# Ilium Plugin Developer Manual

> Developer manual for Ilium plugins: WebAssembly components (wasm32-wasip2) written in Rust or TypeScript that add tree decorations, commands, settings, panels, pane kinds, widgets and ambient scenes to the Ilium terminal multiplexer. The contract is the WIT package plus the manifest.

<!-- source: http://127.0.0.1:4327/pages/landing.md -->
# Plugin manual

## Ilium plugin manual

A plugin adds features to Ilium. It can decorate tree rows with badges, add commands and keybindings, add settings pages, open panels and dialogs, provide a pane kind, add toolbar buttons to agent panes, raise desktop notices and toasts, extend the tree toolbar and the status bar, and draw an ambient scene. The kernel owns the project tree, the panes and the terminals. A plugin never changes them directly. It receives events, returns intents for the kernel to apply, and calls host functions for everything else.

The contract is wide enough that every feature of the Ilium client that is not kernel machinery can be written as a plugin. This manual explains each part of that contract, how to build and install a plugin, and how the kernel loads, restarts and disables one. Every example is given in Rust and in TypeScript. If you are new to plugins, read [What a plugin is](/pages/getting-started-overview/) first, then [Set up a toolchain](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/). The tutorial builds plugins in eleven steps, and each step adds one concept. Twelve standalone tutorials follow: six on basic topics and six on advanced ones, including extension points, hooks and replacing a core plugin. To change how Ilium itself behaves, read [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/).

### What a plugin draws

The screen below is a full Ilium window with three plugin contributions. The agent icons and spinners in the tree on the left come from a server plugin that decorates rows. The panel on the right is a client panel that draws a `table` and three `leader-row` lines. The status bar segment and the key hints at the bottom are the kernel's, with one segment added by the plugin. None of these is part of the kernel.

### Contract version

Every plugin declares the contract it targets in the manifest key `api`. The contract is `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. The contract `ilium:plugin@0.1.0` has 56 events, 42 intents, 51 widgets, 18 settings row types, 68 capabilities, 39 host interfaces and 16 export interfaces. Every plugin declares `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. Each component carries an `ilium:api-version` section with the same version, and the host refuses a package where the two differ. A package whose `api` is not 0.1.x is refused. Items marked unstable (`gpu.kernels`, WebSocket, `ui-calendar`) need an entry in the manifest `unstable` list.

### What you need

| Need | Rule | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Ilium | Installing Ilium installs the `ilium plugin` commands. There is no separate tool. | Build, pack, install, dev reload |
| Rust | Stable 1.90 or later, with the target `wasm32-wasip2` | Rust plugins, crate `ilium-plugin-sdk` |
| TypeScript | Bun 1.2 or later | TypeScript plugins, package `@ilium/plugin-sdk` |
| Grants | Each capability is listed in `capabilities` for its side | Every import that needs one |
| Publisher key | Only for signed packages | Tier T2 installs, see sharing |

`bun install` in a TypeScript plugin installs the component tooling locally. Nothing is installed globally.

Each plugin has one tier. T0 is the kernel itself. T1 is bundled with Ilium. T2 is signed by a publisher key the user trusts. T3 is an unsigned local package. A T3 package installs only with `--allow-unsigned` or through `ilium plugin dev`. It carries a `dev` badge and runs under the T2 sandbox and ceilings. A T1 plugin may set `limits_tier: "first-party"` to use the higher resource ceilings that a feature as large as a board or an editor needs.

### Sides and worlds

Each plugin has one component per side it uses. A side runs in one kernel process, and each side has its own world, which fixes what the component may import and export.

| Side | Manifest key | World | Required exports | Optional exports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Server | `server` | `ilium:server/base@0.1.0` | `lifecycle`, `handler` | `detector`, `job-runner`, `service-provider`, `inference-provider`, `catalog-provider`, `virtual-rows-provider` |
| Client | `client` | `ilium:client/base@0.1.0` | `lifecycle`, `handler` | `views`, `annotator`, `job-runner`, `service-provider`, `inference-provider`, `catalog-provider`, `menu-provider`, `virtual-rows-provider`, `token-provider` |
| Scene | `scene` | `ilium:anim/base@0.1.0` | `lifecycle`, `renderer` | `job-runner` |

The client world adds the UI, command, key, clipboard, audio, media, location, geocoding, help, keymap and plugin-management imports, plus the editor and basic primitives. The server world adds the CLI, HTTP API, workspace, cross-session and long-lived child process imports. The scene world is the smallest: logging, clocks, storage, file access, codecs, jobs, HTTP, audio, media, location and the scene surface. Required exports are never listed in `exports`. The manifest lists only the optional ones, by interface name, and the host refuses a component whose exports differ from that set. [Sides and worlds](/pages/worlds-and-sides/) has the full import matrix.

#### Widgets

51 widgets in 7 families. A view returns a tree of nodes, and the host draws it with the same glyphs and colours as the built-in panels.

[Widget catalogue](/pages/widgets-index/) holds the common props, keys, focus rules, tooltips and the overlays that are built from these parts (tooltip, popover, context menu, toast, command palette). [UI model](/pages/ui-model/), [Layout](/pages/layout/), [Retained mode](/pages/retained-mode/) and [Accessibility and theming](/pages/accessibility-and-theming/) explain how a tree becomes pixels of text.

#### Settings

A plugin adds a settings tab, a section in a kernel tab, or its own view-rendered tab. There are 18 row types, from `toggle` and `choice` to `location`, `map`, `multi-choice` and `meter`. See [Settings extension](/pages/settings-extension/), [Settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/) and [Settings schema reference](/pages/reference-settings-schema/).

#### Capabilities

One grant per feature, such as `tree.decorate`, `agent.read` or `fs.read:<scope>`. There are 19 further grants, nine of them high risk. The user sees every grant in the review dialog before it takes effect. The [capability reference](/pages/capabilities/) lists them all with their sides and risk. The pages in the groups below describe each grant and what it unlocks.

### Worked example: a server plugin

This plugin logs when it activates. It puts a badge on each pane whose agent starts working. The manifest comes first and is the same for both languages.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.hello",
  "name": "Hello",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example",
  "server": { "entry": "server.wasm", "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "server": ["agent.read", "tree.decorate"] },
  "contributes": {
    "decoration_slots": [{ "id": "hello", "placement": "badge", "priority": 50 }]
  }
}
```

The Rust code uses the SDK paths of the Rust module layout. The `#[ilium_plugin]` attribute generates the export glue, so the struct only implements traits.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::Activation;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::AgentActivityEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SetDecorationSpec;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::AgentActivity;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Hello;

impl Lifecycle for Hello {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("hello from {}", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for Hello {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::AgentActivityChanged(AgentActivityEvent { node, current, .. }) = event
            else {
                continue;
            };
            if current != AgentActivity::Working {
                continue;
            }
            submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
                node,
                slot: "hello".into(),
                content: vec![Span::plain("hi")],
                icon: None,
                sort_key: None,
                persist: false,
            })));
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

`Submission::new` takes the next SDK correlation number and no dedup key. `Submission::keyed(intent, key)` sets a key.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'agent-activity-changed') continue;
      if (event.val.current !== 'working') continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'set-decoration',
          val: {
            node: event.val.node,
            slot: 'hello',
            content: [{ text: 'hi' }],
            icon: undefined,
            sortKey: undefined,
            persist: false,
          },
        },
        correlation: 1n,
        dedupKey: undefined,
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

The plugin builds and installs with the commands below. The Rust and TypeScript projects use the same commands.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin build
{"type":"progress","step":"compile","message":"Compiling server.wasm"}
{"type":"artifact","path":"server.wasm","sha256":"3f2a9c01...","bytes":184320}
<span class="t-ok">{"type":"result","ok":true}</span>
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin install com.example.hello-0.1.0.iliumpkg
<span class="t-err">{"type":"error","code":"manifest.grant-unknown",</span>
<span class="t-err"> "message":"capability \"tree.wrte\" is not known to plugin API</span>

</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The first lines show a successful build. The last lines show a manifest typo refused at install.</figcaption>
</figure>

And this is what the user sees in the tree while the agent works. The badge `hi` is drawn after the title, and the row keeps the identity icon and the spinner of the kernel.

### Worked example: a client plugin

This client plugin answers its own command with a desktop notice. The manifest declares the command and the grant that the notice needs.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.hello",
  "name": "Hello",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example",
  "client": { "entry": "client.wasm", "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "client": ["notify.desktop"] },
  "contributes": {
    "commands": [{ "id": "greet", "title": "Say hello" }]
  }
}
```

The command id is `com.example.hello/greet`, because the global id is the plugin id, a slash and the local id.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::Activation;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::CommandInvokedEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::{NotifySpec, Urgency};

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Hello;

impl Lifecycle for Hello {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("hello from {}", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for Hello {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::CommandInvoked(CommandInvokedEvent { command, .. }) = event else {
                continue;
            };
            if command != "com.example.hello/greet" {
                continue;
            }
            submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::Notify(NotifySpec {
                title: "Hello".into(),
                body: "from a plugin".into(),
                urgency: Urgency::Normal,
                sound: None,
            })));
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'command-invoked') continue;
      if (event.val.command !== 'com.example.hello/greet') continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'notify',
          val: { title: 'Hello', body: 'from a plugin', urgency: 'normal', sound: undefined },
        },
        correlation: 1n,
        dedupKey: undefined,
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

`definePlugin` returns one object per export it uses. Here that is `lifecycle` and `handler`, which the entry module must export. Ids such as `correlation` are `bigint` values, because every `u64` is a `bigint` in TypeScript.

### Commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ilium plugin new <dir> --id <id> --lang rust\|typescript --side server\|client\|both\|scene` | Create a project |
| `ilium plugin build [<dir>] [--debug] [--side <side>]` | Build the components of the project |
| `ilium plugin pack [<dir>] [--out <file>]` | Write `dist/<id>-<version>.iliumpkg` |
| `ilium plugin install <file> [--allow-unsigned]` | Install a package |
| `ilium plugin dev` | Watch the directory and reload on change |
| `ilium plugin logs [<id>]` and `ilium plugin grants <id>` | Read the plugin log, and list or revoke grants |

Every command prints JSONL with one object per line. The `type` field is `progress`, `warning`, `error`, `artifact` or `result`. Errors name a `code`, and when known, a `file` and `line`.

### Errors and edge cases

Install and build refuse a package with a code in the manifest group. The common codes are below. [Reference: errors and limits](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/) lists the 15 runtime error codes.

| Code | Cause |
|---|---|
| `manifest.grant-unknown` | The grant is not known to the plugin API |
| `manifest.grant-argument-missing` | A grant such as `fs.read` needs an argument after the colon |
| `manifest.exports-mismatch` | The component exports differ from required plus listed exports |
| `manifest.cli-name-reserved` | The CLI name is a kernel command |
| `manifest.cli-name-taken` | Another installed plugin already owns the CLI name |
| `manifest.contribution-limit` | A contribution key holds more entries than its fixed cap |

At run time every fallible call returns a `plugin-error` with one of these codes. Retry means the same call may succeed later.

| Code | Meaning | Retry |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | No grant, the user declined it, or a policy forbids the action | No |
| `not-found` | The node, pane, file, command or other target does not exist | No |
| `invalid-argument` | A rule the plugin can check before the call failed | No, fix the call |
| `conflict` | State changed or is held, so re-read it first | Yes |
| `quota-exceeded` | A stored or held quota is full | After freeing resources |
| `rate-limited` | A rate rule throttled the call | Yes, after `retry-after-ms` |
| `busy` | Transient capacity is full | Yes, later |
| `timed-out` | A deadline passed | Yes |
| `cancelled` | The plugin, the user or a shutdown cancelled the request | Maybe |
| `unsupported` | The host or platform cannot do it | No |
| `pane-not-ready` | A restored terminal pane has not started its process | Yes, after `pane-created` |
| `revoked` | The grants changed during the call | No, the plugin is re-activated |
| `io` | An operating system I/O error other than a missing file | Maybe |
| `network` | DNS, connect, TLS or transport failure | Yes |
| `internal` | A host bug or a trap in a job instance | No |

A trap, which is a Rust panic or an uncaught TypeScript exception in a handler, counts as a failure. The kernel restarts the plugin after 1 second, then after 5 seconds. A third failure inside 10 minutes disables the plugin on that side. The user turns it on again in Settings > Plugins. A manual re-enable resets the count.

### What the user sees

- **Review dialog:** before a T2 or T3 package installs, the dialog lists each requested capability with a checkbox, drawn as `[x]` and `[ ]`. Declined rows are dimmed. High-risk capabilities start unchecked and are drawn in the warning style.
- **First activation of a bundled plugin:** a T1 plugin with high-risk capabilities asks once, with the buttons `Allow selected` and `Not now`. `Not now` asks again at the next server start, at most three times.
- **Disabled plugins:** the tree footer shows the notice below. Settings > Plugins lists the same plugin with its last error.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Plugins ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ <span class="t-warn">! Plugin Hello stopped after 3 failures in 10 minutes:</span>                     │
│ <span class="t-warn">on-events trap (handler). Turn it on again in Settings &gt; Plugins.</span>          │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative. The notice text is fixed by the kernel: <code>Plugin &lt;name&gt; stopped after 3 failures in 10 minutes: &lt;export&gt; &lt;code or trap&gt; (&lt;view&gt;). Turn it on again in Settings &gt; Plugins.</code></figcaption>
</figure>

- **Windows and macOS:** third-party plugins need the plugin sandbox, which is not available there. The install is refused with `Cannot install <name> <version>.` followed by `Third-party plugins need the plugin sandbox, which is not available on Windows yet.` Bundled plugins keep working. macOS uses the same text with `macOS`.

### Sharing

A package is a file. A registry is optional and none is set up by default. Pack the project with `ilium plugin pack`, sign it with a key from `ilium plugin keygen`, and pass the `.iliumpkg` file on. The recipient runs `ilium plugin install`. Tutorial step 9 walks through the whole path.

<div class="note">
<p>The renders on these pages are illustrative, not generated. They use the glyphs that the Ilium client draws, but exact text and spacing may differ in a release.</p>
</div>

# Your first plugin in five minutes

## Your first plugin in five minutes

This page takes you from an empty folder to a badge on an agent row. You create a server-side plugin from the template, change one line of Rust, and run the plugin in dev mode. The page shows the tree before and after the change. The full build of a plugin with state, commands and tests is the subject of the [tutorial series](/pages/tutorial-01-agent-badge/).

### How the plugin works

The host sends a plugin a batch of events. When an agent changes activity, the host sends an `agent-activity-changed` event for that agent's row in the tree. The plugin reads the event and returns a list of submissions. A submission carries an intent. The intent `set-decoration` puts styled text into a named slot on the row, and `clear-decoration` removes it. The host draws the slot as a badge.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 250" role="img" aria-label="Event, handler, intent and badge in four steps">
  <title>Event to badge</title>
  <desc>The host sends an agent activity event to the plugin handler. The handler returns an intent, and the host draws a badge on the row.</desc>
  <defs>
    <marker id="arrow-first-plugin" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="110" y="8" width="180" height="40" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="200" y="32" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Agent activity changes</text>
  <line x1="200" y1="48" x2="200" y2="70" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arrow-first-plugin)"/>
  <rect x="110" y="70" width="180" height="40" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>

  <rect x="40" y="132" width="320" height="40" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="200" y="156" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">set-decoration or clear-decoration intent</text>

  <rect x="90" y="194" width="220" height="40" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>

<figcaption>The plugin never draws anything itself. It returns an intent, and the host draws the badge in the slot that the intent names.</figcaption>

### What you need

- A Rust toolchain of version 1.90 or later with the `wasm32-wasip2` target. [Set up a toolchain](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/) shows the install steps.
- An Ilium build with the `ilium plugin` commands. Installing Ilium installs them.
- Two grants, both on the server side. The manifest lists them, and the install dialog shows each one as a row that you check to allow it.

| Grant | Dialog row text | What the plugin may do with it |
|---|---|---|
| `agent.read` | See agent status | Receive `agent-activity-changed` events for agent panes |
| `tree.decorate` | Add badges, icons and rows to the tree | Send `set-decoration` and `clear-decoration` intents |

A declined grant stays unchecked and dimmed in the dialog, and the plugin does not receive it in its activation context. Without `agent.read` the plugin gets no activity events, so it never draws a badge. Without `tree.decorate` the host refuses the whole batch that holds a decoration intent.

### Create the project

Run the command in a directory that is not inside a project you care about. The `--id`, `--lang` and `--side` flags are required. `--name` is optional and sets the display name.

**Rust**

```bash
ilium plugin new agent-tools --id example.agent-tools --lang rust --side server --name "Agent tools"
cd agent-tools
ilium plugin build
```

| Flag or argument | Value in this page | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `<dir>` | `agent-tools` | Folder to create. |
| `--id` | `example.agent-tools` | Plugin id. Global command ids start with it, for example `example.agent-tools/greet`. |
| `--lang` | `rust` | `rust` or `typescript`. |
| `--side` | `server` | `server`, `client`, `both` or `scene`. |
| `--name` | `Agent tools` | Display name shown in the install dialog and in settings. |

The command prints JSON lines. Each line has a `type` field, so a script can read the result.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin new agent-tools --id example.agent-tools \
    --lang rust --side server
{"type":"progress","step":"template","message":"Writing the Rust template"}
{"type":"result","ok":true}
{"type":"summary","duration_ms":412,"warnings":0,"errors":0}
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The new command writes three files and prints one result line.</figcaption>
</figure>

The template writes three files:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `manifest.json` | Plugin id, version, grants and contributions. The next section shows the file. |
| `Cargo.toml` | Crate settings. The crate builds as a component for `wasm32-wasip2`. |
| `src/lib.rs` | The server side. It holds the badge text function and the handler. |

The template handler already submits one intent for each activity event. While `badge_text` returns an empty string for every activity, each event clears the slot, so the template draws no badge. The first render in this page shows that state.

### The manifest

The manifest below is the one the template writes. It declares both grants and the `badge` slot that the plugin writes to. The `files` inventory is written by `ilium plugin pack`, so a source manifest may omit it.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "example.agent-tools",
  "name": "Agent tools",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example Developer",
  "server": {
    "entry": "server.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": []
  },
  "capabilities": {
    "server": ["agent.read", "tree.decorate"]
  },
  "contributes": {
    "decoration_slots": [
      { "id": "badge", "placement": "badge", "priority": 10 }
    ]
  }
}
```

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `api` | string | `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. |
| `id` | string | Plugin id. It must match the `--id` given to `new`. |
| `name` | string | Display name in the install dialog and in settings. |
| `version` | string | Plugin version. A higher version of an installed id is an update. |
| `publisher` | string | Publisher name shown in the install dialog. |
| `server.entry` | string | Component file. `server.wasm` for the server side. |
| `server.world` | string | WIT world. `ilium:server/base@0.1.0` for the server side. |
| `server.exports` | list | Optional exports: `views`, `detector`, `job-runner`, `service-provider`, `inference-provider` and `annotator`. The handler needs no entry. |
| `capabilities.server` | list | Grants of the server side, as in the grants table above. |
| `contributes.decoration_slots` | list | Each entry has `id`, `placement` and `priority`. `placement` is one of `badge`, `icon`, `subtitle` or `footer`. A lower `priority` is drawn first within the same placement. |

### Worked example: the complete server side in both languages

This is the complete server side after the change in the next section, in Rust (`src/lib.rs`) and in TypeScript (`src/server.ts`). Both plugins build as they stand.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::{DecorationKey, SetDecorationSpec};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::AgentActivity;

const BADGE_SLOT: &str = "badge";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct AgentTools;

/// Text for the badge slot. An empty string clears the slot.
fn badge_text(activity: AgentActivity) -> &'static str {
    match activity {
        AgentActivity::Working => "working",
        _ => "",
    }
}

impl Handler for AgentTools {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::AgentActivityChanged(change) = event else { continue };
            let text = badge_text(change.current);
            let intent = if text.is_empty() {
                Intent::ClearDecoration(DecorationKey {
                    node: change.node,
                    slot: BADGE_SLOT.into(),
                })
            } else {
                Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
                    node: change.node,
                    slot: BADGE_SLOT.into(),
                    content: vec![Span::plain(text)],
                    icon: None,
                    sort_key: None,
                    persist: false,
                })
            };
            submissions.push(Submission::new(intent));
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

The handler reads two fields from each event. `change.node` names the row, and `change.current` holds the new activity. It writes one intent for each event. `persist: false` means the badge is dropped when the plugin shuts down.

### The one changed line

In the template, the `AgentActivity::Working` arm returns an empty string, so the badge never has text. Change that arm to return the word `working`:

**Rust**

```rust
        AgentActivity::Working => "working",   // was: ""
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
    case 'working':
      return 'working';   // was: ''
```

Nothing else changes. Build the plugin again with `ilium plugin build`.

### Build and run in dev mode

Run dev mode from the project folder. Dev mode installs the plugin as an unsigned development package, which the tree shows with a `dev` badge. The plugin reloads each time a file in the project changes.

```bash
ilium plugin build
ilium plugin dev
```

The dev command prints one `reload` line each time it loads a new build.

<span class="t-ok">watching</span> agent-tools/ for changes
<span class="t-hi">reloaded</span> example.agent-tools 0.1.0
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The same reload appears as a JSON line with type <code>reload</code>, shown below.</figcaption>
</figure>

```json
{"type":"reload","plugin":"example.agent-tools","version":"0.1.0","restored_bytes":0}
```

When the agent leaves the working state, the plugin receives a new `agent-activity-changed` event. The handler then returns `clear-decoration`, and the badge disappears.

### Create the TypeScript project

The TypeScript form is created with `--lang typescript`. Its manifest is the same, except for the id.

**TypeScript**

```bash
ilium plugin new agent-tools-ts --id example.agent-tools-ts \
  --lang typescript --side server --name "Agent tools"
cd agent-tools-ts
bun install
ilium plugin build
ilium plugin dev
```

Bun 1.2 or later is the only tool you install globally. `bun install` fetches the pinned `@ilium/plugin-sdk`, which provides the types and the component build. The entry file is `src/server.ts`.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { span } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import type { AgentActivity } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/agent';

const BADGE_SLOT = 'badge';

/** Text for the badge slot. An empty string clears the slot. */
function badgeText(activity: AgentActivity): string {
  switch (activity) {
    case 'working':
      return 'working';
    default:
      return '';
  }
}

export const { handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    batch.forEach((event, index) => {
      if (event.tag !== 'agent-activity-changed') return;
      const { node, current } = event.val;
      const text = badgeText(current);
      const intent = text === ''
        ? { tag: 'clear-decoration' as const, val: { node, slot: BADGE_SLOT } }
        : {
            tag: 'set-decoration' as const,
            val: {
              node,
              slot: BADGE_SLOT,
              content: [span(text)],
              icon: undefined,
              sortKey: undefined,
              persist: false,
            },
          };
      submissions.push({ intent, correlation: BigInt(index), dedupKey: undefined });
    });
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

The TypeScript template differs in one line: its `'working'` case returns an empty string until you change it, as in the Rust template.

The contract lets the same intent carry more than text. The extended `set-decoration` adds styled spans, a tooltip, a frame animation and trailing segments, so the badge could be a spinner or a meter instead of the word. Tutorial step 1 uses these fields. Node ids are `bigint` values. The event index serves as the `correlation` number, which is unique within one batch.

### Surface used on this page

| Item | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Server side | `#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]` | `definePlugin({ side: 'server' })` | Declares the side. |
| Handler | `impl Handler`, `fn on_events` | `onEvents(batch)` | Receives a batch and returns submissions. |
| Activity event | `Event::AgentActivityChanged(change)` | `event.tag === 'agent-activity-changed'`, `event.val` | Fields `node`, `previous`, `current` and `revision`. |
| Activity values | `AgentActivity::Working` | `'working'` | `none`, `working`, `idle`, `awaiting-approval`, `done` and `menu`. |
| Set badge | `Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec)` | tag `'set-decoration'` | Writes styled text into a slot. |
| Clear badge | `Intent::ClearDecoration(DecorationKey)` | tag `'clear-decoration'` | Empties a slot. Clearing an empty slot returns `ok`. |
| Text | `Span::plain(text)` | `span(text)` | One unstyled run of text. |
| Submission | `Submission::new(intent)` | object with `intent`, `correlation` and `dedupKey` | One intent in the returned list. |

`SetDecorationSpec` has these fields:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `node` | node id | Tree row that receives the decoration. |
| `slot` | string | Slot id. It must match an id in `contributes.decoration_slots`. |
| `content` | list of spans | Text. A badge is at most 12 cells wide. Wider text is cut and ends with `…`. |
| `icon` | optional string | Tabler icon name. `None` draws no icon. |
| `sort_key` | optional integer | Orders decorations that share a row. Lower sorts first. |
| `persist` | boolean | `true` keeps the decoration across a server restart, shown as stale. `false` drops it at shutdown. |

### Edge cases and errors

| Situation | Result | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| The manifest asks for a grant that does not exist | Build error `manifest.grant-unknown` | The text is `capability "<grant>" is not known to plugin API <api>`. Fix the spelling in `capabilities.server`. |
| The slot id is not declared in the manifest | `refused(invalid-argument)` | Only that submission is refused. The other submissions of the batch run. |
| The node was removed before the intent is applied | `refused(not-found)` | The row no longer exists. Nothing is drawn. |
| The plugin already holds the maximum number of decorations | `refused(quota-exceeded)` | The default limit is 4,096 decorations for each plugin. |
| A batch holds a decoration intent without `tree.decorate` | `refused(not-permitted)` for the whole batch | A missing grant refuses the batch. |
| The user declines `agent.read` | No activity events | No badge is drawn. The row in the install dialog stays unchecked. |
| The user revokes `tree.decorate` later | Decorations are withdrawn | The plugin is re-activated with the reduced grant set. The restart does not count as a failure. |
| `on_events` panics or traps | Plugin restart | The plugin restarts after 1 s, then 5 s. A third failure within 10 minutes disables the plugin, and the tree footer shows a notice. |
| The plugin restarts after a crash | Decorations stay, marked stale | Stale badges are drawn in the muted colour until the plugin sets or clears them again. |

<div class="note">
<p>An empty string from <code>badge_text</code> is a valid state. The handler uses it to clear the slot when an agent is idle, done or waiting for approval. Clearing an empty slot returns <code>ok</code>, so the plugin does not need to check whether a badge exists.</p>
</div>

<div class="warn">
<p>The slot id in the code and in <code>contributes.decoration_slots</code> must match exactly. A mismatch does not stop the build. Each submission then fails with <code>refused(invalid-argument)</code>, and no badge appears.</p>
</div>

- [Testing](/pages/testing/) shows how to test `on_events` without a running Ilium.

# What a plugin is

## What a plugin is

Ilium splits its work into two parts. The kernel is the part that must not break. It owns the project tree, the pane processes, the terminal emulator, input routing and the saved state. A plugin adds behaviour on top of the kernel. It reads the tree, reacts to events, and asks the kernel to change things by submitting intents. A plugin never writes to the terminal, opens a pty or draws the screen on its own. Each thing a plugin may do is a capability, and the user grants it.

This page covers the parts, the call model, the trust tiers and a first plugin in Rust and TypeScript.

### You will need

- No grants. The first plugin on this page asks for none.
- The `ilium` binary. The `ilium plugin` commands are subcommands of `ilium` itself, so there is no separate tool to install.
- For Rust: Rust 1.90 or later with the `wasm32-wasip2` target. For TypeScript: Bun 1.2 or later. Both are set up in [Set up a toolchain](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/).
- The contract version. The baseline is `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`, and every event, intent, widget, grant, host interface and settings row belongs to that one contract. A plugin names `ilium:plugin@0.1.0` in its `api` key.

### Parts of a plugin

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Kernel | The Ilium code that owns the state: tree, panes, terminal, input and snapshots. |
| Plugin host | The kernel part that runs plugin instances. It delivers events, takes submissions, checks grants and enforces limits. |
| Package | A `.iliumpkg` file: `manifest.json`, one WebAssembly component per side, and optional assets, help topics, sounds and a signature. |
| Side | One WebAssembly component built for one world: server, client or scene. |
| Export | A function set that the host calls, such as `lifecycle` or `handler`. |
| Capability | A permission named by a grant string such as `tree.decorate`. The user grants it. |

### Three sides

A plugin has up to three sides. The manifest lists the sides under the keys `server`, `client` and `scene`. A plugin with only a badge needs only the server side. A plugin with a panel needs a client side as well.

- **Server side** runs with the server. It sees the tree, the panes, the agent state, jobs, the files it was granted and its own settings.
- **Client side** runs inside the terminal interface. It opens panels, provides pane kinds, handles keys and clicks, and reads the screen mirror.
- **Scene side** draws an ambient background, one frame at a time.

Each side has a fixed set of required and optional exports. The SDK checks them at compile time.

| Side | Manifest key | World | Required exports | Optional exports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Server | `server` | `ilium:server/base` | `lifecycle`, `handler` | `detector`, `job-runner`, `service-provider`, `inference-provider`, `catalog-provider`, `virtual-rows-provider` |
| Client | `client` | `ilium:client/base` | `lifecycle`, `handler` | `views`, `annotator`, `job-runner`, `service-provider`, `inference-provider`, `catalog-provider`, `menu-provider`, `virtual-rows-provider`, `token-provider` |
| Scene | `scene` | `ilium:anim/base` | `lifecycle`, `renderer` | `job-runner` |

In Rust, the `#[ilium_plugin]` attribute sets the side and the optional exports:

```rust
#[ilium_plugin(side = "server", exports = ["detector"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct MyPlugin { /* state */ }
```

A listed export without a matching trait implementation is a compile error.

**TypeScript**

```ts
export const { lifecycle, handler, detector } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  exports: ['detector'],
  // activate, onEvents, identify and classify go here
});
```

`definePlugin` returns one object per export, named in camelCase. The optional exports are `catalog-provider` (option lists for `choice` rows and widgets), `menu-provider` (dynamic context menu items), `virtual-rows-provider` (children of virtual tree rows) and `token-provider` (syntax tokens for the editor).

### How the host calls a plugin

A plugin does not run a loop and does not draw every frame. The host gives a plugin a batch of events through `on-events`, and the plugin returns a list of submissions. Each submission carries one intent, such as `set-decoration`, and a correlation number. In Rust, `Submission::new(intent)` assigns the number; `Submission::keyed(intent, key)` adds a dedup key.

A slow host call returns a request id at once and completes later as a `request-completed` event. In Rust, `fs::read_all(path).await` hides this: the SDK resolves the future when the completion arrives. In TypeScript, `await readAll(path)` does the same with a promise.

A view works the same way. The host calls `render` when a view first opens, after `ui.invalidate`, and on resize. The host keeps the widget state, such as the selected row, and paints the tree. The only per-frame callback is the `render` call of a scene.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-label="Events go in, submissions come out">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ov-flow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <title>Events in, submissions out</title>
  <desc>The kernel sends a batch of events to the plugin. The plugin returns submissions. The kernel checks the batch against the grants and applies the intents in order.</desc>
  <rect x="8" y="20" width="110" height="90" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="63" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Kernel</text>
  <text x="63" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">grants, order</text>
  <rect x="282" y="20" width="110" height="90" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/>
  <text x="337" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Plugin</text>
  <text x="337" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">your code</text>
  <line x1="118" y1="50" x2="282" y2="50" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#ov-flow)"/>
  <text x="200" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">on-events(batch)</text>
  <line x1="282" y1="92" x2="118" y2="92" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#ov-flow)"/>
  <text x="200" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">submissions</text>
  <text x="8" y="136" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">The kernel checks the batch against the grants.</text>
  <text x="8" y="152" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">It applies the submissions in order.</text>
  <text x="8" y="168" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Each submission gets exactly one outcome.</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>One round trip: a batch of events in, a list of submissions out. The host returns one outcome per submission.</figcaption>
</figure>

A batch holds at most 256 events, and one `on-events` call may return at most 256 submissions; more is a trap. The host checks the batch against the grants, then applies the submissions in order.

### Capabilities and grants

A grant is a name, or a name with one argument after the first colon, such as `tree.read` or `http:api.example.com`. A plugin lists its grants per side in `capabilities`. Grants are recorded per side and per user configuration, not per project. Normal grants are checked by default in the install dialog. High-risk grants, marked H, are never checked by default. A bundled plugin gets its normal grants up to the manifest ceiling and is asked once for each H grant at first activation.

The contract includes 19 further grants for terminal cell reads, history and raw input, pane lifecycle, tree restructuring, attention marks, client chrome, external opening, cross-session control, long-lived children, kernel settings and keymap reads, agent transcripts, geocoding, embeddings, toasts and the pane journal. Nine of them are high risk. The [capability reference](/pages/capabilities/) lists every one.

Two outcomes matter when you write code:

- A capability the user declined returns `not-permitted` from its functions. Your code gets an error value and keeps running.
- An import that the manifest never requested is a trap. That is a bug in the plugin, and the host restarts it.

Some imports need no grant at all, such as `log`, `clock`, `timers`, `storage` and `codec`.

A user can revoke a grant in Settings > Plugins > the plugin > Capabilities, or with `ilium plugin grants <id> --revoke <grant>`. The plugin then receives `deactivate(revoked)` and starts again with the smaller grant set.

### Trust tiers

Every installed plugin has one tier. The tier decides where its code runs and how far its limits go.

| Tier | Who it is for | Where it runs | How it gets installed |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | The kernel itself | Server process | Not a plugin |
| T1 | Bundled plugins shipped with Ilium | The process that hosts its side (server, client or CLI process), as precompiled `.cwasm` | Ships with Ilium |
| T2 | Signed packages from a publisher key the user trusts | Sandbox helper process | Install dialog with the review list |
| T3 | Unsigned local packages | Sandbox helper process, shown with a `dev` badge | `--allow-unsigned` or `ilium plugin dev` |

The limits differ by tier. The manifest asks for values in `limits`, and the host clamps them to the tier ceiling. A request above the ceiling is clamped and logged, never refused.

A T1 plugin may also set the top-level manifest key `limits_tier` to `"first-party"`. The host verifies the tier and then applies the higher ceilings of [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/). The table below shows the standard ceilings.

| Limit | Default | T1 ceiling | T2 and T3 ceiling |
|---|---|---|---|
| `memory_mib` | 32 | 256 | 128 |
| `table_elements` | 10,000 | 50,000 | 20,000 |
| `event_deadline_ms` | 20 | 50 | 20 |

A package signed by a key the user does not trust is offered for trust at install. Declining refuses the install. On Windows and macOS, the kernel refuses T2 and T3 packages until a sandbox exists there. The refusal reads:

```text
Cannot install <name> <version>.
Third-party plugins need the plugin sandbox, which is not available on Windows yet.
Bundled plugins keep working.
```

macOS shows the same text with `macOS` in place of `Windows`.

### Lifecycle in brief

The host starts plugins in a fixed order. On the server, it restores the saved state, verifies every installed manifest and registers its static contributions without running any code. Then it activates the plugins with the `startup` trigger, and gives each one a single `tree-changed` batch that covers the restored nodes. A plugin without an `activation` key starts on first use of one of its contributions.

When a plugin stops, the host calls `deactivate` with a reason such as `shutdown`, `disabled` or `revoked`. A trap or a missed deadline restarts the instance after 1 s, then 5 s. A third failure within 10 minutes disables the plugin until the user enables it again. The full sequence is on the [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/) page.

### The manifest

The manifest is JSON with snake_case keys. The host refuses unknown keys.

| Key | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `api` | yes | Contract version, `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. |
| `id` | yes | Reverse-DNS-like id, for example `example.hello`. |
| `name`, `version`, `publisher` | yes | Display name, semver version and publisher name. |
| `server`, `client`, `scene` | one of them | Object with `entry`, `world` and `exports`. |
| `capabilities` | no | Grant strings for each side. |
| `activation` | no | Triggers that start the plugin, such as `startup`. |
| `contributes` | no | Static contributions such as commands, settings, decoration slots, panels, `tree_toolbar`, `row_actions`, `tree_orderings`, `status_segments`, `pane_frame_slots`, `display_modes`, `catalogs`, `client_requests` and `languages`. |
| `limits`, `limits_tier` | no | Requested limits, clamped by tier, and the optional `first-party` tier for T1. |
| `unstable` | no | Opt-in list for unstable features such as `gpu-kernels`. |
| `files` | packed only | Length and SHA-256 of each package entry. `ilium plugin pack` writes it. |

### Your first plugin in Rust

This server-side plugin logs once when it starts and logs the size of each event batch. It needs no grants. The `Lifecycle` trait has a default `deactivate`, so the plugin implements only `activate`.

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Hello;

impl Lifecycle for Hello {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("hello from {}", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for Hello {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        log::log(Level::Debug, &format!("{} events", batch.len()));
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

The prelude brings in the export traits and the common types. The log function takes a `Level` value, not a string.

### Your first plugin in TypeScript

The TypeScript version has the same contract. `definePlugin` returns the `lifecycle` and `handler` objects, and each one has the method names from the Rust trait in camelCase.

```typescript
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  deactivate(reason) {
    return undefined;
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    log('debug', `${batch.length} events`);
    return [];
  },
});
```

Log levels are kebab-case strings in TypeScript: `'trace'`, `'debug'`, `'info'`, `'warn'` and `'error'`.

The manifest is the same for both versions. It names the entry file, the world the component was built for, and the exports it provides. The `exports` list is empty because `lifecycle` and `handler` are required. This source manifest omits `files`, which `ilium plugin pack` adds later.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "example.hello",
  "name": "Hello",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example Developer",
  "server": {
    "entry": "server.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": []
  }
}
```

### SDK import paths

Each WIT interface has one Rust module and one TypeScript subpath with the same name. Most plugins use a handful of them.

| Rust module | TypeScript import | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log` | `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log` | Write log lines. |
| `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::tree` | `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/tree` | Read nodes. Needs `tree.read`. |
| `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::ui` | `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/ui` | Client side: theme and invalidation. |
| `ilium_plugin_sdk::anim::renderer` | `@ilium/plugin-sdk/anim/renderer` | Scene renderer. |

Each import has its own API page, such as [Log](/pages/api-log/) and [Tree](/pages/api-tree/).

### What you see

The `activate` line goes to the plugin log once, when the plugin starts. The `debug` line appears once for each event batch.

<figure>
<pre class="term">
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs example.hello
2026-10-11 12:04:08 info  example.hello hello from example.hello
2026-10-11 12:04:08 debug example.hello 3 events
2026-10-11 12:04:09 debug example.hello 1 events
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The log format is the one `ilium plugin logs` prints: timestamp, level padded to five characters, plugin id and message. The batch sizes depend on the project's activity.</figcaption>
</figure>

The tree does not change, because this plugin decorates nothing. A plugin that adds a badge to each pane needs the `tree.decorate` grant in its manifest's `capabilities.server` list.

### What the user sees at install

Before a T2 or T3 plugin installs, Ilium shows the review dialog. Each requested grant is a checkbox row with a dotted leader to its meaning. High-risk grants start unchecked and use the warning style. The user can decline a grant and still install. Declined features return `not-permitted`.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Install Hello 0.1.0? ───────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Publisher: Example Developer (trusted)                             │
│ This plugin asks for:                                              │
│                                                                    │
│ [x] tree.read ………………………… read the project tree                     │
│ [x] tree.decorate ………………… add badges to tree rows                  │
│ [ ] <span class="t-warn">terminal.raw-input</span> ………… <span class="t-warn">send raw bytes to a pane</span>               │
│                                                                    │
│      Esc Cancel          Enter Install                             │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter install · Esc cancel</span>                          │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, 70 columns. A modal dialog with a rounded border, checkbox rows with <code>…</code> leaders, a Neutral and a Primary button, and the footer hint line with <code>·</code> separators.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Edge cases and errors

Every fallible call returns a `plugin-error` with one of these codes. The retry column says whether the same call can succeed later.

| Code | Meaning | Retry |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | No grant, the user declined it, or a path or policy blocks the call. | No |
| `not-found` | The node, pane, file, command or plugin does not exist any more. | No |
| `invalid-argument` | The argument breaks a rule the plugin can check, such as a size cap. | No, fix the call |
| `conflict` | State changed or is held, such as a stale revision or a locked file. | Yes, after re-reading |
| `quota-exceeded` | A stored or held quota is full. | After freeing resources |
| `rate-limited` | A rate rule throttles the call. `retry-after-ms` is set. | Yes, after the delay |
| `busy` | Transient capacity is full, such as the job queue. | Yes, later |
| `timed-out` | A deadline passed. | Yes |
| `cancelled` | The plugin, the user or a shutdown cancelled the request. | Maybe |
| `unsupported` | The host or platform cannot do it. | No |
| `pane-not-ready` | A restored terminal pane has not started its process yet. | Yes |
| `revoked` | The grant set changed during the call. The plugin is re-activated. | No |
| `io` | An operating system I/O error other than a missing file. | Maybe |
| `network` | DNS, connect, TLS or transport failure. | Yes |
| `internal` | A host bug or a trap inside a job instance. | No |

Rules that apply to every plugin:

- A trap, such as a panic in `on-events`, drops the instance. The server keeps running, and the plugin restarts after its back-off.
- Log lines over 16 KiB are cut and end with `…[truncated]`. Other oversize values give `invalid-argument` before anything is written.
- Events marked "drop oldest, counted" are dropped when the plugin falls behind. The next batch starts with an `events-dropped` event that gives the count.

# Set up a toolchain

## Set up a toolchain

This page explains what you install to build a plugin in Rust or TypeScript, and what each `ilium plugin` command does with your source. A plugin is built as a WebAssembly component that targets WASI Preview 2. You install the language tools once. The `ilium` binary runs the rest of the pipeline: it compiles the source, wraps the result as a component, and later packs the components into a `.iliumpkg` file that the host loads.

The `ilium plugin` commands are part of the `ilium` binary. Installing Ilium installs them. There is no separate tool to add.

### What you need

| Requirement | Rust plugin | TypeScript plugin |
|---|---|---|
| Ilium with the `ilium plugin` commands | Yes, from the Ilium install | Yes, from the Ilium install |
| Language toolchain | Rust stable 1.90 or later, with the `wasm32-wasip2` target | Bun 1.2 or later |
| Other global tools | None. The component step is built into `ilium` | None. `bun install` fetches the rest |
| Grants | None | None |

Grants apply to a plugin, not to its build. You grant capabilities when you install the package on your machine, and the review dialog lists them. Read [What a plugin is](/pages/getting-started-overview/) first if you have not seen the three sides of a plugin.

Plugin builds run on your own machine. You do not need a remote service to build or install a plugin.

### Install the Rust toolchain

**Rust**

```bash
rustup target add wasm32-wasip2
rustc --version
```

`rustc --version` must print 1.90.0 or later. The build needs no other tool. The component step uses the `wit-component` library linked into `ilium`, so `wasm-tools` does not need to be on your path.

### Install the TypeScript toolchain

Bun is the only global tool for TypeScript. Inside the plugin directory, run `bun install`. It reads the `@ilium/plugin-sdk` dependency and installs the exact versions of `componentize-js` and `jco` that the SDK pins. Nothing is installed globally.

**TypeScript**

```bash
bun --version
bun install
```

The build reads the WIT files from `node_modules/@ilium/plugin-sdk/wit/`. It never copies them into your project. You do not call `componentize-js` or `jco` yourself.

### The ilium plugin commands

The full list of commands, flags, exit codes and output records is [Plugin command-line reference](/pages/reference-plugin-cli/). The four commands you use first:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ilium plugin new <dir> --id <plugin-id> --lang <rust or typescript> --template <name>` | Writes a template project. `--side server`, `client`, `both` or `scene` is an alias for the template of that name. The eight templates and their files are in [Project templates](/pages/reference-project-templates/). |
| `ilium plugin build [<dir>]` | Compiles the project and writes the components to `<dir>/dist/`. `--side <side>` builds one side, `--debug` keeps debug information, `--watch` rebuilds on each change. |
| `ilium plugin dev [<dir>]` | Builds, installs as T3, activates, and rebuilds and reloads after each change. |
| `ilium plugin pack [<dir>]` | Writes `<dir>/dist/<id>-<version>.iliumpkg`. It refuses a debug build and does not sign. |

Other commands: `check` and `lint` validate a project, `test` runs the tests, `inspect` and `doctor` show the state of a package or the machine, and `logs`, `trace` and `profile` show a running plugin ([Debugging tools](/pages/reference-debugging-tools/)). `ilium plugin doctor` is the quick way to verify this page: it reports each missing tool with the fix.

`<dir>` defaults to the current directory. The build detects the language from the files. A `Cargo.toml` means Rust, and a `package.json` means TypeScript. If both files exist, or neither does, the build stops with an error (see the error table below). `--debug` keeps DWARF debug information, so traps show `file:line` in the plugin log. Read [Debugging](/pages/debugging/) before you use it.

A person who only installs and manages plugins does not need this toolchain. They use [Plugins for users](/pages/user-plugins-overview/) and [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/). To open the Plugins tab, press `Ctrl+B` then `:` and choose Plugins ([Settings plugin](/pages/core-plugin-settings/#the-plugins-tab)).

The install, signing and trust commands (`ilium plugin install`, `keygen`, `sign` and `trust`) are covered in [Package and share](/pages/tutorial-09-package-and-share/) and defined in [Distribution commands](/pages/reference-plugin-distribution-cli/).

### The sides and the toolchain

`--side both` writes a server and a client entry in one project, and `--side scene` writes a scene entry. The component step still produces one component per side. A plugin sets `"api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0"` in the manifest, and the build checks the component against that version. The host refuses a plugin built for a newer minor than it supports.

### Output lines

Every command prints one JSON object per line, each with a `type` field. A script can read the output without parsing free text.

| Type | Fields | Printed by |
|---|---|---|
| `progress` | `step` (`compile`, `bundle`, `component` or `pack`), `message` | all commands |
| `warning` | `code`, `message` | all commands |
| `error` | `code`, `message`, and `file` and `line` when known | all commands |
| `artifact` | `path`, `sha256`, `bytes` | `build`, `pack` |
| `summary` | `duration_ms`, `warnings`, `errors` | all commands |
| `result` | `ok` (`true` or `false`) | all commands |
| `reload` | `plugin`, `version`, `restored_bytes` | `dev` |
| `log` | `plugin`, `side` (`server`, `client` or `scene`), `level`, `message` | `dev` |

### Worked example: a server plugin

This example creates a server-side plugin with no exports. It logs once on activation. The two languages use the same command with a different `--lang`.

**Rust**

```bash
ilium plugin new agent-tools --id example.agent-tools --lang rust --side server \
  --name "Agent tools"
cd agent-tools
ilium plugin build
```

**TypeScript**

```bash
ilium plugin new agent-tools --id example.agent-tools --lang typescript --side server \
  --name "Agent tools"
cd agent-tools
bun install
ilium plugin build
```

The command writes three files in either language. `manifest.json` declares the server side:

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "example.agent-tools",
  "name": "Agent tools",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example Developer",
  "server": {
    "entry": "server.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": []
  }
}
```

**Rust**: `Cargo.toml` builds a library for the component and depends on the SDK:

```toml
[package]
name = "agent-tools"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
ilium-plugin-sdk = "0.1"
```

**Rust**: `src/lib.rs` holds the plugin. The `#[ilium_plugin]` attribute generates the component glue, and the
default `Lifecycle` methods cover activation:

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct AgentTools;

impl Lifecycle for AgentTools {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("hello from {}", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**: `package.json` pins the SDK version exactly, and `src/server.ts` is the entry module:

```json
{
  "name": "agent-tools",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": {
    "@ilium/plugin-sdk": "0.1.0"
  }
}
```

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents() {
    return [];
  },
});
```

### Worked example: a client plugin

This example creates a client-side plugin. In TypeScript it needs `bun install` once before the first build.

**TypeScript**

```bash
ilium plugin new agent-tools --id example.agent-tools --lang typescript --side client \
  --name "Agent tools"
cd agent-tools
bun install
ilium plugin build
```

**Rust**

```bash
ilium plugin new agent-tools --id example.agent-tools --lang rust --side client \
  --name "Agent tools"
cd agent-tools
ilium plugin build
```

The `package.json` of the TypeScript project is the one shown above. The manifest of a client plugin names the client world:

```json
"client": { "entry": "client.wasm", "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] }
```

**TypeScript**: `src/client.ts` is the entry module. `ilium plugin build` bundles it with Bun and treats `ilium:*` and
`wasi:*` as external imports:

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents() {
    return [];
  },
});
```

**Rust**: `src/lib.rs` of the client plugin differs from the server plugin only in the side name:

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct AgentTools;

impl Lifecycle for AgentTools {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("hello from {}", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for AgentTools {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

### Build, watch and reload

`ilium plugin build` writes one component per declared side into `dist/`, and prints one `artifact` line for
each. The figure shows a successful build of the server plugin, which writes `dist/server.wasm`. Hashes
are shortened.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin build
{"type":"progress","step":"compile","message":"Compiling agent-tools"}
{"type":"progress","step":"component","message":"Writing server.wasm"}
{"type":"artifact","path":"dist/server.wasm","sha256":"3f9a..","bytes":412806}
{"type":"summary","duration_ms":8120,"warnings":0,"errors":0}
{"type":"result","ok":true}
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. Hashes are shortened, and the timings are examples.</figcaption>
</figure>

`ilium plugin dev` runs the same build, then activates the plugin and watches the project. It starts a rebuild
300 ms after the last change. A failed rebuild keeps the running instance, prints the compiler error, and
sends no `deactivate`. A successful rebuild deactivates the old instance with the reason `upgrade`, activates
the new build, and passes the bytes that the old `deactivate` returned as `restored`. A plugin that returns
no bytes reports `restored_bytes` as 0.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin dev
{"type":"progress","step":"compile","message":"Compiling agent-tools"}
{"type":"reload","plugin":"example.tools","version":"0.1.0","restored_bytes":0}
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The reload follows a change to <code>src/lib.rs</code>. The plugin
id is shortened to fit the figure. Each line is one JSON object, as in the table above.</figcaption>
</figure>

### The build pipeline

Source becomes a component, a component goes into a package, and the host loads the package at install time.
The package format is `.iliumpkg`, a deterministic ZIP archive that holds `manifest.json`, one `.wasm` file per
declared side, and an inventory of every file. Each `.wasm` file is a component that targets the world named
in the manifest.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Toolchain pipeline from source to host">
  <title>Toolchain pipeline</title>
  <desc>Source is compiled into components. The pack step writes a package. The host loads the package at install.</desc>
  <defs>

    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="8" y="52" width="80" height="36" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>

The dashed box is the running host, which is not part of the toolchain.</figcaption>

### How a development plugin looks to the user

While `ilium plugin dev` runs, the plugin is installed as a T3 package. Settings > Plugins lists it with a `dev` badge next to its id. The user can open its details, review the grants, and read its log from the same list.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Settings · Plugins ───────────────────╮
│ <span class="t-hi">Plugin</span>              Tier  State   Grants     │
│ ──────────────────────────────────────────   │
│ example.agent-tools [dev] T3 <span class="t-ok">running</span>  2/2    │
│ ilium.badges               T1 <span class="t-ok">running</span>  3/3   │
│ ilium.tasks                T1 <span class="t-dim">disabled</span> 0/1   │
│                                              │
│ <span class="t-dim">↑/↓ move · Enter details · Space enable</span>      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The panel uses a rounded border and the chrome title. The header row has a <code>─</code> rule under it, and the hint line below the rows uses <code>·</code> separators.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Pinned versions

| Component | Version | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Rust | Stable 1.90 or later | `rustup` |
| Rust target | `wasm32-wasip2` | `rustup target add` |
| Bun | 1.2 or later | Installed by you, the only global TypeScript tool |
| `@ilium/plugin-sdk` | 0.1.0 | `package.json` in the TypeScript project |
| `componentize-js`, `jco` | Pinned by the SDK | `bun install` |
| `ilium-plugin-sdk` | 0.1 | `Cargo.toml` in the Rust project |
| `wit-bindgen`, `wit-component` | Pinned by the SDK to match the host | Cargo, through the SDK |

### Errors

Build and dev stop with an `error` line and exit with status 1. The `file` and `line` fields are set when a
file is involved. Manifest errors, such as an unknown capability name, use the `manifest.*` codes listed in
[Packages and manifests](/pages/packages/). Errors from the compiler are printed with the compiler's text.

| Code | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `toolchain.rust-target` | The `wasm32-wasip2` target is not installed | Run `rustup target add wasm32-wasip2` |
| `toolchain.rust-version` | `rustc` is older than 1.90 | Run `rustup update stable` |
| `toolchain.bun-version` | Bun is older than 1.2 | Upgrade Bun |
| `toolchain.sdk-missing` | `node_modules/@ilium/plugin-sdk` is not installed | Run `bun install` in the project |
| `toolchain.language-ambiguous` | Both `Cargo.toml` and `package.json` exist | Keep one of the two files |
| `toolchain.language-unknown` | Neither `Cargo.toml` nor `package.json` exists | Run the command in the project directory |

<div class="note">
<p>Under <code>dev</code>, a failed rebuild keeps the running instance and sends it no <code>deactivate</code>.
Fix the error, and the next change triggers a new build.</p>
</div>

### Check the setup

Run `ilium plugin build` in the template project. A successful build prints `artifact` lines for each side
and ends with `"ok":true` on the `result` line. If the build fails on the target, check the `rustup` output
first. A TypeScript build that fails with `toolchain.sdk-missing` needs `bun install`, not a global install.

- [Rust SDK](/pages/rust-sdk/) and [TypeScript SDK](/pages/typescript-sdk/) describe the imports used above.
- [Packages and manifests](/pages/packages/) and [Manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/) describe the files the build reads.

- [Package and share](/pages/tutorial-09-package-and-share/) covers `pack`, signing and installing.

# Core plugins

## Core plugins

A core plugin is the plugin form of a feature Ilium has today. Ilium ships and maintains all 30 of them, and each one has an id of the form `ilium.core.<name>`. Where a feature is native to the kernel, such as starting a process in a pane, the terminal emulator, the layout solver, the keymap or snapshots, the page says so and shows the plugin driving that kernel surface through contract version 0.1. See [What a plugin is](/pages/getting-started-overview/) and [Worlds and sides](/pages/worlds-and-sides/) for the background.

| [Diagnostics](/pages/core-plugin-diagnostics/) | `ilium.core.diagnostics` | both | File logging, log levels and the diagnostics report. |

### Which core plugins can be disabled

All 30 core plugins can be disabled except the essential set: `ilium.core.tree`, `ilium.core.layout`, `ilium.core.settings` and `ilium.core.sessions`. Safe mode keeps the essential set running ([Safe mode and recovery](/pages/user-safe-mode-and-troubleshooting/)). The Plugins screen shows a lock in the "Can be disabled" column for them. If the restart rule disables an essential plugin, the kernel fallback in [Host architecture](/pages/reference-host-architecture/) applies. [LIF-276]

- [LIF-276] The Plugins screen MUST not offer a disable switch for the four essential plugins. Test: render the list and press Space on each.

### How other plugins work with core plugins

Core plugins use only the public contract, so every way a third-party plugin can reach them is documented. There are five: observe (events and topics), drive (services and commands), extend (fill an extension point), offer (declare your own points) and replace (`replaces`). Every core page ends with an "Extension points" section that lists its points, services, topics and whether it can be replaced. [Core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/) lists all of them. [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/) explains when to use which, and [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/) is the reference.

### Coverage

Every user-visible feature of Ilium maps to exactly one core plugin. Each plugin page lists the features it covers by their names in the user documentation, so you can start from a feature you know and find the plugin that implements it.

### How the samples teach the ABI

The samples on these pages are short and focused. Together they illustrate the whole ABI: the matrix assigns each ABI area (API pages, widgets, settings row types, services, events and intents) one primary plugin, and that plugin's samples use it. Across the 30 pages there are 395 ABI pages linked from the "ABI used" sections, between 8 and 20 per plugin (counted by script over `core-plugin-*.md`). Each sample is given in Rust and in TypeScript, and every name in it appears on the linked ABI page. The `calendar` and `api-gpu` areas are unstable and the samples say so.

Renders and samples marked Illustrative are not test oracles. When a page differs from `src/docs` at the baseline commit, `src/docs` wins and the page is a defect. The exact values a test uses are in the "Behaviour contract" table of each page: a table with one row per rule, an id of the form `<plugin>-B<nn>`, the exact value or text, and the baseline source (`src/docs/<file>.md#<anchor>`, or the source file of the baseline crate when the user documentation is silent). The test oracle for a plugin is that table, checked against the baseline binary through the golden outputs in [CLI compatibility](/pages/reference-cli-compatibility/).

### Security

Replacement of core plugins follows [SEC-300] to [SEC-306] in [Extension security](/pages/reference-extension-security/).

# Tree

## Tree

The Tree plugin (`ilium.core.tree`, side both) owns the project tree as the user sees it: groups, folders and top-level destinations, moving, renaming and closing entries, the tree order, bookmarks, locks and the automatic removal of empty groups. The tree itself is a kernel structure. The plugin reads it with the [`tree` import](/pages/api-tree/) and changes it only through intents, so this page shows how a plugin drives a kernel surface without drawing it.

### What it covers

- The project tree: groups, folders and panes in one outline (Panes and layout, The tree).
- Groups, folders and top-level destinations (Panes and layout, Groups).
- Moving, reordering and renaming entries, and rearranging without stopping any process (Panes and layout, Moving, ordering and renaming).
- Tree ordering (Settings, User Interface tab).
- Bookmarks, locks and automatic removal of empty groups (Panes and layout, Groups and Closing).
- Closing panes and groups (Panes and layout, Closing).
