The server holds all the logic and all the high-risk grants. The client side only shows the status topic, and it cannot hold `panes.lifecycle`.

### Step 2: the state, saved to storage

A run holds an id, a phase, a UTC deadline and one entry per reviewer (worktree path, pane node, `ended` flag, diff summary). The plugin saves it to storage after every step. A value is at most 1 MiB, so each diff summary is cut to 20 KiB.

Keep every decision in one pure function. It takes the run and one input, and returns the new run and a list of actions. The host calls live in a thin layer outside it. That split makes each phase testable without a host.

**Rust**

```rust
// src/plan.rs
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

pub const MAX_REVIEWERS: usize = 8;
pub const DIFF_BYTES: usize = 20 * 1024;

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum Phase { Creating, Working, Collecting, Done, Cancelled, Failed }

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Reviewer { pub worktree: Option<String>, pub pane: Option<u64>, pub ended: bool, pub diff: Option<String> }

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Run { pub run: String, pub phase: Phase, pub deadline: i64, pub reviewers: Vec<Reviewer> }

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub enum Action { CreateWorktree(usize), CreatePane(usize), Broadcast, CollectDiff(usize), StopPane(u64), Notify(String) }

#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum Input {
    WorktreeReady(usize, String), PaneReady(usize, u64), PaneEnded(u64),
    DiffReady(usize, String), Deadline, Cancel, StepFailed(String),
}

/// A count the user typed, clamped to a safe range.
pub fn clamp_count(asked: i64) -> usize { asked.clamp(1, MAX_REVIEWERS as i64) as usize }

pub fn start(run: &str, count: usize, now: i64, window_ms: i64) -> (Run, Vec<Action>) {
    let blank = Reviewer { worktree: None, pane: None, ended: false, diff: None };
    let state = Run { run: run.into(), phase: Phase::Creating, deadline: now + window_ms, reviewers: vec![blank; count] };
    (state, (0..count).map(Action::CreateWorktree).collect())
}

fn stop_all(state: &Run) -> Vec<Action> {
    state.reviewers.iter().filter(|r| !r.ended).filter_map(|r| r.pane).map(Action::StopPane).collect()
}

/// One pure step. Any input after the run has finished changes nothing.
pub fn step(mut state: Run, input: Input) -> (Run, Vec<Action>) {
    if matches!(state.phase, Phase::Done | Phase::Cancelled | Phase::Failed) {
        return (state, vec![]);
    }
    let mut actions = vec![];
    let collect = |s: &Run| (0..s.reviewers.len()).map(Action::CollectDiff).collect::<Vec<_>>();
    match input {
        Input::WorktreeReady(i, path) => {
            if let Some(r) = state.reviewers.get_mut(i) { r.worktree = Some(path); actions.push(Action::CreatePane(i)); }
        }
        Input::PaneReady(i, node) => {
            if let Some(r) = state.reviewers.get_mut(i) { r.pane = Some(node); }
            if state.reviewers.iter().all(|r| r.pane.is_some()) { state.phase = Phase::Working; actions.push(Action::Broadcast); }
        }
        Input::PaneEnded(node) => {
            state.reviewers.iter_mut().filter(|r| r.pane == Some(node)).for_each(|r| r.ended = true);
            if state.reviewers.iter().all(|r| r.ended) { state.phase = Phase::Collecting; actions = collect(&state); }
        }
        Input::Deadline => {
            // Stop what still runs, then collect what the agents wrote.
            actions = stop_all(&state);
            state.reviewers.iter_mut().for_each(|r| r.ended = true);
            state.phase = Phase::Collecting;
            actions.extend(collect(&state));
        }
        Input::DiffReady(i, text) => {
            if let Some(r) = state.reviewers.get_mut(i) { r.diff = Some(text.chars().take(DIFF_BYTES).collect()); }
            if state.phase == Phase::Collecting && state.reviewers.iter().all(|r| r.diff.is_some()) {
                state.phase = Phase::Done;
                let changed = state.reviewers.iter().filter(|r| r.diff.as_deref().is_some_and(|d| !d.is_empty())).count();
                actions.push(Action::Notify(format!("Review swarm done: {changed} of {} reviewers changed files.", state.reviewers.len())));
            }
        }
        Input::Cancel => { actions = stop_all(&state); state.phase = Phase::Cancelled; }
        Input::StepFailed(reason) => {
            actions = stop_all(&state);
            state.phase = Phase::Failed;
            actions.push(Action::Notify(format!("Review swarm failed: {reason}")));
        }
    }
    (state, actions)
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
// src/plan.ts
export const MAX_REVIEWERS = 8;
export const DIFF_BYTES = 20 * 1024;

export type Phase = 'creating' | 'working' | 'collecting' | 'done' | 'cancelled' | 'failed';
export interface Reviewer { worktree?: string; pane?: number; ended: boolean; diff?: string }
export interface Run { run: string; phase: Phase; deadline: number; reviewers: Reviewer[] }

export type Action =
  | { kind: 'create-worktree' | 'create-pane' | 'collect-diff'; index: number }
  | { kind: 'broadcast' }
  | { kind: 'stop-pane'; node: number }
  | { kind: 'notify'; text: string };

export type Input =
  | { kind: 'worktree-ready'; index: number; path: string }
  | { kind: 'pane-ready'; index: number; node: number }
  | { kind: 'pane-ended'; node: number }
  | { kind: 'diff-ready'; index: number; text: string }
  | { kind: 'deadline' | 'cancel' }
  | { kind: 'step-failed'; reason: string };

/** A count the user typed, clamped to a safe range. */
export function clampCount(asked: number): number {
  return Math.min(MAX_REVIEWERS, Math.max(1, Math.trunc(asked) || 1));
}

export function start(run: string, count: number, now: number, windowMs: number): { state: Run; actions: Action[] } {
  const reviewers: Reviewer[] = Array.from({ length: count }, () => ({ ended: false }));
  const actions = reviewers.map((_, index): Action => ({ kind: 'create-worktree', index }));
  return { state: { run, phase: 'creating', deadline: now + windowMs, reviewers }, actions };
}

const FINISHED: Phase[] = ['done', 'cancelled', 'failed'];

/** One pure step. Any input after the run has finished changes nothing. */
export function step(old: Run, input: Input): { state: Run; actions: Action[] } {
  const state: Run = structuredClone(old);
  let actions: Action[] = [];
  if (FINISHED.includes(state.phase)) return { state, actions };
  const collect = (): Action[] => state.reviewers.map((_, index) => ({ kind: 'collect-diff', index }));
  const stopAll = (): Action[] =>
    state.reviewers.filter((r) => !r.ended && r.pane !== undefined).map((r) => ({ kind: 'stop-pane', node: r.pane! }));
  switch (input.kind) {
    case 'worktree-ready':
      if (state.reviewers[input.index]) {
        state.reviewers[input.index].worktree = input.path;
        actions.push({ kind: 'create-pane', index: input.index });
      }
      break;
    case 'pane-ready':
      if (state.reviewers[input.index]) state.reviewers[input.index].pane = input.node;
      if (state.reviewers.every((r) => r.pane !== undefined)) { state.phase = 'working'; actions.push({ kind: 'broadcast' }); }
      break;
    case 'pane-ended':
      state.reviewers.filter((r) => r.pane === input.node).forEach((r) => { r.ended = true; });
      if (state.reviewers.every((r) => r.ended)) { state.phase = 'collecting'; actions = collect(); }
      break;
    case 'deadline':
      // Stop what still runs, then collect what the agents wrote.
      actions = [...stopAll(), ...collect()];
      state.reviewers.forEach((r) => { r.ended = true; });
      state.phase = 'collecting';
      break;
    case 'diff-ready':
      if (state.reviewers[input.index]) state.reviewers[input.index].diff = input.text.slice(0, DIFF_BYTES);
      if (state.phase === 'collecting' && state.reviewers.every((r) => r.diff !== undefined)) {
        state.phase = 'done';
        const changed = state.reviewers.filter((r) => r.diff !== '').length;
        actions.push({ kind: 'notify', text: `Review swarm done: ${changed} of ${state.reviewers.length} reviewers changed files.` });
      }
      break;
    case 'cancel': actions = stopAll(); state.phase = 'cancelled'; break;
    case 'step-failed':
      actions = [...stopAll(), { kind: 'notify', text: `Review swarm failed: ${input.reason}` }];
      state.phase = 'failed';
      break;
  }
  return { state, actions };
}
```

### Step 3: the host calls

The thin layer turns each action into a host call. Every call that changes the world has a dedup key, or an id in its payload, so a repeat after a restart is harmless. A repeat inside the 10-minute window gives `duplicate`, and the layer treats that as success.

The payloads of the core services below are the shapes this page uses. Check the fields against [Reference: core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/) for the version you run. The functions `pane_intent` and `stop_intent` build the `CreatePaneSpec` (title `Review 1`, content kind `ilium.terminal`, the worktree as `cwd`, the command `claude`) and the terminate intent with a grace period.

**Rust**

```rust
// src/lib.rs
use std::collections::HashMap;

use ilium_plugin_sdk::dedup;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{clock, jobs, services, storage, timers, topics};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use serde_json::{json, Value};
mod plan;
use plan::{Action, Input, Phase, Run};

const WINDOW_MS: i64 = 20 * 60_000;
enum Waiting { Worktree(usize), Service, Diff(usize) }

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server", exports = ["handler", "job-runner"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Swarm { run: Option<Run>, waiting: HashMap<RequestId, Waiting> }

impl Lifecycle for Swarm {
    fn activate(&mut self) {
        // Restart recovery: read the saved run. Step 5 says what happens next.
        let saved = storage::get("project", "run").ok().flatten();
        self.run = saved.and_then(|text| serde_json::from_str(&text).ok());
    }
}

impl Handler for Swarm {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let input = match event {
                Event::CommandInvoked(c) if c.command == "example.swarm/start" => {
                    let args: Value = serde_json::from_str(&c.arguments_json).unwrap_or(Value::Null);
                    let now = clock::now_unix_millis();
                    let (state, actions) = plan::start(&format!("{now:x}"), plan::clamp_count(args["count"].as_i64().unwrap_or(3)), now, WINDOW_MS);
                    let _ = timers::at(state.deadline, "deadline");
                    self.run = Some(state);
                    self.perform(actions, &mut out);
                    None
                }
                Event::CommandInvoked(c) if c.command == "example.swarm/cancel" => Some(Input::Cancel),
                Event::DurableTimerFired { name, .. } if name == "deadline" => Some(Input::Deadline),
                Event::PaneLifecycleChanged(change) if change.ended => Some(Input::PaneEnded(change.node)),
                Event::RequestCompleted(done) => self.completed(done),
                _ => None,
            };
            if let (Some(input), Some(run)) = (input, self.run.take()) {
                let (next, actions) = plan::step(run, input);
                if matches!(next.phase, Phase::Done | Phase::Cancelled | Phase::Failed) {
                    let _ = timers::cancel_durable("deadline");
                }
                self.run = Some(next);
                self.perform(actions, &mut out);
            }
        }
        if let Some(run) = &self.run {
            let _ = storage::put("project", "run", &serde_json::to_string(run).unwrap_or_default());
            let _ = topics::publish("example.swarm/status", &json!({ "run": run.run, "phase": run.phase }).to_string());
        }
        out
    }
}

impl Swarm {
    fn call(&mut self, service: &str, payload: Value, why: Waiting) {
        if let Ok(id) = services::call_request(service, "send", &payload.to_string()) {
            self.waiting.insert(id, why);
        }
    }

    fn perform(&mut self, actions: Vec<Action>, out: &mut Vec<Submission>) {
        let Some(run) = self.run.clone() else { return };
        for action in actions {
            match action {
                Action::CreateWorktree(i) => self.call("ilium.core.worktrees/create",
                    json!({ "branch": format!("swarm/{}/{i}", run.run), "agent": "review" }), Waiting::Worktree(i)),
                Action::CreatePane(i) => out.push(Submission::keyed(
                    pane_intent(&run, i), dedup::key_for(&["swarm", &run.run, "pane", &i.to_string()]))),
                Action::Broadcast => self.call("ilium.core.fleet/broadcast",
                    json!({ "message": "Review the diff against main. List risks only.", "run": run.run }), Waiting::Service),
                Action::CollectDiff(i) => {
                    let path = run.reviewers[i].worktree.clone().unwrap_or_default();
                    if let Ok(id) = jobs::start_json("example.swarm/diff", &json!({ "path": path }).to_string()) {
                        self.waiting.insert(id, Waiting::Diff(i));
                    }
                }
                Action::StopPane(node) => out.push(Submission::keyed(
                    stop_intent(node), dedup::key_for(&["swarm", &run.run, "stop", &node.to_string()]))),
                Action::Notify(text) => self.call("ilium.core.notifications/notify",
                    json!({ "title": "Review swarm", "body": text, "urgency": "normal", "run": run.run }), Waiting::Service),
            }
        }
    }

    fn completed(&mut self, done: RequestResult) -> Option<Input> {
        match self.waiting.remove(&done.request)? {
            Waiting::Service => None,
            Waiting::Diff(i) => Some(Input::DiffReady(i, jobs::take_output(done.request).unwrap_or_default())),
            Waiting::Worktree(i) => match services::take_reply(done.request) {
                Ok(text) => {
                    let path = serde_json::from_str::<Value>(&text).ok()?["path"].as_str()?.to_string();
                    Some(Input::WorktreeReady(i, path))
                }
                Err(error) => Some(Input::StepFailed(error.code)),
            },
        }
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
// src/index.ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { nowUnixMillis } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clock';
import { startJson, takeOutput } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/jobs';
import { callRequest, takeReply } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/services';
import { get, put } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/storage';
import { at, cancelDurable } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/timers';
import { publish } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/topics';
import { clampCount, start, step, type Action, type Input, type Run } from './plan';
const WINDOW_MS = 20 * 60_000;
type Waiting = { kind: 'worktree' | 'diff'; index: number } | { kind: 'service' };

let run: Run | undefined;
const waiting = new Map<bigint, Waiting>();
let correlation = 1n;

function keyed(intent: Submission['intent'], ...parts: string[]): Submission {
  const dedupKey = parts.join(':').replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9._:/-]/g, '-').slice(0, 128);
  return { intent, correlation: correlation++, dedupKey };
}

function call(service: string, payload: object, why: Waiting): void {
  try { waiting.set(callRequest(service, 'send', JSON.stringify(payload)), why); } catch { /* the host logs it */ }
}

function perform(actions: Action[], out: Submission[]): void {
  if (!run) return;
  for (const a of actions) {
    if (a.kind === 'create-worktree') {
      call('ilium.core.worktrees/create', { branch: `swarm/${run.run}/${a.index}`, agent: 'review' }, { kind: 'worktree', index: a.index });
    } else if (a.kind === 'create-pane') {
      out.push(keyed(paneIntent(run, a.index), 'swarm', run.run, 'pane', String(a.index)));
    } else if (a.kind === 'broadcast') {
      call('ilium.core.fleet/broadcast', { message: 'Review the diff against main. List risks only.', run: run.run }, { kind: 'service' });
    } else if (a.kind === 'collect-diff') {
      try {
        const id = startJson('example.swarm/diff', JSON.stringify({ path: run.reviewers[a.index].worktree ?? '' }));
        waiting.set(id, { kind: 'diff', index: a.index });
      } catch { /* the host logs it */ }
    } else if (a.kind === 'stop-pane') {
      out.push(keyed(stopIntent(a.node), 'swarm', run.run, 'stop', String(a.node)));
    } else {
      call('ilium.core.notifications/notify', { title: 'Review swarm', body: a.text, urgency: 'normal', run: run.run }, { kind: 'service' });
    }
  }
}

function completed(request: bigint): Input | undefined {
  const entry = waiting.get(request);
  waiting.delete(request);
  if (!entry || entry.kind === 'service') return undefined;
  if (entry.kind === 'diff') return { kind: 'diff-ready', index: entry.index, text: takeOutput(request) ?? '' };
  try {
    const path = (JSON.parse(takeReply(request)) as { path?: string }).path;
    return path ? { kind: 'worktree-ready', index: entry.index, path } : { kind: 'step-failed', reason: 'no worktree path' };
  } catch (error) {
    return { kind: 'step-failed', reason: (error as { code?: string }).code ?? 'failed' };
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler, jobRunner } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate() {
    // Restart recovery: read the saved run. Step 5 says what happens next.
    const saved = get('project', 'run');
    run = saved ? (JSON.parse(saved) as Run) : undefined;
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const out: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      let input: Input | undefined;
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === 'example.swarm/start') {
        const args = JSON.parse(event.val.argumentsJson) as { count?: number };
        const now = Number(nowUnixMillis());
        const started = start(now.toString(16), clampCount(args.count ?? 3), now, WINDOW_MS);
        run = started.state;
        at(BigInt(run.deadline), 'deadline');
        perform(started.actions, out);
      } else if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === 'example.swarm/cancel') {
        input = { kind: 'cancel' };
      } else if (event.tag === 'durable-timer-fired' && event.val.name === 'deadline') {
        input = { kind: 'deadline' };
      } else if (event.tag === 'pane-lifecycle-changed' && event.val.ended) {
        input = { kind: 'pane-ended', node: Number(event.val.node) };
      } else if (event.tag === 'request-completed') {
        input = completed(event.val.request);
      }
      if (input && run) {
        const result = step(run, input);
        run = result.state;
        if (['done', 'cancelled', 'failed'].includes(run.phase)) cancelDurable('deadline');
        perform(result.actions, out);
      }
    }
    if (run) {
      put('project', 'run', JSON.stringify(run));
      publish('example.swarm/status', JSON.stringify({ run: run.run, phase: run.phase }));
    }
    return out;
  },
});
```

A restart loses `waiting`, the map from a request to its purpose. The saved run survives. Step 5 covers recovery.

### Step 4: the diff job

The job runs in its own instance with its own limits. It runs `git diff --stat` in one worktree, so the output stays short.

**Rust**

```rust
// src/job.rs
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::process::{self, ProcessSpec};

impl JobRunner for Swarm {
    fn run(&mut self, job: JobCall) -> JobResult {
        let params: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&job.payload_json).unwrap_or_default();
        let path = params["path"].as_str().unwrap_or("");
        let args = ["-C", path, "diff", "--stat", "HEAD"].map(String::from).to_vec();
        match process::run(&ProcessSpec { command: "git".into(), args, timeout_millis: 20_000 }) {
            Ok(output) => JobResult::Done(output.stdout.chars().take(20 * 1024).collect()),
            Err(error) => JobResult::Failed(error.code),
        }
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
// src/job.ts
import { run as runProcess } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/process';

export function runJob(payloadJson: string): { tag: 'done' | 'failed'; val: string } {
  const { path = '' } = JSON.parse(payloadJson) as { path?: string };
  try {
    const args = ['-C', path, 'diff', '--stat', 'HEAD'];
    return { tag: 'done', val: runProcess({ command: 'git', args, timeoutMillis: 20_000 }).stdout.slice(0, 20 * 1024) };
  } catch (error) {
    return { tag: 'failed', val: (error as { code?: string }).code ?? 'failed' };
  }
}
```

### Step 5: restart, cancel and duplicates

Three events can cut a run short.

- **Ilium restarts.** `activate` reads the saved run. The `waiting` map is gone, so the listing does not match old replies. Resume by phase: in `creating` ask again for worktrees that have no path, in `working` wait for pane events and the durable deadline, in `collecting` start the diffs that are empty.
- **The user cancels.** `Cancel` stops every running pane with `terminate-pane-process` and a grace period, and the layer cancels the timer. Worktrees stay on disk for the user to inspect.
- **A second start.** Refuse the command while the saved phase is `creating`, `working` or `collecting`. One run at a time.

Recovery works because every action is safe to repeat. A pane intent has a dedup key, so a repeat inside 10 minutes gives `duplicate`. After that window create a pane only when the saved reviewer has none. The worktree call uses a fixed branch name, so a repeat should return the existing path. Check this against the worktrees plugin you run. Replies after a cancel are dropped, because `step` ignores every input in a finished run. The listing above restores the run but leaves the resume loop and the second-start guard to you.

### Step 6: test it

`FakeHost` has fake panes and jobs, and `FakeSession.install_core` adds stubs of the core plugins. Test the pure plan, then the pane and job calls with the fakes. Follow [Testing](/pages/testing/) and [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/). Check the real core services in the app.

**Rust**

```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::plan::*;

    fn working(count: usize) -> Run {
        let (mut state, _) = start("r1", count, 1_000, 60_000);
        for i in 0..count {
            state = step(state, Input::WorktreeReady(i, format!("/w/{i}"))).0;
            state = step(state, Input::PaneReady(i, 10 + i as u64)).0;
        }
        state
    }

    #[test]
    fn deadline_stops_only_running_panes_then_one_notification() {
        assert_eq!(clamp_count(500), MAX_REVIEWERS);
        let (state, _) = step(working(2), Input::PaneEnded(10));
        let (state, actions) = step(state, Input::Deadline);
        assert!(actions.contains(&Action::StopPane(11)) && !actions.contains(&Action::StopPane(10)));
        let (state, none) = step(state, Input::DiffReady(0, "a".into()));
        assert!(none.is_empty());
        let (state, done) = step(state, Input::DiffReady(1, "".into()));
        assert_eq!(state.phase, Phase::Done);
        assert_eq!(done, vec![Action::Notify("Review swarm done: 1 of 2 reviewers changed files.".into())]);
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
// src/plan.test.ts
import { expect, test } from 'bun:test';
import { clampCount, MAX_REVIEWERS, start, step, type Run } from './plan';

function working(count: number): Run {
  let { state } = start('r1', count, 1000, 60000);
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    state = step(state, { kind: 'worktree-ready', index: i, path: `/w/${i}` }).state;
    state = step(state, { kind: 'pane-ready', index: i, node: 10 + i }).state;
  }
  return state;
}

test('deadline stops only running panes, then one notification', () => {
  expect(clampCount(500)).toBe(MAX_REVIEWERS);
  const ended = step(working(2), { kind: 'pane-ended', node: 10 }).state;
  const result = step(ended, { kind: 'deadline' });
  expect(result.actions).toContainEqual({ kind: 'stop-pane', node: 11 });
  expect(result.actions).not.toContainEqual({ kind: 'stop-pane', node: 10 });
  const none = step(result.state, { kind: 'diff-ready', index: 0, text: 'a' });
  expect(none.actions).toEqual([]);
  const done = step(none.state, { kind: 'diff-ready', index: 1, text: '' });
  expect(done.state.phase).toBe('done');
  expect(done.actions).toEqual([{ kind: 'notify', text: 'Review swarm done: 1 of 2 reviewers changed files.' }]);
});

```

Run `cargo test` or `bun test`. Then check the live path with the steps in [Debugging](/pages/debugging/):

1. Pack and install as in [tutorial 9](/pages/tutorial-09-package-and-share/). Read the three high-risk rows before you confirm.
2. Run `Start a review swarm` with count 2 in a Git project. Two panes appear.
3. Run `Cancel the review swarm`, then read `ilium plugin logs example.swarm --tail 20`.

### Edge cases and errors: what can go wrong

| Code or symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` on a service | A `services.use` grant is missing or revoked | Grant it. The run ends as failed with this code. |
| `not-found` on a service | The core plugin is off | Turn it on. The run ends as failed. |
| `refused` on `create-pane` | `panes.create` or `fs.read` is missing | Grant it. Check `ilium plugin grants example.swarm`. |
| `refused` on stop | `panes.lifecycle` was left off | Tick it, or stop the agents by hand. |
| `timed-out` on a service | A core plugin took over 30 s | The run fails. Start again. |
| Job `failed` | Git is not allowed or the path is gone | Check `process.run:git`. A failed diff gives an empty summary. |
| Restart in the middle | Ilium restarted | The saved run is read. Resume by phase (step 5). |

# Architecture

## Architecture

Ilium keeps the code that runs per byte, per keystroke or per frame in the kernel. Everything else that a feature needs can be a plugin. Plugins run inside a plugin host, behind a fixed contract, `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`, which lists every function a plugin may call. This page explains where the boundary sits, what sits on each side of it, and what happens when a plugin breaks the rules.

In short, a plugin never touches the terminal, the tree or the disk directly. It calls an SDK function. The host checks the plugin's grants, the kernel does the work, and the result returns to the plugin as an event or as an outcome.

## You will need

Nothing beyond the overview. The later concept pages describe each component in detail.

To write a plugin you need the toolchain from [Getting started toolchain](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/). Rust plugins need Rust stable 1.90 or later with the `wasm32-wasip2` target. TypeScript plugins need Bun 1.2 or later. Both SDKs pin their binding generators, so nothing is installed globally.

## The kernel

The kernel is the native part of Ilium. It runs in the processes that host plugins (the session server, each client and the CLI process; see [Host architecture](/pages/reference-host-architecture/)) and owns the components below. A plugin never reaches into these parts directly. It asks for an operation through a host import, and the kernel checks the plugin's grants before it acts.

| Component | What it owns | How a plugin reaches it |
|---|---|---|
| Process and session lifecycle | Sessions, the CLI dispatcher, server and client processes | `cli` and `http-api` imports, `cli-invoked` events |
| PTY and screen state | PTY spawn, input delivery, vt100 parsing, screen state | `terminal` and `agent` primitives, `send-input` intent |
| Generic tree | Groups and panes, plus plugin metadata the kernel stores but never reads | `tree` and `panes` imports, `tree-changed` events, intents |
| Snapshot writer | The snapshot file and plugin-owned sections | Bytes returned from `deactivate` are stored as restore state |
| Layout and compositor | Split geometry, PTY sizing, the shared animation look, dithering | `ui` widget trees, `anim` scenes |
| Input routing | Keymap, mouse hit-testing, focus, the modal stack | `keys` import, `keys.grab` |
| Commands and settings | The command registry and the settings store | `commands` and `settings` imports |
| Event bus and quotas | Per-plugin queues, timers, the execution quota group | `on-events` export, `timers` import |
| Host services | HTTP, file access by preopen, process runner, sound, notifications, clipboard, audio, video, inference transport | Imports that a grant unlocks |

The terminal and agent pane primitives stay native, because they handle the per-byte path. The editor primitive is native. The contract keeps the same split: its events, intents, grants and widgets let plugins reach much of the kernel without moving any per-byte work into a plugin.

The map below shows the three layers. Solid boxes are kernel components. The dashed box is the plugin host. The double line is the sandbox boundary, which applies to third-party plugins (tiers T2 and T3).

## The plugin host

The plugin host runs plugin components inside Wasmtime. It verifies each package and records the grants. Every plugin side (server, client or scene) gets its own instance and limits. See [Worlds and sides](/pages/worlds-and-sides/).

The host sorts plugins into four tiers. The tier decides where a plugin runs and what it may ask for.

| Tier | Who signs it | Where it runs | How it installs |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | The kernel itself | Native code in the server and the client | Not a plugin |
| T1 | Ilium, embedded in the release as precompiled `.cwasm` | The process that hosts its side (server, client or CLI process), on every platform | Granted up to the manifest ceiling; high-risk grants asked once |
| T2 | A publisher key that the user trusts | The sandbox helper process | Review dialog; grants are remembered |
| T3 | Nobody (unsigned local package) | The sandbox helper process | Only with `--allow-unsigned` or `ilium plugin dev`; shown with a `dev` badge |

A T1 plugin that asks for a high-risk (H) capability runs without it until the user allows it in a single prompt at first activation.

On Windows and macOS, T2 and T3 packages are refused until a native sandbox exists there. The refusal text is:

```
Cannot install acme-agent 1.0.0.
Third-party plugins need the plugin sandbox, which is not available on Windows yet.
Bundled plugins keep working.
```

On macOS the same text names macOS instead of Windows.

<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:12:03</span> <span class="t-ok">load</span>    demo-notes 0.1.0, tier T1, server and client
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:12:03</span> <span class="t-ok">load</span>    acme-agent 1.0.0, tier T2, server, sandbox helper
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:12:04</span> <span class="t-ok">restore</span> snapshot restored, one tree-changed batch
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:12:04</span> <span class="t-warn">refuse</span>  vendor-ext 0.1.0, tier T3, no sandbox on macOS
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:40</span> <span class="t-dim">stop</span>    plugins stopped before the final snapshot write
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. A host log that shows which plugins load, which one is refused on a platform without a sandbox, and when the host stops. The names are placeholders.

### The sandbox helper

T2 and T3 components run in a separate helper process. The helper confines itself with a seccomp filter and a bubblewrap mount namespace. The namespace holds only the scopes that the plugin was granted, mounted read-only for read grants, plus read-only `/usr`, `/bin`, `/lib*` and `/etc`. A component that imports `wasi:sockets` or `wasi:http` is refused at load, so network access goes through the `http` import, which the kernel performs for the plugin.

Child processes that a plugin starts with `process.run` inherit the same confinement. T1 children run without confinement, at low priority.

  <text x="6" y="168" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">A declined grant returns not-permitted before the kernel runs.</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>A call leaves the plugin through an SDK wrapper. The grant check runs first, the kernel acts only when the check passes, and the outcome returns to the plugin.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Kernel and core plugin split

The kernel keeps PTY and vt100, the tree model, IPC, the snapshot writer, the config store, the keymap, layout and the compositor, the look painter, the scene host, the plugin host, the recovery page, the HTTP listener and the parsing of kernel CLI commands. Everything else is a core plugin. The full list, the boot order of both sides, the minimum kernel that runs with `--no-plugins` and the safe start are on [kernel and boot](/pages/reference-kernel-and-boot/). The owner of every Ilium feature is on [feature traceability](/pages/reference-feature-traceability/). [COR-010] [COR-020]

## Start and stop order

On the server, the host starts in this order:

1. The kernel boots and loads the configuration.
2. The snapshot is restored.
3. The plugin host verifies every installed manifest and registers its static contributions. Nothing is instantiated yet.
4. `startup` plugins are instantiated and activated. Service providers activate before the consumers that require them. Cycles are refused at install.
5. Each activated plugin receives one `tree-changed` batch for all restored nodes. It never replays the restore.

On shutdown, the order is reversed in the places where it matters:

1. Services stop in reverse activation order.
2. The host refuses plugin submissions. They complete as `cancelled`.
3. Each active plugin receives `deactivate(shutdown)` in reverse activation order, within `deactivate_deadline_ms`. The bytes it returns become its restore state.
4. Pending requests are cancelled, instances are dropped and quotas are released.
5. The final snapshot is written. No plugin intent can reach the snapshot after the writer stops.

A client connects with a handshake that carries the plugin protocol number, the contract version and its plugin set. A protocol or contract mismatch is refused with `ipc.protocol-mismatch` and the client exits with code 76. A plugin that differs between client and server loses only its client half. See [Plugin traffic over IPC](/pages/reference-host-ipc/).

## Boundary rules

- Plugins depend only on the SDK packages: the crate `ilium-plugin-sdk` for Rust and `@ilium/plugin-sdk` for TypeScript. They never depend on Ilium crates.
- Every call is checked against the grant set in force at that moment. A declined grant links its imports to stubs that return `not-permitted`. An interface that no requested capability unlocks is refused at install with `manifest.import-not-requested`. A function of a never-requested capability inside a linked interface traps the instance with `host.capability-not-requested`. See [Host runtime](/pages/reference-host-runtime/).
- Each plugin has one bounded event queue, sized by `event_queue` (1,024 by default). Plugins hold no event-journal cursors of their own. Events with the drop policy are counted in an `events-dropped` event.
- The dispatcher charges each plugin's bytes and CPU time to the execution quota group. When that budget is spent, calls return `quota-exceeded` with `retry-after-ms`.
- Plugins never print raw terminal escape sequences. They describe widgets as data, and the kernel applies the theme, icon widths and the stable-glyph preference. The host removes escape sequences from text fields and logs one warning per view.

### Limits

The manifest may request a limit. The host clamps the request to the ceiling for the tier and logs the clamp; it never refuses the package. The user sets the same keys under `[plugins.limits]` in `config.toml`, for every plugin or for the whole session. The main keys are below. The full list is in [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/).

| Key | Default | T1 ceiling | T2 and T3 ceiling | Effect on breach |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `memory_mib` | 32 | 256 | 128 | Trap |
| `event_deadline_ms` | 20 | 50 | 20 | Trap |
| `render_deadline_ms` | 10 | 20 | 10 | Trap |
| `job_deadline_ms` (CPU) | 2,000 | 60,000 | 10,000 | `failed(timed-out)` |
| `event_queue` | 1,024 | 4,096 | 1,024 | Stuck plugin restart |
| `ui_tree_nodes` | 4,096 | 16,384 | 4,096 | Trap |
| `storage_bucket_mib` | 16 | 256 | 16 | `quota-exceeded` |
| `http_response_mib` | 8 | 64 | 8 | `failed(quota-exceeded)` |

The session keys cap the sum over all plugins in one process. For example, `session_memory_mib` is 1,024 MiB. A new instance that would exceed it is refused and logged. It does not count as a failure. The session keys and the exact failure list are in [Errors and limits](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/#host-rules-for-limits-and-restarts).

## Hook chains

An owner can run a hook chain through the `extensions` host interface. The host looks up the extensions of that point, sorts them by priority (lower first, ties by plugin id) and calls each handler through the contributor's `hook-handler` export, one after the other. The reply of each handler is checked against the point's mode and `reply_schema` before the next handler runs. Hooks fail open. A handler that times out, traps or errors counts as a pass, three breaches in a row stop that extension until its plugin restarts, and the whole chain is capped at 100 ms. Handlers after the cap are skipped and logged. `run-hook` is asynchronous: it returns a request id at once and the chain runs without blocking the owner's call. Handlers run strictly one after another, the 100 ms cap is measured from the start of the first handler, and a hook never crosses a process: a client-owned point runs only the handlers in that client. T1 handlers run in the process that hosts the owner's side. T2 and T3 handlers cost one helper round trip, which counts inside the handler deadline. See [extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/) and [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/).

## Failures and restarts

A trap or a deadline breach drops the instance, cancels its pending requests and keeps its decorations, marked stale. The host then restarts the plugin on a back-off:

- The first failure restarts after 1 second.
- The second failure restarts after 5 seconds.
- The third failure within the 10-minute window stops that side; there is no 30-second step.
- A third failure inside a sliding 10-minute window disables the plugin on that side. On the client, each client counts separately.

A revocation, a disable, an upgrade or a shutdown never counts as a failure. When the host disables a plugin, the tree footer shows a notice in this form:

`Plugin Acme Agent stopped after 3 failures in 10 minutes: views.render trap (sidebar). Turn it on again in Settings > Plugins.`

The part in parentheses names the view only when the failing export was `views.render`.

## Worked example 1: a Rust server plugin

This plugin runs on the server. It places a badge on every pane whose agent starts working. The manifest asks for two grants: `agent.read` to receive activity events and `tree.decorate` to set the badge.

```json
{
  "server": { "entry": "server.wasm", "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "server": ["agent.read", "tree.decorate"] },
  "contributes": {
    "decoration_slots": [{ "id": "hello", "placement": "badge", "priority": 50 }]
  }
}
```

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::AgentActivityEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SetDecorationSpec;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::AgentActivity;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Hello;

impl Lifecycle for Hello {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("hello from {}", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for Hello {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::AgentActivityChanged(change) = event else { continue };
            if change.current != AgentActivity::Working { continue; }
            submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
                node: change.node,
                slot: "hello".into(),
                content: vec![Span::plain("hi")],
                icon: None,
                sort_key: None,
                persist: false,
            })));
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

The path through the boundary is as follows:

1. The dispatcher delivers `agent-activity-changed` into the plugin's queue. Delivery requires `agent.read`.
2. `log::log` is an always-granted import. Its line goes to the plugin log.
3. The returned `Submission` is checked when the batch is accepted. The kernel verifies `tree.decorate`, the node and the slot `hello`, which the manifest declares.
4. If the user declined `tree.decorate`, the kernel answers `refused(not-permitted)` for that submission. The batch is refused as a whole only for a malformed submission or a missing grant.

## Worked example 2: a TypeScript client plugin

This plugin runs in the client. It answers its own command with a desktop notice. It needs the `notify.desktop` grant, and the command `com.example.hello/greet` must be declared under `contributes.commands`.

```json
{
  "client": { "entry": "client.js", "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "client": ["notify.desktop"] }
}
```

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'command-invoked') continue;
      if (event.val.command !== 'com.example.hello/greet') continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'notify',
          val: { title: 'Hello', body: 'from a plugin', urgency: 'normal', sound: undefined },
        },
        correlation: 1n,
        dedupKey: undefined,
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

The returned submissions are checked by the kernel. A `notify` intent is limited to 6 per minute per plugin; a seventh returns `refused(rate-limited)`.

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs com.example.hello --tail 3
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:02</span> <span class="t-ok">info </span> com.example.hello hello from com.example.hello
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:31</span> <span class="t-warn">warn </span> com.example.hello 2 lines dropped in the last second
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:15:07</span> <span class="t-err">error</span> com.example.hello restart after 1 s, handler trap
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The log lines of one client plugin, as `ilium plugin logs` prints them. The plugin id, the level and the message follow the timestamp.

## Errors and edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Function of a capability the manifest never requested, in a linked interface | The instance traps with `host.capability-not-requested` and counts as a failure. An interface that is not unlocked at all is refused at install |
| Grant declined by the user | The call returns `not-permitted`; the plugin keeps running |
| Component exports differ from required plus listed | Install refused with `manifest.exports-mismatch` |
| Component imports `wasi:sockets` or `wasi:http` | Refused at load |
| Windows or macOS, T2 or T3 package | Install refused with the text above |
| Session memory limit reached | New instance refused and logged; not counted as a failure (`host-capacity`) |
| Third failure inside 10 minutes | Plugin disabled with the notice above |
| Grant revoked while a call is in flight | Call returns `revoked`; the plugin is re-activated with the reduced grants |

## What the user sees

The tree footer shows disable notices. Settings > Plugins lists each plugin with its tier, grants and an on/off switch; a T3 plugin carries a `dev` badge. Decorations appear in the pane rows they name, such as the `hi` badge in example 1. Logs appear through `ilium plugin logs <id>`.

# Background jobs

## Background jobs

An event handler has a deadline of 20 ms by default, so it cannot parse a large file or search a whole workspace. A background job moves that work out of the handler. The plugin starts a job with a kind and an input of bytes. The host runs the plugin's `job-runner` export in a second instance of the same component, under its own CPU deadline, wall-clock deadline and memory limit. The plugin then receives progress as events and reads the output once the job completes. This page covers when to use a job, how to declare and start one, the full surface, progress, cancellation, outcomes and the limits that apply.

## You will need

- The `jobs.run` grant, which the user reviews in the install dialog (see [capability jobs.run](/pages/capability-jobs-run/)).
- A `contributes.jobs` entry for each job kind the plugin runs.
- `job-runner` in the `exports` list of the side that runs the job (see [exports](/pages/api-exports/)).
- The grants of every import the job calls, such as `fs.read` or `http`, on that same side.
- A Rust plugin with `ilium-plugin-sdk`, or a TypeScript plugin with `@ilium/plugin-sdk` (see [Rust SDK](/pages/rust-sdk/) and [TypeScript SDK](/pages/typescript-sdk/)).
- Familiarity with [requests and outcomes](/pages/requests-and-outcomes/), because every job is a request.

## When to use a job

Use a job for work that takes longer than an event deadline: parsing a saved world, preparing a large image, searching a workspace or building an index. Do not use a job for one HTTP request or a short file read. Those already return through request ids, and the host completes them without a job.

## Declaring a job kind

Each kind is listed under `contributes.jobs`. The plugin also lists `job-runner` in its `exports`.

```json
{
  "server": {
    "entry": "server.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": ["job-runner"]
  },
  "capabilities": { "server": ["jobs.run"] },
  "contributes": {
    "jobs": [{ "kind": "parse-world", "deadline_ms": 10000, "memory_mib": 128 }]
  }
}
```

`deadline_ms` is the CPU deadline, and `memory_mib` is the memory limit. Both are optional. A kind that declares no values uses the defaults in the table below. The host clamps a value above the tier ceiling to that ceiling and logs the clamp.

| Limit | Default | Ceiling T1 | Ceiling T2 and T3 | Over the limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPU deadline (`deadline_ms`) | 2,000 ms | 60,000 ms | 10,000 ms | `failed(timed-out)` |
| Wall-clock deadline (`job_wall_ms`) | 20,000 ms | 600,000 ms | 100,000 ms | `failed(timed-out)` |
| Memory (`memory_mib`) | 64 MiB | 512 MiB | 256 MiB | `failed(quota-exceeded)` |
| Input, and output, each | 16 MiB | 64 MiB | 16 MiB | Input: `invalid-argument` at the call. Output: `failed(invalid-argument)` |
| Concurrent jobs | 2 | 8 | 2 | Extra jobs wait in the queue |
| Queued jobs | 16 | 64 | 16 | `busy` at the start call |

The CPU deadline counts CPU time only. Time spent in `wait-request` or waiting for the disk counts against the wall-clock deadline instead.

## The surface

The `jobs` import has five functions. Two of them are callable only inside the job, and the `job-runner` export is the code the host calls.

| Function | Rust | TypeScript | Callable from | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `start` | `jobs::start(kind, input).await` returns `Result<Vec<u8>, PluginError>`; the raw `jobs::start_request` returns `Result<RequestId, PluginError>` | `await start(kind, input)` returns `Promise<Uint8Array>`; the raw `startRequest` returns `bigint` | Plugin | Starts a job of a declared kind. The awaited form resolves with the output |
| `cancel` | `jobs::cancel(job)` | `cancel(job)` | Plugin | Asks the job to stop |
| `take-output` | `jobs::take_output(job)` returns `Option<Vec<u8>>` | `takeOutput(job)` returns `Uint8Array \| undefined` | Plugin | Returns the output once |
| `report-progress` | `jobs::report_progress(percent)` takes `f32` | `reportProgress(percent)` | Inside `run` | Reports 0 to 100. NaN is ignored, other values are clamped |
| `is-cancelled` | `jobs::is_cancelled()` returns `bool` | `isCancelled()` | Inside `run` | True after a cancel request |
| `wait-request` | `jobs::wait_request(request, timeout_millis)` | `waitRequest(request, timeoutMillis)` | Inside `run` | Blocks until a slow call completes, so the job can read a file and then take the result |
| `run` (export) | `JobRunner::run(&mut self, kind: String, input: Vec<u8>)` | `run(kind, input)` member of `definePlugin` | Host calls it | Does the work. Returns the output bytes or a `PluginError` |

The SDKs also provide JSON helpers. `jobs::start_json(kind, &value)` in Rust and `startJson(kind, value)` in TypeScript encode a value as JSON bytes. The job decodes the bytes itself, so the host never looks inside an input or an output.

The job's events are `job-progress` and `request-completed`. Both are described under progress and cancellation below.

## How a job runs

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 150" role="img" aria-label="A handler starts a job that runs in a second instance and reports back">
  <title>Job flow between the handler and the job instance</title>
  <defs>

      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="10" y="50" width="110" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="65" y="68" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Plugin handler</text>
  <text x="65" y="84" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">server instance</text>
  <rect x="270" y="50" width="120" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="330" y="68" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Job instance</text>
  <text x="330" y="84" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">run(kind, input)</text>
  <line x1="120" y1="72" x2="268" y2="72" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#job-arrow)"/>
  <text x="195" y="64" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">jobs.start</text>
  <line x1="268" y1="104" x2="120" y2="104" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#job-arrow)"/>
  <text x="195" y="122" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">job-progress</text>
  <text x="195" y="138" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">request-completed</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The handler starts the job and receives progress and completion as events. It never runs the job code itself.</figcaption>
</figure>

A job instance has three rules that differ from the plugin's own instance:

- It is never activated. `activate` does not run, and the job has no event handler.
- It has the grants of its side. It may call `log`, `clock`, `codec`, `fs`, `http`, `process`, `inference`, `storage.get`, `storage.keys`, `report-progress`, `is-cancelled` and `wait-request`. Every other import, including `jobs.start`, returns `unsupported`. Imports without a result do nothing.
- It never shares memory with the instance that started it. The host keeps a pool of job instances per plugin, at most `concurrent_jobs`, and reuses them between jobs of that plugin.

The host runs jobs on the session job worker bank. The bank has `min(4, cores / 2)` threads, and at least one. Jobs beyond the concurrency limit wait in the queue.

## Example: a job

**Rust**

This server plugin starts an import job when a command runs. The job parses the bytes in chunks and reports progress after each chunk. The `run` export and the handler share one `#[ilium_plugin]` struct.

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{jobs, log::{self, Level}};

const PARSE_KIND: &str = "parse-world";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server", exports = ["job-runner"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct WorldImporter;

impl Handler for WorldImporter {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::CommandInvoked(command) = event else { continue };
            if command.command != "com.example.worlds/import" { continue; }
            // Replace with the bytes of the saved world file, read with fs::read_all first.
            let world_bytes: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
            task::spawn(async move {
                match jobs::start(PARSE_KIND.into(), world_bytes).await {
                    Ok(output) => {
                        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("imported {} bytes", output.len()))
                    }
                    Err(error) => {
                        log::log(Level::Error, &format!("import failed: {}", error.message))
                    }
                }
            });
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl JobRunner for WorldImporter {
    fn run(&mut self, kind: String, input: Vec<u8>) -> Result<Vec<u8>, PluginError> {
        if kind != PARSE_KIND {
            return Err(PluginError {
                code: ErrorCode::InvalidArgument,
                message: format!("unknown job kind {kind}"),
                retry_after_ms: None,
            });
        }
        let chunk_size = input.len().div_ceil(100).max(1);
        let chunks: Vec<&[u8]> = input.chunks(chunk_size).collect();
        let mut output = Vec::new();
        for (index, chunk) in chunks.iter().enumerate() {
            if jobs::is_cancelled() {
                return Err(PluginError {
                    code: ErrorCode::Cancelled,
                    message: "stopped".into(),
                    retry_after_ms: None,
                });
            }
            output.extend(parse_chunk(chunk));
            jobs::report_progress((index + 1) as f32 * 100.0 / chunks.len() as f32);
        }
        Ok(output)
    }
}

// The parser for one chunk of the world file. This example copies the bytes.
fn parse_chunk(chunk: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    chunk.to_vec()
}
```

The manifest for this example lists `"exports": ["job-runner"]` and `"jobs.run"` as shown in the declaration section.

**TypeScript**

This server plugin keeps the request id of its running job, so a second command can cancel it. It reads the output with `takeOutput` when the completion event arrives. The raw `startRequest` form is used because the completion is handled in `onEvents`, not in an awaited call.

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import {
  cancel, isCancelled, reportProgress, startRequest, takeOutput,
} from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/jobs';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const PARSE_KIND = 'parse-world';
let activeJob: bigint | undefined;

// Replace with the real parser for one part of the world file. This example copies the bytes.
function parseChunk(chunk: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
  return chunk.slice();
}

function concatenate(parts: Uint8Array[]): Uint8Array {
  const output = new Uint8Array(parts.reduce((sum, part) => sum + part.length, 0));
  let offset = 0;
  for (const part of parts) {
    output.set(part, offset);
    offset += part.length;
  }
  return output;
}

export const { lifecycle, handler, jobRunner } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate() {},
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === 'com.example.worlds/import') {
        // Replace the empty input with the bytes of the saved world file.
        activeJob = startRequest(PARSE_KIND, new Uint8Array(0));
      }
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === 'com.example.worlds/cancel') {
        if (activeJob !== undefined) cancel(activeJob);
      }
      if (event.tag === 'request-completed' && event.val.request.tag === 'call'
        && event.val.request.val === activeJob) {
        if (event.val.outcome.tag === 'ok' && activeJob !== undefined) {
          log('info', `parsed ${takeOutput(activeJob)?.length ?? 0} bytes`);
        } else {
          log('info', `import ended with ${event.val.outcome.tag}`);
        }
        activeJob = undefined;
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
  run(kind: string, input: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
    if (kind !== PARSE_KIND) {
      throw new PluginError('invalid-argument', `unknown job kind ${kind}`);
    }
    const chunkSize = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(input.length / 100));
    const chunkCount = Math.ceil(input.length / chunkSize);
    const parts: Uint8Array[] = [];
    for (let index = 0; index < chunkCount; index += 1) {
      if (isCancelled()) {
        throw new PluginError('cancelled', 'job stopped');
      }
      const start = index * chunkSize;
      parts.push(parseChunk(input.subarray(start, start + chunkSize)));
      reportProgress(((index + 1) * 100) / chunkCount);
    }
    return concatenate(parts);
  },
});
```

Both examples follow the same job loop: check for cancellation before each chunk, do the work, then report the percentage. A loop that skips the cancellation check keeps running after the user has cancelled, until the deadline stops it.

## Other long-running work

A job is for CPU work in the plugin's own sandbox. Three further surfaces cover other kinds of long work.

| Work | Use | Grant | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| A program that keeps running and prints output | `process.spawn` with a `child` handle | `process.long-lived` and `process.run:<program>`, high risk | `children`, 2 by default; 16 per session (`session_processes`), shared by `process.run` (`busy`) and `process.spawn` (`quota-exceeded`) |
| A response that arrives in pieces (SSE, NDJSON) | `http.stream` | `http:<host-pattern>` | `http_streams`, 4 by default, 64 session wide |
| Work at a later time that must survive a restart | `timers.at(epoch, name)` durable timer | None | `durable_timers`, 64 by default |

Spawned output arrives as `child-output` events, whole lines when `line-mode` is set, and the end as `child-exited`. Dropping the handle, or stopping the plugin, ends the child with SIGTERM and then SIGKILL after 2 s. A durable timer fires as `durable-timer-fired` with `late-by-millis`. If Ilium was not running at the due time, it fires once after the next activation. The same name replaces an earlier timer.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{process, timers};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

// Grants: process.long-lived and process.run:ffmpeg on the server side.
pub fn start_encode(spec: ProcessSpec) -> Result<Child, PluginError> {
    process::spawn(SpawnSpec { process: spec, stdin_open: false, line_mode: true })
}

// Run the nightly cleanup at the given time, even if Ilium restarts before then.
pub fn schedule_cleanup(due_epoch_millis: u64) -> Result<TimerId, PluginError> {
    timers::at(due_epoch_millis, "nightly-cleanup")
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { spawn } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/process';
import { at } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/timers';

// Grants: process.long-lived and process.run:ffmpeg on the server side.
export function startEncode(spec: ProcessSpec) {
  return spawn({ process: spec, stdinOpen: false, lineMode: true });
}

// Run the nightly cleanup at the given time, even if Ilium restarts before then.
export function scheduleCleanup(dueEpochMillis: bigint) {
  return at(dueEpochMillis, 'nightly-cleanup');
}
```

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Encode ───────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ ffmpeg ………………………………………………………………………………………………… <span class="t-ok">▶ RUNNING</span>   │
│ <span class="t-dim">frame= 1204 fps=48 q=28.0 size= 5120kB</span>                   │
│ <span class="t-dim">child-exited status 0</span>  <span class="t-ok">✓ DONE</span>                            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A spawned child process shown as a leader row, with its last output line and its exit.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Progress

While a job runs, the plugin receives `job-progress` events. In Rust the event is `Event::JobProgress(JobProgressEvent { request_id, percent })`. In TypeScript it is `{ tag: 'job-progress', val: { requestId, percent } }`. Progress events are coalesced by job: when several arrive before the handler runs, only the newest percentage remains, at the position of its newest occurrence. A fast job therefore does not flood the event queue.

The host shows no job progress by itself. The plugin draws it. A panel uses a `progress-row` (state, percentage and bar in one row), a `gauge` or a `line-gauge` widget (see [data display widgets](/pages/widgets-data-display/)), and the plugin updates the tree with `ui.invalidate` when the percentage changes. Keep updates under the 10 per second widget rate.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Import: Survival world 2026-10-02 ────────────────╮
│ <span class="t-ok">▶ RUNNING</span>  42%  <span class="t-hi">█████████████</span><span class="t-dim">░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░</span>           │
│ <span class="t-dim">Parsing chunk 42 of 100 in the world file.</span>               │
│ <span class="t-hi">⠋</span> Working   <span class="t-dim">Stop at any time.</span>                            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A progress row and a spinner while a world file is imported in the background.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Cancellation

Cancellation has two sides. The plugin calls `cancel` with the request id, and the job sees the request through `is-cancelled`. The job can stop at its next check, but the outcome does not depend on what the job returns:

- Once `cancel` is requested, the outcome is `cancelled` even if `run` returns output. The output is dropped, so `take-output` returns `none`.
- A queued job that is cancelled before it starts never runs.
- Cancelling a job that has already completed does nothing.

The plugin stops, is disabled or is uninstalled: its pending jobs complete as `cancelled`. Losing the `jobs.run` grant is different. The authorization epoch changes, and the job completes as `failed(revoked)`. A job that ends this way never counts toward the restart rule.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Import: Survival world 2026-10-02 ────────────────╮
│ <span class="t-warn">! cancelled</span>  58%  <span class="t-warn">███████████████████</span><span class="t-dim">░░░░░░░░░░░</span>         │
│ <span class="t-dim">Stopped at chunk 58 of 100. Nothing imported.</span>            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The same import panel after the user cancels the job at 58 percent.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Outcomes and errors

A job completes once, and a `request-completed` event carries the outcome. The outcome is `ok`, `cancelled` or `failed(code)`. The job takes its output with `take-output`. The SDK wrapper in `jobs::start` returns the output directly, or the error as `Err`.

| Situation | Outcome or error |
|---|---|
| Job returns output within limits | `ok`; take the output |
| CPU or wall-clock deadline passed | `failed(timed-out)` |
| Memory limit passed | `failed(quota-exceeded)` |
| Output over `job_io_mib` | `failed(invalid-argument)` |
| `run` returns a `plugin-error` | `failed`, carrying that error's code and message |
| Trap in the job instance | `failed(internal)`, with the trap text |
| Cancel requested, or the plugin stops | `cancelled` |
| Grant revoked during the job | `failed(revoked)` |
| Kind not declared, or input over the job input limit | `invalid-argument` at the start call |
| Job queue full | `busy` at the start call |
| CPU budget of the quota group spent | `quota-exceeded` at the start call, with `retry-after-ms` |
| `wait-request` outside `run` | `unsupported` |
| `take-output` after the 30 s hold, a second take, or an unknown id | `none` |

Every failed job is reported to the plugin and never counts toward the restart rule. A trap in the plugin's own instance, by contrast, counts. See [errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/) for the restart and disable rule.

<div class="warn">
<p>A job cannot start another job. <code>jobs.start</code> returns <code>unsupported</code> inside <code>run</code>. Start the second job from the plugin's own instance, after the first one completes.</p>
</div>

## What the user sees

A job itself is invisible. The user sees what the plugin draws: a progress gauge, a status line or a notification when the job completes. A cancelled job shows the state the plugin sets, because the plugin receives the `cancelled` outcome. A failed job appears only if the plugin reports it, so a plugin that wants the user to see a failure must draw or notify it.

## See also

- [Requests and outcomes](/pages/requests-and-outcomes/)
- [API: jobs](/pages/api-jobs/)
- [Capability: jobs.run](/pages/capability-jobs-run/)
- [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/)
- [Services](/pages/services/)
- [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/)

API version checked: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Capabilities and grants

## Capabilities and grants

A plugin can use only the parts of the host that it asks for. It lists the capabilities it needs in
its manifest, one list per side. The user grants them when a package is installed or first
activated. For bundled plugins the kernel grants everything up to the manifest ceiling, except the
high-risk capabilities.

This page covers the grant syntax, the full capability surface, the tiers and the review dialog,
what happens to an import that is granted, declined or never requested, the always-granted set,
revocation and the error codes.

## You will need

- A manifest with a `capabilities` object. See [Packages and manifests](/pages/packages/).
- The server, client and scene sides. See [Worlds and sides](/pages/worlds-and-sides/).
- The Rust SDK (`ilium-plugin-sdk`) or the TypeScript SDK (`@ilium/plugin-sdk`). Both expose the
  granted list in the activation context. See [Rust SDK](/pages/rust-sdk/) and
  [TypeScript SDK](/pages/typescript-sdk/).

## Grant syntax

A grant is a name, optionally followed by a colon and an argument. The first colon separates the
name from the argument. Later colons belong to the argument.

```text
grant    = name [ ":" argument ]
name     = segment *( "." segment )      segment = [a-z][a-z0-9-]*
argument = 1*char                         everything after the first colon
```

The grants `commands.invoke`, `fs.read`, `fs.write`, `fs.watch`, `http`, `process.run`,
`services.use`, `services.provide`, `messages.peer`, `topics.subscribe` and `http-api.route` require
an argument. Every other grant takes no argument, and `tree.read:x` is a manifest error. A service
name has no version. The grant `services.use:ilium:inference/provider` has the name
`services.use` and the argument `ilium:inference/provider`.

The manifest holds one list per side under `capabilities`. The scene side uses the key `scene`:

```json
"capabilities": {
  "server": ["tree.read", "fs.read:project", "http:api.example.com", "http:*.example.org"],
  "client": ["ui.panels", "panes.read"],
  "scene": []
}
```

Grants are per side. A `server` grant does not apply to the `client` side, and each side keeps its
own list.

## Capability surface

Each grant below unlocks the functions or events named in the API specification. **H** marks a
high-risk grant. It always needs an explicit grant, even for a T1 bundled plugin.

Sides: S is the server world, C is the client world and A is the animation (scene) world. Each page link leads to the full description of the grant.

### Extended grants

The grants below cover the wider kernel surface: tree restructuring, pane lifecycle, terminal and agent data, chrome, sessions, inference and process control. Nine of them are high risk and always need an explicit grant, even for a T1 bundled plugin: `terminal.history`, `terminal.input-lock`, `terminal.raw-input`, `panes.lifecycle`, `tree.restructure`, `sessions.cross`, `process.long-lived`, `agent.transcript` and `settings.read-kernel:api`. The grant `gpu.kernels` is unstable and exists only in development builds. Both `extensions.*` grants take exactly one global point id and refuse wildcards (`manifest.grant-wildcard`). `extensions.contribute` is high risk only for a point that declares `risk: "high"`; the review dialog then shows a warning. Four argument forms are worth knowing: `http:setting:<key>` (the host comes from one of the plugin's own settings, and the user confirms a changed host before the first request), `fs.read:agent-sessions:gemini` with `fs.read:agent-config:gemini`, `fs.read:agent-config:antigravity`, and `settings.read-kernel:<kernel-tab-id>` (argument required, no wildcard).

### Wildcards and scopes

- `commands.invoke:<pattern>` takes an exact global id, `<plugin-id>/*` for all commands of one
  plugin, or a bare `*` for all commands (H). A `*` never crosses `/`.
- `http:<host>` takes an exact host, `*.<domain>` for any subdomain at any depth (not the bare
  domain), and an optional port. `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` allow plain HTTP. A bare `*`
  is refused.
- `topics.subscribe:<pattern>` takes an exact topic, `<prefix>/*` or a bare `*` (H).
- `process.run:*` is refused with `manifest.grant-wildcard`. `process.run:sh` is valid and H.
- `messages.peer:<plugin-id>` takes one exact plugin id and no wildcard.
- `extensions.provide` and `extensions.contribute` take one exact `<plugin-id>/<point>` and no wildcard. There is no `extensions.contribute-any`. List each point.

File scopes are the argument of `fs.read`, `fs.write` and `fs.watch`:

- `project` is the project folder. It excludes the project's `.ilium` folder.
- `worktrees` is the project's Git worktrees. `fs.write:worktrees` is H.
- `picked` is each path the user chose in `fs.pick`.
- `data` and `cache` are the plugin's own folders. Their read and write grants are always granted.
- `package` is the plugin's own package. It is always readable and never watchable.
- `agent-sessions:<agent>` holds transcripts and is H. It is read only.
- `agent-config:<agent>` holds agent configuration. Writes are H.
- `minecraft-saves` is the platform's saves folder.
- `path:<template>` is a path template. It starts with a placeholder (`{home}`, `{config}`,
  `{data}`, `{cache}`, `{project}`, `{worktrees}`) or with a literal absolute path. A literal path
  is always H. The template ends with a name or with `/**`. A `*` anywhere else is refused.

## Tiers and the review dialog

The kernel grants capabilities differently depending on the tier of the package.

| Tier | Source | Grants |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | First-party component embedded in the release | The manifest ceiling is granted automatically, except H capabilities. |
| T2 | Package signed by a key the user trusts | The review dialog shows each capability. The user's choices are remembered. |
| T3 | Unsigned local or development package | The same review dialog, with a persistent development badge. |

Install of a T2 or T3 package shows the review dialog. The plugin installs with the grants that the
user leaves checked. H rows start unchecked. A declined row is dimmed and its grant is absent from
the granted list.

For a T1 bundled plugin, activation starts without its H capabilities. The first activation shows
one prompt per plugin, `Plugin <name> asks for: <list>`, with the buttons `Allow selected` and
`Not now`. `Not now` asks again at the next server start, at most three times, and then never
again. The user can grant the capability at any time from Settings > Plugins.

There is no prompt per call. A grant stays in force until it is revoked. The dialog below is drawn
at 72 columns for a signed notes package.

<figure>

<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Notes 0.1.0 by Example Labs (T2, signed)                                   │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Reads the workspace tree <span class="t-dim">……………………………………………………………………………………………</span> tree.read │
│ [x] Reads files in this project <span class="t-dim">……………………………………………………………………</span> fs.read:project │
│ <span class="t-warn">! [ ] Runs the program git</span> <span class="t-dim">…………………………………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-warn">process.run:git</span> │

## Declined, unrequested and granted

The kernel links each import to one of three targets. The diagram shows them side by side.

<figcaption>The same import behaves differently depending on whether the user granted it, declined
it or the manifest never requested it.</figcaption>
