# File access

## File access

A plugin reaches files only through named scopes. A scope is a directory the user has granted, such as the project folder, or a directory the plugin owns, such as its private data folder. The kernel resolves each grant to one canonical directory once. The plugin then reads and writes through paths relative to that scope, and it never learns the real path on the user's disk.

Use this page to choose a scope, read and write files in Rust or TypeScript, watch a folder for changes, take a lock on a shared file, and ask the user to choose a file with the picker. Every call listed here is in the `fs` interface of `ilium:host/fs`, version `0.1.0`.

## You will need

- A manifest with a `capabilities` object for the side that makes the call. Each file operation needs the grant for its scope. See [Capabilities and grants](/pages/capabilities/).
- The SDK for your language: `ilium_plugin_sdk` for Rust, or `@ilium/plugin-sdk` for TypeScript. See [Rust SDK](/pages/rust-sdk/) and [TypeScript SDK](/pages/typescript-sdk/).
- Familiarity with request ids and completions. Slow calls return a request id, and the result arrives later. See [Requests and outcomes](/pages/requests-and-outcomes/).

The manifest lists grants per side:

```json
"capabilities": {
  "server": ["fs.read:project", "fs.write:data", "fs.pick", "fs.read:picked"]
}
```

## Scopes

A grant names a scope, and the scope names a directory. The plugin sees each scope as a preopened directory at the path shown below. The kernel holds the real location.

| Scope | Preopen | Root | Default | Write | Watch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `package` | `/package` | Unpacked package `assets/` | Always, read only | No | No |
| `data` | `/data` | The plugin's private data directory | Always | Always | Always |
| `cache` | `/cache` | The plugin's private cache, evictable | Always | Always | Always |
| `project` | `/project` | The canonical project directory | Grant | Grant | Grant |
| `picked` | `/picked/<n>` | Each path the user chose in the picker | Grant per pick | Grant | Folders only |
| `agent-sessions:claude`, `:codex`, `:antigravity` | `/agent-sessions/<agent>` | The agent's transcript directory | Grant, high risk | Refused | Grant |
| `agent-config:claude`, `:codex` | `/agent-config/<agent>` | The agent's configuration directory | Grant, high risk | Grant, high risk | Grant |
| `minecraft-saves` | `/minecraft-saves` | The platform's saves directory | Grant | Grant | Grant |
| `worktrees` | `/worktrees` | The root set by `workspace.worktree_root` | Grant | High risk | Grant |
| `path:<template>` | `/paths/<n>` | A template, see below | Grant | Grant | Grant |

The `project` scope excludes the project's `.ilium` folder. Listing hides it, and every access returns `not-permitted`. Session snapshots are never exposed.

The `package` scope is never watchable, because the package does not change at run time.

`fs.read:<scope>` allows reads, `fs.write:<scope>` allows changes, and `fs.watch:<scope>` allows watching folders. Writes outside `data` and `cache` need an explicit user grant, even for bundled plugins.

### Path templates

A `path:<template>` grant starts with a placeholder (`{home}`, `{config}`, `{data}`, `{cache}`, `{project}` or `{worktrees}`) or with a literal absolute path. It ends with a file or folder name, which matches that item and its direct children, or with `/**`, which matches the whole subtree. A `*` anywhere else is refused at install.

- `fs.read:path:{home}/Pictures/**` reads the Pictures tree under the user's home directory, and nothing outside it.
- A literal absolute path such as `fs.read:path:/srv/logs/**` is always high risk.
- `fs.write:path:` with a literal absolute path is available to bundled plugins only.

The kernel names each `path:` grant `paths/<n>`, counting from 0 in manifest order, so the first grant appears as `/paths/0`.

## Calls

Synchronous calls return at once. Calls that need the disk, another process or the user return a request id, and the result is taken with the matching `take-*` function. The Rust and TypeScript SDKs wrap each slow call in one `async` function, so most code never touches a request id. Rust uses snake_case names, such as `read_all`, and TypeScript uses camelCase, such as `readAll`.

| Call | Kind | Result | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `roots()` | Sync | `list<tuple<string, bool>>` | Granted scopes and whether each is writable |
| `metadata(path)` | Sync | `fs-metadata` | Kind, length, modified time and read-only flag |
| `list-dir(path, max-entries)` | Sync | `list<dir-entry>` | Direct children, at most 4,096 |
| `read(path, offset, max-bytes)` | Sync | `list<u8>` | Up to 1 MiB from an offset |
| `read-all(path)` | Async | `take-bytes` | Whole file, up to 64 MiB by default |
| `scan(path, glob, max-entries)` | Async | `take-entries` | Matching entries, at most 65,536 |
| `write(path, data, mode)` | Async | `()` | Write one call of up to 16 MiB |
| `create-dir(path)` | Sync | `()` | Create a folder; an existing folder is success |
| `remove(path)` | Async | `()` | Remove a file, or a folder recursively |
| `rename(source, target)` | Async | `()` | Rename within one scope; a target file is replaced |
| `watch(path, recursive)` | Sync | `watch-id` | Start a watch on an existing folder |
| `unwatch(watch)` | Sync | none | Stop a watch; an unknown id is ignored |
| `lock(path, exclusive, timeout-millis)` | Async | `take-lock` | Take an advisory lock |
| `unlock(lock)` | Sync | none | Release a lock |
| `pick(spec)` | Async | `take-picked` | Ask the user to choose a file or folder |
| `read-with-revision(path)` | Async | `take-revisioned` | Whole file plus a revision token |
| `write-atomic(path, data, expected)` | Async | `take-written` | Write to a temporary file, then rename over the target; `expected` makes it a compare-and-swap |
| `tail(path, cursor, max-bytes)` | Sync | `tail-chunk` | New bytes after a cursor, at most 1 MiB |

The key record and enum types are:

| Type | Fields or cases |
|---|---|
| `fs-path` | `scope: string`, `path: string`, with `/` as separator and relative to the scope root |
| `fs-metadata` | `kind` (`file`, `directory`, `symlink`, `other`), `length: u64`, `modified-unix-millis`, `read-only` |
| `dir-entry` | `name: string`, `metadata: fs-metadata` |
| `write-mode` | `create-new`, `replace`, `append` |
| `pick-kind` | `open-file`, `open-directory`, `save-file` |

In Rust these types are `FsPath`, `FsMetadata`, `DirEntry`, `WriteMode` and `PickKind`, with cases
such as `WriteMode::Replace` and `PickKind::OpenFile`. In TypeScript the cases are kebab-case
strings, such as `'replace'` and `'open-file'`.

Every call that returns a request id also returns `busy` when the plugin has too many pending requests, and `quota-exceeded` when its CPU budget is spent.

## Synchronous reads and std::fs

Synchronous code works against the preopens, so a Rust or JavaScript plugin can use the standard library directly for small reads. No Ilium call is needed. The path is the preopen, not the path on disk.

```rust
// Needs the grant fs.read:project in the manifest.
// The path is the preopen, not the path on the user's disk.
let readme_bytes = std::fs::read("/project/README.md")?;
```

Paths that leave the scope through `..` or through a symbolic link are refused with `not-permitted`. A symbolic link is reported as kind `symlink` by `metadata` and `list-dir`, and it is not followed. Other operations follow a link only when its target stays inside the same scope root.

## Examples

### Read a project file and write a summary

This example reads a file from the project and writes a summary to the plugin's data folder. It needs `fs.read:project` and `fs.write:data`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::fs::{self, WriteMode};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

// Manifest grants: fs.read:project and fs.write:data on the server side.
pub async fn save_readme_size() -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let readme = FsPath { scope: "project".into(), path: "README.md".into() };
    let bytes = fs::read_all(readme).await?;

    // create_dir is synchronous and succeeds when the folder already exists.
    fs::create_dir(FsPath { scope: "data".into(), path: "reports".into() })?;

    let summary = format!("README.md is {} bytes\n", bytes.len());
    let target = FsPath { scope: "data".into(), path: "reports/readme-size.txt".into() };
    fs::write(target, summary.into_bytes(), WriteMode::Replace).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { createDir, readAll, write } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/fs';

// Manifest grants: fs.read:project and fs.write:data on the server side.
export async function saveReadmeSize(): Promise<void> {
  const bytes = await readAll({ scope: 'project', path: 'README.md' });
  createDir({ scope: 'data', path: 'reports' });
  const summary = new TextEncoder().encode(`README.md is ${bytes.length} bytes\n`);
  await write({ scope: 'data', path: 'reports/readme-size.txt' }, summary, 'replace');
}
```

### Append to a shared file under a lock

This example appends one line to a file that another process also writes. It takes an exclusive
lock and waits at most 2 seconds. It releases the lock on both the success and the error path.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::fs::{self, WriteMode};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

pub async fn append_journal_line(line: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let journal = FsPath { scope: "data".into(), path: "journal.log".into() };
    let lock = fs::lock(journal.clone(), true, 2_000).await?;
    let result = fs::write(journal, format!("{line}\n").into_bytes(), WriteMode::Append).await;
    fs::unlock(lock);
    result
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { lock, unlock, write } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/fs';

export async function appendJournalLine(line: string): Promise<void> {
  const journal = { scope: 'data', path: 'journal.log' };
  const held = await lock(journal, true, 2_000);
  try {
    await write(journal, new TextEncoder().encode(`${line}\n`), 'append');
  } finally {
    unlock(held);
  }
}
```

### Pick a note and count its headings

This example asks the user to choose a Markdown file, reads it, and writes the count to the data
folder. It needs `fs.pick`, `fs.read:picked` and `fs.write:data`.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { pick, readAll, write } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/fs';

// Manifest grants: fs.pick, fs.read:picked and fs.write:data on the server side.
export async function countHeadings(): Promise<number> {
  const chosen = await pick({
    kind: 'open-file',
    title: 'Choose a Markdown note',
    extensions: ['md'],
  });
  const text = new TextDecoder().decode(await readAll(chosen));
  const headings = text.split('\n').filter((line) => line.startsWith('#')).length;
  const report = new TextEncoder().encode(`headings: ${headings}\n`);
  await write({ scope: 'data', path: 'heading-count.txt' }, report, 'replace');
  return headings;
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::fs::{self, PickKind, PickSpec, WriteMode};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

// Manifest grants: fs.pick, fs.read:picked and fs.write:data on the server side.
pub async fn count_headings() -> Result<usize, PluginError> {
    let chosen = fs::pick(PickSpec {
        kind: PickKind::OpenFile,
        title: "Choose a Markdown note".into(),
        extensions: vec!["md".into()],
    })
    .await?;
    let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(&fs::read_all(chosen).await?).into_owned();
    let headings = text.lines().filter(|line| line.starts_with('#')).count();
    let report = FsPath { scope: "data".into(), path: "heading-count.txt".into() };
    fs::write(report, format!("headings: {headings}\n").into_bytes(), WriteMode::Replace).await?;
    Ok(headings)
}
```

## Writes

A write takes one of three modes.

- `create-new` creates the file. If the file exists, the call completes as `failed(conflict)`.
- `replace` writes the whole file atomically. The kernel writes a temporary sibling file and then renames it over the target.
- `append` adds the data to the end of the file. It creates the file if it is missing.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 110" role="img" aria-label="Atomic replace through a temporary sibling">

    </marker>
  </defs>

  <text x="56" y="66" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">mode: replace</text>
  <line x1="106" y1="56" x2="130" y2="56" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#fa-arrow)"/>
  <rect x="130" y="36" width="122" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>

  <line x1="252" y1="56" x2="294" y2="56" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#fa-arrow)"/>
  <text x="273" y="49" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">rename</text>

  <text x="344" y="66" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">notes.md</text>
  <text x="6" y="100" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">A reader sees the old file or the new file, never half of one.</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>A replace write creates a temporary sibling, then renames it over the target in one step.</figcaption>
</figure>

A `write` with `replace` on a path that names an existing folder completes as `failed(conflict)`. A `write` whose parent folder is missing completes as `not-found`. Create the folder with `create-dir` first.

A write outside `data` and `cache` is logged at level info, with the scope, path, operation and byte count. To write more than 16 MiB, split the data into `append` calls, or let a [background job](/pages/background-jobs/) produce the file.

## Reading large files and scans

`read-all` returns the whole file when it is 64 MiB or smaller. A larger file completes as `failed(quota-exceeded)`. Read a large file in pieces with the synchronous `read` call, which returns at most 1 MiB per call. A `read` at or past the end of the file returns an empty list, not an error.

`scan` matches a glob against paths relative to the scope root. `*` matches within one segment, a whole `**` segment matches any depth, and `?` matches one character. Braces and character classes are not supported. Matches are sorted by path bytes, and dotfiles are included. More matches than `max-entries` complete as `failed(quota-exceeded)`, never as a silent truncation.

## Revisions, atomic writes and tailing

Two plugins, or a plugin and an agent CLI, often share one file. Use `read-with-revision` to read the bytes and a revision token together. The token is a hash of the content, the size and the modification time. Pass it as `expected` to `write-atomic`: the host writes a temporary file in the same directory and renames it over the target, so a reader never sees a half-written file. If the file changed since the read, the call fails with `conflict` and the plugin reads again. With `expected` set to none, the call creates the file and fails with `conflict` when it exists.

`tail` reads what a growing file gained. The plugin keeps the `cursor` from the last chunk. When the chunk has `truncated: true`, the file shrank or was replaced, and the next read restarts at 0. One call returns at most 1 MiB.

Further scopes are `agent-sessions:gemini`, `agent-config:gemini` and `agent-config:antigravity`, with the same risk as the Claude and Codex ones.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭ Write ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ <span class="t-hi">read-with-revision</span>   counter.txt  <span class="t-dim">rev 9f2c</span>                 │
│ <span class="t-dim">another writer saves the file: rev 71ab</span>                    │
│ <span class="t-hi">write-atomic</span>         expected 9f2c                         │
│ <span class="t-err">✗ failed: conflict</span>  <span class="t-dim">read again and retry</span>                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A compare-and-swap write that loses to another writer and retries.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::fs;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

pub async fn bump_counter() -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let path = FsPath { scope: "data".into(), path: "counter.txt".into() };
    for _attempt in 0..3 {
        let current = fs::read_with_revision(path.clone()).await?;
        let value: u64 = String::from_utf8_lossy(&current.bytes).trim().parse().unwrap_or(0);
        let next = format!("{}\n", value + 1).into_bytes();
        match fs::write_atomic(path.clone(), next, Some(current.revision)).await {
            Ok(_) => return Ok(()),
            Err(error) if error.code == ErrorCode::Conflict => continue,
            Err(error) => return Err(error),
        }
    }
    Err(PluginError::new(ErrorCode::Conflict, "the counter kept changing"))
}

pub fn read_new_log_bytes(path: FsPath, cursor: u64) -> Result<(Vec<u8>, u64), PluginError> {
    let chunk = fs::tail(path, cursor, 65_536)?;
    let next = if chunk.truncated { 0 } else { chunk.cursor };
    Ok((chunk.bytes, next))
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { readWithRevision, tail, writeAtomic } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/fs';

export async function bumpCounter(): Promise<void> {
  const path = { scope: 'data', path: 'counter.txt' };
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const current = await readWithRevision(path);
    const value = Number.parseInt(new TextDecoder().decode(current.bytes).trim(), 10) || 0;
    try {
      await writeAtomic(path, new TextEncoder().encode(`${value + 1}\n`), current.revision);
      return;
    } catch (error) {
      if ((error as { code?: string }).code !== 'conflict') throw error;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('the counter kept changing');
}

export function readNewLogBytes(path: { scope: string; path: string }, cursor: bigint) {
  const chunk = tail(path, cursor, 65_536);
  return { bytes: chunk.bytes, next: chunk.truncated ? 0n : chunk.cursor };
}
```

## Watching folders

`watch(path, recursive)` takes an existing folder. A file gives `invalid-argument`, a missing path gives `not-found`, and a symbolic link gives `not-permitted`. Changes arrive as `fs-changed` events, and each event is a record with the `watch` id and a list of `paths`.

- The host waits 200 ms after the first change and sends one event for all changes in that time. A watch sends at most five events per second.
- An event lists at most 1,024 paths. A larger batch becomes one event that lists only the watched path, and the plugin must read that folder again.
- A non-recursive watch reports only the direct children. A recursive watch reports every changed path below the folder. A rename lists the old and the new path.
- A plugin may hold 64 watches. A recursive watch counts once.
- Watch ids do not survive a restart. Watch again in `activate`.

The event goes only to the instance that made the watch call. A watch ends when its instance deactivates or restarts, when the plugin is disabled, or when it loses the grant. When the watched folder is removed or renamed, one event lists the watched path, and the watch then ends.

## Locks

A lock coordinates plugins with each other, and with any program that takes the same lock. The lock is advisory. A program that does not take the lock is not blocked. The file does not need to exist.

- `exclusive: true` waits behind any other holder. `exclusive: false` shares the lock with other shared holders.
- A held lock that is still held when `timeout-millis` ends completes as `timed-out`.
- A request with timeout `0` on a held lock returns `conflict` at once.
- Locks are keyed by the resolved path. They are released when the plugin is deactivated, disabled, or loses the grant.

## The file picker

A plugin cannot choose a file itself. It calls `pick` with the `fs.pick` grant, and the host draws a modal picker. The user chooses the path, and the plugin receives an `fs-path` in the `picked/<n>` scope. Reading the result needs `fs.read:picked`, and saving to it needs `fs.write:picked`. Without the read or write grant, `fs.pick` fails the install with `manifest.grant-dependency`.

| Kind | Result | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `open-file` | `picked/<n>` with the file path | Read it with `fs.read:picked` |
| `open-directory` | `picked/<n>` with path `""` | The folder itself; paths inside it are relative to it |
| `save-file` | `picked/<n>` with path `""` | The file may not exist yet; `write` needs `fs.write:picked` |

The `extensions` list is written in lower case without a dot. It matches case-insensitively, and an empty list allows every file.

The picker accepts Enter to open a folder or confirm, Backspace to go to the parent folder, Tab to move between the input, the list and the buttons, Ctrl+H to show hidden files, and Escape to cancel. A cancelled pick fails with `cancelled`. A second pick while a picker is open fails at once with `busy`, and no second dialog opens.

Picked paths are recorded with the plugin's grants and survive restarts. The plugin keeps up to 64 picked paths. When it picks a 65th, the oldest is forgotten. The `<n>` counter never repeats, so a picked scope keeps its name until its grant is revoked.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Open file ────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ <span class="t-dim">Notes wants a file</span>                                       │
│ Folder ……………………………………………………… /home/arthur/dev/app/docs   │
│   ..                                                     │
│   <span class="t-hi">meeting-2026-10-09.md</span>                                  │
│   release-checklist.md                                   │
│   plan.md                                                │
│ Filter ………………………………………………………………………………………………………………… .md   │
│ <span class="t-dim">Enter open · Backspace parent · Tab move · Esc cancel</span>    │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The host file picker. The folder is an example. The chosen file is shared with the plugin until the user revokes it.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Scope resolution

A grant becomes a preopen once. The kernel does this work through the platform layer, and the plugin never sees a path it was not granted.

## Errors

Every call returns a plugin error with one of these codes. The table lists the codes beyond the universal `not-permitted`, `revoked` and `internal`.

| Call | Synchronous errors | Completion errors |
|---|---|---|
| `metadata`, `list-dir`, `read` | `not-found`, `invalid-argument` (bad path, limits exceeded, wrong kind), `io` | None |
| `read-all` | `invalid-argument` (bad path) | `not-found`, `io`, `quota-exceeded` (over 64 MiB) |
| `scan` | `invalid-argument` (bad path or glob, `max-entries` over 65,536) | `not-found`, `io`, `quota-exceeded` |
| `write` | `invalid-argument` (bad path, over 16 MiB) | `conflict` (`create-new` found a file, or a lock holds it), `not-found`, `quota-exceeded`, `io` |
| `create-dir` | `conflict` (a file has that name), `not-found`, `io` | None |
| `remove` | `invalid-argument` (scope root) | `not-found`, `conflict` (lock), `io` |
| `rename` | `invalid-argument` (two different scopes) | `not-found`, `conflict` (target is a non-empty folder or locked), `io` |
| `watch` | `not-found`, `invalid-argument` (not watchable), `quota-exceeded` (64 watches) | None |
| `lock` | `invalid-argument` (bad path) | `conflict` (held and timeout 0), `timed-out`, `not-found` |
| `pick` | `busy` (a picker is already open) | `cancelled` when the user cancels |

## What the user sees

- High-risk scopes appear in the review dialog unchecked, and the user must check each one. See [Capabilities and grants](/pages/capabilities/).
- A call refused for a missing or declined grant writes one refusal line to the plugin log, with the capability, the call and the reason:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs notes
<span class="t-err">refusal</span> capability=fs.read:project function=fs.read reason=declined
<span class="t-ok">info</span>    write scope=project path=docs/notes.md op=replace bytes=2048
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The fields are the ones the plugin log records, in an example layout.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Edge cases

- An empty `path` names the scope root. `write` and `remove` refuse it at once, with `invalid-argument`. On a `picked/<n>` scope, an empty path names the picked item itself.
- A declined grant makes every call on that scope return `not-permitted`. A revoked grant ends the plugin's locks and watches.

## Rules

- Ask for the narrowest scope. Prefer a path template to the whole project when only one folder is needed.
- Write your own state to `data`, and use the picker when the user has to choose a file.
- Use `replace` for any file that another reader must never see half-written.
- Take a lock on any file another process writes, and release it on every path.

# Layout constraints

## Layout constraints

A plugin never works out where a widget goes. It describes the sizes it wants with constraints, and the host runs the solver of ratatui 0.29. This page gives the constraint kinds, the flex, spacing and margin rules, the order in which the solver works, and how a plugin reads the space it is given. It shows six layouts with renders drawn at 60 columns, the layout parts of other widgets (`split`, `scroll-view`, `popup`, `dialog` and table columns), the errors a layout can raise, and a responsive view in Rust and in TypeScript.

## You will need

- Grants: none for the layout widget itself. The view that holds it needs `ui.panels` for a panel ([Panels](/pages/capability-ui-panels/)) or `panes.provide-kind` for a basic pane ([Basic panes](/pages/capability-panes-provide-kind/)).
- A language: Rust with the `ilium-plugin-sdk` crate, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk` (built with Bun 1.2 or later).
- Reading: [The UI model](/pages/ui-model/) for the flat tree and the `render` export, and [Retained mode](/pages/retained-mode/) for when a view is redrawn.

## The layout widget

A `layout` widget has a direction, a list of constraints, a flex rule, a spacing rule and a margin. It has one child for each constraint, in the same order: the child at index 0 gets the first segment, the child at index 1 the second, and so on. A different number of children and constraints makes the tree invalid.

| Prop | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `direction` | `horizontal` or `vertical` | required | The axis that the segments divide. |
| `constraints` | `list<constraint>` | required | One constraint for each child. |
| `flex` | `flex` | `start` | Where the space that no segment uses goes. |
| `spacing` | `spacing` | `space(0)` | A gap between segments, or an overlap. |
| `margin` | `margin` | 0 by 0 | Cells removed from the area before the segments are placed. |

The constraint kinds follow ratatui:

| Constraint | Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `length` | `u16` | An exact number of cells. |
| `min` | `u16` | A segment at least this large. |
| `max` | `u16` | A segment at most this large. |
| `percentage` | `u16` | A share of the available space, in per cent. |
| `ratio` | `tuple<u32, u32>` | A fraction of the available space: numerator and denominator. The denominator must not be 0. |
| `fill` | `u16` | A weight. Fill segments share the space that is left, in proportion to their weights. |

**Rust**

```rust
// ilium_plugin_sdk::types::layout::{Constraint, Direction, Flex, Spacing, Margin}
let row = tree
    .layout(Direction::Horizontal, [
        Constraint::Length(20),          // exactly 20 cells
        Constraint::Min(30),             // at least 30
        Constraint::Max(10),             // at most 10
        Constraint::Percentage(25),      // 25 % of the area
        Constraint::Ratio(1, 3),         // one third
        Constraint::Fill(2),             // twice the weight of Fill(1)
    ])
    .flex(Flex::SpaceBetween)
    .spacing(Spacing::Space(1))
    .margin(Margin { horizontal: 1, vertical: 0 });
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { layout, length, fill } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/ui/build';

const row = layout({
  direction: 'horizontal',
  constraints: [
    length(20),                        // exactly 20 cells
    { tag: 'min', val: 30 },           // at least 30
    { tag: 'max', val: 10 },           // at most 10
    { tag: 'percentage', val: 25 },    // 25 % of the area
    { tag: 'ratio', val: [1, 3] },     // one third
    fill(2),                           // twice the weight of fill(1)
  ],
  flex: 'space-between',
  spacing: { tag: 'space', val: 1 },
  margin: { horizontal: 1, vertical: 0 },
}, children);
```

The flex rule decides where leftover space goes when no segment takes it:

| Flex | Effect |
|---|---|
| `legacy` | The last segment takes the leftover space, as in ratatui's legacy rule. |
| `start` | Segments pack at the start. The leftover space goes at the end. |
| `end` | Segments pack at the end. |
| `center` | Segments are centred, with equal space on each side. |
| `space-between` | The leftover space is split into equal gaps between segments. The first and last segments sit at the edges. |
| `space-around` | Each segment has equal space on both sides. The edges get half a gap. |
| `space-evenly` | Every gap, including the edges, is the same size. |

The spacing rule is either `space(n)`, which puts `n` cells between segments, or `overlap(n)`, which lets neighbouring segments share `n` cells. `margin` takes a `horizontal` and a `vertical` count and removes that many cells on each side of the area before anything else happens. The solver is ratatui 0.29 `Layout::split`, with these rules pinned.

- The margin is applied first. `percentage` and `ratio` are relative to the area after the margin, before spacing.
- A `ratio` above 1 is clamped to 1.
- `fill(0)` gets 0 cells unless every constraint is `fill(0)`.
- The SDK builders default `flex` to `start`. The wire default, an absent field, is `legacy`.
- The segments plus gaps never exceed the area. With `legacy` flex they fill it exactly.

Three numeric examples serve as goldens. Each is solved on a row.

| Area | Constraints | Flex | Segment widths |
|---|---|---|---|
| 80 | `length(20)`, `fill(1)`, `percentage(25)` | `start` | 20, 40, 20 |
| 60 | `percentage(25)`, `ratio(1, 3)`, `fill(1)` | `start` | 15, 20, 25 |
| 60 | `length(8)`, `length(8)`, `length(8)` | `space-between` | 8, 8, 8 with gaps of 18 |

## How the solver divides one row

The solver works in this order. It removes the margin from the area. It sizes the segments with `length`, `min`, `max`, `percentage` and `ratio`. It divides the remaining cells among the `fill` segments by weight. Then it places any space left over according to `flex`. When the segments cannot all fit, ratatui's priority rules apply and trailing segments shrink; a segment that gets 0 cells draws nothing.

<figure>

  <defs>

    </marker>
  </defs>

A plugin never sees a rectangle. When it needs a size, it reads the `area` argument of `render`, or the size of a basic pane (see "Reading the area" below).

  │fill(1)                  │  │fill(1)                  │
  │                         │  │                         │
  │                         │  │                         │
  ╰─────────────────────────╯  ╰─────────────────────────╯

</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 60 columns and 7 rows. Margin 2 by 1 and <code>space(2)</code>. The blank first and last rows and the two blank columns at each side are the margin.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Overlap

`overlap(1)` lets two neighbours share one cell. Nodes paint in pre-order, so a later sibling overdraws an earlier one cell by cell. Where bordered blocks share cells, the host uses the box-drawing merge rule. In a horizontal layout the shared vertical edge becomes `┬` at the top and `┴` at the bottom. In a vertical layout the shared horizontal edge becomes `├` at the left and `┤` at the right. Rounded corners that become joints use the plain joints. When the two border types differ, the later sibling's glyph wins. Popups, then tooltips, paint after all content.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">0         1         2         3         4         5
012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789</span>
╭─ Left ──────────────────────┬─ Right ────────────────────╮
│fill(1)                      │fill(1)                     │
│                             │                            │
│                             │                            │
╰─────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 60 columns. <code>overlap(1)</code>. The two panels share column 30, and the host draws the shared edge with the joints <code>┬</code> and <code>┴</code>.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Reading the area

`render` receives `area`, the `columns` and `rows` the view may use. The kernel calls `render` again when that size changes, so a plugin can pick a different layout for a narrow view. A basic pane reads its size with `basic.size`. The plugin gets sizes only, never positions.

| Source | Gives | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `area` in `render` | `columns` and `rows` of the view | Choosing a direction or a segment count. |
| `basic.size` | Columns and rows of a basic pane | Sizing an own character grid. |
| `ui.display-width(text)` | Cell width of a string, with icon widths | Measuring a label before choosing `length`. |
| `ui.theme-extras().density` | `compact`, `normal` or `comfortable` | Choosing spacing and margins. |

Do not guess a width from the character count of a string that holds icons or wide glyphs; use `display-width`. Do not tune a layout to one terminal size. Express the ratios with `fill`, `percentage` and `ratio`, and use `length` only for things with a fixed size such as a button or a gutter.

## Sizes elsewhere in the widget catalogue

Several other widgets take sizes with the same vocabulary. The solver rules above apply to all of them.

| Widget | Where sizes appear | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `popup`, `dialog` | `width` and `height` as `constraint`; `centered((width, height))` anchors | A `percentage` is of the view, a `length` is in cells. The host clamps a popup to the screen. |
| `split` | `position` in per mille (50 to 950), `min-first` and `min-second` in cells | The user moves the divider; the position is host state `widget-state::split`. |
| `scroll-view` | `content-rows` | The single child is laid out at that height and clipped to the area. |
| `table` | `columns` with `width: constraint`, `min-width` and `priority` | Narrow areas drop columns with the lowest priority first, never below `min-width`. |
| `layout` slot of `length(0)` | A child that takes no space | Keeps a closed dialog or an empty notice in the tree without drawing it. |

See [Layout and containers](/pages/widgets-layout-and-containers/) for these widgets.

## Worked example in Rust

This view stacks its two parts when it is narrower than 60 columns. It reads `area.columns` to decide, and it redraws on resize because the kernel calls `render` again.

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::layout::{Area, Constraint, Direction, Margin};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ui::{UiTree, ViewTarget};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::ui::build::Tree;

const NARROW_COLUMNS: u16 = 60;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client", exports = ["views"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct NotesPanel;

impl Lifecycle for NotesPanel {}

impl Handler for NotesPanel {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl Views for NotesPanel {
    fn render(&mut self, _view: ViewTarget, area: Area) -> UiTree {
        let mut tree = Tree::new();
        let sidebar = tree.paragraph(vec![vec![Span::plain("Notes")]]).key("sidebar");
        let body = tree.paragraph(vec![vec![Span::plain("Select a note to read it.")]]).key("body");
        let (direction, constraints) = if area.columns < NARROW_COLUMNS {
            (Direction::Vertical, [Constraint::Length(4), Constraint::Fill(1)])
        } else {
            (Direction::Horizontal, [Constraint::Length(20), Constraint::Fill(1)])
        };
        let root = tree
            .layout(direction, constraints)
            .margin(Margin { horizontal: 1, vertical: 0 })
            .child(sidebar)
            .child(body);
        tree.finish(root)
    }
}
```

## Worked example in TypeScript

The same view. It also puts three buttons in a footer row with `space-between`, under a body that takes all the remaining rows.

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission, Area, ViewTarget } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { button, fill, layout, length, paragraph, span, tree } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/ui/build';

const NARROW_COLUMNS = 60;

export const { lifecycle, handler, views } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  onEvents(_batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    return [];
  },
  render(_view: ViewTarget, area: Area) {
    const narrow = area.columns < NARROW_COLUMNS;
    const split = layout({
      direction: narrow ? 'vertical' : 'horizontal',
      constraints: narrow ? [length(4), fill(1)] : [length(20), fill(1)],
      margin: { horizontal: 1, vertical: 0 },
    }, [
      paragraph([[span('Notes')]], { key: 'sidebar' }),
      paragraph([[span('Select a note to read it.')]], { key: 'body' }),
    ]);
    const footer = layout({
      direction: 'horizontal',
      constraints: [length(8), length(8), length(8)],
      flex: 'space-between',
    }, [
      button('Open', { key: 'open' }),
      button('Save', { key: 'save' }),
      button('Quit', { key: 'quit' }),
    ]);
    return tree(layout({ direction: 'vertical', constraints: [fill(1), length(3)] }, [split, footer]));
  },
});
```

## Errors and edge cases

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Number of children differs from the number of constraints | The builder stops the render with a message that names the layout key. A hand-built invalid tree traps the instance. |
| `ratio` with a denominator of 0 | The tree is invalid and traps the instance with `ui.invalid-tree`. |
| Constraints that need more cells than the area has | The solver follows ratatui's priority rules; trailing segments shrink, and a segment with 0 cells draws nothing. |
| `percentage` above 100 | The segment is clamped to the available space. |
| `ratio` above 1 | Clamped to 1. |
| `fill(0)` | 0 cells, unless every constraint is `fill(0)`. |
| A margin larger than the area | The inner area is empty and nothing is drawn. |
| `spacing: overlap(n)` with bordered children | The shared edge is drawn once with joint glyphs. |
| A tree of more nodes than the effective `ui_tree_nodes` limit (4,096 by default, up to 16,384 for T1) | The tree is invalid and traps the instance with `ui.too-large`. |

A trap ends the plugin instance, and the host applies the [restart and disable rule](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/#restart-and-disable-rule): restart after 1 s, then 5 s, and disable at the third failure in 10 minutes.

## What the user sees

The user sees panels that follow the size of the view and reflow when the terminal is resized or the user drags the sidebar width. They never see a constraint. Because the host owns the solver, two plugins with the same constraints align exactly, and a view looks the same on every platform.

Requirement ids for this page: [WID-004], [WID-005], [WID-006], [WID-007]. See the [requirements index](/pages/reference-requirements/).

## Narrow terminals

A pane can be as narrow as 40 columns, and the solver gives each segment only what is left. A plugin SHOULD test every view at 40 columns by 12 rows, which is the size `lint.widget-missing-key` renders at, and SHOULD give a `min` constraint to a segment that must stay readable. [AUT-505] A fixed width in cells is wrong for text whose length depends on the language. A plugin SHOULD prefer `fill` and `percentage` for text segments. [AUT-506]

## See also

- [Layout and containers](/pages/widgets-layout-and-containers/) for `layout`, `block`, `split`, `scroll-view` and the other containers
- [The UI model](/pages/ui-model/)
- [Widget catalogue](/pages/widgets-index/)
- [Accessibility and theming](/pages/accessibility-and-theming/) for density and reduced motion
- [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/)

API version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Lifecycle

## Lifecycle

A plugin moves through install, activation, running, stopping and, when something goes wrong, failure, revocation or disable. The host decides when each stage happens. Your code receives two calls, `activate` and `deactivate`. The bytes you return from `deactivate` come back as `restored` on the next activation, so a cursor or a scroll position can survive a restart.

## You will need

- A package with a `manifest.json`. Add the `activation` key for every trigger that must fire without a user action. See [Packages and manifests](/pages/packages/) and [Reference: manifest](/pages/reference-manifest/).
- Every component exports `lifecycle` and `handler`. The manifest lists only the optional exports, such as `views` or `detector`.
- For Rust: a stable Rust toolchain with the WASI Preview 2 component target, and the `ilium-plugin-sdk` crate. For TypeScript: Bun and `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. The SDK release pins the toolchain versions it needs, so nothing is installed globally.
- The grants your code uses. A plugin runs without any grant, and it sees only the grants listed in `granted`. See [Capabilities and grants](/pages/capabilities/).

## Install

Installing verifies the package and records the grants the user accepts.

- `ilium plugin install <file.iliumpkg> [--allow-unsigned]` installs a package. The check covers the layout, the file inventory, the `api` field and the `ilium:api-version` section of each component. A component built for a newer minor version than the host is refused, and the error names both versions.
- Tier T2 needs a signature from a publisher key the user trusts. `ilium plugin trust add <publisher.pub>` adds a key. An unknown key is offered for trust with its fingerprint, and declining refuses the install. T3 packages install only with `--allow-unsigned` or through `ilium plugin dev`.
- For a T2 or T3 package, the review dialog lists every capability with its risk. Normal capabilities are checked by default, high-risk ones are unchecked. An unchecked capability is not granted.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives its manifest ceiling automatically. Its high-risk capabilities are asked once, at first activation, with `Allow selected` and `Not now`. `Not now` asks again at the next server start, at most three times. The counter is stored with the grants record and is reset by an update ([LIF-275]).
- Installing a newer version is an update, and the dialog shows only the new capabilities. A lower version is refused unless you pass `--allow-downgrade`. The full pipeline, rollback and uninstall are specified in [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/).
- On Windows and macOS, T2 and T3 packages are refused with `Cannot install <name> <version>.` and the sandbox message. Bundled plugins keep working.

## Activation

A plugin is not instantiated at install. The host instantiates it when one of its triggers fires. Without an `activation` key, the plugin is instantiated on the first use of any of its contributions. That is lazy loading. A plugin that publishes decorations from the start must declare `"activation": ["startup"]`.

| Trigger | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `startup` | the server starts, or the client starts for client-side plugins |
| `event:<event-name>` | the named event is delivered to the plugin |
| `command:<id>` | a command of the plugin is invoked |
| `view:<id>` | the plugin's view is opened |
| `pane-kind:<id>` | a pane of the plugin's kind is created or restored |
| `scene:<id>` | the plugin's scene is shown |
| `cli:<name>` | the plugin's subcommand runs |
| `http:<path>` | a request arrives on the plugin's route |
| `service:<interface>` | a caller invokes the service, which waits for activation |
| `topic:<topic>` | the exact topic is published; a pattern subscriber uses `startup` |
| `settings:<tab-id>` | the plugin's own settings tab is opened, or a built-in tab that carries one of its sections is opened |

`activate` receives a context record. Its fields are the same in every language.

| WIT field | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `plugin` | `plugin` | `plugin` | the plugin id |
| `api` | `api` | `api` | the API version string |
| `instance` | `instance: u64` | `instance: bigint` | the instance number, unique per run |
| `side` | `side` | `side` | `server`, `client` or `scene` |
| `settings-json` | `settings_json` | `settingsJson` | the current settings as a JSON object |
| `granted` | `granted: Vec<String>` | `granted: string[]` | grants the user accepted; declined ones are absent |
| `restored` | `restored: Option<Vec<u8>>` | `restored: Uint8Array \| undefined` | bytes from the last `deactivate`, or none |

The WIT signatures are `activate: func(context: activation) -> result<_, plugin-error>` and `deactivate: func(reason: deactivation-reason) -> option<list<u8>>`.

The `activate` call may yield. Its deadline is 2 s by default and 5 s for T1 plugins (`activate_deadline_ms`). A breach is a trap. The `deactivate` call has 500 ms by default and 1 s for T1 plugins (`deactivate_deadline_ms`). When it misses that deadline, the instance is dropped and no restore bytes are kept. The defaults are the same for every tier, and the figures for T1 are ceilings. Every deadline, its breach effect and whether it counts as a failure are in the call-class table of [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/#call-classes).

The reasons passed to `deactivate` are:

| Reason | Sent when | Counts as a failure | Returned bytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shutdown` | the server stops, after its services stop | no | stored as restore state |
| `disabled` | the user switches the plugin off | no | kept for the next activation |
| `upgrade` | an installed update replaces the running version, or `ilium plugin dev` rebuilds it | no | passed to the new version as `restored` when its `data_version` is unchanged |
| `revoked` | a granted capability is revoked | no | passed back as `restored` |
| `granted` | a capability is added | no | passed back as `restored` |
| `crash-restart` | reserved, never sent [ABI-028]; a trap drops the instance without a call | not applicable | none |

The enum `deactivation-reason` has six cases in a fixed order: `shutdown`, `disabled`, `upgrade`, `crash-restart`, `revoked`, `granted`. Five are delivered. A client that disconnects has no case of its own: the host deactivates that instance with `shutdown` and the returned bytes are stored as restore state, see [persistence and restart](/pages/reference-persistence-and-restart/).

- [LIF-043] The enum `deactivation-reason` MUST have the six values above, and the host MUST send `crash-restart` never. Test: enumerate the reasons seen across a full lifecycle test.
- [LIF-044] A production update MUST send `upgrade` to every live instance of the old version before the swap. Test: update an active plugin and read the reason.

Revocations and grant changes re-activate the plugin with the new `granted` list, so read `granted` on every activation.

## Durable timers and further triggers

Ordinary timers end with the instance. A durable timer (`timers.at`, always granted) survives a server restart. It fires as `durable-timer-fired` with `timer`, `name` and `late-by-millis`. If Ilium was not running at the due time, it fires once after the next activation, with the lateness. The same `name` replaces an earlier timer. Durable timers and journal entries also survive a deactivation.

Further activation triggers are `catalog:<id>`, `menu:<id>`, `virtual-rows:<row-kind>`, `language:<id>`, `client-request:<kind>` and `durable-timer`. On stop, the host also closes the plugin's HTTP streams, ends its spawned children, releases its input locks, withdraws its status segments, frame slots, toasts and row actions, and fails its open client requests with `cancelled`. After a trap the host does the same for the dead instance, and also cancels the jobs and ends the helper processes it started ([LIF-271]). A `cli` entry with `requires_server: false` activates the server component in the CLI process and deactivates it with the reason `shutdown` at the end of the command.

**Rust**

```rust
// Re-arm after every activation. The same name replaces an earlier timer.
timers::at(clock::now_unix_millis() + 86_400_000, "nightly-scan")?;
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
// Re-arm after every activation. The same name replaces an earlier timer.
timers.at(clock.nowUnixMillis() + 86_400_000n, 'nightly-scan');
```

## Activation order

The host decides which plugins start and in which order. This section is normative.

### Start order

On the server, the kernel starts in this order:

1. Boot and configuration load.
2. The snapshot is restored.
3. The plugin host verifies each installed manifest, applies policy and safe mode, and registers static contributions. Nothing is instantiated yet.
4. Plugins with the `startup` trigger are activated, in the order below.
5. Each activated plugin receives one `tree-changed` batch for all restored nodes.

The `startup` trigger fires when the server starts for server-side plugins, and when the client starts for client-side plugins.

- [LIF-045] The host MUST compute the start order of `startup` plugins with Kahn's algorithm over the edges of the non-optional `requires.plugins` entries and of the `requires.services` entries to their providers. A provider's `activate` MUST return before any consumer that requires it begins `activate`. Test: three plugins, A requires B requires C, record the order of `activate.begin`.
- [LIF-046] At each step of that algorithm the host MUST take the ready node with the smallest key: the tier number (T1 first), then the plugin id in ascending byte order. Test: install T1 `b`, T2 `a` and T1 `a` with no dependencies and assert the order T1 `a`, T1 `b`, T2 `a`.
- [LIF-047] Independent plugins MAY activate in parallel. The host MUST run at most 4 concurrent activations per side, and MUST start them in the order of LIF-046. Test: 12 independent plugins, each blocking in `activate`, and assert the peak is 4 and that the begin order is the key order.
- [LIF-048] A cycle in the non-optional `requires.services` entries MUST be refused at install, at stage 10, with `manifest.service-cycle`. A cycle in `requires.plugins` is refused with `dependency.cycle`. The rules for both are in [Versions and dependencies](/pages/reference-dependency-resolution/). Test: install two plugins that require each other's services and read the code and the cycle order.
- [LIF-049] Dependencies are `requires.plugins` and `requires.services`. The host version is checked only through `requires.host`, which is refused with `dependency.host-version` at stage 10. A key named `engines` is refused with `manifest.unknown-key`. Test: install a manifest with `requires.host` above the running release, and one with an `engines` key.

### Stop order

- [LIF-050] On server stop the host MUST call `deactivate(shutdown)` in the exact reverse of the start order, one at a time, so that a consumer stops before the providers it requires. The order of completion of the starts does not matter. Test: record the order of `deactivate` calls after a start in which activations finished in a different order.

### When a provider is not available

A consumer is a plugin that requires a service interface. A consumer is never deactivated because its provider changed state.

| Provider state | What a call to the service returns |
|---|---|
| `activating` or `inactive` | The call waits for activation, up to the call deadline (`service:` trigger). |
| `restart-scheduled` | `busy` with `retry-after-ms` set to the time left on the timer. |
| `stopped-by-failure`, `installed-disabled-by-user`, `disabled-untrusted`, `disabled-blocked`, refused or uninstalled | `not-found`. |

- [LIF-051] A consumer MUST stay active when its provider fails, is disabled or is uninstalled. Test: disable the provider and assert the consumer state.
- [LIF-052] The host MUST return the code in the table for a service call. Test: one case per row.
- [LIF-053] The host MUST send the event `service-availability-changed` (`interface`, `available`, `provider`) to every active consumer when the availability of a required interface changes. Test: disable and enable the provider and read the events.
- [LIF-054] When the user disables a plugin that is a provider for other plugins, the disable dialog MUST list the dependants, and the CLI MUST print a `warning` line for each dependant. The disable is not blocked. Test: disable a provider and read the dialog text.

### Extension owners and contributors

- [LIF-055] The host MUST activate the owner of an extension point before its contributors. After the owner's `activate` returns, the host MUST activate in the background the lazy contributors of its points, so that a contribution needs no trigger of its own. Test: a lazy contributor to a hook point becomes `active` after the owner activates.
- [LIF-056] A hook call MUST NOT wait for a contributor that is not yet `active`. The host skips it, treats it as `pass` and logs `extension.contributor-not-ready`. Test: call a hook while the contributor is `activating`.

### Client handshake and version skew

The client handshake carries the plugin id, version and API version of every installed plugin. A mismatch in the API version fails loudly, as before. A difference in plugin version is allowed during an update.

- [LIF-057] If the server and a client run different versions of one plugin, each side MUST keep running the version it has until it receives the change notice for the update. The host MUST NOT block messages between the sides. Test: update a plugin while a client is attached and assert both sides finish on the new version.
- [LIF-058] A client whose API version differs from the server's MUST be refused at the handshake with the message `api-version mismatch` naming both versions. Test: connect a client with a different API version.

### Startup budget

- [LIF-059] The client SHOULD render its first frame when the essential client plugins are active, or after 1,000 ms, whichever comes first. Plugins that are not active by then continue to activate in the background, and the first frame shows a `starting plugins` mark. Test: delay a non-essential plugin by 3 s and assert the first frame appears within 1,100 ms.

## Core plugins at boot

The `startup` trigger applies per side: a server side with `startup` starts when the server host starts, and a client side with `startup` starts when the client host starts. The core plugins that start at boot and those that start on first use are listed in [startup and lazy activation](/pages/reference-kernel-and-boot/#startup-and-lazy-activation-of-the-30-core-plugins). Safe start (`--safe-plugins`) loads only the essential set, and `--no-plugins` loads none. [COR-020] [COR-021]

## Running

The host calls the exports in response to events, views, commands and scene frames. Each call has its own deadline, for example 20 ms for `handler.on-events`. A breach counts as a failure. See [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/).

## Stop and the final save

On server shutdown, the services stop first. Then the plugin host refuses new plugin submissions, which complete as `cancelled`. Each active plugin receives `deactivate(shutdown)` in reverse start order (consumers before the providers they require), and its returned bytes become its restore state. Pending requests are cancelled and instances are dropped. The final snapshot is written last, so no plugin intent can reach it after the writer stops.

## Worked example: keep a cursor across restarts

The Rust example is a client plugin. It keeps a line number in memory, saves it on shutdown and reads it back on the next activation. It moves the cursor on a command, and it moves it only when the user granted `fs.read:project`. Both exports are required, so the plugin implements `Handler` as well as `Lifecycle`.

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{Activation, DeactivationReason};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};

const NEXT_COMMAND: &str = "com.example.cursor/next";
const FILE_READ_GRANT: &str = "fs.read:project";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct CursorKeeper {
    cursor_line: u32,
    can_read_files: bool,
}

impl Lifecycle for CursorKeeper {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        self.can_read_files = context.granted.iter().any(|grant| grant.as_str() == FILE_READ_GRANT);
        if let Some(saved) = context.restored.as_deref() {
            if let Ok(four_bytes) = <[u8; 4]>::try_from(saved) {
                self.cursor_line = u32::from_le_bytes(four_bytes);
            }
        }
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("cursor at line {}", self.cursor_line));
        Ok(())
    }

    fn deactivate(&mut self, reason: DeactivationReason) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
        match reason {
            DeactivationReason::Shutdown => Some(self.cursor_line.to_le_bytes().to_vec()),
            _ => None,
        }
    }
}

impl Handler for CursorKeeper {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            if let Event::CommandInvoked(invoked) = event {
                if invoked.command == NEXT_COMMAND && self.can_read_files {
                    self.cursor_line += 1;
                }
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

The TypeScript version uses the same manifest and the same behaviour. `definePlugin` infers the types of `context` and `reason`, so no import is needed for them.

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const NEXT_COMMAND = 'com.example.cursor/next';
const FILE_READ_GRANT = 'fs.read:project';

let cursorLine = 0;
let canReadFiles = false;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    canReadFiles = context.granted.includes(FILE_READ_GRANT);
    if (context.restored !== undefined && context.restored.byteLength === 4) {
      const view = new DataView(context.restored.buffer, context.restored.byteOffset, 4);
      cursorLine = view.getUint32(0, true);
    }
    const reads = canReadFiles ? 'allowed' : 'hidden';
    log('info', `cursor at line ${cursorLine}, file reads ${reads}`);
  },
  deactivate(reason) {
    if (reason !== 'shutdown') return undefined;
    const bytes = new Uint8Array(4);
    new DataView(bytes.buffer).setUint32(0, cursorLine, true);
    return bytes;
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === NEXT_COMMAND && canReadFiles) {
        cursorLine += 1;
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

Both versions store the cursor as four little-endian bytes and check the length before decoding.

## Failure counting and restart

This section is the single normative source for what counts as a failure and for restart delays. Other pages link here and do not restate the numbers.

A failure is an event that makes the host drop a running instance because of the plugin. When the host drops an instance after a failure, it withdraws the instance's dynamic contributions, keeps its decorations marked stale, cancels its pending requests, records the failure and then either schedules a restart or stops the side.

### The failure window

- [LIF-025] The host MUST keep one failure window for each combination of plugin id, side and scope. The scope is the session server for the `server` side, and one attached client connection for the `client` and `scene` sides. Test: attach two clients, trap the plugin twice on client A and once on client B, and assert that `failures-in-window` is 2 and 1.
- [LIF-026] Two clients MUST NOT share a window. Disabling the plugin by failure on client A MUST NOT stop it on client B or on the server. Test: as above, with a third trap on client A.
- [LIF-027] A window MUST be a sliding window of 10 minutes on a monotonic clock. A failure counts while its age is less than 600 s. Test: with the FakeHost `advance_clock`, trap at 0 s, advance 599 s and assert the failure counts, advance 2 s more and assert it does not.
- [LIF-285] The failure window is per plugin, per side, per scope and per version. It MUST be emptied when the active version changes, on `ilium plugin dev` reload and on a manual enable. The first activation failure of an update candidate is not counted (LIF-075), and a manual `ilium plugin restart <id>` neither counts nor empties the window. Test: trap twice, change the active version and trap again and assert 1 failure; repeat for dev reload and enable; fail a candidate's first activation and assert the window is empty; restart manually and assert the count is unchanged.
- [LIF-028] The first counted failure in a window MUST schedule a restart after 1 s. Test: trap once and read `restart-at`.
- [LIF-029] The second counted failure in a window MUST schedule a restart after 5 s. Test: trap twice within 10 minutes.
- [LIF-030] The third counted failure in a window MUST stop that side with the instance state `stopped-by-failure` and MUST NOT schedule a restart. The package state stays `installed-enabled`. Test: trap three times within 10 minutes and assert no activation follows.
- [LIF-031] The host MUST NOT use any other restart delay. There is no step after the second, because the third failure stops the side. Test: after a stop, advance the clock one hour and assert the side is still stopped.
- [LIF-032] The host MUST NOT add random jitter. The delay timer starts when the instance is dropped. The next activation MUST NOT begin earlier than the delay, and SHOULD begin within 250 ms after it. Test: assert the begin time is in the range delay to delay plus 250 ms.

Failures older than 10 minutes drop out of the count on their own, so a plugin that runs for 10 minutes without a failure starts again from zero. A stable run needs no separate reset rule. For example, failures at 0 s, 300 s and 660 s: the failure at 660 s sees only the one at 300 s in the window, so it is the second counted failure and restarts after 5 s.

### What counts

| Kind of failure | Counts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Trap in any export | yes | Includes a Rust panic and a thrown TypeScript exception that escapes an export. |
| `activate` returns an error | yes | Also when a `service:` or `cli:` call triggered the activation. |
| `activate` misses its deadline | yes | |
| `handler.on-events`, `views.render` or another export misses its deadline | yes | |
| `deactivate` misses its deadline, reason `disabled` or `shutdown` | no | The plugin is leaving anyway. The instance is dropped and a warn line is logged. |
| `deactivate` misses its deadline, reason `upgrade` or `revoked` | yes | The plugin was to continue. |
| Event queue overflow (more than 1,024 events by default) | yes | |
| Memory limit of the instance reached | yes | A trap. |
| Instantiation refused because the session memory pool is full | no | Host capacity, see below. |
| Service provider fails to start when a call needs it | yes | It is an `activate` failure. The caller gets `busy` or `not-found`. |
| Failed job (trap, deadline, memory) | never | The job request completes as failed. The plugin keeps running. |
| Extension handler timeout, trap or error | not for restart | It counts only toward the 3-breach stop of that extension. See [extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/). |
| Sandbox helper process crash or hang (T2, T3) | one failure for the plugin whose export was running, none for the others | The other plugins in the helper restart without a count. See [health and watchdog](/pages/reference-health-and-watchdog/). |
| Revocation, grant, disable, update, shutdown, detach | never | These are deliberate stops. |

- [LIF-033] The host MUST count each kind in the table as the table says. Test: a parametrised test, one case per row, reading `failures-in-window`.
- [LIF-034] A refusal caused by host capacity MUST NOT count against the plugin. The instance stays `inactive` with the reason `host-capacity`. The host MUST retry the activation when pool memory is released, and in any case 1 s, 5 s and 30 s after the refusal, then every 60 s without end while the plugin is enabled. Test: fill the pool, trigger activation, assert `failures-in-window` is 0, free memory and assert the activation runs.
- [LIF-035] A failed job MUST NOT count. Test: trap inside a job and assert `failures-in-window` is unchanged.

### Reset and persistence

- [LIF-036] Enabling the plugin, the command `ilium plugin reset-failures <id>`, the Enable action of the recovery page and installing an update MUST clear the failure window of the affected sides. Test: two traps, then each action, then one trap restarts after 1 s.
- [LIF-037] The instance state `stopped-by-failure` of the server side MUST be written to `failure_stopped` in `installed.json` and MUST survive a server restart. The failure window itself MUST NOT; it starts empty. The state of a client or scene side MUST be dropped when its client detaches. Test: stop the server after a stop-by-failure and assert the state after the restart; detach and reattach a client and assert the client side runs again.

### Restart timer and other events

- [LIF-038] When a server stop begins, the host MUST cancel all pending restart timers and MUST NOT schedule a new one. A failure during shutdown is logged and not counted. Test: schedule a restart, begin a stop and assert no activation.
- [LIF-039] When the user disables the plugin while a restart is pending, the host MUST cancel the timer and move the side to `installed-disabled-by-user`. Test: schedule, disable, advance the clock past the delay and assert no activation.
- [LIF-040] When an update arrives while a restart is pending, the host MUST cancel the timer, clear the window and activate the new version by its normal triggers. Test: schedule, update, assert the new version activates.
- [LIF-041] A revocation or grant while a restart is pending MUST keep the timer. The new instance MUST receive the current `granted` list. Test: schedule, revoke a grant, assert the restarted instance sees the shorter list.
- [LIF-042] An essential core plugin (see [Core plugins](/pages/core-plugins/)) MUST never be stopped by failure. Its third and later failures in a window MUST restart after 5 s and MUST raise the essential-failure banner. Test: trap `ilium.core.tree` three times and assert it restarts and the banner shows.

When the host stops a side, the tree footer shows one notice, called N14 in this manual, and Settings > Plugins lists the same text. This is the only place where the notice is defined. Other pages link here.

- [USR-130] The notice N14 MUST read `Plugin <name> stopped after 3 failures in 10 minutes: <export> <code or trap>. Turn it on again in Settings > Plugins.` The `<export>` is the failing export. It names the view, as in `views.render trap (sidebar)`, only when the failing export was `views.render`. The tree footer and the row in Settings > Plugins MUST show the same text. Test: trap a plugin three times and compare the footer text and the row text with the template.

A user re-enables a stopped plugin in Settings > Plugins. That clears the failure window, as LIF-036 says. A call to `plugins.set-enabled(id, true)` on a failed plugin clears its `failed` state the same way.

## Dormant extensions

A plugin may contribute to a point whose owner is not installed or not enabled. Install does not fail. The contribution stays in the package and counts for nothing, and Settings > Plugins shows `waiting for <owner>`. When the owner appears, the host activates the contribution and sends the owner `ilium.extensions/changed`. When the owner is disabled, its points drop their contributions in the same way, and they return when it is enabled again. A contributor that was stopped after three breaches in a row stays stopped until its plugin instance restarts or the user presses Reset. The stop is not saved across a server restart ([LIF-270]). See [extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/).

## Disable and enable

`plugins.set-enabled(id, false)` and the Settings switch take effect at once. The call returns `ok` when the change is recorded. Then the plugin receives `deactivate(disabled)` within its deadline, its contributions are withdrawn, its locks are released and its requests are cancelled. Enabling records the change and activates the plugin by its normal rules: a `startup` plugin at once, a lazy plugin at its next trigger.

Disabling or uninstalling removes all decorations of the plugin. A disable keeps the plugin's `data` directory and its storage. An uninstall keeps or deletes them by the rules in [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/). A session bucket is deleted with its session.

### Uninstall cascade

An uninstall changes what other plugins see. Nothing is deleted from them. The table is the one rule set for every page. The user-facing wording is in [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/#remove-a-plugin).

| What depended on the removed plugin | What happens |
|---|---|
| A contribution to a point it owned | The contribution goes dormant and Settings shows `waiting for <owner>`. It wakes when the owner returns. |
| A consumer of one of its services | The consumer stays active. Calls return `not-found` ([LIF-051]). |
| A contribution it made to another plugin's point | It disappears from that point at once. |
| A core plugin it replaced | The core plugin turns back on. Its data was never touched. |
| A pane of a kind it provided | The pane stays in the tree as a placeholder, described in [Panes](/pages/api-panes/#a-pane-whose-plugin-is-gone). |
| Keys, menu items, status segments, toolbar buttons | They disappear. |
| The user's order for its points | The entries are deleted. |

- [USR-172] An uninstall MUST apply the effects of the table above in the same host step that removes the plugin from the registry. Test: remove a provider with a consumer, a contributor and a pane, and check each row.

### Settings rows by state

Settings rows follow the plugin's state. A value is never deleted by disable, failure, upgrade or uninstall.

| State | Plugin tab | Section in a built-in tab | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enabled, not yet started | normal; starts when the tab opens (`settings:<tab-id>`) | normal | editable |
| Running | normal | normal | editable |
| Restarting after a failure | a notice names the attempt and the delay | the divider shows `plugin · restarting` | editable, unless the plugin exports `settings-validate`, then read-only |
| Disabled by the user | dim in the rail, with a button to the recovery page | the divider shows `plugin · off`; rows dim and read-only | kept, read-only |
| Disabled after repeated failures | the same as disabled, with the reason | the divider shows `plugin · disabled` | kept, read-only |
| Refused at load (API or schema) | dim, with the required API version | as disabled | kept, untouched |
| Uninstalled | gone from the rail | gone | kept until the user purges them with `ilium plugin uninstall --purge` or "Forget settings" on the recovery page |

A reinstalled plugin reads its kept values again. The recovery page is the only settings screen that stays reachable when the plugin is disabled.

## Revocation and grant changes

Revoking a grant in Settings > Plugins > Capabilities, or with `ilium plugin grants <id> --revoke <grant>`, bumps the authorization epoch. Calls in flight return `revoked`, and pending requests that need the capability complete as `failed(revoked)`. The plugin receives `deactivate(revoked)` and is activated again with the reduced grant set and its restore bytes. Decorations, toolbar state, grabs, claims, highlights, filters, watches and routes that need the capability are withdrawn.

A capability added later by the user, or by an accepted upgrade, produces `deactivate(shutdown)` and a re-activation with the new set. Neither revocation nor a grant change counts as a failure.

## Development reload

`ilium plugin dev`, run in the package directory, watches the sources and reloads the plugin in a running session. This section is normative. The walkthrough is in [Debugging](/pages/debugging/).

- [LIF-220] `ilium plugin dev` MUST attach to the session of `--cwd` (the current directory by default), or to the session named by `--session <name>`. When no server runs for it, the command MUST exit with code 2 and the error code `dev.no-server`, unless `--start-server` is given. Test: run it with no server.
- [LIF-221] A development package MUST shadow an installed package with the same id for that session only. When `ilium plugin dev` ends, the installed version MUST become active again. Test: install version 1, run dev with version 2, end dev and read the version.
- [LIF-222] A rebuild MUST start 300 ms after the last change in the directory. Test: touch a file twice 100 ms apart and assert one build.
- [LIF-223] The reload steps MUST run in this order: build, validate the manifest, compare grants, deactivate the server side with `upgrade`, deactivate each attached client side with `upgrade` in attach order, swap, activate the server side, then each client side, each with `restored`. Test: record the log order with two clients.
- [LIF-224] New grants MUST produce a review prompt in the dev terminal, and grants that are no longer in the manifest MUST be revoked without a prompt. With `--grant <name>` the named grants are accepted without a prompt. A new high-risk grant that is not accepted MUST NOT be granted, and the reload MUST continue with the smaller set. Test: add a grant to the manifest and assert the prompt.
- [LIF-225] A change to contributions or activation triggers MUST be re-registered at the swap and MUST be followed by `ilium.extensions/changed` for the affected points. Test: add an extension contribution and read the event.
- [LIF-226] In dev mode, failures MUST be counted and shown but MUST NOT stop the plugin. The third and later failures restart after 5 s. A successful reload MUST clear the window. Test: trap three times and assert the plugin restarts.
- [LIF-227] A failed build or a manifest error MUST keep the running instance and print one `build-error` line. No `deactivate` MUST be sent. Test: introduce a compile error.
- [LIF-228] Restore bytes MUST be passed to the new build only when its `data_version` equals the one of the build that produced them. Otherwise they are dropped and the host logs `restore.dropped-data-version`. Test: change `data_version` between two builds.
- [LIF-229] The dev instance MUST be held by a lease. The `ilium plugin dev` process renews it every 2 s over its connection. The server MUST remove the dev package and restore the installed version when the lease is not renewed for 10 s, or when the connection closes. Test: kill the dev process with SIGKILL and assert the installed version returns within 10 s.

The command prints JSON lines. Every line has a `type`.

| `type` | Fields | When |
|---|---|---|
| `dev-start` | `plugin`, `session`, `version` | the command attached |
| `build` | `plugin`, `ok`, `millis` | a build ended |
| `build-error` | `plugin`, `message`, `file`, `line` | a build or manifest check failed |
| `grant-review` | `plugin`, `added`, `removed` | the grants changed |
| `reload` | `plugin`, `version`, `restored_bytes`, `sides` | a reload finished |
| `plugin-failure` | `plugin`, `side`, `code`, `failures_in_window` | a counted failure in dev mode |
| `dev-stop` | `plugin`, `restored_version` | the command ended |

```text
{"type":"reload","plugin":"<id>","version":"<version>","restored_bytes":<n>,"sides":["server","client"]}
```

A development package carries a `dev` badge in Settings, and it uses the T3 sandbox and ceilings. Plugin logs appear in `ilium plugin logs <id>`.

## What `activate` does not tell you

The `activate` call receives the activation context and the restore bytes, and nothing else about the past. There is no `previous-version` value and no flag that says "this is the first run after an update" in `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. A plugin that must act once after an update uses one of these two ways, in this order of preference:

1. Put the work in a `migrator` export and raise `data_version`. The host calls it once per side before `activate`, with the old and new data versions ([Data migration](/pages/guide-data-migration/)).
2. Store the version that last ran under a storage key such as `last_version`, compare it in `activate` and write the new value after the work succeeds.

A plugin MUST NOT rely on a deactivate reason or a restore value to detect that an update happened, because `upgrade` is also the reason used by `ilium plugin dev`. [AUT-215] The author rules for updates are in [Compatibility and upgrades](/pages/guide-compatibility-and-upgrades/).

## Edge cases and errors

| Situation | What happens | Code the caller sees |
|---|---|---|
| `activate` returns an error | the error is logged at level error with its code and message; counts as a failure | none; the instance is not active |
| `activate` passes its deadline | trap; counts as a failure | none |
| call in flight during revocation | fails | `revoked` |
| pending request when the plugin stops or is disabled | cancelled | `cancelled` |
| HTTP route call open when the plugin stops | answered with a 503 response | `503 Service Unavailable` |
| message to a plugin whose activation fails | discarded; the sender's `ok` stands | none |
| watch or video id used after a restart | the id no longer exists; watch again in `activate` | `not-found` |
| input to a restored pane before its process starts | refused | `pane-not-ready` |
| restore bytes over 1 MiB | dropped; the next activation gets no `restored` value | none; one warn log line |
| contribution to a point whose owner is missing or disabled | dormant until the owner is enabled | none; Settings shows `waiting for <owner>` |
| `deactivate` passes its deadline | instance dropped without restore bytes | none; one warn log line |
| activation refused because the session memory pool is full | the side stays `inactive` with reason `host-capacity`; not a failure | none; the list shows `waiting for memory` |
| trap while a restart is already scheduled | impossible: there is no instance; a second failure needs a new instance | none |
| server stops with a restart scheduled | the timer is cancelled | none |

## What the user sees

The tree footer shows notice N14 when the host stopped a plugin. Settings > Plugins shows the plugin state and its capabilities, with the state words of the row state table. The install review dialog lists the capabilities before installation. `ilium plugin logs <id>` shows every trap, restart, deadline breach and dropped restore value.

<div class="warn">
<p>Restore bytes are not a migration. If a new build changes their layout, it must check the length and fall back to defaults when the bytes do not fit.</p>
</div>
