## Declaring a provider

The provider's schema file maps each method to a `params` schema and a `result` schema. The schemas use the keyword subset of JSON Schema draft 2020-12 that the [settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/) also use.

```json
{
  "exports": ["service-provider"],
  "contributes": {
    "services": {
      "provides": [
        {
          "name": "com.example.titles/suggest",
          "version": "0.1.0",
          "schema": "schemas/suggest.json"
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "unstable": ["plugin-services"]
}
```

```json
{
  "suggest": {
    "params": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": { "text": { "type": "string" } },
      "required": ["text"]
    },
    "result": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": { "title": { "type": "string" } },
      "required": ["title"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Declaring a consumer

The consumer names the service with its version in `requires.services`. Its activation waits for a compatible provider. A provider is compatible when its major version equals the required major version and its minor version is at least the required minor version. For major version 0 the rule is stricter, because 0.x versions are unstable: the minor version must be equal, and the patch version is ignored. A consumer that requires `0.1.0` accepts a provider at `0.1.0` or `0.1.5`, and refuses `0.9.0` and any `0.2.x` release. A consumer that requires `1.2.0` accepts `1.2.0` and `1.4.0`, and refuses `1.1.0` and `2.0.0` [SVC-006]. A provider has at most 64 calls in flight at once; a 65th call returns `busy` at the call [SVC-014].

```json
{
  "requires": { "services": ["com.example.titles/suggest@0.1.0"] },
  "unstable": ["plugin-services"]
}
```

## The call surface

| Name | Side | Rust | TypeScript | Grant | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `call` | caller | `services::call(service, method, payload_json).await` | `await call(service, method, payloadJson)` | `services.use` | Sends the call, waits and resolves with the reply JSON. Fails with the completion code. |
| `call-request` | caller | `services::call_request(...)` | `callRequest(...)` | `services.use` | Sends the call and returns a request id at once. |
| `take-reply` | caller | `services::take_reply(request)` | `takeReply(request)` | `services.use` | Returns the reply JSON once. `None` or `undefined` after a failure, a cancel or a second take. |
| `handle` | provider | `ServiceProvider::handle(&mut self, call)` | `handle(call)` in `definePlugin` | `services.provide` | Receives each checked call and returns a `ServiceReply`. |
| `reply` | provider | `services::reply(call, outcome)` | `reply(call, outcome)` | `services.provide` | Answers a deferred call with `Ok(json)` or `Err(error)`. |

| Type | Field or case | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ServiceCall` | `call` (`u64`; `bigint` in TypeScript) | The number to pass back to `reply`. |
| `ServiceCall` | `service`, `method`, `payload_json` | The name, the method, and the payload already checked against `params`. |
| `ServiceCall` | `caller` | The id of the calling plugin. |
| `ServiceReply` | `Done(String)` or `{ tag: 'done', val }` | Answers now with JSON that matches `result`. |
| `ServiceReply` | `Deferred` or `{ tag: 'deferred' }` | Promises a later `reply` with the same call number. |

The `ServiceCall`, `ServiceReply` and `ServiceProvider` names live in `ilium_plugin_sdk::exports` in Rust. In TypeScript they come from `@ilium/plugin-sdk`.

</svg>

</figure>

The payload is checked against `params` before the provider runs, and a failing payload never reaches it. A `Done` answer or a `reply` value must match `result`. The caller has 30 seconds from the call to receive its reply.

## Activation order

At startup the kernel starts service providers before the consumers that require them. A provider that is installed but not running is started by the first call to its service, through the trigger `service:<name>`. The call waits up to the provider's activation deadline, then for the reply. At shutdown, services stop in their declared order. A cycle, where two plugins each require the other, is refused at install.

<pre class="term">
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs com.example.notes-ui
<span class="t-dim">info</span>  services.call com.example.titles/suggest
      <span class="t-dim">provider inactive, activation started (2000 ms)</span>
<span class="t-err">error</span> services.call com.example.titles/suggest
      <span class="t-err">failed(timed-out)</span>: provider did not start
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The provider was installed but not running, and it did not start before its activation deadline.

## Errors and limits

| Code | Returned by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `not-found` | `call` | No installed and enabled provider. Returned at once. |
| `not-permitted` | `call`, `reply` | The plugin lacks the grant. |
| `invalid-argument` | `call` | The payload is over 1 MiB or fails `params`. The provider is not called. |
| `unsupported` | `call` | The method is not in the schema. |
| `busy`, `quota-exceeded` | `call` | Too many pending requests, or the CPU budget is spent. |
| `invalid-argument` | `reply` | The reply is over 1 MiB or fails `result`. |
| `not-found` | `reply`, `take-reply` | The call is unknown, answered or expired. |
| `timed-out` | caller | No reply within 30 seconds, or the provider did not start in time. |
| `cancelled` | caller | The provider stopped, restarted or was disabled before answering. |
| provider's code | caller | A failed `reply` passes its `plugin-error` on to the caller. |

A `Done` answer that fails `result` completes the caller's request as `failed(invalid-argument)`, and the provider logs the failure at level error.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Payload of one call, or one reply | 1 MiB |
| Wait for the reply | 30 seconds from the call |
| Provider activation | `activate_deadline_ms`: 2 seconds by default, 5 seconds at most |

<div class="warn">
<p>Plugin-defined services are unstable in 0.1 and may change within 0.x. Update both plugins when the API changes.</p>
</div>

## Worked example: a provider and a caller

The provider answers short notes at once and defers long ones to a task. The caller submits a note when a command runs. Each plugin is its own `src/lib.rs`.

**Rust**

Provider:

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{
    Handler, Lifecycle, ServiceCall, ServiceProvider, ServiceReply,
};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::services;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::task;

/// Notes shorter than this many bytes are answered at once.
const SHORT_NOTE_BYTES: usize = 200;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server", exports = ["service-provider"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct TitleProvider;

impl Lifecycle for TitleProvider {}

impl Handler for TitleProvider {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl ServiceProvider for TitleProvider {
    fn handle(&mut self, call: ServiceCall) -> ServiceReply {
        // The host has already checked the payload against the params schema.
        if call.payload_json.len() < SHORT_NOTE_BYTES {
            return ServiceReply::Done(r#"{"title":"Fix the parser"}"#.to_string());
        }
        let call_number = call.call;
        task::spawn(async move {
            // Stand-in for real work. A real provider computes the title first.
            let outcome = Ok(r#"{"title":"Long note"}"#.to_string());
            if let Err(error) = services::reply(call_number, outcome) {
                log::log(Level::Error, &error.message);
            }
        });
        ServiceReply::Deferred
    }
}
```

Caller:

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{Handler, Lifecycle};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::services;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::task;

const TITLE_SERVICE: &str = "com.example.titles/suggest";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct NoteCaller;

impl Lifecycle for NoteCaller {}

impl Handler for NoteCaller {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::CommandInvoked(invoked) = event else {
                continue;
            };
            if invoked.command == "com.example.notes/suggest-title" {
                task::spawn(ask_for_title("Fix the parser crash on empty input".to_string()));
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

async fn ask_for_title(note: String) {
    // A real plugin builds the payload with a JSON library, so quotes in the note are escaped.
    let payload_json = format!(r#"{{"text":"{note}"}}"#);
    match services::call(TITLE_SERVICE, "suggest", &payload_json).await {
        Ok(reply_json) => log::log(Level::Info, &format!("title: {reply_json}")),
        Err(error) => log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("title failed: {}", error.message)),
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

The same pair in TypeScript. The provider returns the `ServiceReply` union in the jco form. The caller awaits `call`, which resolves with the reply text or throws the completion code.

Provider, `src/index.ts`:

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type ServiceCall, type ServiceReply } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { reply } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/services';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

// Notes shorter than this many characters are answered at once.
const SHORT_NOTE_CHARACTERS = 200;

export const { lifecycle, handler, serviceProvider } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(_batch: Event[]) {
    return [];
  },
  handle(call: ServiceCall): ServiceReply {
    if (call.payloadJson.length < SHORT_NOTE_CHARACTERS) {
      return { tag: 'done', val: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Fix the parser' }) };
    }
    answerLater(call.call);
    return { tag: 'deferred' };
  },
});

function answerLater(callNumber: bigint): void {
  // Stand-in for real work. A real provider computes the title first.
  queueMicrotask(() => {
    const outcome = reply(callNumber, { tag: 'ok', val: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Long note' }) });
    if (outcome.tag === 'err') {
      log('error', `reply failed: ${outcome.val.message}`);
    }
  });
}
```

Caller, `src/index.ts` of the second plugin:

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { call } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/services';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const TITLE_SERVICE = 'com.example.titles/suggest';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      const isTitleCommand =
        event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === 'com.example.notes/suggest-title';
      if (isTitleCommand) {
        void askForTitle('Fix the parser crash on empty input');
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});

async function askForTitle(note: string): Promise<void> {
  const payloadJson = JSON.stringify({ text: note });
  try {
    const replyJson = await call(TITLE_SERVICE, 'suggest', payloadJson);
    log('info', `title: ${replyJson}`);
  } catch (error: unknown) {
    log('warn', `title failed: ${String(error)}`);
  }
}
```

## When to use extension points instead

A service has one provider and many callers, and the caller pulls an answer. If many plugins should add to one plugin's behaviour, the owner declares an extension point and the others fill it. Use a collect point for data the owner reads, and a hook when the others' code must run inside the owner's flow. See [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/) and [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/).

## Other ways two parts of a plugin talk

A plugin service is for two different plugins. Two other channels cover the cases that look similar.

| Need | Use | Grant |
|---|---|---|
| The server side asks its own client side a question only a client can answer (terminal size, clipboard, theme) | `client-requests` | None for own sides |
| One plugin runs a command in another running Ilium session | `sessions.list-live`, `sessions.send` | `sessions.cross`, high risk |
| Choose from a list that a plugin provides | A plugin catalogue, see [Catalogs](/pages/api-catalogs/) | `catalogs.provide` |

`client-requests` needs the request `kind` declared in `contributes.client_requests`, with an optional `timeout_ms` from 1 to 30,000 and 5,000 by default. The client side receives a `client-request` event and answers with `respond`. A client that is detached completes the request with `not-found`. No answer in time completes it with `timed-out`.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭ client-requests ───────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ server  <span class="t-hi">request</span>(client, "terminal-size", 2000 ms)              │
│ client  <span class="t-hi">client-request</span> {call: 7, kind: terminal-size}          │
│ client  <span class="t-hi">respond</span>(7, ok)                                         │
│ server  <span class="t-ok">✓ request-completed: ok</span>                                │
│ <span class="t-dim">no client attached</span>  <span class="t-err">✗ failed(not-found)</span>                        │
│ <span class="t-dim">no answer in time</span>   <span class="t-err">✗ failed(timed-out)</span>                        │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The order of events of one client request and its two failure outcomes.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::client_requests;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

// Server side: ask the attached client for its terminal size.
pub async fn ask_client_size(client: ClientId) -> Result<String, PluginError> {
    client_requests::request(client, "terminal-size", "{}", 2_000).await
}

// Client side: answer the request. `call` is the number in the client-request event.
pub fn answer_size(call: u64, columns: u16, rows: u16) {
    let payload = format!("{{\"columns\":{columns},\"rows\":{rows}}}");
    client_requests::respond(call, Ok(payload));
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { request, respond } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/client-requests';

// Server side: ask the attached client for its terminal size.
export async function askClientSize(client: bigint): Promise<string> {
  return request(client, 'terminal-size', '{}', 2_000);
}

// Client side: answer the request. `call` is the number in the client-request event.
export function answerSize(call: bigint, columns: number, rows: number): void {
  respond(call, { tag: 'ok', val: JSON.stringify({ columns, rows }) });
}
```

## Kernel-known services: the inference provider

The inference provider is the typed service that most consumers use. A plugin that exports `inference-provider` must hold `inference.provide`. Its WIT shape is:

```wit
// Provider exports
record provider-call { call: u64, request: completion-request }
complete: func(call: provider-call) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
models: func() -> list<string>;

// Provider import, needs inference.provide
provider-reply: func(call: u64, outcome: result<completion, plugin-error>);
```

`complete` accepts the call and returns at once. Network work runs in a task that answers through `provider-reply` with the same call number. A consumer that must wait for a provider declares `requires.services` with `ilium:inference/provider@0.1.0`. The full contract is in [Inference provider](/pages/capability-inference-provide/).

## What the user sees

- The install review lists each grant, such as `services.use:com.example.titles/suggest`.
- If the user declines `services.provide`, the provider stays installed but is never registered. Every caller gets `not-found`.
- Failed calls appear in the caller's plugin log.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs com.example.notes-ui
<span class="t-warn">warn</span>  services.call com.example.titles/suggest
      <span class="t-err">not-found</span>: no installed and enabled provider
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The caller's log line for a service with no enabled provider.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Common mistakes

- Expecting `call` to wait for a provider that is not installed or is disabled. It returns `not-found` at once.
- Putting a version in a grant. Grants carry the bare name.
- Replying to a deferred call after 30 seconds. The late `reply` returns `not-found`.
- Sending large payloads. Each call and each reply is capped at 1 MiB, so pass identifiers and short summaries.
- Assuming that the consumer can read the provider's data. The consumer sees only the reply it asked for.

### Provider lifecycle

A provider stops after its consumers, in reverse activation order. When a provider fails, its consumers move to `waiting` and requests in flight complete as `cancelled`. They are not counted as consumer failures. When the provider restarts, waiting consumers resume. See [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/) and [Plugin lifecycle states](/pages/reference-plugin-lifecycle-states/). [LIF-280]

- [LIF-280] A provider failure MUST NOT count as a failure of its consumers. Test: trap a provider and read the consumer window.


Requirement ids for this page: [SVC-002], [SVC-003], [SVC-004], [SVC-006], [SVC-009], [SVC-012], [SVC-013], [SVC-014]. See the [requirements index](/pages/reference-requirements/).

# Extending core plugins

## Extending core plugins

Many features of Ilium are core plugins: titles, cost, fleet, notifications, search and more. [Core plugins](/pages/core-plugins/) lists them. This page answers one question: how does another plugin control, change or build on one of those features? It also answers a second one: how does a plugin let others build on it?

The short answer is that there are five ways, from light to heavy, and every core plugin supports the first four in the same way. The fifth is available for all core plugins except two. All five use the public contract `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. A third-party plugin gets nothing less than a core plugin gets.

### What you need

- **A grant for each way.** Observing needs a topic grant. Driving needs a service or command grant. Extending needs [extensions.contribute](/pages/capability-extensions-contribute/). Offering needs [extensions.provide](/pages/capability-extensions-provide/). Replacing needs no grant, but the user confirms it.
- **The page of the core plugin.** Every core plugin page has an **Extension points** section that lists its points, services and topics. [Reference: core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/) lists all of them in one place.
- **An SDK.** Rust: stable 1.90 or later with the `wasm32-wasip2` target and the `ilium-plugin-sdk` crate. TypeScript: Bun 1.2 or later and `@ilium/plugin-sdk`.

### The dogfooding rule

Core plugins are ordinary plugins. They are bundled, they have an id that starts with `ilium.`, and they are first-party (tier T1). They use only the public contract. They have no private API and no hidden hooks. Everything a core plugin can do, a third-party plugin can do with the same grants.

Two things follow from this rule.

- **If a core plugin lets you change something, it says so.** The lever is a service, a topic, a command, a pane kind or an extension point. It is documented on its page.
- **If you need a lever that does not exist, ask for a new point, not a private path.** A new point is a normal change to the core plugin's manifest. It gets a version, a risk level and a review.

The kernel keeps only the primitives: the PTY, the tree storage, rendering, the plugin host, the grants and the four pane primitives (terminal, agent, editor, basic). Core plugins own the behaviour on top of them. See [architecture](/pages/architecture/) and [primitives](/pages/primitives/).

### Five ways to work with a core feature

| Way | What you do | Weight | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Observe** | Read events, topics, catalogues and decoration slots. | Lightest. Read only. | A topic grant, for example `topics.subscribe:ilium.core.notifications/raised`. |
| **Drive** | Call a service or a command of the core plugin, or send an intent that it also uses. | You act, the core plugin runs the feature. | `services.use:<id>/<name>` or `commands.invoke:<id>/<command>`. |
| **Extend** | Fill an extension point: a collect entry (data) or a hook (code in the core plugin's flow). | You change what the core plugin does. It stays in charge. | `extensions.contribute:<id>/<point>`. |
| **Offer** | Declare your own extension points so others can extend you. | You become the owner of a slot. | `extensions.provide:<your-id>/<point>`. |
| **Replace** | Install a plugin that takes over the whole surface of a core plugin. | Heaviest. The built-in plugin is turned off. | `replaces` in the manifest and the user's confirmation. |

Pick the lightest way that does the job. Each step up costs more review, more risk and more work to keep in step with the core plugin.

#### I want to ... use ...

| I want to ... | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Know when a notice was raised | Observe | The topic `ilium.core.notifications/raised` pushes it to you. |
| Raise a notice myself | Drive | The service `ilium.core.notifications/notify` takes a title, a body and an urgency. |
| Stop some notices at night | Extend (hook) | `before-notify` is a `veto` hook. A handler that refuses stops the notice. |
| Add a chat webhook as a delivery channel | Extend (collect) | `channels` is a collect point. Your entry names a service of yours. |
| Rewrite text before it is copied | Extend (hook) | `ilium.core.smart-copy/after-copy` is a `transform` hook. |
| Add a new kind of thing to select in Smart Copy | Extend (collect) | `recognisers` is a collect point. |
| Let others add card actions to my board plugin | Offer | Declare `card-actions` as a collect point of your own. |
| Draw something next to a tree row | Observe and a kernel slot | Decoration slots are a kernel slot, not an extension point. See [tree.decorate](/pages/capability-tree-decorate/). |
| Change how the whole tree sorts and groups | Replace | No point covers the whole feature. |
| Show a fixed text in a menu | A provider | Use [menu provider](/pages/api-menu-provider/), a kernel slot. |

### One running scenario: quiet hours for notifications

The goal: the user wants no low-urgency notices between 22:00 and 07:00. The notifications feature is the core plugin `ilium.core.notifications`. Its surface, from [its page](/pages/core-plugin-notifications/):

- Service: `ilium.core.notifications/notify` (method `send`).
- Topic: `ilium.core.notifications/raised`, with `{ event, pane, urgency }`.
- Points: `before-notify` (hook, `veto`) and `channels` (collect).

Each way solves part of the goal, or a neighbouring goal. The sections below show the code.

#### Way 1: observe

Observe when you only need to know. This plugin counts how many notices were raised and writes the number to its log. It needs `topics.subscribe:ilium.core.notifications/raised` in its capabilities and lists the topic under `contributes.topics.subscribes`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct NoticeCounter {
    raised: u32,
}

impl Lifecycle for NoticeCounter {}

impl Handler for NoticeCounter {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            if let Event::TopicPublished(published) = event {
                if published.topic == "ilium.core.notifications/raised" {
                    self.raised += 1;
                    log::log(Level::Info, &format!("notices raised: {}", self.raised));
                }
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

let raised = 0;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'topic-published' && event.val.topic === 'ilium.core.notifications/raised') {
        raised += 1;
        log('info', `notices raised: ${raised}`);
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

An observer cannot change anything. It also never slows the core plugin down. See [messages and topics](/pages/api-messages-and-topics/).

#### Way 2: drive

Drive when you want the core plugin to do its job for you. This plugin raises a notice when its own job ends. It needs `services.use:ilium.core.notifications/notify`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::services;

// manifest: "services.use:ilium.core.notifications/notify"
async fn tell_user(title: &str) {
    let payload = format!(r#"{{"title":"{title}","body":"","urgency":"low"}}"#);
    if let Err(error) = services::call("ilium.core.notifications/notify", "send", &payload).await {
        log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("notify failed: {}", error.message));
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { call } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/services';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

// manifest: "services.use:ilium.core.notifications/notify"
export async function tellUser(title: string): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await call(
      'ilium.core.notifications/notify',
      'send',
      JSON.stringify({ title, body: '', urgency: 'low' }),
    );
  } catch (error) {
    log('warn', `notify failed: ${String(error)}`);
  }
}
```

The call passes through the same `before-notify` chain as every other notice, so a quiet hours extension affects your notice too. Services follow the rules in [services](/pages/services/) and [services API](/pages/api-services/).

#### Way 3: extend

Extend when you want to change what the core plugin does. This is the way that solves the quiet hours goal. The extension is a `veto` handler on `before-notify`. It refuses a notice of urgency `low` at night.

Manifest of the extension package:

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.quiet-hours",
  "exports": ["hook-handler"],
  "capabilities": {
    "server": ["extensions.contribute:ilium.core.notifications/before-notify"]
  },
  "contributes": {
    "extensions": [
      { "point": "ilium.core.notifications/before-notify@0.1.0", "id": "quiet-hours",
        "priority": 40, "handler": "quiet_hours" }
    ]
  }
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{HookCall, HookHandler, HookReply};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server", exports = ["hook-handler"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct QuietHours;

impl Lifecycle for QuietHours {}

impl Handler for QuietHours {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl HookHandler for QuietHours {
    fn handle_hook(&mut self, call: HookCall) -> HookReply {
        if call.extension != "quiet_hours" {
            return HookReply::Pass;
        }
        // Parse call.payload_json with a JSON library in a real plugin.
        let is_low = call.payload_json.contains(r#""urgency":"low""#);
        if is_low && is_quiet_time() {
            return HookReply::Refuse("quiet hours".to_string());
        }
        HookReply::Pass
    }
}

fn is_quiet_time() -> bool {
    false // stand-in for a clock read and the user's setting
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type HookCall, type HookReply } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';

function isQuietTime(): boolean {
  const hour = new Date().getHours();
  return hour >= 22 || hour < 7;
}

export const { lifecycle, handler, hookHandler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents() {
    return [];
  },
  handleHook(call: HookCall): HookReply {
    if (call.extension !== 'quiet_hours') {
      return { tag: 'pass' };
    }
    const payload = JSON.parse(call.payloadJson) as { urgency?: string };
    if (payload.urgency === 'low' && isQuietTime()) {
      return { tag: 'refuse', val: 'quiet hours' };
    }
    return { tag: 'pass' };
  },
});
```

The handler sees the payload of `before-notify` (event, pane, title, urgency, channels) and nothing else. If it is slow or fails, the notice goes out. This is called fail-open and it is explained below.

A collect extension is simpler. It holds an entry instead of code. This manifest adds a delivery channel to the `channels` point. The entry names a service of the same plugin that delivers one notice.

```json
{
  "point": "ilium.core.notifications/channels",
  "id": "team-chat",
  "entry": { "id": "team-chat", "title": "Team chat", "service": "com.example.chat/deliver" }
}
```

#### Way 4: offer

Offer when your own plugin has a place where others could add something. This plugin shows a dashboard. It declares a collect point `tiles` so that other plugins can add tiles. It needs `extensions.provide:com.example.dash/tiles`. The full owner code is in [extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/).

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.dash",
  "capabilities": { "server": ["extensions.provide:com.example.dash/tiles"] },
  "contributes": {
    "extension_points": [
      { "id": "tiles", "kind": "collect", "title": "Dashboard tiles",
        "entry_schema": { "type": "object", "required": ["id", "title"],
          "properties": { "id": { "type": "string" }, "title": { "type": "string" } } },
        "max_entries": 32, "version": "0.1.0" }
    ]
  }
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::extensions;

// manifest: "extensions.provide:com.example.dash/tiles"
fn tile_titles() -> Vec<String> {
    extensions::list("com.example.dash/tiles")
        .map(|entries| entries.into_iter().map(|entry| entry.entry_json).collect())
        .unwrap_or_default()
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { list } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/extensions';

// manifest: "extensions.provide:com.example.dash/tiles"
export function tileTitles(): string[] {
  return list('com.example.dash/tiles').map((entry) => entry.entryJson);
}
```

Offering is how a plugin of yours becomes a platform for other plugins. A core plugin is no different: its points are offered the same way.

<a id="replace"></a>

#### Way 5: replace

Replace when no lever is enough, for example when you want a different notification system. You install a plugin with `replaces`. It must provide the whole surface of the core plugin. Here the replacement is a plugin that offers notices in its own way and keeps the same service, topic and points.

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.notices",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "replaces": ["ilium.core.notifications"],
  "capabilities": {
    "server": [
      "services.provide:ilium.core.notifications/notify",
      "extensions.provide:ilium.core.notifications/before-notify",
      "extensions.provide:ilium.core.notifications/channels"
    ]
  }
}
```

The rules of replacement are in the section "Replacing a core plugin" below.

### Reading the surface of any core plugin

A core plugin lists what it offers in three places.

1. **Its own page.** Every `core-plugin-*` page has an **Extension points** section. It has a table of points (kind, what it does, payload, risk), a list of services, a list of topics and a **Replaceable** line.
2. **The reference.** [Reference: core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/) lists the points of all core plugins in one table. Use it to search.
3. **The Plugins screen.** Settings > Plugins > the plugin shows its **Surface**: the services, points, topics, commands and pane kinds it offers. The manifest carries the same list in `surface`. See [reference: manifest](/pages/reference-manifest/).

Names follow one pattern:

| Item | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Point | `<plugin-id>/<point>` | `ilium.core.fleet/before-broadcast` |
| Service | `<plugin-id>/<name>` | `ilium.core.fleet/broadcast` |
| Topic | `<plugin-id>/<name>` | `ilium.core.tree/changed` |
| Command | `<plugin-id>/<command>` | `ilium.core.kanban/open-board` |

A third-party plugin that wants a core topic lists it in `contributes.topics.subscribes` and holds the matching topic grant. A core service uses the normal `services.provide` and `services.use` grants. Services named `ilium.core.<plugin>/<name>` are stable and need no `unstable` opt-in, to call them or to provide them as a replacement ([Versioning](/pages/versioning/)). See [capability: services](/pages/capability-services/).

### Timing of hooks on core points

A hook on a core plugin's point runs on the side that owns the point (see the Side column of [Core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/)), one handler after another, under the deadlines in [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/) (20 ms per handler on every core hook, 100 ms for the chain, measured from the first handler). For `veto`, `transform` and `first` points the core plugin holds that one action until the chain completes (at most the 100 ms cap plus one deadline) and keeps serving other events meanwhile. For `observe` points the action does not wait, and observe handlers may run after it. [EXT-029] See [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/).

### Ordering, priorities and the user

- **Priority.** A contribution has a priority from 0 to 100, 50 by default. Lower runs first. Among contributions of equal priority, T1 comes before T2 and T3, then plugin id order, then extension id order. The declared priority is kept.
- **User order.** On the owner's Extensions tab the user can move any contributor up or down and turn it off. The user's order is a stored list per point. It overrides priority and tier, a contributor installed later runs after the stored items, and an update keeps the stored position. The host stores it, not the plugin.
- **Chains.** A `transform` chain passes each handler the output of the previous one. A `veto` chain stops at the first refusal. A `first` chain stops at the first answer. An `observe` chain calls everyone.
- **Fail open.** A handler that times out, traps or errors counts as `pass`. A timeout never vetoes. A breach is a timeout, a trap, an error return, an oversize or schema-failing reply, a CPU overrun or a skip because the instance was busy. Three consecutive breaches stop that extension until the contributor's instance restarts or the user presses Reset. The user sees `stopped after 3 failures` and a Reset button. The whole chain has a cap of 100 ms, and handlers that have not started by then are skipped.
- **Dormant contributions.** A contribution is dormant when its owner is not installed, is disabled, or does not satisfy its `@version`. It stays in the package and does nothing. It becomes active when the owner appears, and the Plugins screen shows `waiting for <owner-id>` until then. Install never fails because an owner is missing. See [lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/).
- **Point versions.** Every point has a semver `version` for its schema. A contributor can write `<point>@<minimum-version>`. The match is: same major; minor at least the requested one; for major 0 the minor must be equal; patch is ignored. A contribution without `@version` matches any owner version. A contribution that does not match stays dormant. See [versioning](/pages/versioning/).

A short rule for choosing a mode when you offer a point: use `observe` when you only tell others, `transform` when others may change data, `veto` when others may stop an action, and `first` when exactly one answer is needed.

### Security and consent

- **Grants are per point.** `extensions.contribute:<plugin-id>/<point>` names one point. Wildcards are refused. There is no grant that covers every point. See [capability: extensions.contribute](/pages/capability-extensions-contribute/).
- **High-risk points.** An owner marks a point `risk: "high"` when its handlers can see or change sensitive data or stop sensitive actions. Examples are text sent to a terminal, a broadcast to many agents, a text trigger about to fire and a scheduled input about to be sent. Contributing to such a point is a high-risk (H) grant. The review dialog shows a warning, and the row starts unchecked.
- **What a hook can see.** Only the payload of the owner's `payload_schema`. Payload fields are chosen by the owner, and they are listed in the table of the core plugin. A handler cannot read the owner's state or the other handlers.
- **What a hook can do.** Only what the mode allows. Replies the mode does not allow count as `pass`.
- **The user stays in charge.** The review dialog groups the package's extensions under **Adds to other plugins**. The user can turn any extension off later.
- **Replacement is a consent.** The user must confirm that the built-in plugin is turned off. See below.

See [security](/pages/security/) for the grant risk table and [packages](/pages/packages/) for the review dialog.

### Replacing a core plugin

A package with `"replaces": ["ilium.core.titles"]` can take the place of a core plugin. The list has at most 4 ids.

- **Which plugins.** A core plugin that can be replaced carries `"replaceable": true` and a `surface` list in its manifest (fields in [Manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/#top-level-keys)). `ilium.core.sessions` and `ilium.core.settings` are not replaceable, because they protect saved sessions and they host the Plugins screen itself.
- **The whole surface.** The replacement must provide every `surface` item of the replaced plugin: its services, points, commands, pane kinds, topics and cli commands. Values in `surface` are `kind:name` pairs. A `points` item matches only with the same kind, the same mode and the same major version; a `services` item needs the same method names and the same major version. Otherwise `manifest.replaces-surface-incomplete` names the item and the reason. The error lists the missing items. The surface is checked again at each enable and after each Ilium update. An enabled replacement that no longer covers the surface is turned off, the built-in plugin comes back, and a notice names the missing items. [EXT-051]
- **One at a time.** Several installed packages may replace one core plugin, and at most one is enabled. Enabling another one asks the user and turns the previous replacement off. Only one of the pair (built-in and replacement) is enabled. When the user enables the replacement, the dialog says `Replaces Titles and organisation. The built-in plugin is turned off while this one is on.` The user confirms. Turning the replacement off or uninstalling it turns the built-in plugin back on.
- **Uninstall of the replacement.** Removing the replacement, or turning it off, turns the built-in plugin back on. See the [uninstall cascade](/pages/lifecycle/#uninstall-cascade). The built-in plugin's data was never read or changed by the replacement.
- **Contributions carry over.** Standard contributions of other plugins to the replaced points move to the replacement after a notice. High-risk ones are suspended until the user confirms them for the new owner ([SEC-304]).
- **What is lost.** The settings tabs, commands and pane kinds of the replaced plugin disappear while it is off. Its stored data stays on disk and is not read by the replacement. When the built-in plugin comes back, it finds its data as it left it.
- **Install errors.** `manifest.replaces-unknown` (no such plugin), `manifest.replaces-not-replaceable`, `manifest.replaces-surface-incomplete`, `manifest.replaces-cycle` (a package lists its own id, or an id twice). A list of more than 4 ids fails with `manifest.schema`.

A replacement carries a real cost. It must keep up with every new point of the core plugin. Prefer extending when you can.

### What the user keeps when a core plugin is off

Extending or replacing a core plugin never removes what the user already has. When the plugin is disabled, the kernel fallback applies and the stored data stays. The table for all 30 core plugins is in [kernel and boot](/pages/reference-kernel-and-boot/). A replacement MUST provide the `surface` of the plugin it replaces, and it MUST keep the CLI commands of the replaced plugin (see [CLI compatibility](/pages/reference-cli-compatibility/)). [COR-022] [COR-040]

### Testing and debugging

- **Unit tests.** The fake host in [testing](/pages/testing/) runs one plugin instance with the grants you give it, and `FakeSession` runs several plugins and core extension point stubs together. Deliver a batch of events and check the submissions. A hook handler is a plain function over a payload, so you can also call it directly in a test.
- **Requests.** `run-hook` is a request. A test completes it by hand with `host.complete(request_id, outcome)` and checks the log. The method is described in [testing](/pages/testing/) under requests, jobs and services.
- **Fixtures.** `ilium plugin test` runs every fixture, compares its expectation file, and exits 3 when one differs. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).
- **Logs.** `ilium plugin logs <id> --tail 20` shows the log of one plugin. The host writes the extension codes there: `extension.handler-timeout`, `extension.reply-not-allowed`, `extension.schema-mismatch`, `extension.disabled`. [Debugging](/pages/debugging/) explains the log format and traps.
- **Development reload.** `ilium plugin dev` reloads a plugin when you rebuild it. See [debugging](/pages/debugging/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Is there one place to see everything a core plugin exposes?**
Yes. The **Extension points** section of its page, and the **Surface** on the Plugins screen. [Reference: core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/) has all of them in one list.

**Can I add a hook to a core plugin that has no point for it?**
No. A hook exists only where the owner declared a point. If you need one, ask for a new point on that core plugin. It is a normal manifest change with a version.

**Can a hook break the core plugin?**
A hook can refuse or change data only where the mode allows it. A hook that is late, traps or errors is ignored, and three consecutive breaches stop it. A hook cannot crash the owner.

**Does a hook slow the feature down?**
A little. T1 handlers share the process. T2 and T3 handlers cost one helper round trip. A handler gets 5 to 50 ms (20 by default) and a chain gets 100 ms. Owners should not put hooks on a path hotter than about 100 calls per second.

**What if the owner is not installed?**
Your contribution is dormant. It does nothing, and the Plugins screen shows `waiting for <owner-id>`. It becomes active when the owner appears.

**What is the difference between a service and an extension point?**
A service has one provider and many callers, and a caller pulls an answer. An extension point has one owner and many contributors, and the owner decides when to read data or run handlers. See [services](/pages/services/).

**What is the difference between an extension point and a kernel slot?**
A kernel slot, such as a decoration slot, a menu provider or a status segment, is defined by the kernel. An extension point is defined by any plugin. Extension points do not replace kernel slots.

**Can two plugins fill the same point?**
Yes. Up to `max_handlers` handlers (8) or `max_entries` entries (64 on core points) per point. They run in the order described above, and the user can reorder them. Contributors beyond the cap are dormant with the reason `point full (<n>)`.

**Can I replace a core plugin and keep its data?**
No. The replacement does not read the replaced plugin's stored data. The data stays on disk for the built-in plugin to use when it returns.

**Can I replace the sessions or settings plugin?**
No. `ilium.core.sessions` and `ilium.core.settings` have `replaceable: false`.

**Does a wildcard grant exist?**
No. `manifest.grant-wildcard` refuses it. List each point.

When a replacement plugin is disabled by failure, the built-in core plugin it replaced turns on again and a notice says so. The replacement returns only when you enable it. [LIF-273]

- [LIF-273] A replacement disabled by failure MUST re-enable the replaced core plugin with a visible notice. Test: the replacement is disabled by the restart and disable rule (three crashes).

### See also

- [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/) for the full interface, the hook modes and the error codes.
- [Reference: core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/) for the points of every core plugin.
- [extensions.provide](/pages/capability-extensions-provide/) and [extensions.contribute](/pages/capability-extensions-contribute/) for the grants.
- [Core plugins](/pages/core-plugins/) for the list of core plugins.
- [Services](/pages/services/), [services API](/pages/api-services/), [messages and topics](/pages/api-messages-and-topics/) and [menu provider](/pages/api-menu-provider/) for the other mechanisms.

- [Testing](/pages/testing/) and [debugging](/pages/debugging/) for tools.

Checked against `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

### Security

Risk marks follow [SEC-280]; replacement rules are [SEC-300] to [SEC-306] in [Extension security](/pages/reference-extension-security/).

# Testing plugins

## Testing plugins

This page is the how-to. The exact contract of the harness, with every method, error code and limit, is [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/). If this page and the reference differ, the reference wins.

A plugin is tested against the same contract that the host runs it under. You write the test in Rust or in TypeScript. The test creates a fake host, grants the capabilities the plugin asks for, delivers events and checks the submissions that come back. For a view, the test renders the view into a grid of cells and compares the text. None of this needs a terminal, a window, a running Ilium or a real agent, so a test runs in milliseconds.

Ilium's conformance suite uses fixtures of this kind. Each WIT interface has its own corpus, and the Rust and the TypeScript guest of the suite must both pass a fixture before the interface is released. The fixtures ship with Ilium's test suite, not with user plugins. You can read them as examples and write fixtures for your own plugin in the same shape.

## You will need

- A Rust plugin with the `testing` feature of `ilium-plugin-sdk`, or a TypeScript plugin with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`.
- The capabilities of the plugin in its manifest. The test grants the same ones with `grant(...)`. A capability that the test does not grant is declined, as it is when the user says no.
- No WebAssembly target. The `testing` feature replaces the host calls with the fake host, so `cargo test` links the plugin code for the host target.
- Knowledge of [events and intents](/pages/events-and-intents/) and of [the UI model](/pages/ui-model/).

| Task | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|
| Harness | `ilium_plugin_sdk::testing::FakeHost` | `createFakeHost()` from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/testing` |
| Runner | `cargo test` | `bun test` against the source |
| Grant a capability | `.grant("tree.read")` | `.grant('tree.read')` |
| Start the plugin | `host.activate::<MyPlugin>()` | `host.activate({ lifecycle, handler })` |
| Deliver events | `host.deliver(events)` returns the submissions | `host.deliver(events)` |
| Render a view | `host.render(view, width, height)` | `host.render(view, width, height)` |

## Fixture files

A fixture is a JSON file with a `schema` key and the state keys that the test needs. An unknown key fails with `fixture.unknown-key`. It describes the state that the plugin reads and the events that the test delivers.

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "tree": [],
  "panes": [],
  "agents": [],
  "settings": {},
  "events": [
    {
      "tag": "agent-activity-changed",
      "val": { "node": 42, "previous": "idle", "current": "working", "revision": 1 }
    }
  ]
}
```

| Key | Holds |
|---|---|
| `schema` | Always 1 |
| `tree` | Node views that the tree returns to the plugin |
| `panes` | Pane information for terminal and basic panes |
| `agents` | Agent panes and their current activity |
| `settings` | Current values of the plugin's settings |
| `events` | Events that the test delivers, each written as `{"tag", "val"}` |

The full key list, with `grants`, `tier`, `side`, `clock`, `storage`, `files`, `http`, `processes`, `completions`, `lifecycle` and `expect_state`, is in [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/#fixtures-and-expectation-files). `with_fixture(path)` loads the state keys into the fake host. `fixture_events()` returns the decoded `events` list, so the test can pass it to `deliver`. A fixture holds inputs only. The expected submissions and outcomes are asserted in test code, where the test names them.

## The fake host

A fake host runs one plugin instance. It keeps the grants, the limits and the error codes of the real host. Its main methods are:

| Method | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `new()` | `FakeHost` | A host with no grants |
| `grant(name)` | `FakeHost` | Grants one capability, for example `tree.decorate` |
| `with_fixture(path)` | `FakeHost` | Loads the state and events of a fixture file |
| `activate::<P>()` | `PluginHandle` | Runs the activation of a Rust plugin type that is `Default`. Panics if activation fails. `try_activate` returns a `Result`. |
| `deliver(events)` | `Vec<Submission>` | Runs `on-events` once for the batch |
| `render(view, width, height)` | `Screen` | Runs `views.render` and draws the tree into cells |
| `complete(request_id, outcome)` | none | Completes a request that the plugin started |
| `settle()` | none | Delivers queued `request-completed` events until the queues are empty |
| `grant_now(name)`, `revoke(name)` | none | Change a grant after activation |
| `fixture_events()` | `Vec<Event>` | The events of the loaded fixture |
| `outcomes()` | `Vec<Outcome>` | Completions of the submissions, in submission order |
| `pending_requests()` | `Vec<RequestId>` | Requests the plugin started and the test has not completed |
| `logs()` | `Vec<LogLine>` | Lines that the plugin wrote to its log |

In TypeScript the same methods use camelCase names, and `activateModule(path)` imports a fresh copy of the plugin module for each test. Outcomes are queued as `request-completed` events, and `settle()` delivers them. `FakeHost::for_manifest(path)` takes the grants, side and tier from the manifest. `Screen` has `row(index)`, which returns the text of one row, and `cell(row, column)`, which returns the symbol and the style of one cell.

## Worked example: a handler test

The plugin below sets a badge on an agent's node when the agent starts working. It is the server side of the Rust SDK described on [the Rust SDK page](/pages/rust-sdk/). The tests follow it in the same file. The TypeScript version follows the Rust one.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::AgentActivityEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SetDecorationSpec;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::AgentActivity;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Hello;

impl Lifecycle for Hello {
    fn activate(&mut self, _context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for Hello {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::AgentActivityChanged(AgentActivityEvent { node, current, .. }) = event
            else {
                continue;
            };
            if current != AgentActivity::Working {
                continue;
            }
            submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
                node,
                slot: "hello".into(),
                content: vec![Span::plain("hi")],
                icon: None,
                sort_key: None,
                persist: false,
            })));
        }
        submissions
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use ilium_plugin_sdk::testing::FakeHost;

    fn became(current: AgentActivity) -> Event {
        Event::AgentActivityChanged(AgentActivityEvent {
            node: 42,
            previous: AgentActivity::Idle,
            current,
            revision: 1,
        })
    }

    fn host_with_grants() -> FakeHost {
        FakeHost::new().grant("agent.read").grant("tree.decorate")
    }

    #[test]
    fn working_agent_gets_a_badge() {
        let mut host = host_with_grants();
        host.activate::<Hello>();
        let submissions = host.deliver(vec![became(AgentActivity::Working)]);
        assert_eq!(submissions.len(), 1);
        assert!(matches!(submissions[0].intent, Intent::SetDecoration(_)));
    }

    #[test]
    fn idle_agent_gets_no_badge() {
        let mut host = host_with_grants();
        host.activate::<Hello>();
        assert!(host.deliver(vec![became(AgentActivity::Idle)]).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn fixture_events_produce_one_badge() {
        let mut host = host_with_grants().with_fixture("tests/fixtures/agent-working.json");
        host.activate::<Hello>();
        let events = host.fixture_events();
        assert_eq!(host.deliver(events).len(), 1);
    }
}
```

Run the tests from the plugin directory with `cargo test badge`. The filter selects the tests whose names contain `badge`.

**TypeScript**

The TypeScript plugin behaves the same way. Its handler is exported as the pair that `definePlugin` returns, and the test runs it with `bun test`.

```typescript
// src/plugin.ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { span, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

let nextCorrelation = 1n;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'agent-activity-changed') continue;
      if (event.val.current !== 'working') continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'set-decoration',
          val: {
            node: event.val.node,
            slot: 'hello',
            content: [span('hi')],
            icon: undefined,
            sortKey: undefined,
            persist: false,
          },
        },
        correlation: nextCorrelation++,
        dedupKey: undefined,
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/plugin.test.ts
import { expect, test } from 'bun:test';
import type { Event } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { createFakeHost } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/testing';
import { handler, lifecycle } from './plugin';

function activity(current: 'working' | 'idle'): Event {
  return {
    tag: 'agent-activity-changed',
    val: { node: 42n, previous: 'idle', current, revision: 1n },
  };
}

test('working agent gets a badge', async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().grant('agent.read').grant('tree.decorate');
  await host.activate({ lifecycle, handler });
  const submissions = host.deliver([activity('working')]);
  expect(submissions.length).toBe(1);
  expect(submissions[0].intent.tag).toBe('set-decoration');
});

test('idle agent gets no badge', async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().grant('agent.read').grant('tree.decorate');
  await host.activate({ lifecycle, handler });
  expect(host.deliver([activity('idle')])).toEqual([]);
});
```

## Render tests

A render test draws a view on the headless host and compares the text of the rows. The host draws the tree that `views.render` returns into a buffer of cells, so the test reads exactly the text and the styles that a user would see. Borders are the rounded `╭╮╰╯` corners, and a `leader-row` shows its `…` leaders, so the expected strings contain the same characters as the real Ilium.

**Rust**

```rust
#[test]
fn notes_panel_lists_open_counts() {
    let mut host = FakeHost::new()
        .grant("tree.read")
        .with_fixture("tests/fixtures/notes-panel.json");
    host.activate::<NotesPane>();
    let screen = host.render(ViewTarget::Pane(42), 40, 4);
    assert_eq!(screen.row(1), "│ claude-review …………………………… [2 open] │");
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { expect, test } from 'bun:test';
import { createFakeHost } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/testing';
import { handler, lifecycle, views } from './plugin';

test('notes panel lists open counts', async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().grant('tree.read').withFixture('tests/fixtures/notes-panel.json');
  await host.activate({ lifecycle, handler, views });
  const screen = host.render({ tag: 'pane', val: 42n }, 40, 4);
  expect(screen.row(1)).toBe('│ claude-review …………………………… [2 open] │');
});
```

When a row differs, the assertion prints the expected and the actual text. The render below shows such a failure for a notes panel where the count of open notes is missing.

<figure>
<pre class="term">
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> cargo test notes_panel_lists_open_counts
<span class="t-err">assertion `left == right` failed</span>
  left: <span class="t-err">"│ claude-review …………………………… [0 open] │"</span>
 right: <span class="t-dim">"│ claude-review …………………………… [2 open] │"</span>
<span class="t-err">test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed</span>
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. A render assertion failure: the count of open notes is wrong in the row.</figcaption>
</figure>

Render tests check the text and the styles of the cells. They do not show how the output looks in a real terminal. Fonts, colour contrast and animation still need a person to look at the result.

## Testing views with the extended widgets

The extended widgets are drawn by the same fake host, so a test of a `check-list`, a `meter`, a `notice`, a `progress-row` or a `dialog` reads their rows the same way. Three rules keep these tests stable:

- Assert the characters the user sees (`[x]`, `█`, `▶ RUNNING`), not the widget props. The props are the plugin's business, and the render is the contract.
- A widget that animates, such as `spinner`, shows its first frame in the fake host, and one static frame when the test sets reduced motion. Do not assert later frames.
- Give every widget a `key`, so a test can send an action to it by name.

The render below is what a member picker draws when one of three items is checked.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Members ────────────────────────╮
│ <span class="t-dim">Pick the agents to include</span>             │
│ [x] claude: refactor                   │
│ [ ] codex: tests                       │
│ [ ] codex: docs <span class="t-dim">(frozen)</span>               │
╰────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. A check-list inside a block. The first item is checked.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Rust**

```rust
#[test]
fn picking_a_member_updates_the_checklist() {
    let mut host = FakeHost::new().grant("panes.read");
    host.activate::<MemberPicker>();
    let first = host.render(ViewTarget::Pane(7), 40, 6);
    assert_eq!(first.row(2), "│ [x] claude: refactor                   │");

    host.deliver(vec![action("members", ActionKind::Changed, Some(ActionValue::ItemState("p2".into(), TriState::On)))]);
    let second = host.render(ViewTarget::Pane(7), 40, 6);
    assert_eq!(second.row(3), "│ [x] codex: tests                       │");
}

fn action(key: &str, kind: ActionKind, value: Option<ActionValue>) -> Event {
    Event::UiAction(UiAction {
        view: ViewTarget::Pane(7),
        key: key.into(),
        action_id: key.into(),
        kind,
        value,
    })
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
function action(key: string, kind: ActionKind, value?: ActionValue): Event {
  return { tag: 'ui-action', val: { view: { tag: 'pane', val: 7n }, key, actionId: key, kind, value } };
}

test('picking a member updates the checklist', async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().grant('panes.read');
  await host.activate({ lifecycle, handler, views });
  expect(host.render(view, 40, 6).row(2)).toBe('│ [x] claude: refactor                   │');

  host.deliver([action('members', 'changed', { tag: 'item-state', val: ['p2', 'on'] })]);
  expect(host.render(view, 40, 6).row(3)).toBe('│ [x] codex: tests                       │');
});
```

## Testing pointer and keyboard input

A node with `pointer-events` sends `pointer` actions with a `view-pointer` value: the kind (`down`, `up`, `move`, `drag`, wheel kinds), the button, the modifiers, the cell inside the widget, the position inside the cell from 0 to 255 (128 when the terminal reports whole cells), and the click count. A test builds that value and delivers it like any other action. The same pattern covers `hover-enter`, `hover-leave`, `drag-over` and `resized`.

**Rust**

```rust
#[test]
fn double_click_on_a_cell_opens_the_file() {
    let mut host = FakeHost::new().grant("fs.read:project");
    host.activate::<Explorer>();
    let pointer = ViewPointer {
        kind: PointerKind::Down,
        button: PointerButton::Left,
        modifiers: PointerModifiers::empty(),
        column: 4,
        row: 2,
        sub_x: 128,
        sub_y: 128,
        clicks: 2,
    };
    let submissions = host.deliver(vec![action("files", ActionKind::Pointer, Some(ActionValue::Pointer(pointer)))]);
    assert!(matches!(submissions[0].intent, Intent::EditorOpen(_)));
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
test('double click on a cell opens the file', async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().grant('fs.read:project');
  await host.activate({ lifecycle, handler, views });
  const pointer = {
    kind: 'down', button: 'left',
    modifiers: { shift: false, control: false, alt: false },
    column: 4, row: 2, subX: 128, subY: 128, clicks: 2,
  } as const;
  const submissions = host.deliver([action('files', 'pointer', { tag: 'pointer', val: pointer })]);
  expect(submissions[0].intent.tag).toBe('editor-open');
});
```

Keyboard input is tested the same way, one level up: send the `ui-action` that the widget would send after the key (`changed`, `submitted`, `activated`), because the host, not the plugin, handles the key itself. The key table of each widget is in [Widget catalogue](/pages/widgets-index/).

## Golden renders

A golden render is a text file that holds the expected rows of a whole view. The test draws the view, joins the rows with line breaks, and compares the result with the file. A mismatch prints the first differing row. `assert_golden` (`assertGolden` in TypeScript) reads the file, converts line endings and prints the diff; `ILIUM_PLUGIN_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1` rewrites it. Keep golden files next to the fixtures, for example `tests/golden/files-panel.txt`, and review each change to a golden file like a change to code.

**Rust**

```rust
fn screen_text(screen: &Screen, height: u16) -> String {
    (0..height).map(|index| screen.row(index)).collect::<Vec<_>>().join("\n")
}

#[test]
fn files_panel_matches_golden() {
    let mut host = FakeHost::new().with_fixture("tests/fixtures/files.json");
    host.activate::<Explorer>();
    let drawn = screen_text(&host.render(ViewTarget::Pane(42), 40, 6), 6);
    assert_golden("tests/golden/files-panel.txt", &drawn);
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
function screenText(screen: Screen, height: number): string {
  return Array.from({ length: height }, (_, index) => screen.row(index)).join('\n');
}

test('files panel matches golden', async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().withFixture('tests/fixtures/files.json');
  await host.activate({ lifecycle, handler, views });
  const drawn = screenText(host.render({ tag: 'pane', val: 42n }, 40, 6), 6);
  assertGolden('tests/golden/files-panel.txt', drawn);
});
```

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Files ──────────────────────────╮
│ README.md ………………………………………………………… <span class="t-dim">2 KiB</span> │
│ CHANGELOG.md ………………………………………………… <span class="t-dim">9 KiB</span> │
│ <span class="t-dim">Esc close · Enter open</span>                 │
╰────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The content of a golden file for a small file panel: rounded border, title icons, leader dots and a hint line. The test compares it character by character.</figcaption>
</figure>

Golden files hold the Unicode characters of the real UI. Never replace `…`, `╭`, `▶` or `⠋` with ASCII stand-ins in a golden file: the test would then pass while the real render differs. The stable-glyph mode is a user setting, and a test for it sets the fake host's icon mode and keeps a second golden file.

## Testing requests, jobs and services

A call that returns a request id, such as `fs.read-all`, `jobs.start`, `services.call`, `catalogs.query-async` or `geocode.search`, is tested by completing the request by hand: the test calls `host.complete(request_id, outcome)` with the outcome the real host would send, then delivers the `request-completed` event that follows. This covers `ok`, `cancelled` and each `failed(code)` without a network, a disk or a second plugin.

**Rust**

```rust
#[test]
fn failed_import_is_logged_not_trapped() {
    let mut host = FakeHost::new().grant("jobs.run");
    host.activate::<WorldImporter>();
    host.deliver(vec![command("com.example.worlds/import")]);
    let request = host.pending_requests()[0];
    host.complete(request, Outcome::Failed(PluginError::timed_out("import timed out")));
    assert!(host.logs().iter().any(|line| line.message.contains("import failed")));
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
test('failed import is logged, not trapped', async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().grant('jobs.run');
  await host.activate({ lifecycle, handler });
  host.deliver([command('com.example.worlds/import')]);
  const request = host.pendingRequests()[0];
  host.complete(request, { tag: 'failed', val: { code: 'timed-out', message: 'import timed out' } });
  expect(host.logs().some((line) => line.message.includes('import failed'))).toBe(true);
});
```

## Running tests from the command line

`ilium plugin test` is the gate for fixtures. It runs every fixture against the built component, compares each expectation file, and exits 3 when one differs or the component traps. Run the project's own unit tests with `cargo test` or `bun test`, and put both in CI. The full flags are in [Plugin command-line reference](/pages/reference-plugin-cli/).

<figure>
<pre class="term">
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin test
agent-working.json   pass  12 ms
agent-idle.json      pass   9 ms
summary: 2 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped (21 ms)
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. Text output on a terminal: one line per fixture and a summary line. Piped output or `--json` prints JSONL records instead. The exit code is 0.</figcaption>
</figure>

The command compares the output of each fixture with its `.expect.json` file. A fixture without an expectation file only has to run without a trap. Expectation files use the match modes `exact`, `ordered` and `subset`, which [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/) defines.

## Faking the world

The fake host also fakes the clock, the file system, processes, the network, storage and settings. Each fake is deterministic, and an unexpected call to a fake process or network fails the test. Register what the plugin may call before you deliver the events.

```rust
let mut host = FakeHost::for_manifest("manifest.json").unwrap();
host.processes().expect("git", &["status", "--short"]).returns("M src/lib.rs\n", 0);
host.fs().write("project:notes.md", b"# Notes");
host.activate::<Plugin>();
host.advance_clock(60_000);
host.settle();
```

```ts
const host = createFakeHost().forManifest('manifest.json');
host.processes().expect('git', ['status', '--short']).returns('M src/lib.rs\n', 0);
host.fs().write('project:notes.md', new TextEncoder().encode('# Notes'));
await host.activateModule('../src/server');
host.advanceClock(60_000);
await host.settle();
```

## Tests with more than one plugin

Use `FakeSession` when the behaviour crosses a boundary: two sides of one plugin, a service call between plugins, or a core extension point. `FakeHost` runs one plugin.

```rust
let mut session = FakeSession::new();
session.install("../provider").install("../consumer").start();
session.plugin("example.consumer").deliver(vec![ask_event()]);
session.pump();
assert_eq!(session.plugin("example.consumer").outcomes(), vec![Outcome::Ok]);
```

## Failure injection, replay and coverage

- `inject_trap(code)` and `inject_failure(import, error)` make the next call fail, so you can test the restart rule and error paths.
- `fuzz_run(seed, rounds)` delivers random valid event batches. A failure prints the seed.
- `record_to(path)` and `replay(path)` record and re-run a session.
- `ilium plugin test --coverage --min-coverage 80` also runs your unit tests under a coverage tool and exits 3 below the minimum.
- `ilium plugin test --conformance` runs the [conformance suite](/pages/reference-conformance-suite/).

## Test lanes

A plugin usually has three lanes of tests. Fixture and render tests run on the headless host. End-to-end checks run the installed package in a real Ilium.

## Lifecycle tests

The fake host can drive the lifecycle of [Plugin lifecycle states](/pages/reference-plugin-lifecycle-states/) without a real server. These methods exist on `FakeHost` for contract `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `deactivate(reason)` | Calls `deactivate` with a reason and returns the restore bytes. |
| `restart_with(bytes)` | Activates a new instance with `restored` set. |
| `inject_trap(code)` | Traps the instance with a trap code as a failure and applies the restart rule. |
| `advance_clock(ms)` | Moves the fixture clock, so back-off and windows pass at once. |
| `revoke(grant)`, `grant_now(grant)` | Fire the `revoked` and `granted` reasons. |
| `with_storage_snapshot(path)` | Starts with the storage of a JSON file. |
| `with_data_version(n)` | Sets the stored data version before activation. |
| `crash_after_journal_write()` | Traps after the next journal append is committed. |
| `failures()` | Returns the failure window of the plugin side. |

```rust
#[test]
fn third_failure_disables() {
    let mut host = FakeHost::for_manifest("manifest.json").unwrap();
    host.activate::<Plugin>();
    host.inject_trap("trap.panic");   // restarts after 1 s
    host.advance_clock(1_000);
    host.inject_trap("trap.panic");   // restarts after 5 s
    host.advance_clock(5_000);
    host.inject_trap("trap.panic");   // third failure
    assert_eq!(host.lifecycle_state(), LifecycleState::StoppedByFailure);
    assert_eq!(host.failures().len(), 3);
}
```

```ts
test("restore bytes survive an upgrade", async () => {
  const host = createFakeHost().forManifest("manifest.json");
  await host.activateModule("../src/server");
  const bytes = await host.deactivate("upgrade");
  await host.restartWith(bytes!);
  expect(host.restored()).toEqual(bytes);
});
```

In an `ilium plugin test` fixture file, the keys `lifecycle` (a list of steps such as `trap`, `advance`, `deactivate`) and `expect_state` run the same steps.

### Host conformance checklist

A host implementation passes when each line holds. Each line cites the requirement that defines it.

- Back-off is 1 s then 5 s and the third failure disables (LIF-025 to LIF-042).
- Activation order follows dependencies (LIF-045 to LIF-059).
- Package and instance transitions match the tables (LIF-001 to LIF-020).
- Install, update and rollback follow the pipeline (LIF-065 to LIF-094).
- Migration runs once, with backup (LIF-100 to LIF-116).
- Health and deadline bounds hold (LIF-122 to LIF-138).
- Capacity refusals do not count as failures (LIF-141).
- The survival matrix holds (LIF-150 to LIF-157).

- [LIF-279] The fake host MUST offer the methods in the table, and its results MUST match the real host for the lines above. Test: run the same fixtures against both.

## Edge cases and error codes

A test should cover the refusal path as well as the success path. The fake host returns the same codes as the real host.

| Situation | What the test sees | Code and retry |
|---|---|---|
| The tree capability is declined or not requested | No tree events arrive. `get` returns none and `find` returns an empty list. The plugin log gets one warn line that names `tree.read`. | No error code |
| An intent needs a grant that the test did not give | The offending submission is `refused(not-permitted)`. The other submissions of the batch are `refused(cancelled)` with the message `batch refused: submission <index>`. | `not-permitted`, no retry |
| A submission is malformed, such as a missing dedup key for `send-input` | The whole batch is refused. | `invalid-argument`, fix the call |
| A decoration uses a slot that the manifest does not declare | The submission is `refused(invalid-argument)`. | `invalid-argument`, fix the call |
| A decoration targets a node that no longer exists | The submission is `refused(not-found)`. | `not-found`, no retry |
| The decoration quota is full | The submission is `refused(quota-exceeded)`. | `quota-exceeded`, free resources first |
| A restored pane refuses input | The submission is `refused(pane-not-ready)`. | `pane-not-ready`, retry after `tree-changed` |

A panic in a Rust test or a thrown exception in a TypeScript test fails that test. In the real host the same failure is a trap. The host writes it to the plugin log as `trap in <export>` with the reason. See [debugging](/pages/debugging/) for how to read the trap entry.

## What the user sees

Tests run on the developer's machine only. `cargo test` reports each test with `ok` or `FAILED`, and it prints the values of a failed assertion. `ilium plugin test` prints the JSON lines shown above. The end user sees none of this. A user sees the result only when the built package runs in Ilium, for example as a badge on a node in the tree or as a panel row with the right text.

## Advice

- Write one fixture for each event that the plugin handles, and one for each error that it expects.
- Keep fixtures small. A fixture that checks one behaviour is easy to read when it fails.
- Grant exactly the capabilities in the manifest. A test that grants more than the manifest asks for hides a missing entry.
- Test the refusal path too: a missing grant should produce `not-permitted`, and the plugin should hide the feature without a trap.
- Check text in render tests, and check the look by hand in a real terminal.
