### Grants

A plugin needs no grant for its own tab or for sections in its own tab. The always-granted `settings` access covers the plugin's own values.

To add sections to a built-in tab, the plugin needs one grant per tab: `settings.contribute:<tab-id>`, for example `settings.contribute:terminal`. The grant takes one tab id with no wildcard. It gives permission to draw sections in that tab and nothing else. The review dialog shows it as "Adds settings to the Terminal tab". The grant is low risk and gives no read or write access to built-in values.

`settings.read-all` and `settings.write-all` are a different grant and stay high risk. Neither grant implies `settings.contribute`, and the reverse is also true. See [capability: settings.read-all and settings.write-all](/pages/capability-settings-all/).

### Row types

A row is one setting line group: a label, a control and a description. Rows are declared inline in the manifest. The table lists the 18 types. Every type, in every state, is on the [row gallery](/pages/reference-settings-rows/).

| Type | Stores | What the user gets |
|---|---|---|
| `toggle` | boolean | `‹ On ›` or `‹ Off ›`, or `[x]` and `[ ]` with `style: "checkbox"` |
| `choice` | string or integer | A short list of `options`, stepped with Left and Right, or a filterable dialog |
| `number` | integer or decimal | A stepper `- 42 + *`, or a slider with a `●` thumb |
| `text` | string | A single line, optionally masked with `secret` as `••••` |
| `text-area` | string | A multi-line editor opened with Enter |
| `path` | string | A file or folder picker; stores the path as text only |
| `color` | `#rrggbb` | A swatch picker with hex entry |
| `keybinding` | key chord | A capture of a chord for one of the plugin's own commands |
| `button` | nothing | A button that runs one of the plugin's commands |
| `info` | nothing | Read-only text; can be updated at runtime if `live` is set |
| `group` | nothing | A folding heading that holds up to 12 child rows |
| `list` | array | A list editor for strings or small objects of up to 8 fields |
| `location` | `{ lat, lon, label? }` | The world-map picker with an address search |
| `preview` | nothing | A live area drawn by the plugin; own tabs only |
| `notice` | nothing | A banner with a tone; can be dismissed |
| `map` | object | An editor for string keys and their values |
| `multi-choice` | array | A checklist, or a dialog with check marks |
| `meter` | nothing | A segmented bar, updated by the plugin |

Every value row has a `key`, a `title` and a `default`. The kernel turns each value row into one property of a JSON schema, so the same validation and merge rules apply to plugin rows and built-in rows. A row whose default does not match its own schema refuses the package at install time.

Three fields of every value row change how a row behaves:

- `depends_on` makes the row read-only when its condition is false. The row stays visible and focusable and says `Unavailable: <title> is <value>.`
- `visible_when` hides the row when its condition is false. A hidden row keeps its value and search skips it.
- `scope: "project"` stores the value in the project's `.ilium/` settings under `[plugins."<plugin-id>"]`. The project value wins while that project is open.
- `applies: "restart"` draws the marker `↻` after the value and the note `Applies after restart.`

Use `depends_on` when the user should see where a setting lives. Hiding a row moves the rows under the cursor.

### Safety rules

Plugins can add to Settings. They cannot change what is already there.

- A plugin cannot hide, disable, reorder, relabel or restyle a built-in row, and it cannot change the rows of a built-in section.
- Plugin keys are stored only in `[plugins."<plugin-id>"]`. A section in the Terminal tab never writes the `[terminal]` table.
- The kernel handles Up, Down, Tab, Esc, `q`, `?`, `/` and `r` before any plugin row sees input. Plugin rows receive values, never raw key events.
- Plugin text (titles, descriptions, info text) is plain text. The kernel strips control characters and bidirectional overrides and draws the text in its own styles. A plugin cannot draw a fake built-in divider or a fake close button.

The user always sees who added a section. A plugin tab shows its name and version in the first line of the page, and its frame title ends with `· plugin`. A plugin block inside a built-in tab starts with a divider line of the form `▏ <glyph> <PLUGIN NAME> ──── plugin ─`. Every line of plugin content carries a dim `▏` gutter in column 0, so the label stays visible after the user scrolls past the divider.

### Limits

| Item | Limit |
|---|---|
| Tabs per plugin | 2 |
| Sections per plugin tab | 8 |
| Sections per plugin, per built-in tab | 2 |
| Plugin sections in one built-in tab, all plugins | 6 |
| Rows per section (a group counts its children) | 24 |
| Value keys per plugin | 128 |
| Segments in a meter, entries in a map | 8 and 64 |
| Choice options | 64 |
| List items, and fields per item object | 64, and 8 |
| Text value | 4,096 characters (text area: 65,536) |
| All values of one plugin, serialized | 256 KiB |
| Manifest titles, section titles, descriptions, info text, button labels | 48, 40, 200, 120 and 20 characters |

When the limit for plugin sections in one built-in tab is reached, the extra sections are not drawn. They are listed on the recovery page with the warning `settings.section-dropped`. Install-time errors name the item, its path in the manifest and the limit.

### Values and saving

Values for a plugin's settings are stored in its own table in `config.toml`:

```toml
[plugins."example.clipboard-history"]
enabled = true
max_entries = 500
ignore_patterns = ["^sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}$", "^ghp_"]
record_panes = true
```

A row's key follows its section's `scope`. A row with `scope: "project"` is written to the project's `.ilium/` settings instead of `config.toml`; the project value wins while that project is open. The `scope` of a `settings-changed` event names the receiving side. Client-scope keys are read on the client. Server-scope keys are checked by the client against the same schema, written to the same table and passed to the server through the normal configuration refresh. A section has a single scope, so a plugin that needs both sides declares two sections.

Changes are saved as the user makes them. There is no Save button.

| Interaction | Saved |
|---|---|
| Toggle, choice step, choice picked from a list | At once |
| Number steps | 600 ms after the last step; steps within the window become one write |
| Typed number or text | 600 ms after the last keystroke, or at once on Enter or when leaving the row |
| Text area | 1 s after the last keystroke, and at once when the editor closes |
| Path, colour, keybinding, list item | At once, when the dialog is confirmed |
| Plugin call `set-json` | At once, without a delay |

While a write is pending, the row shows a dim `◌` after the value. A row whose value differs from its default shows a dim `•` after the label, and the `r` key resets the focused row to its default.

A save runs three checks in order: the schema, then the plugin's optional `settings-validate` export, then the write. The export has a deadline of 100 ms. A failed check keeps the previous value and puts the message in place of the row's description. Closing Settings writes every pending change at once.

### Live content

Eight calls let a plugin update its own rows while it runs. They need no grant and are limited to 10 per second per plugin. A plugin tab can also draw its whole page with a view. A built-in tab never runs plugin code while it paints.

| Call | Effect |
|---|---|
| `set-info`, `set-info-rich` | the text of a live `info` row |
| `set-choices`, `set-choice-items` | the options of a dynamic `choice` or `multi-choice` row |
| `set-row-note` | a dim note under the description |
| `set-row-state` | `idle`, `loading`, `pending` or `error` on a row, with a message of at most 80 characters |
| `set-item-states` | the state of single list items |
| `set-meter` | the segments of a `meter` row |

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::{RowState, RowStateKind};

fn mark_loading() -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    settings::set_row_state("stars", &RowState {
        kind: RowStateKind::Loading,
        message: Some("asking the server".into()),
    })
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { setRowState } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';

export function markLoading(): void {
  setRowState('stars', { kind: 'loading', message: 'asking the server' });
}
```

A plugin that needs a built-in value can read it. The grant `settings.read-kernel:<tab-id>` and the import `kernel-settings` return the values of that tab as read-only JSON, with secrets replaced by `<redacted>`. No plugin writes a built-in value; a link with `ilium://settings/<tab-id>#<key>` opens Settings at that row.

### Search

Settings has a filter. Press `/` or `Ctrl+F` to open it, and type part of a name. The field replaces the `Esc or q to close` hint on the second header line. The filter matches tab titles, row titles, descriptions, section titles, keywords and keys, and for plugin rows the plugin name and id. A row hidden by `visible_when` is skipped. The rail then shows only the tabs with matches, each with a count, and the content shows only the matching rows, each with its section title and, for plugin rows, the plugin divider. Esc clears the filter, and a second Esc closes Settings.

<span class="t-hi">│ ⎘  Clipboard 1   │</span> │<span class="t-hi">  CAPTURE                                                </span>│
│                  │ │  Maximum entries ………………………………………………………… -   500    + *  │

Plugins need no search code. To make a row easier to find, give it `keywords`, at most 4 per row.

### Reset to default

The `r` key on a focused value row sends the patch `{ "<key>": null }` and needs no confirmation. The section title of a plugin tab, and the divider of a plugin block, carry a `[ Reset ]` control. It sets every key of the section that has `reset: true` to `null`, after the question `Reset <n> settings of <plugin name>?`. A section reset has the origin `reset` in `settings-changed`. Built-in rows have no reset key.

### Declaring and reading, in both languages

A tab and a section differ only in the entry. The values are read the same way in both cases.

```json
{ "contributes": { "settings": [
  { "kind": "section", "id": "terminal-capture", "tab": "terminal",
    "placement": "end", "title": "Terminal capture", "scope": "client",
    "rows": [ { "type": "toggle", "key": "record_panes", "title": "Record pane copies",
                "default": true } ] }
] } }
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings;

fn record_panes() -> bool {
    let values: serde_json::Value =
        serde_json::from_str(&settings::get_json()).unwrap_or_default();
    values["record_panes"].as_bool().unwrap_or(true)
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { getJson } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';

export function recordPanes(): boolean {
  const values = JSON.parse(getJson()) as { record_panes?: boolean };
  return values.record_panes ?? true;
}
```

The section needs the grant `settings.contribute:terminal` in the manifest. The full build is [tutorial 11](/pages/tutorial-11-settings-extend-tab/).

### Lifecycle

Settings outlive the plugin. The table shows each state.

| State | Plugin tab | Section in a built-in tab | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Running | Normal | Normal | Editable |
| Restarting after a failure | Notice with the attempt number and wait time | Divider shows `plugin · restarting` | Editable, unless the plugin has `settings-validate`; then read-only |
| Turned off by the user | Rail entry dimmed, with a link to the Plugins page | Divider shows `plugin · off`; rows dimmed | Kept, read-only |
| Disabled after repeated failures | The stop notice and a link to the Plugins page | Divider shows `plugin · disabled`; rows dimmed | Kept, read-only |
| Refused at load (API or schema mismatch) | Dimmed, with the required API version | As disabled | Kept, untouched |
| Uninstalled | Gone from the rail | Gone | Kept until the user purges them |

A plugin that fails three times within 10 minutes is disabled. Disabling, crashes, upgrades and uninstalls never delete values. An upgrade can narrow a range, so a stored value may stop matching its row. The kernel then ignores it, uses the default and lists it on the recovery page as `settings.value-ignored`. The stored text stays in the file. Only `ilium plugin uninstall --purge` or "Forget settings" on the recovery page deletes values. A reinstall reads them again.

<div class="warn">

A plugin that declares `settings-validate` has its rows read-only while it restarts, because the kernel cannot check a new value without the plugin. Plugins without that export keep their rows editable during a restart.

</div>

### What the user sees

The renders are 80 columns wide, with the geometry of the Settings screen at 80 by 32: a navigation frame of 20 columns, a gap of 1 and a content frame of 59. They are built from the layout code of the client. `◂` marks the selected rail entry, which the real rail shows with the selected style (lavender, near-black text), not with a glyph. The scrollbar is a `│` track with a `┃` thumb. The microphone glyph of Voice control is one cell in the width tables of the client, so a browser that draws it two cells wide shifts that one line. The same holds for the lightning glyph of the Inference tab in the rails below.

The plugin tab `Clipboard history` uses its `short_title` `Clipboard`, because 17 cells do not fit the 14 cells the rail leaves for a label at this width. It sits after `Text Triggers` and before the pinned tail.

### How the pieces fit

The kernel keeps one settings registry. It is built when the client starts and rebuilt when a plugin is installed, enabled, disabled or upgraded. It holds the tabs in rail order, the anchors of each built-in tab and the plugin blocks for each anchor. Keys, mouse, help and search all read the same row list, so plugin rows behave like built-in rows.

### Security

Project-scope values are ignored until the user trusts the project ([SEC-310], [SEC-311]). See [Extension security](/pages/reference-extension-security/).

Requirements for this page: [Settings requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-settings/).

<!-- source: http://127.0.0.1:4327/pages/api-audio.md -->
# audio

## audio

The `audio` import lists the sound devices, opens a capture stream from a microphone or from a loopback of the desktop output, and plays samples. Captured audio arrives as `audio-frames` events, one event for each 20 ms chunk. A plugin that captures audio hears everything the device records, so capture is a high-risk capability (marked H) and the user must allow it explicitly.

Use this import in client plugins and scenes. The server world has no audio import.

### What you need

- **Grants.** `audio.capture` opens a microphone (H). `audio.loopback` captures what the computer plays (H). `audio.playback` plays samples. Listing devices needs no grant of its own: `audio.devices` returns only the devices that your granted capabilities allow.
- **Worlds.** The import is in the client world (`ilium:client`) and the animation world (`ilium:anim`).
- **Manifest.** Declare each grant under the side that uses it in `manifest.json`:

```json
{
  "capabilities": { "client": ["audio.capture", "ui.panels"] }
}
```

- **Consent.** The user answers one prompt per plugin at first activation. Each H capability is listed unchecked, and the user must tick it. A declined grant makes every call that needs it return `not-permitted`.

### Surface

| Rust (`ilium_plugin_sdk::host::audio`) | TypeScript (`@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/audio`) | Grant | Call | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `audio::devices()` | `audio.devices()` | any audio grant | sync | `Vec<AudioDevice>` | Lists the devices the grants allow. |
| `audio::open_capture(device, sample_rate, channels)` | `audio.openCapture(device, sampleRate, channels)` | `audio.capture` | sync | `Result<u64, PluginError>` | Opens a microphone and returns a capture id. `None` or `undefined` selects the default input. |
| `audio::open_loopback(sample_rate, channels)` | `audio.openLoopback(sampleRate, channels)` | `audio.loopback` | sync | `Result<u64, PluginError>` | Opens a capture of the desktop output. |
| `audio::close_capture(capture)` | `audio.closeCapture(capture)` | the grant that opened it | sync | nothing | Stops the capture and releases the device. |
| `audio::play(samples, sample_rate, channels).await` | `await audio.play(samples, sampleRate, channels)` | `audio.playback` | async | `Result<(), PluginError>` | Plays samples. Completes when playback ends. |

Types and events:

| Name | Rust | TypeScript | Fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| Device record | `AudioDevice` | `AudioDevice` | `id: String`, `name: String`, `is_input: bool`, `is_default: bool` (TypeScript: `isInput`, `isDefault`) |
| Capture event | `Event::AudioFrames(AudioFramesEvent)` | `{ tag: 'audio-frames', val }` | `capture: u64` (TypeScript `bigint`), `samples: Vec<i16>` (TypeScript `Int16Array`) |

The WIT form, for reference:

```wit
record audio-device { id: string, name: string, is-input: bool, is-default: bool }
record audio-frames-event { capture: u64, samples: list<s16> }
devices: func() -> list<audio-device>;
open-capture: func(device: option<string>, sample-rate: u32, channels: u8)
  -> result<u64, plugin-error>;
open-loopback: func(sample-rate: u32, channels: u8) -> result<u64, plugin-error>;
close-capture: func(capture: u64);
play: func(samples: list<s16>, sample-rate: u32, channels: u8)
  -> result<request-id, plugin-error>;
```

### Sample format

Samples are signed 16-bit integers (`s16`) from -32,768 to 32,767, with 0 as silence. They are interleaved: each frame holds one sample per channel, left before right. The same layout applies to `audio-frames` and to `play`.

Each `audio-frames` event holds 20 ms of audio. The number of samples is `sample_rate / 50 * channels`. At 16 kHz mono, one event carries 320 samples. At 48 kHz stereo, one event carries 1,920 samples.

The host resamples natively between your requested rate and the device rate, so you never need a fallback rate. Any rate from 8,000 to 192,000 Hz is accepted.

### Delivery and backpressure

`audio-frames` uses the policy *drop oldest, counted*. A slow handler loses old frames and never blocks the device. When frames are dropped, the next batch starts with an `events-dropped` event whose `event` field is `audio-frames` and whose `source` field is the capture id. The count tells you how much audio you missed.

### Worked example: level meter (Rust)

The plugin opens the default microphone on activation, computes the peak level of each 20 ms chunk, and keeps the last 60 levels. A panel can draw them as a sparkline (see [UI](/pages/api-ui/)).

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{Activation, DeactivationReason, Handler, Lifecycle};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::audio;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

const LEVEL_HISTORY: usize = 60;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct LevelMeter {
    capture: Option<u64>,
    levels: Vec<u8>,
}

impl Lifecycle for LevelMeter {
    fn activate(&mut self, _context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        self.capture = Some(audio::open_capture(None, 16_000, 1)?);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn deactivate(&mut self, _reason: DeactivationReason) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
        if let Some(capture) = self.capture.take() {
            audio::close_capture(capture);
        }
        None
    }
}

impl Handler for LevelMeter {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::AudioFrames(frames) = event else { continue };
            if Some(frames.capture) != self.capture {
                continue;
            }
            let peak = frames.samples.iter().map(|sample| sample.unsigned_abs()).max();
            let level = (u32::from(peak.unwrap_or(0)) * 100 / 32_768).min(100) as u8;
            if self.levels.len() == LEVEL_HISTORY {
                self.levels.remove(0);
            }
            self.levels.push(level);
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

The `audio::open_capture` call is synchronous, so `activate` can return its error at once. A `not-permitted` error means the user declined `audio.capture`, and the plugin should keep working without the meter.

### Worked example: tone playback (TypeScript)

The plugin plays a one-second 440 Hz tone when the user runs its command. The command is declared in the manifest. The `play` call is async: `await` resolves when the sound has finished.

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import * as audio from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/audio';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const SAMPLE_RATE = 16_000;
const TONE_HZ = 440;
const TONE_SECONDS = 1;
const PLAY_COMMAND = 'com.example.tone/play';

function makeTone(): Int16Array {
  const samples = new Int16Array(SAMPLE_RATE * TONE_SECONDS);
  for (let index = 0; index < samples.length; index++) {
    const phase = (2 * Math.PI * TONE_HZ * index) / SAMPLE_RATE;
    samples[index] = Math.round(Math.sin(phase) * 8_000);
  }
  return samples;
}

async function playTone(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await audio.play(makeTone(), SAMPLE_RATE, 1);
    log('info', 'tone finished');
  } catch (error) {
    const code = error instanceof PluginError ? error.code : 'unknown';
    log('warn', `tone not played: ${code}`);
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {
    log('info', 'tone plugin ready');
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === PLAY_COMMAND) {
        void playTone();
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

The `playTone` promise is not awaited inside `onEvents`. The SDK drains pending promises before it returns from each export call, so the play request finishes on its own. Errors are caught here because an unhandled rejection would be a trap.

### Audio in scenes and video

The animation world has the same `audio` import, so a scene can open a capture or a loopback for a spectrum scene; the grants are listed under `capabilities.scene`. The `video` widget and the media import play with the sound muted unless the plugin also holds `audio.playback`. Frame pacing, dithering and the shared look still apply to anything the scene draws from audio. See [media](/pages/api-media/).

**Rust**

```rust
// In a scene: loopback for a spectrum, 20 ms chunks arrive as audio-frames events.
let capture = audio::open_loopback(48_000, 2)?;
// Closing is the plugin's job; the host also closes it on deactivate or revoke.
audio::close_capture(capture);
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
const capture = audio.openLoopback(48000, 2);
audio.closeCapture(capture);
```

### Limits

| Limit | Value | Over the limit |
|---|---|---|
| Channels per stream | 1 or 2 | `unsupported` above 2; `invalid-argument` for 0 |
| Sample rate | 8,000 to 192,000 Hz | `invalid-argument` outside the range |
| Open captures per plugin | 2 by default, 4 at the T1 ceiling, 2 at the T2 and T3 ceiling | `quota-exceeded` |
| `audio.play` per call | 30 s or 16 MiB of samples | `invalid-argument` |
| Samples per `play` call | a multiple of `channels` | `invalid-argument` |

### Errors

| Call | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| `devices` | none | Returns an empty list when every audio grant is declined. A plugin with no audio grant in its manifest traps when it calls `devices`. |
| `open-capture` | `not-permitted` | `audio.capture` is missing, declined or revoked. |
| `open-capture` | `not-found` | The device id does not exist. |
| `open-capture` | `busy` | Another client holds the device exclusively. |
| `open-capture` | `unsupported` | More than 2 channels. |
| `open-loopback` | `unsupported` | The platform has no monitor source for the desktop output. |
| `play` | `io` | The output device failed during playback. |

A grant revoked while a stream is open makes its frames stop, and `not-permitted` is returned by the next call that needs the grant. Streams close on their own when the plugin deactivates, is disabled or is uninstalled, so a plugin does not leak devices if it forgets `close-capture`.

### Used by

- A voice session that opens a capture and reads `audio-frames`, then sends the audio to its provider with `http.fetch`.
- A voice onboarding demo that captures a short sample and plays it back with `audio.play`.
- A device picker that lists devices with `audio.devices` and offers the choice in a `choice` widget (see [Input widgets](/pages/widgets-input/)).

- [Capability: audio](/pages/capability-audio/) for the grant rules and the review dialog.
- [Events](/pages/api-events/) for the `audio-frames` delivery policy and `events-dropped`.

# cli

## cli

The `cli` import lets a server-side plugin add a subcommand to the `ilium` command line. The plugin declares the subcommand in its manifest. When the user runs `ilium <name> [arguments]`, the kernel routes the call to the plugin as a `cli-invoked` event. The plugin writes output, optionally reads standard input, and ends the call with an exit code. The invocation stays open until the plugin calls `finish`, or until the caller disconnects.

The interface provides a JSON-lines output form, a plain text form, a separate standard error stream, bounded standard input, a terminal test, the caller's pane, a shared pane-selector argument group, and commands that run without a server. This page documents the whole contract. CLI dispatch, server auto-start and session control stay in the kernel.

### What you need

- **Grant:** `cli.contribute`, on the server side only. The grant takes no argument (see [capability-cli-contribute](/pages/capability-cli-contribute/)). Every function and event on this page needs it.
- **Manifest:** a `cli` entry under `contributes`, and a `server` component that exports `handler`.
- **Language:** Rust with the `ilium-plugin-sdk` crate, or TypeScript with the `@ilium/plugin-sdk` package. Both are set up by `ilium plugin new` (see [getting started](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/)).
- **Imports:** `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::cli` in Rust, `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/cli` in TypeScript.

### Manifest

The `cli` key under `contributes` declares the subcommands. It holds one object, or a list of at most 8 objects, and the names MUST be unique inside the plugin. A name in the reserved kernel list (see [CLI compatibility](/pages/reference-cli-compatibility/)) is refused with `manifest.cli-name-reserved`. Each entry has these fields; five are optional.

```json
{
  "capabilities": { "server": ["cli.contribute"] },
  "contributes": {
    "cli": {
      "name": "tally",
      "summary": "Count lines of text read from standard input",
      "arguments_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "label": { "type": "string" } } },
      "output": "text",
      "stdin": "optional",
      "requires_server": false,
      "argument_groups": ["pane-selector"]
    }
  }
}
```

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | required | The subcommand. It must match `[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}` and runs as `ilium <name>`. |
| `summary` | string | required | One line shown in `ilium --help`. |
| `arguments_schema` | JSON Schema object | none | Documents the arguments for help. The host passes `argv` unchanged and does not validate it. |
| `output` | `"jsonl"`, `"text"` or `"mixed"` | `"jsonl"` | The output form. It decides which write function is allowed (see "Output forms"). |
| `aliases` | list of strings | empty | Further names for the same command. Each follows the `name` rule. |
| `stdin` | `"none"`, `"optional"` or `"required"` | `"none"` | Whether the command may read standard input. |
| `requires_server` | bool | `true` | With `false`, the command also runs when no server is running (see "Commands without a server"). |
| `argument_groups` | list of strings | empty | `["pane-selector"]` adds `--pane <id\|title\|.>` and `--all-panes`, resolved by the host. |

A name that a kernel command uses is refused at install with `manifest.cli-name-reserved`. A name that another installed plugin owns is refused with `manifest.cli-name-taken`. An invalid `output`, `stdin` or `argument_groups` value is refused with `manifest.cli-field`.

### Surface

#### WIT

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/cli in reference-wit
// ilium:host/cli  (cli.contribute, server side)
write-line:   func(invocation: u64, jsonl: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;       // output "jsonl"
write-error:  func(invocation: u64, text: string)  -> result<_, plugin-error>;       // plain text to stderr
finish:       func(invocation: u64, exit-code: u8);

// further output and input functions
write-text:   func(invocation: u64, text: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;        // output "text"
write-stderr: func(invocation: u64, text: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;        // plain text to the caller's stderr
read-stdin:   func(invocation: u64, max-bytes: u32) -> result<request-id, plugin-error>;   // at most 4 MiB in total
take-stdin:   func(request: request-id) -> option<list<u8>>;                         // empty list: end of input
is-tty:       func(invocation: u64) -> tuple<bool, bool>;                            // stdout, stderr are terminals
caller-pane:  func(invocation: u64) -> option<node-id>;                              // from ILIUM_PANE_ID
record pane-selection { panes: list<node-id>, all: bool }
selected-panes: func(invocation: u64) -> option<pane-selection>;                     // with argument_groups ["pane-selector"]
```

#### Functions

| WIT function | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `write-line` | `cli::write_line(invocation: u64, jsonl: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `writeLine(invocation: bigint, jsonl: string): void` | One JSON object and a newline to standard output. Only for `output: "jsonl"`. |
| `write-error` | `cli::write_error(invocation: u64, text: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `writeError(invocation: bigint, text: string): void` | Plain text and a newline to standard error. |
| `write-text` | `cli::write_text(invocation: u64, text: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `writeText(invocation: bigint, text: string): void` | Plain text to standard output, written as given. Only for `output: "text"`. |
| `write-stderr` | `cli::write_stderr(invocation: u64, text: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `writeStderr(invocation: bigint, text: string): void` | Plain text to standard error, for either output form. |
| `read-stdin` | `cli::read_stdin(invocation: u64, max_bytes: u32) -> Result<RequestId, PluginError>` | `readStdin(invocation: bigint, maxBytes: number): bigint` | Asks for up to `max_bytes` of standard input. The chunk arrives as `request-completed`. |
| `take-stdin` | `cli::take_stdin(request: RequestId) -> Option<Vec<u8>>` | `takeStdin(request: bigint): Uint8Array \| undefined` | Takes the chunk. An empty list means end of input. |
| `is-tty` | `cli::is_tty(invocation: u64) -> (bool, bool)` | `isTty(invocation: bigint): [boolean, boolean]` | Whether standard output and standard error are terminals. |
| `caller-pane` | `cli::caller_pane(invocation: u64) -> Option<NodeId>` | `callerPane(invocation: bigint): bigint \| undefined` | The pane the command ran in, taken from `ILIUM_PANE_ID`. |
| `selected-panes` | `cli::selected_panes(invocation: u64) -> Option<PaneSelection>` | `selectedPanes(invocation: bigint): PaneSelection \| undefined` | The panes chosen by `--pane` or `--all-panes`. |
| `finish` | `cli::finish(invocation: u64, exit_code: u8)` | `finish(invocation: bigint, exitCode: number): void` | Ends the invocation. `exit_code` becomes the process exit status. |

In TypeScript, a failed call throws `PluginError`. `PaneSelection` is `{ panes: bigint[]; all: boolean }` in TypeScript and `PaneSelection { panes: Vec<NodeId>, all: bool }` in Rust.

#### Events

| Event | Payload | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cli-invoked` | `invocation` (u64), `name`, `argv` (list of strings), `cwd` | `Event::CliInvoked(CliInvokedEvent { invocation, name, argv, cwd })` | `{ tag: 'cli-invoked', val: { invocation, name, argv, cwd } }` |
| `cli-cancelled` | `invocation` (u64) | `Event::CliCancelled(u64)` | `{ tag: 'cli-cancelled', val: bigint }` |
| `request-completed` | `request`, `outcome` (for `read-stdin`) | `Event::RequestCompleted(..)` | `{ tag: 'request-completed', val: { request, outcome } }` |

Both CLI events are never dropped. `argv` holds the words after the name as the shell passed them. `cwd` is the absolute path of the caller's working directory.

### Output forms

The manifest `output` key picks the form. `jsonl` and `text` never mix in one command. `mixed` allows both `write-line` and `write-text`, for a command such as `new-pane` that prints a plain line for one argument shape and JSONL for another.

| Form | Allowed output calls | Rule | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `jsonl` (default) | `write-line`, `write-stderr`, `write-error` | Every line is exactly one JSON object with a string `type` field. Agents read this output. | Commands that agents and scripts call. |
| `text` | `write-text`, `write-stderr`, `write-error` | Written as given, no parsing. | Commands a person reads, or that feed a pipe. |

`write-text` on a JSONL command, and `write-line` on a text command, both return `invalid-argument`. The refused write is not sent.

### Standard input

Set `stdin` to `optional` or `required`. The plugin then reads input with the request model: `read-stdin` returns a `request-id`, the host completes it with `request-completed`, and `take-stdin` returns the bytes. An empty list means the caller closed standard input. The total over one invocation is at most 4 MiB. A command with `stdin: "none"` calls `read-stdin` and gets `unsupported`. See [Requests and outcomes](/pages/requests-and-outcomes/).

### Commands without a server

With `requires_server: false`, `ilium <name>` works when no Ilium server is running. The `ilium` process then runs the plugin's server component in a transient host inside the CLI process, with the same grants. The transient host is smaller than a server:

- `tree.*` returns empty results and no panes exist.
- Storage and settings are read from disk. The host neither reads nor writes the `restored` bytes.
- No other plugin and no client side runs there.
- `caller-pane` returns `none`.
- The host ends at `finish`, and the component is deactivated with the reason `shutdown`.

When a server is running, the command runs in the normal instance instead.

### Pane selector

`argument_groups: ["pane-selector"]` gives the command two options without any parsing in the plugin: `--pane <id|title|.>` (a pane id, a title, or `.` for the caller's pane) and `--all-panes`. The host resolves them to node ids. The plugin calls `selected-panes`. It receives the resolved list, or `none` when the caller gave neither option. `caller-pane` is separate: it reports the pane the command ran in, from the `ILIUM_PANE_ID` environment variable, and is `none` outside Ilium.

### Worked example: a tally command

`ilium tally` counts the lines on standard input and prints the result. It declares `output: "text"` and `stdin: "optional"`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::cli;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::CliInvokedEvent;

const CHUNK_BYTES: u32 = 64 * 1024;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Tally {
    /// Open invocation, the read request in flight, and the lines counted so far.
    open: Option<(u64, RequestId, u64)>,
}

impl Lifecycle for Tally {}

impl Handler for Tally {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::CliInvoked(CliInvokedEvent { invocation, name, .. }) if name == "tally" => {
                    self.start(invocation);
                }
                Event::RequestCompleted(done) => self.on_chunk(done.request, done.outcome.is_ok()),
                Event::CliCancelled(invocation) => {
                    if matches!(self.open, Some((open, _, _)) if open == invocation) {
                        self.open = None;
                    }
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl Tally {
    fn start(&mut self, invocation: u64) {
        let (stdout_is_tty, _) = cli::is_tty(invocation);
        if stdout_is_tty {
            let _ = cli::write_stderr(invocation, "tally: pipe some text into this command");
            cli::finish(invocation, 2);
            return;
        }
        match cli::read_stdin(invocation, CHUNK_BYTES) {
            Ok(request) => self.open = Some((invocation, request, 0)),
            Err(error) => {
                let _ = cli::write_stderr(invocation, &error.message);
                cli::finish(invocation, 1);
            }
        }
    }

    fn on_chunk(&mut self, request: RequestId, is_ok: bool) {
        let Some((invocation, open_request, lines)) = self.open else { return };
        if open_request != request {
            return;
        }
        self.open = None;
        let Some(bytes) = cli::take_stdin(request).filter(|_| is_ok) else {
            let _ = cli::write_stderr(invocation, "tally: input failed");
            cli::finish(invocation, 1);
            return;
        };
        if bytes.is_empty() {
            let _ = cli::write_text(invocation, &format!("{lines} lines\n"));
            cli::finish(invocation, 0);
            return;
        }
        let total = lines + bytes.iter().filter(|byte| **byte == b'\n').count() as u64;
        match cli::read_stdin(invocation, CHUNK_BYTES) {
            Ok(next) => self.open = Some((invocation, next, total)),
            Err(_) => cli::finish(invocation, 1),
        }
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import * as cli from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/cli';

const CHUNK_BYTES = 64 * 1024;

interface OpenCall { invocation: bigint; request: bigint; lines: number }
let open: OpenCall | undefined;

function start(invocation: bigint): void {
  const [stdoutIsTty] = cli.isTty(invocation);
  if (stdoutIsTty) {
    cli.writeStderr(invocation, 'tally: pipe some text into this command');
    cli.finish(invocation, 2);
    return;
  }
  open = { invocation, request: cli.readStdin(invocation, CHUNK_BYTES), lines: 0 };
}

function onChunk(request: bigint, isOk: boolean): void {
  if (open === undefined || open.request !== request) return;
  const call = open;
  open = undefined;
  const bytes = isOk ? cli.takeStdin(request) : undefined;
  if (bytes === undefined) {
    cli.writeStderr(call.invocation, 'tally: input failed');
    cli.finish(call.invocation, 1);
    return;
  }
  if (bytes.length === 0) {
    cli.writeText(call.invocation, `${call.lines} lines\n`);
    cli.finish(call.invocation, 0);
    return;
  }
  call.lines += bytes.filter((byte) => byte === 0x0a).length;
  call.request = cli.readStdin(call.invocation, CHUNK_BYTES);
  open = call;
}

export const { handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'cli-invoked' && event.val.name === 'tally') start(event.val.invocation);
      else if (event.tag === 'request-completed') onChunk(event.val.request, event.val.outcome.tag === 'ok');
      else if (event.tag === 'cli-cancelled' && open?.invocation === event.val) open = undefined;
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

Both examples keep one open call and one read request in flight, and call `finish` on every path. A real command keeps a map keyed by invocation, because several invocations can run at once.

### Worked example: JSON lines and the pane selector

A command declared with `output: "jsonl"` and `argument_groups: ["pane-selector"]` reports the selected panes. It writes one object per pane, then a summary.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::cli;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

fn report_panes(invocation: u64) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let Some(selection) = cli::selected_panes(invocation) else {
        cli::write_stderr(invocation, "pass --pane or --all-panes")?;
        cli::finish(invocation, 2);
        return Ok(());
    };
    for pane in &selection.panes {
        cli::write_line(invocation, &format!(r#"{{"type":"pane","id":{}}}"#, pane.0))?;
    }
    cli::write_line(
        invocation,
        &format!(r#"{{"type":"summary","panes":{},"all":{}}}"#, selection.panes.len(), selection.all),
    )?;
    cli::finish(invocation, 0);
    Ok(())
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import * as cli from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/cli';

export function reportPanes(invocation: bigint): void {
  const selection = cli.selectedPanes(invocation);
  if (selection === undefined) {
    cli.writeStderr(invocation, 'pass --pane or --all-panes');
    cli.finish(invocation, 2);
    return;
  }
  for (const pane of selection.panes) {
    cli.writeLine(invocation, JSON.stringify({ type: 'pane', id: Number(pane) }));
  }
  cli.writeLine(
    invocation,
    JSON.stringify({ type: 'summary', panes: selection.panes.length, all: selection.all }),
  );
  cli.finish(invocation, 0);
}
```

For a slow command, start the work with `task::spawn` (Rust) or an async function (TypeScript) and write from it. Keep `on-events` short, because its deadline is 20 ms.

### What the user sees

Help lists the subcommand with its summary. A text command prints what the plugin wrote. A JSONL command prints one object per line. Standard error is a separate stream, so a pipe sees only standard output.

<figure>

<span class="t-prompt">$</span> echo $?

<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium tally
<span class="t-err">tally: pipe some text into this command</span>
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> echo $?

</pre>

<span class="t-dim">{"type":"pane","id":3}</span>

<span class="t-dim">{"type":"summary","panes":2,"all":true}</span>
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium panes-report

When the grant is declined, the subcommand is hidden from help and the command fails:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium tally
<span class="t-err">error</span>: unknown command
</pre>
<figcaption>The plugin never runs, because the grant was declined. Illustrative, not generated.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Error codes

| Function | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| `write-line` | `invalid-argument` | Not exactly one JSON object with a string `type`, a raw newline in the line, over 64 KiB, or the command declares `output: "text"`. |
| `write-text` | `invalid-argument` | The command declares `output: "jsonl"`, or the text is over 64 KiB. |
| `write-error`, `write-stderr` | `invalid-argument` | Text over 64 KiB. |
| every write | `not-found` | The invocation is finished or cancelled. |
| every write | `not-permitted` | The user declined `cli.contribute`. |
| `read-stdin` | `unsupported` | The command declares `stdin: "none"`. |
| `read-stdin` | `quota-exceeded` | The 4 MiB total for this invocation is used up. |
| `read-stdin` completion | `cancelled` | The caller left before the chunk arrived. |
| `finish` | none | An unknown or finished invocation is ignored. |
| manifest | `manifest.cli-field` | A bad `output`, `stdin` or `argument_groups` value. |
| manifest | `manifest.cli-name-taken` | The name belongs to another plugin. |
| manifest | `manifest.cli-name-reserved` | The name is a kernel command. |
| kernel | `cli.owner-disabled` | The owner plugin is disabled. The kernel answers with exit code 1 before any plugin runs. |

### Limits

| Item | Value | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Text of one write | 64 KiB | `invalid-argument` |
| Standard input per invocation | 4 MiB in total | `quota-exceeded` |
| Invocation deadline | none; open until `finish` or the caller disconnects | none |
| `on-events` deadline | 20 ms (50 ms at tier 1) | trap |

### Edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| No `cli.contribute` grant | The subcommand is hidden from help. `ilium <name>` fails with `unknown command`. Calls return `not-permitted`. |
| Caller disconnects early | `cli-cancelled` arrives. Later writes return `not-found`. |
| Plugin restarts, is disabled or is uninstalled while open | The invocation ends with exit code 1 and `plugin stopped` on standard error. |
| Handler traps | The plugin restarts under the rule in [errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/), and the open invocation ends as above. |
| Output form mismatch | `invalid-argument`; the write is dropped. |

<div class="warn">
<p>A plugin that never calls <code>finish</code> leaves the caller waiting with no deadline. Call <code>finish</code> on every path, including the error path and the cancel path.</p>
</div>

<div class="note">
<p>Several invocations can run at once. Each has its own id, and each <code>cli-invoked</code> event arrives in a batch with other events.</p>
</div>

### Used by

- `ilium voice say` is a `cli` subcommand that asks the plugin's own client side to act (see [client requests](/pages/api-client-requests/)).
- `ilium progress` writes its status through `cli.write-line` and `cli.finish`.
- The chatroom commands hold `cli.contribute`.
- `ilium broadcast` (all agent panes, across sessions) is the cross-session case (see [sessions](/pages/api-sessions/)).
- The context-injection hook reads its read position from `storage` when `cli-invoked` arrives.

- [http-api](/pages/api-http-api/) for the other server entry point.
- [Events](/pages/api-events/) for `cli-invoked` and `cli-cancelled`.
- [Exports](/pages/api-exports/) for the `handler` export that receives them.

# clipboard

## clipboard

The `clipboard` import reads and writes plain text on the system clipboard. The clipboard belongs to the user's desktop session, so the client runs this import and a server-side plugin cannot call it. Writing is common and low risk. Reading is high risk: the clipboard often holds passwords and other secrets that the user copied from another program. A plugin must therefore hold the `clipboard.read` grant before it can read, and every read is logged.

Two functions cover the whole import. `read-text` returns the clipboard text. `write-text` replaces it. Both are synchronous: they return at once and never return a `request-id`.

### You will need

| Need | Value |
|---|---|
| Side | Client. The import belongs to the client world, `ilium:client/base`. |
| Grant to write | `clipboard.write`, normal risk. |
| Grant to read | `clipboard.read`, high risk. The user allows it once in the review dialog. |
| Rust | Crate `ilium-plugin-sdk`, Rust stable 1.90 or later, target `wasm32-wasip2`. |
| TypeScript | Package `@ilium/plugin-sdk`, Bun 1.2 or later. `bun install` adds the toolchain. |
| Text format | UTF-8 plain text only. |

Import the module in each language:

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::clipboard;
```

```ts
import * as clipboard from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clipboard';
```

### Interface

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/clipboard in reference-wit
read-text: func() -> option<string>;                        // clipboard.read
write-text: func(text: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;  // clipboard.write
```

### Functions

| WIT function | Rust | TypeScript | Grant | Result | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `read-text` | `clipboard::read_text() -> Option<String>` | `clipboard.readText(): string \| undefined` | `clipboard.read` | `option<string>` | Returns the plain text on the clipboard. Returns nothing when the clipboard holds no text, for example an image. |
| `write-text` | `clipboard::write_text(text: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `clipboard.writeText(text: string): void`, throws `PluginError` | `clipboard.write` | `result<_, plugin-error>` | Replaces the clipboard text with `text`. |

The names follow the binding rules (S5): kebab-case becomes snake_case in Rust and camelCase in TypeScript.

### How the import behaves

- **Plain text only.** Only UTF-8 text is covered. Images and other formats are not part of the contract. `read-text` returns nothing for an image.
- **Write limit.** `write-text` accepts at most 1 MiB, counted in UTF-8 bytes. A larger text returns `invalid-argument`, nothing is written, and the text is never truncated.
- **Route.** The client writes through the system clipboard when it runs on the user's desktop. When it runs in a terminal that supports OSC 52, it writes through an OSC 52 sequence. With neither route, `write-text` returns `unsupported` and `read-text` returns nothing.
- **Logging.** Every successful read writes an info line to the plugin log that records only the length, never the text. The same line goes to the privacy log. The user is not asked before each read.
- **Footer.** After each read, the client footer shows `clipboard read by <plugin name>` for 3 s.
- **Prompts.** The review dialog lists `Read the clipboard` for `clipboard.read` and `Write to the clipboard` for `clipboard.write`. The high-risk grant is asked once, when the plugin first activates. There is no prompt per call.

</figure>

### Grants and refusals

| Situation | `write-text` | `read-text` |
|---|---|---|
| Grant held | Writes the text. | Returns the text, or nothing when the clipboard has no text. |
| Grant declined by the user | `not-permitted`. | Returns nothing. A warn line is written to the plugin log. |
| Grant revoked during the call | `revoked`. The plugin is re-activated. | Returns nothing, because `read-text` has no error result. |
| Grant never requested in the manifest | Traps. The plugin fails and is restarted under the rules in [errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/). | Traps, the same as an audio call without an audio grant. |

### Using the clipboard from the server side

The clipboard belongs to the client, so a server-side plugin cannot call this import. The server side has a typed way to ask its own client side: a client request (see [client requests](/pages/api-client-requests/)). The client side holds the clipboard grant, reads the text, and answers. The server side never gets a grant for the clipboard, and the read is logged on the client as usual.

The full code for this exchange, in Rust and TypeScript, is the second worked example on the [client requests](/pages/api-client-requests/) page.

### Example 1: copy the selected text of a pane

A context-menu item named `copy-selection` copies the selected text of a pane. The plugin reads the selection through the terminal primitive and writes it to the clipboard. It never reads the clipboard. The pane comes from the `context` field of the `command-invoked` event.

**Grants:** `terminal.read-screen`, `clipboard.write`

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::clipboard;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::terminal;

/// Called from the handler of the `copy-selection` command.
fn copy_selection(pane: NodeId) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let Some(selection) = terminal::selection(pane) else {
        return Ok(());
    };
    if selection.text.is_empty() {
        return Ok(());
    }
    clipboard::write_text(&selection.text)
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import * as clipboard from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clipboard';
import * as terminal from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal';

/** Called from the handler of the `copy-selection` command. */
export function copySelection(pane: bigint): void {
  const selection = terminal.selection(pane);
  if (selection === undefined || selection.text.length === 0) {
    return;
  }
  clipboard.writeText(selection.text);
}
```

Outcome: after the menu item runs, the clipboard holds the selected text. Pasting it into another pane gives the same characters. A pane with no selection writes nothing and shows no error.

### Example 2: paste the clipboard into a pane

A command named `paste-clipboard` sends the clipboard text to a pane as a paste. It needs two grants: `clipboard.read` for the text and `terminal.write` for the send. The `send-input` intent requires a `dedup-key`, and its text is limited to 64 KiB. A clipboard text over 64 KiB is therefore skipped with a warn line. It is never truncated.

**Grants:** `clipboard.read`, `terminal.write`

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::clipboard;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::clock;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::{Delivery, SendInputSpec};

const MAX_PASTE_BYTES: usize = 64 * 1024;

/// Builds the paste submission for `pane`, or nothing when there is nothing to paste.
fn paste_clipboard(pane: NodeId) -> Option<Submission> {
    let text = clipboard::read_text()?;
    if text.is_empty() {
        return None;
    }
    if text.len() > MAX_PASTE_BYTES {
        log::log(Level::Warn, "clipboard text over 64 KiB, paste skipped");
        return None;
    }
    let intent = Intent::SendInput(SendInputSpec {
        pane,
        text,
        delivery: Delivery::Pasted,
        prompt_epoch: None,
    });
    let dedup_key = format!("paste:{}", clock::now_unix_millis());
    Some(Submission::keyed(intent, dedup_key))
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import * as clipboard from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clipboard';
import * as clock from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clock';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import type { Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

const MAX_PASTE_BYTES = 64 * 1024;

/** Builds the paste submission for `pane`, or nothing when there is nothing to paste. */
export function pasteClipboard(pane: bigint): Submission | undefined {
  const text = clipboard.readText();
  if (text === undefined || text.length === 0) {
    return undefined;
  }
  if (new TextEncoder().encode(text).length > MAX_PASTE_BYTES) {
    log('warn', 'clipboard text over 64 KiB, paste skipped');
    return undefined;
  }
  return {
    intent: {
      tag: 'send-input',
      val: { pane, text, delivery: 'pasted', promptEpoch: undefined },
    },
    correlation: 0n,
    dedupKey: `paste:${clock.nowUnixMillis()}`,
  };
}
```

The caller returns the submission from `on-events` (Rust) or `onEvents` (TypeScript). The key is built from the current millisecond, so a paste of new text is not swallowed as a duplicate. Two pastes in the same millisecond share a key, and the second completes as `duplicate(original)`.

Outcome: the `send-input` submission completes as `ok` in the next batch, and the text appears at the prompt of the pane as a paste. If the pane is still restoring, the submission completes as `refused(pane-not-ready)`. A refused submission does not reserve its key, so the same key is valid for a retry.

### What the user sees

The plugin log shows one line per call. The footer confirms each read.

2026-10-11 12:04:33 <span class="t-err">error</span> clipboard.write too big
</pre>

### Errors

| Function | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| `write-text` | `invalid-argument` | The text is over 1 MiB in UTF-8 bytes. Nothing is written. |
| `write-text` | `unsupported` | Neither the system clipboard nor OSC 52 is available. |
| `write-text` | `not-permitted` | The user declined `clipboard.write`. |
| `write-text` | `revoked` | The grant was revoked during the call. |
| `write-text` | `internal` | A host bug. |
| `read-text` | none | The clipboard has no text, the grant is declined or revoked, or there is no route. `read-text` has no error result. |

### Limits

| Item | Value | Error |
|---|---|---|
| `write-text` size | 1 MiB in UTF-8 bytes | `invalid-argument`, nothing written |
| Text format | UTF-8 plain text | an image reads as nothing |
| Read frequency | no limit; every read is logged | none |
| Prompt for the high-risk grant | once, at first activation | none |

### Used by

- Text selection and right-click menu (feature 16) writes the selection with `clipboard.write-text`.
- Smart Copy light (feature 65) writes the selection on key release. It uses `clipboard.write-text` with a grab from the keys import.
- Agent toolbar (feature 35) copies text with `clipboard.write`.

# clock and timers

## clock and timers

The `clock` import gives wall-clock time and monotonic time. The `timers` import fires a `timer-fired` event after a delay, and again at a fixed interval when you ask for one. A plugin uses `clock` to read the time and to measure how long work takes. It uses `timers` to run work later or on a schedule, without a thread of its own.

Timers set with `timers.set` are not saved. When Ilium restarts the plugin, every one of them is gone, so the plugin sets its timers again in `activate`. Cancel each timer in `deactivate` so that no event arrives after shutdown. Durable timers are saved in the snapshot and fire at a wall-clock time even after a restart. They have their own page: [durable timers and input journal](/pages/api-durable-timers/).

### What you need

- **Grants:** none. `clock` is always available on the server, client and scene sides. `timers` is always available on the server and client sides.
- **Scene side:** the scene world has no `timers` import. A scene reads time from the frame input instead: `time-millis` counts from the start of the scene, and `wall-millis` counts from the last time the scene became visible.
- **Rust:** the `ilium-plugin-sdk` crate at the release pin, with Rust stable 1.90 or later and the `wasm32-wasip2` target.
- **TypeScript:** the `@ilium/plugin-sdk` package, installed with Bun 1.2 or later.
- **Handler:** timers reach the plugin only through the `handler` export. The plugin must handle `timer-fired` in its event batches.

### The surface

Every timer and clock function is synchronous. The timer id is a `u64` in WIT, `TimerId` in Rust and a `bigint` in TypeScript.

| WIT | Rust | TypeScript | Sides | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `now-unix-millis: func() -> u64` | `clock::now_unix_millis() -> u64` | `nowUnixMillis(): bigint` | S C A | Wall-clock time in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. It can jump when the system clock changes. |
| `monotonic-millis: func() -> u64` | `clock::monotonic_millis() -> u64` | `monotonicMillis(): bigint` | S C A | Milliseconds from a fixed origin. It never goes backwards. Use it for durations. |
| `set: func(after-millis: u32, repeat-millis: option<u32>) -> result<timer-id, plugin-error>` | `timers::set(after_millis: u32, repeat_millis: Option<u32>) -> Result<TimerId, PluginError>` | `timers.set(afterMillis: number, repeatMillis: number or undefined): bigint`, throws `PluginError` | S C | Starts a timer. The first event arrives after `after-millis`. With `repeat-millis`, events keep arriving at that interval until the timer is cancelled. |
| `cancel: func(timer: timer-id)` | `timers::cancel(timer: TimerId)` | `timers.cancel(timer: bigint): void` | S C | Stops a timer. A cancelled timer sends no further events. |
| `timer-fired(timer-id)` event | `Event::TimerFired(TimerId)` | `{ tag: 'timer-fired', timerId: bigint }` | S C | Delivered in the `handler` batch. One event per timer per batch. |

Rust and TypeScript names follow the binding rules in the Rust SDK and TypeScript SDK pages. The Rust path for `TimerId` is `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ids`.

### WIT

```wit
// ilium:host/clock  (S C A, always)
now-unix-millis: func() -> u64;
monotonic-millis: func() -> u64;

// ilium:host/timers  (S C, always)
set:    func(after-millis: u32, repeat-millis: option<u32>) -> result<timer-id, plugin-error>;
cancel: func(timer: timer-id);
// at and cancel-durable: see durable timers
```

The `timer-fired` event carries the `timer-id`, and events for one timer are coalesced while they wait. Timers fire on the side that set them. A timer set by the server side does not reach the client side, and the reverse.

### Choosing a clock and a timer

| Need | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Show a time of day or stamp a record | `now-unix-millis` | It follows the system clock and matches `epoch-ms` values in the journal and in durable timers. |
| Measure how long work took | `monotonic-millis` | It never goes backwards, even when the system clock is corrected. |
| Run something every few seconds while Ilium runs | `timers.set` with `repeat-millis` | In memory, cheap, lost on restart. |
| Wait once, then act | `timers.set` with no repeat | In memory. Use a debounce pattern to restart it. |
| Act at a wall-clock time, even across a restart | `timers.at` | Persisted. Fires once, late if Ilium was down. |

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Ordinary timers compared with durable timers across a restart">
  <title>Ordinary and durable timers across a restart</title>
  <defs>
    <marker id="clock-compare-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <text x="10" y="22" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">timers.set</text>
  <line x1="90" y1="18" x2="200" y2="18" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#clock-compare-arrow)"/>
  <text x="210" y="22" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">restart: timer is gone, activate arms it again</text>

<figcaption>What survives a restart. Only durable timers are stored; ordinary timers must be set again in <code>activate</code>.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Rules

- **Minimum interval:** 50 ms. Both `after-millis` and `repeat-millis` must be at least 50. A value under 50, including 0, is refused.
- **Held timers:** 64 per plugin by default (the same default applies separately to durable timers). A manifest `limits` entry can raise the limit for tier 1 (bundled) plugins to 256. Tier 2 and tier 3 plugins stay at 64.
- **Coalescing:** events for one timer merge while they wait in the queue. A handler that runs late sees one `timer-fired` for that timer with the current state, not one event per missed tick.
- **Identity:** the handler matches `timer-fired` against the ids the plugin stored. Ignore an event whose id the plugin no longer tracks.
- **Delivery:** a timer never fires inside the call that set it. The first `timer-fired` is queued after the delay, counted from the return of `timers.set` on the monotonic clock, and arrives in the next batch [API-074].
- **One-shot timers:** the id is freed when its `timer-fired` is queued. `timers.cancel` of a freed, unknown or already cancelled id does nothing and returns no error.
- **Cancel:** `timers.cancel` also removes a `timer-fired` of that timer that is queued and not yet delivered, so a cancelled timer never reaches the handler [API-074].
- **Repeat:** a repeating timer keeps its drift-free schedule (`first + n * repeat-millis`). Ticks missed while the queue holds a pending `timer-fired` of that timer merge into it.
- **Restart:** every ordinary timer is dropped when the instance ends, and no `timer-fired` of the old instance reaches the new one.
- **Deadline:** the `handler` call must return within the event deadline, 20 ms by default and 50 ms at tier 1. Start slow work as a request and read the result later as `request-completed`. See [Requests and outcomes](/pages/requests-and-outcomes/).

### Example 1: a repeating status poll (server)

The plugin reads a status file every five seconds in the server world. It cancels the timer when it is deactivated.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{clock, timers};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ids::TimerId;

const POLL_MILLIS: u32 = 5_000;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct StatusPoll {
    poll_timer: Option<TimerId>,
}

impl Lifecycle for StatusPoll {
    fn activate(&mut self, _context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        self.poll_timer = Some(timers::set(POLL_MILLIS, Some(POLL_MILLIS))?);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn deactivate(&mut self, _reason: DeactivationReason) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
        if let Some(timer) = self.poll_timer.take() {
            timers::cancel(timer);
        }
        None
    }
}

impl Handler for StatusPoll {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            if let Event::TimerFired(timer) = event {
                if Some(timer) == self.poll_timer {
                    let started = clock::monotonic_millis();
                    start_status_read();
                    let elapsed = clock::monotonic_millis() - started;
                    log::log(Level::Debug, &format!("status read started in {elapsed} ms"));
                }
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { monotonicMillis } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clock';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import * as timers from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/timers';

const POLL_MILLIS = 5_000;
let pollTimer: bigint | undefined;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate() {
    pollTimer = timers.set(POLL_MILLIS, POLL_MILLIS);
  },
  deactivate() {
    if (pollTimer !== undefined) {
      timers.cancel(pollTimer);
      pollTimer = undefined;
    }
    return undefined;
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'timer-fired' && event.timerId === pollTimer) {
        const started = monotonicMillis();
        startStatusRead();
        const elapsed = monotonicMillis() - started;
        log('debug', `status read started in ${elapsed} ms`);
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

`start_status_read` and `startStatusRead` are the plugin's own helpers. They start a read through the request model and return at once. The read result arrives later as a `request-completed` event.

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs example.status-poll --tail 3
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:00:05</span> <span class="t-dim">debug</span> status read started in 0 ms
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:00:10</span> <span class="t-dim">debug</span> status read started in 0 ms
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:00:15</span> <span class="t-ok">info </span> deactivating: disabled, timer 7 cancelled
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> <span class="t-dim">3 lines shown</span>
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The last ticks of the status poll, then the timer is cancelled when the plugin is disabled.

### Example 2: debouncing a search field (client)

The client waits for 300 ms without edits before it searches. Each edit cancels the pending timer and arms a new one. Call `query_edited` from the handler when the search field changes.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::timers;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ids::TimerId;

const DEBOUNCE_MILLIS: u32 = 300;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct SearchBox {
    pending_timer: Option<TimerId>,
}

impl Lifecycle for SearchBox {}

impl SearchBox {
    fn query_edited(&mut self) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if let Some(previous) = self.pending_timer.take() {
            timers::cancel(previous);
        }
        self.pending_timer = Some(timers::set(DEBOUNCE_MILLIS, None)?);
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for SearchBox {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            if let Event::TimerFired(timer) = event {
                if Some(timer) == self.pending_timer {
                    self.pending_timer = None;
                    refresh_results();
                }
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import * as timers from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/timers';

const DEBOUNCE_MILLIS = 300;
let pendingTimer: bigint | undefined;

function queryEdited(): void {
  if (pendingTimer !== undefined) {
    timers.cancel(pendingTimer);
  }
  pendingTimer = timers.set(DEBOUNCE_MILLIS, undefined);
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {},
  deactivate() {
    if (pendingTimer !== undefined) {
      timers.cancel(pendingTimer);
      pendingTimer = undefined;
    }
    return undefined;
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'timer-fired' && event.timerId === pendingTimer) {
        pendingTimer = undefined;
        refreshResults();
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

### What the user sees

Timers draw nothing. The status poll writes only to the plugin log, which `ilium plugin logs` shows. The search box updates its results about 300 ms after the last keystroke. A user who types quickly sees one refresh at the end of the burst.

### Edge cases and errors

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| `after-millis` or `repeat-millis` under 50, including 0 | `invalid-argument`. No timer is armed. |
| The plugin already holds its limit of timers | `quota-exceeded`. Cancel an unused timer and retry. |
| `set` returns `internal`, `revoked` or `not-permitted` | The plugin has no timer. Treat the failure like any other host error. |
| `cancel` with an unknown or finished id | Nothing happens. No error is returned. |
| Clock functions | Never fail. |
| `handler` runs past the event deadline | The plugin traps. Move slow work to a request. |
| The event queue fills because the handler does not return | The plugin restarts. Its timers are lost, so `activate` must arm them again. |

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs example.status-poll --tail 2
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:02</span> <span class="t-err">error</span> timers.set: invalid-argument
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:02</span> <span class="t-warn">warn </span> interval 20 ms is under 50 ms
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> <span class="t-dim">2 lines shown</span>
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. A plugin that asks for a 20 ms interval logs the refusal from its own error handler.

### Time zones and locale

`now-unix-millis` is UTC. `ilium:plugin@0.1.0` has no function for the user's UTC offset, time zone or locale, and a clock import does not add one. A plugin MUST store time as UTC milliseconds and MUST state the zone or show relative time when it displays a time. [AUT-616] Patterns for formatting are in [Internationalisation](/pages/guide-internationalisation/). The test clock starts at 2030-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and moves only with `advance_clock`. See [Patterns cookbook](/pages/guide-patterns-cookbook/) for debounce, throttle and retry built on timers.

### Used by

- Sound alerts (feature 47) and desktop notifications (feature 48) use timers to coalesce bursts of activity.
- Reset planning (feature 88) runs an hourly timer that fetches a feed.
- Scheduled input (feature 55) and the progress monitor (feature 59) use timers for their intervals.

### Units and conventions

Times are `epoch-ms` (`u64`, milliseconds since the Unix epoch, UTC) and durations are milliseconds. Correlation numbers below 2^63 belong to the plugin and the rest to the SDK. A limit in characters counts Unicode scalar values. The rules are stated once in the [conventions of the WIT reference](/pages/reference-wit/#2-conventions).

### See also

- [log](/pages/api-log/) for writing timer results to the plugin log.
- [Events](/pages/api-events/) for the `timer-fired` delivery policy.
- [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/) for `activate` and `deactivate`, where timers are armed and cancelled.
- [Durable timers and input journal](/pages/api-durable-timers/) for timers that survive a restart.
- [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/) for the event deadline and the full error code list.
- [Rust SDK reference](/pages/rust-sdk/) and [TypeScript SDK reference](/pages/typescript-sdk/) for the binding rules.

Contract: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# codec

## codec

The `codec` import does the byte-level work that plugins need without shipping their own libraries. It inflates and deflates data, reads image sizes, decodes images to RGBA pixels, computes SHA-256 digests and rasterises text into a grey image. Every function is synchronous and runs in the host's native code, so a plugin never bundles a decoder and never pays for one in WebAssembly.

`codec` does no input or output itself. A plugin gets its bytes from [fs](/pages/api-fs/) or [http](/pages/api-http/), passes them to `codec`, and writes the result to a pane or a file.

**You will need:**

- No grant. `codec` is always granted in the server, client and scene worlds, and in job instances.
- Rust: the `ilium-plugin-sdk` crate, module `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::codec`.
- TypeScript: the `@ilium/plugin-sdk` package, subpath `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/codec`.
- Inputs of up to 16 MiB per call. Larger work belongs in a job, see [background jobs](/pages/background-jobs/).

### Interface

Interface version: `ilium:host/codec@0.1.0`.

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/codec in reference-wit
enum compression { zlib, gzip, deflate-raw }
record image-info { width: u32, height: u32, frames: u32 }
record decoded-image { width: u32, height: u32, rgba: list<u8> }
record raster-text { text: string, size-px: u16, max-width-px: u32 }
inflate: func(format: compression, data: list<u8>, max-output: u32)
    -> result<list<u8>, plugin-error>;
deflate: func(format: compression, data: list<u8>, level: u8)
    -> result<list<u8>, plugin-error>;
image-info: func(data: list<u8>) -> result<image-info, plugin-error>;
decode-image: func(data: list<u8>, frame: u32, max-pixels: u32)
    -> result<decoded-image, plugin-error>;
sha256: func(data: list<u8>) -> list<u8>;
rasterize-text: func(request: raster-text) -> result<decoded-image, plugin-error>;
```

Names follow the SDK naming rules. In Rust the functions are snake_case and the enum cases are `Compression::Zlib`, `Compression::Gzip` and `Compression::DeflateRaw`. In TypeScript the functions are camelCase (`imageInfo`, `decodeImage`) and the format is the string `'zlib'`, `'gzip'` or `'deflate-raw'`.

### Functions

| Function | Parameters | Returns | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `inflate` | `format`, `data`, `max-output: u32` | bytes | Decompresses zlib, gzip or raw deflate data. Refused if the output is longer than `max-output`, which may be at most 64 MiB. |
| `deflate` | `format`, `data`, `level: u8` | bytes | Compresses data. `level` runs from 0 to 9. Higher levels are slower and produce smaller output. |
| `image-info` | `data` | `image-info` | Reads the width, height and frame count from the header. It does not decode any pixels. |
| `decode-image` | `data`, `frame: u32`, `max-pixels: u32` | `decoded-image` | Decodes one frame, counted from 0, to 8-bit RGBA. Refused if the image has more pixels than `max-pixels`. |
| `sha256` | `data` | 32 bytes | Returns the SHA-256 digest. It never fails. |
| `rasterize-text` | `request: raster-text` | `decoded-image` | Draws text as white pixels. The alpha channel holds the ink tone: 0 is background, 255 is full ink. Text wraps at word boundaries to `max-width-px`. |

Records:

| Record | Fields | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `image-info` | `width`, `height`, `frames` (all `u32`) | Size in pixels and number of frames. A still image has one frame. |
| `decoded-image` | `width`, `height` (`u32`), `rgba` (bytes) | Pixels in RGBA order, 4 bytes per pixel, so `rgba` is `width × height × 4` bytes. |
| `raster-text` | `text` (string), `size-px` (`u16`), `max-width-px` (`u32`) | The text, its font size in pixels and the widest line allowed. |

Each function is synchronous, so Rust and TypeScript code call it directly. Errors arrive as `PluginError`, see [errors](/pages/errors-and-limits/).

The native crates behind the import are flate2, the image decoders, sha2 and cosmic-text. A plugin cannot choose another decoder.

### Limits

| Limit | Value | Refused with |
|---|---|---|
| Input of any function | 16 MiB | `invalid-argument` |
| `inflate` `max-output` | at most 64 MiB | `invalid-argument` |
| Pixels in `decode-image` | `max-pixels`, and never more than 67,108,864 | `invalid-argument` |
| `rasterize-text` text | 64 KiB | `invalid-argument` |
| `rasterize-text` `size-px` | 1 to 512 | `invalid-argument` |
| `rasterize-text` `max-width-px` | 1 to 16,384 | `invalid-argument` |

### Example 1: decode a PNG into a surface

The plugin reads a picture that the user picked, checks its size from the header, and decodes the first frame. The RGBA bytes then go to a `surface` in the plugin's pane. The `fs.read` call returns at most 1 MiB, so this example handles pictures up to that size. Read a larger file with `fs.read-all`, see [fs](/pages/api-fs/).

**Grants:** `fs.read:picked`

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::codec::{self, DecodedImage, ImageInfo};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{fs, ui};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ui::{PixelFormat, ViewTarget};

const MAX_PIXELS: u32 = 4_000_000;

fn load_picture(path: FsPath) -> Result<DecodedImage, PluginError> {
    let bytes = fs::read(&path, 0, 1_048_576)?;
    let info: ImageInfo = codec::image_info(&bytes)?;
    if u64::from(info.width) * u64::from(info.height) > u64::from(MAX_PIXELS) {
        return Err(PluginError {
            code: ErrorCode::InvalidArgument,
            message: "the picture has more than 4 megapixels".to_string(),
            retry_after_ms: None,
        });
    }
    codec::decode_image(&bytes, 0, MAX_PIXELS)
}

fn show_picture(view: ViewTarget, picture: &DecodedImage) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    ui::write_surface(&view, "picture", 0, PixelFormat::Rgba8, &picture.rgba)
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import * as codec from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/codec';
import * as fs from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/fs';
import * as ui from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/ui';
import type { FsPath, ViewTarget } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

const MAX_PIXELS = 4_000_000;

export function loadPicture(path: FsPath): codec.DecodedImage {
  const bytes = fs.read(path, 0n, 1_048_576);
  const info = codec.imageInfo(bytes);
  if (info.width * info.height > MAX_PIXELS) {
    throw new PluginError('invalid-argument', 'the picture has more than 4 megapixels');
  }
  return codec.decodeImage(bytes, 0, MAX_PIXELS);
}

export function showPicture(view: ViewTarget, picture: codec.DecodedImage): void {
  ui.writeSurface(view, 'picture', 0, 'rgba8', picture.rgba);
}
```

For a 640 × 480 picture, `image_info` returns `width 640, height 480, frames 1`. The decoded image holds 640 × 480 × 4 = 1,228,800 bytes. The size cap of 4,000,000 pixels gives 16,000,000 bytes of RGBA, which fits the 16 MiB limit of `ui.write-surface`.
