### Edge cases and error codes

Errors that come back at once from `call` or `reply` are returned as a `plugin-error`. Errors found later arrive in the caller's completion as `failed(code)`.

| Code | When | Retry |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | The caller lacks `services.use:<name>`, or the provider lacks `services.provide:<name>`. | No |
| `not-found` | No installed and enabled provider (at call). The call id is unknown, answered or expired (at `reply`). | No |
| `invalid-argument` | Payload over 1 MiB or failing `params`. Reply over 1 MiB or failing `result`. | No, fix the call |
| `unsupported` | The method is not in the provider's schema. | No |
| `busy` | The plugin already has 64 pending requests (`pending_requests`). | Yes, later |
| `quota-exceeded` | The CPU budget of the execution quota group is spent. `retry-after-ms` is set. | Yes, after the delay |
| `failed(timed-out)` | No reply 30 seconds after the call, or the provider did not start in time. | Yes |
| `failed(cancelled)` | The provider stopped, restarted or was disabled before it answered. | Maybe |
| `failed(<code>)` | The provider returned that code from `done` or from a failed job. | As that code says |

Further edge cases:

- Two calls to the same service return two request ids. Each completion carries its own request, so take each reply by its id.
- `take-reply` gives the JSON once. A second call for the same request returns `None` or `undefined`.
- A deferred reply that arrives after 30 seconds returns `not-found`. The provider should log it and drop the work.
- A provider that restarts after a failure (see the restart and disable rule) loses its deferred calls. Their callers receive `failed(cancelled)`. If the restart was caused by the provider breaching its 50 ms call deadline, the caller of the breaching call receives `failed(timed-out)` and every other deferred caller receives `failed(cancelled)`.

### When to use extension points instead

A service has one provider. If several plugins should add data or handlers to one owner, declare an extension point. See [extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/).

### Used by

- Custom instruction inputs (feature 45) use `services.use:ilium.instructions/inputs`.
- The agent auto-compact trigger reader (feature 83) uses `services.use:ilium.compact/trigger`.

### Services of the host and catalogue services

Two more things use the service machinery in this contract.

- **Catalogues of another plugin.** `catalogs.query` on the catalogue of plugin `P` needs `services.use:catalog/P`. The provider is the `catalog-provider` export, not a `service-provider` method, so the plugin declares it in `exports`. See [catalogs](/pages/api-catalogs/).
- **Typed host services.** Some services have their own typed interfaces rather than JSON payloads: `inference`, the editor provider, `geocode`, `vector` and `catalogs`. They are listed in [geocode](/pages/api-geocode/) and [inference](/pages/api-inference/); a plugin that serves one of them uses the matching export.

| Need | Interface | Grant |
|---|---|---|
| Call another plugin's JSON service | `services.call` | `services.use:<name>` |
| Read another plugin's catalogue | `catalogs.query` | `services.use:catalog/<plugin-id>` |
| Ask a client a question | `client-requests.request` | none |
| Run a command in another session | `sessions.send` | `sessions.cross` |

Deadlines for the provider exports are fixed: `query-catalog` 20 ms, `menu-items` 20 ms, `list-virtual-children` 20 ms and `tokens` 10 ms per call. A breach counts like any deadline breach; `menu-items` and `tokens` fall back to static content instead of failing the action.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::catalogs::{self, CatalogQuery};

// manifest: "client": ["services.use:catalog/example.layouts"]
fn other_layouts() -> Vec<String> {
    let query = CatalogQuery { catalog: "example.layouts/layouts".into(), filter: String::new(), cursor: None, limit: 50 };
    catalogs::query_async(&query).map(|id| vec![format!("request {id:?} started")]).unwrap_or_default()
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { queryAsync } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/catalogs';

// manifest: "client": ["services.use:catalog/example.layouts"]
export const otherLayouts = () =>
  queryAsync({ catalog: 'example.layouts/layouts', filter: '', cursor: undefined, limit: 50 });

Requirement ids for this page: [SVC-001], [SVC-005], [SVC-007], [SVC-008], [SVC-010], [SVC-011]. See the [requirements index](/pages/reference-requirements/).

# extension points

## extension points

An extension point is a named slot that one plugin owns and other plugins fill. The owner decides what the slot means and when it is used. There are two kinds. A **collect** point holds data: contributors add entries and the owner reads the list when it needs it. A **hook** point holds code: contributors add handlers and the owner runs them at a fixed place in its own flow. Core plugins use the same mechanism as every other plugin, so a third-party plugin can extend a core plugin, and a third-party plugin can offer points of its own. The kernel checks the grants, the schemas and the deadlines on every use.

Extension points do not replace services, topics or the kernel slots. A service has one provider and many callers. A topic has one publisher and many subscribers. An extension point has one owner and many contributors. [Services](/pages/services/) explains the other choice. [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/) shows all five ways side by side.

### What you need

- **Grants.** The owner needs `extensions.provide:<plugin-id>/<point>` for each point it owns. A contributor needs `extensions.contribute:<plugin-id>/<point>` for each point it fills. There is no wildcard and no "contribute to any" grant. See [extensions.provide](/pages/capability-extensions-provide/) and [extensions.contribute](/pages/capability-extensions-contribute/).
- **Manifest.** The owner lists its points in `contributes.extension_points`. A contributor lists its entries and handlers in `contributes.extensions`. Any side that has hook extensions lists `hook-handler` in `exports`. See [reference: manifest](/pages/reference-manifest/).
- **Worlds.** The `extensions` import and the `hook-handler` export exist in `ilium:server/base` and `ilium:client/base`. The scene world has neither.
- **Toolchain.** Rust: stable 1.90 or later with the `wasm32-wasip2` target and the `ilium-plugin-sdk` crate. TypeScript: Bun 1.2 or later and `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. Nothing is installed globally.

### Names and manifest entries

| Item | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Point id | 1 to 64 characters from `a-z`, `0-9` and `-` | `after-copy` |
| Global point name | `<plugin-id>/<id>`; the prefix is the owner's plugin id | `ilium.core.smart-copy/after-copy` |
| Owner grant | `extensions.provide:<plugin-id>/<point>` | `extensions.provide:com.example.notes/before-export` |
| Contributor grant | `extensions.contribute:<plugin-id>/<point>` | `extensions.contribute:com.example.notes/before-export` |
| Owner manifest entry | object in `contributes.extension_points` | see below |
| Contributor manifest entry | object in `contributes.extensions` | see below |

A grant carries the bare global name, with no version and no wildcard. A plugin owns at most 16 points and contributes at most 64 extensions.

The fields of an owner entry (`id`, `kind`, `title`, `mode`, the schemas, `risk`, `deadline_ms`, `max_handlers`, `max_entries`, `dynamic`, `version`, `on_failure`, `final_check`) and of a contributor entry (`point`, `id`, `priority`, `entry`, `handler`, `guard`) are defined once, in [Manifest reference, extension points](/pages/reference-manifest/#extension-points-and-replacement). The schemas use the keywords listed in [Data schema subset](/pages/reference-settings-schema/#data-schema-subset); any other keyword fails the install with `manifest.schema-keyword`.

Owner manifest, with one collect point and one hook point:

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.notes",
  "capabilities": {
    "server": [
      "extensions.provide:com.example.notes/recognisers",
      "extensions.provide:com.example.notes/before-export"
    ]
  },
  "contributes": {
    "extension_points": [
      { "id": "recognisers", "kind": "collect", "title": "Note recognisers",
        "entry_schema": { "type": "object", "required": ["id", "regex"],
          "properties": { "id": { "type": "string" },
                          "regex": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 512 } } },
        "max_entries": 64, "version": "0.1.0" },
      { "id": "before-export", "kind": "hook", "mode": "transform",
        "title": "Before export",
        "payload_schema": { "type": "object",
          "properties": { "text": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 65536 } } },
        "reply_schema": { "type": "object",
          "properties": { "text": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 65536 } } },
        "risk": "standard", "deadline_ms": 20, "max_handlers": 8, "version": "0.1.0" }
    ]
  }
}
```

The owner does not export `hook-handler`, because it runs hooks and does not handle them. A plugin that also contributes hooks to other points adds the export.

Contributor manifest:

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.tickets",
  "exports": ["hook-handler"],
  "capabilities": {
    "server": [
      "extensions.contribute:com.example.notes/recognisers",
      "extensions.contribute:com.example.notes/before-export"
    ]
  },
  "contributes": {
    "extensions": [
      { "point": "com.example.notes/recognisers", "id": "jira-key", "priority": 50,
        "entry": { "id": "jira", "regex": "[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-[0-9]+" } },
      { "point": "com.example.notes/before-export@0.1.0", "id": "strip-tokens",
        "priority": 30, "handler": "strip_tokens" }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Interface

```wit
// ilium:host/extensions, imported by owners and contributors
interface extensions {
  record extension-entry {
    extension: string,      // contributor-chosen id, unique per contributor and point
    contributor: plugin-id,
    priority: u8,
    entry-json: string,     // the validated entry
  }
  enum extension-error {
    unknown-point, not-granted, schema-mismatch, cap-exceeded,
    reentrant, not-dynamic, not-found,
  }

  // owner side (needs extensions.provide:<point>)
  list: func(point: string) -> result<list<extension-entry>, extension-error>;
  run-hook: func(point: string, payload-json: string) -> result<request-id, extension-error>;
  take-reply: func(request: request-id) -> option<string>;

  // contributor side, collect points with dynamic = true (needs extensions.contribute:<point>)
  register: func(point: string, extension: string, priority: u8, entry-json: string)
    -> result<_, extension-error>;
  unregister: func(point: string, extension: string) -> result<_, extension-error>;
}

// export fragment `with-hook-handler`, listed as "hook-handler" in `exports`
variant hook-reply { pass, replace(string), refuse(string), answer(string) }
record hook-call { point: string, extension: string, call: u64, payload-json: string }
handle-hook: func(call: hook-call) -> hook-reply;
```

### Functions

| Function | Grant | Rust | TypeScript | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `list` | `extensions.provide:<point>` | `extensions::list(point)` | `list(point)` | Returns the active entries of a point, sorted by the user's order, then tier band, priority, plugin id and extension id (see Order below). Dormant and disabled entries are left out. |
| `run-hook` | `extensions.provide:<point>` | `extensions::run_hook(point, payload_json).await` | `await runHook(point, payloadJson)` | Runs the chain and resolves when it ends. The raw form returns a request id: `extensions::run_hook_request` and `runHookRequest`. |
| `take-reply` | `extensions.provide:<point>` | `extensions::take_reply(request)` | `takeReply(request)` | Returns the final payload of a `transform` chain only when at least one `replace` was accepted, or the answer of a `first` chain. Returns nothing for `observe` and `veto`, for a `transform` chain in which every handler passed (the owner then uses its original payload), and on a second take. |
| `register` | `extensions.contribute:<point>` | `extensions::register(point, extension, priority, entry_json)` | `register(point, extension, priority, entryJson)` | Adds or replaces an entry of a `dynamic` collect point. The entry is validated again. |
| `unregister` | `extensions.contribute:<point>` | `extensions::unregister(point, extension)` | `unregister(point, extension)` | Removes an entry that this plugin registered. |
| `handle-hook` | export `hook-handler` | `HookHandler::handle_hook` | `handleHook` in `definePlugin` | Receives one hook call and returns one reply. |

The `HookHandler` trait, `HookCall` and `HookReply` are in `ilium_plugin_sdk::exports` in Rust. In TypeScript the types come from `@ilium/plugin-sdk` and the handler is the `handleHook` member of `definePlugin`.

| Field or case | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ExtensionEntry.extension` | string | The id the contributor gave the entry in its manifest or in `register`. It is the identity of the entry. The owner shows and stores it as `<contributor-id>/<id>`, so equal ids from two plugins never collide. |
| `ExtensionEntry.contributor` | plugin id | The plugin that contributed the entry. |
| `ExtensionEntry.priority` | `u8` | The declared priority (0 to 100), unchanged by tier. The list is already in run order. |
| `ExtensionEntry.entry_json` | string | The validated entry. |
| `HookCall.point` | string | The global point name. |
| `HookCall.extension` | string | The `handler` name from the manifest. Dispatch on it. |
| `HookCall.call` | `u64` (`bigint` in TypeScript) | The number of this call. Useful in log lines. |
| `HookCall.payload_json` | string | The payload. For `transform` it is the output of the previous handler. |
| `HookReply::Pass` | none | No opinion. Always allowed. |
| `HookReply::Replace(json)` | JSON string | A new payload. Allowed in `transform` only. |
| `HookReply::Refuse(reason)` | string | Stops the action. Allowed in `veto` only. The reason is shown in logs and notices. |
| `HookReply::Answer(json)` | JSON string | The answer. Allowed in `first` only. |

In TypeScript the replies are `{ tag: 'pass' }`, `{ tag: 'replace', val }`, `{ tag: 'refuse', val }` and `{ tag: 'answer', val }`.

`register` takes a `u8` priority, but the manifest range is 0 to 100. A `register` with a priority above 100 fails with base code `invalid-argument` and a message that starts with `extension.schema-mismatch`.

<a id="hooks"></a>

### Hook modes

| Mode | Handlers called | Reply allowed | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `observe` | All, in priority order. Replies are ignored. | `pass` | Outcome `ok`. `take-reply` returns nothing. |
| `transform` | In run order. Each handler gets the output of the previous one. | `pass`, `replace(json)` | Outcome `ok`. `take-reply` returns the final payload when at least one replace was accepted, otherwise nothing. |
| `veto` | In priority order, until one refuses. | `pass`, `refuse(reason)` | `refused` with code `extension.vetoed` on the first refusal, otherwise `ok`. |
| `first` | In priority order, until one answers. | `pass`, `answer(json)` | Outcome `ok`. `take-reply` returns the answer, or nothing when nobody answered. |
| `guard` (after a `transform` chain whose point sets `final_check`) | Each contributor that declared `guard: true`, once, after the transform chain, with the final payload. | `pass`, `refuse(reason)` | Any `refuse` ends the chain as `refused(conflict)` with `extension.vetoed`. Otherwise the outcome is `ok`. |

A reply that the mode does not allow counts as `pass` and is logged as `extension.reply-not-allowed`. An `answer` on a `first` point that fails `reply_schema` counts as `pass` and is logged as `extension.schema-mismatch`.

For `transform`, a `replace` carries the whole payload. The host validates it against `payload_schema` and checks that every field not listed in `reply_schema.properties` equals its input value. Otherwise the reply counts as `pass` and is logged as `extension.schema-mismatch` (a breach). `reply_schema` on a `transform` point therefore lists the changeable fields only, and the next handler always gets the `payload_schema` shape. [EXT-014]

**Guards and failure policy.** A `transform` owner whose result drives a privileged action sets `final_check: true`. After the transform chain, the host calls once each contributor entry that has `guard: true` (it needs a `handler`) with the final payload. A guard replies `pass` or `refuse`. On a `high` point of mode `veto` or `transform`, the owner may set `on_failure` to `pass` or `refuse` (default `refuse`): with `refuse`, a handler that fails on a plugin-started action refuses it with `extension.vetoed` (reason `guard-failed`). [SEC-284] [SEC-287]

**User override.** A `veto` chain, or a guard, on an action the user started can be overridden by the user: see [SEC-291]. After an override the chain completes `ok` with no reply, and the owner's log gets `extension.veto-overridden` with the contributor and the point. The core points that allow it are marked in the **User override** column of [Core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/).

### Rules for payloads, deadlines, ordering and failure

- **Payloads.** A payload, a reply and a hook chain result are each capped at 64 KiB. An entry is capped at 16 KiB. The host checks the payload against `payload_schema` before the first handler runs. A failing payload returns `schema-mismatch` from `run-hook` and no handler runs.
- **What a contributor sees.** A handler gets the payload of the owner's `payload_schema` and nothing else. It does not see the owner's state, the other handlers or the other contributors.
- **Deadlines.** Each handler gets `deadline_ms`, between 5 and 50 milliseconds, 20 by default. The whole chain gets 100 milliseconds. Handlers that have not started when the chain reaches 100 ms are skipped and logged (see Chain cap).
- **Order.** The user order is a stored list of (plugin id, extension id) per point. Items in it run first, in that order. Items not in it follow, sorted by tier band (T1 before T2 and T3), then priority (lower first), then plugin id, then extension id (byte-wise ASCII comparison). A contributor installed after the user reordered therefore lands after the stored items. An update keeps the stored position, and an uninstall removes it. The same order applies to `list` on collect points. Declared priorities are kept: `ExtensionEntry.priority` returns the declared value. [EXT-007] [EXT-008]
- **Fail open.** A handler that times out, traps or errors counts as `pass`. A timeout never vetoes. A **breach** is a timeout, a trap, an error return, a reply over 64 KiB, a `replace` or `answer` that fails its schema, a CPU budget overrun, or a skip because the contributor's instance was busy. `reply-not-allowed` and a chain-cap skip are not breaches. The counter is per contributor, point and extension id. Any call that returns an accepted reply within its deadline resets it to 0. The third consecutive breach stops the extension. The stop ends when the contributor's instance restarts or the user presses Reset, and it is not persisted. The user sees a notice and a Reset button. [EXT-021]
- **Re-entry.** A `run-hook` on any point that is already on the current chain stack, directly or indirectly (A runs B, and B's handler runs A), fails with `extension.reentrant`.
- **Other host calls.** A handler may call other host functions that its grants allow. The calls must finish within its deadline, and they must be synchronous. A handler can only start an inner chain with `run-hook` (see Nested chains); it cannot wait for it.
- **Where handlers run.** A handler runs in the contributor's own instance, in the process that hosts the owner's side. T1 handlers run in that process. T2 and T3 handlers cost one helper round trip, and that round trip counts inside the handler deadline (a 5 ms handler has about 4.5 ms for its own work). Do not put a hook on a path hotter than about 100 calls per second.
- **Asynchronous chain.** `run-hook` does not block the owner's current call. It returns a request id at once, the chain runs on the host, and the result arrives as `request-completed`, where `take-reply` returns the reply. The SDK `await` form hides this. The 100 ms chain cap therefore does not conflict with the owner's 20 ms `on-events` deadline. An owner that needs the answer inside the same call cannot use a hook; it keeps its own default and applies the reply when it arrives.
- **Sequential.** The handlers of one chain run strictly one after another in priority order, never in parallel. A handler that cannot start within its own deadline (its plugin is busy) is skipped as `pass` and counts a breach. A handler whose instance is still activating is skipped as `pass` and is not a breach.
- **Chain cap.** The 100 ms cap is measured from the start of the first handler call. A handler that starts before 100 ms runs until its own `deadline_ms`, even if that ends after the cap. Handlers not started at 100 ms are skipped as `pass`, are logged `extension.chain-cap` and are not breaches. [EXT-005]
- **Does the action wait?** For `veto`, `transform` and `first` points the owner holds that one action until the chain completes (at most the 100 ms cap plus one deadline) and keeps serving other events meanwhile. For `observe` points the action does not wait, and handlers may run after it. [EXT-029]
- **No process crossing.** A hook runs only handlers hosted by the process that owns the point. A client-owned point runs only the handlers in that client, never in another client or in the server. A server-owned point runs only server handlers.
- **Nested chains.** The outermost chain is depth 1. A `run-hook` from a handler at depth 3 fails at once with `extension-error` `reentrant`, base code `conflict` and a message that starts with `extension.depth-exceeded`. It counts as `pass` for that handler and not as a breach. The inner chain runs after the handler returns. Its completion arrives at the handler's plugin as `request-completed`, and its time does not count toward the outer deadline.
- **Side.** A handler runs on the side that owns the call: server for a server-owned point, client for a client-owned point. A contributor declares its handler on the same side.
- **[HST-470]** `run-hook` MUST NOT block the owner's current call. It MUST return a request id at once and complete as `request-completed`.
- **[HST-471]** Handlers of one chain MUST run strictly one after another in priority order, and a handler that cannot start within its own deadline MUST be skipped as `pass` and count a breach.
- **[HST-472]** The 100 ms chain cap MUST be measured from the start of the first handler, and handlers not started at the cap MUST be skipped and logged `extension.chain-cap`.
- **[HST-473]** The helper round trip of a T2 or T3 handler MUST count inside the handler deadline.
- **[HST-474]** A hook MUST run only the handlers hosted by the process that owns the point.
- **[HST-475]** A chain started inside a handler MUST be limited to depth 3. The inner chain MUST run after the handler returns and MUST NOT count toward the outer deadline.
- **Contributions change.** The kernel sends the topic `ilium.extensions/changed` to the owner once per point after any change to its active set: install, uninstall, update, enable or disable of a contributor, `register`, `unregister`, a user toggle or reorder, a breach stop, a Reset, or a dormant/active change. The payload is `{ "point": "<global point name>" }`. Changes within 50 ms are merged into one event. Nobody but the owner gets it. No `contributes.topics.subscribes` entry or grant is needed; listing it is allowed and has no effect. The owner calls `list` again. [EXT-026]
- **Dormant contributions.** A contribution is dormant when its owner is not installed, is disabled, or does not satisfy its `@version`. An inactive owner does not make it dormant. A dormant contribution stays in the package and counts for nothing. It becomes active when the owner appears. Install never fails because an owner is missing.
- **Point full.** Install never fails because a point is full. The active set is the first `max_handlers` handlers (or `max_entries` entries) in run order. The rest are dormant with the reason `point full (<n>)`. A reorder by the user or a removal recomputes the set and sends `ilium.extensions/changed`. [EXT-030]

### Example: Rust owner

The owner `com.example.notes` has one collect point, `recognisers`, and one `transform` hook point, `before-export`. On a command it reads the recognisers and runs the hook over the note text. When the topic `ilium.extensions/changed` arrives, it reads the list again.

`src/lib.rs`:

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::extensions;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::task;

const RECOGNISERS: &str = "com.example.notes/recognisers";
const BEFORE_EXPORT: &str = "com.example.notes/before-export";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Notes {
    recogniser_entries: Vec<String>,
}

impl Lifecycle for Notes {
    fn activate(&mut self) {
        self.reload_recognisers();
    }
}

impl Notes {
    fn reload_recognisers(&mut self) {
        match extensions::list(RECOGNISERS) {
            Ok(entries) => {
                self.recogniser_entries = entries.into_iter().map(|e| e.entry_json).collect();
            }
            Err(error) => log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("list failed: {error:?}")),
        }
    }
}

impl Handler for Notes {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::TopicPublished(published) if published.topic == "ilium.extensions/changed" => {
                    self.reload_recognisers();
                }
                Event::CommandInvoked(invoked) if invoked.command == "com.example.notes/export" => {
                    task::spawn(export_note("Release notes for Friday".to_string()));
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

async fn export_note(text: String) {
    // Escape the text with a JSON library in a real plugin.
    let payload = format!(r#"{{"text":"{text}"}}"#);
    match extensions::run_hook(BEFORE_EXPORT, &payload).await {
        Ok(Some(final_payload)) => log::log(Level::Info, &format!("export: {final_payload}")),
        Ok(None) => log::log(Level::Info, "export: no handler changed the text"),
        Err(error) => log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("export failed: {}", error.message)),
    }
}
```

`run_hook` resolves with `Some(json)` for `transform` and `first` chains, with `None` for `observe` and `veto`, and with `Err` when the chain ended in `refused` or `failed`. For a `veto` point the owner checks `error.extension_code() == Some("extension.vetoed")` and does not perform the action. For a `transform` point the owner uses the original text when `take_reply` finds nothing.

### Example: Rust contributor

The contributor `com.example.tickets` handles the hook by name. The `extension` field of the call is the `handler` value from the manifest.

`src/lib.rs`:

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{HookCall, HookHandler, HookReply};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server", exports = ["hook-handler"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Tickets;

impl Lifecycle for Tickets {}

impl Handler for Tickets {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl HookHandler for Tickets {
    fn handle_hook(&mut self, call: HookCall) -> HookReply {
        match call.extension.as_str() {
            "strip_tokens" => strip_tokens(&call.payload_json),
            _ => HookReply::Pass,
        }
    }
}

fn strip_tokens(payload_json: &str) -> HookReply {
    // Parse with a JSON library in a real plugin. This stand-in keeps the example short.
    if !payload_json.contains("ghp_") {
        return HookReply::Pass;
    }
    HookReply::Replace(payload_json.replace("ghp_", "[removed]"))
}
```

The contributor's package needs the manifest shown above. A handler must stay under its deadline and must not block. Return `Pass` when you have nothing to change.

### Example: TypeScript owner

The same owner in TypeScript. `runHook` resolves with the final payload, or `undefined` when the mode returns none.

`src/index.ts`:

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { list, runHook } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/extensions';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const RECOGNISERS = 'com.example.notes/recognisers';
const BEFORE_EXPORT = 'com.example.notes/before-export';

let recogniserEntries: string[] = [];

function reloadRecognisers(): void {
  try {
    recogniserEntries = list(RECOGNISERS).map((entry) => entry.entryJson);
  } catch (error) {
    log('warn', `list failed: ${String(error)}`);
  }
}

async function exportNote(text: string): Promise<void> {
  try {
    const finalPayload = await runHook(BEFORE_EXPORT, JSON.stringify({ text }));
    log('info', finalPayload === undefined ? 'export: unchanged' : `export: ${finalPayload}`);
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof PluginError && error.extensionCode === 'extension.vetoed') {
      log('info', `export refused: ${error.message}`);
      return;
    }
    log('warn', `export failed: ${String(error)}`);
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate() {
    reloadRecognisers();
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'topic-published' && event.val.topic === 'ilium.extensions/changed') {
        reloadRecognisers();
      }
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === 'com.example.notes/export') {
        void exportNote('Release notes for Friday');
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

### Example: TypeScript contributor

`src/index.ts`:

```ts
import { definePlugin, type HookCall, type HookReply } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';

export const { lifecycle, handler, hookHandler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents() {
    return [];
  },
  handleHook(call: HookCall): HookReply {
    if (call.extension !== 'strip_tokens') {
      return { tag: 'pass' };
    }
    const payload = JSON.parse(call.payloadJson) as { text?: string };
    const text = payload.text ?? '';
    const cleaned = text.replace(/ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}/g, '[removed]');
    if (cleaned === text) {
      return { tag: 'pass' };
    }
    return { tag: 'replace', val: JSON.stringify({ ...payload, text: cleaned }) };
  },
});
```

### Entry-bound services

Some collect entries carry a `service` field: `compaction/techniques`, `cost/quota-sources`, `notifications/channels`, `recap/fact-sources`, `scenes/scene-data-sources`, `scheduler/schedule-sources`, `search/sources`, `session-convert/formats`, `settings/config-importers`, `keys-and-help/help-sources` and `diagnostics/report-sections`.

An entry field `service` names a service whose prefix is the contributor's own id and that the contributor provides, or the entry fails with `manifest.extension-entry-invalid`. The owner of the point may call it without its own `services.use` grant: the kernel admits the call because the entry is active. The normal 30 second timeout and the 1 MiB caps apply. The method, parameters and result of each point are fixed on the core plugin's page, in the row for that point. [EXT-043]

### Dynamic collect points

A collect point with `"dynamic": true` lets a contributor add and remove entries at run time. A static point takes entries from the manifest only. The owner sees both kinds in `list`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::extensions;

// manifest: "extensions.contribute:com.example.notes/recognisers"
fn add_project_key(key_prefix: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
    let entry = format!(r#"{{"id":"project","regex":"{key_prefix}-[0-9]+"}}"#);
    extensions::register("com.example.notes/recognisers", "project-key", 50, &entry)
        .map_err(|error| format!("{error:?}"))
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { register } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/extensions';

// manifest: "extensions.contribute:com.example.notes/recognisers"
export function addProjectKey(keyPrefix: string): void {
  const entry = JSON.stringify({ id: 'project', regex: `${keyPrefix}-[0-9]+` });
  register('com.example.notes/recognisers', 'project-key', 50, entry);
}
```

Dynamic is a property of the point, and the core points that allow it are marked in the **Dynamic** column of [Core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/). `register` with an id that the plugin already used replaces that entry. A plugin can only remove entries it registered. A call on a point that is not `dynamic` returns `not-dynamic`.

### What the user sees

The review dialog groups a package's extensions under **Adds to other plugins**. Each line names the owner, the point and what the handler can do. A high-risk point carries a warning.

On Settings > Plugins, the plugin page has an **Extensions** tab. For each point the plugin owns, it lists the contributors in run order, each with a toggle and move up and down buttons. For each extension the plugin contributes, it lists the point and a toggle. The user's order overrides the priority. The host stores the toggles, not the plugin.

╭──────────────────────────────────────────────╮

</figure>

Two states need a note.

- **Dormant.** An extension that is dormant shows the reason `waiting for <owner-id>` (owner missing or disabled), `needs <point>@<version>, <owner-id> has <version>` (version mismatch) or `point full (<n> handlers)`. It does nothing, and the toggle stays as the user set it.
- **Stopped.** An extension that breached three times in a row, whatever the cause, shows `stopped after 3 failures` and a Reset button. The stop lasts until the instance restarts or Reset is pressed, and it is not saved to disk. [LIF-270]

- [LIF-270] A stop after three breaches MUST end at an instance restart of the contributor or Reset and MUST NOT be persisted. Test: stop an extension, restart the contributor, and call it.

### Edge cases and error codes

Extension codes do not add a case to the 15-case `error-code` enum. Each extension code is carried by a normal `plugin-error`: the `code` field holds the mapped base code from the table below, and the `message` field starts with the extension code, a colon and a space, for example `extension.vetoed: com.example.quiet-hours: quiet hours are on` [EXT-003]. The message names the contributor's plugin id; the user interface shows the display name instead (host prefix rule [SEC-292]). The SDKs parse this prefix and expose it as `error.extension_code()` in Rust and `error.extensionCode` in TypeScript, so a plugin never matches on free text. The prefix is the only part of `message` that is a contract.

The WIT `extension-error` variant (7 cases) is the sync result of `list`, `run-hook`, `register` and `unregister`; the SDK converts each case to the mapped `plugin-error`. Codes found later arrive as `refused(...)` or `failed(...)` in the completion of the `run-hook` request, with the same mapping. Codes marked log-only never reach the caller; they are written to the log of the plugin that caused them.

| Extension code | Base `code` | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| `extension.unknown-point` | `not-found` | sync |
| `extension.not-granted` | `not-permitted` | sync |
| `extension.schema-mismatch` | `invalid-argument` | sync for a caller payload or entry; log-only for a bad handler reply |
| `extension.cap-exceeded` | `invalid-argument` for a payload, reply or entry over its size cap; `quota-exceeded` when a point already holds `max_entries` | sync |
| `extension.reentrant` | `conflict` | sync |
| `extension.not-dynamic` | `unsupported` | sync |
| `extension.vetoed` | `conflict` | completion `refused(conflict)` |
| `extension.depth-exceeded` | `conflict` | sync; travels as `reentrant` |
| `extension.entry-rejected` | `invalid-argument` | log-only, to the contributor's log and the owner's log |
| `rate-limited` (no extension prefix) | `rate-limited` | sync from `run-hook`, with `retry-after-ms`, above 200 calls per second per point |
| `extension.handler-timeout`, `extension.reply-not-allowed`, `extension.disabled`, `extension.chain-cap`, `extension.veto-overridden` | none | log-only |

The 7-case `extension-error` enum is unchanged: `extension.depth-exceeded` travels as `reentrant`, and `rate-limited` is the base error code.

A payload over 64 KiB is always `extension.cap-exceeded` (base `invalid-argument`), not `extension.schema-mismatch`; a payload that fits the size cap but fails `payload_schema` is `extension.schema-mismatch` [EXT-004]. When a chain reaches 100 ms, the handlers after the cap are skipped and each skipped handler is logged with `extension.chain-cap` [EXT-005].

| Code | When | Retry |
|---|---|---|
| `extension.unknown-point` | The point is not declared by an installed and enabled owner. | No |
| `extension.not-granted` | The caller lacks `extensions.provide` or `extensions.contribute` for the point. | No |
| `extension.schema-mismatch` | The payload or an entry fails its schema. A bad `replace` or `answer` is logged with this code and counts as `pass`. | No, fix the data |
| `extension.cap-exceeded` | The point already holds `max_entries` entries, or the payload, reply or entry is over its size cap. | No |
| `extension.reentrant` | A handler called `run-hook` on a point already on the current chain, or the chain is deeper than 3. | No |
| `extension.depth-exceeded` | A `run-hook` from a handler at depth 3. Counts as `pass`, not as a breach. | No |
| `extension.entry-rejected` | The owner refused an entry outside its allowlist ([SEC-283]). | No, fix the entry |
| `rate-limited` | More than 200 `run-hook` calls per second on one point. | After `retry-after-ms` |
| `extension.not-dynamic` | `register` or `unregister` on a point that is not `dynamic`. | No |
| `not-found` (host error) | `unregister` for an entry this plugin did not register. | No |
| `extension.handler-timeout` | A handler passed its deadline. Counts as `pass` and as one breach. | No |
| `extension.reply-not-allowed` | The reply is not allowed in the point's mode. Counts as `pass`. | No |
| `extension.vetoed` | A `veto` handler or a guard refused. The completion is `refused(conflict)`, the message is `extension.vetoed: <contributor plugin id>: <reason>`. | Not by the owner, the action stays refused |
| `extension.disabled` | The extension was stopped after three breaches in a row or turned off by the user. Not called. Log-only. | After the user presses Reset in Settings > Plugins. A breach stop also ends when the plugin restarts. A user turn-off persists across restarts |

Install errors:

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `manifest.extension-point-duplicate` | Two points have the same id in one plugin. |
| `manifest.extension-point-invalid` | A bad id, kind, mode or schema. |
| `manifest.extension-entry-invalid` | An entry fails the point's `entry_schema`. |
| `manifest.extension-side` | A handler is declared on a different side from the owner's call. |
| `manifest.extension-limit` | More than 16 points or 64 extensions in one plugin. |
| `manifest.grant-missing-extension` | An extension has no `extensions.contribute` grant, or a point has no `extensions.provide` grant. |
| `manifest.exports-mismatch` | A plugin with hook extensions does not list `hook-handler` in `exports`. |
| `manifest.grant-wildcard` | A grant for a point ends in `*`. |
| `manifest.point-risk` | An owner declares `risk: "standard"` for a point that meets [SEC-280]. |
| `manifest.grant-dependency` | A contributor to a point with a sensitive data class lacks the matching read grant ([SEC-282]), or a command-running entry lacks `process.run`. |
| `manifest.replaces-tier` | A T3 package, or a T2 package whose surface needs T1-only grants, replaces a core plugin. |
| `policy.replacement` | The admin policy `extensions.allow_replacement = false` refuses a replacement. |
| `manifest.schema-keyword` | A data schema uses a keyword outside the [Data schema subset](/pages/reference-settings-schema/#data-schema-subset). |

Further edge cases:

- **Owner disabled.** The contributions to its points go dormant at once. Handlers in a running chain finish or time out.
- **Contributor removed while a chain runs.** The chain skips its handler and logs `extension.disabled`.
- **Equal priority.** Two extensions on one point with the same priority run in plugin id order, then in extension id order [EXT-007].
- **Two contributors, same id.** The id is unique per contributor and point, so both stay. The user sees them as two rows.
- **Version mismatch.** A contribution asks for `point@X.Y.Z`. The rule is the one for services: same major; minor at least the requested one; for major 0 the minor must be equal; patch is ignored. Otherwise it stays dormant and the Plugins screen says why. A contribution without `@version` matches any owner version. Examples with an owner at `1.2.0`: `@1.0.0` accepted, `@1.2.0` accepted, `@1.3.0` dormant, `@2.0.0` dormant. With an owner at `0.1.2`: `@0.1.0` and `@0.1.9` accepted, `@0.2.0` dormant [EXT-006].
- **Hook with no handlers.** `run-hook` resolves at once with outcome `ok` and no reply. The owner continues with its original data.
- **Slow owner path.** The owner pays for the chain. The action waits for a `veto`, `transform` or `first` chain, at most the 100 ms cap plus one deadline. A handler that is skipped at the cap counts as `pass`, so a `veto` chain that never reached a refusal lets the action go on.
- **No retry by the kernel.** The kernel never re-runs a failed chain. The owner decides.

### Used by

- Every core plugin that has an **Extension points** section uses this mechanism for it. [Reference: core extension points](/pages/reference-core-extension-points/) lists them all.
- [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/) shows the quiet hours scenario: a `veto` hook on `ilium.core.notifications/before-notify`.

The host pre-activates the inactive contributors of an active owner in the background, so the first call does not wait for a cold start. A handler skipped because its instance is still activating counts as `pass`, not as a breach. [LIF-274]

- [LIF-274] The host MUST activate inactive contributors of an active owner in the background. Test: owner activates, contributor is `active` without a call.

See the [requirements index](/pages/reference-requirements/).

# settings

## settings

Each plugin declares its settings in its manifest, under `contributes.settings`. A plugin can add a tab of its own to the Settings screen, and it can add sections of rows to a built-in tab such as Terminal or Editor. Each row is one value, and the kernel validates every change against the schema that the rows compile to. The kernel saves the values, draws the rows, and tells the plugin which keys changed. A plugin reads and writes its own values with no grant. A settings screen can also read and write the values of other plugins, but only with the all-settings grants.

The `settings` import lives in `ilium:host/settings`. It has five functions and one event for values. Eight row-update calls, one read-only import for built-in values and one client-side `open` call sit beside them (see [Dynamic content](#dynamic-content)). The 18 row types are shown on the [row gallery](/pages/reference-settings-rows/).

**You need:**

- No grant for the plugin's own values. `get-json` and `set-json` are always granted on the `server` and `client` sides. A plugin's own tab needs no other grant.
- `settings.contribute:<tab-id>` for each built-in tab where the plugin adds a section, for example `settings.contribute:terminal`. It allows drawing sections in that tab and nothing else. It is low risk, and it neither implies nor is implied by the two all-settings grants. See [settings.read-all and settings.write-all](/pages/capability-settings-all/).
- `settings.read-kernel:<tab-id>` for the read-only `kernel-settings.read` call. It is low risk, takes one tab id and gives no write access.
- `settings.read-all` for `list-settings` and `get-plugin-json`. This grant is high risk and available only to bundled first-party (T1) plugins.
- `settings.write-all` for `set-plugin-json`. It also needs `settings.read-all`. It is high risk and T1 only.
- A language: Rust with `ilium_plugin_sdk`, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`.
- A `contributes.settings` entry in the manifest, if the plugin has settings. Without one, `get-json` returns `{}`.

<div class="note">
<p>The scene side has no settings import. A scene receives its own settings as the JSON string in its constructor argument (api-scenes).</p>
</div>

The SDK names of the calls on this page, including the `_request` / `Request` starting forms and the `_json` / `Json` names, follow [Wrapper names in the SDKs](/pages/reference-wit/#wrapper-names-in-the-sdks).

### Surface

| Name | Rust | TypeScript | Grant | Sides | Result and effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `get-json` | `settings::get_json() -> String` | `getJson(): string` | always | server, client | Returns the plugin's own values for its side as one JSON object, from its tabs and sections alike. |
| `set-json` | `settings::set_json(&str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `setJson(patch: string): void`, throws `PluginError` | always | server, client | Applies a merge patch to the own values after validation. |
| `list-settings` | `settings::list_settings() -> Vec<SettingsRef>` | `listSettings(): SettingsRef[]` | `settings.read-all` | server, client | Lists the tabs and sections that every plugin with settings declares. |
| `get-plugin-json` | `settings::get_plugin_json(&str) -> Result<String, PluginError>` | `getPluginJson(plugin: string): string` | `settings.read-all` | server, client | Returns all values of another plugin. Secret values are empty strings. |
| `set-plugin-json` | `settings::set_plugin_json(&str, &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `setPluginJson(plugin: string, patch: string): void` | `settings.write-all` | server, client | Applies a merge patch to another plugin's values, validated against that plugin's schema. |
| `settings-changed` | `Event::SettingsChanged(SettingsChange)` | `{ tag: 'settings-changed', val: SettingsChange }` | always | server, client | Carries the changed keys, the origin and the receiving side. Coalesced per batch. |

The `SettingsRef` record has these fields: `plugin` (the plugin id), `tab` (the global tab id `<plugin-id>/<tab-id>`, or the built-in tab id for a section in a built-in tab), `section` (the global section id, when the entry is a section), `title`, `scope` (`server` or `client`) and `kernel-tab` (an optional built-in tab id). In Rust it is imported from `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings`. In TypeScript it is imported as a type from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings`.

The `SettingsChange` record has three fields: `keys` (the changed keys, sorted, no duplicates), `origin` and `scope` (the receiving side, `server` or `client`). The origin is one of:

- `user`: a row on the Settings screen changed, or the `r` key reset a row.
- `plugin`: the plugin's own `set-json` call.
- `reset`: a section's `[ Reset ]` control ran.
- `other-plugin`: a plugin with `settings.write-all` changed this plugin's values.
- `file`: `config.toml` was edited on disk and reloaded.

`settings-changed` arrives for every change to the plugin's own values. That includes a change the plugin makes with `set-json` and a change the user makes on the page. A plugin therefore has one code path for both. If writes with different origins are coalesced into one event, `origin` is the last one and `keys` is the union.

### Manifest: rows and their schema

A `tab` or `section` entry in `contributes.settings` holds rows. Each value row has a `type`, a `key`, a `title` and a `default`. The kernel compiles every value row into one property of a JSON-Schema subset validated with draft 2020-12, so the same checks run for rows and for `set-json`. The full field tables are in the [settings schema reference](/pages/reference-settings-schema/).

```json
{
  "contributes": {
    "settings": [
      {
        "kind": "section",
        "id": "notes-editing",
        "tab": "editor",
        "placement": "end",
        "title": "Notes",
        "scope": "client",
        "rows": [
          { "type": "toggle", "key": "sound_enabled", "title": "Play a sound",
            "default": true },
          { "type": "number", "key": "indent_width", "title": "Indent width",
            "minimum": 1, "maximum": 8, "step": 1, "unit": "spaces",
            "default": 4 },
          { "type": "number", "key": "zoom", "title": "Zoom", "integer": false,
            "minimum": 0.5, "maximum": 2, "step": 0.1, "default": 1 },
          { "type": "text", "key": "sync_token", "title": "Sync token",
            "secret": true, "default": "" },
          { "type": "text-area", "key": "template", "title": "Template",
            "default": "" },
          { "type": "choice", "key": "density", "title": "Density",
            "default": "comfortable",
            "options": [
              { "value": "compact", "title": "Compact" },
              { "value": "comfortable", "title": "Comfortable" }
            ] }
        ]
      },
      {
        "kind": "tab",
        "id": "notes",
        "title": "Notes",
        "icon": "notes",
        "render": "view"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The `Notes` tab in the example is a custom page: it has `"render": "view"`, so the plugin's `views` export draws it. A plugin declares its custom pages this way, as tabs, and not in a separate list.

The keywords that a row's schema may use are fixed. Any other keyword is refused at install with `manifest.schema-keyword`.

| Keyword | Applies to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | all | `object`, `boolean`, `integer`, `number`, `string` or `array`. The `enum` form is a `string` or `integer` with `enum`. |
| `enum` | `string`, `integer` | The allowed values. Any other value is `invalid-argument`. |
| `enum_titles` | `enum` | Display strings for the `enum` values, same length and order. |
| `items`, `maxItems` | `array` | One primitive type, or an object of at most eight primitive fields, for a `list` row. At most 64 items. |
| `title`, `help`, `description` | all | Row label, help text shown with the field, and documentation text. |
| `default` | all | The value used before the user or the plugin sets one. |
| `minimum`, `maximum`, `step` | `integer`, `number` | Range and the step of the control. |
| `unit` | `integer`, `number` | Text shown after the value, such as `spaces`. |
| `pattern`, `maxLength`, `required` | `string`, `object` | Standard JSON-Schema checks. |
| `secret` | `string` | The field is masked on the page, and the value is redacted from logs. |
| `multiline` | `string` | The field is a text area. |
| `picker` | `string` | `"file"` or `"directory"`, with optional `extensions`. Adds a path chooser. |
| `x-visible-when` | all value rows | Compiled from `visible_when`. A false condition hides the row. It is a UI annotation and never takes part in validation. |
| `x-scope` | all value rows | Compiled from `scope: "project"`. The value is stored per project. |
| `x-applies` | all value rows | Compiled from `applies: "restart"`. Draws `↻` and the note `Applies after restart.` |
| `x-steps`, `x-special-values` | `integer`, `number` | Compiled from `steps` and `special_values`. A ladder of allowed stops, and values drawn as a title. |

The error codes `manifest.catalog-unknown` (a choice `source` names an unknown catalogue) and `manifest.settings-source` (`source` together with `options`) are install-time manifest errors.

Row keys must be unique within one plugin, across all its tabs and sections. A duplicate is refused at install with `manifest.settings-key-clash`.

### Live reload of settings

The kernel store is the single copy of every value. A write by the user, by a file edit, or by a tab owner (`settings.write-kernel`) reaches a running plugin as the event `settings-changed` (own keys) or `kernel-settings-changed` (kernel tabs) without a restart. Values that need a restart are listed in [kernel and boot](/pages/reference-kernel-and-boot/), table "Live reload and restart". [COR-024]

### Writing values: merge patch

`set-json` and `set-plugin-json` take a JSON merge patch (RFC 7396). A key in the patch replaces the stored value. A key that is absent is unchanged. A key set to `null` resets that key to its schema `default`. The patch is applied as a whole: if one key fails, nothing is stored. A patch that changes no value succeeds and sends no `settings-changed` event.

A key that belongs to the other side (see the scope rule below) is `invalid-argument`, and so is a key that is not in the schema. `set-json` is not debounced, and it does not call the plugin's own `settings-validate` export, because the plugin already knows its rules.

### Optional validation: settings-validate

A plugin may export `settings-validate` on the side that owns the keys. The kernel calls it after the schema check and before a save, for changes made by the user and for resets. It is never called for `set-json` or `set-plugin-json`.

```wit
record field-error { key: string, message: string }   // message <= 120 characters
settings-validate: func(patch: string, merged: string) -> result<_, list<field-error>>;
```

The call has a deadline of 100 ms. A timeout, a trap or a stopped plugin refuses the save, and the previous value stays. Each `field-error` replaces the matching row's description line in the warning style.

### Dynamic content

These calls change a row while the plugin runs. They need no grant, because they cover only the plugin's own rows. They are limited to 10 calls per second per plugin, in total, and they are coalesced per row. A call over the limit returns `rate-limited`. A call that names an unknown key or id returns `not-found`.

| Call | Rust | TypeScript | Applies to | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `set-info(key, text)` | `settings::set_info` | `setInfo` | an `info` row with `live: true` | Replaces the text, at most 120 characters. |
| `set-info-rich(key, spans)` | `settings::set_info_rich` | `setInfoRich` | a live `info` row with `rich` | Replaces the spans `{ text, tone, bold, command }`. |
| `set-choices(key, options)` | `settings::set_choices` | `setChoices` | a `choice` row with `dynamic: true` | Replaces the options, 1 to 64. A stored value that is no longer offered shows as `‹ value (unavailable) ›`. |
| `set-choice-items(key, items)` | `settings::set_choice_items` | `setChoiceItems` | a `choice` or `multi-choice` row with a `source` catalogue | Replaces the items of the catalogue, with description, preview and disabled reason. |
| `set-row-note(key, note)` | `settings::set_row_note` | `setRowNote` | any row | Sets or clears a dim note under the description, at most 120 characters. |
| `set-row-state(key, state)` | `settings::set_row_state` | `setRowState` | any value row | Sets `idle`, `loading`, `pending` or `error`, with a message of at most 80 characters. |
| `set-item-states(key, states)` | `settings::set_item_states` | `setItemStates` | a `list` row with `remote` or `item_status` | Sets the state of single items. |
| `set-meter(id, segments)` | `settings::set_meter` | `setMeter` | a `meter` row | Replaces up to 8 segments `{ label, value, tone }`. |

`open(target)` is a client import. It opens Settings at a plugin's tab, at one of its sections, or at one row. The targets are `<plugin-id>/<tab-id>`, `<plugin-id>/<section-id>` and `<plugin-id>/<section-id>/<key>`. A target of another plugin is refused with `invalid-argument`.

`kernel-settings.read(tab)` returns the values of one built-in tab as JSON, read-only, with secrets replaced by `<redacted>`. It needs `settings.read-kernel:<tab-id>`. A change arrives as the event `kernel-settings-changed`. To point the user at a built-in row, open the link `ilium://settings/<tab-id>#<key>` with `open-external`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings::{self, MeterSegment, RowState, RowStateKind, Tone};

fn show_budget(used: f64) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    settings::set_meter("budget", &[
        MeterSegment { label: "used".into(), value: used, tone: Tone::Success },
    ])?;
    settings::set_row_state("api_key", &RowState {
        kind: RowStateKind::Loading,
        message: Some("checking the key".into()),
    })
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { setMeter, setRowState } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';

export function showBudget(used: number): void {
  setMeter('budget', [{ label: 'used', value: used, tone: 'success' }]);
  setRowState('api_key', { kind: 'loading', message: 'checking the key' });
}
```

### Examples

Both examples use the always-granted own values. The Rust example adds the `serde_json` crate to the plugin's `Cargo.toml` to build and read JSON.

**Example 1: write and read own values**

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings;

fn remember_density(choice: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let patch = serde_json::json!({ "density": choice }).to_string();
    settings::set_json(&patch)
}

fn read_indent() -> u32 {
    let values: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&settings::get_json())
        .unwrap_or(serde_json::Value::Null);
    values["indent_width"].as_u64().unwrap_or(4) as u32
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { getJson, setJson } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';

export function rememberDensity(choice: 'compact' | 'comfortable'): void {
  setJson(JSON.stringify({ density: choice }));
}

export function readIndent(): number {
  const values: Record<string, unknown> = JSON.parse(getJson());
  const indent = values['indent_width'];
  return typeof indent === 'number' ? indent : 4;
}
```

Calling `set_json` with `{"indent_width": 12}` fails with `invalid-argument`, because the maximum is 8. The message names the key. Nothing is stored.

**Example 2: react to a change**

This client-side handler keeps the indent in memory and refreshes it only when `indent_width` changes. The change can come from the plugin or from the user.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct IndentWatcher {
    indent: u32,
}

impl Handler for IndentWatcher {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::SettingsChanged(change) = event else { continue };
            if change.keys.iter().any(|key| key == "indent_width") {
                let values: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&settings::get_json())
                    .unwrap_or(serde_json::Value::Null);
                self.indent = values["indent_width"].as_u64().unwrap_or(4) as u32;
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { getJson } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';

let indent = 4;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'settings-changed') continue;
      if (!event.val.keys.includes('indent_width')) continue;
      const values: Record<string, unknown> = JSON.parse(getJson());
      const next = values['indent_width'];
      indent = typeof next === 'number' ? next : 4;
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

**Example 3: read the settings of other plugins (T1 only)**

A settings screen lists the tabs and sections of every plugin and reads one plugin's values. The plugin needs `settings.read-all` in its manifest and the user must grant it.

```ts
import { getPluginJson, listSettings } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';

export function dumpNotesSettings(): string[] {
  const lines: string[] = [];
  for (const entry of listSettings()) {
    lines.push(`${entry.plugin} / ${entry.tab} (${entry.scope}): ${entry.title}`);
  }
  lines.push(getPluginJson('ilium.notes'));
  return lines;
}
```

### Scope and access

Each entry's `scope` decides which side owns its keys. A `client` key is read and written by the client instance of the plugin, and a `server` key by the server instance. `get-json` on a side returns only that side's keys, `set-json` with a key of the other side is `invalid-argument`, and `settings-changed` goes only to the owning side. A section must be single-scope. A plugin that needs both sides declares two sections.

A settings screen uses `list-settings` to find the tabs and sections. A section is drawn as rows inside its tab. A plugin tab with `"render": "view"` is drawn by the plugin's `views` export through the `settings-page("<tab-id>")` view target. See [Building settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/).

### Errors

| Code | Returned by | When |
|---|---|---|
| `invalid-argument` | `set-json`, `set-plugin-json`, `open`, row-update calls | The patch is not one JSON object, breaks the schema, names an unknown key or a key of the other side, or is over 256 KiB. An `open` target of another plugin is refused too. |
| `not-found` | `get-plugin-json`, `set-plugin-json`, row-update calls | The named plugin is not installed, or a row key or id is unknown. |
| `rate-limited` | row-update calls | More than 10 calls per second. |
| `not-permitted` | `list-settings`, `get-plugin-json`, `set-plugin-json`, `kernel-settings.read` | The grant is missing or was declined. Universal. |
| `revoked`, `internal` | all | Universal. `revoked` means the plugin is re-activated. |

`get-json` has no error code of its own. A tab or section that a plugin does not declare is simply left out of `list-settings` (A37).

### What the user sees

- **A plugin tab** appears in the Settings rail, next to the built-in tabs. Its frame title ends with `· plugin`, and its first line names the plugin and its version.
- **A section in a built-in tab** sits under a divider line that names the plugin and the word `plugin`. Every line of the plugin's rows carries a dim gutter, so the user can always tell whose rows they are.
- Each row has a label, dotted leaders and a control. Secret fields show `••••`, and the last characters when `reveal_last` is set. A changed value has a dim `•` after its label, and a pending write has a dim `◌` after the value.
- A change saved on the page reaches the plugin as `settings-changed` in its next event batch.
- A rejected value is not saved. The reason names the key, so the user can correct the field.
- A disabled plugin's rows stay visible, but read-only and dimmed. Its values are kept.
- The kernel recovery page stays reachable when the settings plugin itself fails. It can re-enable any plugin, so a broken plugin never hides its own repair switch.

### Edge cases

- **Concurrent writes.** Each patch is applied to the stored values at the moment the kernel handles it. Two patches in one batch apply in order.
- **Types.** An `integer` field rejects `4.5`. A `number` field accepts `4`. A string over `maxLength` is `invalid-argument`.
- **Unset keys.** A key with a `default` and no stored value reads as its default in `get-json`.
- **Secrets.** A `secret` value is kept out of logs and out of the snapshot. Other plugins see an empty string from `get-plugin-json`.
- **Restarts.** A restart does not reset stored values. A plugin that restarts after a failure reads them again with `get-json`. Rows of a restarting plugin stay editable, unless the plugin exports `settings-validate`.
- **Disable and uninstall.** Disabling or uninstalling a plugin never deletes its values. They stay in `[plugins."<plugin-id>"]` until the user purges them. See [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/).

# storage

## storage

The `storage` import keeps small key-value data for a plugin. Every value lives in one of three buckets: `global`, `project` or `session`. The bucket decides which projects or sessions can see the value and how long it lasts. Each `put` replaces one value atomically, so a reader never sees half of a write. Storage is for small state such as counters, cursors and settings-like flags. For large data, use [fs](/pages/api-fs/).

**You need:**

- **Grant:** none. Storage is always granted in the server (S), client (C) and scene (A) worlds, so the manifest does not list it.
- **Language:** Rust with the SDK, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. Both wrap the same interface.
- **Import:** Rust `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::storage`; TypeScript `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/storage`.
- **Toolchain:** the SDK pins its own versions. See [Rust SDK](/pages/rust-sdk/) or [TypeScript SDK](/pages/typescript-sdk/).

### Interface

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/storage in reference-wit
enum bucket { global, project, session }
get: func(bucket: bucket, key: string) -> option<list<u8>>;
put: func(bucket: bucket, key: string, value: list<u8>) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
remove: func(bucket: bucket, key: string);
keys: func(bucket: bucket, prefix: string) -> list<string>;
record entry { key: string, value: option<list<u8>> }   // none removes the key
write-batch: func(bucket: bucket, entries: list<entry>) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
```

### Surface

| Function | Rust | TypeScript | Returns | Error codes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `get` | `get(bucket, key) -> Option<Vec<u8>>` | `get(bucket, key): Uint8Array \| undefined` | the value, or nothing | none |
| `put` | `put(bucket, key, &[u8]) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `put(bucket, key, Uint8Array): void`, throws | nothing | `invalid-argument`, `quota-exceeded` |
| `remove` | `remove(bucket, key)` | `remove(bucket, key): void` | nothing | none |
| `keys` | `keys(bucket, prefix) -> Vec<String>` | `keys(bucket, prefix): string[]` | matching keys | none |
| `write-batch` | `write_batch(bucket, &[Entry]) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `writeBatch(bucket, entries): void`, throws | nothing | `invalid-argument`, `quota-exceeded`, `conflict` |

The bucket type is the enum `Bucket` with the variants `Global`, `Project` and `Session` in Rust. In TypeScript it is the string `'global'`, `'project'` or `'session'`. All four functions are synchronous: each call returns when the host has applied it, with no request id to wait for.

`put` also returns the universal codes `not-permitted`, `revoked` and `internal` (see [errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/)). In practice these appear only when the grant is revoked during a call.

### Buckets

| Bucket | Shared with | Lifetime | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `global` | every project on this machine, for this plugin | until the plugin's data is deleted | a preference that applies everywhere |
| `project` | every session that opens the same canonical project directory | until the project's data is deleted | counters, last-run markers, per-project state |
| `session` | only the one named session | deleted when that session is deleted | cursors, pane state |

A session's name comes from its file under `.ilium/sessions/`. The bare `ilium` command owns the `default` session. When a pane's kind declares `persist: "storage"`, the kernel deletes that pane's session keys under `pane/<node-id>/` when the pane closes.

### Rules

- **Keys:** a non-empty UTF-8 string of at most 256 bytes. The host stores the key byte for byte, with no trimming or case folding. A slash has no special meaning to the host; the `pane/<node-id>/` pattern above is a convention.
- **Values:** a byte array of at most 1 MiB per `put`. An empty value is allowed.
- **Quota:** each bucket holds 16 MiB by default. The manifest field `limits.storage_bucket_mib` may request less, or more up to the host ceiling: 256 MiB for tier 1 and 16 MiB for tiers 2 and 3. The size of a bucket is the sum of its key bytes and value bytes. A `put` that replaces a value counts only the difference.
- **Atomic replacement:** a `put` either replaces the whole value or changes nothing. A refused `put` keeps the previous value.
- **Keys listing:** `keys` returns every key that starts with the prefix, sorted by byte order. An empty prefix returns all keys of the bucket. Results are not paged.
- **Missing keys:** `get` returns nothing, and `remove` does nothing. Neither is an error.

### Batches, durability and concurrency

- [LIF-117] `write-batch` MUST apply all its entries or none of them. A batch holds at most 256 entries and at most 4 MiB of key and value bytes together; more is `invalid-argument`. A refused batch keeps every previous value. Test: write a batch whose last entry breaks the quota and read all keys.
- [LIF-118] `put`, `remove` and `write-batch` MUST return only after the change is flushed to stable storage, so that a crash or power loss after the return cannot lose it. A crash before the return leaves the previous value. Test: kill the process in the middle of a batch and read back.
- [LIF-119] A write that fails because the disk is full MUST return `io` with the message `no-space`, never `quota-exceeded`, which is only for the plugin's own quota. Test: fill the disk and `put`. See [offline and low disk](/pages/reference-offline-and-low-disk/).
- [LIF-120] Several session servers can write the same `global` or `project` bucket. The host MUST serialise writers with a lock per bucket, so that each `put` and each batch is atomic across processes, and the last writer of a key wins. There is no compare-and-set; use a version key and `write-batch` if you need one. Test: two servers write the same key and read it back.
- [LIF-121] The bucket also carries a data version stamp that the plugin cannot see. A write from an instance older than the stamp MUST return `conflict` with the message `stale-data-version`. See [data migration](/pages/guide-data-migration/). Test: see LIF-113.

A storage database that fails its integrity check is moved aside and the plugin starts with empty storage ([offline and low disk](/pages/reference-offline-and-low-disk/)).

### Example 1: a save counter per project

The counter lives in the `project` bucket. Two projects get two counters, because each project directory is its own bucket scope.

**Grants:** none (always granted)

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::storage::{self, Bucket};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

const COUNTER_KEY: &str = "saves";

fn read_counter() -> u64 {
    storage::get(Bucket::Project, COUNTER_KEY)
        .and_then(|bytes| <[u8; 8]>::try_from(bytes).ok())
        .map_or(0, u64::from_le_bytes)
}

fn increment_counter() -> Result<u64, PluginError> {
    let next = read_counter() + 1;
    storage::put(Bucket::Project, COUNTER_KEY, &next.to_le_bytes())?;
    Ok(next)
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import * as storage from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/storage';

const COUNTER_KEY = 'saves';

export function readCounter(): bigint {
  const bytes = storage.get('project', COUNTER_KEY);
  if (bytes === undefined || bytes.length !== 8) {
    return 0n;
  }
  return new DataView(bytes.buffer, bytes.byteOffset, 8).getBigUint64(0, true);
}

export function incrementCounter(): bigint {
  const next = readCounter() + 1n;
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(8);
  new DataView(bytes.buffer).setBigUint64(0, next, true);
  storage.put('project', COUNTER_KEY, bytes);
  return next;
}
```

After two saves in the same project, `increment_counter()` returns `2`. The TypeScript `incrementCounter()` returns `2n`. In another project the same call starts again at `1`.

### Example 2: a cursor per pane, with a key listing

This example stores one cursor per pane in the `session` bucket. It uses the `pane/<node-id>/`
convention, so `keys` can list the panes and `remove` can forget one. The pane identifier is passed in
as a string, so the example does not depend on how `NodeId` is represented.

**Grants:** none (always granted)

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::storage::{self, Bucket};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

fn cursor_key(pane_key: &str) -> String {
    format!("pane/{pane_key}/cursor")
}

fn save_cursor(pane_key: &str, cursor: u32) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    storage::put(Bucket::Session, &cursor_key(pane_key), &cursor.to_le_bytes())
}

fn load_cursor(pane_key: &str) -> u32 {
    storage::get(Bucket::Session, &cursor_key(pane_key))
        .and_then(|bytes| <[u8; 4]>::try_from(bytes).ok())
        .map_or(0, u32::from_le_bytes)
}

fn panes_with_cursor() -> Vec<String> {
    storage::keys(Bucket::Session, "pane/")
        .into_iter()
        .filter_map(|key| {
            let pane_key = key.strip_prefix("pane/")?.strip_suffix("/cursor")?;
            Some(pane_key.to_owned())
        })
        .collect()
}

fn forget_cursor(pane_key: &str) {
    storage::remove(Bucket::Session, &cursor_key(pane_key));
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import * as storage from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/storage';

function cursorKey(paneKey: string): string {
  return `pane/${paneKey}/cursor`;
}

export function saveCursor(paneKey: string, cursor: number): void {
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(4);
  new DataView(bytes.buffer).setUint32(0, cursor, true);
  storage.put('session', cursorKey(paneKey), bytes);
}

export function loadCursor(paneKey: string): number {
  const bytes = storage.get('session', cursorKey(paneKey));
  if (bytes === undefined || bytes.length !== 4) {
    return 0;
  }
  return new DataView(bytes.buffer, bytes.byteOffset, 4).getUint32(0, true);
}

export function panesWithCursor(): string[] {
  return storage
    .keys('session', 'pane/')
    .filter((key) => key.endsWith('/cursor'))
    .map((key) => key.slice('pane/'.length, -'/cursor'.length));
}

export function forgetCursor(paneKey: string): void {
  storage.remove('session', cursorKey(paneKey));
}
```

Saving cursor `7` for pane `p3` and then calling `panes_with_cursor()` returns `["p3"]`. After
`forget_cursor("p3")`, the list is empty and `load_cursor("p3")` returns `0`.

### What the user sees

Storage has no screen of its own. A refused `put` is a return value to the plugin, so the user sees
the failure only where the plugin reports it, for example in its log. The plugin log line has the
format `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss`, the level, the plugin id and the message:

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs demo-plugin --tail 3
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:02</span> <span class="t-ok">info </span> demo-plugin saves now 2
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:31</span> <span class="t-err">error</span> demo-plugin put saves failed: quota-exceeded
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:31</span> <span class="t-warn">warn </span> demo-plugin kept the value from 09:14:02
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The plugin writes these lines itself; the host only stores them and
formats them. The key, values and times are placeholders.

When a plugin is uninstalled, the user chooses whether to keep or delete its data and storage. A
deleted session bucket goes with its session.

### Errors

| Code | Raised by | Cause | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `invalid-argument` | `put` | key empty or over 256 bytes, or value over 1 MiB | fix the call; nothing is written |
| `quota-exceeded` | `put` | the bucket or the disk limit (`data` plus `cache`) would be passed | remove keys or shrink values, then retry |

A value over 1 MiB is always `invalid-argument`, never `quota-exceeded`. This lets a plugin tell a bad
call from a full bucket. The host never truncates a value.

### The shared bucket and the lease

The enum gains a fourth case, `shared`. It is one cache bucket per plugin, shared by the plugin's server side, all its client sides and every session of the same user. The host may clear it at any time, so it holds only data that can be rebuilt: a downloaded index, a rendered image, a geocoding answer. Entries beyond `shared_cache_mib` (64 MiB by default; 256 for tier 1, 128 for tiers 2 and 3) evict the oldest first.

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/storage in reference-wit
enum bucket { global, project, session, shared }
lease: func(key: string, ttl-millis: u32) -> bool;     // true for the one caller that may refresh
```

Several sessions can notice at the same moment that a cache entry is stale. The lease makes only one of them refresh it: `lease` returns true to exactly one caller per `key` until `ttl-millis` passes, and false to the rest, who should read the old value or wait. The lease is not a lock for correctness; it prevents duplicate work.

| Bucket | Shared with | Cleared by the host | Count against |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shared` | server side, client sides and all sessions of the user | any time | `shared_cache_mib` |

<figure>

<figcaption>Only one caller per key refreshes the entry while its lease is open.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::storage::{self, Bucket};

fn index_bytes() -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
    if storage::lease("index", 60_000) {
        let fresh = rebuild_index();                       // slow work, done once
        let _ = storage::put(Bucket::Shared, "index", &fresh);
        return Some(fresh);
    }
    storage::get(Bucket::Shared, "index")                  // someone else refreshes
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { get, put, lease } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/storage';

export function indexBytes(): Uint8Array | undefined {
  if (lease('index', 60_000)) {
    const fresh = rebuildIndex();
    put('shared', 'index', fresh);
    return fresh;
  }
  return get('shared', 'index');
}
```

Errors: `put` into `shared` returns `quota-exceeded` only when one value alone is larger than `shared_cache_mib`; otherwise the oldest entries go. The key rules are those of the other buckets.
