### When the grant is declined, revoked or missing

| Situation | What the call returns | What happens to streams |
|---|---|---|
| The user declined the grant | `not-permitted` from `open-capture`, `open-loopback` and `play` | none opened |
| The grant was revoked while a stream was open | `revoked` for calls in flight | the stream closes, the plugin gets `deactivate(revoked)` and activates again with the reduced grant set |
| The manifest never requested the grant | the call traps | the plugin fails |

Handle a declined grant in `activate` and keep the plugin working without audio. The example below does this, and it is the pattern to copy for any optional grant.

### Worked example: voice input that survives a declined grant (Rust)

The plugin opens the default microphone at 16 kHz mono on activation. If the user declined `audio.capture`, the plugin stays active and counts nothing. It counts chunks whose peak level passes a threshold, and it adds up the frames that the host dropped.

Manifest excerpt:

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.voice",
  "capabilities": { "client": ["audio.capture"] }
}
```

Plugin source:

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{Handler, Lifecycle};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::audio;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

const CAPTURE_RATE: u32 = 16_000;
const SPEECH_PEAK: u16 = 4_000;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct VoiceInput {
    capture: Option<u64>,
    speech_chunks: u32,
    dropped_frames: u32,
}

impl Lifecycle for VoiceInput {
    fn activate(&mut self, _context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        match audio::open_capture(None, CAPTURE_RATE, 1) {
            Ok(capture) => self.capture = Some(capture),
            // The user declined audio.capture. Stay active without voice input.
            Err(error) if error.code == ErrorCode::NotPermitted => {}
            Err(error) => return Err(error),
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    fn deactivate(&mut self, _reason: DeactivationReason) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
        if let Some(capture) = self.capture.take() {
            audio::close_capture(capture);
        }
        None
    }
}

impl Handler for VoiceInput {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::AudioFrames(frames) if Some(frames.capture) == self.capture => {
                    let peak = frames.samples.iter().map(|sample| sample.unsigned_abs()).max();
                    if peak.unwrap_or(0) > SPEECH_PEAK {
                        self.speech_chunks += 1;
                    }
                }
                Event::EventsDropped(counts) => {
                    self.dropped_frames += counts
                        .iter()
                        .filter(|count| count.event == "audio-frames")
                        .map(|count| count.count)
                        .sum::<u32>();
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

Any other error is returned from `activate` unchanged. A `not-permitted` error is not a failure of the plugin, so the plugin does not return it.

### Worked example: loopback recorder (TypeScript)

The plugin records five seconds of desktop output when the user runs its command. It records 250 chunks of 20 ms, closes the stream, and logs the result. It also closes the stream if the plugin deactivates first. The manifest declares `audio.loopback` under `capabilities.client`, and a `contributes.commands` entry for the command id.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import * as audio from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/audio';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const RECORD_COMMAND = 'com.example.clip/record-output';
const SAMPLE_RATE = 48_000;
const CHANNELS = 2;
const CHUNKS_TO_RECORD = 250; // 250 chunks of 20 ms is five seconds

let recording: bigint | undefined;
let chunksSeen = 0;

function startRecording(): void {
  if (recording !== undefined) {
    return;
  }
  try {
    recording = audio.openLoopback(SAMPLE_RATE, CHANNELS);
    chunksSeen = 0;
    log('info', `loopback ${recording} opened`);
  } catch (error) {
    const code = error instanceof PluginError ? error.code : 'unknown';
    log('warn', `loopback not opened: ${code}`);
  }
}

function stopRecording(reason: string): void {
  if (recording === undefined) {
    return;
  }
  audio.closeCapture(recording);
  log('info', `loopback closed (${reason}) after ${chunksSeen} chunks`);
  recording = undefined;
}

function onFrames(capture: bigint): void {
  if (capture !== recording) {
    return;
  }
  chunksSeen += 1;
  if (chunksSeen >= CHUNKS_TO_RECORD) {
    stopRecording('complete');
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {},
  deactivate() {
    stopRecording('deactivate');
    return undefined;
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === RECORD_COMMAND) {
        startRecording();
      } else if (event.tag === 'audio-frames') {
        onFrames(event.val.capture);
      } else if (event.tag === 'events-dropped') {
        for (const count of event.val) {
          if (count.event === 'audio-frames') {
            log('warn', `${count.count} loopback frames dropped`);
          }
        }
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

The `openLoopback` call throws a `PluginError` when the grant is declined or the platform has no monitor source. The plugin catches it and logs the code, so it never traps. A real recorder would copy the samples of each `audio-frames` event into a buffer.

### Edge cases and error codes

| Call | Code | Cause and response |
|---|---|---|
| `open-capture`, `open-loopback`, `play` | `not-permitted` | grant declined or revoked; keep working without audio |
| `open-capture` | `not-found` | the device id is not in `devices()`; list devices again |
| `open-capture`, `open-loopback` | `invalid-argument` | rate outside 8,000 to 192,000 Hz, or zero channels |
| `open-capture`, `open-loopback` | `unsupported` | more than two channels, or loopback with no monitor source |
| `open-capture` | `busy` | the device is held exclusively by another application |
| `open-capture`, `open-loopback` | `quota-exceeded` | too many open streams; the default is 2, and the ceiling is 4 for T1 and 2 for T2 and T3 |
| `play` | `invalid-argument` | longer than 30 s, larger than 16 MiB, or a sample count that is not a multiple of `channels` |
| `play` | `io` (completion) | the output device failed during playback |
| `audio-frames` | `events-dropped` | the handler was too slow; the event names `audio-frames` and the capture id |
| `close-capture` | none | an unknown or already closed id does nothing |

Stream rules that the plugin can rely on:

- A stream closes when its plugin deactivates, is disabled or is uninstalled. No `audio-frames` event arrives after that.
- Frames that do not fit the queue are dropped oldest first. The loss is counted in `events-dropped`, and the drop never blocks the device.
- A `play` call completes when playback ends, not when it starts. The Rust function returns after playback, and the TypeScript `await` resolves to `undefined` at the same point.

### What the user sees

The host shows the install dialog for a T2 or T3 plugin and the first-activation prompt for a T1 plugin. The plugin's own log shows what it did with the streams. `ilium plugin logs` prints it:

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs voice-input
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:02</span> <span class="t-ok">info</span>  capture 4 opened: 16000 Hz, 1 channel
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:07</span> <span class="t-warn">warn</span>  device usb-mic-2 is gone, reopening the default input
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:07</span> <span class="t-ok">info</span>  capture 5 opened: 16000 Hz, 1 channel
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:09</span> <span class="t-warn">warn</span>  2 audio-frames events dropped (capture 5)
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> <span class="t-dim">4 lines shown, 0 dropped</span>
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The log of a voice plugin that reopens its microphone after the device is removed. The plugin writes the reopen lines, and the device name is a placeholder.

### Who requests it

First-party plugins from `feature-mapping.md`:

- 50 Voice session: `audio.capture`.
- 53 Voice onboarding demo: `audio.capture` and `audio.playback`.
- 54 Voice device selection and reconnect: `audio.capture`.
- 101 Media scenes: `audio.loopback` and `audio.capture`.

# Capability: cli.contribute

## cli.contribute

The `cli.contribute` grant lets a server-side plugin add one subcommand to the `ilium` command
line. The plugin declares the subcommand in its manifest. When the user runs
`ilium <name> [arguments]`, the server sends a `cli-invoked` event to the plugin, and the plugin
answers with JSON lines on standard output and ends the call with an exit code. Every output line
must be one JSON object with a `type` field, because agents read this output.

The grant decides whether the subcommand exists for the user at all. If the user declines it, the
subcommand is hidden from help and cannot be run. The grant is server-side only, and it takes no
argument: the subcommand name belongs in the `cli` contribution.

**You will need:**

- the `cli.contribute` grant on the `server` side of the manifest, with no argument;
- a `cli` object under `contributes` that names the subcommand;
- a `server` component that exports `handler`;
- Rust with `ilium_plugin_sdk` 0.1, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. Create a project with
  `ilium plugin new notes --id com.example.notes --lang rust --side server`.

### Grant syntax

| Grant | Valid | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `cli.contribute` | yes | the only form |
| `cli.contribute:notes` | no | refused at install with `manifest.grant-argument` |
| `cli:contribute` | no | the separator is a dot; refused with `manifest.grant-unknown` |

The install error for the first row reads
`capability "cli.contribute" takes no argument (got "cli.contribute:notes")`.

### Manifest

A plugin declares its subcommands in the `cli` key. The key holds one object, or a list of at most 8 objects when the plugin owns several commands (the fleet plugin owns `panes`, `broadcast` and `new-pane`). Names MUST be unique inside the plugin:

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.notes",
  "capabilities": { "server": ["cli.contribute"] },
  "server": {
    "entry": "server.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": []
  },
  "contributes": {
    "cli": {
      "name": "notes",
      "summary": "List notes",
      "arguments_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": { "type": "string" } } },
      "output": "jsonl"
    }
  }
}
```

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | The subcommand. It must match `[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}`. It runs as `ilium <name>`. |
| `summary` | string | One line shown in `ilium --help`. |
| `arguments_schema` | JSON Schema object | Documents the arguments for help. The host passes `argv` unchanged and does not validate it. |
| `output` | `"jsonl"`, `"text"` or `"mixed"` | The output form. `mixed` allows both `write-line` and `write-text` (used by `new-pane`). |
| `aliases` | list of strings | Further names for the same command, for example `wait` for `progress wait`. Same name rule. |

A name that a kernel command uses is refused at install with `manifest.cli-name-reserved`; a name
that another installed plugin owns is refused with `manifest.cli-name-taken`. A plugin starts for the subcommand on its first use when its activation
rule is `cli:<name>`, or on first use of any contribution when no activation rule is set.

### Surface

The import interface is `ilium:host/cli@0.1.0`. In Rust it is `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::cli`, and in
TypeScript it is `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/cli`.

| Function | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning | Errors beyond the universal set |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `write-line` | `cli::write_line(invocation: u64, jsonl: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `writeLine(invocation: bigint, jsonl: string): void` | Writes one JSON object and a newline to the caller's standard output. | `not-found` (finished or cancelled), `invalid-argument` (not one object with a string `type`, a raw newline, or over 64 KiB) |
| `write-error` | `cli::write_error(invocation: u64, text: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `writeError(invocation: bigint, text: string): void` | Writes plain text and a newline to standard error. | `not-found`, `invalid-argument` (over 64 KiB) |
| `finish` | `cli::finish(invocation: u64, exit_code: u8)` | `finish(invocation: bigint, exitCode: number): void` | Ends the invocation. `exit_code` becomes the process exit status. | none; an unknown invocation is ignored |

In TypeScript a failed `writeLine` or `writeError` throws a `PluginError`. The universal codes
`not-permitted`, `revoked` and `internal` can also appear (see
[errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/)).

| Event | Payload | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cli-invoked` | `invocation` (u64), `name` (string), `argv` (list of strings), `cwd` (string) | `Event::CliInvoked(CliInvokedEvent { invocation, name, argv, cwd })` | `{ tag: 'cli-invoked', val: { invocation, name, argv, cwd } }` |
| `cli-cancelled` | `invocation` (u64) | `Event::CliCancelled(u64)` | `{ tag: 'cli-cancelled', val: bigint }` |

`name` is the subcommand name. `argv` holds the words after the name, exactly as the shell passed
them. `cwd` is the absolute path of the caller's working directory. Invocation ids are assigned by
the host and are unique for the life of the server. Both events are never dropped.

The WIT form of the three imports is:

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/cli in reference-wit
// cli (cli.contribute)
write-line: func(invocation: u64, jsonl: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
write-error: func(invocation: u64, text: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
finish: func(invocation: u64, exit-code: u8);
```

### How an invocation runs

  </defs>

  <rect x="60" y="60" width="280" height="34" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>

  <text x="300" y="137" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Declined: hidden from help</text>
  <line x1="100" y1="150" x2="100" y2="172" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#cli-cap-arrow)"/>
  <line x1="300" y1="150" x2="300" y2="172" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#cli-cap-arrow)"/>
  <rect x="10" y="172" width="180" height="34" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="100" y="193" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">cli-invoked reaches plugin</text>
  <rect x="210" y="172" width="180" height="34" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="300" y="193" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Fails: unknown command</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The grant decides at install whether the subcommand exists. A declined subcommand never
reaches the plugin.</figcaption>
</figure>

Once the command runs, the plugin writes its output and calls `finish`:

1. The host sends `cli-invoked` with the invocation id, the name, the arguments and the working
   directory.
2. The plugin calls `write-line` once per JSON object. Each line is written as it arrives.
3. The plugin calls `finish` with the exit code. The invocation closes.

The invocation has no deadline of its own. It stays open until `finish`, or until the caller
disconnects, which sends `cli-cancelled`. Several invocations can run at once, and each has its own
id. Keep the handler short, because it runs inside the plugin's event deadline. Start slow work in
a task and write from it.

### Risk, review and revocation

- **Risk:** normal. The capability table does not mark the grant as high risk.
- **Tier T1 (bundled):** granted automatically up to the manifest ceiling.
- **Tier T2 and T3:** the review dialog lists the grant as a checked row, and the user can uncheck
  it before installing. The row text is `Add ilium commands`.
- **Other grants:** the subcommand runs inside the plugin, so the plugin's other grants still
  apply to anything the subcommand reads or writes.
- **Revoke:** in Settings > Plugins > (plugin) > Capabilities, or with
  `ilium plugin grants com.example.notes --revoke cli.contribute`. The subcommand is withdrawn at
  once. Calls already in flight return `revoked`.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.cli 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                       │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Adds commands to the ilium program <span class="t-dim">……………………………………………………</span> cli.contribute │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>The review dialog for a package that requests cli.contribute, drawn with the client's dialog characters: rounded corners, dotted leaders and the hint bar. Checked rows are granted; a high-risk row starts unchecked.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Worked example in Rust

This plugin answers `ilium notes` with one JSON line per note. It uses two sample titles. A real
plugin reads its notes with `storage` or with `fs.read`, which need their own grants.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::cli;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

const SAMPLE_NOTES: [&str; 2] = ["Weekly plan", "Release checklist"];

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct NotesCommand;

impl Lifecycle for NotesCommand {}

impl Handler for NotesCommand {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::CliInvoked(invoked) = event else {
                continue;
            };
            if invoked.name == "notes" {
                list_notes(invoked.invocation);
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

fn list_notes(invocation: u64) {
    for title in SAMPLE_NOTES {
        let line = format!(r#"{{"type":"note","title":"{title}"}}"#);
        if let Err(error) = cli::write_line(invocation, &line) {
            let _ = cli::write_error(invocation, &error.message);
            cli::finish(invocation, 1);
            return;
        }
    }
    cli::finish(invocation, 0);
}
```

### Worked example in TypeScript

The same behaviour in TypeScript, with the manifest shown above. `JSON.stringify` does the
escaping, and `finish` is called on both the success and the error path.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { finish, writeError, writeLine } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/cli';

const SAMPLE_NOTES = ['Weekly plan', 'Release checklist'];

function listNotes(invocation: bigint): void {
  try {
    for (const title of SAMPLE_NOTES) {
      writeLine(invocation, JSON.stringify({ type: 'note', title }));
    }
    finish(invocation, 0);
  } catch (error) {
    const message = error instanceof PluginError ? error.message : String(error);
    writeError(invocation, message);
    finish(invocation, 1);
  }
}

export const { handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'cli-invoked' && event.val.name === 'notes') {
        listNotes(event.val.invocation);
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

### What the user sees

With the grant granted, the subcommand appears in help and prints one JSON object per line:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium --help
Commands:
  <span class="t-hi">notes</span>    List notes
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium notes
<span class="t-dim">{"type":"note","title":"Weekly plan"}</span>
<span class="t-dim">{"type":"note","title":"Release checklist"}</span>
<span class="t-ok">exit 0</span>
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A granted subcommand, from help to a successful
run.</figcaption>
</figure>

With the grant declined, the subcommand is hidden and cannot run. The grant list still shows it:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium notes
<span class="t-err">error</span>: unknown command
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin grants com.example.notes
  server  cli.contribute  <span class="t-warn">declined</span>
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A declined subcommand and its grant state.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Edge cases and errors

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Grant declined at install | The subcommand is hidden from `ilium --help`. `ilium <name>` fails with `unknown command`. No `cli-invoked` arrives. |
| Grant revoked while running | In-flight calls return `revoked`. The plugin is re-activated with the reduced grant set. An open invocation ends with exit code 1 and `grant revoked` on standard error. |
| Grant with an argument | Install refused with `manifest.grant-argument`. |
| Unknown grant spelling | Install refused with `manifest.grant-unknown`. |
| Name outside `[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}` | Install refused. |
| Name used by a kernel command | Install refused with `manifest.cli-name-reserved`. |
| Name owned by another installed plugin | Install refused with `manifest.cli-name-taken`. |
| `write-line` text is not one JSON object with a string `type` | `invalid-argument`. The line is not written. |
| `write-line` text contains a raw newline | `invalid-argument`. The host adds the newline itself. |
| `write-line` or `write-error` text over 64 KiB | `invalid-argument`. |
| `write-line` or `write-error` after `finish` or after cancel | `not-found`. |
| `finish` for an unknown or finished invocation | Ignored. |
| Caller disconnects early | `cli-cancelled` arrives. Later writes return `not-found`. |
| Plugin restarts, is disabled or is uninstalled while open | The invocation ends with exit code 1 and `plugin stopped` on standard error. |

<div class="warn">
<p>A plugin that never calls <code>finish</code> leaves the caller waiting, with no deadline.
Call <code>finish</code> on every path, including the error path.</p>
</div>

<div class="note">
<p>The host does not check <code>argv</code> against <code>arguments_schema</code>. The schema
only documents the arguments for help, so the plugin validates them itself.</p>
</div>

### Used by

First-party plugins from `feature-mapping.md` that hold this grant:

- 52 `ilium voice say`, which sends a `message` to the plugin's own client side.
- 60 `ilium progress`, which writes its status with `write-line` and `finish`.
- 62 Chatroom, which adds its own CLI commands.
- 64 Context-injection hook, which reads its read position from `storage` when `cli-invoked`
  arrives.
- 109 `ilium panes`.
- 110 `ilium broadcast`.

- [api-cli](/pages/api-cli/) for the full import reference and the Rust and TypeScript SDK paths.

  the loopback HTTP API.

  project.

# Capability: clipboard

## clipboard.read and clipboard.write

The `clipboard.read` and `clipboard.write` grants let a client plugin read and write plain text on the system clipboard. Writing is common and low risk. Reading is high risk, because the clipboard often holds passwords and tokens that the user copied from another program. Each direction is a separate grant, and a plugin asks only for the direction it uses.

The grants cover one import, `clipboard`, which belongs to the client world. A server plugin cannot call it, because the clipboard belongs to the user's desktop session.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="Client plugin calls write-text and read-text on the host clipboard, each under its own grant">
  <defs>
    <marker id="clip-arrow" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="10" y="30" width="130" height="100" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="75" y="58" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Client plugin</text>
  <text x="75" y="76" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">com.example.notes</text>
  <rect x="260" y="30" width="130" height="100" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="325" y="58" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Host clipboard</text>

## You will need

| Need | Value |
|---|---|
| Side | Client. The import is part of `ilium:client/base@0.1.0`. |
| Grant to write | `clipboard.write`, normal risk. Checked by default in the review dialog. |
| Grant to read | `clipboard.read`, high risk (H). Unchecked by default, and the user checks it. |
| Rust | Crate `ilium-plugin-sdk`, Rust stable 1.90 or later, target `wasm32-wasip2`. |
| TypeScript | Package `@ilium/plugin-sdk`, Bun 1.2 or later. `bun install` adds the toolchain. |
| Text format | UTF-8 plain text. Images and other formats are not supported. |

Import the module in each language:

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::clipboard;
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import * as clipboard from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clipboard';
```

## Grant syntax

A clipboard grant takes no argument. The name is the whole grant string.

| Grant | Valid | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `clipboard.read` | yes | The read direction. High risk. |
| `clipboard.write` | yes | The write direction. Normal risk. |
| `clipboard` | no | The direction is missing. The manifest is refused. |
| `clipboard.read:text` | no | The grant takes no argument. The manifest is refused with `manifest.grant-argument`. |

## The surface

The import has two functions and no records.

| WIT function | Rust | TypeScript | Grant | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `read-text` | `clipboard::read_text() -> Option<String>` | `clipboard.readText(): string \| undefined` | `clipboard.read` | `option<string>` | The clipboard text, or nothing when the clipboard holds no text. |
| `write-text` | `clipboard::write_text(text: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `clipboard.writeText(text: string): void`, throws `PluginError` | `clipboard.write` | `result<_, plugin-error>` | Replaces the clipboard text with `text`. |

Both functions are synchronous. They return at once and never return a request id. The names
follow the plugin binding rules: kebab-case becomes snake_case in Rust and
camelCase in TypeScript.

## What the user sees

The review dialog lists one row per grant, in the Client group. The `clipboard.read` row carries
the HIGH mark. A T2 or T3 package shows this dialog at install. A T1 bundled plugin is activated
first without its high-risk grants, and the user sees one prompt per plugin at first activation.

<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.clipboard 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                 │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Client side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Writes to the clipboard <span class="t-dim">………………………………………………………………………………</span> clipboard.write │
│ <span class="t-warn">! [ ] Reads the clipboard</span> <span class="t-dim">………………………………………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-warn">clipboard.read</span> │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-warn">! marks a high-risk grant. It starts unchecked and is</span>                      │
│ <span class="t-warn">always asked for, even for bundled plugins.</span>                                │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>

The client never asks again on each read. A successful read writes an info line to the plugin
log that records only the length of the text, never the text itself. The same line goes to the
privacy log. The client footer also shows the read for 3 s:

<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">Client footer, 3 seconds after a successful read</span>
<span class="t-hi">clipboard read by Example Notes</span>
</pre>

The client chooses a route for each write. The route decides whether the text reaches the desktop
clipboard at all.

## Behaviour, edge cases and errors

| Situation | `write-text` | `read-text` |
|---|---|---|
| Grant held, text on the clipboard | Writes the text. Returns `ok`. | Returns the text. |
| Clipboard holds no text (an image, or nothing) | Not applicable. | Returns `none`. No error. |
| Empty string written | Accepted. Replaces the clipboard text with an empty text. Returns `ok`. | Returns an empty string. |
| Text larger than 1 MiB (1,048,576 UTF-8 bytes) | `invalid-argument`. Nothing is written. The text is never truncated. | Not applicable. |
| No route on this client | `unsupported`. | Returns `none`. |
| Grant declined by the user | `not-permitted`. | Returns `none`. A warn line goes to the plugin log. |
| Grant revoked during the call | `revoked`. The plugin is re-activated with the reduced grant set. | Returns `none`, because `read-text` has no error result. A warn line goes to the plugin log. |
| Grant never requested in the manifest | The plugin traps and counts as a failure. | The plugin traps and counts as a failure. |

Rules that follow from the table:

- A declined or revoked read is not reported as an error. The plugin cannot tell "no text" from
  "not allowed" by the return value alone. The warn line in the plugin log is the only record of
  a refused read.
- `write-text` counts the 1 MiB limit in UTF-8 bytes, not in characters. A text of 300,000
  characters that take four bytes each is 1.2 MB, so it is refused.
- A revoked grant does not make the plugin fail. Revocation re-activates the plugin, as described
  in the grant lifecycle.

## Example 1: copy a note link (Rust)

The manifest requests only the write direction. The plugin copies a link to a note when the user
runs the `copy-note-link` command.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.notes",
  "name": "Example Notes",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example Corp",
  "client": {
    "entry": "client.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": []
  },
  "capabilities": { "client": ["clipboard.write"] }
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::clipboard;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

const NOTE_LINK_PREFIX: &str = "notes://";

/// Runs when the user invokes the `copy-note-link` command.
/// `note_path` comes from the command arguments, for example "today/weekly-plan".
fn copy_note_link(note_path: &str) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let link = format!("{NOTE_LINK_PREFIX}{note_path}");
    // Errors (not-permitted, unsupported, invalid-argument) pass to the caller.
    clipboard::write_text(&link)
}
```

The command handler maps `Err(PluginError)` to a message in the plugin's own pane, so the user
can copy the link by hand when the write fails.

## Example 2: read a note link and handle a missing grant (TypeScript)

This plugin reads the clipboard to open a note that the user copied from elsewhere. It needs both
directions, because it also copies links. The read grant is high risk, so the manifest must say
why the plugin needs it in its `description`.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.notes",
  "name": "Example Notes",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example Corp",
  "description": "Opens a note whose link you copied. Reads the clipboard only when you ask it to.",
  "client": {
    "entry": "client.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": []
  },
  "capabilities": { "client": ["clipboard.read", "clipboard.write"] }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import * as clipboard from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/clipboard';

const NOTE_LINK_PREFIX = 'notes://';

/** Returns the note path on the clipboard, or undefined when no note link is there. */
export function noteFromClipboard(): string | undefined {
  // undefined covers an empty clipboard, an image, a declined grant and a revoked grant.
  const text = clipboard.readText();
  if (text === undefined) {
    return undefined;
  }
  const link = text.trim();
  if (!link.startsWith(NOTE_LINK_PREFIX)) {
    return undefined;
  }
  return link.slice(NOTE_LINK_PREFIX.length);
}

/** Copies a note link and reports the outcome, so the caller can fall back to a visible link. */
export function copyNoteLink(notePath: string): 'copied' | 'unsupported' | 'not-permitted' {
  try {
    clipboard.writeText(`${NOTE_LINK_PREFIX}${notePath}`);
    return 'copied';
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof PluginError && error.code === 'unsupported') {
      return 'unsupported';
    }
    if (error instanceof PluginError && error.code === 'not-permitted') {
      return 'not-permitted';
    }
    throw error;
  }
}
```

Error codes arrive as kebab-case strings in TypeScript. A `PluginError` carries `code`, `message`
and `retryAfterMs` (present only for rate and quota errors). Any other thrown value is a bug, so
the example rethrows it.

## Who requests it

Among the first-party plugins in the feature map, four request `clipboard.write`: the text
selection and right-click menu, the agent toolbar, and the two Smart Copy plugins (light and AI).
No first-party plugin requests `clipboard.read`.

### Security

**[SEC-044]** Clipboard reads are high risk and are logged to the privacy log; a write never reads. See [Secrets](/pages/reference-secrets/).

# commands.invoke

## Overview

The `commands.invoke` grant lets a plugin run commands that belong to other plugins, or to the kernel, by their global id. A plugin can start a git status refresh, a compaction or a voice command without knowing how those features work inside. You name the command by its id, and the kernel runs it.

Every call passes one check. The kernel compares the global id of the command with the pattern in your grant. A match runs the command. Anything else returns `not-permitted`, and the command does not run. The grant reaches only the ids that its pattern matches, so a narrow pattern keeps the reach small. The pattern `*` reaches every command of every plugin. It is a high-risk grant.

Your own commands need no grant. You invoke them without the check, and their invocations arrive as `command-invoked` events.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 230" role="img" aria-label="A caller plugin sends invoke to the kernel grant check, which runs a matching command or returns not-permitted">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arrow-invoke" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="20" y="10" width="360" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="200" y="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Caller plugin</text>
  <text x="200" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">holds commands.invoke:ilium.git/*</text>
  <line x1="200" y1="60" x2="200" y2="84" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arrow-invoke)"/>
  <text x="210" y="76" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">invoke(command, arguments-json)</text>
  <rect x="20" y="84" width="360" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="200" y="104" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Kernel grant check</text>
  <text x="200" y="122" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">does the pattern match the global id?</text>
  <line x1="110" y1="134" x2="110" y2="166" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arrow-invoke)"/>
  <text x="118" y="154" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">match</text>
  <line x1="290" y1="134" x2="290" y2="166" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arrow-invoke)"/>
  <text x="282" y="154" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">no match</text>
  <rect x="20" y="166" width="170" height="52" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="105" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">ilium.git/status runs</text>
  <text x="105" y="204" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">and returns its outcome</text>
  <rect x="210" y="166" width="170" height="52" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="295" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">not-permitted</text>
  <text x="295" y="204" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">the command does not run</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>A call that matches the granted pattern runs the command. Any other call returns not-permitted, and the command does not run.</figcaption>
</figure>

## You will need

- A grant `commands.invoke:<pattern>` on every side that makes the call. The `invoke` call exists on the server side and on the client side. A client handler needs the grant in `capabilities.client`, and a server handler needs it in `capabilities.server`.
- The global id of each command you call. A global id is the plugin id, a slash and the local id, for example `ilium.git/status`.
- Nothing else for your own commands. Only commands of other plugins, and kernel commands, need the grant.

## Grant syntax

The first colon in the grant separates the name from the pattern, and the pattern is required. A `*` is a whole-segment wildcard. It never crosses the slash between the plugin id and the local id, so `ilium.git/*` covers the local ids of one plugin and nothing else.

| Pattern | Matches | Result at install |
|---|---|---|
| `ilium.git/status` | exactly one command | valid |
| `ilium.git/*` | every command of the git plugin | valid |
| `*` | every command of every plugin | valid, high risk (H) |
| `ilium.git*` | a wildcard inside a word | rejected |
| `ilium.git/prefix*` | a wildcard inside the local id | rejected |
| `*/status` | a wildcard in the plugin id | rejected |
| `commands.invoke` | no pattern at all | rejected |

## Surface

The grant unlocks four call forms and one intent. The Rust and TypeScript wrappers wait for the outcome, so most plugins use them. The raw forms return the request id at once, and the outcome arrives later as an event.

| Form | Side | Signature | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| WIT `invoke` | server, client | `invoke(command: string, arguments-json: string) -> result<request-id, plugin-error>` | A request id. The outcome arrives later as `request-completed`. |
| Rust wrapper | server, client | `commands::invoke(command, arguments_json).await` | `Result<(), PluginError>`, once the command has finished |
| Rust raw form | server, client | `commands::invoke_request(command, arguments_json)` | `Result<RequestId, PluginError>` |
| TypeScript wrapper | server, client | `invoke(command, argumentsJson)`, from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/commands` | `Promise<void>`, which rejects with the plugin error |
| TypeScript raw form | server, client | `invokeRequest(command, argumentsJson)` | `Promise<bigint>`, the request id |
| Intent `invoke-command` | server, client | Fields `command` and `arguments-json` in a submission | `ok` once the command has run |

Every form takes the same two arguments.

| Argument | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `command` | string | An exact global id. Patterns are not accepted here. |
| `arguments-json` | string | One JSON object, at most 64 KiB. The target's `arguments_schema` checks it when the target declares one. Without a schema, any object is accepted. |

The outcome of a raw call arrives as `request-completed`. Its `request-ref` is `call(<request-id>)`, and its outcome is one of these:

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ok` | The command ran and succeeded. |
| `failed(code)` | The command reported its own failure, or the call timed out. |
| `refused(code)` | The kernel refused the call before the command ran. |
| `cancelled` | The call was cancelled before it ran. |

A command returns an outcome only, `ok` or `failed`. It cannot return data. If you need a value from another plugin, use a service (see [api-services](/pages/api-services/)).

Your own commands arrive as `command-invoked` events, with an `origin` of `keybinding`, `palette`, `toolbar`, `menu`, `voice` or `cli`. See [api-events](/pages/api-events/) for the event record.

## Worked example in Rust

The client handler below refreshes git status when the user runs one of its own commands. It needs the grant `commands.invoke:ilium.git/status` in `capabilities.client`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::commands;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::task;

// Manifest, client side: "commands.invoke:ilium.git/status"
const GIT_STATUS: &str = "ilium.git/status";

// Starts the git status command. The call returns at once. The task waits for the
// outcome, so the event handler never blocks.
fn refresh_git_status() {
    task::spawn(async {
        match commands::invoke(GIT_STATUS, "{}").await {
            Ok(()) => log::log(Level::Info, "git status refreshed"),
            Err(error) => {
                log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("git status failed: {}", error.message));
            }
        }
    });
}
```

## Worked example in TypeScript

The same action in TypeScript. Any rejection counts as a failed refresh, and the handler logs the reason. The arguments are an empty JSON object because the status command takes none.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { invoke } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/commands';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const GIT_STATUS = 'ilium.git/status';

// Returns true when the git plugin ran the status command.
async function refreshGitStatus(): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    await invoke(GIT_STATUS, '{}');
    log('info', 'git status refreshed');
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    log('warn', `git status failed: ${String(error)}`);
    return false;
  }
}
```

A command that takes arguments needs a JSON object that matches its schema, for example `JSON.stringify({ target: 'line' })`. Build the string with `JSON.stringify` rather than by hand, so the quoting stays valid.

## Edge cases and errors

Each call returns one of these codes, either at once or as the outcome of the request.

| Code | When it happens | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | The pattern does not cover the id, the grant was declined or revoked, or the plugin lacks the grant on this side. | Do not retry. Hide the action. A grant change deactivates the plugin with reason `revoked`. Read the `granted` list on the next activation before you show the action again. |
| `not-found` | No command has that id. | Check the id against the owning plugin's manifest. |
| `conflict` | The command is disabled by its owner. The `invoke-command` intent gives `refused(conflict)`. | Retry after the owner enables it. |
| `invalid-argument` | The arguments are not one JSON object, are over 64 KiB, or fail the target's schema. | Fix the call. Do not retry it unchanged. |
| `timed-out` | The command did not reply within 30 s. The outcome is `failed(timed-out)`. | Retry later. The command may still finish, so make the action idempotent. |
| `busy` | The plugin's pending request limit is full. | Retry after a short delay. See [errors-and-limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/) for the limits. |
| `quota-exceeded` | The plugin's CPU budget is spent. | Retry after `retry-after-ms`. |

Three more rules apply:

- The `when` expression of a command only shows or hides its palette, menu and keybinding entries. It never blocks `commands.invoke`.
- A refused call writes a refusal line to the plugin log. The line has the form that [reference-capabilities](/pages/reference-capabilities/) describes.
- Invoking a disabled command is not an error in the plugin. The call returns `conflict`, and the plugin decides what to show.

<div class="warn">
<p>Do not use the pattern <code>*</code> to save work. It grants every command of every plugin, including commands that change git state or run agents. Use <code>ilium.git/*</code> or a single id.</p>
</div>

## What the user sees

At install, the review dialog lists each grant with its pattern as written, so the user can judge its width before approving it. A T2 or T3 plugin's `commands.invoke` grant is listed and checked by default, and the user can uncheck it. A T1 bundled plugin receives a narrow pattern up to its manifest ceiling. The bare `*` pattern is unchecked by default, and a T1 plugin asks for it once, at first activation.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.commands 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                  │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Runs commands of ilium.git <span class="t-dim">………………………………………</span> commands.invoke:ilium.git/* │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>The review dialog for a package that requests commands.invoke:ilium.git/*, drawn with the client's dialog characters: rounded corners, dotted leaders and the hint bar. Checked rows are granted; a high-risk row starts unchecked.</figcaption>
</figure>

When a call is refused, the palette shows nothing new. The refusal goes to the plugin log, which the user reads with `ilium plugin logs`.

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs example-notes
<span class="t-warn">warn</span> 2026-10-11 09:14:02 invoke refused, command outside grant
{"type":"refusal","capability":"commands.invoke:ilium.compaction/compact",
 "function":"commands.invoke","reason":"not-granted"}
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The refusal line has the same shape as the other refusal lines in the plugin log.

# editor.edit

## Overview

The `editor.edit` grant lets a client-side plugin change text in the Ilium editor. With it, a plugin can create an in-memory buffer, load a file into a buffer, save a buffer to a file, close a buffer, apply text edits to an open buffer and open a file in an editor pane.

Every edit names the revision of the buffer that the plugin read. Each buffer keeps a revision number that rises with every change, whether the user types or a plugin's edit lands. When the buffer has moved on, the kernel refuses the whole edit with `conflict` and applies none of it. The plugin then reads the buffer again, works out the edit again and submits it against the new revision. An edit made against old text therefore never lands in the wrong place.

## What you need

- The grant `editor.edit`, on the client side only. Server-side plugins cannot hold it.
- The grant [`editor.read`](/pages/capability-editor-read/). The plugin reads the buffer list, the revision and the lines before it edits. The revision comes only from a `buffer-ref`, which needs `editor.read`.
- `fs.read` on the file's scope for `load-file`, and for the path of `editor-open`. `fs.write` on the file's scope for `save-buffer`. Scopes are named in the path, for example `project`. See [File access](/pages/file-access/).
- The SDK for your language: `ilium-plugin-sdk` for Rust, `@ilium/plugin-sdk` for TypeScript. Both expose the editor functions under `primitives/editor`.

The grant takes no argument. `editor.edit` is valid. `editor.edit:project` is invalid, because files are reached through their file scope, not through this grant.

## The surface

The primitive functions belong to the editor interface, `ilium:primitives/editor`. The table lists every function this grant covers, with its SDK form.

| Function | Rust (`primitives::editor`) | TypeScript (`primitives/editor`) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `create-buffer(initial, language)` | `create_buffer(initial: &str, language: Option<&str>)` | `createBuffer(initial: string, language?: string)` | `Result<BufferId, PluginError>`; `bigint`, throws |
| `load-file(path)` | `load_file(path).await`; raw `load_file_request(path)` | `loadFile(path)` | `Result<BufferId, PluginError>`; `Promise<bigint>` |
| `take-buffer(request)` | `take_buffer(request)` (raw, re-exported) | `takeBuffer(request)` | `Option<BufferId>`; `bigint \| undefined` |
| `save-buffer(buffer, path)` | `save_buffer(buffer, path: Option<FsPath>).await` | `saveBuffer(buffer, path?)` | `Result<(), PluginError>`; `Promise<void>` |
| `close-buffer(buffer)` | `close_buffer(buffer)` | `closeBuffer(buffer)` | nothing |

`load-file` and `save-buffer` are slow calls. Their Rust `async` wrappers wait for the completion and return its result. `load-file` takes the buffer from the completion for you, so the plugin does not call `take-buffer` itself. The raw `_request` form returns a `RequestId` and leaves the rest to the plugin.

The edit intents are submitted, not called. They are listed in the next table with their outcomes.

| Intent | Payload | Outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| `editor-apply-edits` | `buffer: buffer-id`, `base-revision: u64`, `edits: list<text-edit>` | `ok`; `refused(not-found)`, `refused(conflict)`, `refused(invalid-argument)` |
| `editor-open` | `path: fs-path`, `line: option<u32>`, `placement: editor-placement` | `ok-node(node-id)`, the pane that opened; `refused(not-permitted)`, `failed(not-found)`, `failed(io)` |

The payload records are defined in `ilium:types/editing` and in the `editor-placement` enum:

```wit
record text-position { line: u32, column: u32 }
record text-range { start: text-position, end: text-position }
record text-edit { range: text-range, replacement: string }
record editor-apply-edits-spec {
  buffer: buffer-id, base-revision: u64, edits: list<text-edit>,
}
enum editor-placement { new-pane, split, replace }
record editor-open-spec {
  path: fs-path, line: option<u32>, placement: editor-placement,
}
```

`line` and `column` are 0-based. `column` counts Unicode scalar values, not bytes or UTF-16 units. The user interface shows line numbers from 1, so a plugin converts with `line - 1` when it reads a number from the user. A range with `start` equal to `end` is an insertion. In Rust the placement is `EditorPlacement::{NewPane, Split, Replace}`. In TypeScript it is the string `'new-pane'`, `'split'` or `'replace'`.

### Events that need `editor.read`

The grant `editor.edit` does not deliver events. A plugin that wants to follow buffer changes also needs `editor.read`.

| Event | Payload | Delivery |
|---|---|---|
| `editor-opened`, `editor-closed` | `buffer-ref` | never dropped |
| `editor-changed` | `buffer`, `revision`, `first-line`, `last-line` | coalesced per buffer, debounced 100 ms |
| `editor-saved` | `buffer`, `path` | never dropped |

A `buffer-ref` carries `buffer`, `pane`, `path`, `language`, `revision`, `line-count` and `dirty`. The same record comes from `buffers()`.

## The stale revision rule

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 260" role="img" aria-label="A stale edit is refused, and the plugin retries with the new revision">

</marker>
</defs>

</svg>
<figcaption>A stale edit is refused as a whole. The plugin reads the buffer again and submits the edit against the current revision.</figcaption>
</figure>

The rule has three parts:

- All edits in one `editor-apply-edits` refer to the text at `base-revision`. They must not overlap. Overlapping edits give `refused(invalid-argument)`.
- The kernel applies the edits of one submission as one change, so the revision rises by one, not once per edit.
- The only code for a stale revision is `conflict`. The plugin decides whether to retry. The safe retry reads the buffer again, checks whether the change is still needed, and submits again.

## Worked example in Rust

This client-side plugin adds a heading to the top of `NOTES.md` when the user runs its command. It reads the buffer list, skips the edit when the heading is already there, and retries when a submission comes back as `conflict`. The manifest grants `editor.read` and `editor.edit` on the client side.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::editor;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::editing::{BufferRef, TextEdit, TextPosition, TextRange};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::EditorApplyEditsSpec;

const STAMP_COMMAND: &str = "com.example.notes/stamp-heading";
const HEADING: &str = "# Notes";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct NotesStamp;

impl Lifecycle for NotesStamp {}

impl Handler for NotesStamp {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::CommandInvoked(invoked) if invoked.command == STAMP_COMMAND => {
                    task::spawn(stamp_heading());
                }
                Event::RequestCompleted(result) => {
                    // Only a stale revision is retried; the retry reads the new revision.
                    if let Outcome::Refused(error) = result.outcome {
                        if error.code == ErrorCode::Conflict {
                            task::spawn(stamp_heading());
                        }
                    }
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

async fn stamp_heading() {
    let buffers = editor::buffers();
    let Some(target) = buffers.into_iter().find(is_notes_buffer) else { return };
    let Ok(first_lines) = editor::read_lines(target.buffer, 0, 1) else { return };
    if first_lines.first().map(String::as_str) == Some(HEADING) {
        return;
    }
    let spec = EditorApplyEditsSpec {
        buffer: target.buffer,
        base_revision: target.revision,
        edits: vec![TextEdit {
            range: TextRange {
                start: TextPosition { line: 0, column: 0 },
                end: TextPosition { line: 0, column: 0 },
            },
            replacement: format!("{HEADING}\n"),
        }],
    };
    task::submit(Submission::new(Intent::EditorApplyEdits(spec)));
}

fn is_notes_buffer(buffer: &BufferRef) -> bool {
    buffer
        .path
        .as_ref()
        .is_some_and(|path| path.scope == "project" && path.path == "NOTES.md")
}
```

`task::submit` appends the submission to the batch that the handler returns. The outcome comes back as a `request-completed` event. The handler checks the outcome, and only a `conflict` starts another attempt.

To create a buffer that a code view can show, call the SDK function directly:

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ids::BufferId;

let buffer: BufferId = editor::create_buffer("fn main() {}\n", Some("rust"))?;
```

## Worked example in TypeScript

This client-side plugin loads `NOTES.md` when it activates, keeps the buffer id, and submits the same heading edit when its command runs. The SDK drains the promise queue before each export returns, so the result of `loadFile` is in place before the next `onEvents` call.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import { buffers, loadFile } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/editor';
import type { FsPath } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

const STAMP_COMMAND = 'com.example.notes/stamp-heading';
const NOTES_PATH: FsPath = { scope: 'project', path: 'NOTES.md' };
const HEADING = '# Notes\n';

let notesBuffer: bigint | undefined;
let nextCorrelation = 1n;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {
    loadFile(NOTES_PATH)
      .then((buffer) => {
        notesBuffer = buffer;
      })
      .catch((error: unknown) => {
        if (error instanceof PluginError) {
          log('warn', `load NOTES.md failed: ${error.code}: ${error.message}`);
        }
      });
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'command-invoked' || event.val.command !== STAMP_COMMAND) continue;
      const submission = stampHeading();
      if (submission) submissions.push(submission);
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});

function stampHeading(): Submission | undefined {
  if (notesBuffer === undefined) return undefined;
  const target = buffers().find((candidate) => candidate.buffer === notesBuffer);
  if (!target) return undefined;
  const correlation = nextCorrelation;
  nextCorrelation += 1n;
  return {
    intent: {
      tag: 'editor-apply-edits',
      val: {
        buffer: target.buffer,
        baseRevision: target.revision,
        edits: [
          {
            range: { start: { line: 0, column: 0 }, end: { line: 0, column: 0 } },
            replacement: HEADING,
          },
        ],
      },
    },
    correlation,
    dedupKey: undefined,
  };
}
```

`buffers()` returns `buffer-ref` records, so `revision` is a `bigint` and matches `baseRevision` without conversion. Correlation numbers below 2^63 belong to the plugin, which is why the counter starts at 1.

## Edge cases and errors

Synchronous checks fail at the call. Checks that need the disk, the user or the editor's apply step come back in the completion as `failed(code)`.

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Grant declined, or revoked during the call | `not-permitted` at once; `revoked` for a call in flight, then re-activation |
| `create-buffer` with more than 16 MiB of text | `invalid-argument` |
| 65th buffer held by one plugin (64 allowed) | `quota-exceeded` |
| `load-file` with a bad path | `invalid-argument` at once |
| `load-file`, file missing | `failed(not-found)` in the completion |
| `load-file`, binary file or over 16 MiB | `failed(invalid-argument)` in the completion |
| `save-buffer` with `path: none` on a buffer without a path | `invalid-argument` at once |
| `save-buffer`, file changed on disk since it was loaded | `failed(conflict)` in the completion |
| `save-buffer`, no `fs.write` for the scope | `not-permitted` at once |
| `editor-apply-edits`, stale `base-revision` | `refused(conflict)`; no edit applied |
| `editor-apply-edits`, overlapping or out-of-range edits | `refused(invalid-argument)`; no edit applied |
| `editor-apply-edits`, more than 10,000 edits | `refused(invalid-argument)` |
| `editor-apply-edits`, unknown or closed buffer | `refused(not-found)` |
| `editor-apply-edits`, buffer closed after acceptance | `failed(not-found)` |
| `editor-apply-edits`, empty `edits` list | `ok`; the revision does not change |
| `editor-open`, path without `fs.read` | `refused(not-permitted)` |
| `editor-open`, file missing or unreadable | `failed(not-found)` or `failed(io)` |

A plugin that saves right after an edit waits for the edit's `ok` outcome before it calls `save-buffer`. The save then writes the edited text, and the `editor-saved` event follows it.

A language name that the editor does not know opens the buffer as plain text. That is not an error. Use lowercase names, as the editor reports them in `buffer-ref.language`.

## Buffer lifetime

Buffers stay open when the plugin stops, is disabled or is re-activated. The editor keeps their text, because the text belongs to the user. A re-activated plugin finds its buffers again with `buffers()`. Closing a buffer with `close-buffer` frees its slot in the 64-buffer quota.

A completed `load-file` is held for 30 seconds for `take-buffer`. If the plugin takes the buffer later than that, the buffer is still open, and `buffers()` finds it.

## Risk and tier rules

- This grant is normal risk, not high risk.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives it automatically up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin shows the grant in the review dialog, listed and checked by default. The user's choice is remembered.
- An edit changes the user's text. A plugin should edit only for an action the user asked for, and should show the change in the editor, not hide it.

## What the user sees

The review dialog lists the grant when the plugin is installed. If the user declines it, the editor works as before, and every call of this grant returns `not-permitted`. A code view or file explorer that needs to open files should then show that opening is unavailable.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.editor 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                    │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Client side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Edits open files and buffers <span class="t-dim">……………………………………………………………………………</span> editor.edit │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>The review dialog for a package that requests editor.edit, drawn with the client's dialog characters: rounded corners, dotted leaders and the hint bar. Checked rows are granted; a high-risk row starts unchecked.</figcaption>
</figure>

After the stamp command runs, the heading appears on line 1 of the buffer, and the revision has risen by one. The user sees the change in the editor like any other edit:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ NOTES.md (project) ───────────────────────────────── revision 18 ─╮</span>
│ 1 <span class="t-ok"># Notes</span>                                                          │
│ 2 Ideas for the next release.                                      │
│ 3 <span class="t-dim">Open questions for the design review.</span>                            │
<span class="t-hi">╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</span>
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The heading line added by the edit, with the buffer revision after it.</figcaption>
</figure>

A code view that shows a buffer the plugin created with `create-buffer` needs `editor.edit` only. Showing any other buffer also needs `editor.read`. Without the grant, the widget draws an empty frame with the text `not permitted`.

## Manifest

The manifest requests the grant on the client side, together with the read grant that gives the revision:

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "client": ["editor.read", "editor.edit"]
  }
}
```

- [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/): the error codes and caps used on this page.
- [Tutorial 05: TODO scanner](/pages/tutorial-05-todo-scanner/): opening files with `editor-open`.

# editor.provide

<div class="warn">
<p>Status: reserved, not available in `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. A package that names `editor.provide` is refused with `manifest.grant-unknown`, and the interface `editor-provider` is not in the [WIT reference](/pages/reference-wit/). The editor is a built-in pane kind. A plugin that needs its own text pane uses the `basic` primitive with `panes.provide-kind`. The rest of this page describes the design planned for a later version.</p>
</div>

The `editor.provide` grant lets a client-side plugin replace the native editor. The plugin exports the `editor-provider` interface, which has every function of `ilium:primitives/editor` plus two handover calls, `adopt` and `release`. When the provider starts, the native editor hands its open buffers to the plugin. While the provider runs, every other plugin's `editor` calls reach the provider instead of the native editor. When the provider stops, the buffers return to the native editor.

<div class="warn">

High risk. The grant is high risk (H) and for T1 bundled plugins only. By default the native editor serves `ilium:primitives/editor`, and no other feature depends on this grant.

</div>

## Overview

A provider is a client-side plugin that owns the text of every open buffer while it runs. The native editor keeps no copy of the text during that time. The provider answers every editor call, so decorations, gutter marks, edits and file loads all go through the provider. The kernel still checks grants on each call. The buffers stay the user's work: a provider that stops or traps must not silently lose them (see the lifecycle below).

Only one editor provider runs at a time.

## You will need

- A T1 bundled plugin. A T2 or T3 package gets `manifest.grant-tier` at install.
- The API string `ilium:plugin@0.1.0` in the manifest `api` key.
- A client-side build. A grant or export on the server side gives `manifest.grant-side`.
- The calls that the provider implements are described on [editor.read](/pages/capability-editor-read/) and [editor.edit](/pages/capability-editor-edit/). The provider needs no extra grant for them, because it is the implementation.
- `fs.read` and `fs.write` only if the provider reads or writes files itself, for `load-file` and `save-buffer`.

## Grant and export syntax

- Valid grant: `editor.provide`.
- Invalid: `editor.provide:code-view`. The grant takes no argument, so the install error is `manifest.grant-argument`: `capability "editor.provide" takes no argument (got "editor.provide:code-view")`.
- Manifest export: `"editor-provider"` in the client `exports` list. Listing it without the grant gives `manifest.export-grant`.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "capabilities": { "client": ["editor.provide"] },
  "client": {
    "entry": "client.wasm",
    "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0",
    "exports": ["editor-provider"]
  }
}
```

## Full surface

| Name | Kind | Signature (WIT) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `adopt` | export | `adopt(buffers: list<adopted-buffer>)` | Receives every open buffer at start. Returns nothing. |
| `release` | export | `release() -> list<adopted-buffer>` | Returns every buffer at stop, with its current text. |
| `apply-edits` | export | `(buffer, base-revision: u64, edits: list<text-edit>) -> result<u64, plugin-error>` | Answers the intent `editor-apply-edits`. Returns the new revision. |
| `buffers` | export | `() -> list<buffer-ref>` | As `ilium:primitives/editor`. |
| `buffer-for-pane` | export | `(pane: node-id) -> option<buffer-ref>` | As `ilium:primitives/editor`. |
| `read-lines` | export | `(buffer, first-line: u32, count: u32) -> result<list<string>, plugin-error>` | As the editor primitive. At most 10,000 lines per call. |
| `selections` | export | `(buffer) -> list<text-range>` | As the editor primitive. |
| `set-decorations` | export | `(buffer, layer: string, items: list<range-decoration>) -> result<_, plugin-error>` | As the editor primitive. |
| `set-gutter` | export | `(buffer, layer: string, marks: list<gutter-mark>) -> result<_, plugin-error>` | As the editor primitive. |
| `create-buffer` | export | `(initial: string, language: option<string>) -> result<buffer-id, plugin-error>` | As the editor primitive. |
| `load-file` | export | `(path: fs-path) -> result<request-id, plugin-error>` | As the editor primitive. Also answers the intent `editor-open`. |
| `take-buffer` | export | `(request: request-id) -> option<buffer-id>` | As the editor primitive. |
| `save-buffer` | export | `(buffer, path: option<fs-path>) -> result<request-id, plugin-error>` | As the editor primitive. |
| `close-buffer` | export | `(buffer)` | As the editor primitive. |

The record `adopted-buffer` has the fields `buffer: buffer-id`, `path: option<fs-path>`, `text: string`, `language: option<string>`, `cursor: text-position` and `dirty: bool`. The `buffer` id is the one the native editor issued, so a plugin that stored it keeps working after the handover. A buffer that the provider creates gets a new id from the provider's own counter, and that counter never reuses an adopted id.

The record `text-edit` has the fields `range: text-range` and `replacement: string`.

In Rust, the trait is `ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::EditorProvider`, with the same twelve methods in snake_case (`read_lines`, `apply_edits` and so on). In TypeScript, the methods sit flat in the `definePlugin` object beside `lifecycle` and `handler`, in camelCase.

## Lifecycle of a provider

1. **Grant.** A T1 plugin activates first without its H capabilities, and then the prompt appears (see below). If the user declines, the provider role does not start and the native editor keeps serving the interface.
2. **Activate.** `activate` runs under `activate_deadline_ms`: 2,000 ms by default, 5,000 ms ceiling for T1.
3. **Adopt.** The kernel calls `adopt` with every open buffer. A buffer with unsaved changes carries `dirty: true`. `adopt` runs under the same activation deadline. A trap or a missed deadline stops the provider, and the native editor keeps its buffers.
4. **Run.** Other plugins' `editor` calls reach the provider. Decorations and gutter layers stay per plugin and clear when that plugin stops.
5. **Release.** On a clean stop, `deactivate` runs, then `release` returns the buffers under `deactivate_deadline_ms`: 500 ms by default, 1,000 ms ceiling. The native editor takes them back before the final snapshot is written.
6. **Trap or restart.** A trap hands the buffers back to the native editor at the text the provider last adopted. Edits made after `adopt` and not saved are lost, and the tree footer shows a warn line that names the plugin. The provider follows the [restart and disable rule](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/#restart-and-disable-rule): restart after 1 s, then 5 s, disabled at the third failure in 10 minutes. On restart the kernel calls `adopt` again with the buffers the native editor holds.
7. **Revocation.** Revoking `editor.provide` makes calls in flight fail with `revoked`. The plugin receives `deactivate(revoked)`, and its buffers return to the native editor (see [Editor primitives](/pages/primitives-editor/)).

## Worked example: Rust

This provider keeps the adopted buffers in memory. It implements `adopt`, `release` and `read_lines`. The other methods listed above follow the same pattern. The trait does not compile until all twelve exist.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::EditorProvider;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::editor_provider::AdoptedBuffer;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ids::BufferId;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client", exports = ["editor-provider"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct BufferKeeper {
    buffers: Vec<AdoptedBuffer>,
}

impl BufferKeeper {
    fn find(&mut self, buffer: BufferId) -> Result<&mut AdoptedBuffer, PluginError> {
        self.buffers
            .iter_mut()
            .find(|entry| entry.buffer == buffer)
            .ok_or_else(|| error(ErrorCode::NotFound, "no such buffer"))
    }
}

fn error(code: ErrorCode, message: &str) -> PluginError {
    PluginError { code, message: message.to_owned(), retry_after_ms: None }
}

impl Lifecycle for BufferKeeper {}

impl Handler for BufferKeeper {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl EditorProvider for BufferKeeper {
    fn adopt(&mut self, buffers: Vec<AdoptedBuffer>) {
        self.buffers = buffers;
    }

    fn release(&mut self) -> Vec<AdoptedBuffer> {
        std::mem::take(&mut self.buffers)
    }

    fn read_lines(
        &mut self,
        buffer: BufferId,
        first_line: u32,
        count: u32,
    ) -> Result<Vec<String>, PluginError> {
        if count > 10_000 {
            return Err(error(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, "at most 10,000 lines per call"));
        }
        let entry = self.find(buffer)?;
        let line_total = entry.text.lines().count();
        if first_line as usize > line_total {
            return Err(error(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, "line past the end of the buffer"));
        }
        let lines = entry.text.lines().skip(first_line as usize).take(count as usize);
        Ok(lines.map(str::to_owned).collect())
    }

    // buffers, buffer_for_pane, selections, set_decorations, set_gutter,
    // create_buffer, load_file, take_buffer, save_buffer, close_buffer and apply_edits
    // are implemented the same way, as listed in the table above.
}
```

## Worked example: TypeScript

The same provider in TypeScript. `definePlugin` returns the `editorProvider` export. A thrown `PluginError` becomes the `plugin-error` record that the host sees.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { AdoptedBuffer } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/editor-provider';

const buffers = new Map<bigint, AdoptedBuffer>();

function requireBuffer(buffer: bigint): AdoptedBuffer {
  const found = buffers.get(buffer);
  if (found === undefined) {
    throw new PluginError('not-found', 'no such buffer');
  }
  return found;
}

export const { lifecycle, handler, editorProvider } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {},
  deactivate() { return undefined; },
  onEvents() { return []; },
  adopt(adopted: AdoptedBuffer[]) {
    buffers.clear();
    for (const entry of adopted) buffers.set(entry.buffer, entry);
  },
  release() {
    const returned = [...buffers.values()];
    buffers.clear();
    return returned;
  },
  readLines(buffer: bigint, firstLine: number, count: number) {
    if (count > 10_000) {
      throw new PluginError('invalid-argument', 'at most 10,000 lines per call');
    }
    const lines = requireBuffer(buffer).text.split('\n');
    if (firstLine > lines.length) {
      throw new PluginError('invalid-argument', 'line past the end of the buffer');
    }
    return lines.slice(firstLine, firstLine + count);
  },
  // The other editor functions follow the same pattern, in camelCase.
});
```

## Edge cases and errors

| Code | Where it comes from | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | Any call | The grant was declined or revoked during the call. |
| `revoked` | Any call | The authorization epoch changed. The plugin is re-activated. |
| `not-found` | Buffer calls | The buffer id is unknown. |
| `invalid-argument` | `read-lines`, `apply-edits` | A line past the end of the buffer, more than 10,000 lines, or overlapping edits. |
| `conflict` | `apply-edits` | The `base-revision` is stale. Read the buffer again and retry. |
| trap | `adopt`, `release`, any call | A deadline breach, a wrong record shape or a guest panic. The instance is dropped (see [Editor primitives](/pages/primitives-editor/)). |

Install errors:

| Code | Cause |
|---|---|
| `manifest.grant-tier` | A T2 or T3 package asks for the grant. |
| `manifest.grant-side` | The grant or export is on the server side. |
| `manifest.grant-unknown` | The `api` key names an unknown API version. |
| `manifest.export-grant` | `editor-provider` is listed without the grant. |

A second provider does not start. It logs a warn line, and the user frees the role by disabling the other plugin in settings.

## What the user sees

When a T1 plugin with the grant starts for the first time, the user gets one prompt. The H capability is unticked until the user ticks it.

# editor.read

The `editor.read` grant lets a client-side plugin read the editor's buffers: the open files, their lines, the selections and whether they have unsaved changes. It also lets the plugin mark those buffers with decorations and gutter icons, and it delivers the editor lifecycle events. The plugin never changes the text itself. Changing text needs `editor.edit`.
