<!-- source: http://127.0.0.1:4327/pages/capability-panes-provide-kind.md -->
# panes.provide-kind

## Overview

The `panes.provide-kind` grant lets a client-side plugin add a new kind of pane. A kind is a
named type of pane, such as a file explorer, a board or a Markdown view. The plugin declares the
kind in the manifest, and the host creates panes of that kind when the user or another plugin asks
for them.

The pane is a basic pane. The host draws its frame: the title bar, the status line in the footer,
and the focus border. The plugin draws only the body, through the `views` export, which returns a
UI tree for each pane of its kind. The plugin keeps its own state, either in node metadata or in
storage, so a restored pane can show the same content after a restart.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 200" role="img" aria-label="A basic pane: the plugin draws the body through views.render, and the host draws the frame, title and status line">
  <defs>
    <marker id="pk-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <text x="200" y="24" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Pane kind: example.tree-explorer.files</text>
  <rect x="10" y="40" width="150" height="110" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="85" y="62" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Plugin</text>
  <text x="85" y="84" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">views.render</text>
  <text x="85" y="102" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">set-title, set-status</text>
  <text x="85" y="120" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">Node metadata</text>
  <rect x="240" y="40" width="150" height="110" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="315" y="62" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Host frame</text>
  <text x="315" y="84" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">Title and status line</text>
  <text x="315" y="102" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">Focus and frame</text>
  <text x="315" y="120" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">Body area</text>
  <line x1="162" y1="80" x2="236" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#pk-arrow)"/>
  <text x="200" y="72" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">ui tree</text>
  <line x1="238" y1="110" x2="164" y2="110" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#pk-arrow)"/>
  <text x="200" y="130" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">key-pressed</text>
  <text x="200" y="180" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">Grant: panes.provide-kind (client side)</text>

<figcaption>A basic pane. The plugin draws the body and handles keys. The host draws the frame,
the title and the footer status line, which the plugin sets with the basic primitive.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What you need

- The grant `panes.provide-kind`, on the client side only. Its risk is not marked high.
- A `pane_kinds` entry in the manifest for each kind the plugin provides.
- A client build of the plugin with a `handler` export, which is required on the client side and
  receives `key-pressed` events when the kind wants keys, and a `views` export, which renders the
  body. The manifest lists `"views"` in its `exports` array, because it is an optional export.
- The SDK for the language you write in. The Rust SDK is `ilium_plugin_sdk`; the TypeScript SDK is
  `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. Both expose the basic primitive as one module (see the table below).
- [ui.panels](/pages/capability-ui-panels/) only if the body opens panels or popups as well.
- Read access for the data the body shows. A basic pane has no access to the file system or the
  terminal by itself. Its reads need their own grants, such as `fs.read:project`.

`ui.invalidate` for the views the plugin contributes is always granted, so a basic pane can redraw
its body without asking for more.

## Manifest contribution

The grant allows the `pane_kinds` contribution. Each entry declares one kind:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | Local id. The global kind id is `<plugin-id>.<id>`. |
| `title` | string | Display name of the kind in menus. |
| `icon` | string | A Tabler icon name. |
| `primitive` | `"basic"` | The primitive the kind uses. Only `basic` is valid for this grant. |
| `wants_keys` | bool | When `true`, keys the focused widget does not consume arrive as `key-pressed`. |
| `persist` | `"metadata"`, `"storage"` or `"none"` | How the pane's state survives a restart (see below). |

```json
{
  "contributes": {
    "pane_kinds": [
      {
        "id": "files",
        "title": "Files",
        "icon": "folder",
        "primitive": "basic",
        "wants_keys": true,
        "persist": "metadata"
      }
    ]
  },
  "capabilities": {
    "client": ["panes.provide-kind", "fs.read:project"]
  }
}
```

With this manifest, the global kind id of the example is `example.tree-explorer.files` when the
plugin id is `example.tree-explorer`.

### The persist values

| Value | Where the state lives | After a restart |
|---|---|---|
| `metadata` | Node metadata: the plugin's own byte map on the node, at most 64 KiB per node. | The node is restored with its metadata, and the view can read it. |
| `storage` | The plugin's storage buckets. Keys under `pane/<node-id>/` are deleted when the pane is closed. | The node is restored empty, as with `none`. The plugin reads its own storage. |
| `none` | Nothing is kept. | The node is recreated empty, and the view starts without state. |

### Grant syntax and tiers

- Valid: `panes.provide-kind`.
- Invalid: `panes.provide-kind:explorer`. The kind is declared in `pane_kinds`, not in the grant.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives the grant automatically, up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin needs an explicit grant in the review dialog, and the grant is remembered.

## The basic primitive

The `basic` primitive gives the plugin four calls for each of its panes. The plugin passes the
node id of the pane, which the host gives it in `views.render` and in events.

| Function | Rust (`ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::basic`) | TypeScript (`@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/basic`) | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `set-title` | `set_title(pane: NodeId, title: &str)` | `setTitle(pane: bigint, title: string)` | `Result<(), PluginError>` | Sets the title in the frame. At most 256 characters. |
| `set-status` | `set_status(pane: NodeId, status: StyledText)` | `setStatus(pane: bigint, status: StyledText)` | `Result<(), PluginError>` | Sets one line of styled text in the footer. |
| `request-focus` | `request_focus(pane: NodeId)` | `requestFocus(pane: bigint)` | `Result<(), PluginError>` | Asks the kernel to focus the pane. |
| `size` | `size(pane: NodeId) -> Option<(u16, u16)>` | `size(pane: bigint): [number, number] \| undefined` | option | Inner columns and rows of the body. `None` for a node that is not a pane of the plugin's kinds. |

The body is drawn by the `views` export. Its Rust trait method is
`fn render(&mut self, view: ViewTarget, area: Area) -> UiTree`, and its TypeScript form is
`render(view, area)`. The host calls it when the view first opens, after `ui.invalidate` for the
pane, and on resize. It is not called for each frame. The render deadline is 10 ms on the client
by default. A render that runs over the deadline traps.

A key the focused widget does not consume arrives as an event for the pane:

| Event | Payload | Delivery |
|---|---|---|
| `key-pressed` | `grab: option<u64>`, `pane: option<node-id>`, `chord`, `repeat` | Only when `wants_keys` is `true`. Never dropped. |
| `key-released` | Same fields as `key-pressed`. | Same rule. |

Rust receives it as `Event::KeyPressed(key)`, and TypeScript as `{ tag: 'key-pressed', val: ... }`.

## Worked example in Rust

The example is a file explorer pane. Its body lists the rows of a folder, its title shows the
folder, and its footer shows the row count. The cursor row is kept in node metadata, so it survives
a restart with `persist: "metadata"`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{tree, ui};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::basic;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::layout::Area;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ui::{UiTree, ViewTarget};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::ui::build::Tree;

const ROW_COUNT: u32 = 5;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client", exports = ["views"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct TreeExplorer;

impl Lifecycle for TreeExplorer {}

impl Handler for TreeExplorer {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::KeyPressed(key) = event else { continue };
            let Some(node) = key.pane else { continue };
            let cursor = (read_cursor(node) + 1) % ROW_COUNT;
            // Example only: a production plugin handles these errors.
            let _ = write_cursor(node, cursor);
            let _ = basic::set_title(node, "Files: src");
            let _ = basic::set_status(node, vec![Span::plain(&format!("{ROW_COUNT} items"))]);
            let _ = ui::invalidate(ViewTarget::Pane(node));
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl Views for TreeExplorer {
    fn render(&mut self, view: ViewTarget, _area: Area) -> UiTree {
        // Only pane views are registered for this kind, so any other target is a bug.
        let ViewTarget::Pane(node) = view else { unreachable!("only pane views are registered") };
        let line = format!("Cursor at row {} of {ROW_COUNT}", read_cursor(node) + 1);
        let mut builder = Tree::new();
        let body = builder.paragraph(vec![vec![Span::plain(&line)]]);
        let root = builder.block().title("Files").child(body);
        builder.finish(root)
    }
}

fn read_cursor(node: NodeId) -> u32 {
    tree::metadata(node)
        .and_then(|bytes| <[u8; 4]>::try_from(bytes.as_slice()).ok())
        .map_or(0, u32::from_le_bytes)
}

fn write_cursor(node: NodeId, cursor: u32) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    tree::set_metadata(node, cursor.to_le_bytes().to_vec())
}
```

The `Lifecycle` implementation uses the default `activate` and `deactivate`, so it needs no body.
The `handler` and `views` exports both run in the client instance of the plugin.

## Worked example in TypeScript

The same pane in TypeScript. The entry module exports the three objects that `definePlugin`
returns: `lifecycle`, `handler` and `views`.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import * as basic from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/basic';
import * as treeHost from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/tree';
import * as ui from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/ui';
import { block, paragraph, span, tree as buildTree } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/ui/build';

const ROW_COUNT = 5;

function readCursor(node: bigint): number {
  const bytes = treeHost.metadata(node);
  if (!bytes || bytes.length !== 4) return 0;
  return new DataView(bytes.buffer, bytes.byteOffset, 4).getUint32(0, true);
}

function writeCursor(node: bigint, cursor: number): void {
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(4);
  new DataView(bytes.buffer).setUint32(0, cursor, true);
  treeHost.setMetadata(node, bytes);
}

export const { lifecycle, handler, views } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {},
  deactivate() { return undefined; },
  onEvents(batch) {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'key-pressed' || event.val.pane === undefined) continue;
      const node = event.val.pane;
      writeCursor(node, (readCursor(node) + 1) % ROW_COUNT);
      basic.setTitle(node, 'Files: src');
      basic.setStatus(node, [span(`${ROW_COUNT} items`)]);
      ui.invalidate({ tag: 'pane', val: node });
    }
    return [];
  },
  render(view) {
    // Only pane views are registered for this kind.
    const node = view.val;
    const line = `Cursor at row ${readCursor(node) + 1} of ${ROW_COUNT}`;
    const body = paragraph([[span(line)]]);
    return buildTree(block({ title: 'Files' }, [body]));
  },
});
```

Both examples keep the state in node metadata. The TypeScript `bigint` node id comes from the
`pane` field of the event, and TypeScript receives the variant `view-target` as `{ tag, val }`.

## What the user sees

The user opens a pane of the kind from the pane menu or from a command. The host draws the frame,
the plugin's title and the footer status. The body is the UI tree the plugin returns. Pressing a
key moves the cursor, and the view redraws without a restart.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Files: src ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</span>
│ ▸ app/                                                             │
│     lib.rs              1.2 KB                                     │
│     main.rs             0.4 KB                                     │
│ <span class="t-dim">▸ tests/                                                          </span> │
│     smoke.rs            2.9 KB                                     │
│                                                                    │
│ <span class="t-hi">Cursor at row 3 of 5                                              </span> │
<span class="t-dim">├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤</span>
│ <span class="t-ok">5 items</span>                                                            │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A basic pane with a body drawn by the plugin and a
footer set by `set-status`. The file names are placeholders.</figcaption>
</figure>

On the review dialog for a T2 or T3 plugin, the grant appears as "Add a pane kind drawn by the
plugin". The grant is remembered once the user accepts it.

## Errors and edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| The grant is declined or revoked | The `pane_kinds` contribution is not registered, so the kind is not offered. The `basic` calls return `not-permitted`. |
| `set-title` on a node that is not a pane of one of the plugin's kinds | `not-permitted`. |
| `set-title` with a title over 256 characters | `invalid-argument`. |
| `set-status`, `request-focus` on a foreign node | `not-permitted`. |
| `size` on a foreign node | `None`. The function has no result, so it has no error code. |
| Grant revoked at run time | `revoked` on the next call. |
| Basic panes and restore | A basic pane has no process, so `pane-not-ready` never applies to it. Calls work at once after a restore. |
| `views.render` over 10 ms | The plugin traps. Three failures in 10 minutes disable the plugin (see [lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/)). |
| `wants_keys` is `false` | No `key-pressed` or `key-released` events reach the pane. |

Only the codes listed here are specific to the basic primitive. Every call can also return
`revoked` and `internal`.

## First-party features that request it

- Feature 22, file explorer and picker, which provides the `files` kind.
- Feature 24, kanban boards, in Phase 7. In v1 the board is native.
- Feature 21, Markdown source and rendered views, in Phase 7.

# panes.read

The `panes.read` grant lets a plugin see the panes that exist: their size, title, kind, focus and whether a restored pane is still waiting for its process. It also delivers the pane lifecycle events, so a plugin learns when a pane is created, exits, gains focus, resizes or changes its title. The grant reads pane state only. It does not type into a pane, start one or stop one.

Two calls read state on demand: `info` returns the record of one pane, and `focused` returns the focused pane. Events report changes as they happen. A plugin should react to the events and call `info` only when it needs a pane's current record. It should not call the functions in a loop.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 170" role="img" aria-label="A plugin asks the kernel for pane state and receives pane events">
  <defs><marker id="arr-panes-read" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>
  <rect x="8" y="30" width="100" height="110" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="58" y="88" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Plugin</text>
  <text x="58" y="104" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">needs panes.read</text>
  <rect x="252" y="30" width="100" height="110" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="302" y="88" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Pane state</text>
  <text x="302" y="104" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">server or client</text>
  <line x1="108" y1="60" x2="252" y2="60" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-panes-read)"/>
  <text x="180" y="54" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">info(pane), focused()</text>
  <line x1="252" y1="100" x2="108" y2="100" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-panes-read)"/>
  <text x="180" y="94" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">pane-info, node id</text>
  <line x1="252" y1="128" x2="108" y2="128" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-panes-read)"/>
  <text x="180" y="122" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">pane events</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Pane state reaches the plugin in two ways: info and focused return pane records on request, and pane events such as pane-exited arrive as they happen. The grant does not start or type into a pane.</figcaption>
</figure>

## You will need

- The grant `panes.read` on each side that calls the functions or receives the events. A server-side plugin lists it under `capabilities.server`, and a client-side plugin under `capabilities.client`.
- A Rust plugin built with `ilium-plugin-sdk` 0.1 or a TypeScript plugin built with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. Both need the toolchain of the SDK release (Rust 1.90 or later, or Bun 1.2 or later).
- [tree.read](/pages/capability-tree-read/) if the plugin also needs the node that holds each pane, for example to walk from a pane to its folder.

## Grant syntax

- Valid: `panes.read`
- Invalid: `panes.read:terminal`. The grant takes no argument. The primitive kind is part of the pane information the plugin reads, not of the grant.

## Functions

Both functions are synchronous. They return at once, without a request id, and they have no error code (see the edge cases below).

| Function | Rust | TypeScript | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `info(pane)` | `panes::info(node)` | `info(node)` | `option<pane-info>` | The record of one pane. `none` for a node that is not a pane or no longer exists. |
| `focused()` | `panes::focused()` | `focused()` | `option<node-id>` | The focused pane, or `none` when no pane has focus. |

Rust names come from `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::panes`. TypeScript names come from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/panes`. A node id is a `u64` in Rust and a `bigint` in TypeScript.

## Records and types

`pane-info` is a record in `ilium:types/tree`. Its fields are:

| Field | WIT type | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `node` | `node-id` | `NodeId` | `bigint` | The tree node of the pane. |
| `content-kind` | `string` | `String` | `string` | `ilium.terminal`, `ilium.editor`, or `<plugin-id>.<kind>` for a pane kind a plugin provides. |
| `primitive` | `primitive-kind` | `PrimitiveKind` | `'terminal' \| 'editor' \| 'basic'` | The kind of body the pane has. |
| `columns` | `u16` | `u16` | `number` | Inner width in cells. |
| `rows` | `u16` | `u16` | `number` | Inner height in cells. |
| `focused` | `bool` | `bool` | `boolean` | The pane has focus. |
| `title` | `string` | `String` | `string` | The current title. |
| `is-restored` | `bool` | `bool` | `boolean` | A restored pane is waiting for its process to start. |

The WIT declarations, with the grant on each line:

```wit
// ilium:types/tree
record pane-info {
    node: node-id, content-kind: string, primitive: primitive-kind,
    columns: u16, rows: u16, focused: bool, title: string, is-restored: bool,
}
enum primitive-kind { terminal, editor, basic }

// ilium:host/panes (panes.read)
info: func(pane: node-id) -> option<pane-info>;
focused: func() -> option<node-id>;
```

## Events

The grant opens five events. Each arrives in the plugin's batch, in kernel order, through `on-events`.

| Event | Payload | Delivery | Rust variant | TypeScript tag and value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pane-created` | `pane-info` | never dropped | `Event::PaneCreated(PaneInfo)` | `'pane-created'`, a `PaneInfo` |
| `pane-exited` | `node`, `status`, `signal` | never dropped | `Event::PaneExited(PaneExitedEvent)` | `'pane-exited'`, `{ node, status, signal }` |
| `pane-focused` | `option<node-id>` | coalesced | `Event::PaneFocused(Option<NodeId>)` | `'pane-focused'`, `bigint \| undefined` |
| `pane-resized` | `node`, `columns`, `rows` | coalesced by node | `Event::PaneResized(PaneResizedEvent)` | `'pane-resized'`, `{ node, columns, rows }` |
| `pane-title-changed` | `node`, `title`, `source` | coalesced by node | `Event::PaneTitleChanged(PaneTitleChangedEvent)` | `'pane-title-changed'`, `{ node, title, source }` |

- `status` is `option<s32>`: the exit code of the process. `signal` is `option<string>`: the name of the signal that ended it, such as `SIGKILL`. For a terminal pane whose end the kernel recorded, exactly one of the two is set. Editor and basic panes have no process, so they never send `pane-exited`.
- `coalesced` means that when several events of the same kind reach the queue before the plugin runs, only the newest is delivered. `pane-exited` and `pane-created` are never merged.
- `source` is `osc` (the program set the title with an escape sequence), `manual` (the user renamed the pane) or `inferred` (the kernel chose the title from the program name). Rust `TitleOrigin::{Osc, Manual, Inferred}`; TypeScript `'osc' | 'manual' | 'inferred'`.
- A restored pane reports its saved size until the client lays it out. Then `pane-resized` arrives with the real size. A size is never zero.

## Worked example: Rust, server side

This plugin logs every pane exit with the title and the way the process ended. It needs only `panes.read`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::panes;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::PaneExitedEvent;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct ExitWatch;

impl Handler for ExitWatch {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::PaneExited(PaneExitedEvent { node, status, signal }) = event else {
                continue;
            };
            let title = panes::info(node)
                .map(|info| info.title)
                .unwrap_or_else(|| String::from("(closed)"));
            let outcome = match (status, signal) {
                (Some(code), _) => format!("exit status {code}"),
                (None, Some(name)) => format!("killed by {name}"),
                (None, None) => String::from("ended, status unknown"),
            };
            log::log(Level::Info, &format!("pane {node} \"{title}\" {outcome}"));
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

The manifest excerpt for this plugin:

```json
{
  "server": { "entry": "server.wasm", "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "server": ["panes.read"] }
}
```

## Worked example: TypeScript, client side

This client plugin logs the focused pane each time focus moves. It also handles the case where no pane has focus.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { info } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/panes';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `focus watch started in ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'pane-focused') continue;
      const node = event.val;
      if (node === undefined) {
        log('info', 'no pane has focus');
        continue;
      }
      const pane = info(node);
      if (pane === undefined) continue;
      log('info', `focus on "${pane.title}" (${pane.primitive}, ${pane.columns}x${pane.rows})`);
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

## What the user sees

The grant changes no pane. The user sees the plugin's log lines with `ilium plugin logs`:

## Risk and tier rules

- This grant is not marked high risk.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives it automatically up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin needs an explicit grant in the review dialog, and the grant is remembered.
- The grant does not allow starting, stopping or typing into a pane. Those need `panes.create`, `panes.signal` or `terminal.write`.

## What the review dialog says

## Edge cases and errors

- **Grant declined or revoked.** `info` and `focused` return `none`, because their signatures have no error channel. The first refused call of each plugin instance writes one warn line to the plugin log, naming `panes.read` and the reason (`declined`). Pane events are not delivered. A grant revoked while the plugin runs stops events from the next batch on.
- **Node that is not a pane.** `info` returns `none` for a folder, a container, a removed node or an unknown id.
- **Exited pane.** A pane node stays in the tree after its process exits, until it is closed. `info` still returns it, with its last title and size. `is-restored` is `false`.
- **Restored pane.** `is-restored` is `true` while a restored pane waits for its first process start. Input to such a pane is refused with `pane-not-ready` by the sending grant, such as `terminal.write`. Re-check `is-restored` before each write.
- **New pane.** `pane-created` arrives before any other event for that node, and before its process starts.
- **Error codes.** No function in this grant returns a code. The universal codes of the error table do not apply, because the calls have no result.
- **Event overflow.** Pane events are never dropped. A plugin whose queue overflows is treated as stuck and restarted. The restart counts toward the disable rule (after three failures in ten minutes the plugin is disabled). The new instance re-reads state with `info` and `focused`.

## First-party features that request it

- Feature 17, screen transfer between panes.
- Feature 18, pane title from the terminal.
- Feature 47, sound alerts, through `pane-exited`.
- Feature 109, the `ilium panes` command.

# panes.signal

## Overview

The `panes.signal` grant lets a server-side plugin send a POSIX signal to the process that runs inside a terminal pane. The plugin does this by submitting the `signal-pane` intent with a pane id and one of four signal names: `interrupt`, `terminate`, `kill` or `hangup`. The host checks the grant, sends the signal and completes the submission with `ok`.

The grant is high risk (H). Stopping a process can lose the user's work, so the user must check it in the review dialog, even for a bundled T1 plugin. It covers stopping only. It does not let a plugin read a pane's output or type into it; those need [terminal.read-screen](/pages/capability-terminal-read-screen/) and [terminal.write](/pages/capability-terminal-write/).

<div class="warn">

A signal can end a running agent or a build without warning, and `kill` cannot be caught, so the process gets no chance to save its work. Grant `panes.signal` only to a plugin whose purpose is stopping processes, and read the plugin's source before you grant it.

</div>

## You will need

- **The grant** `panes.signal` in `capabilities.server` of the manifest. The grant takes no argument.
- **Server side only.** Submit the intent from the server handler. Do not declare the grant under `capabilities.client`.
- **A pane id.** The intent needs a `NodeId` (Rust) or `bigint` (TypeScript). Get it from the `pane-focused` or `pane-exited` events, which need [panes.read](/pages/capability-panes-read/). Without `panes.read`, the plugin receives no pane events, so it can only signal panes whose ids it already holds.
- **The SDK path.** Rust `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::Signal` and `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SignalPaneSpec` with `Intent::SignalPane`. TypeScript `@ilium/plugin-sdk/types` for the `Signal` type, and the `signal-pane` tag in an intent literal.

## Grant syntax

| Manifest entry | Result |
|---|---|
| `"panes.signal"` | Valid. |
| `"panes.signal:kill"` | Refused at install with `manifest.grant-argument`: `capability "panes.signal" takes no argument (got "panes.signal:kill")`. |

The signal is a field of the intent, chosen on every call. The grant itself never names a signal.

## The intent: signal-pane

The WIT declaration in `ilium:types/intents` is:

```wit
record signal-pane-spec { pane: node-id, signal: signal }
enum signal { interrupt, terminate, kill, hangup }
// in variant intent: signal-pane(signal-pane-spec)
```

| Name | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intent | `Intent::SignalPane(SignalPaneSpec { pane, signal })` | `{ tag: 'signal-pane', val: { pane, signal } }` | Asks the host to send the signal. |
| `pane` | `NodeId` | `bigint` | The pane whose process receives the signal. |
| `signal` | `Signal` | `'interrupt' \| 'terminate' \| 'kill' \| 'hangup'` | The signal to send. |
| Outcome | completes with `ok` or a refusal | same | See the outcome table below. |

The signal values map to POSIX signals as follows:

| Value | POSIX signal | Can the process catch it | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `interrupt` | `SIGINT` | yes | Ask a program to stop its current task, as Ctrl+C does. |
| `terminate` | `SIGTERM` | yes | Ask a program to exit. |
| `kill` | `SIGKILL` | no | Stop a process that ignored `terminate`. |
| `hangup` | `SIGHUP` | yes | Tell a process that its terminal went away. |

Escalate in order: send `interrupt`, then `terminate`, and send `kill` only when `terminate` has failed to end the process. The signal goes to the child process that the pane started. An `ok` outcome means the signal was sent, not that the process exited. To confirm the exit, wait for the `pane-exited` event. It carries `status` and `signal`, for example `SIGKILL`, and `status` is `None` when a signal ended the process.

Each submission completes exactly once. The completion arrives as a `request-completed` event whose request reference is `submission(<correlation>)`. The `signal-pane` intent does not need a dedup key, because only `send-input` and `agent-action` require one. Without a key, every submission sends its signal. With a key, a repeat of that key within 10 minutes completes as `duplicate` and sends nothing.

## Outcomes and errors

| Situation | Outcome | Retry |
|---|---|---|
| The signal was sent | `ok` | The process may still run. Watch `pane-exited`. |
| The grant is missing or the user declined it | `refused(not-permitted)` for the signal. The whole batch is refused: every other submission in it completes as `refused(cancelled)` with `batch refused: submission <index>`. | No. Ask the user to grant it. |
| The pane id names no node, or a node that is not a pane | `refused(not-found)` | No. |
| The process has exited, or the pane has no process (for example a basic pane) | `refused(not-found)` with the message `no running process` | No. |
| A restored pane whose process has not started | `refused(pane-not-ready)` | Yes, after `pane-created` or `tree-changed` for that pane. |

Edge cases to handle in code:

- **Refused batches.** When the grant is missing, the whole batch is refused, including other submissions such as `send-input`. Submit signals in their own batch when the other submissions must still run.
- **Pane closed before the host handles the signal.** The outcome is `refused(not-found)`. Treat the pane as already stopped.
- **Ignored signals.** A program may ignore `interrupt` or `terminate`. Escalate only after the process has had time to respond, and check `pane-exited` first.
- **Revocation.** The user can revoke the grant in Settings > Plugins > the plugin > Capabilities, or with `ilium plugin grants <id> --revoke panes.signal`. The plugin then receives `deactivate(revoked)`. Pending requests that need the revoked capability complete as `failed(revoked)`.
- **Grant added later.** When the user grants `panes.signal` after install, the plugin receives `deactivate(granted)` and is re-activated with the new set.

## Risk and tier rules

- **H grant.** The user must check it. It is never granted by default.
- **T2 and T3 packages.** The install review dialog lists it as a HIGH row, unchecked. The plugin installs with the rows the user leaves checked.
- **T1 bundled plugins.** The plugin activates first without the grant. On first activation the user sees one prompt, `Plugin <name> asks for: <list>`. The prompt has a checkbox per H capability and the buttons `Allow selected` and `Not now`. `Not now` asks again at the next server start, at most three times, and then never again. Settings > Plugins can grant it at any time.
- **No prompt per call.** A granted `panes.signal` stays in force until it is revoked.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: interrupt on a key, kill on a second key in Rust

**Grants:** `panes.read` and `panes.signal`, both in `capabilities.server`.

The plugin tracks the focused pane. The `runner/interrupt` command sends `interrupt`, and the `runner/kill` command sends `kill`. Declare both commands in the manifest's `contributes.commands`, as the [commands](/pages/api-commands/) page describes.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::Signal;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SignalPaneSpec;

const INTERRUPT_COMMAND: &str = "com.example.runner/interrupt";
const KILL_COMMAND: &str = "com.example.runner/kill";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct PaneSignaller {
    focused_pane: Option<NodeId>,
}

impl Lifecycle for PaneSignaller {}

impl Handler for PaneSignaller {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::PaneFocused(pane) => self.focused_pane = pane,
                Event::CommandInvoked(invoked) => {
                    let signal = match invoked.command.as_str() {
                        INTERRUPT_COMMAND => Signal::Interrupt,
                        KILL_COMMAND => Signal::Kill,
                        _ => continue,
                    };
                    let Some(pane) = self.focused_pane else { continue };
                    let spec = SignalPaneSpec { pane, signal };
                    submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::SignalPane(spec)));
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

`Submission::new` assigns the next correlation number, so the plugin needs no counter. The `ok` outcome arrives later as a `request-completed` event, and the plugin ignores it here.

### Example 2: the same escalation in TypeScript

**Grants:** `panes.read` and `panes.signal`, both in `capabilities.server`.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { NodeId, Signal } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

const SIGNAL_BY_COMMAND: Record<string, Signal> = {
  'com.example.runner/interrupt': 'interrupt',
  'com.example.runner/kill': 'kill',
};
let focusedPane: NodeId | undefined;
let nextCorrelation = 1n;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'pane-focused') {
        focusedPane = event.val;
        continue;
      }
      if (event.tag !== 'command-invoked') continue;
      const signal = SIGNAL_BY_COMMAND[event.val.command];
      if (signal === undefined || focusedPane === undefined) continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: { tag: 'signal-pane', val: { pane: focusedPane, signal } },
        correlation: nextCorrelation,
        dedupKey: undefined,
      });
      nextCorrelation += 1n;
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

Both examples use the generated names of the SDK binding rules: `Signal` and `SignalPaneSpec` in Rust, and the kebab-case tag `signal-pane` with string values such as `'interrupt'` in TypeScript. The Rust `Lifecycle` implementation uses the default `activate` and `deactivate`. Keep `correlation` values unique within the plugin, as the TypeScript example does.

## First-party features that request it

No first-party feature in v1 requests `panes.signal`. The progress monitor runs its probe commands under `process.run:sh`, which is a different grant. A plugin that stops work must explain to the user, in its description, why it needs `panes.signal`.

# Capability: plugins.manage

## plugins.manage

The `plugins.manage` grant lets a client-side plugin list every installed plugin and turn each one on or off. Only a bundled first-party plugin at tier T1 can hold it, because turning a plugin off stops that plugin's work at once. The guided setup plugin is the intended holder. A plugin that is turned off withdraws all its contributions, cancels its pending requests and stays off until someone turns it on again.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" role="img" aria-label="The setup plugin calls set-enabled on the plugin registry, which deactivates the disabled plugin">

      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="20" y="10" width="360" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="200" y="35" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Setup plugin (client, T1, plugins.manage)</text>
  <line x1="200" y1="50" x2="200" y2="82" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-plugins-disable)"/>
  <text x="212" y="70" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">set-enabled(id, false)</text>
  <rect x="20" y="82" width="360" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="200" y="107" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Plugin registry</text>

  <text x="200" y="220" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">Requests cancelled, quotas released, data kept.</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The setup plugin turns one plugin off through the registry. The call returns once the change is recorded. The disabled plugin then receives its deactivate call and loses its contributions.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div class="warn">
<p>A disabled plugin stops at once: its contributions are withdrawn and its pending requests are cancelled. Grant <code>plugins.manage</code> only to the guided setup plugin, and make the setup plugin ask the user before it calls <code>set-enabled</code>.</p>
</div>

### What you need

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Grant | `plugins.manage`, risk H. It always needs an explicit allow from the user. |
| Tier | T1 bundled only. A T2 or T3 package that asks for it is refused at install. |
| Side | `client`. The `plugins` import is part of the `ilium:client/base` world. A server-side plugin cannot call it. |
| Language | Rust with `ilium-plugin-sdk`, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. |
| Manifest | The grant under `capabilities.client`, and a command if the plugin offers one. |

The grant takes no argument. The valid and invalid forms are:

| Grant | Valid | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `plugins.manage` | yes | The only form. |
| `plugins.list` | no | `plugins.list` is the name of the function, not a grant. |
| `plugins.manage:set-enabled` | no | The grant takes no argument. |

A T2 or T3 manifest that requests the grant fails at install with the code `manifest.grant-tier` and the message `capability "plugins.manage" is available to bundled plugins only`.

### The surface

Rust paths start at `ilium_plugin_sdk::host`. TypeScript paths start at `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host`. Both functions are synchronous and return no request id.

| Function | Rust | TypeScript | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `%list` (`plugins.list`) | `plugins::list() -> Vec<PluginInfo>` | `list()` returns `PluginInfo[]` | `list<plugin-info>` | Every installed plugin, including disabled and failed ones. |
| `set-enabled` | `plugins::set_enabled(plugin: &str, enabled: bool) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `setEnabled(plugin, enabled)` returns `void` and throws `PluginError` | `result<_, plugin-error>` | Turns the plugin on or off. Returns once the change is recorded. |

The WIT form, as the SDK receives it:

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/plugins in reference-wit
record plugin-info {
  id: plugin-id, name: string, version: string, tier: string, enabled: bool, failed: bool,
  state: package-state, side-states: list<side-state>, scope: string,
  disabled-reason: option<string>, health: health-state,
  publisher: string, publisher-key: option<string>,
  source: string, channel: string, pinned: bool,
  update-available: option<string>, deprecated: bool, yanked: bool
}
%list: func() -> list<plugin-info>;
set-enabled: func(plugin: plugin-id, enabled: bool, scope: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
```

The record `plugin-info` has nineteen fields. The first six are `id`, `name`, `version`, `tier`, `enabled` and `failed`, as before. Five fields are new: `state` (package state), `side-states` (a list of `side-state` records), `scope` (`global` in 0.1.0), `disabled-reason` and `health`. Eight more describe distribution: `publisher`, `publisher-key` (the key id, none for T3), `source` (`file`, `url` or `registry`), `channel`, `pinned`, `update-available` (the newest allowed version known from cached registry data, never fetched by this call), `deprecated` and `yanked`. Their types and rules are in [Plugin lifecycle states](/pages/reference-plugin-lifecycle-states/).

The first six fields:

| Field | Type (Rust, TypeScript) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `String`, `string` | Plugin id, such as `com.example.notes`. |
| `name` | `String`, `string` | Display name from the manifest. |
| `version` | `String`, `string` | Version of the installed package. |
| `tier` | `String`, `string` | `T1` (bundled), `T2` (signed) or `T3` (unsigned local package). |
| `enabled` | `bool`, `boolean` | `true` when the plugin is turned on. |
| `failed` | `bool`, `boolean` | `true` when the host turned the plugin off after repeated failures. |

The `scope` parameter is `global`, `project` or `session`; see [Plugin scope and sessions](/pages/reference-plugin-scope-and-sessions/). A global change propagates to every running session within 2 seconds. Calling `set-enabled` with the state a plugin already has returns `ok` and changes nothing. Calling `set-enabled(id, true)` on a failed plugin also clears `failed` and starts the plugin again.

### What a disable does

1. The call returns `ok` once the host has recorded the change. It does not wait for the plugin to stop.
2. The plugin receives `deactivate(disabled)`. It has 500 ms to finish, or 1 s at the T1 ceiling. If it misses the deadline, the host drops the instance and keeps no restore bytes.
3. Its contributions are withdrawn: decorations, toolbar state, grabs, claims, highlights, filters, watches and routes.
4. Its pending requests are cancelled and its quotas are released.
5. Its `data` and storage stay in place, unless the user chooses to delete them.

A disable never counts as a failure, so it does not count toward the restart and disable rule. Enabling records the change and activates the plugin by its activation rule: a `startup` plugin starts at once, and a lazy plugin starts at its next trigger. The full lifecycle is on the [lifecycle page](/pages/lifecycle/).

### Risk and tier rules

- `plugins.manage` is a high-risk grant (H). On first activation of a T1 plugin, the host shows one prompt, and the grant stays off until the user allows it.
- Only T1 bundled plugins can hold it. A T2 or T3 package cannot receive it, even when the user trusts the publisher.
- The grant is per plugin and per side. It is recorded in the user configuration, not in the project.

A bundled plugin that requests the grant gets the first-start prompt, not the install dialog ([Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/#first-start-of-a-bundled-plugin)). The high-risk row starts unchecked, as in the canonical review dialog of [Security](/pages/security/#verifying-a-package).

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Settings wants more access ─────────────────╮</span>
│ ilium.core.settings 0.1.0 · bundled (T1)     │
│                                              │
│ <span class="t-dim">Client</span>                                       │
│ [ ] <span class="t-warn">HIGH</span> Turn plugins on and off             │
│     plugins.manage                           │
│                                              │
│ <span class="t-hi"> Esc </span> Not now   <span class="t-hi"> Enter </span> Allow selected       │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The first-start prompt of a bundled plugin that requests plugins.manage. The row starts unchecked.</figcaption>
</figure>

A T2 or T3 package that requests the grant never reaches a dialog. The install stops at the manifest check:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin install notes-switcher-0.1.0.iliumpkg
<span class="t-err">error</span> manifest.grant-tier
       Cannot install com.example.switcher 0.1.0.
       Capability "plugins.manage" is available to
       bundled plugins only.
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The error for a T2 or T3 package that requests plugins.manage. Nothing is installed.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Errors and edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| The user declined the grant, or it was revoked | `list()` returns an empty list. `set-enabled` returns `not-permitted`. |
| The grant is revoked while a call is in flight | The call returns `revoked`. The plugin receives `deactivate(revoked)` and restarts with the reduced grant set. |
| The plugin id is not installed | `set-enabled` returns `not-found`. |
| The plugin is already in the requested state | `set-enabled` returns `ok` and changes nothing. |
| The plugin provides a service that a consumer calls | The disable does not cascade. Later `services.call` requests from consumers return `not-found`. |
| The user declined the prompt with "Not now" | The prompt returns at the next server start, at most three times. After that, the user grants the grant from Settings > Plugins. |
| The user turns the plugin off in Settings | No notice appears. The footer notice N14 (see [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/#failure-counting-and-restart)) appears only for a plugin the host turned off after failures. |

Universal codes apply as well: any call may return `internal`. A plugin that does not handle `not-permitted` should show the user where to turn the grant on, instead of retrying.

The footer notice for a plugin that the host turned off after repeated failures is notice N14. Its text and render are defined once in [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/#failure-counting-and-restart). The `failed` flag of that plugin is `true`.

### Manifest

The examples below use this manifest for the Settings plugin, which is bundled (T1):

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "ilium.core.settings",
  "name": "Settings",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Ilium",
  "client": { "entry": "client.wasm", "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "client": ["plugins.manage"] },
  "contributes": { "commands": [{ "id": "disable-notes", "title": "Disable notes" }] }
}
```

The command id is global: `ilium.core.settings/disable-notes`.

### Worked example in Rust

This client plugin turns off `com.example.notes` when the user runs the command from the palette. It checks that the plugin is installed first, so the log shows a clear reason when it is not.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::Activation;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::plugins;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::CommandInvokedEvent;

const TARGET_PLUGIN: &str = "com.example.notes";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct SetupPlugin;

impl Lifecycle for SetupPlugin {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("setup active for {}", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for SetupPlugin {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            let Event::CommandInvoked(CommandInvokedEvent { command, .. }) = event else {
                continue;
            };
            if command == "ilium.core.settings/disable-notes" {
                disable_target();
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

fn disable_target() {
    let installed = plugins::list();
    if !installed.iter().any(|plugin| plugin.id == TARGET_PLUGIN) {
        log::log(Level::Warn, "the notes plugin is not installed");
        return;
    }
    match plugins::set_enabled(TARGET_PLUGIN, false) {
        Ok(()) => log::log(Level::Info, "the notes plugin is turned off"),
        Err(error) => log::log(
            Level::Error,
            &format!("set-enabled failed: {:?}: {}", error.code, error.message),
        ),
    }
}
```

The handler returns no submissions, because the disable is a direct call and not an intent. The SDK runs `set_enabled` synchronously, so the `match` sees the result at once.

### Worked example in TypeScript

The same plugin in TypeScript. `PluginError` carries the `code` and `message` fields of the `plugin-error` record.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import { list, setEnabled } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/plugins';

const TARGET_PLUGIN = 'com.example.notes';

function disableTarget(): void {
  const installed = list();
  if (!installed.some((plugin) => plugin.id === TARGET_PLUGIN)) {
    log('warn', 'the notes plugin is not installed');
    return;
  }
  try {
    setEnabled(TARGET_PLUGIN, false);
    log('info', 'the notes plugin is turned off');
  } catch (error) {
    if (!(error instanceof PluginError)) {
      throw error;
    }
    log('error', `set-enabled failed: ${error.code}: ${error.message}`);
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `setup active for ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === 'ilium.core.settings/disable-notes') {
        disableTarget();
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

### Who requests it

- The Settings plugin (`ilium.core.settings`) holds `plugins.manage` and calls `set-enabled` for the plugins the user picks.

<!-- source: http://127.0.0.1:4327/pages/capability-process-run.md -->
# Capability: process.run

## process.run:&lt;program&gt;

The `process.run:<program>` capability lets a plugin start one named external program, wait for it to exit, and read its exit status and output. The grant names the program. Arguments, working folder, environment and timeout are chosen on each call, inside the limits on this page.

This is a high-risk capability (H). A plugin that can run programs can do nearly anything the user can do at a command line, so the user decides on every grant, even for a bundled plugin.

<div class="warn">
<p>Granting <code>process.run</code> lets the plugin run the named program with the user's permissions. Grant it only to a program whose behaviour you can review. Grant a shell (<code>sh</code>) only when the plugin's purpose needs one, because a shell can start any other program.</p>
</div>

### What you need

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Grant | `process.run:<program>` for each program, on the side that starts it (`server` or `client`). Each side holds its own grants. |
| Working folder | `fs.read` for the scope that holds the `cwd` you pass. No grant exists per folder. |
| Job code | A job instance may call `process.run` with the same grants as its plugin side. |
| Rust | `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::process`, with `process::run`, `ProcessSpec` and `ProcessExit`. |
| TypeScript | `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/process`, with `run`, `ProcessSpec` and `ProcessExit`. |
| Packages | T1 bundled plugins ask for the grant once, at first activation. T2 and T3 packages run the helper in a sandbox, and they are refused on Windows and macOS until a native sandbox exists. |

The manifest lists each grant under the side that uses it:

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.notes",
  "capabilities": { "server": ["process.run:git", "fs.read:project"] }
}
```

### Grant syntax

The argument is either a program name, resolved through `PATH`, or an absolute path, which pins one exact file. Install checks each grant with the rules of the grant grammar and these program rules:

| Grant | Result at install | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `process.run:git` | accepted | a program name, resolved through `PATH` |
| `process.run:/usr/bin/git` | accepted | an absolute path; the grant names one file |
| `process.run:sh` | accepted for T1 only, H | a shell can start any program, so the grant is very wide |
| `process.run` | `manifest.grant-argument-missing` | a program is required |
| `process.run:*` | `manifest.grant-wildcard` | wildcards are refused for this grant |
| `process.run:git status` | `manifest.grant-program` | arguments belong in `arguments`; a program name has no spaces |

A T2 or T3 package that asks for `process.run:sh` fails with `manifest.grant-tier`.

### The surface

| Name (Rust / TypeScript) | WIT form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `process::run` / `run` | `run(spec) -> result<request-id, plugin-error>`, wrapped as async | Starts the program and resolves with `ProcessExit` when it exits. A non-zero exit code is not an error. A failed run rejects with `PluginError`. |
| `process::run_request` / `runRequest` | the raw `run` | Returns a `RequestId`. The exit arrives later as a `request-completed` event. |
| `process::take_exit` / `takeExit` | `take-exit(request) -> option<process-exit>` | Returns the exit of a raw request once. The result is held for 30 seconds or until taken. Async code does not need it. |

The records:

| Field | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `process-spec.program` | `String` | `string` | Program name or absolute path. It must match a grant. |
| `process-spec.arguments` | `Vec<String>` | `string[]` | Arguments after the program. At most 1,024. |
| `process-spec.cwd` | `Option<FsPath>` | `FsPath \| undefined` | Working folder. It must lie in a scope the plugin can read. |
| `process-spec.stdin` | `Option<Vec<u8>>` | `Uint8Array \| undefined` | Standard input. At most 4 MiB. |
| `process-spec.environment` | `Vec<(String, String)>` | `[string, string][]` | Each pair replaces the inherited variable of the same name. At most 64 pairs. |
| `process-spec.timeout_millis` | `u32` | `number` | Required. From 1 to 600,000 ms. |
| `process-exit.status` | `Option<i32>` | `number \| undefined` | Exit code. `None` when a signal ended the process. |
| `process-exit.signal` | `Option<String>` | `string \| undefined` | POSIX name such as `SIGKILL`. Set only when a signal ended the process. |
| `process-exit.stdout` | `Vec<u8>` | `Uint8Array` | Standard output. |
| `process-exit.stderr` | `Vec<u8>` | `Uint8Array` | Standard error, kept apart from stdout. |

### How the helper runs

<figure>

<svg viewBox="0 0 420 260" role="img" aria-label="Path of a process.run call from plugin to helper and back">

      <path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 z" fill="currentColor"/>

  </defs>
  <rect x="110" y="10" width="200" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="210" y="34" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Plugin instance (server or job)</text>
  <line x1="210" y1="50" x2="210" y2="78" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#pr-arrow)"/>
  <text x="220" y="68" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">process.run(spec)</text>
  <rect x="110" y="78" width="200" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="210" y="102" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Grant check and limits</text>
  <line x1="210" y1="118" x2="210" y2="146" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#pr-arrow)"/>
  <text x="220" y="136" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">starts helper</text>
  <rect x="40" y="146" width="340" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="72" y="166" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Helper: low priority, CPU quota, timeout</text>
  <text x="72" y="182" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Environment: PATH, HOME, LANG and given pairs</text>
  <text x="72" y="198" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Output cap; T2 and T3 add confinement</text>
  <line x1="210" y1="206" x2="210" y2="226" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#pr-arrow)"/>
  <text x="220" y="219" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">exit</text>
  <rect x="40" y="226" width="340" height="26" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="210" y="243" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Completion: status, signal, stdout, stderr</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The grant check runs before the helper starts, and it refuses a call at once. The helper runs inside its limits. The plugin receives only the exit and the two output streams.</figcaption>
</figure>

When the plugin calls `run`:

1. **Grant check.** A program that matches no grant, including a grant the user declined, returns `invalid-argument` at once. A `cwd` outside a readable scope returns `not-permitted`. A value over a fixed cap returns `invalid-argument`. Nothing starts.
2. **Program lookup.** A bare name is resolved through `PATH`. An absolute path runs exactly that file.
3. **Environment.** The helper starts with `PATH`, `HOME` and `LANG` only. Each `environment` pair then replaces or adds one variable.
4. **Priority and quota.** The helper runs at low priority, and its CPU time is charged to the plugin's CPU quota.
5. **Confinement.** On T2 and T3 packages the helper runs in a bubblewrap mount namespace with a seccomp filter. It sees only the plugin's granted scopes (read-only for read grants), plus read-only `/usr`, `/bin`, `/lib*` and `/etc`, and it has no network. On T1 bundled plugins the helper runs unconfined, at low priority.
6. **Timeout.** The helper is killed when `timeout_millis` passes, and the completion is `failed(timed-out)`.
7. **Output cap.** When stdout and stderr together pass the cap, the helper is killed and the completion is `failed(quota-exceeded)`. No partial output is delivered.
8. **Logging.** Each run is written to the plugin log at level info, with the program and its full argument list.

### Limits

| Limit | Default | T1 ceiling | Breach |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stdout plus stderr (`process_output_mib`) | 4 MiB | 32 MiB | `failed(quota-exceeded)`; process killed |
| Standard input | 4 MiB | 4 MiB | `invalid-argument` |
| Arguments / environment pairs | 1,024 / 64 | 1,024 / 64 | `invalid-argument` |
| `timeout_millis` | required, 1 to 600,000 | same | `invalid-argument` |
| Concurrent children per session (`session_processes`, 16 per session, shared by `process.run` and `process.spawn`) | 16 | 16 | `busy` for `process.run`; `process.spawn` returns `quota-exceeded` |
| Pending requests per plugin (`pending_requests`) | 64 | 256 | `busy` |

### Risk and the review dialog

The review dialog lists the program name from each grant. It does not show arguments, because they are not known at install. Every run and its argument list appear in the plugin log, so the user can see what ran after the fact.

### Errors and edge cases

| Where | Code | When it happens |
|---|---|---|
| `run`, sync | `invalid-argument` | The program matches no grant, or a declined grant leaves none. `timeout_millis` is 0 or over 600,000. Stdin is over 4 MiB. There are more than 1,024 arguments or 64 pairs. |
| `run`, sync | `not-permitted` | `cwd` lies outside a scope the plugin can read. |
| `run`, sync | `busy` | The session runs 16 children, or the plugin's pending requests are full. |
| Completion | `failed(not-found)` | The program is not on `PATH`, or `cwd` does not exist. |
| Completion | `failed(io)` | The program was found but could not start. |
| Completion | `failed(timed-out)` | The timeout passed. The helper was killed first. |
| Completion | `failed(quota-exceeded)` | Output passed the cap. The helper was killed, and no output is delivered. |
| Completion | `cancelled` | The plugin was disabled, stopped or shut down while the program ran. The helper is killed. |

Edge cases to handle in code:

- **A non-zero exit is not an error for `run`.** Check `status` yourself. `grep` exits with 1 when nothing matches, which is a normal answer.
- **A signal ends the process.** Then `status` is `None` and `signal` holds a name such as `SIGKILL`. Treat that as a failure.
- **Only one completion.** The exit and the output arrive together, once the helper has exited.
- **A missing program is not a grant error.** The grant matched, so the failure is `failed(not-found)`, not `invalid-argument`.
- **Timeouts are required.** Choose a value that fits the work, and keep it under 600,000 ms.

### Worked example 1: Rust

This example runs `git status --short` in a project folder and reports the outcome to the log. It needs `process.run:git` and `fs.read` for the project scope.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::process::{self, ProcessExit, ProcessSpec};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::task;

/// Returns the short status of a project folder, or the reason it could not be read.
pub async fn short_status(project: FsPath) -> Result<String, String> {
    let spec = ProcessSpec {
        program: "git".to_string(),
        arguments: vec!["status".to_string(), "--short".to_string()],
        cwd: Some(project),
        stdin: None,
        environment: Vec::new(),
        timeout_millis: 10_000,
    };
    let exit: ProcessExit = process::run(spec)
        .await
        .map_err(|error| format!("git did not run: {:?}", error.code))?;
    if let Some(signal) = exit.signal {
        return Err(format!("git was stopped by {signal}"));
    }
    if exit.status != Some(0) {
        return Err(format!("git exited with {:?}", exit.status));
    }
    Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&exit.stdout).into_owned())
}

/// Called from a command handler. The SDK runs the task on its executor.
pub fn on_refresh_requested(project: FsPath) {
    task::spawn(async move {
        match short_status(project).await {
            Ok(text) => log::log(Level::Info, &format!("git status:\n{text}")),
            Err(reason) => log::log(Level::Warn, &reason),
        }
    });
}
```

`process::run(spec).await` resolves when the helper exits. The `?` operator passes a refused or failed run out as a message. The plugin never calls `take_exit`.

### Worked example 2: TypeScript

This example counts `TODO` lines with `grep`. It needs `process.run:grep`. It treats exit code 1 as zero matches, and it reports a signal or any other failure as an error.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import { run, type ProcessExit } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/process';
import type { FsPath } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

/** Counts TODO lines under a project folder. Returns undefined when grep fails. */
export async function countTodos(project: FsPath): Promise<number | undefined> {
  let exit: ProcessExit;
  try {
    exit = await run({
      program: 'grep',
      arguments: ['-r', '--count', 'TODO', '.'],
      cwd: project,
      stdin: undefined,
      environment: [],
      timeoutMillis: 5_000,
    });
  } catch (error) {
    const code = error instanceof PluginError ? error.code : 'internal';
    log('warn', `grep could not run: ${code}`);
    return undefined;
  }
  if (exit.signal !== undefined) {
    log('warn', `grep was stopped by ${exit.signal}`);
    return undefined;
  }
  if (exit.status === 1) return 0;
  if (exit.status !== 0) {
    log('warn', `grep exited with ${exit.status}`);
    return undefined;
  }
  const lines = new TextDecoder().decode(exit.stdout).split('\n');
  return lines
    .filter((line) => line.length > 0)
    .reduce((total, line) => total + Number(line.split(':').pop() ?? 0), 0);
}
```

The `run` call rejects with `PluginError` only when the run fails. A grep that finds nothing resolves with `status` 1, so the function returns 0 rather than an error.

### Who requests it

First-party plugins from `feature-mapping.md`:

- 59 Progress monitor: `process.run:sh`, to run arbitrary probe commands. Only a T1 bundled plugin can hold this grant.
- 67, 68, 69 and 70 Git worktree features: `process.run:git`.
- 71 Worktree include copy and post-create command: `process.run:sh`.

Requirement ids for this page: [CAP-009]. See the [requirements index](/pages/reference-requirements/).

### See also

- [Process control](/pages/api-process-control/) for the full `process` import and the `signal-pane` intent.
- [Capability: signal panes](/pages/capability-panes-signal/) for the `panes.signal` grant that stops a pane's process.
- [Capability: fs.read](/pages/capability-fs-read/) for the scope that holds a working folder.
- [Capability: workspace.manage](/pages/capability-workspace-manage/), which creates worktrees through the kernel and uses this grant for Git commands.

- [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/) for the full error table.

Targets `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

### Security

Children get a rebuilt environment: `LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` and `PATH` cannot be set (`invalid-argument`, [SEC-033]), `PATH` is fixed, the data folder is mounted `noexec`, the child has no network, and secrets are redacted from captured output ([SEC-243]). A refused program returns `not-permitted`. See [Sandbox reference](/pages/reference-sandbox/).

# Capability: services

## services.use:&lt;name&gt; and services.provide:&lt;name&gt;

The `services.use:<name>` and `services.provide:<name>` grants let plugins call each other through named services. A provider exports `service-provider` and answers calls. A consumer calls the service by name, then takes the reply later. The payload is JSON. The kernel checks every payload against the schema that the provider declares in its manifest.

Plugin-defined services are `@unstable`. A plugin that uses them must list `plugin-services` in its manifest `unstable` key. Kernel-known services, such as `ilium:inference/provider`, have typed interfaces instead, and they are covered on their own pages.

### What you need

- **A grant on each side.** A consumer needs `services.use:<name>`. A provider needs `services.provide:<name>` and the `service-provider` export.
- **The `unstable` opt-in.** Add `"unstable": ["plugin-services"]` to the manifest of both plugins.
- **A language SDK.** Rust: crate `ilium-plugin-sdk`, module `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::services`. TypeScript: `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/services`.
- **A side.** Services exist on the server and the client side. Each side has its own grants.

### Names and grants

A grant takes the service name as its argument. The first colon separates the grant name from the argument, so `services.use:ilium:inference/provider` is valid. A name has one of two forms:

- A plugin-defined service is `<plugin-id>/<name>`. The `<name>` part is 1 to 64 characters from `[a-z0-9-]`.
- A kernel-known typed interface is `ilium:<package>/<interface>`.

A version is never part of a grant. It appears only in `requires` and `provides`.

| Grant | Valid | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `services.use:com.example.notes/search` | yes | consumer grant for one service |
| `services.provide:com.example.notes/search` | yes | provider grant for the same service |
| `services.use:ilium:inference/provider` | yes | kernel-known typed interface |
| `services.use` | no | `manifest.grant-argument-missing`: the argument is required |
| `services.use:com.example.notes/*` | no | `manifest.grant-wildcard`: wildcards are refused |
| `services.use:com.example.notes/search@0.1.0` | no | a version is never part of a grant |
| `services.call` | no | `manifest.grant-unknown`: `call` is a function, not a grant |

### The full surface

Functions and records of the service interface. The Rust names are the SDK names; the WIT names are the same in kebab-case.

| Item | Side and grant | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `call(service, method, payload-json)` | consumer, `services.use` | `services::call_request` returns `Result<RequestId, PluginError>`; `services::call(...).await` returns `Result<String, PluginError>` | `callRequest` returns `bigint`; `call` returns `Promise<string>` | Starts a call. Checks the grant, the schema and the size caps at once. |
| `take-reply(request)` | consumer | `services::take_reply` returns `Option<String>` | `takeReply` returns `string \| undefined` | Returns the JSON of an `ok` completion. Nothing for a failed or cancelled call, or on a second take. |
| `handle(call: service-call)` | provider export | `ServiceProvider::handle` returns `ServiceReply` | `handle` in `definePlugin` | Answers the call at once, or defers it. |
| `reply(call, outcome)` | provider, `services.provide` | `services::reply` returns `Result<(), PluginError>` | `reply(call, outcome)` | Answers a deferred call. `outcome` is `ok` with a JSON string, or `err` with a `PluginError`. |

The records:

| Type | Fields |
|---|---|
| `ServiceCall` (WIT `service-call`) | `call: u64`, `service: string`, `method: string`, `payload_json: String`, `caller: plugin-id` |
| `ServiceReply` (WIT `service-reply`) | `Done(String)` or `Deferred`. In TypeScript `{ tag: 'done', val }` or `{ tag: 'deferred' }` |
| `PluginError` (WIT `plugin-error`) | `code`, `message`, `retry_after_ms: Option<u32>` |

Call numbers (`call`) and request ids are `u64`, so TypeScript uses `bigint` for them.
