### Manifest entries

A consumer lists the services it needs in `requires`. A provider lists each service it answers in `contributes.services.provides`, with a version and a schema file. The grant itself goes in `capabilities`.

Consumer manifest, with a kernel-known service:

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.search-ui",
  "unstable": ["plugin-services"],
  "requires": { "services": ["ilium:inference/provider@0.1.0"] },
  "capabilities": { "server": ["services.use:com.example.notes/search"] }
}
```

Provider manifest:

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.notes",
  "unstable": ["plugin-services"],
  "capabilities": { "server": ["services.provide:com.example.notes/search"] },
  "contributes": {
    "services": {
      "provides": [
        { "name": "com.example.notes/search", "version": "0.1.0",
          "schema": "schemas/search.json" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The schema file maps each method to its `params` and `result` schemas. It uses the settings subset of the JSON schema, draft 2020-12. Allowed keywords are `type`, `properties`, `required`, `enum`, `title`, `description`, `default`, `minimum`, `maximum`, `pattern`, `maxLength` and `items` for arrays. Any other keyword makes install fail with `manifest.schema-keyword`.

```json
{
  "query": {
    "params": {
      "type": "object", "required": ["text"],
      "properties": {
        "text": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 200 },
        "limit": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 50 }
      }
    },
    "result": {
      "type": "object", "required": ["hits"],
      "properties": { "hits": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } } }
    }
  }
}
```

A component that exports `service-provider` without a `services.provide` grant is refused at install with `manifest.export-grant`.

### Worked example: a provider in Rust

This complete server-side provider answers `query` calls with a fixed hit list. A real provider parses `payload_json` and searches its notes. The kernel has already checked the payload against the schema, so the provider reads only the fields the schema declares.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{ServiceCall, ServiceReply};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server", exports = ["service-provider"])]
#[derive(Default)]
struct NotesSearch;

impl Lifecycle for NotesSearch {}

impl Handler for NotesSearch {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

impl ServiceProvider for NotesSearch {
    fn handle(&mut self, call: ServiceCall) -> ServiceReply {
        // The SDK has already validated call.payload_json against search.json.
        let _query_text = &call.payload_json;
        ServiceReply::Done(r#"{"hits":["2026-10-01 release plan"]}"#.to_string())
    }
}
```

The `Lifecycle` trait has default methods, so the empty `impl` is enough. The `Handler` export is required on every server component, even when the plugin handles no events.

### Worked example: a consumer in TypeScript

This server-side consumer calls the provider once on activation. It logs the reply, or the error code when the call fails.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError, type Event } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import { call } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/services';

async function searchNotes(text: string): Promise<void> {
  try {
    const reply = await call(
      'com.example.notes/search',
      'query',
      JSON.stringify({ text, limit: 5 }),
    );
    log('info', `search reply: ${reply}`);
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof PluginError) {
      log('warn', `search failed: ${error.code}: ${error.message}`);
    }
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate() {
    void searchNotes('release plan');
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]) {
    return [];
  },
});
```

`call` resolves with the reply JSON. The SDK resolves the promise when the completion arrives, and the `definePlugin` wrapper drains pending promises before it returns from each export.

### Deferred replies

A provider that cannot answer at once returns `Deferred` and keeps the call number. It answers later with `reply`. The call number is `u64`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{ServiceCall, ServiceProvider, ServiceReply};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::services;

#[derive(Default)]
struct SlowSearch { waiting: Vec<u64> }

impl ServiceProvider for SlowSearch {
    fn handle(&mut self, call: ServiceCall) -> ServiceReply {
        self.waiting.push(call.call);
        ServiceReply::Deferred
    }
}

// Later, from a task or another export call. reply returns
// Result<(), PluginError>; it fails with not-found after the 30 s deadline.
fn answer_later(call_number: u64) {
    if let Err(error) = services::reply(call_number, Ok(r#"{"hits":[]}"#.to_string())) {
        log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("reply refused: {:?}", error.code));
    }
}
```

A deferred call that gets no reply within 30 seconds fails the caller's request with `timed-out`. A `reply` that arrives after that returns `not-found`.

### Errors and completions

A call returns a `request-id` or a synchronous error. Everything that needs the provider is reported in the completion of the request as a `request-completed` event, or to the Rust future.

| Code | When | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | consumer grant missing, declined or revoked | synchronous |
| `not-found` | no installed and enabled provider; `reply` for an unknown or expired call | synchronous |
| `invalid-argument` | payload over 1 MiB or fails the schema; `reply` over 1 MiB or fails the result schema | synchronous |
| `unsupported` | the method is not in the provider schema | synchronous |
| `busy` | the pending request queue is full | synchronous |
| `quota-exceeded` | CPU budget of the execution quota group spent, with `retry-after-ms` | synchronous |
| `timed-out` | the provider did not activate within `activate_deadline_ms` (2,000), or no reply within 30 seconds | completion |
| `cancelled` | the provider stopped or restarted before it answered | completion |
| `invalid-argument` | a `done` answer fails the provider's result schema | completion; the provider logs it at level error |
| the provider's own code | the provider answered with an error | completion |

Revocation, disable and upgrade behave as the other capabilities do. A grant revoked during a call makes that call return `revoked`. A disabled provider is treated as not installed, so new calls return `not-found`.

### Limits and timing

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Payload size, call and reply | 1 MiB |
| Provider activation wait | 2,000 ms (`activate_deadline_ms`) |
| Reply deadline for a call | 30 seconds from the call |
| Service name after the slash | 1 to 64 characters from `[a-z0-9-]` |

A call that finds the provider installed but not running starts it with the trigger `service:<name>`. The call then waits for the provider's activation, then for its reply.

### Declined grants and edge cases

- **Consumer declined.** Every `call` returns `not-permitted`. Each refusal is written to the plugin log with the grant name.
- **Provider declined.** The provider is installed, but its service is never registered and its `handle` export is never called. Callers get `not-found`.
- **Provider not installed or disabled.** `call` returns `not-found` at once.
- **Provider cycle.** Two plugins that require each other's services are refused at install (section 16.3 of the API).
- **Failing provider.** A provider that stops or restarts before it answers fails its pending callers with `cancelled`. Three failures within 10 minutes disable it.

### Review dialog and what the user sees

The install dialog lists the consumer grant as a row of its own. The row is unchecked for high-risk grants. `services.use` and `services.provide` are normal risk, so they are checked by default. A provider sees the payload of every call made to it, so review providers before you grant them to other plugins.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">Review permissions: com.example.search-ui 0.1.0</span>
  Use the service com.example.notes/search
  services.use:com.example.notes/search
<span class="t-dim">[allow]  [decline]</span>
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The review row for a consumer grant. The service name is an example.</figcaption>
</figure>

When a declined grant blocks a call, the plugin log shows the refusal:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs com.example.search-ui
<span class="t-warn">warn</span>  services.call com.example.notes/search
      <span class="t-err">not-permitted</span> (declined)
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The refusal line of a declined consumer grant.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Who uses it in the first-party plugins

Two first-party features use services. Feature 45, custom instruction inputs, is a consumer of `services.use:ilium.instructions/inputs`, and the `ilium.instructions` plugin provides it. Feature 83, the agent auto-compact trigger, is a consumer of `services.use:ilium.compact/trigger`, and the `ilium.compact` plugin provides it. Both providers declare `services.provide` for those names.

# Capability: settings.read-all and settings.write-all

## settings.read-all and settings.write-all

The `settings.read-all` and `settings.write-all` capabilities let a plugin read and change the settings of other plugins. They exist for one purpose: the settings screen itself. Only a bundled first-party (T1) plugin can hold either grant. A T2 or T3 package that asks for one fails the manifest check, so a third-party plugin never reaches the user with these grants.

The two grants unlock three functions of the `settings` import: `list-settings` lists the tabs and sections that every installed plugin declares, `get-plugin-json` reads all values of one plugin, and `set-plugin-json` changes some of them. A plugin's own values stay under `get-json` and `set-json`, which need no grant.

### settings.contribute:<tab-id>, a different grant

`settings.contribute:<tab-id>` is a separate, low-risk grant. A plugin needs it to add a section of rows to one built-in tab, for example `settings.contribute:terminal`. It is the only grant that lets a plugin draw anything in a built-in tab, and it allows nothing else:

| Grant | Risk | Argument | Allows | Does not allow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `settings.read-all` | high, T1 only | none | Reading the values of other plugins and the list of tabs and sections | Changing any value |
| `settings.write-all` | high, T1 only | none | Changing the values of other plugins (needs `settings.read-all`) | Reading kernel values |
| `settings.contribute:<tab-id>` | low, all tiers | one built-in tab id, required | Drawing sections in that one built-in tab | Reading or writing any value, including kernel values |

The two groups are independent. `settings.read-all` and `settings.write-all` never imply `settings.contribute:<tab-id>`, and `settings.contribute:<tab-id>` never implies either of them. A plugin's own tabs need no grant at all, because the always-granted `settings` import covers their values. The review dialog lists each contribute grant as `Adds settings to the Terminal tab`. The argument must be one built-in tab id. A wildcard is refused, and an unknown or closed tab id fails at install (`manifest.settings-target-unknown`, `manifest.settings-target-closed`). See [Plugin settings extension](/pages/settings-extension/) for the tab ids.

<div class="note">
<p>See also: <a href="/pages/settings-extension/">Plugin settings extension</a> for how sections are placed in a tab.</p>
</div>

<div class="warn">
<p>Writing another plugin's settings can change how that plugin behaves, including settings that control network hosts or agent behaviour. Keep <code>settings.write-all</code> to the settings screen and the guided setup plugin.</p>
</div>

<div class="note">
<p>The settings store, its validation and the kernel recovery page stay in the kernel. A plugin that uses these grants does not replace them.</p>
</div>

**You will need:**

- `settings.read-all` for `list-settings` and `get-plugin-json`. A plugin that only reads settings needs this grant alone.
- `settings.write-all` for `set-plugin-json`. It also needs `settings.read-all`. Without it, the install fails with `manifest.grant-dependency`.
- A bundled T1 plugin. Both grants are high risk (H) and are declared under `capabilities.client`, the side of the settings screen.
- A language: Rust with `ilium-plugin-sdk`, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`.
- Nothing else. Neither grant takes an argument.

### Grant syntax

| Grant | Valid | Result when used |
|---|---|---|
| `settings.read-all` | yes | T1 only |
| `settings.write-all` | yes | T1 only, and only together with `settings.read-all` |
| `settings.read` | no | `manifest.grant-unknown`: the grant name is `settings.read-all` |
| `settings.write-all:com.example.notes` | no | `manifest.grant-argument`: the grant takes no argument |
| `settings.all` | no | `manifest.grant-unknown` |

### Surface

| Function | Rust | TypeScript | Grant | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `list-settings` | `settings::list_settings()` | `listSettings()` | `settings.read-all` | `Vec<SettingsRef>` / `SettingsRef[]` | The tabs and sections that installed plugins declare. Plugins without settings are not listed. |
| `get-plugin-json` | `settings::get_plugin_json(plugin)` | `getPluginJson(plugin)` | `settings.read-all` | `Result<String, PluginError>` / `string` | All values of one plugin as one JSON object, for every scope. |
| `set-plugin-json` | `settings::set_plugin_json(plugin, patch)` | `setPluginJson(plugin, patch)` | `settings.write-all` | `Result<(), PluginError>` / `void` | Applies a merge patch to one plugin's values. |

The Rust module is `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings`. The TypeScript import is `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings`. The plugin id is a string. The `SettingsRef` record has these fields:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `plugin` | plugin id | The plugin that declares the tab or section. |
| `tab` | string | The global tab id `<plugin-id>/<tab-id>`, for example `com.example.notes/notes`, or the built-in tab id for a section in a built-in tab. |
| `section` | string, optional | The global section id, when the entry is a section. |
| `title` | string | The title the settings screen shows. |
| `side` | `plugin-side` | `server` or `client`, the side that owns the values. |
| `kernel-tab` | string, optional | The built-in tab that holds the section, for example `terminal`. |

The WIT form, with the grant of each function written above it:

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/settings in reference-wit
// settings.read-all
record settings-ref {
  plugin: plugin-id, tab: string, section: option<string>,
  title: string, side: plugin-side, kernel-tab: option<string>
}
list-settings: func() -> list<settings-ref>;
get-plugin-json: func(plugin: plugin-id) -> result<string, plugin-error>;

// settings.write-all
set-plugin-json: func(plugin: plugin-id, patch: string) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
```

### How a patch is applied

`set-plugin-json` reads its `patch` as an RFC 7396 JSON merge patch, the same rule as `set-json` for a plugin's own values:

- The patch must be one JSON object of at most 256 KiB. Anything else is `invalid-argument`.
- The patch is validated against the target plugin's schema before anything is stored.
- A key that is not in the schema is `invalid-argument`, and the message names that key.
- The patch is all or nothing. One invalid key stores nothing.
- A key set to `null` resets that key to its schema `default`.
- A patch that changes no stored value succeeds and sends no event (P4).

When a patch changes values, the target plugin receives `settings-changed` with the changed keys, on the side that owns them. The writer gets no event of its own.

`get-plugin-json` returns the keys of every scope, so a settings screen needs one call per plugin. A plugin without settings returns `{}`. A `secret` field comes back as the empty string to every plugin except its owner, so the screen can show a masked field without seeing the value.

### Risk and tier rules

- Both grants are high risk (H). They always need an explicit grant from the user.
- A T2 or T3 package that declares either grant fails with `manifest.grant-tier`. The install review dialog never lists them.
- A T1 plugin is activated first without the grants. The user then answers the prompt described below.

<figure>

<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.settings 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                  │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Client side</span>                                                                │
│ <span class="t-warn">! [ ] Reads all plugin settings</span> <span class="t-dim">………………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-warn">settings.read-all</span> │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-warn">! marks a high-risk grant. It starts unchecked and is</span>                      │
│ <span class="t-warn">always asked for, even for bundled plugins.</span>                                │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

### Minimal manifest

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "ilium.settings",
  "capabilities": {
    "client": ["settings.read-all", "settings.write-all", "help.read"]
  }
}
```

### Rust example

This settings screen logs the tabs of every plugin when it activates, and sets one value of another plugin when it receives a command. A declined grant is logged and not raised: an error from `activate` counts as a crash.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::settings;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

const NOTES_PLUGIN: &str = "com.example.notes";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct SettingsScreen;

impl Lifecycle for SettingsScreen {
    fn activate(&mut self, _context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        for entry in settings::list_settings() {
            log::log(Level::Info, &format!("settings tab {} ({})", entry.tab, entry.scope));
        }
        match settings::get_plugin_json(NOTES_PLUGIN) {
            Ok(values) => log::log(Level::Info, &format!("notes values: {values}")),
            Err(error) => log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("cannot read notes: {}", error.message)),
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for SettingsScreen {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            if let Event::SettingsChanged(change) = event {
                log::log(Level::Debug, &format!("own settings changed: {}", change.keys.join(", ")));
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}

/// Sets the sync interval of the notes plugin and returns a message on refusal.
fn set_sync_interval(seconds: u32) -> Result<(), String> {
    let patch = format!("{{\"sync_interval_seconds\": {seconds}}}");
    match settings::set_plugin_json(NOTES_PLUGIN, &patch) {
        Ok(()) => Ok(()),
        Err(error) if matches!(error.code, ErrorCode::NotPermitted) => {
            Err("settings.write-all is not granted".into())
        }
        Err(error) => Err(error.message),
    }
}
```

### TypeScript example

The same plugin in TypeScript. The entry module exports only `lifecycle` and `handler`, as the manifest lists them.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import { getPluginJson, listSettings, setPluginJson } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';

const NOTES_PLUGIN = 'com.example.notes';
const SET_INTERVAL_COMMAND = 'ilium.settings/set-sync-interval';

/** Returns undefined on success, or a message that the settings screen can show. */
function setSyncInterval(seconds: number): string | undefined {
  try {
    setPluginJson(NOTES_PLUGIN, JSON.stringify({ sync_interval_seconds: seconds }));
    return undefined;
  } catch (error) {
    if (!(error instanceof PluginError)) throw error;
    return `${error.code}: ${error.message}`;
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {
    for (const entry of listSettings()) {
      log('info', `settings tab ${entry.tab} (${entry.scope})`);
    }
    try {
      log('info', `notes values: ${getPluginJson(NOTES_PLUGIN)}`);
    } catch (error) {
      if (!(error instanceof PluginError)) throw error;
      log('warn', `cannot read notes: ${error.message}`);
    }
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'settings-changed') {
        log('debug', `own settings changed: ${event.val.keys.join(', ')}`);
      }
      if (event.tag === 'command-invoked' && event.val.command === SET_INTERVAL_COMMAND) {
        const refusal = setSyncInterval(300);
        if (refusal) log('warn', refusal);
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

### Errors

Every call can return `not-permitted`, `revoked` and `internal`. The grant-specific cases are:

| Situation | Code | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| The grant is not held, or the user declined it | `not-permitted` | Every call fails. Retrying does not help. |
| The grant is revoked during a call | `revoked` | The plugin is re-activated with the reduced grant set. This is not counted as a failure. |
| The plugin id is not installed | `not-found` | `get-plugin-json` and `set-plugin-json` fail. |
| The patch is not one JSON object, is over 256 KiB, has a key outside the schema, or breaks a rule of the schema | `invalid-argument` | Nothing is stored. The message names the key. |
| The target plugin has no settings | none | `get-plugin-json` returns `{}`. A non-empty patch is `invalid-argument`. |

The manifest checks that run at install or build time, with their exact text:

| Code | Text |
|---|---|
| `manifest.grant-tier` | `capability "settings.read-all" is available to bundled plugins only` |
| `manifest.grant-dependency` | `capability "settings.write-all" also needs "settings.read-all"` |
| `manifest.grant-argument` | `capability "settings.write-all" takes no argument (got "settings.write-all:x")` |
| `manifest.settings-target-grant` | `settings section "<id>" in tab "<tab>" needs capability "settings.contribute:<tab>"` |
| `manifest.settings-target-unknown` | `settings section "<id>" targets unknown tab "<tab>"` |
| `manifest.settings-target-closed` | `settings tab "<tab>" does not accept plugin sections` |

<figure>

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin build
<span class="t-err">error</span> manifest.grant-dependency
     capability "settings.write-all" also needs "settings.read-all"
</pre>

<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A manifest that asks for write without read fails the build.</figcaption>
</figure>

First-party plugins from `feature-mapping.md`:

- Feature 89, guided setup: `settings.read-all`, `settings.write-all` and `plugins.manage`.
- Feature 90, settings UI: `settings.read-all`, `settings.write-all` and `help.read`. The settings store, its validation and the recovery page stay in the kernel.

# Capability: sound.play

## sound.play

The `sound.play` capability lets a plugin ask the Ilium client to play a short sound. The plugin does not open an audio device. It submits the intent `play-sound` with a sound id. The host checks the grant and the sound catalogue, and only an accepted id reaches the audio output. The sound comes either from the set bundled with Ilium or from the plugin's own `contributes.sounds` list.

### What you need

- **A grant.** `sound.play` on the side that submits the intent. Client plugins request it under `capabilities.client`. It is a normal-risk grant, not a high-risk one. T1 bundled plugins receive it up to their manifest ceiling. T2 and T3 packages list it in the review dialog, checked by default.
- **A language.** Rust with `ilium_plugin_sdk`, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. The toolchain is described in [Toolchain](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/).
- **A sound id.** Either a bundled id or an id from your own `contributes.sounds` list.

### Grant syntax

The grant takes no argument.

| Grant | Valid | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `sound.play` | yes | the only form |
| `sound.play:bell` | no | the grant takes no argument; name the sound in the intent |
| `sound` | no | the grant name is incomplete |

### The surface

| Name | Kind | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `play-sound` | intent, grant `sound.play` | `Intent::PlaySound(String)` | `{ tag: 'play-sound', val: 'done' }` | Asks the client to play the sound with that id. The outcome is in the request result. |
| `catalog` | host function, always granted | `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::sounds::catalog() -> Vec<String>` | `catalog(): string[]` from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/sound` | Returns the sound ids this plugin may play. It is synchronous and has no error code. |
| `contributes.sounds` | manifest key | not applicable | not applicable | A list of `{ "id", "file" }` entries. Each file lives in the `sounds/` folder of the package. |
| `dedup-key` | submission field | `Submission::keyed(intent, key)` | `dedupKey`, an optional string | An optional key that stops a repeat within 10 minutes. |

The Rust prelude brings in `Intent` and `Submission`. Import `sound` from `ilium_plugin_sdk::host` explicitly.

### Sound ids and files

- **Bundled ids.** Ilium ships one bundled sound: `chirping`. It is embedded in the client, so it plays with no sound package installed.
- **Contributed ids.** Each `contributes.sounds` entry adds one id. The id is the plain string you write, such as `done`.
- **Catalogue scope.** `catalog()` and `play-sound` see the bundled ids and the plugin's own ids. A plugin cannot play another plugin's sounds. Such an id is refused with `not-found`.
- **Id rules.** An id must be unique within the manifest, and it must not be `chirping`. A repeated id or a clash with `chirping` fails the package check at install with `manifest.sound-id-taken`.
- **File format.** A sound file must be WAV with PCM samples, or OGG Vorbis. A file that is missing or in another format fails the package check at install, and the plugin is not installed.

The manifest for both examples below:

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.notes",
  "capabilities": { "client": ["sound.play"] },
  "contributes": {
    "sounds": [ { "id": "done", "file": "sounds/done.ogg" } ],
    "commands": [ { "id": "finish", "title": "Finish note" } ]
  }
}
```

### Worked example 1: Rust, client side

The plugin plays `done` when the user runs its `finish` command. It checks the catalogue first, so it never submits an id that the host would refuse.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::sounds;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::CommandInvokedEvent;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct NotesSound;

impl Handler for NotesSound {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::CommandInvoked(CommandInvokedEvent { command, .. }) = event else {
                continue;
            };
            if command != "com.example.notes/finish" {
                continue;
            }
            if !sounds::catalog().iter().any(|id| id == "done") {
                continue;
            }
            submissions.push(Submission::keyed(
                Intent::PlaySound("done".to_string()),
                "notes-done-2026-10-11",
            ));
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

The `Submission::keyed` call sets the dedup key. Use a key that names one logical event, such as one note and its revision. A fixed key, as here, only suppresses repeats within the 10-minute window.

### Worked example 2: TypeScript, client side

The same behaviour in TypeScript. The submission is a literal, and `correlation` is a number below 2^63 that the plugin chooses. Every `u64` is a `bigint`.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { catalog } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/sounds';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const out: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'command-invoked') continue;
      if (event.val.command !== 'com.example.notes/finish') continue;
      if (!catalog().includes('done')) continue;
      out.push({
        intent: { tag: 'play-sound', val: 'done' },
        correlation: 1n,
        dedupKey: 'notes-done-2026-10-11',
      });
    }
    return out;
  },
});
```

The host answers each submission with a `request-completed` event. The SDK passes that event to `onEvents` unless a future is waiting for it. Check the outcome when a sound matters to the user; a refusal is not an error that stops the plugin.

### Errors and edge cases

| Outcome | When it happens | What the plugin does |
|---|---|---|
| `ok` | The id is in the catalogue and the sound is sent to the audio output. | Nothing. |
| `refused(not-permitted)` | The grant is missing, declined or revoked during the call. Every later submission in the same batch completes as `refused(cancelled)`. | Do not retry. Tell the user the grant is needed. |
| `refused(not-found)` | The id is not in `catalog()`. Only this submission is refused. | Check `catalog()` first. Do not retry the same id. |
| `refused(rate-limited)` | More than 4 `play-sound` submissions per second from this plugin. The result carries `retry-after-ms`. | Wait for `retry-after-ms`, or drop the sound. The key is not reserved, so a retry with the same key is valid. |
| `duplicate(original)` | The same key was reserved within the last 10 minutes. The `original` field names the earlier submission. | Nothing. The earlier sound was already accepted. |
| `failed(io)` | The client has no audio output, or the device fails. | Log it. A retry of a failed play needs a new key. |
| `refused(invalid-argument)` | The `dedup-key` is malformed. | Fix the key. The malformed submission refuses its whole batch. |

A key is 1 to 128 characters from `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `.`, `_`, `:`, `/` and `-`.

Edge cases:

- A plugin that submits 5 `play-sound` intents inside one second gets `ok` for 4 and `refused(rate-limited)` for the fifth.
- A sound file that is missing or not WAV or OGG Vorbis fails the install. It never fails at play time.
- A `play-sound` on a client without an audio device completes as `failed(io)`. The plugin keeps running and no failure is counted.
- A grant revoked while a batch is in flight refuses the current submission with `not-permitted` and the later ones with `refused(cancelled)`. The plugin is re-activated with the reduced grants.

### Rate and dedup rules

- **Rate.** Each plugin may submit 4 `play-sound` intents per second. Its `notify` intents have a separate budget of 6 per minute. Sounds that repeat often should use a dedup key rather than a retry loop.
- **Dedup window.** A key stays reserved for 10 minutes from the moment it is accepted. A refused submission does not reserve its key. A submission that was accepted keeps its key, even when playback later fails.
- **Retries.** Do not retry a refusal in a loop. Retry `rate-limited` after `retry-after-ms`. Do not retry `not-permitted` at all until the user grants the capability.

### What the user sees

The review dialog shows one row for the capability. For a T2 package it looks like this:

<figure>

│ com.example.sound 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                     │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Plays sounds <span class="t-dim">…………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………</span> sound.play │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>

The row text is "Play sounds", and the grant string follows it on the right. A declined row is shown unchecked and dimmed. The plugin then receives no `sound.play` grant, and its calls are refused as described above. The sound itself comes out of the audio output of the Ilium client, and the plugin shows no notice of its own.

To change the grant later, open Settings > Plugins > the plugin > Capabilities, or run `ilium plugin grants com.example.notes --revoke sound.play`. Calls in flight then return `revoked`, and the plugin is re-activated with the reduced set.

# terminal.output-filter

The `terminal.output-filter` grant lets a server-side plugin watch the output of terminal panes for lines that match a regular expression. The host matches the lines itself, so the plugin never sees the full output stream. For each match the plugin receives one `output-matched` event. A rate limit on each filter stops a noisy pane from flooding the plugin: matches above the limit are dropped and counted.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 320 200" role="img" aria-label="Terminal output passes through the host filter, which sends output-matched events to the plugin">
  <defs><marker id="arr-output-filter" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>
  <rect x="50" y="10" width="220" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="160" y="36" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Terminal pane output</text>
  <line x1="110" y1="54" x2="110" y2="78" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-output-filter)"/>
  <text x="124" y="70" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">output lines</text>
  <rect x="50" y="78" width="220" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="160" y="104" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Host filter (regex, rate limit)</text>
  <line x1="110" y1="122" x2="110" y2="146" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-output-filter)"/>
  <text x="124" y="138" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">output-matched</text>
  <rect x="50" y="146" width="220" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Server plugin</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The host matches each completed output line against the plugin's filters. The rate limit applies before delivery, so only accepted matches reach the plugin as output-matched events.</figcaption>
</figure>

## You will need

- The grant `terminal.output-filter`, on the server side only. The grant is per side: a client-side plugin cannot use it.
- A server-side plugin. Rust plugins depend on the crate `ilium-plugin-sdk` and TypeScript plugins on `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. See [Toolchain](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/) for the build setup.
- Either a `output_filters` entry in the manifest, for filters known at install time, or a runtime call to `add-output-filter`, for rules that the user switches on. Runtime filters need the grant but no manifest entry.

## Grant syntax

- Valid: `terminal.output-filter`.
- Invalid: `terminal.output-filter:agents`. The pane selection is a field of the filter, not of the grant.

## Surface

### Manifest entry

Each entry in `contributes.output_filters` is installed when the plugin starts.

| Field | Type | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | yes | none | Filter id, unique within the plugin. It appears in `output-matched` events. |
| `regex` | string | yes | none | Pattern, see [Matching](#matching). Up to 1 KiB. |
| `panes` | `"all"`, `"agents"` or `"terminals"` | yes | none | Which panes the filter watches. |
| `rate_per_second` | integer, 1 to 100 | no | 10 | Accepted matches per second, per pane. |

### Runtime calls

Both calls are synchronous and live in the `ilium:primitives/terminal` interface.

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:primitives/terminal in reference-wit
record output-filter { id: string, regex: string, rate-per-second: u16 }
add-output-filter: func(pane: node-id, filter: output-filter) -> result<_, plugin-error>;
remove-output-filter: func(pane: node-id, filter-id: string);
```

| WIT | Rust (`ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::terminal`) | TypeScript (`@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal`) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `add-output-filter` | `add_output_filter(pane, OutputFilter)` returns `Result<(), PluginError>` | `addOutputFilter(pane, filter)` returns `void`, throws `PluginError` | Adds a rule for one pane. An existing id on that pane is replaced. |
| `remove-output-filter` | `remove_output_filter(pane, filter_id)` | `removeOutputFilter(pane, filterId)` | Removes a rule by id. No result, no error code. |
| `output-filter` record | struct `OutputFilter { id, regex, rate_per_second }` | `{ id, regex, ratePerSecond }` | The filter. `rate-per-second` is `u16`. |

The pane is a `NodeId` in Rust and a `bigint` in TypeScript, because node ids are `u64`.

### Event

| WIT field | Rust (`OutputMatchedEvent`) | TypeScript (`val` of `output-matched`) | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `node` | `node` | `node` | `u64` | The pane that printed the line. |
| `filter-id` | `filter_id` | `filterId` | string | The id of the filter that matched. |
| `line` | `line` | `line` | string | The completed line, with escape sequences removed. |
| `row` | `row` | `row` | `u32` | Zero-based line number in the pane's output since it started. |

The event arrives in `on_events` (Rust) or `onEvents` (TypeScript) as `Event::OutputMatched(...)` or `{ tag: 'output-matched', val: ... }`.

## Matching

- The host matches each completed line, after escape sequences are removed, so colour codes do not hide a match. A partial line that has not received its line end is not matched yet.
- The dialect is the Rust `regex` crate. It has no look-around and no back-references. A pattern matches anywhere in the line; use `^` and `$` to anchor it.
- One line can match several filters. Each matching filter raises its own event.
- A pane selection of `all` means every terminal pane. `agents` means panes whose agent is identified, and `terminals` means terminal panes with no identified agent.

## Rate limit

Each filter instance on each pane has its own limit of `rate_per_second` accepted matches. A match above the limit is dropped and counted, not delivered. The next batch that the plugin receives starts with one `events-dropped` event. It carries a list of `{ event, source, count }` records, where `event` is `output-matched` and `source` is the filter id. The `events-dropped` event itself is never dropped.

## Limits

| Limit | Default | Ceiling T1 | Ceiling T2 and T3 | Over the limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Filters per plugin | 32 | 128 | 32 | `quota-exceeded` |
| Filters across all plugins | n/a | 512 | 512 | `quota-exceeded` |
| Queued `output-matched` events per plugin | 1,024 | 4,096 | 1,024 | Oldest dropped, counted |

Events of a plugin are dropped oldest first when its event queue is full, and the drop is counted in `events-dropped`.

## Risk and tier rules

- This grant is not marked high risk in the capability table.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives it automatically up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin needs an explicit grant in the review dialog, and the user's choice is remembered.
- Filters see the output of the panes they select. A filter on `all` sees every terminal, so use `agents` or `terminals` when the plugin does not need more.

## Worked example 1: a manifest filter in Rust

This plugin counts rate-limit messages from the model service in agent panes. The manifest asks for the grant on the server side and declares the filter. The rate limit is two accepted matches per second per pane.

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "server": ["terminal.output-filter"]
  },
  "contributes": {
    "output_filters": [
      {
        "id": "rate-limit-seen",
        "regex": "rate limit (reached|exceeded)",
        "panes": "agents",
        "rate_per_second": 2
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The Rust code implements the server-side traits. Lifecycle uses the defaults, so the manifest
filter needs no code to install.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct RateLimitWatcher {
    accepted_matches: u32,
}

impl Lifecycle for RateLimitWatcher {}

impl Handler for RateLimitWatcher {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::OutputMatched(matched) if matched.filter_id == "rate-limit-seen" => {
                    self.accepted_matches += 1;
                }
                // Drops are counted by the host (Event::EventsDropped); nothing to do here.
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

The `Event` and `Submission` names come from the prelude. Matches above the rate limit never
reach `on_events`, so `accepted_matches` counts only delivered matches.

## Worked example 2: a runtime filter in TypeScript

This text trigger watches one pane for a Rust compiler error code. The user turns it on and off
from a setting. The filter fires at most once per second. The host removes the filter when the
plugin deactivates, so the plugin does not need to remove it there.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { addOutputFilter, removeOutputFilter } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal';

const BUILD_FILTER_ID = 'build-failed';
const watchedPanes = new Set<bigint>();

/** Turns the trigger on for one pane. Returns false when the grant is declined. */
export function enableTrigger(pane: bigint): boolean {
  try {
    addOutputFilter(pane, {
      id: BUILD_FILTER_ID,
      regex: 'error\\[E',
      ratePerSecond: 1,
    });
    watchedPanes.add(pane);
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    const pluginError = error as PluginError;
    if (pluginError.code === 'not-permitted') {
      return false;
    }
    throw error;
  }
}

export function disableTrigger(pane: bigint): void {
  removeOutputFilter(pane, BUILD_FILTER_ID);
  watchedPanes.delete(pane);
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate() {
    return;
  },
  deactivate() {
    watchedPanes.clear();
    return undefined;
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]) {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'output-matched' && event.val.filterId === BUILD_FILTER_ID) {
        // A text trigger runs its actions here, for example a sound or a notice.
        // The intents that do that are on the notifications page.
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

## Edge cases and errors

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Grant declined or revoked | `add-output-filter` returns `not-permitted`. Manifest filters are not installed. No events arrive. |
| Pane does not exist | `not-found`. |
| Regex does not compile, or the pattern is over 1 KiB, or the compiled program is over 1 MiB | `invalid-argument`. |
| `rate_per_second` is 0 or over 100, or the id is empty | `invalid-argument`. |
| More than 32 filters on T2 or T3 (128 on T1), or 512 across all plugins | `quota-exceeded`. |
| Same id added twice on one pane | The second call replaces the first. |
| Same id on another pane | Allowed. Filter ids are scoped to the pane. |
| Matches above `rate_per_second` | Dropped and counted in `events-dropped`. |
| Pane closes | Its runtime filters are removed. No event is raised. |
| Plugin deactivates | All of its runtime filters are removed. |

Every refused call is written to the plugin log, which `ilium plugin logs` shows.

## What the user sees

The review dialog lists the grant as a checkbox. A declined grant is shown dimmed, and the plugin
keeps its other features.

<figure>

│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │

│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │

<figure>

A text trigger that cannot watch output should say so in its settings page rather than fail
silently.

<div class="warn">
<p>A filter on <code>all</code> reads every terminal's output, including panes that show secrets such as tokens printed by a command. Prefer <code>agents</code> or <code>terminals</code>, and keep the regex narrow.</p>
</div>

<div class="note">
<p>A filter sees only completed lines. A prompt that waits for input without a newline is not matched until the line ends.</p>
</div>

# terminal.pointer

## Overview

The `terminal.pointer` grant lets a client-side plugin take the mouse in a terminal pane. The plugin claims a pane, receives every pointer event for that pane, and draws highlight regions over its text. Copy features use it so the user can select a block of output with the mouse. The grant never changes the text in the pane.

A claim belongs to one plugin per pane. While it is held, the host stops sending mouse input to the pane's program, stops its own text selection on that pane, and stops the wheel from scrolling the scrollback. All three return when the claim ends.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 150" role="img" aria-label="Pointer events go from the pane to the claiming plugin, and the plugin sends highlights back to the pane">
  <defs><marker id="arr-pointer-flow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>

  <rect x="20" y="100" width="360" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="200" y="125" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Terminal pane (display and mouse)</text>
  <line x1="120" y1="100" x2="120" y2="54" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-pointer-flow)"/>

</svg>
<figcaption>While the plugin holds the claim, the pane's pointer events go to the plugin and not to the pane. Highlights are drawn over the pane, and the text stays the same.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What you need

- The grant `terminal.pointer`, on the client side only. The grant is normal risk. A bundled T1 plugin receives it up to its manifest ceiling. A T2 or T3 plugin needs an explicit grant in the review dialog, and the grant is remembered.
- The grant [`terminal.read-screen`](/pages/capability-terminal-read-screen/) when the plugin reads the text under the highlights.
- The Rust crate `ilium-plugin-sdk` (Rust 1.90 or later, target `wasm32-wasip2`), or the npm package `@ilium/plugin-sdk`.

The grant takes no argument. `terminal.pointer:claim` is refused at build time with `manifest.grant-argument`: `capability "terminal.pointer" takes no argument (got "terminal.pointer:claim")`. The claim is a call made at run time, not a grant argument.

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "client": ["terminal.read-screen", "terminal.pointer", "clipboard.write"]
  }
}
```

## The surface

| Function | Rust (`primitives::terminal`) | TypeScript (`primitives/terminal`) | Result | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `claim-pointer` | `claim_pointer(pane)` | `claimPointer(pane)` | `Result<(), PluginError>`, throws | Sends the pane's pointer events to this plugin until it is released. |
| `release-pointer` | `release_pointer(pane)` | `releasePointer(pane)` | none | Gives the pointer back to the host. It never fails. |
| `set-highlights` | `set_highlights(pane, layer, &[CellRegion])` | `setHighlights(pane, layer, regions)` | `Result<(), PluginError>`, throws | Replaces every region of one layer. |
| `clear-highlights` | `clear_highlights(pane, layer)` | `clearHighlights(pane, layer)` | none | Removes one layer and its regions. |

In Rust, `pane` is a `NodeId`. In TypeScript it is a `bigint`, because every `u64` node id is a `bigint` in TypeScript. A layer is a string.

A highlight is a `CellRegion`:

| Field | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| first row | `first_row: u32` | `firstRow: number` | First row, counted from the top visible row (0). |
| first column | `first_column: u16` | `firstColumn: number` | First column, counted from the left (0). |
| last row | `last_row: u32` | `lastRow: number` | Last row, inclusive. |
| last column | `last_column: u16` | `lastColumn: number` | Last column, inclusive. |
| style | `style: Style` | `style: Style` | Foreground, background and text modifiers. |
| label | `label: Option<String>` | `label: string \| undefined` | Optional text for a tooltip, at most 128 characters. |

Pointer events arrive in the `on_events` batch as `Event::Pointer` in Rust, or as `{ tag: 'pointer', val }` in TypeScript. The payload is a `PointerEvent`:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `node` | `node-id` | The terminal pane. |
| `row` | `u32` | Visible row of the pointer, from the top (0). The scrollback offset is not applied. |
| `column` | `u16` | Column of the pointer, from the left (0). |
| `kind` | `down`, `up`, `move`, `drag`, `wheel-up`, `wheel-down`, `wheel-left` or `wheel-right` | What happened. |
| `button` | `left`, `middle`, `right` or `none` | The button. `none` for wheel and move events. |

The WIT forms are:

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:types/ui in reference-wit
enum pointer-kind { down, up, move, drag, wheel-up, wheel-down, wheel-left, wheel-right }
enum pointer-button { none, left, middle, right }
```

The event record `pointer-event` is defined in `ilium:types/events` and also carries `modifiers`, `sub-x` and `sub-y`. The button is `none` for a wheel event and for `move`.

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:primitives/terminal in reference-wit
record cell-region {
  first-row: u32, first-column: u16, last-row: u32, last-column: u16,
  style: style, label: option<string>,
}
```

## How a claim behaves

- **Events.** While the claim is held, every mouse event for the pane goes to the plugin. Drag events are coalesced, so a fast drag produces fewer events than the mouse moved. Use the row of the latest event, not a sum of movements.
- **Wheel.** A wheel event (`wheel-up`, `wheel-down`, `wheel-left` or `wheel-right`) goes to the plugin and does not scroll the scrollback. The plugin decides what the wheel means.
- **Typing.** Keyboard input is not affected. Typing into the pane needs `terminal.write`, not a claim.
- **One owner.** A pane has at most one claim. A second plugin gets `conflict`. Calling `claim-pointer` again from the plugin that already holds the claim returns `ok` and changes nothing.
- **Release.** `release-pointer` without a claim does nothing and returns no error.
- **Lifetime.** A claim ends on `release-pointer`, when the plugin is deactivated for any reason, and when the pane is removed. When the `terminal.pointer` grant is revoked, the host releases the claim and re-activates the plugin with the reduced grant set.

Release the claim as soon as the feature no longer needs the mouse. A claim that stays open blocks the normal mouse behaviour of the pane.

## How highlights behave

- **Layer names** match `[a-z0-9-]{1,32}`. A layer belongs to the calling plugin, so two plugins can both use a layer called `search` without touching each other.
- **Limits.** A layer holds at most 4,096 regions. A plugin may hold at most 16 layers in one pane. Both limits are checked before anything is written.
- **Clipping.** A region outside the visible screen is clipped to it without an error. A region whose first row or column is after its last is `invalid-argument`.
- **Overlap.** Regions of one layer are painted in list order. Where two regions overlap, the later region sets the foreground and background. The `add` and `remove` modifiers of all overlapping regions are combined.
- **Labels.** The label is not drawn in the pane. The client shows it as a tooltip when the pointer rests on the region for 500 ms.
- **Lifetime.** Highlights survive `release-pointer`, so a plugin can give the mouse back and keep the result on screen. They are withdrawn when the plugin is disabled, when its grant is revoked, or when the pane is removed.

## Errors

Each call checks its grant, the pane and the arguments before it writes anything. On an error, nothing changes.

| Code | Call | When | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | all four | The grant is missing or was declined. | Offer a keyboard path. Do not retry. |
| `not-found` | claim, set, clear | The pane does not exist. | Read the tree again. |
| `unsupported` | claim, set | The node exists but is not a terminal pane. | Check the node kind before calling. |
| `conflict` | claim | Another plugin holds the claim. | Wait for it to release, or fall back. Retry after reading the state. |
| `invalid-argument` | set | First row or column after the last, over 4,096 regions, a bad layer name, or a label over 128 characters. | Fix the call. Do not retry it unchanged. |
| `quota-exceeded` | set | The plugin already holds 16 layers in this pane. | Clear a layer it no longer uses. |
| `revoked` | all | The grant was revoked during the call. | Do not retry. The plugin is re-activated. |

## What the user sees

While a claim is held, the pane behaves as described above. The highlighted rows use the colour of the style. The label appears only as a tooltip.

## Example 1: select a block of rows with the mouse (Rust)

The plugin starts a pick from a command the user triggers. A left press sets the first row. Dragging extends the highlight, and the release keeps it and gives the pointer back. The region spans the full width of the pane, and the host clips any part beyond the screen.

**Grants:** `terminal.pointer`

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::terminal::{self, CellRegion};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::ui::{PointerButton, PointerKind};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::PointerEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::text::{Color, ColorRole, Modifiers};

/// Selects whole rows of one pane with the mouse.
#[derive(Default)]
struct BlockCopy {
    pane: Option<NodeId>,
    anchor_row: Option<u32>,
    current_row: u32,
}

impl BlockCopy {
    /// Called from a command the user triggers. The claim can be refused.
    fn start(&mut self, pane: NodeId) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        terminal::claim_pointer(pane)?;
        self.pane = Some(pane);
        self.anchor_row = None;
        Ok(())
    }

    fn on_pointer(&mut self, pointer: PointerEvent) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if self.pane != Some(pointer.node) {
            return Ok(());
        }
        match pointer.kind {
            PointerKind::Down if matches!(pointer.button, Some(PointerButton::Left)) => {
                self.anchor_row = Some(pointer.row);
                self.current_row = pointer.row;
                self.paint()
            }
            PointerKind::Drag => {
                self.current_row = pointer.row;
                self.paint()
            }
            PointerKind::Up => {
                self.current_row = pointer.row;
                self.paint()?;
                self.finish();
                Ok(())
            }
            _ => Ok(()),
        }
    }

    fn paint(&self) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        let (Some(pane), Some(anchor_row)) = (self.pane, self.anchor_row) else {
            return Ok(());
        };
        let region = CellRegion {
            first_row: anchor_row.min(self.current_row),
            first_column: 0,
            last_row: anchor_row.max(self.current_row),
            last_column: 79,
            style: Style {
                fg: Some(Color::Role(ColorRole::Accent)),
                bg: None,
                add: Modifiers::empty(),
                remove: Modifiers::empty(),
            },
            label: Some("Output block".to_string()),
        };
        terminal::set_highlights(pane, "copy-block", &[region])
    }

    /// Gives the pointer back. The highlight stays on screen.
    fn finish(&mut self) {
        if let Some(pane) = self.pane.take() {
            terminal::release_pointer(pane);
        }
        self.anchor_row = None;
    }
}

impl Handler for BlockCopy {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            if let Event::Pointer(pointer) = event {
                // A failed call means the pane or the grant went away. The host has already
                // ended the claim on that path, so the error needs no further action here.
                let _ = self.on_pointer(pointer);
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

Outcome: after the user drags from row 10 to row 14, the pane shows an accent highlight over rows 10 to 14, and the claim is released. The mouse selects text again as soon as `finish` runs.

## Example 2: fall back to the keyboard when the grant is declined (TypeScript)

The same feature in TypeScript. The start function treats `not-permitted` and `conflict` as a reason to offer the keyboard path instead of failing. The handler marks one clicked row and releases the claim.

**Grants:** `terminal.pointer`

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { PluginError, definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { claimPointer, releasePointer, setHighlights } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

let activePane: bigint | undefined;

/** Starts a mouse pick. Returns the input mode the UI should show. */
export function startBlockPick(pane: bigint): 'mouse' | 'keyboard' {
  try {
    claimPointer(pane);
  } catch (error) {
    const is_declined = error instanceof PluginError
      && (error.code === 'not-permitted' || error.code === 'conflict');
    if (is_declined) {
      return 'keyboard';
    }
    throw error;
  }
  activePane = pane;
  return 'mouse';
}

export default definePlugin({
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'pointer' || event.val.node !== activePane) {
        continue;
      }
      if (event.val.kind === 'up' && event.val.button === 'left') {
        setHighlights(event.val.node, 'copy-block', [{
          firstRow: event.val.row, firstColumn: 0, lastRow: event.val.row, lastColumn: 79,
          style: { fg: { tag: 'role', val: 'accent' }, bg: undefined, add: {}, remove: {} },
          label: 'Output row',
        }]);
        releasePointer(event.val.node);
        activePane = undefined;
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

Outcome: with the grant, the user clicks a row and that row is highlighted. Without it, `startBlockPick` returns `keyboard`, the pane keeps its normal mouse behaviour, and the feature shows its keyboard path.

## Who requests it

- Feature 65, Smart Copy light.
- Feature 66, Smart Copy AI.

## See also

- [terminal.read-screen](/pages/capability-terminal-read-screen/) for the text that a highlight covers.
- [Terminal primitive](/pages/primitives-terminal/) for the full terminal import and the output filters.
- [Events](/pages/api-events/) for the `pointer` event in the full event list.
- [clipboard](/pages/capability-clipboard/) for copying the selected text.
- [Errors and limits](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/) for the error codes in general.

Checked against the API version `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# terminal.read-screen

The `terminal.read-screen` grant lets a plugin read the text that a terminal pane shows: the visible rows, the scrollback above them and the user's current selection. The server reads the authoritative screen. The client reads its own mirror of the same screen. Many first-party features need this grant, so it is common, but it exposes everything printed in the pane. Tell the user what the plugin reads before they grant it.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 170" role="img" aria-label="The plugin calls read-screen for a pane and receives the screen record or none">
  <defs><marker id="arr-read-screen" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>
  <rect x="20" y="10" width="320" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="180" y="36" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Plugin (needs terminal.read-screen)</text>
  <rect x="20" y="110" width="320" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <text x="180" y="136" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Terminal pane screen</text>
  <line x1="60" y1="54" x2="60" y2="110" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-read-screen)"/>
  <text x="74" y="76" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">read-screen(pane, part, max-rows)</text>
  <line x1="320" y1="110" x2="320" y2="54" stroke="currentColor" marker-end="url(#arr-read-screen)"/>
  <text x="312" y="102" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-size="10">screen record or none</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The plugin asks for the visible or scrollback rows of one pane. The host returns a screen record, or none when the grant is missing or the pane is not a terminal. Typing into a pane needs terminal.write instead.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div class="warn">

A terminal screen can show secrets: tokens printed by a command, passwords typed at a prompt, private file contents and the text of a private conversation. A plugin that holds this grant can read all of it. Explain this to the user in the plugin's description, and read only the rows the feature needs.

</div>

## You will need

- The grant `terminal.read-screen` on every side that reads screens. Grants are per side: a server-side read needs the grant on the server side, and a client-side read needs it on the client side.
- [panes.read](/pages/capability-panes-read/) if the plugin must discover which panes exist and what kind they are. An event such as `agent-activity-changed` already carries the pane's node id, so a plugin that reacts to events needs no extra grant to get the id.
- A plugin written in Rust with `ilium-plugin-sdk`, or in TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. The two read functions are synchronous, so they need no `await`.

## Grant syntax

- Valid: `terminal.read-screen`
- Invalid: `terminal.read-screen:visible`. The part of the screen is an argument of the call, not of the grant. A grant with an argument fails the install with `manifest.grant-argument`.

## The surface

The grant opens two functions of the `terminal` primitive (`ilium:primitives/terminal`). Both are synchronous and return an option.

| Rust (`primitives::terminal`) | TypeScript (`@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal`) | Arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `read_screen(pane, part, max_rows)` | `readScreen(pane, part, maxRows)` | `pane`: node id (`NodeId`, a `bigint` in TypeScript). `part`: `ScreenPart::Visible` or `ScreenPart::Scrollback` (`'visible'` or `'scrollback'`). `max_rows`: `u32` | `Option<Screen>`, or `undefined` |
| `selection(pane)` | `selection(pane)` | `pane`: node id | `Option<Selection>`, or `undefined` |

The `Screen` record has these fields:

| Field (Rust / TypeScript) | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `columns` / `columns` | `u16` / `number` | Width of the screen in terminal cells. |
| `rows` / `rows` | `Vec<String>` / `string[]` | The returned rows, top to bottom. |
| `cursor_row` / `cursorRow` | `u16` / `number` | Cursor row, counted in the returned rows. |
| `cursor_column` / `cursorColumn` | `u16` / `number` | Cursor column, counted in terminal cells. |
| `title` / `title` | `Option<String>` / `string` or `undefined` | The title the program set, or none. |
| `revision` / `revision` | `u64` / `bigint` | Counter that rises when the screen changes. |

The `Selection` record has `first_row`, `first_column`, `last_row` and `last_column` (`u32` and `u16`; `number` in TypeScript), and `text` (`String`; `string`).

`max_rows` is clamped to 10,000. A larger value does not fail: the host returns at most 10,000 rows.

## How the reads behave

- **Visible part.** `ScreenPart::Visible` returns the bottom `max_rows` rows of the visible area, top to bottom. The newest output and the prompt sit at the bottom, so this is the part most features need. The cursor row and column refer to the returned rows, and row 0 is the first returned row. When the cursor sits above the returned rows, `cursor_row` is the number of returned rows and `cursor_column` is 0.
- **Scrollback part.** `ScreenPart::Scrollback` returns the rows directly above the visible area. The host counts upward from the newest scrollback row and returns the rows top to bottom, oldest first. When the history holds fewer rows than `max_rows`, the record has fewer rows. When there is no history, `rows` is empty.
- **Zero rows.** `max_rows` of 0 returns a record with an empty `rows` list. The revision and the cursor are still filled in.
- **Row text.** Each row is the printed characters of its cells, with escape sequences and trailing blanks removed. A wide character, such as a CJK glyph, appears once in the string, and its second cell is not repeated.
- **Revision.** The revision is a counter per pane. It starts at 0 when the host starts the pane and rises whenever either part changes. It is not saved in the snapshot, so it starts again after a restart. Compare revisions only within one run of the plugin. When `revision` equals the value you stored, the screen has not changed and you can skip the work.
- **Selection.** The coordinates count from the top of the visible area. `text` holds only the part of the selection inside the visible area, with lines joined by a newline. A selection that lies entirely in the scrollback returns none.
- **Snapshot semantics.** Each call is a snapshot. A later call can return different rows, and the host does not push screen changes. To react to new output, use [terminal.output-filter](/pages/capability-terminal-output-filter/) for text patterns, or [agent.read](/pages/capability-agent-read/) for activity changes, and then read the screen.

## Risk and tier rules

- The grant is not marked H (high risk). The review dialog still shows the privacy warning above, and the user should read it before granting.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives it automatically, up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin lists the grant in the review dialog, checked by default. The user can uncheck it before installing and can revoke it later. Revoking ends in-flight calls with `revoked`.
- The grant reads screens only. Typing into them needs `terminal.write`, and mouse control needs `terminal.pointer`.

## When the grant is declined

A declined or revoked grant does not raise an error. The screen reads return none, because the functions have no error result. The host writes one refusal line to the plugin log, as the location and editor reads do. A plugin that shows screen text, such as a workspace search, must show its empty state. It must not show an error that suggests the pane is broken.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:02</span> <span class="t-ok">info</span>  node 42 idle: 2 rows hold "error"
<span class="t-dim">2026-10-11 09:14:03</span> <span class="t-warn">warn</span>  terminal.read-screen not granted, node 57 skipped
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. Two plugin log lines: one successful read and one read refused by a missing grant. The wording of the lines is a placeholder.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Worked example in Rust

This server-side plugin reacts when an agent in a pane goes idle. It reads the last 40 visible rows, counts the rows that contain the word `error`, and sets a badge on the pane. The badge needs `tree.decorate` and a declared `errors` decoration slot.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::terminal::{self, ScreenPart};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::AgentActivityEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SetDecorationSpec;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::AgentActivity;

const ROWS_TO_READ: u32 = 40;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct ErrorBadge;

impl Lifecycle for ErrorBadge {}

impl Handler for ErrorBadge {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::AgentActivityChanged(AgentActivityEvent { node, current, .. }) =
                event
            else {
                continue;
            };
            if current != AgentActivity::Idle {
                continue;
            }
            // None means the grant is missing or the pane is not a terminal.
            let Some(screen) = terminal::read_screen(node, ScreenPart::Visible, ROWS_TO_READ)
            else {
                continue;
            };
            let error_rows = screen.rows.iter().filter(|row| row.contains("error")).count();
            submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
                node,
                slot: "errors".into(),
                content: vec![Span::styled(
                    format!("{error_rows} errors"),
                    Style::role(ColorRole::Danger),
                )],
                icon: None,
                sort_key: None,
                persist: false,
            })));
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

The manifest requests the grant on the server side and declares the slot:

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "server": ["terminal.read-screen", "tree.decorate"]
  },
  "contributes": {
    "decoration_slots": [{ "id": "errors", "placement": "badge", "priority": 40 }]
  }
}
```

## Worked example in TypeScript

The same feature in TypeScript. The `readScreen` call takes the `bigint` node id from the event. The `span` and `role` helpers come from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/ui/build`.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { readScreen } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal';
import { role, span } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/ui/build';

const ROWS_TO_READ = 40;
let nextCorrelation = 1n;

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'agent-activity-changed') continue;
      const { node, current } = event.val;
      if (current !== 'idle') continue;
      // undefined means the grant is missing or the pane is not a terminal.
      const screen = readScreen(node, 'visible', ROWS_TO_READ);
      if (screen === undefined) continue;
      const errorRows = screen.rows.filter((row) => row.includes('error')).length;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'set-decoration',
          val: {
            node,
            slot: 'errors',
            content: [span(`${errorRows} errors`, { fg: role('danger') })],
            icon: undefined,
            sortKey: undefined,
            persist: false,
          },
        },
        correlation: nextCorrelation++,
        dedupKey: undefined,
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

## Edge cases and errors

The two functions have no error codes. A failed read is a none, and the plugin log shows the reason only when the grant is missing.

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Grant missing, declined or revoked | none, and one refusal line in the plugin log |
| Pane is not a terminal, or the node id is unknown | none, with no log line |
| Pane has no selection (`selection`) | none |
| `max_rows` above 10,000 | clamped to 10,000 rows |
| `max_rows` of 0 | empty `rows`, with the revision and the cursor |
| Scrollback shorter than `max_rows` | fewer rows, no error |

A plugin should treat none as "nothing to show now". It should not retry in a loop. When the grant is the reason, the user must grant it again in Settings.

## What the user sees

- In the review dialog, the row "Read text shown in terminals" with the grant name at the right edge.
- In a first-party feature that needs the grant, such as workspace search, an empty state when the grant is declined.
- In a `terminal-view` widget, which embeds a pane's screen (W30). Without the grant the widget draws an empty frame with the text `not permitted`.

# terminal.write

The `terminal.write` grant lets a plugin type text into a terminal pane, as if the user had typed it. It is the only way a plugin sends input to a running agent or shell. A plugin uses it to run a scheduled command in a shell, to answer an agent's approval prompt, to transfer a screen between panes or to pass a message to an agent. Each send is a `send-input` intent. The plugin names a pane and a text, and the kernel checks the request in a fixed order before it writes the text to the pane.

The grant is high risk (H): whatever a plugin sends runs with the rights of the process in that pane, so the user must grant it explicitly, even for a T1 bundled plugin.

<div class="warn">

Input sent to a pane runs there with the permissions of that process. A plugin with this grant can start commands in a shell, approve an agent's prompt or submit text to an agent. Grant it only to plugins whose purpose needs it, and check the plugin's source before you grant it.

</div>

## You will need

- The grant `terminal.write`, on each side (server or client) whose code sends input. Each side needs its own grant.
- The SDK for your language: the Rust crate `ilium-plugin-sdk` or the npm package `@ilium/plugin-sdk`, at the versions pinned by the SDK release.
- [panes.read](/pages/capability-panes-read/) to find the pane and check that it is restored and ready.
- [agent.read-prompts](/pages/capability-agent-read-prompts/) when the plugin needs the `input-submitted` event, which carries the prompt epoch.
- [terminal.read-screen](/pages/capability-terminal-read-screen/) when the plugin reads the prompt text before it decides what to send.

## Grant syntax

- Valid: `terminal.write`
- Invalid: `terminal.write:agents`. The grant takes no argument, and the manifest check refuses the scoped form with `manifest.grant-argument`. Choosing the pane is part of the intent.

## The surface

| Name | Kind | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `send-input` | intent | record `send-input-spec { pane, text, delivery, prompt-epoch }` | Writes `text` to the pane. Rust: `SendInputSpec` in `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents`. TypeScript: `{ tag: 'send-input', val: {...} }`. |
| `pane` | field | `node-id` | The terminal pane that receives the text. |
| `text` | field | `string`, at most 64 KiB | The text to type. |
| `delivery` | field | enum `typed`, `submitted`, `pasted` | How the text is written (see Delivery modes). |
| `prompt-epoch` | field | `option<u64>` | Optional. The prompt epoch the plugin read before it decided to send. |
| `dedup-key` | submission field | `string`, 1 to 128 characters | Mandatory for `send-input`. See Dedup keys. |
| `terminal.prompt-epoch` | sync function | `func(pane: node-id) -> option<u64>` | Returns the pane's current prompt epoch. |
| `epoch` | field of `input-submitted-event` | `u64` | The epoch of the prompt recorded by that event. Needs `agent.read-prompts`. |
| `submit_keys` | signature field | string, default `"\r"` | The keys that `submitted` sends for panes of that signature. |
| `initial-input` | field of `create-pane-spec` | `string`, at most 64 KiB | Text typed into a new pane. It needs this grant as well. |

Rust names are snake_case: `Delivery::Submitted`, `prompt_epoch`, `ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives::terminal::prompt_epoch`. TypeScript names are camelCase: `promptEpoch`, `promptEpoch(pane)` from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal`. The `delivery` strings in TypeScript are `'typed'`, `'submitted'` and `'pasted'`.

## Submitting text

The kernel checks every `send-input` submission in this order. The first failing check decides the outcome, and a submission that fails any check does not reach the pane.
