<text x="226" y="243" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">refused: conflict</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The eight checks of a send-input submission. A failed check stops the submission and returns the outcome beside it. The key of a refused submission is not reserved, so a retry with the same key is valid after the cause is fixed.</figcaption>
</figure>

Two rules apply to the whole batch, not to one submission. A batch is refused as a whole when a submission is malformed (wrong shape, a missing `dedup-key`, or more than 256 submissions) or when the plugin lacks the grant. In that case every submission of the batch completes as `refused(cancelled)` with the message `batch refused: submission <index>`, except the offending one. All other checks run per submission.

## Dedup keys

A plugin can lose track of whether a send worked, for example after a restart. Sending the same text again would then type it twice. The `dedup-key` prevents that.

- The key is mandatory for `send-input` and `agent-action`. A submission without one is malformed.
- The key has 1 to 128 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9._:/-]`. Another character makes the submission malformed.
- The key is reserved for the pair of plugin id and key, for 10 minutes. From build phase 5, the kernel also journals `send-input` keys in the session snapshot before the write. A server restart then does not repeat input. Before that phase, keys live in memory only.
- A submission whose key is reserved completes as `duplicate(original)`, where `original` names the submission that reserved the key. It has no effect.
- A key is reserved only after every check passed. A refused submission keeps its key free, so a retry is valid. An accepted submission keeps its key reserved even if it later fails, so a retry of a failed send needs a new key.

Derive the key from the work, never from the clock or a random value. A new random key on every attempt defeats the purpose. The SDK helper `dedup::key_for` (Rust) joins its parts with `:` and replaces disallowed characters with `-`. TypeScript has no helper, so the plugin builds the string itself.

## Delivery modes

| Delivery | What the pane receives |
|---|---|
| `typed` | The text only. The program sees the characters as if typed. |
| `submitted` | The text, then the submit keys of the pane's signature. The default submit key is `"\r"`. A signature can set `submit_keys` to another sequence. |
| `pasted` | The text inside bracketed paste markers when the program enabled bracketed paste (DEC mode 2004). Otherwise the text is sent like `typed`. |

A pane without a signature always receives `"\r"` for `submitted`.

```json
{
  "contributes": {
    "signatures": [
      { "id": "example-repl", "process_names": ["example-repl"], "submit_keys": "\r\n" }
    ]
  }
}
```

## Prompt epochs

A prompt epoch identifies the prompt an agent pane was showing. It guards against answering a prompt the plugin did not read.

- The kernel keeps a `u64` counter for each terminal pane. It starts at 0 and increases each time the kernel records a submitted prompt for that pane. That is the same moment it emits `input-submitted`. The counter is saved in the snapshot.
- `terminal.prompt-epoch(pane)` returns the current value, or `none` when the pane has no epoch.
- A `send-input` with `prompt-epoch: some(n)` is refused with `conflict` when `n` is not the current epoch. The check runs after the rate check and before the write. The plugin reads the screen again and decides again.
- Without the epoch, the answer reaches whatever prompt is on the screen at write time.

## Risk and tier rules

- This grant is high risk (H). A T1 bundled plugin does not receive it automatically. The user must grant it explicitly.
- A T2 or T3 plugin needs the same explicit grant, and the review dialog shows the line with the H mark.
- Grants are per side. The server and client sides each need their own explicit grant.

## What the review dialog says

<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.terminal 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                  │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │
│ <span class="t-warn">! [ ] Types into terminals</span> <span class="t-dim">……………………………………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-warn">terminal.write</span> │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-warn">! marks a high-risk grant. It starts unchecked and is</span>                      │

## When the grant is declined

A declined grant refuses the batch with `refused(not-permitted)`, and no text is written. A plugin that schedules or queues input must keep its queue, mark the item as not sent and tell the user that sending is unavailable. It must not drop the item.

## Worked example in Rust

This server-side function builds the submission for one due run of a scheduled command. The key comes from the schedule id and the due time, so a restart that replays the same due run is answered with `duplicate(original)`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::dedup;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::{Delivery, SendInputSpec};

/// Builds the submission for one due run of a scheduled command.
/// The due time comes from the schedule's own state, never from the clock.
pub fn scheduled_run(
    pane: NodeId,
    schedule_id: &str,
    due_at: &str,
    command: &str,
) -> Submission {
    let key = dedup::key_for(&["nightly", schedule_id, due_at]);
    let spec = SendInputSpec {
        pane,
        text: command.to_string(),
        delivery: Delivery::Submitted,
        prompt_epoch: None,
    };
    Submission::keyed(Intent::SendInput(spec), key)
}
```

The plugin calls `scheduled_run` from its `on_events` when a schedule comes due, and it returns the result in the list of submissions. With `prompt_epoch: None`, the kernel skips the epoch check, which is correct for a shell that has no prompt to answer.

## Worked example in TypeScript

This server-side plugin answers an agent's approval prompt. It stores the epoch of the prompt when the agent enters `awaiting-approval`. When the user presses an approve command, it sends `y` with that stored epoch. If the prompt changed in between, the kernel refuses the send with `conflict`.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';
import { promptEpoch } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/primitives/terminal';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';

const APPROVE_COMMAND = 'com.example.approve/yes';
const APPROVAL_ACTIVITY = 'awaiting-approval';

const epochByPane = new Map<bigint, bigint>();
let nextCorrelation = 1n;

function rememberEpoch(pane: bigint, current: string): void {
  if (current !== APPROVAL_ACTIVITY) {
    epochByPane.delete(pane);
    return;
  }
  const epoch = promptEpoch(pane);
  if (epoch !== undefined) {
    epochByPane.set(pane, epoch);
  }
}

function approve(command: string, pane: bigint | undefined): Submission | undefined {
  if (command !== APPROVE_COMMAND || pane === undefined) {
    return undefined;
  }
  const epoch = epochByPane.get(pane);
  if (epoch === undefined) {
    log('info', 'No approval prompt was read for this pane. Nothing was sent.');
    return undefined;
  }
  const correlation = nextCorrelation;
  nextCorrelation += 1n;
  return {
    intent: {
      tag: 'send-input',
      val: { pane, text: 'y', delivery: 'submitted', promptEpoch: epoch },
    },
    correlation,
    dedupKey: `approve:${pane}:${epoch}`,
  };
}

export const { handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'agent-activity-changed') {
        rememberEpoch(event.val.node, event.val.current);
      } else if (event.tag === 'command-invoked') {
        const submission = approve(event.val.command, event.val.context.pane);
        if (submission !== undefined) {
          submissions.push(submission);
        }
      }
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

The manifest needs `"server": ["agent.read", "terminal.write"]` for this plugin. The `dedupKey` uses the epoch, so a double click on the same prompt sends once. A refused `conflict` reserves nothing, so the plugin can read the prompt again and retry.

## What the user sees

The text appears at the pane's prompt as if the user had typed it. With `submitted`, the program then receives the submit keys, so a shell runs the command or an agent starts its turn. The grant is the only consent: the kernel does not ask the user before each send.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">Shell pane 42, written by the scheduled run</span>
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> cargo test --workspace
<span class="t-ok">test result: ok. 412 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored</span>
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> <span class="t-hi">_</span>
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The shell pane after a submitted send of cargo test.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Errors and edge cases

| Outcome | Cause | Retry |
|---|---|---|
| `ok` | The text was written. | Not needed. |
| `duplicate(original)` | The key is reserved within the last 10 minutes. | No. The original was written. |
| `refused(invalid-argument)` | Text over 64 KiB, a missing or malformed key, or a malformed batch. | No. Fix the call. |
| `refused(not-permitted)` | The grant is missing or declined. | No. Ask the user to grant it. |
| `refused(not-found)` | The pane no longer exists. | No. |
| `refused(unsupported)` | The node is not a terminal pane. | No. |
| `refused(pane-not-ready)` | A restored pane has not started its process. | Yes, after `pane-created` or `tree-changed` for that pane. |
| `refused(rate-limited)` | More than 20 submissions per second to one pane. | Yes, after `retry-after-ms`. |
| `refused(conflict)` | The prompt epoch is stale. | Yes, after reading the prompt again. |
| `refused(cancelled)` | Another submission of the same batch was refused. | Maybe. |

Check `is-restored` again before each write, because a pane can be restored after the plugin read it. Keep the queued text until you see `ok`, `duplicate(original)` or a refusal that will not clear.

Limits:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Text per submission | 64 KiB |
| Dedup key | 1 to 128 characters |
| Dedup window | 10 minutes |
| Dedup journal | 24 hours or 4,096 entries per session, whichever is smaller |
| Rate | 20 per second per pane per plugin |
| Submissions per batch | 256 |

## First-party features that request it

- Feature 17, screen transfer between panes.
- Feature 23, create an agent from an editor line, through `initial-input`.
- Feature 36, agent messaging.
- Feature 51, voice confirmations.
- Feature 55, scheduled input.
- Feature 56, text triggers, from Phase 5.
- Feature 57, prompt queue.
- Feature 62, chatroom, for the `@name` routing.
- Feature 80, remote compaction.
- Feature 110, `ilium broadcast`.

# Capability: topics.subscribe

## topics.subscribe:&lt;topic-pattern&gt;

The `topics.subscribe:<topic-pattern>` capability lets a plugin receive the topics that other plugins publish. A topic is a named channel such as `ilium.progress/finished`. Each publish on a matching topic reaches the subscriber as one `topic-published` event with the topic name, the publishing plugin id and the JSON payload.

Topics let plugins share state without knowing each other. A message (see [messages.peer](/pages/capability-messages-peer/)) goes to one named receiver. A topic goes to every subscriber whose pattern matches, and the publisher never learns who they are.

Subscribing is declarative. There is no subscribe call and no unsubscribe call. The grant and the manifest decide what a plugin receives, and the kernel checks both on every publish.

### What you need

- **A grant per pattern.** Each `topics.subscribe:<topic-pattern>` string is one grant. Grants are per side, so a server half and a client half that both need topics each list their own grant.
- **A manifest entry.** List every topic you react to under `contributes.topics.subscribes`. The entries use the same pattern syntax as the grant. An invalid entry fails the install check.
- **An activation trigger.** A plugin that is not active receives no events. Use `"startup"` in `activation`, or `"topic:<exact-topic>"` for each exact topic. A pattern cannot be a trigger, so a plugin with a pattern subscription uses `"startup"`.
- **A language SDK.** Rust uses the crate `ilium-plugin-sdk` (imported as `ilium_plugin_sdk`). TypeScript uses `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. Both need the toolchain from [getting started](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/).
- **No grant to publish.** A plugin that publishes a topic needs its own id prefix and a `contributes.topics.publishes` entry, not this grant. See [messages and topics](/pages/api-messages-and-topics/).

### Patterns

| Pattern | Matches | Risk | Accepted |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ilium.progress/finished` | that one topic | normal | yes |
| `ilium.progress/*` | every topic under `ilium.progress/`, any depth | normal | yes |
| `*` | every topic | high (H) | yes |
| `ilium.*`, `*/finished`, `ilium.progress*` | none | not applicable | no, `manifest.grant-wildcard` |
| `topics.subscribe` | none | not applicable | no, `manifest.grant-argument-missing` |

A prefix pattern matches a topic only when the topic continues past the slash, so `ilium.progress/*` does not match the bare name `ilium.progress`. A topic name is at most 128 characters.

### The full surface

| Name | Kind | Types | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `topics.subscribe:<topic-pattern>` | grant, sides server and client | pattern string | Lets the side receive matching topics. |
| `contributes.topics.subscribes` | manifest list | topic patterns | Declares the topics the plugin reacts to. |
| `topic:<exact-topic>` | activation trigger | exact topic name | Activates the plugin when that topic is published. |
| `topic-published` | event | `topic: string`, `from: plugin-id`, `payload-json: string` | One publish on a matching topic. Drop oldest, counted. |
| `events-dropped` | event | `list<dropped-count>` | Reports lost events. `dropped-count` holds `event`, `source` (the topic name) and `count`. Never dropped. |
| `granted` | field of the activation context | `list<string>` | The grant strings actually granted. A declined grant is absent. |

Bindings for the event:

| Language | Event | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| Rust | `Event::TopicPublished(TopicPublishedEvent { topic, from, payload_json })` | snake_case fields |
| TypeScript | `{ tag: 'topic-published', val: { topic, from, payloadJson } }` | camelCase fields |

The payload is the JSON text the publisher sent, unchanged. The kernel does not parse it.

### Worked example: the progress notice in Rust (server side)

The plugin keeps a server-side record of finished jobs. It checks at activation that the grant is present, and it logs each notice it receives.

Manifest excerpt for both examples in this page:

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.jobwatch",
  "activation": ["startup"],
  "contributes": {
    "topics": { "publishes": [], "subscribes": ["ilium.progress/finished"] }
  },
  "capabilities": {
    "server": ["topics.subscribe:ilium.progress/finished"],
    "client": ["topics.subscribe:ilium.progress/finished"]
  }
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::TopicPublishedEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::exports::{Activation, DeactivationReason};

const JOB_FINISHED_TOPIC: &str = "ilium.progress/finished";
const JOB_FINISHED_GRANT: &str = "topics.subscribe:ilium.progress/finished";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct JobWatch;

impl Lifecycle for JobWatch {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if !context.granted.iter().any(|grant| grant == JOB_FINISHED_GRANT) {
            log::log(Level::Warn, "job notices declined; no topic events will arrive");
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    fn deactivate(&mut self, _reason: DeactivationReason) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
        None
    }
}

impl Handler for JobWatch {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::TopicPublished(TopicPublishedEvent { topic, from, payload_json })
                    if topic == JOB_FINISHED_TOPIC =>
                {
                    log::log(Level::Info, &format!("{from} published {topic}: {payload_json}"));
                }
                Event::EventsDropped(_) => {
                    log::log(Level::Warn, "topic events were dropped; re-read the job state");
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

The handler only logs and returns no submissions. It must finish inside the `on-events` deadline (see edge cases).

### Worked example: the progress notice in TypeScript (client side)

The client half parses the payload. The keys inside the JSON keep the catalogue spelling (`job_id`), because the publisher wrote them that way.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const JOB_FINISHED_TOPIC = 'ilium.progress/finished';

interface JobFinishedPayload {
  pane: number;
  job_id: string;
  status: 'done' | 'error';
  percent: number;
  message: string;
  details: string | null;
}

function describeJobNotice(payloadJson: string): string {
  try {
    const payload = JSON.parse(payloadJson) as JobFinishedPayload;
    return `job ${payload.job_id} ${payload.status}: ${payload.message}`;
  } catch {
    return 'job notice with an unreadable payload';
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {
    log('info', 'job notice plugin ready');
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'topic-published' && event.val.topic === JOB_FINISHED_TOPIC) {
        log('info', describeJobNotice(event.val.payloadJson));
      }
      if (event.tag === 'events-dropped') {
        log('warn', 'topic events were dropped; re-read the job state');
      }
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

### The progress payload

The kernel publishes `ilium.progress/finished` when a background job ends. The payload is:

```json
{"pane": 42, "job_id": "release-build", "status": "done", "percent": 100,
 "message": "Release build finished", "details": null}
```

`pane` is the node id as a JSON number. `status` is `"done"` or `"error"`. `percent` runs from 0 to 100. `message` is one line. `details` is text or `null`.

### What the user sees

The review dialog shows one row per grant. A normal grant is checked by default. A bare `*` is a high-risk row: it is unchecked on a T2 or T3 install, and a T1 bundled plugin asks once at first activation.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.topics 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                    │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Listens to topics build/* <span class="t-dim">…………………………………………………</span> topics.subscribe:build/* │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>The review dialog for a package that requests topics.subscribe:build/*, drawn with the client's dialog characters: rounded corners, dotted leaders and the hint bar. Checked rows are granted; a high-risk row starts unchecked.</figcaption>
</figure>

For a T1 bundled plugin with the high-risk `*` grant, the first activation shows one prompt, "Plugin <name> asks for:", with `Allow selected` and `Not now`. `Not now` asks again at the next server start, up to three times. Settings > Plugins lets the user grant it at any time.

### Edge cases and errors

| Situation | What happens | Signal to the plugin |
|---|---|---|
| Grant declined at install or in the prompt | No events for the pattern. | No error. The `granted` list omits the string. |
| Grant revoked while running | The plugin is deactivated with reason `revoked` and reactivated with the new set. | Lifecycle only. |
| Grant added while running | The plugin is deactivated with reason `granted` and reactivated with the new set. | Lifecycle only. |
| Queue full (1,024 events by default) | The oldest event is dropped. The next batch starts with `events-dropped`. | `events-dropped` with `event: "topic-published"`, `source` set to the topic and `count`. |
| Handler too slow | The `on-events` deadline is 20 ms by default and 50 ms at the T1 ceiling. A breach counts as a plugin failure. | Counted as a failure. The plugin keeps its other events. |
| Plugin not active | Nothing is delivered. | None. Use a `startup` or `topic:` trigger. |
| Plugin publishes a topic it also subscribes to | It receives its own publish when it holds the matching grant. | Ordinary `topic-published`. |
| Invalid pattern in the grant | The install check refuses the package. | `manifest.grant-wildcard` or `manifest.grant-argument-missing`. |
| Invalid entry in `subscribes` | The install check refuses the package. | The same codes. |

The publisher enforces two limits, and the subscriber inherits them. A topic payload is valid JSON of at most 64 KiB, and a publisher may call `publish` at most 100 times per second, with `rate-limited` and `retry-after-ms` above that.

### Who requests it

First-party plugins from the feature mapping use this capability:

- AI triggers (feature 44) hold `topics.subscribe:*`, as a T1 plugin with the user's grant.
- Semantic animation (feature 103) holds `topics.subscribe:ilium.organise/*`, to receive topics from the tree organisation plugin.

The progress monitor (feature 59) publishes `ilium.progress/finished`. It needs no subscription grant for that.

# tree.decorate

The `tree.decorate` grant lets a plugin add small pieces of information to rows in the project tree: a badge, an icon, a subtitle line or a footer line. It also sorts sibling rows with a sort key, and it adds virtual rows such as "Chatroom". A plugin decorates a row; it never draws the tree itself. The host places each decoration in a slot that the manifest declared, draws the row, and reports the outcome of each intent back to the plugin.

## You will need

- The grant `tree.decorate` in the manifest `capabilities` list of the side that sends the intents. The examples below run on the server side.
- A `decoration_slots` entry for each slot the plugin fills. A slot must be declared before the plugin can use it.
- A `virtual_rows` entry for each virtual row kind the plugin fills, and a `commands` entry for each command a row invokes.
- Either the Rust SDK (`ilium_plugin_sdk`) or the TypeScript SDK (`@ilium/plugin-sdk`). Both expose the same three intents.
- [tree.read](/pages/capability-tree-read/) if the plugin chooses the rows to decorate by their content.

## Grant syntax

- Valid: `tree.decorate`
- Invalid: `tree.decorate:badge`. The slot is named in the manifest and in the intent, not in the grant.

## Intents

The grant opens three intents. Each one completes with an outcome, as described in [requests and outcomes](/pages/requests-and-outcomes/).

| Intent | Payload | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `set-decoration` | `node: node-id`, `slot: string`, `content: styled-text`, `icon: option<string>`, `sort-key: option<s64>`, `persist: bool` | `ok` |
| `clear-decoration` | `node: node-id`, `slot: string` | `ok` |
| `set-virtual-rows` | `row-kind: string`, `rows: list<virtual-row>`; a `virtual-row` has `id`, `label`, `icon` and `command` | `ok` |

In Rust the payloads are `SetDecorationSpec`, `DecorationKey` and `SetVirtualRowsSpec` (with `VirtualRow`), all in `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents`. In TypeScript they are the objects of the same names in camelCase, for example `sortKey` and `rowKind`.

Field rules:

- `content` is a `styled-text`: a list of spans. Build one span with `Span::plain("2")` in Rust or `span('2')` in TypeScript.
- `icon` is a Tabler icon name, such as `checks` or `messages`. It is not a file path.
- `node` is the id from `tree.read` or from an event. A node keeps its id when it is renamed or moved.
- `set-decoration` on a node and slot that already hold a decoration replaces it. It does not add a second one.
- `set-virtual-rows` replaces every row of that kind that the plugin owns. An empty `rows` list removes them all.
- `command` is the global id of one of the plugin's commands, `<plugin-id>/<id>`. When the user activates the row, the plugin receives `command-invoked` for that command.

## Slots and placements

The manifest declares the slots and the parent of each virtual row:

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.review-agent",
  "capabilities": { "server": ["agent.read", "tree.decorate"] },
  "contributes": {
    "decoration_slots": [
      { "id": "review-count", "placement": "badge", "priority": 10 },
      { "id": "branch-line", "placement": "subtitle", "priority": 20 }
    ],
    "virtual_rows": [
      { "id": "chatroom", "title": "Chatroom", "icon": "messages", "parent": "project" }
    ],
    "commands": [{ "id": "open-chatroom", "title": "Open chatroom" }]
  }
}
```

The four placements are:

| Placement | Where it appears | Size limit |
|---|---|---|
| `icon` | Before the title | 2 cells |
| `badge` | On the right of the title line | 12 cells |
| `subtitle` | Under the title | The width of the row |
| `footer` | The bottom line of the row | The width of the row |

Text wider than its limit is cut and ends with `…`. Widths use the host's display-width rules, so a wide glyph counts as two cells. Use the `display-width` function of the host when you need to measure text before you send it.

The `priority` value orders the slots of one placement: a lower number is drawn first, to the left or higher. Use one slot per kind of information, so that a plugin's badges do not replace each other.

## Sorting and virtual rows

A `sort-key` orders a row among its siblings, lowest first. A row with several decorations uses its lowest key. Rows without a key come after the keyed rows, in their usual order. The feature that sorts the tree by cost uses this field.

A virtual row is a row that the plugin owns, not a node of the workspace. The manifest sets its parent to `project` (a row under the project) or `session` (a row under each session). The row kind in `row-kind` must match the `id` of a `virtual_rows` entry.

## Persistence and restarts

`persist: true` stores the decoration in the snapshot, so it survives a restart of the server. After a restart it is shown in the muted colour, marked as stale, until the plugin sets or clears it again after its activation. `persist: false` decorations are dropped at shutdown.

A crash restart keeps every decoration of the plugin, marked as stale. Disabling or uninstalling the plugin removes all of its decorations. Closing a node removes the decorations on that node.

## Risk and tier rules

- This grant is not marked high risk.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives it automatically, up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin needs an explicit grant in the review dialog. The grant is remembered.
- A virtual row kind is declared in the manifest with its parent. Only the declared kinds can be filled.

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.tree 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                      │

</figure>

## Limits

<div class="note">

A plugin may hold 4,096 decorations on T2 and T3 and 16,384 on the T1 ceiling. All plugins together may hold 65,536 decorations per session. A plugin that writes the same decoration again should use the same slot and node, so that it replaces the old one rather than adding a second.

</div>

## What the user sees

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">Project tree</span>
▾ api-service
  <span class="t-ok">◉</span> review-agent                              <span class="t-hi">[done]</span>
      feature/parser-rewrite, 3 files changed
      <span class="t-dim">14 min   0.42 EUR</span>
  ▸ Chatroom
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. One project with an agent row and a virtual row. The icon is before the title, the badge on the right, the subtitle under the title and the footer at the bottom. Exact positions depend on the host layout.</figcaption>
</figure>

A stale decoration looks the same, but in the muted colour. A decoration of a plugin that has been stopped disappears with the plugin.

## Worked example in Rust

This server-side plugin puts a `done` badge on each agent row when the agent finishes. It removes the badge when the agent starts working again. The badge persists across restarts.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::events::AgentActivityEvent;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::{DecorationKey, SetDecorationSpec};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::AgentActivity;

const REVIEW_SLOT: &str = "review-count";

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct ReviewBadge;

impl Handler for ReviewBadge {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            let Event::AgentActivityChanged(AgentActivityEvent { node, current, .. })
                = event
            else {
                continue;
            };
            match current {
                AgentActivity::Done => {
                    submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
                        node,
                        slot: REVIEW_SLOT.into(),
                        content: vec![Span::plain("done")],
                        icon: Some("checks".into()),
                        sort_key: Some(0),
                        persist: true,
                    })));
                }
                AgentActivity::Working => {
                    submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::ClearDecoration(DecorationKey {
                        node,
                        slot: REVIEW_SLOT.into(),
                    })));
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

The `Event` and `Submission` names come from the prelude. Each submission gets the next correlation number when `Submission::new` is called. Use `Submission::keyed(intent, key)` when a repeated submission must not be applied twice.

## Worked example in TypeScript

This server-side plugin declares a "Chatroom" virtual row under the project. The row runs the plugin's `open-chatroom` command. The row is set again on every `tree-changed` batch. Setting the same rows again is safe, because the intent replaces every row of the kind.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';

const CHATROOM_ROW_KIND = 'chatroom';
const OPEN_CHATROOM_COMMAND = 'com.example.review-agent/open-chatroom';

let nextCorrelation = 1n;

export const { handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'tree-changed') continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'set-virtual-rows',
          val: {
            rowKind: CHATROOM_ROW_KIND,
            rows: [
              {
                id: 'chatroom',
                label: 'Chatroom',
                icon: 'messages',
                command: OPEN_CHATROOM_COMMAND,
              },
            ],
          },
        },
        correlation: nextCorrelation++,
        dedupKey: undefined,
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

The TypeScript intent objects use the `tag` and `val` shape of the event and intent variants. The `correlation` value is a `bigint`, so the counter starts at `1n`.

## Edge cases and errors

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Grant declined | Each intent completes `refused(not-permitted)`. Decorations on screen stay, but the plugin cannot change them. |
| Grant revoked while running | Pending calls complete `revoked`. The decorations are withdrawn and the plugin is re-activated with the reduced grants. |
| Slot not declared in the manifest | `refused(invalid-argument)` |
| Row kind not declared in the manifest | `refused(invalid-argument)` from `set-virtual-rows` |
| Node does not exist, or was removed | `refused(not-found)` from `set-decoration` and `clear-decoration` |
| Quota full | `refused(quota-exceeded)`. Clear decorations you no longer need, then retry. |
| `clear-decoration` on a slot with no decoration | `ok`. Nothing changes. |
| Icon name not in the icon set | The icon is not drawn; the content still shows. |
| Text wider than the placement | Cut to the size limit and ends with `…`. |
| Plugin traps or misses its deadline | Its decorations stay on screen, marked stale, until the plugin restarts and sets them again. |

A plugin that cannot decorate should still work through its other features, such as commands and panels.

## See also

- [tree.read](/pages/capability-tree-read/) for choosing the rows to decorate.
- [tree.metadata](/pages/capability-tree-metadata/) for data that the plugin keeps on a row without drawing it.
- [panes.read](/pages/capability-panes-read/) for the pane state that a status badge usually shows.
- [agent.read](/pages/capability-agent-read/) for the agent activity events that drive most badges.
- [Retained mode](/pages/retained-mode/) for how decorations and virtual rows are replicated to the client.
- [Tutorial: agent badge](/pages/tutorial-01-agent-badge/) for a complete first plugin that uses a badge.

# tree.metadata

## Overview

The `tree.metadata` grant lets a plugin keep its own bytes on a workspace tree node. Each plugin
has a separate byte map on each node, so no plugin can read or write another plugin's entry
through this grant. The host saves the maps in the session snapshot and restores them when the
server starts. A node keeps its metadata when it is moved or renamed, and the host removes the
metadata when the node closes.

Use metadata for small state that belongs to one node: a bookmark flag, a schedule, a position in
a queue. Use [storage](/pages/api-storage/) for anything larger, or for state that is not tied to a
node.

## You will need

- The grant `tree.metadata` on each side that calls the functions. Grants are per side, so a
  server-side call needs a server grant and a client-side call needs a client grant.
- The Rust SDK `ilium-plugin-sdk` or the TypeScript SDK `@ilium/plugin-sdk`, both at the versions
  pinned for the release. Plugins built with either SDK use the same imports.
- The grant [tree.read](/pages/capability-tree-read/) when the plugin also needs to find the nodes
  that carry metadata, for example with `find`.

## Grant syntax and risk

- Valid: `tree.metadata`.
- Invalid: `tree.metadata:own`. The grant takes no argument. The manifest fails with
  `manifest.grant-argument` and the text `capability "tree.metadata" takes no argument (got
  "tree.metadata:own")`.
- Risk: `normal`. The grant is not marked high risk, so it is never off by default.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives the grant automatically, up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin lists the grant in the install review dialog, checked by default. The user
  confirms the install. The choice is recorded per plugin and per side.

## Surface

| Function | Rust | TypeScript | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `metadata` | `tree::metadata(node: NodeId) -> Option<Vec<u8>>` | `metadata(node: bigint): Uint8Array \| undefined` | option | The plugin's own bytes for the node. `None` or `undefined` when nothing is stored. |
| `set-metadata` | `tree::set_metadata(node: NodeId, bytes: Vec<u8>) -> Result<(), PluginError>` | `setMetadata(node: bigint, bytes: Uint8Array): void` | result | Replaces the plugin's bytes for the node. Throws `PluginError` in TypeScript. |

Both functions live in the `tree` interface, so the Rust module is `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::tree`
and the TypeScript import is `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/tree`. The WIT signatures are:

```wit
// Excerpt of ilium:host/tree in reference-wit
// ilium:host/tree
metadata: func(node: node-id) -> option<list<u8>>;                  // tree.metadata
set-metadata: func(node: node-id, bytes: list<u8>) -> result<_, plugin-error>;  // tree.metadata
```

`node-id` is a `u64`. In TypeScript it is a `bigint`, including every node id that comes from an
event. `list<u8>` is `Vec<u8>` in Rust and `Uint8Array` in TypeScript.

An empty list clears the entry. The host has no delete call. After an empty write, `metadata`
returns an empty list, not `none`. Treat an empty list and `none` as "no value" in your code.

### Size limits

The limit is per node, per plugin, and it is the manifest key `node_metadata_kib`:

| Tier | Default | Ceiling | Bytes at the ceiling |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 bundled | 64 KiB | 256 KiB | 262,144 |
| T2 and T3 | 64 KiB | 64 KiB | 65,536 |

A manifest request above the ceiling is clamped and logged, never refused. The user can set the
same key under `[plugins.limits]` in `config.toml`.

Metadata bytes are opaque to the host. The host never reads them, so a plugin that stores
structured data must choose its own format and write a version byte first. A later version of
your plugin can then tell old bytes from new ones.

## Rules that affect your code

- **Client and server share one map.** Both sides of a plugin read and write the same map for
  each node. The server holds it and replicates it to the client. A value written on one side is
  visible on the other.
- **Revision and events do not change.** `set-metadata` does not change the node's `revision` and
  emits no `tree-changed` event. A plugin that caches metadata must update its cache from its own
  writes, or re-read the value when it needs it.
- **Restore at boot.** Metadata is part of the snapshot. After a server restart, `metadata` returns
  the saved bytes before the plugin writes anything new.
- **No cross-plugin access.** Another plugin's entry is invisible. The grant gives no way to list
  the keys of other plugins.

## Worked example, Rust (server side)

The manifest requests the grant on the server side and caps the size at 16 KiB, which is well
under the T2 ceiling. The module stores a bookmark flag on a node.

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "server": ["tree.metadata", "tree.read"]
  },
  "limits": {
    "node_metadata_kib": 16
  }
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::tree;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

/// Version byte written first, so a later format can be told apart from this one.
const BOOKMARK_FORMAT_VERSION: u8 = 1;
const BOOKMARKED_FLAG: u8 = 1;

/// True when the node carries the bookmark. Absent metadata, a cleared flag and a declined
/// grant (which returns `None`) all read as "not bookmarked".
pub fn is_bookmarked(node: NodeId) -> bool {
    tree::metadata(node).is_some_and(|bytes| bytes == [BOOKMARK_FORMAT_VERSION, BOOKMARKED_FLAG])
}

/// Sets or clears the bookmark. Clearing writes an empty list, which leaves an empty entry.
pub fn set_bookmark(node: NodeId, bookmarked: bool) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
    let bytes = if bookmarked {
        vec![BOOKMARK_FORMAT_VERSION, BOOKMARKED_FLAG]
    } else {
        Vec::new()
    };
    tree::set_metadata(node, bytes)
}

/// Flips the bookmark and returns the new state. Errors come back to the caller with `?`.
pub fn toggle_bookmark(node: NodeId) -> Result<bool, PluginError> {
    let now_bookmarked = !is_bookmarked(node);
    set_bookmark(node, now_bookmarked)?;
    Ok(now_bookmarked)
}
```

Call `toggle_bookmark` from the handler that reacts to the user's bookmark command. The module
needs no export of its own. It is ordinary code called from the `Handler` implementation.

## Worked example, TypeScript (client side)

The manifest requests the grant on the client side. The helpers use the same byte format as the
Rust example, so a server and a client can read each other's flag.

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "client": ["tree.metadata", "tree.read"]
  }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { metadata, setMetadata } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/tree';

/** Version byte written first, matching the Rust example so both sides read one format. */
const BOOKMARK_FORMAT_VERSION = 1;
const BOOKMARKED_FLAG = 1;

export function isBookmarked(node: bigint): boolean {
  const bytes = metadata(node);
  return bytes !== undefined
    && bytes.length === 2
    && bytes[0] === BOOKMARK_FORMAT_VERSION
    && bytes[1] === BOOKMARKED_FLAG;
}

/** Sets or clears the flag. Throws `PluginError` when the host refuses the write. */
export function setBookmark(node: bigint, bookmarked: boolean): void {
  const bytes = bookmarked
    ? new Uint8Array([BOOKMARK_FORMAT_VERSION, BOOKMARKED_FLAG])
    : new Uint8Array();
  setMetadata(node, bytes);
}
```

Node ids arrive as `bigint` values in the event payloads, so pass them through unchanged.

## Edge cases and errors

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| `set-metadata` with more bytes than the per-node limit | `quota-exceeded`. Nothing is written. The old value stays. |
| Node id not in the tree | `metadata` returns `none`. `set-metadata` returns `not-found`. |
| Node removed during the `set-metadata` call | `not-found`. |
| Node moved or renamed | Metadata moves with the node, and the node keeps its id. |
| Node closed | The host removes its metadata with it. There is no delete call. |
| Grant declined at install | `set-metadata` returns `not-permitted`. `metadata` returns `none`. |
| Grant revoked while running | Calls in flight return `revoked`. The plugin is re-activated without the grant and then behaves as declined. |
| Host bug or trap inside the call | `internal`. |

The `not-permitted` rule follows the rule for `api-location`. The `metadata` function returns an
option, so it has no error code, and a declined grant makes it return `none`.

A plugin that stores per-node state without the grant must keep it in its own storage bucket,
keyed by node id. It must also remove those keys when it receives `node-removed` for that node.

<div class="note">
<p>Metadata is saved with the session snapshot, which lives in the project's `.ilium/sessions/`
folder. Anyone who can read that folder can read the bytes, so do not store secrets there.</p>
</div>

<div class="warn">
<p>Do not treat a missing entry as an error. A new node, a cleared flag and a declined grant all
read as "no value". Code that throws on `none` breaks as soon as the user declines the grant.</p>
</div>

The install review dialog lists the grant for the side that requests it. Settings > Plugins >
[plugin] > Capabilities shows the same grant later, and `ilium plugin grants <id> --revoke
tree.metadata` removes it.

## First-party features that use it

- Feature 6, bookmarks and locks, stores the bookmark flag in metadata.
- Feature 55, scheduled input, keeps the schedule in node metadata.
- Feature 57, prompt queue, keeps the queue in node metadata.
- Pane kinds with `persist: "metadata"` keep their state in node metadata. See
  [panes.provide-kind](/pages/capability-panes-provide-kind/).

- [tree.read](/pages/capability-tree-read/) to find the nodes that carry metadata.
- [tree.write](/pages/capability-tree-write/) to move, rename or close the nodes.
- [tree.decorate](/pages/capability-tree-decorate/) to show a flag next to the node.
- [api-tree](/pages/api-tree/) for the full `tree` interface.
- [api-storage](/pages/api-storage/) for data that is not tied to a node.
- [terminal.write](/pages/capability-terminal-write/) for the input that scheduled and queued work
  sends.

Checked against the API version `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# tree.read

The `tree.read` grant lets a plugin read the project tree. With it, a plugin can list the nodes, learn the kind of each node, see how the nodes are nested, and see which agent runs in a pane. It is the base grant for most tree features. Without it the plugin cannot look up any node, and it receives no tree events.

The grant allows reads only. Changing the tree needs [tree.write](/pages/capability-tree-write/). Storing the plugin's own bytes on a node needs [tree.metadata](/pages/capability-tree-metadata/). Badges and rows need [tree.decorate](/pages/capability-tree-decorate/).

## What you need

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Grant | `tree.read`, on the `server` side, the `client` side, or both |
| Always-granted set | [Always granted](/pages/capability-always-granted/): log, clock, timers, storage and codec |
| `agent.read` | Only if the plugin reads `node-view.agent` or filters with `signature` |
| Language | Rust with `ilium-plugin-sdk`, or TypeScript with `@ilium/plugin-sdk` |

Grant strings take no argument. `tree.read` is valid. `tree.read:*` and `tree.read:project` are not. An install with such a string fails with the error `manifest.grant-argument` and the text `capability "tree.read" takes no argument (got "tree.read:x")`.

## Full surface

All four functions are synchronous. They return at once and never return a request id. None of them returns a `plugin-error`, so a read has no error code to handle.

| Function (WIT, `ilium:host/tree`) | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `get: func(node: node-id) -> option<node-view>` | `none` for a missing node | The view of one node |
| `children: func(node: node-id) -> list<node-id>` | empty list | Direct children, in tree order |
| `roots: func() -> list<node-id>` | empty list | Top-level nodes, in tree order |
| `find: func(query: node-query) -> list<node-id>` | empty list | Nodes that match the query |

The types are declared in `ilium:types/tree` (`node-view`, `node-class`, `agent-view`,
`agent-activity`) and in the host interface (`node-query`).

| Type | Fields or cases | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `node-id` | `u64` | Stable id. It stays the same when the node moves or is renamed |
| `node-query` | `content-kind`, `signature`, `under`, all `option` | Filter for `find` |
| `node-view` | `id`, `parent`, `class`, `content-kind`, `title`, `cwd`, `agent`, `locked`, `revision` | Snapshot of one node |
| `node-class` | `container`, `pane`, `folder` | Kind of node |
| `agent-view` | `signature`, `activity`, `objective`, `goal` | The agent in a pane |
| `agent-activity` | `none`, `working`, `idle`, `awaiting-approval`, `done`, `menu` | Agent state |

Two events come from this grant. The host delivers them in batches to `on-events`.

| Event | Payload | Delivery |
|---|---|---|
| `tree-changed` | `list<node-id>` | Coalesced: pending lists merge into one event whose list holds each node once, in first-seen order, at the position of the newest change |
| `node-removed` | `node-id` | Never dropped |

Rules that the reads follow:

- `children`, `roots` and `find` return ids in tree order. A parent comes before its children,
  and siblings keep their order.
- `under` matches every strict descendant of a node, at any depth. The node itself is not in the
  result. A query with every field unset returns every node.
- `content-kind` and `signature` match by exact string. A query combines its fields with AND.
- `node-view.agent` is `none` unless the plugin holds `agent.read`. A `signature` filter matches
  no pane without that grant. The grant is checked on every call, so a revoked grant takes effect
  on the next call.
- `tree-changed` names each node whose `node-view` fields changed, including nodes that were just
  created. `revision` moves with the same changes. Writing the node's metadata changes neither the
  revision nor the events.

### SDK names

| Item | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|
| Functions | `ilium_plugin_sdk::host::tree::{get, children, roots, find}` | `@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/tree` |
| Query type | `host::tree::NodeQuery { content_kind, signature, under }` | `{ contentKind, signature, under }` |
| View types | `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::{NodeView, NodeClass, AgentView, AgentActivity}` | `NodeView` and the others from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/types` |
| `tree-changed` | `Event::TreeChanged(Vec<NodeId>)` | `{ tag: 'tree-changed', val: bigint[] }` |
| `node-removed` | `Event::NodeRemoved(NodeId)` | `{ tag: 'node-removed', val: bigint }` |

Node ids are `u64` in Rust and `bigint` in TypeScript. Field names change case as the SDK rules
require: `content_kind` in Rust and `contentKind` in TypeScript.

## Risk and tiers

- The grant is not marked high risk. It appears in the review dialog and is checked by default.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives it automatically, up to the ceiling in its manifest.
- A T2 or T3 plugin gets it when the user leaves the row checked in the review dialog. A user
  can also remove it later in Settings > Plugins.
- Grants are per side and per plugin. A plugin that reads the tree only on the server should
  request `tree.read` under `server` and nothing under `client`.
- Revoking the grant: Settings > Plugins > the plugin > Capabilities, or
  `ilium plugin grants <id> --revoke tree.read`.

## What the user sees

Before a T2 or T3 plugin is installed, the review dialog shows one row for the grant. The row text
is fixed: "Read the workspace tree".

╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

</figure>

If the grant is declined, the plugin keeps running. Its log shows one warning, and the plugin
continues with empty answers:

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs com.example.agent-index
2026-10-11 12:04:11 <span class="t-warn">warn</span>  refused tree.read in find (declined)
2026-10-11 12:04:11 <span class="t-ok">info</span>  0 codex panes at activation
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. The plugin log after the user declined tree.read.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Declined, revoked and missing grants

Because the reads have no error channel, a missing grant gives an empty answer, not an error code.

- **Declined at install or on the prompt.** `get` returns `none`. `children`, `roots` and `find`
  return empty lists. The first refused call of each plugin instance writes one warn line that
  names `tree.read` and the reason (`declined`). No tree events are delivered.
- **Revoked while running.** The next read returns `none` or an empty list. The plugin receives
  `deactivate(revoked)`, and it is activated again with the reduced grant set. The restart does not
  count as a failure.
- **Granted later.** The plugin receives `deactivate(granted)` and is activated again with the new
  grant set. Events start arriving after that.
- **Requested but not in the manifest.** A call to an import the manifest never requested is a
  trap, not a refusal. The plugin instance is restarted. Always list `tree.read` in the manifest.

A plugin should treat an empty answer as a normal result. It should turn off the feature that needs
the tree. It should not retry in a loop.

## Worked example 1: Rust, server side

This plugin counts the Codex panes at activation and logs every node change. The manifest excerpt
asks for both grants on the server side.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.agent-index",
  "server": { "entry": "server.wasm", "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "server": ["tree.read", "agent.read"] }
}
```

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::tree::{self, NodeQuery};

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct AgentIndex;

impl Lifecycle for AgentIndex {
    fn activate(&mut self, context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        let codex_panes = tree::find(NodeQuery {
            content_kind: Some("ilium.terminal".into()),
            signature: Some("codex".into()),
            under: None,
        });
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("{} codex panes at activation", codex_panes.len()));
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("plugin {} active", context.plugin));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for AgentIndex {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::TreeChanged(nodes) => {
                    for node in nodes {
                        if let Some(view) = tree::get(node) {
                            let line = format!("node {} is now {}", view.id, view.title);
                            log::log(Level::Info, &line);
                        }
                    }
                }
                Event::NodeRemoved(node) => {
                    log::log(Level::Info, &format!("node {node} removed"));
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

## Worked example 2: TypeScript, client side

The same query on the client. The `signature` filter needs `agent.read` on the client side as well,
so the manifest asks for both grants under `client`.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "com.example.agent-index-ui",
  "client": { "entry": "client.wasm", "world": "ilium:client/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] },
  "capabilities": { "client": ["tree.read", "agent.read"] }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { find, get } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/tree';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    const codexPanes = find({
      contentKind: 'ilium.terminal',
      signature: 'codex',
      under: undefined,
    });
    log('info', `${codexPanes.length} codex panes at activation of ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'tree-changed') {
        for (const node of event.val) {
          const view = get(node);
          if (view) log('info', `node ${view.id} is now "${view.title}"`);
        }
      }
      if (event.tag === 'node-removed') log('info', `node ${event.val} removed`);
    }
    return [];
  },
});
```

## Edge cases

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Node id that does not exist | `get` returns `none`. `children` returns an empty list. Not an error |
| Node removed after an event was queued | `get` returns `none`. Act on the `node-removed` event |
| `find` with `signature` and no `agent.read` | Empty list. Panes without an agent are not matched |
| `under` naming a node that has no children | Empty list |
| Query with every field unset | Every node in tree order |
| Many changes to one node in one batch | One `tree-changed` entry for that node |
| Restored project after a restart | One `tree-changed` batch covers all restored nodes, once |

## Limits

- Event batches hold at most 256 events. The event queue per plugin holds 1,024 events by default for every tier; a T1
  plugin may request up to 4,096 in `limits`. A full queue on a never-dropped event such as `node-removed` restarts the plugin.
- Each `on-events` call has a default deadline of 20 ms for every tier; a T1 plugin may request up to 50 ms in `limits`. Keep the handler
  short, and do the slow work in a job.

## First-party features that request it

These rows of `feature-mapping.md` list `tree.read`: feature 5 (tree ordering), feature 6 (bookmarks,
locks and removal of empty groups), feature 9 (workspace search), feature 42 (session naming),
feature 43 (tree organisation) and feature 109 (the `ilium panes` command).

## See also

- [tree.write](/pages/capability-tree-write/) for the intents that change the tree.
- [tree.metadata](/pages/capability-tree-metadata/) for the plugin's own bytes on a node.
- [tree.decorate](/pages/capability-tree-decorate/) for badges and rows.
- [agent.read](/pages/capability-agent-read/) for the agent data in `node-view.agent`.
- [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/) for the error codes and the trap rules.
- [Events and intents](/pages/events-and-intents/) for batching and delivery order.

Checked against the API version `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# tree.write

## Overview

The `tree.write` grant lets a plugin change the project tree. It can rename a node, move it, close it, or set its lock flag. The plugin never edits the tree itself. It returns submissions from `on-events`, or calls `intents.submit` from a timer or request callback. The kernel checks each batch against the grants, applies the accepted submissions in order, and gives every submission exactly one outcome. That outcome arrives as a `request-completed` event.

The grant keeps two user decisions intact. A title the user typed is never overwritten by a plugin, and a locked node cannot be closed by a plugin.

## You need

- The grant `tree.write` in the manifest, on each side that submits the intents (`server`, `client`, or both). See [capabilities](/pages/capabilities/).
- The grant [tree.read](/pages/capability-tree-read/) when the plugin must find nodes or receive `tree-changed`.
- The grant [panes.read](/pages/capability-panes-read/) when the plugin reacts to `pane-created`, as the examples below do.
- Rust: `use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;` with the `ilium_plugin` attribute and `Handler`. TypeScript: `definePlugin` from `@ilium/plugin-sdk`.

### Grant syntax

- Valid: `tree.write`
- Invalid: `tree.write:tree`. The grant takes no argument. The manifest is refused at install with `manifest.grant-argument`, and the text is `capability "tree.write" takes no argument (got "tree.write:tree")`.

### Risk and tier

- The grant is not marked high risk.
- A T1 bundled plugin receives it automatically, up to its manifest ceiling.
- A T2 or T3 plugin needs an explicit grant in the review dialog. The grant is remembered.
- Grants are per side (`server` and `client`).

## Surface

The grant has no functions. It opens four intents, each returned as a submission. The WIT records below are the payloads.

```wit
record submission { intent: intent, correlation: u64, dedup-key: option<string> }
enum placement { before, after, inside-first, inside-last }
record rename-node-spec { node: node-id, title: string }
record move-node-spec { node: node-id, target: node-id, placement: placement }
record set-node-locked-spec { node: node-id, locked: bool }
```

| Intent | Payload | Meaning | Outcomes beyond `ok` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rename-node` | `rename-node-spec`: `node`, `title` (string) | Sets the title of a node. The title is 1 to 256 characters. | `refused(not-found)`; `refused(conflict)` when the user named the node by hand; `refused(invalid-argument)` for a title of the wrong length |
| `move-node` | `move-node-spec`: `node`, `target` (node-id), `placement` | Moves a node before or after `target`, or into `target` as first or last child. | `refused(not-found)`; `refused(invalid-argument)` when `target` is the node itself or lies inside it |
| `close-node` | `node` (node-id) | Closes the node, as the user does in the tree. | `refused(not-found)`; `refused(conflict)` when the node is locked |
| `set-node-locked` | `set-node-locked-spec`: `node`, `locked` (bool) | Sets or clears the lock flag. | `refused(not-found)` |

Every intent can also return `refused(not-permitted)` when the grant is missing or declined.

The `placement` values, in Rust and TypeScript:

| Value | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|
| Before `target` | `Placement::Before` | `'before'` |
| After `target` | `Placement::After` | `'after'` |
| First child of `target` | `Placement::InsideFirst` | `'inside-first'` |
| Last child of `target` | `Placement::InsideLast` | `'inside-last'` |

Import paths:

- Rust: `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::{Intent, Submission, RenameNodeSpec, MoveNodeSpec, SetNodeLockedSpec}` and `ilium_plugin_sdk::types::tree::Placement`. `Submission::new(intent)` takes the next SDK correlation number. `Submission::keyed(intent, key)` sets a dedup key.
- TypeScript: `Intent` and `Submission` from `@ilium/plugin-sdk/types`. Write the correlation as a `bigint`, for example `1n`.

### Batch and key rules

- A batch holds at most 256 submissions. A return of more than 256 traps the plugin, and none of the batch is applied.
- A batch is refused as a whole for one of two reasons: a malformed submission, or a missing grant. The offending submission gets `refused(invalid-argument)` or `refused(not-permitted)`. Every other submission gets `refused(cancelled)` with the message `batch refused: submission <index>`.
- Submissions apply in order. A node closed by an earlier submission in the batch makes a later submission on it fail with `failed(not-found)`.
- `dedup-key` is optional for these intents. A key of 1 to 128 characters from `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `.`, `_`, `:`, `/` and `-` is reserved for 10 minutes once the submission is accepted. A repeat completes as `duplicate(<original>)`. A refused submission does not reserve its key, so a retry with the same key is valid.

## Manual titles stay with the user

When the user types a title for a node, the kernel marks the node as named by hand. From then on, a `rename-node` on that node returns `refused(conflict)`, whatever plugin sends it. The mark is removed when the user clears the title, which returns the node to automatic naming.

The plugin cannot read the mark, because `node-view` has no field for it. It learns of the mark only from the outcome:

```text
rename-node { node: 42, title: "Build server" }
-> refused(plugin-error { code: conflict,
                          message: "node 42 was named manually",
                          retry-after-ms: none })
```

Treat this outcome as final for that node until the user clears the title. Do not retry in a loop.

## Lock flag

The lock flag has one effect on `tree.write`: a locked node cannot be closed. `close-node` on it returns `refused(conflict)`. A rename or a move of a locked node is applied. A plugin can also clear the flag, so set it only on nodes the plugin owns.

## Examples

### Lock new terminal panes (Rust)

This server-side plugin locks every new terminal pane, so a stray close cannot remove it. It logs any refused lock. The manifest requests `"capabilities": { "server": ["panes.read", "tree.write"] }`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SetNodeLockedSpec;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct LockNewTerminals;

impl Handler for LockNewTerminals {
    fn on_events(&mut self, batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        let mut submissions = Vec::new();
        for event in batch {
            match event {
                Event::PaneCreated(pane) if pane.content_kind == "ilium.terminal" => {
                    let spec = SetNodeLockedSpec { node: pane.node, locked: true };
                    submissions.push(Submission::new(Intent::SetNodeLocked(spec)));
                }
                Event::RequestCompleted(result) => {
                    if let Outcome::Refused(error) = result.outcome {
                        log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("lock refused: {}", error.message));
                    }
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
        submissions
    }
}
```

### Name new terminal panes (TypeScript)

This server-side plugin names each new terminal pane `Shell`. The dedup key stops a repeated event for the same pane from renaming it again within 10 minutes. When the user has already named the pane, the outcome is `conflict`, and the plugin keeps the user's title. The manifest requests the same grants as the Rust example.

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import type { Event, Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/types';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag === 'pane-created' && event.val.contentKind === 'ilium.terminal') {
        submissions.push({
          intent: { tag: 'rename-node', val: { node: event.val.node, title: 'Shell' } },
          correlation: event.val.node,
          dedupKey: `shell-title:${event.val.node}`,
        });
      }
      if (event.tag === 'request-completed') {
        const outcome = event.val.outcome;
        if (outcome.tag === 'refused' && outcome.val.code === 'conflict') {
          log('info', 'the user named this pane, so the title stays');
        }
      }
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

## Edge cases and errors

| Situation | Outcome |
|---|---|
| The node id does not exist, or the node was removed before the batch was accepted | `refused(not-found)` |
| The node was removed by an earlier submission in the same batch | `failed(not-found)` |
| A title is empty or longer than 256 characters | `refused(invalid-argument)` |
| The user named the node by hand | `refused(conflict)` on `rename-node` |
| `close-node` on a locked node | `refused(conflict)` |
| `move-node` with a target inside the moved node | `refused(invalid-argument)` |
| A malformed submission | The whole batch is refused. |
| More than 256 submissions in one return | The plugin traps, and none of the batch is applied. |
| The grant is declined | `refused(not-permitted)` for the first `tree.write` submission in a batch, `refused(cancelled)` for the rest. The plugin's other intents and events are not affected. |
| The grant is revoked | The authorization epoch changes. Calls in flight return `revoked`. The plugin is deactivated with `revoked`, then re-activated with the reduced grant set. |
| A repeat of an accepted `dedup-key` within 10 minutes | `duplicate(<original>)`, with no effect |

Every `not-permitted` refusal is also written to the plugin log, which `ilium plugin logs` shows. Conflicts are not logged by the kernel, so a plugin that needs a record of them writes its own log line, as the examples do.

## What the user sees

The review dialog lists the grant when a T2 or T3 plugin is installed. Each side is shown separately.

<pre class="term">╭─<span class="t-hi"> Review permissions </span>───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ com.example.tree 0.1.0 by Example Ltd                                      │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-hi">Server side</span>                                                                │
│ [x] Renames and moves tree nodes <span class="t-dim">………………………………………………………………………………</span> tree.write │
│                                                                            │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space toggle · Enter allow · Esc decline</span>                                   │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The wording is a placeholder.

A successful rename or lock appears in the tree at once. The user sees the new title, and a lock marker on the node. A conflict or a refusal leaves the tree unchanged, and the user sees no message from the kernel.

<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">project</span>
├─ <span class="t-ok">Build server</span>            <span class="t-dim">pane 42  locked</span>
╰─ Shell                        <span class="t-dim">pane 57</span>
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The node named by hand keeps its title, and the locked node shows its flag.

## Submission flow

# ui.panels

The `ui.panels` grant lets a client-side plugin contribute views to the interface: full-screen or overlay panels, popups, and settings pages. The plugin describes each view as a UI tree. The host lays the tree out, paints it with the theme, keeps the state of each widget and reports the user's actions back to the plugin. The plugin never draws a pixel of its own, except through a `surface` widget that it fills with `ui.write-surface`.

A view is rendered by the `views` export. The host calls `render(view, area)` when the view first opens, after the plugin calls `invalidate`, and when the terminal is resized. The host never calls it per frame.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 140" role="img" aria-label="Host draws the view from the plugin tree and sends actions back">
  <defs><marker id="cap-ui-arrow" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>
  <g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5">
    <rect x="10" y="40" width="110" height="50" rx="4"/>
    <rect x="145" y="40" width="110" height="50" rx="4"/>
    <rect x="280" y="40" width="110" height="50" rx="4"/>
    <line x1="120" y1="65" x2="144" y2="65" marker-end="url(#cap-ui-arrow)"/>
    <line x1="255" y1="65" x2="279" y2="65" marker-end="url(#cap-ui-arrow)"/>
    <path d="M200,90 L200,115 L65,115 L65,92" marker-end="url(#cap-ui-arrow)"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="currentColor" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="65" y="62" font-size="12">views export</text>
    <text x="65" y="78" font-size="11">returns UI tree</text>
    <text x="200" y="62" font-size="12">host layout</text>
    <text x="200" y="78" font-size="11">ratatui solver</text>
    <text x="335" y="62" font-size="12">terminal</text>
    <text x="335" y="78" font-size="11">theme colours</text>
    <text x="132" y="30" font-size="11">tree</text>
    <text x="267" y="30" font-size="11">cells</text>
    <text x="132" y="130" font-size="11">ui-action</text>
  </g>
</svg>
<figcaption>The plugin returns a tree and receives the user's actions. The host lays out and paints the tree.</figcaption>
