# Sandbox reference

## Sandbox reference

This page is the normative definition of the sandbox that confines third-party plugins (tiers T2 and T3). The [Security model](/pages/security/) gives the overview. The [Threat model](/pages/reference-threat-model/) says why. This page says exactly what the host MUST build, so that an implementer can write it and a tester can check it.

Terms. A **helper** is a separate operating-system process that hosts the WebAssembly instance of one plugin side. A **namespace** is a Linux kernel feature that gives a process its own private view of one kind of resource (mounts, process ids, network, and so on). **seccomp** is a Linux filter that lets a process make only listed system calls. A **cgroup** is a Linux group of processes with resource limits. **no_new_privs** is a process flag that stops the process and its children from gaining privileges through set-id programs. **Dispatcher protocol** is the message channel between the Ilium server and a helper.

### You will need

- Linux with user namespaces, cgroup v2 and seccomp. The checks are in the [prerequisite section](#sandbox-unavailable).
- The grant names in the [Capability table](/pages/reference-capabilities/).
- For tests, the hostile fixtures in [Security testing](/pages/reference-security-testing/).

## Topology

**[SEC-020]** The host MUST start one helper process per T2 or T3 plugin and per side. Plugin A and plugin B never share a helper. The server side and the scene side of one plugin run in separate helpers. Client-side T2 plugins run in a helper started by each attached client, with the same confinement. The reason is decision D5: a shared helper would reduce isolation between plugins to Wasmtime alone, and Wasmtime has had sandbox-escape advisories. With one helper per plugin, an escape from Wasmtime reaches only that plugin's own mount namespace.

Consequences accepted by this decision:

- Memory use grows with the number of third-party plugins. Each helper has a fixed memory floor of about 20 MiB plus the plugin's `memory_mib`.
- Start-up takes one process start per plugin side. Lazy activation (D6) keeps this off the start path.
- Plugin to plugin calls (services, peer messages) go through the server, never directly between helpers.

## Process confinement

Every row is a MUST. A helper that cannot be started with all of them is not started ([SEC-055]).

| Id | Requirement | How a tester checks it |
|---|---|---|
| [SEC-021] | The helper runs in new user, mount, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces. Inside the user namespace it has no capabilities outside it. | Hostile fixture reads `/proc/self/ns/*` and compares to the server's. All six differ. |
| [SEC-022] | The network namespace has no interface except a downed loopback. | Fixture calls `socket`+`connect` to loopback and to a public address. Both fail. |
| [SEC-023] | The mount namespace holds only: read-only `/usr`, `/bin`, `/lib`, `/lib64` and `/etc` (a minimal subset, no `/etc/passwd` home lists beyond uid maps); a fresh `/proc` for the PID namespace; a minimal `/dev` with `null`, `zero`, `urandom`, `full`; a tmpfs `/tmp` capped at 64 MiB; and the granted scopes, read-only for read grants. The `data` and `cache` mounts are `noexec,nosuid,nodev`. | Fixture lists `/`; only these paths exist. Executing a binary from `/data` fails with `EACCES`. |
| [SEC-024] | The helper sets `no_new_privs`, installs a seccomp allowlist, and drops every capability before it reads the first plugin byte. | Fixture calls `prctl(PR_GET_NO_NEW_PRIVS)`. Result is 1. |
| [SEC-025] | The sandbox is defence in depth. A bug in Wasmtime that gives native code execution in the helper MUST NOT give access to any asset in the [threat model](/pages/reference-threat-model/) without a second bug in the kernel. | Escape probe suite, see [Security testing](/pages/reference-security-testing/). |
| [SEC-026] | The helper's `/proc` shows only its own PID namespace. It cannot read `/proc/<pid>/environ` of any process outside. `/sys` is not mounted. | Fixture reads `/proc/1/environ` (its own init) and the server's PID path. The second does not exist. |
| [SEC-027] | The helper's environment is rebuilt from an allowlist: `HOME` set to the data mount, `TMPDIR=/tmp`, `LANG=C.UTF-8`, `PATH` set to the fixed value `/usr/bin:/bin`, `ILIUM_PLUGIN_ID`. Nothing else is inherited. In particular `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, `DISPLAY`, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, proxy variables and any `*_TOKEN`, `*_KEY` or `*_SECRET` variable are absent. | Fixture prints `environ`. Only the allowlist appears. |
| [SEC-028] | All file descriptors except the dispatcher channel and stdio on `/dev/null` are closed before the Wasmtime engine starts (close-range with no exceptions). The helper calls `setsid` and has no controlling terminal. Because the helper has no controlling terminal and cannot open the PTY master (it is not inherited), terminal injection through `TIOCSTI` and `TIOCLINUX` is impossible. The seccomp filter also denies those ioctl numbers. | Fixture enumerates `/proc/self/fd`; only fds 0 to 2 and the channel remain. `ioctl(0, TIOCSTI)` fails. |
| [SEC-029] | A cgroup v2 leaf is created per helper with: `memory.max` = plugin `memory_mib` plus 32 MiB overhead; `pids.max` = 64 plus 8 per allowed child; `cpu.weight` = 10 (low priority); `cpu.max` = the manifest `cpu_ms_per_s` quota expressed as a period. A memory kill is reported as a trap `limit-exceeded(memory)` and counts as a failure. | Fixture allocates past the limit; helper is killed; the log has the code. |

### The seccomp allowlist

**[SEC-067]** The filter is an allowlist of the system calls that Wasmtime, the allocator and the dispatcher channel need. Everything else returns `EPERM`, or kills the helper for the entries marked kill. The implementation MUST publish the list as a generated file with the release so tests can compare. These calls are always denied, and the fixture suite calls each of them:

| Group | Calls |
|---|---|
| Debugging and memory of others | `ptrace`, `process_vm_readv`, `process_vm_writev`, `kcmp` |
| Keys and kernel objects | `keyctl`, `add_key`, `request_key`, `bpf`, `perf_event_open`, `userfaultfd`, `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter`, `io_uring_register` |
| Namespaces and mounts | `mount`, `umount2`, `pivot_root`, `chroot`, `unshare`, `setns`, `open_by_handle_at` |
| Kernel modules and boot | `init_module`, `finit_module`, `delete_module`, `kexec_load`, `kexec_file_load`, `reboot` |
| Sockets (all families except the one dispatcher socketpair, which is inherited, not created) | `socket`, `socketpair`, `connect`, `bind`, `listen`, `accept`, `accept4` |
| Terminal injection | `ioctl` with request `TIOCSTI` or `TIOCLINUX` or `TIOCSCTTY` |
| Privilege | `setuid`, `setgid`, `setresuid`, `capset`, `personality` |

### Limits when cgroup delegation is missing

**[SEC-065]** If cgroup v2 is available but the user has no delegated controller (`memory`, `pids`, `cpu`), the host MUST enforce the same limits inside the helper with `setrlimit` (`RLIMIT_AS`, `RLIMIT_NPROC`, `RLIMIT_CPU`) and a watchdog in the server that samples the helper's RSS once a second. The audit log records `sandbox-degraded` with the controller list once per start. If the controllers needed for `memory.max` and `pids.max` are both missing and `setrlimit` cannot bound them, the helper is not started ([SEC-055]).

## Dispatcher protocol trust

**[SEC-050]** The server MUST treat every message from a helper as hostile. The identity of the plugin comes from the channel the message arrived on, never from a field in the message. A message that names another plugin id is dropped and counts as a failure.

**[SEC-051]** The server MUST enforce a maximum message size of 4 MiB (8 MiB for `terminal-view` frames) and a rate of 5,000 messages per second per helper. A larger or faster message ends the helper.

**[SEC-052]** A malformed message (bad framing, bad UTF-8, a schema violation, an unknown message kind, an out-of-range resource handle) kills the helper and counts as a failure toward the restart-and-disable rule. The server never tries to repair the message.

**[SEC-053]** Wasmtime configuration, for T1 and for the helper:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Linear-memory guard pages | On, 2 GiB guard region on 64-bit |
| Spectre mitigations | On (bounds-check hardening for table and memory access) |
| Epoch interruption | On, deadlines set per call; a missed deadline traps |
| `wasi:sockets`, `wasi:http` imports | Refused at load. A component that imports them is not instantiated |
| `wasi:clocks`, `wasi:random` | Virtualised: clocks coarsened ([SEC-370]), random from the host CSPRNG |
| Wasmtime version | Pinned exactly in the release, recorded in the build metadata, see [Trust and supply chain](/pages/reference-trust-and-supply-chain/) |
| Memory and table maximums | From the manifest `limits`, clamped to the tier ceiling |

**[SEC-054]** Compiled module cache. For T2 and T3 the host MUST NOT load a precompiled artefact that was written by a process it cannot verify. If a cache exists it lives in the host's cache directory, owner-only, keyed by the SHA-256 of the component and the Wasmtime version, and its integrity (an HMAC under a per-install key held by the server) is checked before deserialisation. No plugin scope can reach it. When the check fails the module is recompiled. A deployment MAY disable the cache for T2 and T3 with the policy key `[packages] precompiled_cache = false`.

## Sandbox unavailable

**[SEC-055]** If the host cannot create the sandbox exactly as specified, T2 and T3 plugins MUST refuse to load with error code `sandbox.unavailable`. The message names the missing prerequisite (for example `unprivileged user namespaces are disabled: sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone`). There is no silent fallback to in-process or unconfined execution, on any platform and for any reason.

Typical prerequisites and the message the host prints:

| Prerequisite | Typical failure | Message names |
|---|---|---|
| Unprivileged user namespaces | Ubuntu 24.04 AppArmor restriction, container without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, hardened kernels | `user namespaces` and the sysctl or AppArmor profile |
| cgroup v2 | cgroup v1 only | `cgroup v2` |
| seccomp | Kernel built without it | `seccomp` |
| Mount of `/proc` in a PID namespace | Locked-down container | `procfs mount` |

T1 plugins and the kernel are unaffected. The Plugins screen shows an installed T2 or T3 plugin as `Cannot start: sandbox unavailable` with the message. The audit log records `sandbox-unavailable` once per start and prerequisite.

**[SEC-056]** Running as root. If the server's effective uid is 0, the host MUST refuse T2 and T3 plugins with `sandbox.unavailable` and the message `running as root is not supported for third-party plugins`. Root has capabilities that user-namespace rules do not remove for the server itself. A deployment that needs root MAY run Ilium as an unprivileged user instead.

**[SEC-057]** Platform matrix.

| Platform | T1 | T2/T3 | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux, native | Yes | Yes, with the prerequisites above | Full sandbox |
| Linux, container | Yes | Only if the container grants user namespaces and cgroup delegation | Many container defaults refuse |
| WSL 2 | Yes | Yes if the kernel prerequisites hold, otherwise `sandbox.unavailable` | A real Linux kernel |
| WSL 1 | Yes | No | No namespaces |
| macOS | Yes | No (decision D5) | No equivalent sandbox |
| Windows | Yes | No (decision D5) | No equivalent sandbox |

## File scopes

File access is the most common route to harm, so its rules are normative here. The rules apply inside the helper and to the kernel's own file functions for T1.

The authoritative scope table. Other pages link here.

| Scope | Read | Write | Watch | Tiers | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `package` | always | never | always | all | Unpacked `assets/`, read only |
| `data` | always | always | always | all | Plugin's private folder, mounted `noexec,nosuid,nodev` |
| `cache` | always | always | always | all | May be evicted |
| `project` | normal | H | normal | all | The session's project folder; `.ilium/` stays visible but the stores of the deny set do not live there |
| `picked` | per pick | per pick | per pick | all | A path the user chose |
| `worktrees` | normal | H | normal | all | Setting `workspace.worktree_root` |
| `agent-sessions:<agent>` | H | refused | H | all | Transcript folders, read only |
| `agent-config:<agent>` | H | refused | H | all | Configuration folders, credential files excluded ([SEC-063]) |
| `minecraft-saves` | normal | H | normal | all | The game's saves folder, for the Minecraft scenes |
| `path:{project}` / `{data}` / `{cache}` | normal | H | normal | all | Same as the named scope |
| `path:{config}` | H | H | H | all | The Ilium configuration folder; the deny set still applies |
| `path:{home}/...` | normal below a sensitive path-free subtree, H otherwise ([SEC-061], [SEC-062]) | H | same as read | all | Template with `{home}` |
| literal absolute path | H | H | H | all | Review dialog shows the path |

Writes to `agent-sessions` fail at install with `manifest.grant-scope`. Writes to `agent-config:<agent>` are also refused at install with `manifest.grant-scope`. This resolves the earlier disagreement between pages: agent scopes are read-only and `H` for read.

**[SEC-058]** Path resolution uses `openat2` with `RESOLVE_BENEATH | RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS | RESOLVE_NO_XDEV` relative to a file descriptor opened on the scope root (or the closest equivalent where `openat2` is missing, which is an `openat` walk that checks every component with `O_NOFOLLOW`). The kernel never checks a path string and then opens it later. A symlink swap between check and open therefore cannot leave the scope.

**[SEC-059]** Hard links. When a file in a scope has a link count above 1, a write or a read-for-write open is refused when the device and inode differ from the scope's recorded inventory for writable scopes, and always refused when the other link is outside every writable mount (the host reads `st_nlink` and compares `st_dev` with the scope root). The error is `not-permitted`.

**[SEC-060]** The deny set. No scope, for any plugin including T1 plugins other than the owning core plugin, reaches: the Ilium configuration (`config.toml`), the grant store, the trust store, the consent store, the project trust store, the secrets file, the admin policy file, the audit log, the plugin install directory, every other plugin's `data` and `cache`, the runtime directory and the Ilium socket, and the HTTP API token file. A template that resolves into the deny set is refused at install with `manifest.grant-scope`. A path that passes the check at install but resolves into the set at run time (a symlink created later) is refused with `not-permitted`.

**[SEC-061]** The sensitive path set. A grant whose resolved root is, contains or lies below one of the following is high risk, and the review dialog shows the resolved path: `~/.ssh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.aws`, `~/.config/gcloud`, `~/.kube`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.docker/config.json`, OS keyrings (`~/.local/share/keyrings`), browser profiles (`~/.mozilla`, `~/.config/google-chrome`, `~/.config/chromium`), password-manager stores, and agent credential files.

**[SEC-062]** A template whose resolved root is `$HOME`, `/`, or an ancestor of `$HOME` is high risk, because it reaches the sensitive set. `fs.read:path:{home}` is therefore H. `fs.read:path:{home}/Pictures/**` is normal.

**[SEC-063]** Agent credential files are excluded from `agent-config` scopes even with the grant. The named lists, relative to each agent's configuration folder:

| Agent | Excluded files |
|---|---|
| `claude` | `.credentials.json`, `credentials.json`, `.claude.json` keys block (the file is served with `oauthAccount` and key fields removed) |
| `codex` | `auth.json` |
| `gemini` | `oauth_creds.json`, `google_accounts.json` |
| `antigravity` | `auth.json`, `oauth_creds.json` |
| every agent | any file whose name matches `*credentials*`, `*token*`, `*secret*`, `*.pem`, `*.key` |

**[SEC-064]** Errors never include the resolved absolute path. A failing call returns the scope and the path relative to the scope root only.

Case-folding filesystems: the scope check compares resolved file identities (device and inode), not names, so `Data` and `data` cannot cross a boundary. Bind mounts: an `openat2` with `RESOLVE_NO_XDEV` stops at a mount point inside a scope root.

## Escape-hatch review

An escape hatch is a feature whose effect leaves the sandbox by design. Each one has a classification and a required mitigation.

| Feature | Class | Required mitigation | Id |
|---|---|---|---|
| `panes.create` with a `command` | Code execution | Needs the H grant `panes.create-command:<program>`; kernel confirmation on first use; see below | [SEC-040] |
| `panes.lifecycle` restart with a new command | Code execution | Same program grant; the confirmation names the program | [SEC-041] |
| `agent.signatures` resume argv | Code execution | Program must match `process_names` or a `panes.create-command` grant; one argv element for `{session}` | [SEC-042] |
| `terminal.write`, `terminal.raw-input` | Code execution (types into a shell) | H grants; `send-input` dedup and journal; lock rules | existing |
| `agent.control` | Code execution (drives an agent) | H grant | existing |
| `process.run:<program>` | Code execution | H grant per program; env denylist; fixed PATH; noexec data | [SEC-031] to [SEC-035] |
| `process.run:sh` | Code execution | T1 only | existing |
| `fs.write` to dotfiles or agent config | Code execution at next shell start | Write outside `data` and `cache` is H; `agent-config` writes refused; dotfile paths in `{home}` are in the sensitive set | [SEC-061] |
| `clipboard.write` | UI integrity (paste hijack) | Size and control character rules | [SEC-044] |
| `open-external` file targets | Code execution through the desktop handler | Scope, mode bit and extension rules | [SEC-043] |
| `notify.desktop` | UI integrity (spoofing) | Title prefix by the host | [SEC-045] |
| `keys.intercept` | UI integrity (captures keystrokes) | Review wording names it; only active while the plugin's pane or mode has focus; audit | existing, [SEC-102] |
| `editor.provide` | UI integrity and data (sees file text) | H, review wording | [SEC-102] |
| `sessions.cross` | Acts in other sessions | T1 and T2 only; same-plugin commands only | existing |
| `workspace.manage` | Moves or deletes folders | H, review wording | existing |
| `cli.contribute` output read by agents | Prompt injection into agents | Output is plain text with a header `from plugin <id>`; agents are told by `ilium.core.agent-setup` instruction blocks | existing |
| http-api routes | Data egress to local clients | Routes need the token; see [Network egress](/pages/reference-network-egress/) | [SEC-097] |
| `collect` entries driving a T1 owner's action | Code execution via the owner | Owner validates with an allowlist; dialog shows what the entry can do | [SEC-283] |
| Replacement of a core plugin | Everything the core plugin could do | T3 cannot replace; no grant inheritance | [SEC-300] |

**[SEC-030]** Every row in this table MUST have the mitigation implemented. A feature added to the contract later MUST add a row before release.

### Process execution rules

**[SEC-031]** `process.run` and `process.spawn` need a grant for the exact program. A bare name such as `git` is resolved against a fixed system `PATH` that the server captured at start and filtered to system directories (`/usr/bin`, `/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`). It is never resolved against the plugin's own environment or against any writable scope.

**[SEC-032]** Children of T2 and T3 plugins run in the same confinement as the helper and have no network. A program that needs the network, such as `git fetch`, therefore fails by design. A plugin that needs a remote operation uses `http`.

**[SEC-033]** Environment keys are validated. These are refused with `invalid-argument`: `LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `PATH`, `IFS`, `BASH_ENV`, `ENV`, `PYTHON*`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `PERL5*`, `RUBY*`, `GIT_CONFIG*`, `GIT_SSH*`, `GIT_EXEC_PATH`, `GIT_ASKPASS`, plus any key that the admin policy adds under `[processes] deny_env`.

**[SEC-034]** A program may not resolve into `package`, `data`, `cache`, `picked` or any writable scope. Writable mounts of T2 and T3 are `noexec`, so a plugin cannot write a binary and run it. Absolute-path grants (`process.run:/usr/bin/git`) are compared to the resolved real path.

**[SEC-035]** Argument hazards. The review dialog shows for every `process.run:<program>` the line `This program can run other programs.` when the program is on the host's list of known launchers (`git`, `sh`, `bash`, `python*`, `node`, `rg` with `--pre`, `find`, `xargs`, `env`, `make`, `ssh`, `sudo`). The documentation of `process.run` warns of `git -c core.sshCommand=...`, `git` hooks in the repository, and `rg --pre`. The host does not filter arguments, because that cannot be done in general.

**[SEC-066]** A spawn that leaves the confinement (`panes.create` command, `panes.lifecycle` restart) is written to the audit log with the full argv, with secret values replaced by `<redacted>`.

### Pane commands

**[SEC-040]** `create-pane` with a `command` from a T2 or T3 plugin needs the H grant `panes.create-command:<program>`. `panes.create` itself stays normal risk and allows only a shell pane in a cwd below a scope the plugin may read. The pane process starts unconfined, with the user's privileges, so the kernel draws a confirmation the first time each program is started: `Notes Panel wants to run git in a new pane.` and the full argv. The answer is remembered per plugin and program as a consent. A command whose program matches no `panes.create-command` grant completes `refused(not-permitted)` with reason `not-granted` (`declined` when the grant was requested but unchecked). A command-less `create-pane` needs only `panes.create`. The install fails with `manifest.grant-dependency` when the manifest lists `panes.create-command:<program>` without `panes.create` in the same side. PATH is resolved as in [SEC-031]. T1 plugins follow the same rule: the grant is H and is asked at first activation.

**[SEC-041]** `panes.lifecycle` restart with a new command uses the same grant and the same confirmation.

**[SEC-042]** `agent.signatures` rules: the `resume` argv program must equal one of the signature's `process_names` or match a `panes.create-command:<program>` grant of the same plugin, otherwise the resume is not offered. `{session}` is substituted as exactly one argv element, never through a shell, and it is validated against `[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,128}`; a session id outside it makes the resume unavailable. The resume runs only on an explicit user action, and the confirmation shows the full command the first time. `actions.keys` are delivered only when the user or a plugin that holds `agent.control` triggers them. A plugin cannot mark a pane as an agent when the pane's process name does not match the signature's `process_names`. With these constraints `agent.signatures` stays normal risk.

### Other hatches

**[SEC-043]** `open-external` file targets: only paths in scopes the plugin can read; refused when the file has any executable mode bit; refused for the extensions `.desktop`, `.exe`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, `.com`, `.sh`, `.jar`, `.app`, `.appimage`, `.scr`, `.lnk`, `.command`, `.html`, `.htm`, `.svg`, `.js`, `.py`, `.pl`, `.rb`; and refused for MIME types the host treats as active content. Outcome code `refused(not-permitted)` with reason `file-type`. The origin prompt shows the punycode form for hosts that contain non-ASCII characters and highlights the registrable domain. A plugin may have at most one pending consent prompt and 6 per hour ([SEC-105]).

**[SEC-044]** `clipboard.write`: text larger than 64 KiB, or containing any control character other than tab, newline and carriage return, is refused with `invalid-argument`. Text with a newline is allowed. A write is accepted only from a user-initiated command or a keybinding while the user has focus in a terminal pane; a write caused by a timer or an event while the terminal has focus is refused with `not-permitted` reason `not-user-initiated`.

**[SEC-045]** `notify.desktop`: the host prefixes the title with the plugin display name and a colon. The plugin cannot supply the prefix.

**[SEC-046]** Regular expressions supplied by plugins (output filters, settings `pattern`, schema `pattern`, `when` expressions) MUST be compiled with a linear-time engine that has Rust `regex` semantics: no backreferences and no lookaround. A pattern is at most 1,024 bytes, and its compiled automaton is at most 256 KiB. A pattern that fails any limit is refused with `invalid-argument` at registration (code `regex.too-large` or `regex.unsupported`). Matching against a 1 MiB input finishes in time proportional to the input.

## Edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Two plugins ask for the same scope | Each helper gets its own bind mount. They never see each other's `tmp` |
| A scope root is deleted while a plugin runs | Reads return `not-found`; the mount is re-created at next activation |
| Plugin exceeds `pids.max` | `fork` fails inside the helper with `EAGAIN`; the plugin sees `quota-exceeded` for spawns |
| The server is killed | Helpers see the dispatcher channel close and exit within 2 s; children get SIGTERM then SIGKILL |
| A T2 plugin is installed on a machine with no user namespaces | Install succeeds (it is only files). Load fails with `sandbox.unavailable` |

### See also

- [Security model](/pages/security/)
- [Threat model](/pages/reference-threat-model/)
- [Network egress](/pages/reference-network-egress/)
- [Capability: process.run](/pages/capability-process-run/)
- [Security testing](/pages/reference-security-testing/)
- [Design decisions](/pages/design-decisions/)

# Secrets

## Secrets

A **secret** is a value that gives access to something: an API key, a token, a password. This page says where Ilium keeps secrets, who can read them, how they are kept out of logs, and what plugin authors must do. The rules are scattered across the settings pages; this page is the single normative source and the other pages link here.

The attacker classes are A1, A3 and A8 in the [Threat model](/pages/reference-threat-model/). Secrets that never reach the host, such as a publisher's private signing key, are covered by [Trust and supply chain](/pages/reference-trust-and-supply-chain/).

### You will need

- The settings row types in [Settings schema](/pages/reference-settings-schema/), in particular `secret`.
- The settings API in [API: settings](/pages/api-settings/).

## What counts as a secret

**[SEC-240]** The host treats these as secrets: the value of any settings row declared with `"secret": true`; the keys in the built-in `api` settings tab (model provider keys); and webhook URLs of notification channels that contain a token. Publisher private keys are not handled by the host at all.

## Storage at rest

**[SEC-241]** Secret values are never written to `config.toml`, to a project `.ilium/` folder, to session snapshots, to exports or to the pane journal. They are stored in the **secrets store**: the OS keyring when one is available (Secret Service on Linux, Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows), and otherwise `secrets.json` in the user state directory, mode 0600, in the deny set ([SEC-060]). The file has the form `{ "version": 1, "plugins": { "<id>": { "<key>": "<value>" } }, "kernel": { "<tab>.<key>": "<value>" } }` and is written atomically. When the keyring is used, the store holds only an index with no values.

**[SEC-242]** A settings row with `secret` together with `scope: "project"` is refused at install with `manifest.secret-scope`. A secret never comes from a project file. A secret value found in a project file is ignored and audited.

## Who can read a secret

**[SEC-244]** Only the plugin side that owns the row reads its secrets, through `settings.get-json`. `settings.read-all` and `settings.read-kernel` return an empty string for a plugin secret and `<redacted>` for a kernel secret. A secret does not appear in events, in the `settings-changed` payload (the event names the key only), in the review dialog or in `ilium plugin ... --json` output.

**[SEC-245]** The host never forwards a secret value to another plugin: not through `messages.peer`, services, topics or extension points. A plugin that sends its own secret to another plugin does so by its own code; the host cannot stop that, which is a residual risk of inter-plugin channels ([SEC-007]).

**[SEC-250]** Snapshots and exports exclude secrets. After a restore the secret rows are empty and the plugin is told with a `settings-changed` event.

## Redaction

**[SEC-243]** The host replaces secrets in text it writes. Algorithm:

1. Collect the current secret values of all plugins and the kernel that are at least 6 characters long. Shorter values are not redacted (and the settings page warns when a `secret` row accepts values shorter than 6).
2. For each value, build the variants: the raw bytes, the base64 form (standard and URL-safe, with and without padding), the percent-encoded form, and the hexadecimal form.
3. Replace every occurrence of each variant, case-sensitively, with `<redacted>`. Longer values are replaced first.

The step applies to plugin log lines, `process-run` log lines and audit records, trap messages, HTTP request logs, diagnostics report sections ([SEC-249]) and error strings returned to plugins. Limits, stated honestly: a plugin can transform a secret (reverse it, split it, encrypt it) and then write it; redaction stops accidents, not malice.

**[SEC-249]** Diagnostics reports (`ilium.core.diagnostics/report-sections`) pass through redaction before they are shown or saved. A section that contains a secret in a form the algorithm cannot match is the contributor's defect.

**[SEC-246]** Rotation. When a secret changes, the host overwrites the old value in the store, forgets it for redaction purposes after 60 s (so late log lines are still redacted), and keeps no copy.

## Guidance for plugin authors

**[SEC-247]** A plugin SHOULD: never log a secret or a request that carries one; send secrets in headers, not in query strings (URLs are logged on errors and shown in consent prompts); keep a secret in memory only as long as a request needs it and overwrite buffers it controls; avoid placing a secret in a place a command line shows; and name the row clearly so the user knows what to enter. Rust and TypeScript examples follow.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::{http::{self, Request}, settings};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

/// Calls an API with a bearer token read just in time. The token never reaches a log line.
fn call_api() -> Result<Vec<u8>, PluginError> {
    let mut token = settings::get_json("api_token")?.into_bytes();
    let mut request = Request::get("https://api.example.com/v1/me");
    request.header("Authorization", &format!("Bearer {}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&token)));
    let result = http::send(request).map(|response| response.body);
    token.iter_mut().for_each(|byte| *byte = 0); // best effort: shorten the secret's lifetime
    result
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { get } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/settings';
import { send } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/http';

/** Reads the token only when needed and sends it as a header, never in the URL. */
export async function callApi(): Promise<Uint8Array> {
  const token = await get('api_token');
  const response = await send({
    method: 'GET',
    url: 'https://api.example.com/v1/me',
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  return response.body;
}
```

## What the user sees

**[SEC-248]** A secret row is masked with `••••`; `reveal_last` shows up to 8 trailing characters. Settings > Plugins > Secrets lists which plugins hold secrets (names only) and offers **Forget secrets** per plugin and for all. Forgetting removes the values from the store and the keyring and sends the plugin a `settings-changed` event.

## Edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Keyring is locked or unavailable at start | The file store is used; a notice appears once |
| Secret shorter than 6 characters | Stored and masked, not redacted in logs |
| Package declares `secret` with `scope: "project"` | `manifest.secret-scope` at install |
| Plugin uninstalled | Its secrets are removed from the store with its grants |
| Plugin logs a secret split in two lines | Not matched; this is the plugin's defect |

### See also

- [Settings schema](/pages/reference-settings-schema/)
- [API: settings](/pages/api-settings/)
- [Audit log](/pages/reference-audit-log/)
- [Diagnostics core plugin](/pages/core-plugin-diagnostics/)
- [Debugging](/pages/debugging/)

Contract: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Security response

## Security response

This page says how to report a security problem in Ilium or in a plugin, what the Ilium project does with the report, how a bad plugin is stopped, and how a user starts Ilium with third-party code off. It is a process page: the dates and contact are commitments of the project, and a test cannot check them, but the safe-mode behaviour is testable.

### You will need

- For a report: a way to send encrypted email, and a description with steps to reproduce.
- For safe mode: the `ilium` command line.

## Reporting a vulnerability in Ilium

**[SEC-320]** The project publishes a security contact in `SECURITY.md` at the repository root and in `ilium --version --verbose`. Until the project publishes an address the contact is the placeholder `security@ilium.example` and a PGP key published next to it. Reports go there, not to public issues.

A report should say: the version (`ilium --version --verbose`), the platform, what you did, what you expected, what happened, whether a plugin was involved, and whether you have disclosed it elsewhere.

**[SEC-321]** The project acknowledges a report within 3 working days, gives a first assessment within 10 working days, and keeps the reporter informed at least every 14 days. The embargo is 90 days from the report, or until a fix is released, whichever is first. The reporter and the project may agree on a shorter or a longer embargo. The project does not take legal action against good-faith research that follows this process.

**[SEC-322]** A confirmed issue gets a CVE identifier, a security advisory in the repository (`GHSA` style) and an entry in the release notes. An advisory states: affected versions, fixed versions, severity, a description, a workaround if one exists, credit (if the reporter wants it), and the requirement ids concerned (for example `SEC-023`).

**[SEC-323]** Supported versions. The latest minor release of Ilium and the one before it receive security fixes.

**[SEC-324]** Severity. The project rates issues on a four-level scale:

| Level | Examples in this platform |
|---|---|
| Critical | A sandbox escape from a T2 or T3 plugin; a plugin that runs unconfined code without a grant; reading the HTTP API token from a plugin |
| High | A grant check bypass; a consent bypass; reading a file outside a granted scope; a signature bypass; unauthenticated use of the HTTP API |
| Medium | A data leak through an error message or event; a denial of service of the server by a plugin that quotas should stop; spoofing of a kernel dialog |
| Low | A side channel with a small bandwidth; a missing audit line; a wrong error code |

## Reporting a vulnerability in a plugin

**[SEC-325]** A plugin SHOULD set `security_contact` in its manifest ([SEC-268]). The Details view of the install dialog and `ilium plugin inspect` show it. A user who finds a flaw reports it to that contact and not to the Ilium project, unless the flaw is in the host.

**[SEC-326]** When a publisher does not answer a serious report within 30 days, the Ilium project MAY add the package, the plugin id with a version range, or the publisher key to the release blocklist ([SEC-146]) and publish an advisory. The project does not host plugins, so it has no other way to stop a plugin that is spread as files.

## Takedown

**[SEC-327]** When a blocklist entry matches an installed plugin, the plugin is disabled at the next load, its data is kept, the user sees `Blocked: <reason>`, and the audit log records `blocklist-hit` ([SEC-149]). The user can uninstall it. The user cannot re-enable it.

## Safe mode

Safe mode starts Ilium with all third-party code off, for the case where a plugin breaks the client so that the recovery page cannot be reached.

**[SEC-328]** `ilium --safe-mode` without a value is `--safe-mode=third-party`. The environment variable `ILIUM_SAFE_MODE` accepts `third-party`, `all-optional`, `1` (the same as `third-party`) and `0` (off); any other value exits 2 with `usage.invalid-value`. `--safe-plugins` is an alias of `--safe-mode=third-party`, and `--no-plugins` starts no plugin host. The flag wins over the variable. The flags start the server and client in safe mode. In safe mode: all T2 and T3 plugins are disabled; all core plugin replacements are off and the built-in plugins are restored; the admin policy still applies; no plugin is deleted and no grant, consent or data is changed. The flag is not stored: the next normal start returns to the previous state.

**[SEC-329]** A persistent badge `SAFE` is shown in the status bar while safe mode is on. The Plugins screen lists the disabled plugins with `Off in safe mode`, and the user can uninstall them from there.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Safe mode ──────────────────────────────────╮</span>
│ Third-party plugins and replacements are     │
│ off. Built-in plugins are restored.          │
│                                              │
│ example.pane-tools ……………………………………………………… off │
│ example.notes …………………………………………………………………… off │
│                                              │
│ <span class="t-hi"> Enter </span> Continue                             │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The badge SAFE stays in the status bar while safe mode is on.</figcaption>
</figure>

**[SEC-330]** The server writes `safe-mode` to the audit log at start. A project that holds `.ilium/` plugin values is treated as untrusted in safe mode.

## Publisher incident checklist

1. Stop distributing the affected package.
2. If the private key may be exposed: stop signing with it. If you still control it, sign a rotation statement for a new key ([SEC-143]) and ship a fixed version signed by the new key. If you no longer control it, ask the Ilium project for a blocklist entry for the key.
3. Ship a fixed version with a higher version number and a short description of what changed.
4. Tell users: uninstall the old version, trust the new fingerprint (compare it through a channel other than the package), and review the grants.
5. Publish a note with affected versions and the fix.

## Dependency advisories

**[SEC-331]** An advisory in Wasmtime or a codec that applies to the pinned version is handled as in [SEC-171]: a patched release within 14 days of the upstream fix (48 hours when exploited in the wild), a release-blocklist entry for the vulnerable runtime, and a warning in Ilium until the user updates.

## Edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Safe mode and a `force_enabled` plugin from the policy | The plugin stays off if it is third-party; the policy shows `conflict: safe-mode` |
| Safe mode and a bundled T1 plugin | Runs normally |
| Report arrives for a plugin and the host together | Two advisories, one for each party |
| User runs `ilium --safe-mode` against a running server | The command starts a new session in safe mode and does not disturb the running one |

### See also

- [Trust and supply chain](/pages/reference-trust-and-supply-chain/)
- [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/)
- [User security and privacy](/pages/user-plugin-security-and-privacy/)
- [Audit log](/pages/reference-audit-log/)

Contract: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Security testing

## Security testing

This page lists what must be fuzzed, what a hostile test plugin must fail to do, and how each security requirement maps to a test. It is the checklist a test author uses to turn the normative statements in the security pages into test cases. The general test approach is in [Testing](/pages/testing/).

A **fuzz target** is a function that takes arbitrary bytes and must never crash, hang or break an invariant. A **corpus seed** is an example input that starts the fuzzer near interesting cases. A **fixture** is a fixed file or program that a test uses.

### You will need

- The requirement ids from [Security and policy requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-security-policy/).
- A Linux machine that meets the [sandbox prerequisites](/pages/reference-sandbox/).
- A fuzzing tool for Rust (for example `cargo-fuzz`) and the project's test harness.

## Fuzz targets

**[SEC-340]** Each target below MUST exist in the repository, with corpus seeds and the stated invariants. The invariant for every target is: no panic, no out-of-bounds access, no unbounded memory or time (a limit of 1 s and 512 MiB per input), and a defined error code for every rejected input.

| Target | Seeds | Extra invariant |
|---|---|---|
| `.iliumpkg` reader | Valid packages; zip-slip names; duplicate names; ZIP64; header mismatch; overlapping entries; symlink entries; decompression bombs | Nothing is written outside the staging folder; errors are `manifest.zip-*` |
| Manifest parser and validator | Valid manifests; duplicate keys; depth 1,000; 10 MiB strings; unknown keys; bad grant strings | Duplicate keys refused; unknown keys give `manifest.unknown-key` |
| Grant string and host-pattern matcher | Valid and invalid grants | Property test against a reference implementation: the matcher and the reference agree on every input |
| Path canonicaliser and scope resolver | Traversal corpus (`..`, encoded dots, backslashes, long names), symlink loops | A result is always below the scope root, or an error |
| Settings schema compiler and value validator | Valid schemas; huge `oneOf`; recursive refs; bad `pattern` | Limits of the schema reference hold |
| `payload_schema` and `entry_schema` validators | As above, plus `x-ilium-data` annotations | Risk raised to `high` where [SEC-281] applies |
| Every WIT host function's lifting of guest values | Lengths up to `u32::MAX`, invalid UTF-8, bad enum discriminants, stale resource handles | Defined error, never a trap of the host |
| Dispatcher protocol messages from the helper | Truncated, oversized, malformed, wrong-identity messages | Helper ended and counted as a failure ([SEC-052]) |
| Codecs: inflate, image decoders, audio, video headers | Real files, truncated files, huge dimensions | Pixel cap and byte cap hold |
| HTTP API request parser | Smuggling cases; huge headers; wrong Host and Origin | 4xx, never a route call without the token |
| Transcript parsers behind `agent.transcript` | Real transcripts per agent, truncated, hostile JSON | Redaction still applies |
| Detector screen inputs | Real screens, random bytes, escape-sequence storms | Classification returns within the time limit |
| Regex compilation of plugin patterns | Catastrophic patterns (`(a+)+$`), huge classes, nested groups | Compile refused ([SEC-046]) or match is linear in the input |
| Audit record parser (`--verify`) | Tampered chains | The first broken `seq` is reported |

**[SEC-341]** Each fuzz target runs for at least 10 minutes in CI on every change that touches its code, and for at least 4 hours per target before each release. Native code runs under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer in at least one CI job.

**[SEC-342]** A fuzz crash, hang or invariant failure is a release blocker. The input is added to the corpus as a regression test before the fix merges.

## Sandbox escape probe suite

**[SEC-345]** A hostile test plugin (guest) and a hostile child program (started with `process.run`) MUST each attempt the actions below, and each attempt MUST fail with the defined result. The suite runs on every supported Linux configuration of CI and before each release.

| Attempt | Expected result | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Open a socket (TCP, UDP, UNIX, raw) | `EPERM` or no route | [SEC-022] |
| Read `/proc/<server pid>/environ`, `/proc/1/environ` | Path does not exist or `EACCES` | [SEC-026] |
| `ptrace` the server or a sibling helper | `EPERM` | [SEC-024] |
| `ioctl(TIOCSTI)` or `TIOCLINUX` on any fd | `EPERM`; no inherited PTY fd exists | [SEC-028] |
| Reach `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, the Ilium socket, the API token | Not mounted | [SEC-023], [SEC-098] |
| Read `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg` without a grant | Not mounted | [SEC-023] |
| Write outside the granted scope, through `..`, a symlink swap race, a hard link, a bind mount | `not-permitted` | [SEC-058], [SEC-059] |
| Execute a binary written to `data` | `EACCES` | [SEC-023], [SEC-034] |
| Fork-bomb | `EAGAIN` at `pids.max`; helper still responsive | [SEC-029] |
| Allocate beyond `memory.max` | Helper killed; trap `limit-exceeded(memory)` | [SEC-029] |
| Call each denied system call of [SEC-067] | `EPERM` or kill | [SEC-024] |
| Read another plugin's data folder | Not mounted | [SEC-020], [SEC-060] |
| Send a message with another plugin's id | Dropped; failure counted | [SEC-050] |
| Set `LD_PRELOAD` or `PATH` in `process.run` env | `invalid-argument` | [SEC-033] |
| Run `sh -c` through `panes.create` with no `panes.create-command` grant | `refused(not-permitted)` | [SEC-040] |

## Security test checklist

Every row below is a test the project MUST have. Kinds: unit, integration, e2e (end to end with the real client), fuzz, manual.

| SEC id | Kind | Fixture | Expected result |
|---|---|---|---|
| [SEC-141] | unit | A signed package; flip each byte of the manifest and signature | `manifest.signature-invalid` for every flip |
| [SEC-142] | integration | Install `a` signed by key 1, then update signed by key 2 | `package.publisher-key-changed` |
| [SEC-143] | integration | Update with a valid rotation statement | Accepted; dialog says `Signing key rotated` |
| [SEC-145] | integration | Install a lower version | Refused without the flag; audited with the flag |
| [SEC-146], [SEC-149] | integration | A blocklist entry for an installed package | Disabled at next load; `blocklist-hit` |
| [SEC-150] | unit | Archives with each defect of the table | The listed code |
| [SEC-153] | integration | Edit a file in the install folder | `manifest.file-hash`, plugin disabled |
| [SEC-103] | e2e | Hold Enter while the dialog opens | Dialog stays open |
| [SEC-110] | e2e | Decline an origin three times | Fourth call returns `not-permitted` with no prompt |
| [SEC-113] | integration | Add an H grant to `grants.json` by hand | Dropped at start; `store-external-edit` |
| [SEC-116] | e2e | `ilium plugin install --yes` from a pane with no client | `approval.no-client` |
| [SEC-120] | integration | `consents --withdraw` | Next use asks again |
| [SEC-182] | integration | Policy file writable by the user | Ignored; notice; audit |
| [SEC-181] | unit | System and user policy pairs | Merge table of the policy page |
| [SEC-187] | integration | Malformed policy | `policy.invalid`; third parties not loaded |
| [SEC-189] | integration | `plugins.manage` enables a forced-off plugin | `not-permitted` reason `policy` |
| [SEC-221], [SEC-222] | integration | One scripted scenario per event | Exactly one record per event, chain verifies |
| [SEC-226] | unit | Edit a record in the middle | `--verify` names that `seq` |
| [SEC-072], [SEC-073] | integration | A local resolver that answers a public name with `127.0.0.1`, then `93.184.216.34` | Refused; no second resolution |
| [SEC-075], [SEC-076] | integration | Redirect to another origin | Authorization header removed; https to http refused |
| [SEC-077] | integration | Server with an invalid certificate | `network` reason `tls` |
| [SEC-097] | integration | Requests with a wrong Host, a foreign Origin, no token | 403, 403, 401 |
| [SEC-084] | integration | Offline switch | `not-permitted` reason `offline` |
| [SEC-243] | unit | A secret in a log line, in base64, in a URL | `<redacted>` in each |
| [SEC-242] | unit | `secret` with `scope: "project"` | `manifest.secret-scope` |
| [SEC-287] | integration | A veto handler that sleeps | Plugin-initiated send refused with `guard-failed`; user prompt for a paste |
| [SEC-285] | integration | Withdrawn (see HST-472): a handler that starts before 100 ms and burns its deadline | Handlers not started at 100 ms are skipped as pass and logged `extension.chain-cap` |
| [SEC-284] | integration | A transform that returns an invalid payload | Next handler sees the previous valid payload |
| [SEC-289] | integration | Hooks nested three deep | `extension.depth-exceeded` at depth 3 |
| [SEC-290] | integration | Three consecutive breaches | Extension stopped; notice; audit |
| [SEC-300], [SEC-301] | integration | Replace a core plugin as T3 and as T2 | `manifest.replaces-tier`; T2 gets the confirmation |
| [SEC-311] | e2e | Open a repository with hostile `.ilium/` values | Ignored until trusted |
| [SEC-328] | e2e | `ilium --safe-mode` | Third-party plugins off, badge `SAFE` |
| [SEC-380] | unit | A corpus of spoofing strings in every plugin text field | Controls, bidi and fake borders stripped |
| [SEC-346] | manual | Review dialogs at 48 columns | Readable, aligned, screen-reader text present |

**[SEC-346]** The review dialog, trust dialog and consent prompts are checked by hand on each release in a terminal of 48 columns and in one of 120 columns, in light and dark themes.

## Side-channel tests and accepted risks

**[SEC-347]** Tests exist for: clock resolution (a guest reading `clock` twice 100 times sees steps of 1 ms or more, and jitter [SEC-370]); no `screen-changed` event while the pane is in no-echo mode ([SEC-371]); identical errors for a missing and an ungranted plugin ([SEC-373]); no absolute paths in error strings ([SEC-374]). Accepted risks (cache timing between processes, coarse output rhythm, a busy-loop timer) are not tested; they are listed in the [Threat model](/pages/reference-threat-model/).

## Reusing the fixtures

**[SEC-348]** The hostile-input fixtures (archives, manifests, path corpus, spoofing strings, catastrophic patterns) live in `tests/security-fixtures/` of the repository and are released with the SDK. Plugin authors MAY use them to test their own plugins against the same inputs; see [Testing](/pages/testing/).

## Edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| CI machine without user namespaces | The escape suite is skipped with a visible failure; the release cannot be tagged |
| A fuzz target takes more than 1 s on one input | The input is a failure |
| Sanitizer reports a leak in a test-only helper | Fixed or suppressed with a written reason |

- [Testing](/pages/testing/)

# Signing and trust reference

## Signing and trust reference

This page specifies how a package is signed, how the host decides whom to trust, and what happens when a key changes or is revoked. It replaces the short description that older pages gave. A developer can implement the verifier from it. A test author can use the known-answer vector at the end.

A **publisher** is the person or organisation that releases a plugin. A **publisher id** is the machine-readable name of that publisher. A **key** is an Ed25519 key pair. The private half signs. The public half verifies. A **fingerprint**, also called the key id, is a short name for a public key. The **trust store** is the list of keys that a user or an administrator accepts. A **tier** is the trust level that the host assigns to a package at install time: T1 (bundled), T2 (signed by a trusted key) or T3 (unsigned).

Requirement ids such as `PKG-200` can be cited by tests. See [Requirements: manifest and package](/pages/reference-requirements-manifest-package/).

### You will need

- The package layout and the `signature` entry position: [Package format reference](/pages/reference-package-format/).
- The command syntax: [Plugin command line](/pages/reference-plugin-cli/).
- The user-facing dialog: [Finding and installing plugins](/pages/user-plugin-store/).

## Decision summary

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Algorithm | Ed25519 (RFC 8032), pure mode, not prehashed |
| What is signed | A fixed message built from a domain prefix, the publisher id and the SHA-256 of the exact bytes of `manifest.json` |
| Canonical form | None. The exact stored bytes are signed. No canonicalisation step exists |
| Who is trusted | A key, never a free-text name. Each key belongs to exactly one publisher id |
| Trust on first use | Allowed only with an explicit user action that shows the full fingerprint |
| Key change | An update signed by another key is refused unless a valid rotation statement or earlier trust exists |
| T1 root | The release build. Bundled components are checked against a hash list built into the binary |

## The signed message

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-200] | A signature MUST be an Ed25519 signature (RFC 8032, "pure" Ed25519) over the message `M` below. Ed25519ph and Ed25519ctx MUST NOT be used. |
| [PKG-201] | `M` is the concatenation of: the 25 ASCII bytes `ilium-plugin-signature-v1`, one `0x00` byte, the UTF-8 bytes of the publisher id, one `0x00` byte, and the 32 raw bytes of the SHA-256 of `manifest.json`. |
| [PKG-202] | The SHA-256 is computed over the exact bytes of the `manifest.json` entry as stored in the archive. The host MUST NOT parse, normalise or re-serialise the manifest before hashing. |
| [PKG-203] | A verifier MUST reject a signature when the public key is not a valid Ed25519 point or when the signature is not canonical (S not smaller than the group order). RFC 8032 section 5.1.7 rules apply. |

The domain prefix means that a signature made for a package cannot be replayed in another protocol that also uses Ed25519. The publisher id inside the message means that a key cannot be reused to claim a different publisher.

The manifest holds the SHA-256 of every other entry (the inventory). So the signature covers every listed file, transitively. The `signature` entry itself is not listed, and nothing else is exempt: the package format allows no unlisted entry.

Signing is not a hash of the whole archive. The archive bytes change when the `signature` entry is added, so the hash of the archive cannot be signed. That is why the manifest bytes are signed.

## The signature entry

The entry is named `signature` and holds a UTF-8 JSON document.

```json
{
  "format": "ilium-sig/1",
  "signatures": [
    {
      "algorithm": "ed25519",
      "key_id": "56475aa75463474c0285df5dbf2bcab73da651358839e9b77481b2eab107708c",
      "publisher_id": "example",
      "signature": "jv5zcDEiiDljfN-iy3nZLtCgScmbTMJoOv0M3X9r0D9Tm4dvdqE43gpEEAW_cqVod6iYQAjeIR8E0-vFwEplBw",
      "signed_at": "2026-10-12 10:00:00"
    }
  ]
}
```

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-204] | The document MUST have exactly the keys `format` and `signatures`. `format` MUST be `ilium-sig/1`. |
| [PKG-205] | `signatures` MUST hold 1 to 4 objects. Each has exactly the keys `algorithm` (`ed25519`), `key_id`, `publisher_id`, `signature` and `signed_at`. |
| [PKG-206] | `key_id` is 64 characters of lowercase hexadecimal. `signature` is the 64 signature bytes in base64url without padding (86 characters). `signed_at` is `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` in UTC and is informational: the host never uses it for a decision. |
| [PKG-207] | The first object is the publisher signature. A second object MAY be a registry countersignature (see [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/)). The host verifies every object and requires at least one valid object from a trusted key. |
| [PKG-208] | The entry is at most 16 KiB. A document that does not match these rules is refused with `package.signature-format`. A signature that does not verify is refused with `manifest.signature-invalid`. A `key_id` that does not match any key that verifies the signature is `manifest.signature-invalid`. |
| [PKG-209] | The entry sorts like any other entry (bytewise by path). Adding it keeps the archive valid and deterministic ([PKG-148]). |
| [PKG-650] | The signature document is serialised with the rules of [PKG-145]: UTF-8 without a byte order mark, 2-space indentation, LF line endings and one final LF. Keys appear in table order: `format`, `signatures`; in each object `algorithm`, `key_id`, `publisher_id`, `signature`, `signed_at`. Two runs of `sign` with the same key, manifest and `signed_at` MUST give byte-identical packages. |
| [PKG-651] | `signed_at` is taken by `sign` from `--signed-at <time>` (the form `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss`, in UTC), else from the environment variable `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` (seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC), else from the clock. The test vector below was made with `--signed-at "2026-10-12 10:00:00"`. |

## Keys and key files

`ilium plugin keygen --publisher-id <id> --publisher "<name>" --out <dir>` writes two files and refuses to overwrite an existing file (`trust.key-exists`).

**publisher.key** is the private key.

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-210] | `publisher.key` MUST be a PKCS#8 (RFC 5958) private key in PEM, with the label `PRIVATE KEY`, or `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` when protected by a passphrase. |
| [PKG-211] | An encrypted key uses PBES2 with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (at least 600,000 iterations) and AES-256-CBC. `keygen` encrypts when `--passphrase-file` or the environment variable `ILIUM_KEY_PASSPHRASE` is given or when the user types a passphrase at the prompt. An empty passphrase is refused. |
| [PKG-212] | `keygen` MUST create the file with mode 0600 and the folder with mode 0700. `sign` MUST refuse a key file that is readable by group or others (`trust.key-permissions`), on systems that have such modes. |
| [PKG-213] | `sign --key -` reads the PEM from standard input. The environment variable `ILIUM_PUBLISHER_KEY` MAY hold the PEM text for CI use. The host never writes a private key to a log. |

**publisher.pub** is the public key. It is safe to share.

```json
{
  "format": "ilium-pub/1",
  "publisher_id": "example",
  "publisher": "Example Labs",
  "algorithm": "ed25519",
  "public_key": "A6EHv_POEL4dcN0Y50vAmWfk1jCbpQ1fHdyGZBJVMbg",
  "key_id": "56475aa75463474c0285df5dbf2bcab73da651358839e9b77481b2eab107708c",
  "created": "2026-10-12 10:00:00"
}
```

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-214] | `public_key` is the 32 raw bytes in base64url without padding. `key_id` MUST equal the lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 of those 32 bytes. A file with another `key_id` is refused with `trust.key-malformed`. |
| [PKG-215] | `publisher_id` follows the grammar below. `publisher` is a display name of 1 to 64 characters with no control and no bidirectional-override characters. |

**Fingerprint display.** The stored form is the 64-character hex string. The display form groups it in 16 groups of 4 characters separated by single spaces, and the dialog splits it into two lines of 8 groups. [PKG-216] A dialog or prompt that asks the user to trust a key MUST show all 64 characters. It MUST NOT show a truncated fingerprint as the only identification. A short form (the first 8 characters) MAY appear next to the full form in lists.

## Publisher identity

The `publisher` field in the manifest is a display name. Anyone can write any display name. The identity that is checked is the publisher id and the key.

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-217] | A publisher id matches `[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*(\.[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*){0,3}`, is 1 to 64 characters long and has at most 4 segments. |
| [PKG-218] | A signed package's plugin `id` MUST start with `<publisher_id>.` where `publisher_id` is the one in the signature. Otherwise the install is refused with `manifest.id-publisher`. Example: publisher id `com.acme` signs `com.acme.notes`. |
| [PKG-219] | The manifest `publisher` text MUST equal (after Unicode NFC normalisation, case-sensitive) the display name stored with the key in the trust store. A mismatch is refused with `manifest.publisher-mismatch`. |
| [PKG-220] | The prefix `ilium.` is reserved for the release. No key can be trusted for the publisher id `ilium`, `core`, `local` or `test`. Adding such a key is refused with `trust.publisher-reserved`. |

Registry names add homoglyph checks. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/#namespaces).

## The trust store

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-221] | The user store is the file `trust.json` in the Ilium user state folder (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/ilium/trust.json`; `~/.local/state/ilium/trust.json` on Linux when `XDG_STATE_HOME` is unset). It is created with mode 0600. Writes are atomic: write a temporary file in the same folder, fsync, rename. |
| [PKG-222] | The system store is `/etc/ilium/trust.json` on Linux (the platform equivalent through the same crate elsewhere). It is read-only for the host. An administrator owns it. |
| [PKG-223] | The effective trust set is the union of both stores minus every revoked key. A key revoked in either store is revoked. A user cannot remove or override a system entry. |
| [PKG-224] | Each store entry binds one `key_id` to exactly one `publisher_id`. A second entry with the same `key_id` and another publisher id is refused with `trust.publisher-conflict`. One publisher id MAY have several keys (needed for rotation). |

Store format:

```json
{
  "format": "ilium-trust/1",
  "keys": [
    {
      "key_id": "56475aa75463474c0285df5dbf2bcab73da651358839e9b77481b2eab107708c",
      "publisher_id": "example",
      "publisher": "Example Labs",
      "public_key": "A6EHv_POEL4dcN0Y50vAmWfk1jCbpQ1fHdyGZBJVMbg",
      "added": "2026-10-12 10:05:00",
      "added_by": "user",
      "status": "trusted",
      "revoked": null
    }
  ]
}
```

`added_by` is `user`, `admin` or `registry`. `status` is `trusted` or `revoked`. `revoked` is null or an object `{ "reason", "at" }`. An unknown `format` value refuses the whole file with `trust.store-invalid`, and the host then treats the store as empty and shows a warning. It never guesses.

### Trust commands

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ilium plugin trust add <publisher.pub> [--yes]` | Shows the full fingerprint and asks. `--yes` skips the question. The file must pass [PKG-214] |
| `ilium plugin trust add --fingerprint <key_id> <package>` | Trusts the key that signed the package, only if its `key_id` equals the one given. Use this in scripts |
| `ilium plugin trust list [--json]` | Lists the effective set with `key_id`, publisher id, status and source (user or system) |
| `ilium plugin trust remove <key_id> [--force]` | Removes a user entry. See below |
| `ilium plugin trust export <key_id>` | Writes the `publisher.pub` form to standard output |

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-225] | `ilium plugin install --trust <key_id>` trusts that exact key for this install and for later ones. It is the only non-interactive way to trust a key. A package signed by another key is refused with `trust.key-unknown`. |
| [PKG-226] | `trust remove` of a key that signed installed plugins MUST be refused with `trust.in-use` and list the plugins, unless `--force` is given. With `--force` the plugins change to the package state `disabled-untrusted` ([plugin lifecycle states](/pages/reference-plugin-lifecycle-states/#package-states)): they stay installed, are stopped, keep their grants and settings, and show a badge. They leave that state when the key is trusted again, or with `ilium plugin enable <id> --accept-risk`. |
| [PKG-227] | `trust remove` MUST NOT delete any plugin data. `trust remove` of a system entry is refused with `trust.system-entry`. |

## Tier assignment

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-228] | A package with a valid signature from a trusted, non-revoked key is tier T2. |
| [PKG-229] | A package with no `signature` entry is tier T3. It installs only with `--allow-unsigned`, or through `ilium plugin dev`. Without either it is refused with `trust.unsigned`. |
| [PKG-230] | A package with a valid signature from a key that is not in the trust store prompts the user with the key details. If the user accepts, the key is added with `added_by: user` and the install continues as T2. If the user declines, the install stops with `trust.declined`. In a non-interactive run without `--trust`, it stops with `trust.key-unknown`. |
| [PKG-231] | A package with an invalid signature is refused with `manifest.signature-invalid`, whatever the user could choose. There is no flag that installs it. |
| [PKG-232] | A package signed by a revoked key is refused with `trust.key-revoked`. |
| [PKG-233] | T1 is not a trust-store tier. A T1 component is a component embedded in the Ilium release. At build time the release records the SHA-256 of each embedded component in a table inside the binary. At load time the host compares the embedded bytes with the table. A mismatch disables the plugin with `trust.bundled-tampered`. |
| [PKG-234] | A package from any source whose `id` starts with `ilium.` is refused with `manifest.id-reserved`, even when it carries a valid signature. Core plugins change only with a new Ilium release. |
| [PKG-235] | The declared tier never comes from the manifest. There is no manifest key for it. |

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-warn">Unknown signing key</span>
Publisher  Example Labs (example)
Package    example.notes 1.2.0

Fingerprint
5647 5aa7 5463 474c 0285 df5d bf2b cab7
3da6 5135 8839 e9b7 7481 b2ea b107 708c

Ask the publisher for this fingerprint
over another channel before you trust it.

[ Trust key ]  [ Cancel ]
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The trust prompt for an unknown key. All 64 characters are shown.</figcaption>
</figure>

The dialog splits the 16 groups of 4 into two lines of 8 groups. Command output prints the same groups on one line. Both are the same value.

## Publisher key change and rotation

A package update is signed by the same key in nearly every case. The next rules cover the exceptions.

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-236] | When a plugin is installed and an update is signed by a key with another `key_id` than the installed version's key, the host checks the trust store. If the new key is already trusted for the same publisher id, the update continues. |
| [PKG-237] | Otherwise the update MUST be refused with `package.publisher-key-changed`, and the message names both fingerprints. No dialog can override this inside `install`. The user changes the situation first, by importing a rotation statement or by running `trust add --additional`. This decision keeps a stolen distribution channel from replacing a key through a prompt that users click through. |
| [PKG-238] | A **rotation statement** is the document `rotation.json`: `{ "format": "ilium-rot/1", "publisher_id", "old_key_id", "new_key": { "public_key", "key_id" }, "signature", "created" }`. `signature` is made by the old key over the message `ilium-key-rotation-v1`, `0x00`, the publisher id, `0x00`, the 32 raw bytes of the new `key_id`. |
| [PKG-239] | `ilium plugin trust add --rotation <rotation.json>` verifies the statement against the old key in the store. If valid, it adds the new key with `added_by: user` for the same publisher id, and keeps the old key as `trusted` until the user or the publisher revokes it. |
| [PKG-240] | `ilium plugin trust add --additional <publisher.pub>` adds a second key for a publisher id that already has a key. It shows the old and the new fingerprints and requires typing the word `replace` in an interactive session. |
| [PKG-241] | A rotation statement MUST be signed by a key that is currently trusted for the same publisher id. Otherwise `trust.rotation-invalid`. |

## Revocation and distrust

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-242] | A **revocation statement** is the document `{ "format": "ilium-rev/1", "publisher_id", "key_id", "reason", "effective", "signature" }`. `reason` is `compromised`, `superseded` or `retired`. `effective` is `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` in UTC. `signature` is made by the revoked key itself, or by the new key named in a rotation statement, over `ilium-key-revocation-v1`, `0x00`, the publisher id, `0x00`, the 32 raw bytes of `key_id`, `0x00`, the reason text. |
| [PKG-243] | `ilium plugin trust revoke <key_id> --reason <reason>` writes the key as revoked in the user store. A registry (when configured) distributes revocations in its metadata. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/#revocation). The administrator also revokes keys in the system store. |
| [PKG-244] | New installs of a package signed by a revoked key are refused with `trust.key-revoked`, for every reason. |
| [PKG-245] | Installed plugins signed by a key revoked as `compromised` are stopped at once, enter the package state `disabled-blocked` and show the reason. They leave that state only with `ilium plugin enable <id> --accept-risk`, or with an update signed by another trusted key of the same publisher id. |
| [PKG-246] | Installed plugins signed by a key revoked as `superseded` or `retired` keep running at T2 with the badge `key retired`. Updates must come from a trusted key of the same publisher id. |
| [PKG-247] | The host checks the revocation lists whenever the trust stores or the registry metadata change, and at every start. A revocation with an `effective` time in the future applies when that time passes. |

### A compromised key: the publisher runbook

1. Stop signing with the key. Take the signing machine or CI secret out of use.
2. Generate a new key with a new `key_id` and the same publisher id (`keygen`).
3. Publish a revocation statement of the old key with reason `compromised`, signed by the new key if the old key is not safe to use, together with a rotation statement if the old key is still under your control. Send both to the registry and place them on your site.
4. Release a new version of each plugin signed by the new key.
5. Tell your users which versions are affected. Every version signed with the old key after the compromise time is suspect.

If the private key is lost and no copy exists, there is no recovery. Nobody can sign a rotation statement. The publisher must start a new publisher id (and so new plugin ids), and users must trust the new key. This is the cost of having no central account.

## Compared with other schemes

| Scheme | Binding | Why not used here |
|---|---|---|
| Free-text publisher name | None | Anyone can write any name |
| X.509 certificate authorities | A third party vouches for a name | Needs paid infrastructure and a policy for the CA |
| Sigstore keyless signing | An identity provider vouches | Needs network access at install time |
| This design | Key, publisher id and user or admin decision | Works offline. The weakest point is the first trust decision |

## Codes and dialog wording

| Code | Message template |
|---|---|
| `manifest.signature-invalid` | `The signature of {package} does not match its manifest.` |
| `package.signature-format` | `The signature entry of {package} is not a valid signature document: {detail}.` |
| `trust.key-unknown` | `{package} is signed by key {key_id}, which is not trusted. Use --trust {key_id} to trust it.` |
| `trust.declined` | `Key {key_id} was not trusted. Nothing was installed.` |
| `trust.unsigned` | `{package} is not signed. Use --allow-unsigned to install it as a dev (T3) package.` |
| `trust.key-revoked` | `Key {key_id} was revoked ({reason}). Nothing was installed.` |
| `package.publisher-key-changed` | `{id} was signed by {old_key_id}. This update is signed by {new_key_id}. Import a rotation statement first.` |
| `manifest.publisher-mismatch` | `The package says publisher "{manifest_publisher}". The key belongs to "{key_publisher}".` |
| `manifest.id-publisher` | `The id {id} must start with {publisher_id} because the package is signed for that publisher.` |
| `trust.in-use` | `Key {key_id} signed {count} installed plugins: {ids}. Use --force to continue.` |
| `trust.bundled-tampered` | `The bundled plugin {id} does not match this Ilium release.` |

## Test vector

A verifier MUST reproduce the following values. Ed25519 signatures are deterministic (RFC 8032), so any conforming library gives the same 64 bytes for the same seed and message. The values were computed with a reference implementation and checked independently with OpenSSL 3.5.5: the seed is wrapped as a PKCS#8 key (the 16 bytes `302e020100300506032b657004220420` followed by the seed), `openssl pkey -pubout` gives the public key, and `openssl pkeyutl -sign -rawin -inkey <key> -in <M file>` gives the signature.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Private seed (32 bytes) | `000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f101112131415161718191a1b1c1d1e1f` |
| Public key (32 bytes) | `03a107bff3ce10be1d70dd18e74bc09967e4d6309ba50d5f1ddc8664125531b8` |
| `key_id` (SHA-256 of the public key) | `56475aa75463474c0285df5dbf2bcab73da651358839e9b77481b2eab107708c` |
| Publisher id | `example` |
| Manifest | the 402 bytes of the [package format vector](/pages/reference-package-format/#test-vector-a-minimal-package) |
| SHA-256 of the manifest | `350b5e47c5781e72a9bb7b3d6630335fca0390402d0f625a48857a234f99c99d` |
| Message `M` (hex) | `696c69756d2d706c7567696e2d7369676e61747572652d7631006578616d706c6500350b5e47c5781e72a9bb7b3d6630335fca0390402d0f625a48857a234f99c99d` |
| Signature (64 bytes, hex) | `8efe737031228839637cdfa2cb79d92ed0a049c99b4cc2683afd0cdd7f6bd03f539b876f76a138de0a441005bf72a56877a8984008de211f04d3ebc5c04a6507` |
| Signature (base64url) | `jv5zcDEiiDljfN-iy3nZLtCgScmbTMJoOv0M3X9r0D9Tm4dvdqE43gpEEAW_cqVod6iYQAjeIR8E0-vFwEplBw` |

The signed package (1,114 bytes, SHA-256 `d2238076eea48c58ceb4416dbb50438c6ffee23028051d7e9a0cb1f9ae7fc408`) was made with `ilium plugin sign --signed-at "2026-10-12 10:00:00"` and the serialisation of PKG-650. It holds the entries `manifest.json`, `server.wasm` and `signature`, with the signature document shown in the section [The signature entry](#the-signature-entry).

### Negative vectors

Each row changes the vector and expects a refusal.

| Id | Change | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| [PKG-248] | One byte of `manifest.json` changed (and the CRC repaired) | `manifest.signature-invalid` |
| [PKG-249] | One byte of `server.wasm` changed, manifest unchanged | `manifest.file-hash` (stage 5, before the signature) |
| [PKG-250] | One byte of the signature value changed | `manifest.signature-invalid` |
| [PKG-251] | The prefix `ilium-plugin-signature-v2` used to sign | `manifest.signature-invalid` |
| [PKG-252] | The same key signs with publisher id `other` but the document says `example` | `manifest.signature-invalid` |
| [PKG-253] | The document lists `publisher_id: "other"` and the plugin id is `example.minimal` | `manifest.id-publisher` |
| [PKG-254] | `format` is `ilium-sig/2` | `package.signature-format` |
| [PKG-255] | A key not in the trust store, non-interactive, no `--trust` | `trust.key-unknown` |
| [PKG-256] | The key is in the store with display name "Other Labs" | `manifest.publisher-mismatch` |
| [PKG-257] | The key is revoked as `compromised` | `trust.key-revoked` |
| [PKG-258] | An installed `example.minimal` signed by key A, an update signed by key B, no rotation | `package.publisher-key-changed` |

## Edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Two valid signatures, one trusted and one not | The trusted one decides. The package is T2 |
| The same key listed twice in `signatures` | Refused with `package.signature-format` |
| The trust store file is unreadable | The effective set from that store is empty. Signed packages become untrusted. A warning is shown |
| The clock is wrong | No decision depends on the clock, except a future `effective` time of a revocation |
| The publisher edits the manifest after signing | The signature fails. Pack again, then sign again |
