# Install and manage plugins

## Install and manage plugins

This page shows how to install a plugin from a file, trust its publisher, turn it on and off, update it, remove it, and see what it is doing. It covers the Plugins tab in Settings and the matching `ilium plugin` commands. The exact rules for each step are in [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/) and the [CLI reference](/pages/reference-plugin-cli/); this page keeps to what you see and what you decide.

Contract version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. Requirement ids have the form `[USR-nnn]`, collected in [User and administrator requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-user-admin/).

<div class="note">
<p>Decision status. The platform is not implemented. Ilium ships no store, marketplace or registry; a registry is optional (decision D27). A plugin is a local <code>.iliumpkg</code> file that someone gave you.</p>
</div>

### Contents

- Before you start
- Install from a file
- Trust a publisher
- Review the permissions
- First start of a bundled plugin
- Turn a plugin on or off
- Update a plugin
- Remove a plugin
- Look at a plugin
- Settings and the recovery page
- Errors
- Edge cases
- Requirements

### Before you start

You need a package file, for example `notes.iliumpkg`. Check three things first.

- You are on Linux. On Windows and macOS only the bundled plugins run, and the install is refused with "Cannot install <name> <version>."
- You know who made the file. Ilium cannot tell whether a plugin is useful or honest. It can only tell whether the file is intact and whether a key you trust signed it.
- Your administrator has not locked plugins on this machine. If they have, the install says "Blocked by policy". See [Administration guide](/pages/guide-administration/).

Installing needs no network access and does not need administrator rights. Everything is stored in your own folders. See [Plugin files on disk](/pages/reference-plugin-files/).

### Install from a file

There are two ways. Both run the same checks.

1. In the tree, press `Ctrl+B` then `:` to open Settings. Choose **Plugins**, select **Install from file**, and enter the path of the file. Press `Enter`.
2. In a terminal: `ilium plugin install notes.iliumpkg`.

Ilium checks the file before any code in it runs. A file that fails a check is not installed, and the error names the check. The checks run in this order, and the first failure stops the install:

1. The file is a plugin package and every file inside has the length and hash that the package lists.
2. The signature, if any, verifies, and the signer is a key you trust or that you are now asked to trust.
3. The version of the plugin interface fits this version of Ilium.
4. The description of the plugin (the manifest) is valid.
5. Your administrator's policy allows this plugin.
6. You see the permission review and answer it.
7. The files are unpacked and prepared, then recorded.

The complete list with every error code is in [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/#the-install-pipeline).

- [USR-010] Installing MUST NOT run any code of the package before the user has answered the permission review. Test: install a package whose start function writes a file, decline the review, and assert that the file does not exist.
- [USR-011] A failed install MUST leave the installed plugins and their settings unchanged and MUST print one error that names the failed check. Test: install a package with a bad file hash, list plugins before and after, and compare.

Without a terminal, for example in a script, the review cannot be shown. Then `--yes` accepts all normal permissions, and a high-risk permission is accepted only if you name it with `--grant`.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin install notes.iliumpkg
Example Labs, signed (T2), 3F2A…9C01
Installed Notes 1.2.0.
It is on. 4 of 5 permissions given.
<span class="t-dim">Open Settings &gt; Plugins to change them.</span>
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. A successful install on the command line.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Trust a publisher

A signed (T2) package carries the signature of a publisher. A publisher is a person or company with a key. Ilium shows the key's fingerprint, a short code that identifies the key. Trust a publisher only if you have checked the fingerprint with them by another route, for example on their website over HTTPS or by phone. A fingerprint on the same page as the download proves nothing.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Trust this publisher? ──────────────────────╮</span>
│ Example Labs signed Notes 1.2.0.             │
│                                              │
│ Key fingerprint:                             │
│ 3F2A…9C01                                    │
│                                              │
│ You have not trusted this key before.        │
│ Trusting it lets you install and update      │
│ other packages that Example Labs signs.      │
│                                              │
│   [ Trust ]   [ Details ]   [ Cancel ]       │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The trust prompt for an unknown key.</figcaption>
</figure>

Choose **Details** to see the full fingerprint, 32 characters in 8 groups of 4. Choose **Cancel** and the install stops: nothing is installed. A trusted key is stored in your own trust list. You can manage the list with `ilium plugin trust list`, `ilium plugin trust add <publisher.pub>` and `ilium plugin trust remove <publisher>`. Removing a key does not remove the plugins that it signed. They stay installed and show `untrusted`; Ilium does not update them silently, because updates are always your decision.

- [USR-120] Ilium MUST show the full key fingerprint on request and the short form (first 4 and last 4 characters joined by an ellipsis) in the prompt, and MUST NOT trust a key without an explicit user answer. Test: install a package signed by an unknown key and assert that the prompt appears and that declining installs nothing.
- [USR-121] Removing a trusted key MUST NOT remove, disable or change any installed plugin, and MUST mark plugins that it signed as `untrusted` in `ilium plugin list`. Test: remove the key and list.
- [USR-122] An update of a T2 plugin MUST be signed by a trusted key. A key that signed the installed version MUST NOT be replaced silently by a different key. Test: install version 1 signed by key A, then offer version 2 signed by unknown key B, and assert that the trust prompt appears and that the dialog names both fingerprints.

Unsigned packages (T3) carry no signature. They need `--allow-unsigned`. They get a `dev` badge in the list and the permissions of a T2 plugin at most. Install one only if you built it or reviewed it yourself.

### Review the permissions

After the checks, Ilium shows one dialog with every permission the plugin asks for. The dialog is drawn by Ilium. A plugin cannot draw it or change it. Rows marked HIGH start unchecked. Leave a row unchecked if you do not see why the plugin needs it. The plugin installs anyway, and calls that need that permission fail with `not-permitted`. The dialog and the wording of every row are in [Security](/pages/security/#verifying-a-package). The plain meaning of every row is in [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/).

A package that fills other plugins' extension points shows an extra group, **Adds to other plugins**. A package that replaces a core plugin asks one more question. Read both carefully: they change what Ilium does by itself. See [The Extensions tab](/pages/user-extensions-tab/).

- [USR-012] The review dialog MUST list every requested permission, MUST start HIGH rows unchecked, and MUST record exactly the checked rows. Test: install a package with three normal and two HIGH rows, accept the defaults, and assert that the grant file holds three granted and two declined entries.
- [USR-013] The plugin MUST be on after a successful install, unless the user chose to leave it off. Test: install, then run `ilium plugin list` and assert the state.

### First start of a bundled plugin

Bundled plugins (T1) need no install. A few of them ask for a high-risk ability the first time they need it, for example to read your terminal history. Ilium shows one prompt for the plugin with its high-risk rows.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ First start: Voice ─────────────────────────╮</span>
│ Voice wants these extra permissions:         │
│                                              │
│ [ ] Use the microphone <span class="t-dim">…………………</span> audio.capture │
│ [ ] Run the program say <span class="t-dim">…………</span> process.run:say │
│                                              │
│ You can change this later in Settings &gt;      │
│ Plugins &gt; Voice &gt; Capabilities.              │
│                                              │
│  Enter Allow selected      Esc Not now       │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The first-start prompt of a bundled plugin.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Allow selected** gives the checked rows. **Not now** gives none and asks again at the next start. It asks at most 3 more times, then stops asking. The plugin works without those abilities, with those features unavailable. You can give them later in the Capabilities tab.

- [USR-014] The first-start prompt MUST appear at most once per start, MUST NOT block other plugins, and after **Not now** MUST appear at most 3 more times in total. Test: answer Not now at four consecutive starts and assert that the fifth start shows no prompt.

### Turn a plugin on or off

Select the plugin in **Settings > Plugins** and press `Space`. Or run `ilium plugin disable <id>` and `ilium plugin enable <id>`. Turning a plugin off stops it, hides what it added, and keeps its permissions, settings and data. Turning it on starts it again and resets its failure count.

If a plugin keeps failing, Ilium turns it off by itself. It restarts a failing plugin after 1 s, then after 5 s, and at the third failure within 10 minutes it stays off and the row shows the reason. Turning it on again resets the count. See [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/).

Row states in the Plugins tab are defined once, in [Settings, plugin rows](/pages/core-plugin-settings/#plugin-row-states). They are `On`, `Off`, `Failed`, `Restarting`, `Waiting for <owner>`, `Blocked by policy` and `Refused`. A plugin that shows `Failed` is explained in [Plugin health for users](/pages/user-plugin-health/).

### Update a plugin

There is no automatic update. To update, get the new package file and install it: `ilium plugin install notes-1.3.iliumpkg`, or **Install from file** in the Plugins tab. Ilium sees that the id is installed and treats it as an update. The review dialog then shows only what is new. Permissions you already gave stay as they are.

- A newer version asks for new permissions: only the new rows appear. New HIGH rows start unchecked.
- The update fails to start: Ilium puts the old version back and shows `Update failed, rolled back`. Your data is restored from the copy made before the update, if a data migration ran.
- A lower version needs `--allow-downgrade`. Ilium refuses a downgrade if the stored data is newer than the old version can read.

`ilium plugin update <file>` does the same as install but fails if the id is not yet installed. `ilium plugin rollback <id>` returns to the previous version.

- [USR-123] An update MUST show only permissions that the installed version did not request, and MUST keep the answers already given. Test: update from a package with two grants to one with three and assert one new row.
- [USR-124] A failed update MUST restore the previous version and its data and MUST show "Update failed, rolled back". Test: update to a package whose activation fails and assert the version in `ilium plugin list`.
- [USR-125] Ilium MUST NOT check for, download or install updates by itself. Test: with two plugins installed, run for one hour with request logging and assert that no update request is made.

### Remove a plugin

Select the plugin and press `d`, or run `ilium plugin uninstall <id>`. Ilium asks what to do with the plugin's data when a terminal is attached.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Remove Notes? ──────────────────────────────╮</span>
│ Notes 1.2.0 will be removed.                 │
│                                              │
│ Its permissions and cache are deleted.       │
│ Plugins that wait for it will pause.         │
│                                              │
│ What about its data and settings?            │
│  ( ) Keep them for a later reinstall         │
│  ( ) Delete them now (purge)                 │
│                                              │
│   [ Remove ]   [ Cancel ]                    │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The uninstall dialog.</figcaption>
</figure>

On the command line, `--keep-data` keeps the data and `--purge` deletes data, settings and log. The two flags exclude each other. Without a terminal and without a flag, the data is kept. A reinstall of the same id asks for permissions again and may read the kept data. The table of what each choice deletes is in [Plugin files on disk](/pages/reference-plugin-files/#what-each-action-leaves-behind).

Removing a plugin has effects on other plugins. They stop being fed by it but they are not deleted:

| What depended on the removed plugin | What happens |
|---|---|
| A plugin that fills an extension point owned by the removed plugin | It becomes dormant and shows "Waiting for <owner>". It wakes up when the owner is installed again |
| A plugin that requires a service of the removed plugin | It shows "Waiting for <owner>" and its calls to the service return `unavailable` |
| An extension that the removed plugin filled in another plugin | It disappears from that point at once |
| A core plugin that the removed plugin replaced | The core plugin turns back on. Its own data was never touched |
| A pane of a kind the removed plugin provided | The pane stays in the tree and shows a placeholder: "Plugin <name> is not installed" with the kind and the plugin id |
| Keys, menu items, status segments and toolbar buttons the plugin added | They disappear |
| Your order of extensions for the plugin's points | The entries for the removed plugin are deleted |

- [USR-140] Uninstall MUST first mark the plugin as being removed, then stop it, then delete files, and after a crash the next start MUST finish the removal. Test: kill the host after the mark and start again.
- [USR-141] Uninstall MUST NOT delete the data of any other plugin and MUST NOT remove trusted keys. Test: compare the other plugins' folders before and after.
- [USR-142] A pane whose plugin is gone MUST stay in the tree with a placeholder and MUST come back to life when the plugin is installed again. Test: remove, check the placeholder, reinstall, check the pane.
- [USR-143] Plugins that depend on the removed plugin MUST become dormant, not failed, and MUST wake up when it returns. Test: remove the owner, check the state of the dependent plugin, reinstall the owner.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-dim">Plugin Notes is not installed</span>
 
This pane was made by the plugin
com.example.notes (kind: notes).
 
Install the plugin again to see it,
or close this pane.
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. A pane left behind by a removed plugin.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Look at a plugin

| I want to see | In Settings > Plugins | On the command line |
|---|---|---|
| All plugins and their states | the list | `ilium plugin list` |
| One plugin in detail | select it, `Enter` | `ilium plugin info <id>` |
| Its permissions and their state | the Capabilities tab | `ilium plugin grants <id>` |
| What it logged | the Log tab | `ilium plugin logs <id> --tail 50` |
| How much it uses | the Details tab | `ilium plugin stats <id>` |

`ilium plugin list` prints one line per plugin, with the id, version, tier, state and the count of permissions given. Add `--json` for scripts.

### Settings and the recovery page

Each plugin can have its own settings pages inside Settings. Their values are saved as you change them. If a plugin's settings page cannot open, or a bad value stops Ilium from starting the plugin, the recovery page lists the plugin with seven actions, among them **Disable** and **Forget settings**. [Settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/#the-kernel-recovery-page) lists all seven. Forget settings deletes that plugin's values for this user and starts the plugin again with its defaults. It does not touch permissions or data. See [Settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/).

### Errors

| What you see | Code | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Cannot install <name> <version>. (on Windows or macOS) | `policy.tier-denied` | Use Linux for third-party plugins |
| The file is damaged | `package.manifest-missing` or `package.entry-unexpected`, `manifest.file-hash` | Download the file again and compare its checksum |
| The signature does not verify | `manifest.signature-invalid` | Do not install. Ask the publisher |
| The publisher key is not trusted and you declined | `trust.declined` | Trust the key after checking its fingerprint |
| The package is unsigned | `install.unsigned` | Add `--allow-unsigned` only for packages you reviewed |
| The plugin is for another interface version | `package.api-unsupported` | Get a version for your Ilium |
| Blocked by policy | `policy.blocked` | Ask your administrator |
| You declined the review | `install.review-declined` | Run the install again and accept what you need |
| Another install is running | `install.locked` | Wait and try again |
| The disk is full | `install.io` | Free space. Nothing was changed |

### Edge cases

- **Installing the same file twice** does nothing and succeeds. A different file with the same version fails with `install.same-version-different-content`.
- **Two Ilium windows** share the same plugins. A change in one appears in the other within 2 s.
- **The file moves while installing.** Ilium copies it first. Moving it does not harm the install.
- **A plugin id that starts with `ilium.`** is reserved. A third-party package with such an id is refused.
- **A plugin that wants a replaced core plugin** needs your confirmation. Declining installs the plugin without the replacement.

### See also

- [Plugins for users](/pages/user-plugins-overview/)
- [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/)

- [Troubleshooting plugins](/pages/user-troubleshooting/)
- [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/)
- [CLI reference](/pages/reference-plugin-cli/)
- [Security](/pages/security/)

API version checked: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Managing plugins

## Managing plugins

This page shows how to see what your plugins are doing, turn them on and off, deal with failures, and how an administrator restricts them.

Contract version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

### The Plugins screen

Open Settings, then Plugins. Each row shows the name, the tier, the version, the state and the health. Select a row to open its detail tabs.

| Tab | Shows |
|---|---|
| Overview | state, health, version, publisher, scope |
| Capabilities | grants, with a switch for each |
| Resources | memory, execution bucket, storage and disk use |
| Log | the last lines of the plugin log |
| Data | data size, buttons Clear cache and Delete data |

<figure>
<pre class="term"> Plugins
 Name              State    Health
 Notes             on       healthy
 Cursor trail      failed   failed
 Tickets           on       degraded
 [Enter] detail  [Space] on/off
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The Plugins list with a state and a health column.</figcaption>
</figure>

- [LIF-190] The Plugins screen MUST show state and health for each installed plugin, and a detail view with the five tabs. Test: render a fixture list.

### When a plugin fails

After a failure the plugin restarts after a short delay (see [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/#failure-counting-and-restart)). After the third failure in a window it is turned off, and the row shows "failed". You see a notice with three buttons.

1. Enable again. This clears the failure count and starts the plugin.
2. Open log. Shows the lines that explain the failure.
3. Uninstall.

If the failed plugin replaced a built-in one, the built-in plugin is turned on again and a notice says so.

- [LIF-191] Enable on a failed plugin MUST clear the failure window. Test: fail, enable, fail twice more and assert it is not disabled.
- [LIF-192] A replacement disabled by failure MUST re-enable the built-in plugin with a notice. Test: fail a replacement.

### The recovery page

The recovery page lists plugins with state and last failure. It offers: enable or disable, uninstall, reset failures, forget settings, and start in safe mode ([Safe mode](/pages/user-safe-mode-and-troubleshooting/)). Open it with `Ctrl+Alt+R`.

### Update, rollback and uninstall

Select Update on a row, or run `ilium plugin update <id>`. If the new version fails to start within the trial, Ilium puts the old version back. Uninstall asks whether to keep or delete the plugin data ([Plugin files](/pages/reference-plugin-files/)). Details are in [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/).

### Administrator policy

An administrator controls plugins for all users with `/etc/ilium/policy.toml` on Linux. Keys are in [Plugin policy](/pages/reference-plugin-policy/). A plugin that the policy blocks shows "Blocked by policy" and its data stays. A policy may forbid third-party plugins, limit tiers, allow or deny publishers and ids, and forbid grants. On macOS the file is in `/Library/Application Support/ilium/` and on Windows in `%PROGRAMDATA%\ilium\`.

The policy can also block exact versions with `policy.blocked`, force safe mode, or pin a version. These keys are planned and are not in the first policy format. Until they exist, use `plugins.deny_ids` and `plugins.allow_ids`.

- [LIF-193] A plugin blocked by policy MUST show "Blocked by policy" with the code and MUST keep its data. Test: add its id to `denied_ids`.

### See also

- [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/)
- [Safe mode and recovery](/pages/user-safe-mode-and-troubleshooting/)
- [Health and watchdog](/pages/reference-health-and-watchdog/)
- [Security](/pages/security/)
- [Requirements, lifecycle and operations](/pages/reference-requirements-lifecycle-ops/)

API version checked: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Permissions explained

## Permissions explained

A plugin can only do what you let it do. Each ability is a permission, called a grant in the technical pages. This page explains in plain words how permissions work, what every permission means, which ones are risky, and what happens when you say no. Read it before you install a plugin that you did not write.

Contract version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. Requirement ids have the form `[USR-nnn]`, collected in [User and administrator requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-user-admin/). The technical table of every grant is [Capability reference](/pages/reference-capabilities/).

<div class="note">
<p>Decision status. The platform is not implemented. The wording of each permission in the review dialog is a working text that the platform owner confirms.</p>
</div>

### Contents

- How permissions work
- What needs no permission
- Risk levels
- Every permission in plain words
- Questions that are not permissions
- Change a permission later
- What happens when a call is refused
- Limits that protect you
- Errors and edge cases
- Requirements

### How permissions work

- A permission belongs to one plugin and one side of it. A plugin has up to three sides: the server side runs in the background, the client side draws things on your screen, and the scene side draws animated backgrounds. A permission given to the server side does not carry to the client side.
- A permission belongs to you, not to a project. You give it once. It applies in every project you open. Permissions are stored in your own Ilium data, never inside a project folder, so a project you share does not share your permissions. See [Plugin files on disk](/pages/reference-plugin-files/).
- A plugin lists what it wants in its manifest. You see that list in the review dialog when you install. A plugin cannot get a permission that it did not list.
- You can say yes to some rows and no to others. The plugin installs either way.
- You can change your mind at any time in the **Capabilities** tab of the plugin, or with `ilium plugin grants`.

- [USR-020] A permission MUST apply to one plugin and one side, MUST be stored per user, and MUST NOT be shared through a project folder. Test: grant a permission to the client side only, then call it from the server side and assert `not-permitted`.
- [USR-021] A plugin MUST NOT obtain a permission that its manifest does not list. Test: call a host function whose permission is not in the manifest and assert that the call traps with `host.capability-not-requested`.

### What needs no permission

Some abilities cannot reach anything that is yours, so they need no permission and never appear in the dialog. Every plugin has them on every side that carries them:

- Writing lines to its own log, and reading the clock.
- Timers that call back into the plugin.
- Keeping its own notes (storage, up to 16 MiB in each bucket) and its own settings values.
- Compression, image decoding, hashing and text rasterizing.
- Reading and writing its own data folder and cache folder, and reading its own package files.
- Sending messages between its own server side and client side.
- Asking Ilium to draw one of its own views again.

Limits apply even to these: a plugin may write at most 200 log lines per second (extra lines are dropped), and at most 16 MiB to each storage bucket. See [Always-granted capabilities](/pages/capability-always-granted/).

### Risk levels

The dialog marks each row as normal or HIGH. HIGH means the ability could do harm or reveal private information if the plugin were careless or dishonest.

| Level | What it means | Start state in the dialog |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Works inside Ilium, or reads little of yours | checked |
| HIGH | Can read private text, type for you, run programs, reach other sessions or change many things | unchecked |

A quick way to judge a row: ask what the plugin is for. A note-taking plugin that asks to run programs, or a theme that asks to read your terminal history, is asking for more than it should need. Leave the row unchecked, or do not install the plugin.

- [USR-022] The review dialog MUST start every HIGH row unchecked and every normal row checked. Test: open the dialog for a package with both and assert the initial states.

### Every permission in plain words

Names in the first column are the strings you see in the dialog and in `ilium plugin grants`. A name with `<...>` takes an argument: the dialog shows the real value. The last column says what happens if you say no. In all cases the plugin keeps running; only the calls that need the permission fail.

#### The project tree and panes

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `tree.read` | See the groups, panes and their names in your project tree | normal |
| `tree.write` | Add, rename or move items you did not ask it to touch | normal |
| `tree.metadata` | Attach its own notes to tree items | normal |
| `tree.decorate` | Add badges and colors to tree rows | normal |
| `tree.restructure` | Reorganize the tree on a large scale | HIGH |
| `tree.attention` | Mark items as needing your attention | normal |
| `panes.read` | See pane sizes, titles and focus | normal |
| `panes.create` | Open new panes | normal |
| `panes.signal` | Send signals to the programs in panes | HIGH |
| `panes.lifecycle` | Close, restart or kill panes | HIGH |
| `panes.provide-kind` | Offer its own kind of pane, like a notes pane | normal |

#### Terminals and agents

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `terminal.read-screen` | Read the text you see in a terminal pane | normal |
| `terminal.read-cells` | Read the text with its colors and styles | normal |
| `terminal.history` | Read scrollback, the older lines that scrolled out of view | HIGH |
| `terminal.output-filter` | Change terminal output before you see it, such as hiding noise | normal |
| `terminal.write` | Type into a terminal as if you did | HIGH |
| `terminal.input-lock` | Block your keyboard for a moment while it acts | HIGH |
| `terminal.raw-input` | Receive every key you press in a terminal | HIGH |
| `terminal.pointer` | See mouse movement over a terminal | normal |
| `agent.read` | See which coding agents run, and whether each is working or idle | normal |
| `agent.read-prompts` | Read what you typed to an agent | HIGH |
| `agent.control` | Send commands to an agent | HIGH |
| `agent.signatures` | Add rules that tell Ilium how to recognize an agent | normal |
| `agent.transcript` | Read the saved conversation of an agent | HIGH |

Terminal text can hold passwords, tokens and private notes. Terminal rows are the ones to read with care.

#### Editors, screen and keys

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `editor.read` | Read the text of open editor panes | normal |
| `editor.edit` | Change the text of open editor panes | normal |
| `editor.provide` | Offer its own editor, for a new file type | HIGH |
| `ui.panels` | Show its own panels and settings pages | normal |
| `ui.chrome` | Add items to menus, toolbars, status bar and tree rows | normal |
| `keys.intercept` | See your keys before Ilium does and swallow some | HIGH |
| `keymap.read` | Read your key bindings | normal |
| `commands.invoke:<pattern>` | Run Ilium commands. The pattern names which ones. A bare `*` means all | HIGH when `*`, otherwise normal |

#### Files and folders

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `fs.read:<scope>` | Read files in one named place. The place is a scope, see below | normal; HIGH for agent transcripts |
| `fs.write:<scope>` | Create and change files in one named place | HIGH, except its own data and cache |
| `fs.watch:<scope>` | Be told when files in a place change | normal |
| `fs.pick` | Ask you to choose a file or folder, then read that one only | normal |

The scopes you will see: `project` (the project folder you launched Ilium in), `worktrees` (the folder of Git worktrees), `agent-sessions:<agent>` (an agent's saved conversations), `agent-config:<agent>` (an agent's settings), `minecraft-saves`, and `path:<template>` (a custom place built from your home, config, data, cache, project or worktree folders). Its own `data`, `cache` and `package` folders are always allowed. A plugin sees the granted place and nothing around it.

Reading the project folder is a normal-risk permission, because the plugin cannot read anything outside it. Writing there is HIGH.

#### Network, programs and background work

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `http:<host-pattern>` | Talk to one named website or server | normal |
| `http:setting:<key>` | Talk to the host that you type into one of its settings | normal; asks you for each new host |
| `jobs.run` | Run work in the background | normal |
| `process.run:<program>` | Run one named program. Never a wildcard | HIGH |
| `process.long-lived` | Keep a started program running in the background. Needs `process.run` | HIGH |

A started program runs in the same sandbox as the plugin, with no network. Stopping the plugin ends the program.

#### AI, services and messages

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `inference` | Use your configured AI providers to answer a prompt | normal |
| `inference.provide` | Offer itself as an AI provider | normal |
| `inference.embed` | Turn text into embeddings with your AI providers | normal |
| `services.use:<name>` | Call a named service of another plugin | normal |
| `services.provide:<name>` | Offer a named service to other plugins | normal |
| `messages.peer:<plugin-id>` | Exchange messages with one named other plugin | normal |
| `topics.subscribe:<pattern>` | Listen to a named stream of events | normal; HIGH for a bare `*` |
| `journal.read` | Read the host's record of recent events | normal |
| `extensions.provide:<id>/<point>` | Offer its own extension point | normal |
| `extensions.contribute:<id>/<point>` | Fill another plugin's extension point | normal; HIGH if the point is marked high |

#### Sound, alerts, links and the clipboard

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `sound.play` | Play sounds | normal |
| `notify.desktop` | Send desktop notifications | normal |
| `notify.toast` | Show small messages inside Ilium | normal |
| `open-external` | Ask to open a link; you confirm each site | normal |
| `clipboard.read` | Read what you copied | HIGH |
| `clipboard.write` | Put text on the clipboard | normal |
| `audio.capture` | Use the microphone | HIGH |
| `audio.loopback` | Record the sound your computer plays | HIGH |
| `audio.playback` | Play audio streams | normal |
| `media.video` | Show and decode video | normal |
| `location.observer` | Know your approximate location for scenes | HIGH |
| `location.geocode` | Turn a place name into a position, through an online service | normal; asks you first |

#### Sessions, workspace and settings

| Permission | In plain words | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `sessions.cross` | Reach other Ilium sessions on this machine | HIGH |
| `workspace.manage` | Create and remove worktrees and workspaces | HIGH |
| `cli.contribute` | Add its own `ilium` command | normal |
| `http-api.route:<path>` | Answer requests at one path of the local HTTP API | normal |
| `settings.contribute:<tab>` | Add rows to one named built-in Settings tab | normal |
| `settings.read-kernel:<tab>` | Read the values of one built-in Settings tab | normal; HIGH for the api tab |
| `settings.read-all`, `settings.write-all` | Read or change every setting. Bundled plugins only | HIGH |
| `plugins.manage` | Install, remove and turn plugins on and off. Bundled plugins only | HIGH |
| `help.read` | Read the Ilium help topics | normal |
| `gpu.kernels` | Run graphics code. Development builds only | normal |

Rows marked bundled-only or development-only are never shown to you for third-party plugins. A third-party package that asks for them fails to install with `manifest.grant-tier`.

- [USR-080] The Capabilities tab MUST show the plain wording, the grant string, the risk and the state (granted, declined, revoked) of every permission the plugin requests. Test: open the tab for a plugin with ten requested grants and compare.
- [USR-081] A package that requests a bundled-only grant MUST fail to install with `manifest.grant-tier`. Test: request `plugins.manage` in a T2 package.
- [USR-082] A grant string MUST be shown exactly as it will be matched, including its argument, so that the user can see the host, program or place. Test: request `http:api.example.com` and assert the dialog shows that string.

### Questions that are not permissions

Four features ask you at the moment of first use, because Ilium only knows the target then. The answer is stored with the plugin and you can withdraw it in the Capabilities tab.

| Feature | When you are asked | If you say no |
|---|---|---|
| `open-external` | The first time a plugin opens a link to each website | The link does not open |
| `http:setting:<key>` | When the setting holds a host the plugin has not used before | The request fails and the host is not contacted |
| `location.geocode` | The first time a plugin looks up a place. The online service is Photon, with Nominatim as fallback | Calls return `not-permitted` |
| Bundled plugin with HIGH rows | Once, at its first start | It runs without them. You are asked again at the next start, at most 3 more times |

- [USR-083] Ilium MUST ask the user before it opens a link from a plugin, for each target website and plugin, and MUST remember the answer. Test: open two links to the same site and one to another site and count prompts: two.
- [USR-084] Ilium MUST NOT contact a host from a `http:setting` grant until the user has confirmed that host. Test: set a new host in a setting, call, and assert no connection before the answer.

### Change a permission later

Open **Settings > Plugins**, select the plugin, choose **Capabilities**. Each row has a switch. Or run:

```sh
ilium plugin grants com.example.notes
ilium plugin grants com.example.notes --revoke clipboard.read
ilium plugin grants com.example.notes --grant clipboard.read
```

Turning a permission off takes effect at once. A call that is running when you turn it off returns `revoked`, and the plugin is started again with the smaller set, so its screens refresh. Turning a HIGH permission on asks you to confirm. A plugin cannot give itself a permission that its manifest does not list: `--grant` fails with `grants.not-requested`.

- [USR-085] A revoke MUST take effect for calls started after it, MUST make calls in flight return `revoked`, and MUST restart the plugin with the smaller set. Test: start a long call, revoke, and assert `revoked` and a restart in the log.
- [USR-086] A HIGH grant MUST ask for confirmation in the attached client. Test: run `ilium plugin grants <id> --grant terminal.write` with a client attached and assert the prompt.

### What happens when a call is refused

The plugin keeps running. The call returns `not-permitted` (declined), or `revoked` (you turned it off). The host writes one line into the plugin's log:

```text
2026-10-12 09:14:02 warn  com.example.notes refused tree.restructure by restructure (declined)
```

The form is `refused <grant> by <function> (<reason>)`, and the reason is one word such as `declined`, `revoked`, `not-granted`, `policy` or `offline`. You can read the log in the plugin's **Log** tab or with `ilium plugin logs <id>`. A plugin that depends on a declined permission may show an empty panel or a message; that is the plugin's own design, not an Ilium fault.

A call to something the plugin never listed is different. It is a bug in the plugin, not a refusal. The call traps, the plugin instance ends, and Ilium restarts it after a delay. Repeated traps turn the plugin off. See [Troubleshooting plugins](/pages/user-troubleshooting/).

### Limits that protect you

Even with permissions, Ilium limits what a plugin can do to your screen and session:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Toasts from one plugin | 3 per 10 s |
| Input lock (`terminal.input-lock`) | at most 2 s at a time |
| Clipboard use | a footer indicator stays 3 s after each use |
| Log lines | 200 per second |
| Storage | 16 MiB per bucket |

- [USR-087] Ilium MUST show a footer indicator for 3 s after a plugin reads or writes the clipboard. Test: read the clipboard from a test plugin and watch the footer.
- [USR-088] Ilium MUST drop toasts beyond 3 per 10 s per plugin and MUST end an input lock after 2 s. Test: send ten toasts at once, count the visible ones; lock input and time the release.

### Errors and edge cases

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| You decline every row | The plugin installs with the always-granted set only |
| The plugin lists a permission that does not exist | Install fails with `manifest.grant-unknown` |
| The plugin asks for a permission its side cannot hold | Install fails with `manifest.grant-side` |
| An update asks for a new permission | Only the new row is shown |
| Your administrator forbids a permission | The row shows "Blocked by your administrator", off and locked. See [Plugin policy](/pages/reference-plugin-policy/) |
| You uninstall, then reinstall | Permissions are asked again |

### See also

- [Plugins for users](/pages/user-plugins-overview/)
- [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/)
- [Plugin privacy](/pages/user-privacy/)
- [Capability reference](/pages/reference-capabilities/)
- [Security](/pages/security/)

API version checked: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Plugin health for users

## Plugin health for users

A plugin can slow Ilium down or stop working without telling you. Ilium watches every plugin and shows one health word for each. This page explains the words, how to see the reason, and what to do. It uses no technical background.

## You will need

- Ilium with at least one plugin installed. The core plugins that ship with Ilium appear here too.

## The health words

| Word | What it means | What you can do |
|---|---|---|
| healthy | The plugin works and answers on time | Nothing |
| dormant | The plugin is on and waits until something needs it | Nothing |
| degraded | The plugin works but is slow, busy or was restarted once | Open the detail and read the reason. Often it needs no action |
| restarting | The plugin failed and Ilium will start it again in a moment | Wait a few seconds |
| failed | The plugin failed three times in ten minutes and Ilium turned it off | Read the log. Turn it on again with the Space key when you want to try again |
| disabled | You, or your administrator, turned the plugin off | Turn it on in the Plugins screen if the policy allows |
| refused | Ilium would not load the plugin, for example because it needs permissions that your policy forbids | Read the reason in the detail |

## See the health of every plugin

Open Settings, then Plugins. The Health column shows the word.

<figure>
<pre class="term">┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Plugins                                      │
│ Name            State    Health              │
│ Notes           on       healthy             │
│ Tickets         on       degraded            │
│ Cursor trail    on       restarting          │
│ Sketch pad      on       failed              │
│                                              │
│ [Enter] detail   [R] restart   [Space] on/off│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The Plugins list with a Health column.</figcaption>
</figure>

## See why a plugin is degraded

Select the plugin and press Enter. The detail view shows the reason with numbers.

<figure>
<pre class="term">┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Tickets: health                              │
│ Health      degraded                         │
│ Why         near-misses (7 in 5 min)         │
│ Slowest     views.render 9.1 ms of 10 ms     │
│ Queue       812 of 1,024 events              │
│ Failures    0 in the last 10 minutes         │
│                                              │
│ [L] open log   [Esc] back                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The health detail of one plugin.</figcaption>
</figure>

The reasons you can see are:

- **Near-misses.** The plugin answered, but close to the time limit, several times in the last five minutes. If Ilium feels slow while this plugin is busy, turn the plugin off to test.
- **Busy queue.** Many messages wait for the plugin. This passes when the plugin catches up.
- **Held by its quota.** The plugin used its share of time or data and Ilium made it wait. It continues on its own.
- **Waiting for memory.** Ilium has too many plugins running at once. Turn off one you do not use.
- **Restarted.** The plugin failed once and started again. If it happens again, the word changes to failed.

## What happens to what the plugin showed

When a plugin stops, the badges and rows that it added stay on screen for up to a minute, dimmed. This lets you keep working. If the plugin comes back, the items refresh. If it does not, they disappear. A dimmed item that you select shows "plugin is restarting".

## What Ilium never does

Ilium does not send health data anywhere. The numbers stay on your computer. See [Telemetry and plugin health](/pages/reference-host-telemetry/) for what is measured. A health report that you share is made by you, with `ilium plugin status` or the Diagnostics report, and you choose what to send.

## If Ilium itself is slow or does not start

Start Ilium with `--safe-mode` (the alias `--safe-plugins` does the same) to run only the bundled plugins, or with `--no-plugins` to run none. See [Safe mode and troubleshooting](/pages/user-safe-mode-and-troubleshooting/). The recovery page lists the plugins that are not healthy first.

## See also

- [Managing plugins](/pages/user-managing-plugins/) for turning plugins on and off.
- [Troubleshooting](/pages/user-troubleshooting/) for common problems.
- [Health and watchdog](/pages/reference-health-and-watchdog/) for the exact rules.

API version checked: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Plugin security and privacy for users

## Plugin security and privacy for users

This page is for people who use Ilium, not for people who write plugins. It says what Ilium and its plugins keep on your computer, what can leave it, how to read the install screen, and what to do if a plugin misbehaves. The technical rules behind it are in [Security model](/pages/security/).

### You will need

- Ilium with the plugin platform.
- To read the install screen, nothing else. To delete data, the Settings screen or the `ilium plugin` command.

## What Ilium collects

**[SEC-260]** Ilium and its bundled plugins send no telemetry, crash reports or usage data. If a future version collects anything, it will be opt-in, off by default, and listed on this page before it ships.

A third-party plugin can send data only to hosts you allowed in its install screen, and only through the rules in [Network egress](/pages/reference-network-egress/).

## What is stored on your computer

**[SEC-261]** The table lists every place the plugin platform writes. A file in this table is created by Ilium and is readable only by you.

| What | Where (Linux) | Retention | How to delete |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plugin files | `~/.local/share/ilium/plugins/` | Until uninstall | `ilium plugin uninstall <id>` |
| Plugin data and cache | Inside the plugin's own folder | Until uninstall or cache eviction | Uninstall, or Settings > Plugins > Clear data |
| Storage buckets | The plugin's data folder | Per bucket policy | Clear data |
| Grants and consents | `~/.local/state/ilium/grants.json`, `consents.json` | Until you revoke or uninstall | Settings > Plugins |
| Trusted publisher keys | `~/.local/state/ilium/trust.json` | Until you remove them | `ilium plugin trust remove` |
| Secrets | OS keyring, or `~/.local/state/ilium/secrets.json` | Until you forget them | Settings > Plugins > Secrets > Forget |
| Plugin logs | Ilium's log folder | Rotated; the newest 10 MiB per plugin | `ilium plugin logs --clear <id>` |
| Audit log | `~/.local/state/ilium/audit/` | 365 days or 64 MiB | Delete the folder; the next start begins a new chain |
| Privacy log | `~/.local/state/ilium/privacy/inference.jsonl` | 90 days or 16 MiB | Settings > Privacy > Clear |
| Pane journal | Ilium state folder, per session | Newest entries only | Closes with the session |
| Session snapshots | `<project>/.ilium/sessions/` | Until you delete them | Delete the file |

## What can leave your computer

**[SEC-263]** Only the features in the inventory of [Network egress](/pages/reference-network-egress/) send data off the machine. The two that matter most:

- **AI model requests.** The default provider is the remote Kilo Gateway, with no key. Text a plugin sends to the AI model goes to that service. Choose a local provider in Settings > API if you do not want that.
- **Place lookups.** Place names go to a public geocoding service, after you agree once.

**[SEC-264]** The install screen of a plugin that asks for `inference` names the provider that is selected now and says `remote` or `local`.

### The privacy log

**[SEC-265]** Every request to an AI model made through Ilium is recorded in the privacy log, `inference.jsonl`, one JSON object per line: `ts` (UTC, ISO 8601), `plugin` (id), `purpose` (a short label the plugin gives), `provider`, `model`, `tokens_in`, `tokens_out`, `bytes_out`, `bytes_in`, `local` (true or false). It never contains the text. Retention is 90 days or 16 MiB, whichever is smaller. Settings > Privacy shows the log; `ilium privacy log [--since <time>] [--plugin <id>]` prints it as JSONL. The privacy log belongs to the kernel and a replacement of the inference plugin cannot disable it.

## Reading the install screen

- **HIGH** means the permission can change things outside the plugin or read sensitive data (running programs, reading scrollback, typing into terminals). A HIGH row starts off. Turn it on only if you need the feature it names.
- **This plugin can read your data and send data out** means the plugin asked for something that reads your terminal, files or agents, and for something that sends data to a server. Many useful plugins do. Check that you know the plugin and its publisher.
- **Details** (press Tab) shows the full key fingerprint, the file hashes and the publisher's contact.
- **Signed (T2)** means a publisher you trust signed it. **dev** means it is unsigned and runs from a local file.
- The publisher name is what the publisher wrote about itself. Only the key fingerprint is verified.

You can change your mind any time: Settings > Plugins > Capabilities revokes one permission, and **Revoke all** removes them all. If a plugin crashes Ilium or you doubt it, start Ilium with `ilium --safe-mode` to turn off all third-party plugins, then uninstall the one you doubt ([Security response](/pages/reference-security-response/)).

To report a bad plugin, use the contact in its Details. For a flaw in Ilium itself, follow [Security response](/pages/reference-security-response/).

## Rules for plugin authors

**[SEC-266]** A plugin that sends telemetry MUST make it opt-in, through a setting that is visible in its settings page and that defaults to off.

**[SEC-267]** A plugin that collects or sends data other than what its function needs MUST declare it in the optional manifest key `data_use`, a list of objects `{ "what": string, "where": string, "purpose": string, "opt_in": bool }`, with at most 8 entries and 200 characters per field. The review dialog shows each entry under **Data this plugin collects**. The key is part of contract 0.1.0; a host that does not know it refuses the manifest with `manifest.unknown-key`, so the key is listed in the [Manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/).

**[SEC-268]** A plugin SHOULD set `security_contact` (an email address or an https URL, at most 200 characters) in its manifest; Details shows it.

## Edge cases

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Local provider selected | `inference` rows say `local`; nothing leaves the machine |
| Offline switch on | AI requests and lookups fail with `offline` |
| Privacy log disk full | Oldest records are dropped first, a notice is shown |
| You clear the audit log | The next start begins a new hash chain, recorded in the first record |

### See also

- [Security model](/pages/security/)
- [Network egress](/pages/reference-network-egress/)
- [Secrets](/pages/reference-secrets/)
- [Audit log](/pages/reference-audit-log/)
- [Grant review and consent](/pages/reference-grant-review-and-consent/)

Contract: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Plugin store

## Plugin store

The plugin store is where you find plugins in a registry, read about them and install them. A registry is a list of plugins that someone runs and signs. You use the store from Settings, Plugins, Browse, or from the command line. This page shows both.

### You will need

- At least one registry set up. Ilium ships with none. Add one with `ilium plugin registry add <url> --root-key <key_id>`, or ask your administrator ([Plugin administration](/pages/guide-plugin-administration/)).
- To install, read [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/).

Requirement ids such as `PKG-530` are in [Requirements: manifest and package](/pages/reference-requirements-manifest-package/).

## Search

Type words in the Browse tab, or run `ilium plugin search git --category tools`. Results show the name, publisher, latest version, categories and tier badge.

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-530] | The store MUST show one row per plugin id with name, publisher, latest version, tier badge and a short description. |
| [PKG-531] | The category filter MUST offer only the closed category list of [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/#search-and-categories). |
| [PKG-532] | With no registry configured the store MUST show the empty state "No registry is set up" with the command to add one. It MUST NOT contact the network. |
| [PKG-533] | Yanked versions MUST NOT appear in results. A deprecated plugin MUST show a badge and its successor. |
| [PKG-534] | User ratings are not shown (not in 0.1). |

<figure>
<pre class="term">╭  ≡ ● · Browse ───────────────────────────────╮
│ Search: git                                  │
│ Category: tools                              │
│                                              │
│ ▸ Git tools     Example Labs  1.4.2 T2       │
│   Branch and diff helpers.                   │
│ ▸ Git blame lens Acme        0.3.0 T3        │
│   Deprecated. Use Git tools.                 │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative, not generated. Browse tab with two results.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Read before you install

Open a row to see the description, the requested grants, the dependencies, the size, the publisher key fingerprint and whether the key is already trusted.

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-535] | The detail view MUST list every requested grant with its risk level, as the review dialog does. |
| [PKG-536] | The detail view MUST show the publisher id and key status: `trusted`, `unknown` or `revoked`. |
| [PKG-537] | A plugin with a revoked key or a blocked id MUST NOT have an Install button. It shows the reason. |

## Install, update and remove

Press Install, or run `ilium plugin install com.example.git-tools`. The review dialog opens. The store never installs without it. Update with the Update button or `ilium plugin update <id>`. Details: [Install and update](/pages/reference-install-and-update/).

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-538] | Install from the store MUST use the same pipeline and dialog as a file install. |
| [PKG-539] | The store MUST show an update badge when the registry has a newer allowed version. It MUST NOT install it unless the user chooses, or has set `auto_update = install`. |

## When the registry is unreachable

The store shows cached results with their age ("Updated 3 days ago"). Install of a cached package works only if the package file is in the cache.

| Id | Rule |
|---|---|
| [PKG-540] | When offline the store MUST show the cache age and mark the view as stale. |
| [PKG-541] | The store MUST refuse metadata older than the expiry rule and show `registry.metadata-expired`. |

## Edge cases

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Two registries list the same id | The default registry wins. The detail view names the source. |
| Search has no match | The view shows "No plugins found" and keeps the filters. |
| Policy blocks a plugin | The row shows "Blocked by your administrator". |

## See also

- [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/)
- [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/)
- [Plugin administration](/pages/guide-plugin-administration/)

# Plugins for users

## Plugins for users

This page is the start of the user and administrator manual for plugins. It explains in plain words what a plugin is, which plugins you already have, what you can do with them, and what can and cannot go wrong. If you write plugins, start with [What a plugin is](/pages/getting-started-overview/) instead.

Contract version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. Requirement ids have the form `[USR-nnn]`, collected in [User and administrator requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-user-admin/).

<div class="note">
<p>Decision status. The platform is not implemented yet. This page describes the behaviour that the manual specifies. The text is the specification that tests are derived from.</p>
</div>

### Contents

- What a plugin is
- The plugins you already have
- Where plugins come from
- Where plugins run
- What a plugin can do to you
- Where to manage plugins
- Common tasks
- Errors and edge cases
- Requirements

### What a plugin is

A plugin is a small program that adds to Ilium. It can add a pane, a setting, a command, a sound, a background scene or a step in something Ilium already does. A plugin is not a separate application. It runs inside Ilium, in a walled-off space, and it can only do what you allow.

Every feature that Ilium has today is also a plugin. Ilium ships and maintains 30 of them, called core plugins, and their ids start with `ilium.core.`. When you read "tree", "layout" or "Smart Copy" in the Ilium documentation, you are reading about a core plugin. You use them exactly as before.

- [USR-001] The user documentation MUST state that all 30 core plugins ship with Ilium and need no install. Test: search the page for the count 30 and the phrase "ship with Ilium".

### The plugins you already have

| Kind | Id starts with | Who made it | Install needed | Runs where | How trusted |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core plugin | `ilium.core.` | Ilium | no | inside Ilium | fully (T1) |
| Bundled plugin | `ilium.` (not `ilium.core.`) | Ilium | no | inside Ilium | fully (T1) |
| Signed plugin | any other id | a publisher you trust | yes | in a sandbox | by signature (T2) |
| Unsigned plugin | any other id | anyone | yes | in a sandbox | not trusted (T3) |

The tier names T1, T2 and T3 appear in the Plugins screen and in `ilium plugin list`. A T1 plugin is made by the Ilium project. It is not sandboxed, because it is part of the program, but the same permission rules apply to the things it asks you for. A T2 plugin carries a signature from a publisher key that you chose to trust. A T3 plugin has no signature. Ilium shows a `dev` badge on it and asks you to confirm the install with `--allow-unsigned`.

Read [Core plugins](/pages/user-core-plugins/) for the list of the 30 and what each one does.

### Where plugins come from

Ilium ships with no store, marketplace or registry (decision D27); you may add a registry. A plugin is a single file that ends in `.iliumpkg`. Someone gives it to you: a colleague, a website, a repository. You install the file on your own machine. Ilium never searches for plugins, never downloads one by itself and never updates one by itself.

- [USR-002] Ilium MUST NOT fetch, list, recommend or update plugins from the network on its own. Test: run Ilium with all network traffic logged for one hour with two plugins installed and assert that no request is made for a plugin package or a plugin list.

Because the file comes from someone else, Ilium checks it before anything runs. See [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/).

### Where plugins run

Third-party plugins (T2 and T3) run only on Linux, in a sandbox made of three parts: a private view of the file system (bubblewrap), a limit on processor and memory use (cgroups) and a filter on system calls (seccomp). On Windows and macOS the install is refused, and only the bundled plugins run. The refusal reads "Cannot install <name> <version>." and gives the reason.

| System | Core and bundled plugins | Signed and unsigned plugins |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | yes | yes |
| macOS | yes | refused at install |
| Windows | yes | refused at install |

### What a plugin can do to you

Think of a plugin as a guest in a house with locked rooms. The guest can sit in the hall (it can show a panel and store its own notes). Every other room has a lock, and you hold the key. The locks are called grants. A grant is one specific ability, for example "read the text of a terminal pane" or "talk to the host api.example.com". Ilium shows the list when you install the plugin. You can leave a box unchecked. The plugin still installs, and the ability stays locked.

A short list of abilities needs no grant, because they cannot reach anything of yours: writing its own log, reading the clock, using timers, keeping its own settings and notes, and reading and writing its own data and cache folders. The full list and the plain meaning of each grant is in [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/).

What a plugin can never do, whatever you grant:

- Read or write a file outside the folders you granted.
- Start a program that you did not name in a grant.
- Reach the network except hosts you named.
- Draw outside its own panels, or draw the install dialog.
- Stop Ilium from showing you the recovery page.

- [USR-003] Ilium MUST show every grant a plugin requests before the plugin runs, and a grant the user does not give MUST stay locked. Test: install a plugin that requests five grants, leave two unchecked, and assert that calls that need those two return `not-permitted`.

### Where to manage plugins

Open **Settings** with `Ctrl+B` then `:`, or press the gear in the tree footer. Choose the **Plugins** tab. You see one row for each plugin. From there you can turn a plugin on or off, read its permissions and change them, see its log, update it and remove it. The same actions exist on the command line as `ilium plugin ...`. See [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/) and [Settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/).

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Plugins ────────────────────────────────────╮</span>
│ Filter: all plugins                          │
│                                              │
│ ilium.core.tree <span class="t-dim">…………………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-ok">On</span> │
│ ilium.core.layout <span class="t-dim">……………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-ok">On</span> │
│ com.example.notes (T2) <span class="t-dim">………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-ok">On</span> │
│ com.example.old (T3) <span class="t-dim">…………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-dim">Off</span> │
│                                              │
│ Enter details  Space on or off  d remove     │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The Plugins tab with three plugins.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Common tasks

| I want to | Do this | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Add a plugin from a file | `ilium plugin install <file>` or Settings > Plugins > Install from file | [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/) |
| See what a plugin may do | Select it, then the Capabilities tab | [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/) |
| Turn a plugin off without removing it | Space on its row, or `ilium plugin disable <id>` | [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/) |
| Remove a plugin | `ilium plugin uninstall <id>` | [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/) |
| Fix Ilium after a bad plugin | Start with `ilium --safe-mode` | [Troubleshooting plugins](/pages/user-troubleshooting/) |
| Change the order of things plugins add | Settings > Plugins > Extensions | [The Extensions tab](/pages/user-extensions-tab/) |
| Know what is sent where | Read the privacy page | [Plugin privacy](/pages/user-privacy/) |
| Lock plugins on a shared machine | Write a policy file | [Administration guide](/pages/guide-administration/) |
| Find a quick answer | Questions and answers | [Plugin FAQ](/pages/user-faq/) |

### Errors and edge cases

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| You install on Windows or macOS | The install is refused: "Cannot install <name> <version>." Core and bundled plugins keep working |
| A plugin crashes | Ilium restarts it after 1 s, then 5 s, and turns it off at the third failure in 10 minutes |
| You decline a grant | The plugin keeps running and the calls that need the grant return `not-permitted` |
| You remove a plugin that others depend on | The others show "waiting for <owner>" and wake up again when the owner returns |
| A plugin hangs or floods the screen | Ilium limits it (toasts, input lock, log lines) and you can turn it off from the Plugins tab |

### See also

- [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/)
- [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/)
- [Core plugins](/pages/user-core-plugins/)
- [The Extensions tab](/pages/user-extensions-tab/)
- [Troubleshooting plugins](/pages/user-troubleshooting/)
- [Plugin privacy](/pages/user-privacy/)
- [Plugin FAQ](/pages/user-faq/)

# Plugin privacy

## Plugin privacy

This page answers three questions about plugins and your privacy. What can a plugin see? Where can it send what it sees? What does Ilium itself send about plugins? It also tells you where plugin data is stored on your machine and how to delete it.

Contract version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. Requirement ids have the form `[USR-nnn]`, collected in [User and administrator requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-user-admin/).

<div class="note">
<p>Decision status. The platform is not implemented. The statements here are the specified behaviour. A plugin you install is software written by someone else. The permission system limits it, but it cannot make a dishonest plugin honest. Install only what you trust.</p>
</div>

### Contents

- The short version
- What a plugin can see
- Where a plugin can send data
- What Ilium itself sends
- What is stored on your machine
- Delete a plugin's data
- Core plugins and AI providers
- Errors and edge cases
- Requirements

### The short version

- A plugin sees only what you grant, plus its own folders. See [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/).
- A plugin can send data only to hosts you granted, over HTTPS. Plugins cannot open a raw network connection.
- Ilium does not report plugins, their ids or their use to anyone. It has no plugin telemetry.
- Everything about a plugin is stored in your own folders. You can delete it all.

- [USR-060] Ilium MUST NOT send the list of installed plugins, plugin use, plugin logs or plugin errors to any remote party. Test: run Ilium for one hour with five plugins and request logging, and assert that no request carries a plugin id.

### What a plugin can see

| A plugin can see | Only if |
|---|---|
| The names and structure of your project tree | you granted `tree.read` |
| Titles, sizes and focus of panes | you granted `panes.read` |
| The text in a terminal pane | you granted `terminal.read-screen` or `terminal.read-cells` |
| Older terminal lines | you granted `terminal.history` (HIGH) |
| What you typed to a coding agent | you granted `agent.read-prompts` (HIGH) |
| An agent's saved conversation | you granted `agent.transcript` or `fs.read:agent-sessions:<agent>` (HIGH) |
| Files in the project folder | you granted `fs.read:project` |
| Files in other folders | you granted a read of that specific folder |
| What you copied | you granted `clipboard.read` (HIGH) |
| Your voice | you granted `audio.capture` (HIGH) |
| Sound your computer plays | you granted `audio.loopback` (HIGH) |
| Your approximate location | you granted `location.observer` (HIGH) |
| Your key presses | you granted `keys.intercept` (HIGH) |
| Another plugin's data | never directly. Only through a service or a message that the other plugin chose to offer, and you granted |

A plugin never sees the process environment, your home folder as a whole, other users' files, or the memory of Ilium or of other plugins. It sees what Ilium passes to it and nothing else.

Terminal text may contain passwords, keys and private notes. Think twice about terminal permissions for a plugin whose job does not need them.

- [USR-061] A plugin MUST NOT read terminal text, history, agent prompts, transcripts, the clipboard, audio or location without the matching grant. Test: for each item call the function without the grant and assert `not-permitted`.

### Where a plugin can send data

A third-party plugin runs in a sandbox with no network of its own. The only ways data can leave are listed here.

| Way out | What guards it |
|---|---|
| `http:<host>` | You granted that exact host or pattern. Only HTTPS, except for `localhost`. A redirect to another host needs its own grant |
| `http:setting:<key>` | The host comes from a setting. Ilium asks you the first time for each new host |
| `inference` | The plugin uses the AI providers you set up. What it sends goes to the provider you chose, as described in [Inference providers](/pages/core-plugin-inference/) |
| `location.geocode` | A place name goes to an online lookup service, Photon, with Nominatim as fallback. Ilium asks the first time |
| `open-external` | Ilium asks before it opens each site in your browser. The browser then contacts the site |
| `process.run:<program>` | The program runs in the same sandbox, with no network |
| `notify.desktop`, `sound.play` | Local only |
| Messages to another plugin | Needs `messages.peer:<plugin-id>`. The other plugin may have its own grants for the network |

A plugin that holds both a read permission and a network permission can send what it reads to that host. The dialog does not warn you about the combination. Think about it yourself: a notes plugin that reads terminal text and can talk to `*.example.com` can pass that text to example.com.

- [USR-102] A T2 or T3 plugin MUST have no network access except through `http:` grants and the providers named above. Test: from a test plugin, try a raw socket and a request to an ungranted host, and assert failure.
- [USR-103] Ilium MUST refuse a request to a host that the plugin has no grant for, including a redirect target. Test: redirect from a granted host to an ungranted host and assert `not-permitted`.

### What Ilium itself sends

Ilium does not contact any server to check, list, download or update plugins. Installing a plugin does not use the network. Reading a package does not use the network. Verifying a signature does not use the network, because the keys you trust are stored on your machine.

Ilium's own features that use the network are unchanged: for example, AI providers you configure. Core plugins contact the same services as before. Their page in Settings lists them. See [Inference providers](/pages/core-plugin-inference/).

- [USR-062] Install, verify, update, uninstall and list MUST NOT use the network. Test: run each in a network namespace without interfaces and assert success.

### What is stored on your machine

| What | Where | Who can read it |
|---|---|---|
| Installed packages | your plugin store | you |
| Your permissions and answers | one file per plugin | you |
| Plugin settings | your `config.toml` and the project's `.ilium` folder | you, and anyone who gets those files |
| Plugin data and notes | one folder and database per plugin | you and that plugin |
| Plugin logs | one file per plugin | you |
| Audit log | only if your administrator turned it on | you and the administrator |

A project's `.ilium` folder may hold plugin settings and the plugin's project storage. If you share or commit that folder, you share them. Permissions are never stored there. The exact paths are in [Plugin files on disk](/pages/reference-plugin-files/).

Plugin logs are plain text. Plugins are told not to write secrets there, but Ilium cannot check. Read a log before you share it.

### Delete a plugin's data

| I want to delete | Do this |
|---|---|
| Everything of one plugin | `ilium plugin uninstall <id> --purge` |
| A plugin's settings only | Recovery page > Forget settings |
| A plugin's logs | `--purge`, or wait: logs of an uninstalled plugin are deleted after 7 days |
| One project's plugin data | Delete the plugin's files in the project's `.ilium` folder, or use `--purge` while the project is open |
| My trusted publisher keys | `ilium plugin trust remove <publisher>` |
| Everything | Remove the plugin folders listed in [Plugin files on disk](/pages/reference-plugin-files/) with Ilium stopped |

`--purge` also leaves a note so that other projects delete the plugin's project and session data the next time you open them. A plugin that was uninstalled without `--purge` leaves its data inert: no other plugin can read it, and the same plugin reads it again if you reinstall.

### Core plugins and AI providers

Core plugins are made by the Ilium project and follow the same permission rules for high-risk abilities. Some of them send data to services you configure: the Inference plugin sends prompts to the AI provider you pick, the Voice plugin may use a speech service you set up, and the Cost plugin may read agents' usage files. These behave as documented in the user documentation. A third-party plugin that asks for `inference` uses the same providers and the same privacy controls: the provider you choose for each purpose, and the setting that decides whether file names, paths and terminal text may be included in a prompt.

### Errors and edge cases

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| A plugin tries a host without a grant | The call returns `not-permitted`. The log gets `refused http:<host>` |
| You revoke a network grant during a request | The request ends with `revoked` |
| The audit log | Always on. Install, update, grant, consent, trust and block events are recorded. Plugin data and settings values are not. See [Audit log](/pages/reference-audit-log/) |
| You share a project folder | Plugin settings and project storage in `.ilium` go with it. Permissions do not |
| A plugin writes a secret to its log | Ilium cannot detect it. Delete the log with `--purge` or wait for the 7 days |

### See also

- [Plugins for users](/pages/user-plugins-overview/)
- [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/)
- [Plugin files on disk](/pages/reference-plugin-files/)
- [Security](/pages/security/)
- [Plugin FAQ](/pages/user-faq/)

API version checked: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

# Safe mode and recovery

## Safe mode and recovery

When a plugin makes Ilium hard to use, start in safe mode. Safe mode turns plugins off without removing anything, so you can find the cause and fix it. This page also covers the bisect tool and the crash-loop guard.

Contract version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.

### Start in safe mode

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ilium --safe-mode` | The same as `--safe-mode=third-party`. |
| `ilium --safe-mode=third-party` | Runs the bundled plugins only. T2 and T3 plugins are not loaded. `replaces` is ignored. |
| `ilium --safe-mode=all-optional` | Runs only the essential set below. Every other plugin is off. |
| `ILIUM_SAFE_MODE=third-party` | Same as the flag. The flag wins when both are set. The variable also accepts `all-optional`, `1` (the same as `third-party`) and `0` (off). Any other value exits 2 with `usage.invalid-value`. |

The older switches stay as aliases: `--safe-plugins` is `--safe-mode=third-party`, and `--no-plugins` starts no plugin host at all (the kernel only). When more than one is given, the strictest wins.

Safe mode changes nothing on disk. Installed packages, grants, settings and data stay as they were. The footer shows "Safe mode: third-party plugins are off."

- [LIF-180] `--safe-mode=third-party` MUST load no T2 or T3 plugin and ignore `replaces`, and `--safe-mode=all-optional` MUST load only the essential set. Neither MUST change files on disk. Test: start both and compare the profile before and after.
- [LIF-181] The environment variable MUST behave like the flag, and the flag MUST win. Test: set both to different values.
- [LIF-182] Safe mode MUST show an indicator in the footer. Test: capture the footer.

### The essential set

The essential set is the core plugins that the screen needs to stay usable. A plugin outside the set can be turned off in safe mode.

| Plugin | Why essential |
|---|---|
| `ilium.core.tree` | draws the tree |
| `ilium.core.layout` | keeps the split layout |
| `ilium.core.settings` | opens Settings and the recovery page |
| `ilium.core.sessions` | writes the session snapshot |

Core plugins that are not in this table can be disabled. See the column "Can be disabled" in [Core plugins](/pages/core-plugins/).

- [LIF-183] The essential set MUST be exactly the four plugins above in 0.1.0, and MUST load in `all-optional` mode. Test: list running plugins in that mode.

### Find the plugin that causes a problem

`ilium plugin bisect` halves the set of enabled third-party plugins until it finds the one at fault.

| Command | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ilium plugin bisect start` | Saves the enabled set, then enables half of it for this session. |
| `ilium plugin bisect good` | The problem is gone with this half. Test the other half next. |
| `ilium plugin bisect bad` | The problem remains. Narrow this half. |
| `ilium plugin bisect reset` | Restores the saved set. |

State lives in `<data>/plugins/bisect.json`. Each command prints JSONL records of type `bisect` with the enabled list and the remaining candidates. When one plugin remains, the record has `found` set to its id. The bisect changes the session level only, so it never alters your saved choices.

- [LIF-184] Bisect MUST change only the session-level enabled state and MUST restore the saved set on `reset`. Test: run to the end and compare `installed.json`.
- [LIF-185] Bisect MUST finish in at most `ceil(log2(n))` steps for `n` plugins. Test: 16 plugins, 4 steps.

### The crash-loop guard

If the server stops with a crash 3 times within 5 minutes during start, the next start runs in `third-party` safe mode and opens the recovery page. The guard clears after one start that stays up for 5 minutes.

- [LIF-186] Three crashes during start within 5 minutes MUST cause the next start to use `third-party` safe mode. Test: write three crash marks.

### Recovery steps

1. Start with `ilium --safe-mode=third-party`.
2. Open Settings, then Plugins ([Managing plugins](/pages/user-managing-plugins/)).
3. Turn plugins on one at a time, or run `ilium plugin bisect start`.
4. When you find the plugin, update it, disable it, or uninstall it.
5. Start normally.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-warn">Safe mode: third-party plugins are off.</span>
Plugins
 ilium.core.tree       on
 com.example.notes     off  (safe mode)
 com.example.cursor    off  (safe mode)
[b] bisect  [r] leave safe mode
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The Plugins list in safe mode with third-party plugins held off.</figcaption>
</figure>

### See also

- [Managing plugins](/pages/user-managing-plugins/)
- [Plugin lifecycle states](/pages/reference-plugin-lifecycle-states/)
- [Host architecture](/pages/reference-host-architecture/)
- [Requirements, lifecycle and operations](/pages/reference-requirements-lifecycle-ops/)

API version checked: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`.
