# Troubleshooting plugins

## Troubleshooting plugins

This page helps you when a plugin does not install, does not start, keeps stopping, slows Ilium down, floods the screen, or stops Ilium from starting. It starts with a table of symptoms, then explains safe mode, the recovery page, how to find the plugin that causes a problem, how to read a plugin's log, and how to report a problem.

Contract version: `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. Requirement ids have the form `[USR-nnn]`, collected in [User and administrator requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-user-admin/).

<div class="note">
<p>Decision status. The platform is not implemented. The name of the safe mode start flag, <code>--safe-mode</code>, is a working name that the platform owner confirms. The behaviour is specified in <a href="/pages/reference-plugin-lifecycle-states/">Plugin lifecycle states</a>.</p>
</div>

### Contents

- Find your symptom
- Safe mode
- The recovery page
- Find the plugin that causes a problem
- Read the plugin log
- Restart rules you will see
- Protective limits you will see
- Roll back and repair
- Report a problem
- Errors and edge cases
- Requirements

### Find your symptom

| What you see | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| "Cannot install <name> <version>." | You are on Windows or macOS, and the plugin is third-party | Use Linux, or use only bundled plugins |
| Install fails with a code such as `manifest.file-hash` | The file is damaged or was changed | Get the file again and compare its checksum with the publisher's |
| Install fails with `policy.blocked` | Your administrator limits plugins | Ask your administrator. See [Administration guide](/pages/guide-administration/) |
| A plugin shows **Failed** | It failed 3 times within 10 minutes | Read its log, then turn it on again (see below, and [Plugin health for users](/pages/user-plugin-health/)) |
| A plugin shows **Refused** | Ilium checked it at start and refused to run it | Read the code in the row. Reinstall the package or get a new version |
| A plugin shows **Blocked by policy** | Your administrator forbids it | Ask your administrator |
| A plugin shows **Waiting for <owner>** | It depends on a plugin that is off or removed | Turn on or install the owner |
| A panel or pane is empty | A permission was declined, or the plugin is off | Check the Capabilities tab and the log |
| A pane says "Plugin <name> is not installed" | The plugin that made the pane was removed | Install it again, or close the pane |
| A key does nothing | Another binding wins, or the plugin is off | See Settings > Keys. Your own remap wins over plugins |
| Lines of toasts appear | A plugin shows many messages | Ilium shows at most 3 per 10 s per plugin. Turn the plugin off |
| Your keyboard is unresponsive for a moment | A plugin locks input | The lock ends after 2 s. Revoke `terminal.input-lock` |
| Ilium is slow | A plugin uses much processor or memory | Run `ilium plugin stats <id>`. Turn it off |
| Settings does not open | The settings plugin failed | Use the recovery page |
| Ilium does not start well after you installed a plugin | A plugin breaks startup | Start in safe mode |
| An update shows "Update failed, rolled back" | The new version failed to start | The old version is back. Read the log of the new package's id |

### Safe mode

Safe mode starts Ilium with every third-party plugin (T2 and T3) switched off for this run. Core and bundled plugins run. Nothing is deleted, nothing is written to the registry, and the next normal start has every plugin as before.

Start it in one of three ways:

1. From a terminal: `ilium --safe-mode`.
2. From the recovery page, press the Safe mode action. Ilium restarts the client with third-party plugins off.
3. If Ilium fails to start twice in a row while a plugin starts, Ilium offers safe mode at the next start. (Pending decision: the offer after two failed starts is proposed.)

In safe mode, a banner stays at the top of the screen: "Safe mode: third-party plugins are off." The Plugins tab still works. Every third-party row shows **Off** with the reason `safe-mode`. You can read logs, uninstall plugins and use the bisect tool. You cannot turn a third-party plugin on until you leave safe mode.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Plugins (safe mode) ────────────────────────╮</span>
│ <span class="t-warn">Safe mode: third-party plugins are off.</span>      │
│                                              │
│ ilium.core.tree <span class="t-dim">…………………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-ok">On</span> │
│ ilium.core.layout <span class="t-dim">……………………………………………………………</span> <span class="t-ok">On</span> │
│ com.example.notes (T2) <span class="t-dim">………………</span> <span class="t-dim">Off, safe mode</span> │
│ com.example.old (T3) <span class="t-dim">……………………</span> <span class="t-dim">Off, safe mode</span> │
│                                              │
│ Restart Ilium without --safe-mode to leave.  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The Plugins tab in safe mode.</figcaption>
</figure>

- [USR-030] Safe mode MUST switch off every T2 and T3 plugin for the run, MUST leave core and bundled plugins on, and MUST NOT write the state to the registry. Test: start in safe mode, stop, start normally and assert every plugin is as before.
- [USR-031] Safe mode MUST show a banner on every screen and MUST label every third-party row as off with the reason `safe-mode`. Test: render the tree and the Plugins tab in safe mode.

### The recovery page

The recovery page is a screen that belongs to Ilium itself, not to any plugin. No plugin can replace it, hide it or change it. It works even if the Settings plugin has failed. It lists plugins that failed or are off first, and offers these actions: enable, disable, open the raw configuration file, uninstall, reset failures, forget settings and safe mode.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Recovery ───────────────────────────────────╮</span>
│ Failed or disabled plugins come first.       │
│                                              │
│ failed   example.demo 0.1.0 3 in 10 min      │
│ enabled  ilium.cost-view 0.1.0               │
│ enabled  ilium.animations 0.1.0              │
│                                              │
│ e enable   d disable   o open config file    │
│ u uninstall   r reset failures               │
│ f forget settings   s safe mode   q close    │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The recovery page.</figcaption>
</figure>

Open the recovery page from the **Open Plugins page** link on any disabled plugin's rows, or from a failed-start notice, or with `Ctrl+B` then `:` and the Recovery entry when Settings is not available. (Pending decision: the direct key for the recovery page is not set.)

| Action | Effect | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| Enable | Turns the plugin on and clears its failure count | the on or off flag, the failure window |
| Disable | Turns the plugin off | the on or off flag |
| Reset failures | Clears the failure count without starting the plugin | the failure window |
| Forget settings | Deletes this plugin's saved settings for you and starts it with defaults | settings values only |
| Uninstall | Removes the plugin as in [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/) | the plugin |
| Open config file | Opens `config.toml` in an editor | nothing by itself |
| Safe mode | Restarts with third-party plugins off | nothing stored |

- [USR-032] The recovery page MUST stay reachable when the Settings plugin is off or failed, and MUST NOT be replaceable by a plugin. Test: turn off `ilium.core.settings`, open the recovery page, and re-enable it.
- [USR-033] Forget settings MUST delete only that plugin's settings values and MUST NOT delete permissions or data. Test: set a value, forget, and compare the grant file and data folder.

### Find the plugin that causes a problem

If you do not know which plugin is at fault, use the bisect tool. It turns half of your third-party plugins off, asks you whether the problem is still there, and narrows down until one plugin is left.

```sh
ilium plugin bisect start
# check the problem, then answer
ilium plugin bisect good     # the problem is gone with the current set off
ilium plugin bisect bad      # the problem is still there
ilium plugin bisect reset    # stop and put everything back
```

Bisect changes nothing on disk. The plugins it turns off are off for this run, as in safe mode, and `reset` or a restart brings them back. When bisect has found the plugin, it names it and offers to turn it off for good or to open its log.

1. Run `ilium plugin bisect start`.
2. Look at whether the problem is still there. Answer `good` when it is gone, `bad` when it is still there.
3. Repeat until Ilium names one plugin. With 16 plugins this takes at most 4 rounds.
4. Run `ilium plugin bisect reset`.

### Read the plugin log

Every plugin has a log that holds its own lines and the lines that Ilium writes about it: refused calls, failures, restarts and process runs. The log has four columns: time, level, plugin id and message.

```sh
ilium plugin logs com.example.notes --tail 50
ilium plugin logs com.example.notes --level warn --since "2026-10-12 08:00:00"
ilium plugin logs com.example.notes --follow
```

Lines you will often see:

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `refused <grant> by <function> (declined)` | You said no to that permission. Grant it in the Capabilities tab if you want the feature |
| `refused <grant> by <function> (revoked)` | You turned the permission off |
| `refused <grant> by <function> (not-granted)` | The plugin used a value outside what you granted, such as a host or folder you did not allow |
| `restart in 1 s` or `restart in 5 s` | The plugin stopped and Ilium will start it again |
| `disabled after 3 failures in 10 minutes` | The plugin is off and stays off until you turn it on |
| `dropped N log lines` | The plugin wrote more than 200 lines per second |

The log is plain text. Before you paste it into a bug report, read it. A plugin should not write secrets there, but check.

### Restart rules you will see

When a plugin stops with an error, Ilium starts it again after a delay: 1 s after the first failure, 5 s after the second. At the third failure within 10 minutes it stays off, the row shows **Failed**, and a notice names the plugin. Turning it on again, from the Plugins tab, the recovery page or `ilium plugin enable <id>`, starts counting from zero. `ilium plugin reset-failures <id>` clears the count without starting the plugin. See [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/).

If you changed the plugin in the meantime, for example by updating it, the count also starts from zero.

- [USR-100] The plugin MUST restart after 1 s, then after 5 s, and MUST stay off at the third failure within 10 minutes. Test: make a test plugin fail on start and measure.
- [USR-101] Turning a plugin on MUST clear its failure count. Test: reach the stop, turn on, fail once, and assert a restart after 1 s.

### Protective limits you will see

Ilium limits what a plugin can do to your screen, whatever you granted. If you see these effects, a plugin is probably very active:

- **Toasts:** at most 3 per 10 s per plugin. More are dropped. One summary line goes to the log.
- **Input lock:** a plugin can block your keyboard for 2 s at most.
- **Clipboard:** after a plugin reads or writes the clipboard, the footer shows an indicator for 3 s.
- **Log lines:** 200 per second.

### Roll back and repair

| Problem | Command | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| The new version is worse | `ilium plugin rollback <id>` | Activates the previous version |
| The new version cannot read old data | `ilium plugin rollback <id> --restore-backup` | Restores the data copy made before the update. What was written since is lost |
| Store files are damaged | `ilium plugin reinstall <id>` | Rebuilds the store entry from the cached package |
| You want a clean start for one plugin | `ilium plugin uninstall <id> --purge`, then install | Deletes its data, settings and log |
| Many checks at once | `ilium plugin doctor` | Checks the tools, trust store and free disk space |

`ilium plugin doctor` also checks whether the machine allows T2 and T3 plugins and whether the trust store file is readable.

### Report a problem

Give the maintainer of the plugin, not the Ilium project, the report first. Include:

1. The plugin id and version (`ilium plugin list`).
2. Your Ilium version and your system.
3. The last lines of the log, after you read them for secrets.
4. What you did and what you expected.

If you think Ilium itself is at fault, for example a plugin could do something it was not granted, report it to the Ilium project as a security issue and include the log lines.

### Errors and edge cases

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| Safe mode and a policy that blocks plugins | Both apply. The row shows the policy reason first |
| Bisect with one third-party plugin | It names that plugin after the first answer |
| You leave safe mode | Plugins are back as they were. Failed plugins stay failed until you turn them on |
| The log file is missing | The log tab is empty. A new file starts at the next line |
| Two problems at once | Fix one, restart, then check again. Bisect finds one plugin at a time |
| The registry cannot be written | The action fails with `io`, and the state stays as it was |

### See also

- [Plugins for users](/pages/user-plugins-overview/)
- [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/)
- [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/)
- [Plugin FAQ](/pages/user-faq/)
- [Plugin lifecycle states](/pages/reference-plugin-lifecycle-states/)
- [Settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/)

# Design decisions

## Design decisions

The user made seven decisions on 2026-10-11 about the plugin platform, D1 to D7. On the same day the user overrode one earlier rule so that plugins can add tabs and sections to Settings, recorded as SE1 to SE20. On 2026-10-12 the user asked that the API and the widget catalogue express everything Ilium has. That work added 42 additions (AX1 to AX42) and raised fourteen open questions, D8 to D25. This page records each decision: the question it answered, the decision, the reason and the effect on plugin authors.

D1 to D25 and SE1 to SE20 are decided. Each entry states the choice and the alternative that was not taken. Where a decision differs from the original recommendation, the page says so.

In plain terms, a plugin is a WebAssembly component. Rust and TypeScript both compile to that form and run under one contract, one set of limits and one set of capability grants. Third-party code runs in a separate helper process. First-party code runs inside the Ilium process. The decisions set these boundaries, and the other pages apply them.

### You will need

Nothing to install or grant. This page explains design choices and asks nothing of you. Read it when a rule in another page looks strict, for example when a T2 package is refused on Windows, when a timer refuses an interval under 50 ms, or when a high-risk grant is off by default even for a bundled plugin. The [Glossary](/pages/glossary/) defines the terms tier, side and grant that this page uses.

### Summary

| ID | Decision | Status | What it means for you |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | JavaScript and TypeScript compile to WebAssembly components | Decided | Both languages share one contract, one set of limits and one set of grants |
| D2 | Saved-world and file-reading scenes are plugins | Decided | Scenes read files through scoped grants; editor and basic primitives exist to build on |
| D3 | Local and signed packages first, a registry later | Superseded in part by D27 | You can always distribute a file; a T2 package needs a signature from a key the user trusts |
| D4 | Editors and boards are native in version 1 | Decided | Use the editor primitive; a plugin that provides the editor is a post-v1 feature |
| D5 | A separate-process sandbox is mandatory for T2 and T3 | Decided | Third-party code runs in a helper process; Windows and macOS refuse it |
| D6 | Bundled plugins are precompiled and start lazily | Decided | Activation triggers decide when your plugin first runs |
| D7 | One `.iliumpkg` format replaces `.iliumanim` | Decided | Rebuild old packages; the `limits` object gains four fields |
| SE1 to SE20 | Plugins add tabs and sections to Settings | Decided | Rows are declared in the manifest, labelled by the kernel and stored under your plugin id |
| D8 | `path` rows store a string only | Decided | A path picked in Settings gives no file scope |
| D9 | Reading built-in values | Replaced by D13 | See D13 |
| D10 | No user reordering of plugin sections | Decided | Section order is fixed |
| D11 | Kernel rows keep their own reset and debounce behaviour | Decided | Only plugin rows have the `r` reset and the `•` modified mark |
| D12 | First-party limits tier only for bundled `ilium.*` plugins | Decided | `limits_tier: "first-party"` is refused for anyone else |
| D13 | Kernel settings are readable; the tab owner may write | Decided | Any plugin can read a kernel value. Only the one owner plugin of a tab can write it |
| D14 | The host owns geocoding | Decided | You never call a geocoder through `http` |
| D15 | Embeddings only through the selected inference provider | Decided | `vector.embed` can return `unsupported` |
| D16 | Cross-session commands are high risk and same-plugin only | Decided | You can reach only your own commands in other sessions |
| D17 | Raw input and the input lock are high risk | Decided | The lock lasts at most 2 s |
| D18 | GPU access is `@unstable` and host kernels only | Decided | You cannot ship shader code |
| D19 | No `preview` rows in kernel tabs | Decided | Previews live in your own tab |
| D20 | Toasts need a grant and a rate limit | Decided | 3 toasts per 10 s per plugin |
| D21 | Durable timers fire late once; journaled input never replays | Decided | You may get `input-uncertain` after a crash |
| D22 | Agent transcripts are typed turns from the host | Decided | No raw transcript files |
| D23 | A host taken from a setting is confirmed by the user | Decided | The first request to a new host waits for the user |
| D24 | Package assets: 64 MiB, 256 MiB for T1 | Decided | Video and font assets must fit |
| D25 | `open-external` asks once per target origin | Decided | The first open of a site waits for the user |
| D26 | One uniform mechanism for extension points, hooks fail open, replacement needs a declared surface, no wildcard grants | Decided | Any plugin can offer a slot and any plugin can fill it, one point at a time |
| D27 | An optional static registry protocol, no central store | Decided | Anyone can host a signed registry or mirror; Ilium ships with none configured |

## D1: JavaScript and TypeScript compiled to components

**Question.** How does JavaScript or TypeScript run in the platform? The original draft proposed generated V8 glue. The alternative is to compile the code to WebAssembly components.

**Decision.** JavaScript and TypeScript are compiled to a WebAssembly component with `componentize-js`. `componentize-qjs` is not used. The SDK pins `@bytecodealliance/componentize-js` and `@bytecodealliance/jco` as exact dependencies of `@ilium/plugin-sdk`, and Bun 1.2 or later is the only global tool. V8 stays only for the existing animation packages until the animation migration (Phase 4c).

**Reason.** The contract is synchronous by design, so it fits a component build exactly. One host, one linker and one conformance suite then cover both languages. The alternative would need a WIT-to-V8 generator with no upstream, a second dispatcher and a doubled conformance matrix. This decision replaces the original recommendation of generated V8 glue.

**Effect on authors.** A TypeScript plugin faces the same limits, grants and error codes as a Rust plugin. `ilium plugin build` detects the language from the files in the project folder. A `Cargo.toml` means Rust, and a `package.json` means TypeScript. If both are present and `--lang` is absent, the build fails. See the [TypeScript SDK reference](/pages/typescript-sdk/) and the [Rust SDK reference](/pages/rust-sdk/).

## D2: Scope of plugins

**Question.** Which built-in features must be native, and which can be plugins?

**Decision.** The user disagreed with native-by-default for several areas. Saved-world scenes are plugins. They read their files through scoped `fs.read:<scope>` grants and use the codec helpers. File-reading scenes also use scoped reads. Editors get an editor primitive, a host-provided pane kind that plugins extend or build on. The basic primitive is a generic pane kind from which a plugin can build a kanban board, for example. Plugins get a UI-building API that mirrors the ratatui widget model, and that API is enough to build settings screens.

**Reason.** Saved-world and file-reading scenes can be plugins once the ABI gives scoped file access and processing helpers. The primitives let editors and boards be built on the same contract that plugins use, so a later move needs no ABI change.

**Effect on authors.** A scene that reads a folder declares a grant such as `fs.read:<scope>` in its manifest. The user approves that grant in the review dialog. Build screens with `ilium_plugin_sdk::ui::build` in Rust or `@ilium/plugin-sdk/ui/build` in TypeScript. Each widget is listed in the [widget pages](/pages/widgets-index/). The [primitives](/pages/primitives/) and [settings screens](/pages/settings-screens/) pages show the rest of the surface.

## D3: Third-party scope for version 1

**Question.** Should version 1 include a marketplace?

**Decision.** Local and signed packages are the base of the system. A package is a file that users pass on, and `ilium plugin install <file.iliumpkg>` installs it. Ilium ships no central marketplace and no default registry. Decision D27 adds an optional, self-hostable registry protocol on top of the file; it replaces the earlier wording "no registry and no download".

**Reason.** A marketplace costs signing infrastructure, index hosting and a review policy. Local signed files need none of those to be loaded and verified.

**Effect on authors.** A T2 package is signed with Ed25519. The signature covers the canonical bytes of `manifest.json`, and the manifest's `publisher` must match the key's recorded publisher. You create a key with `ilium plugin keygen --publisher "<name>" --out <dir>`. A T3 package is unsigned. It installs only with `--allow-unsigned`, or through `ilium plugin dev`, and it carries a dev badge. The [Security model](/pages/security/) page lists every tier.

## D4: Editors and boards native in version 1

**Question.** Are the editor and boards native pane kinds, or plugins?

**Decision.** Native in version 1. Plugin support for them is a planned phase after v1. The primitives are shaped so that moving the editor and boards later needs no ABI break.

**Reason.** The editor would be the first user of a pane-body contract that needs keymap arbitration, cursor, selection and clipboard semantics. The user chose native in v1 and a planned post-v1 phase, so the primitives are designed to make that move cheap.

**Effect on authors.** The editor primitive exists in v1, and a plugin can use it. A plugin that provides the editor needs the `editor.provide` grant, which only T1 bundled plugins can receive, and it arrives after v1. A calling plugin names the primitive, not a provider, so it does not change when the provider moves. See the [Roadmap](/pages/roadmap/).

## D5: Separate-process sandbox for third-party plugins

**Question.** Should third-party WebAssembly run in the Ilium process?

**Decision.** No. A separate-process sandbox is mandatory for third-party plugins (T2 and T3). The helper process runs the plugin host for those packages inside the sandbox, which opens only the directories the user granted. The sandbox exists on Linux only. Windows and macOS refuse to load third-party packages until a sandbox exists on those platforms.

**Reason.** Running third-party code in-process would rely on Wasmtime alone for isolation. The design record counts twelve Wasmtime advisories in two months, which is the reason for a separate process boundary.

**Effect on authors.** A T2 or T3 plugin runs in the helper and sees only its granted folders. A `process.run:sh` grant is refused for T2 and T3 at install with `manifest.grant-tier`. On Windows and macOS, the install is refused with the message below. First-party T1 plugins run in-process on every platform. See the [Security model](/pages/security/).

## D6: Bundled plugins precompiled and lazy

**Question.** How are first-party WebAssembly plugins delivered and started?

**Decision.** Bundled plugins are embedded in the release precompiled, as `.cwasm`, and start lazily on first need. Wasmtime's on-demand allocator is the default. A plugin starts when one of its activation triggers fires. Without an `activation` list, it starts on the first use of any of its contributions.

**Reason.** Compiling about forty plugins with Cranelift at every start costs time at each launch. The design record notes that Zellij abandoned Wasmtime over that cost. Precompiled components with lazy activation meet the start-time and memory targets of the [performance budget](/pages/performance/): under 5 ms and under 4 MiB resident memory for each precompiled Rust component.

**Effect on authors.** Use `activation` in the manifest to choose the trigger. The triggers are `startup`, `event:<event-name>`, `command:<id>`, `view:<id>`, `pane-kind:<id>`, `scene:<id>`, `cli:<name>`, `http:<path>`, `service:<interface>`, `topic:<topic>` and `settings:<tab-id>`. A plugin that must run at launch declares `startup`. Start order is in the [lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/) page, and the manifest keys are in the [manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/).

## D7: One package format

**Question.** Should the animation package format stay alongside the plugin format?

**Decision.** One `.iliumpkg` format replaces `.iliumanim`, with no compatibility layer. The package is a deterministic ZIP32 archive with stored entries, sorted paths and fixed timestamps. The `limits` object gains memory, table, event-deadline and render-deadline fields. The loader does not accept the old format.

**Reason.** Keeping both formats would mean two loaders to maintain. The project has no users yet, so a one-time rebuild costs little.

**Effect on authors.** An `.iliumanim` package must be rebuilt as a `.iliumpkg`. The [Porting from .iliumanim](/pages/porting-iliumanim/) page lists the changes. The `limits` keys and their ceilings are below. A request above the ceiling is clamped and logged. It is never refused.

| Key | Default | T1 ceiling | T2 and T3 ceiling | Exceeded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `memory_mib` | 32 | 256 | 128 | instance trapped |
| `table_elements` | 10,000 | 50,000 | 20,000 | instance trapped |
| `event_deadline_ms` | 20 | 50 | 20 | instance trapped |
| `command_deadline_ms` | 50 | 100 | 50 | instance trapped |
| `render_deadline_ms` | 10 | 20 | 10 | instance trapped |

### Worked example: a limit request above the ceiling

A signed T2 plugin asks for a longer event deadline than its tier allows. The manifest excerpt below requests 64 MiB of memory and a 30 ms event deadline.

```json
{
  "api": "ilium:plugin@0.1.0",
  "id": "example.notes",
  "name": "Notes",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "publisher": "Example Labs",
  "limits": {
    "memory_mib": 64,
    "event_deadline_ms": 30
  },
  "server": { "entry": "server.wasm", "world": "ilium:server/base@0.1.0", "exports": [] }
}
```

The memory request fits the T2 ceiling of 128 MiB and is used as given. The 30 ms request is above the T2 ceiling of 20 ms, so the host clamps it and writes one line to the log:

<pre class="term"><span class="t-warn">warn</span> example.notes:
     limit event_deadline_ms 30 clamped to 20 (T2 ceiling)
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The log line the host writes when it clamps a manifest limit.

## The Settings extension decisions

On 2026-10-11 the user overrode the earlier rule that a plugin cannot attach to a kernel settings page. The twenty decisions SE1 to SE20 follow from that override. The page [Plugin settings extension](/pages/settings-extension/) explains them in full. In short:

| ID | Decision |
|---|---|
| SE1, SE2 | A plugin may add tabs to Settings and sections to built-in tabs. A custom page is a plugin tab with `"render": "view"`, and `settings_pages` is removed |
| SE3, SE4 | Every kernel tab has a frozen kebab-case id. Kernel tabs expose anchors, which are only ever added |
| SE5 | `animations`, `debug`, `api`, `about`, `setup` and the recovery page accept no plugin sections |
| SE6 | Plugins add, never alter. Values live only under `[plugins."<plugin-id>"]` |
| SE7, SE8 | Rows are declared inline. There are 18 types. Object list items have at most 8 primitive fields |
| SE9 | Plugin tabs carry `· plugin` in the frame title. Plugin blocks in kernel tabs carry one divider per plugin per anchor and a `▏` gutter on every line. Plugin text is plain and sanitized |
| SE10 | Kernel tabs host only static plugin rows plus `set-info`, `set-choices` and `set-row-note`. View-rendered content is allowed only in the plugin's own tab |
| SE11 | The grant `settings.contribute:<kernel-tab-id>` allows sections in that tab and nothing else |
| SE12, SE13 | Limits are enforced at load time. Ordering is anchor, then `order`, then plugin id, then declaration order |
| SE14 | Values are never deleted by disable, failure, upgrade or uninstall. Only `--purge` or "Forget settings" deletes them |
| SE15 | Toggles and choices save at once. Number steps and text save 600 ms after the last change, and text areas after 1 s |
| SE16, SE17 | `settings-changed` carries `keys`, `origin` and `scope`. The optional export `settings-validate` has a 100 ms deadline |
| SE18 to SE20 | Id grammar, a kernel search filter over kernel and plugin rows, and a kernel-owned settings registry |

The extended rows are part of these decisions: SE7's twelve base row types are joined by six more (`location`, `preview`, `notice`, `map`, `multi-choice` and `meter`), SE8's object items may have up to 8 fields, and SE10 still keeps `preview` rows and every view-rendered content out of kernel tabs (D19).

## Decisions D8 to D25

The decisions below are final. Each entry states the choice, and the second half says what the alternative would have changed. The reference for the choices is the design record of the plugin platform; the effect on plugin code is on the pages named in each entry.

### D8, D10, D11: Settings questions

| ID | Question | Decided | If the user chooses otherwise |
|---|---|---|---|
| D8 | Does a `path` row grant file access to the picked path? | No. The row stores a string only. A plugin that must open the file asks for an `fs.read` grant, or uses `path-field`, which returns a picked scope and never a raw path | The plugin could open the picked path without a broad grant, at the cost of a persistent file scope created from Settings |
| D10 | May the user reorder plugin sections inside a built-in tab? | No. The order is anchor, then `order`, then plugin id | A per-user order that must be stored and reconciled when plugins appear or disappear |
| D11 | Do kernel rows adopt the `r` reset, the `•` modified mark and the 600 ms debounce of plugin rows? | Optional follow-up, outside the settings extension | Kernel and plugin rows would behave the same everywhere |

### D12: the first-party limits tier

**Question.** Who may use `limits_tier: "first-party"`, which lifts the settings caps to 8 tabs, 2,048 value keys, 64 rows per section, 1,024 list items and 512 choice options?

**Decision.** Only bundled T1 plugins whose id starts with `ilium.`. Any other package is refused at install with `manifest.limits-tier`. The tier raises only the settings caps and the `list-editor` cap. The ceilings of the requestable limits stay as they are.

**Alternative.** Signed T2 plugins could ask for it too, which a settings-heavy third-party plugin might need. The caps would then stop protecting the Settings screen.

**Effect on authors.** Write `"limits_tier": "standard"` or omit the key. If your package is first-party and bundled, set `"first-party"`, and keep the id under `ilium.`.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin install ./example.notes-1.0.0.iliumpkg
<span class="t-err">error</span> manifest.limits-tier  limits_tier first-party needs a
      bundled plugin whose id starts with ilium.
<span class="t-dim">step</span>  install stopped before any code was loaded
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A third-party package that asks for the first-party tier stops at the install checks.</figcaption>
</figure>

### D13: kernel settings are readable and the tab owner may write

**Question.** May a plugin read a built-in setting, such as a key that Smart Copy uses?

**Decision.** Yes, read for every plugin, write for one owner per tab. The grant `settings.read-kernel:<kernel-tab-id>` allows `kernel-settings.read` for one tab and the event `kernel-settings-changed`. The argument is required and has no wildcard. Secrets are always returned as `<redacted>`. The `api` tab is high risk. The matching `keymap.read` grant returns the keymap and sends `keymap-changed`. The grant `settings.write-kernel:<kernel-tab-id>` allows `kernel-settings.write` for one tab. It is T1 only and high risk, and at most one plugin holds it for a tab (the core plugin that owns the tab, see [config and data migration](/pages/reference-config-and-data-migration/)). No plugin writes the keymap. Every other plugin links to the row with `open-external`.

**Alternative.** Keep D9's "not provided". A plugin that needs a kernel value would then duplicate it as its own setting and drift from the kernel.

**Effect on authors.** Read a value, and when the user must change it, link to the built-in row with the intent `open-external` and the target `ilium://settings/<tab-id>#<key>`. The code below reads one key of one tab. The grant is `settings.read-kernel:terminal`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::kernel_settings;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

/// Reads one value of a built-in tab. Returns `None` when the grant is missing
/// or the kernel has no such key.
fn kernel_value(tab: &str, key: &str) -> Option<serde_json::Value> {
    let json = kernel_settings::read(tab).ok()?;
    let values: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&json).ok()?;
    values.get(key).cloned()
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { read } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/kernel-settings';

/** Reads one value of a built-in tab. Returns undefined when the grant is missing. */
function kernelValue(tab: string, key: string): unknown {
  try {
    const values = JSON.parse(read(tab)) as Record<string, unknown>;
    return values[key];
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof PluginError && error.code === 'not-permitted') {
      return undefined;
    }
    throw error;
  }
}
```

### D14: geocoding

**Question.** Who geocodes place names for `location.geocode` and the location picker?

**Decision.** The host. It uses Photon, with Nominatim as fallback, asks the user once for consent, limits each plugin to 1 request per second and caches results for 24 h.

**Alternative.** Plugins call geocoders through `http`. That offers more choice, but every plugin then ships its own politeness and consent, and the user cannot see where place names go.

**Effect on authors.** Use the `geocode` calls or the `location-picker` widget. See [Security model](/pages/security/) for the consent prompt and for what a declined consent returns.

### D15: embeddings

**Question.** Where do embeddings for `vector.embed` come from?

**Decision.** Only from the selected inference provider. A provider without embeddings makes the call return `unsupported`.

**Alternative.** A bundled local embedding model. It works offline but adds tens of megabytes and a native inference path.

**Effect on authors.** Check for `unsupported` and keep a keyword fallback. The grant is `inference.embed`.

### D16: cross-session commands

**Question.** May a plugin run commands in the user's other Ilium sessions?

**Decision.** Yes, with the high-risk grant `sessions.cross`. It is available to T1 and signed T2 plugins only, and only to the same plugin in the other session, which must have the grant too. Kernel commands of another session are never reachable.

**Alternative.** Available to T3 as well. That is simpler, but an unsigned plugin could drive every open session.

**Effect on authors.** Declare the command in your own manifest, ask for `sessions.cross` on the server side, and expect `not-permitted` when the other session lacks the plugin or the grant.

### D17: raw terminal input and the input lock

**Question.** May a plugin send raw bytes or mouse events to a pane, and hold the keyboard while it types?

**Decision.** Both are high risk (`terminal.raw-input`, `terminal.input-lock`). The lock lasts at most 2 s, and the user's keys are queued during it.

**Alternative.** No raw input. Plugins then cannot drive TUI programs that need mouse or control bytes, so screen-transfer and agent-control plugins stay partial.

**Effect on authors.** Keep a locked sequence short. See [Security model](/pages/security/).

### D18: GPU access

**Question.** Can a plugin use the GPU?

**Decision.** Only through `gpu.kernels`, which is `@unstable(feature = gpu-kernels)` and appears in development builds only. The host runs its own kernels (blur, threshold, palette map, ordered dither, scale). A plugin never ships a shader.

**Alternative.** `wasi:webgpu` once it is mature. That gives full shaders, with a large new attack surface and driver-dependent results.

**Effect on authors.** GPU scenes stay native behind the scene adapter. A manifest that names `device.gpu` is refused with `manifest.grant-unknown`.

### D19: `preview` rows in kernel tabs

**Decision.** No. A `preview` row exists in a plugin's own tab only (SE10), because a kernel tab never runs plugin code while it paints.

**Alternative.** Allow it in kernel tabs, which breaks SE10.

### D20: toasts

**Question.** May a plugin show an in-app toast?

**Decision.** Yes, with the grant `notify.toast`, at most 3 per 10 s per plugin and 3 pending. A toast has a title of at most 60 characters, a body of at most 200 characters and up to 2 actions.

**Alternative.** No grant. Any plugin could then cover the screen with toasts.

**Effect on authors.** The code under D25 sends one toast and asks the host to open a status page. A toast and an `open-external` are submissions, so both can be refused.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Copied 3 regions ───────────────────────╮</span>
│ Select a pane and press Enter to paste.  │
│ <span class="t-ok">━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━</span><span class="t-dim">────────────────────────</span> │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A toast as the client draws it, with the shrinking countdown line below the text. The kernel places the stack.</figcaption>
</figure>

### D25: confirming `open-external`

**Question.** Does the user confirm when a plugin opens a link or file?

**Decision.** The host asks the first time a plugin opens each target origin and remembers the answer per plugin. Only `http`, `https` and `mailto` URLs, files and `ilium://settings/...` targets are allowed.

**Alternative.** Ask every time, which is safer and tedious for link-heavy panels, or never ask, which lets a plugin open any site.

**Effect on authors.** The first open of a site waits for the user. A decline completes the submission as `refused(not-permitted)`.

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::{ExternalTarget, OpenExternalSpec, ToastSpec};

fn status_submissions() -> Vec<Submission> {
    vec![
        Submission::new(Intent::Toast(ToastSpec {
            id: Some("copied".into()),
            tone: Tone::Success,
            title: "Copied 3 regions".into(),
            body: None,
            actions: vec![],
            duration_ms: None,
        })),
        Submission::new(Intent::OpenExternal(OpenExternalSpec {
            target: ExternalTarget::Url("https://status.example.com".into()),
        })),
    ]
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import type { Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';

function statusSubmissions(): Submission[] {
  return [
    {
      intent: { tag: 'toast', val: { id: 'copied', tone: 'success', title: 'Copied 3 regions', body: undefined, actions: [], durationMs: undefined } },
      correlation: 1n,
      dedupKey: undefined,
    },
    {
      intent: { tag: 'open-external', val: { target: { tag: 'url', val: 'https://status.example.com' } } },
      correlation: 2n,
      dedupKey: undefined,
    },
  ];
}
```

### D21: timers and the input journal

**Decision.** Durable timers (`timers.at`) persist across restarts and fire once, late, with the lateness in `durable-timer-fired`. A `send-input` with `journal: true` that was written to the pane but not confirmed before a crash is reported once as `input-uncertain` and never replayed.

**Alternative.** Replay unconfirmed input after a restart. No prompt is lost, and a prompt could be sent twice.

**Effect on authors.** Handle `input-uncertain` by asking the user, not by sending again.

### D22 and D23: transcripts and hosts from a setting

- **D22.** Agent transcripts are typed turns that the host parses, behind the high-risk grant `agent.transcript`. The alternative is raw file access through `fs.read:agent-sessions:*`, where every plugin parses every agent format and the kernel cannot redact.
- **D23.** A host taken from a setting (`http:setting:<key>`) is confirmed by the user before the first request to each new host. The alternative is to trust the setting, which silently opens a new host when the setting changes.

### D24: package asset size

**Decision.** 64 MiB by default and for T2 and T3, up to 256 MiB for T1. A larger package is refused with `manifest.asset-size`. The alternative is 16 MiB everywhere, which makes packages smaller but does not fit the video and font assets of the media scenes.

## D26: extension points, hooks and replacement

**Question.** How do plugins add to each other, and how does a third party change a core plugin, without a private API?

**Decision.** One mechanism serves every plugin, core or not. An owner declares a point under `contributes.extension_points`. A point is either `collect` (the owner reads data entries) or `hook` (handlers run inside the owner's flow, in one of four modes: `observe`, `transform`, `veto`, `first`). A contributor fills it under `contributes.extensions`. Two grants guard it: `extensions.provide:<plugin-id>/<point>` and `extensions.contribute:<plugin-id>/<point>`. A core plugin that can be replaced declares `replaceable` and a `surface`, and a package with `replaces` that provides the whole surface may take its place after the user confirms.

**Why one uniform mechanism.** Core plugins use only the public contract, so everything they can do a third-party plugin can do with the same grants. Services have one provider and topics have no reply. The manual needed a third shape, many contributors to one owner, and building it once keeps one set of limits, one review dialog group and one error table. The existing mechanisms stay.

**Why hooks fail open.** A handler is someone else's code inside the owner's flow. If a timeout, a trap or an error stopped the owner, one slow or broken plugin could freeze text triggers, titles or fleet actions. A failing handler counts as a pass, three breaches in a row stop that extension, and the whole chain is capped at 100 ms. Only a `veto` handler that answers on purpose can stop an action.

**Why replacement needs a surface.** A replacement that provides only part of a core plugin would leave dangling services, commands, pane kinds and topics for other plugins. The `surface` list is the checklist, and `manifest.replaces-surface-incomplete` names what is missing. Replacement needs the user's confirmation, not a grant, because the user decides which built-in behaviour to give up. `ilium.core.sessions` and `ilium.core.settings` are not replaceable, because they protect saved data and the Plugins screen itself.

**Why no wildcard grants.** A wildcard such as "contribute to any point" would let one package place code in every flow. The user could not read the review dialog and decide. Each point is named, so the dialog can show `Text triggers > Before fire: can stop a trigger from sending text (high risk)`. The grant `extensions.contribute-any` does not exist.

**Alternative.** Per-plugin special hooks, which give core plugins a private API, or a single global event bus with veto rights, which cannot show the user what a package may stop.

**Effect on authors.** To let others extend your plugin, declare a point and read it with `list` or `run-hook`. To extend another plugin, ask for the grant for that exact point and list `hook-handler` in `exports` if you add handlers. See [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/) and [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/).

## The API additions and their decisions

The additions AX1 to AX42 are all additive. "Shape" additions add optional fields to a record that already exists, and they are part of the first frozen contract. After that freeze, the same need is met only by new records and new functions. The table lists every addition.

| Addition | What it adds |
|---|---|
| AX1 | Hover, `tooltip` prop, anchored and pinnable non-modal popups |
| AX2 | Catalogue `choice`: option records, typed filter, disabled reasons, previews, paged sources, host catalogues |
| AX3 | Settings row semantics: `visible_when`, step ladders, special values, slider style, project scope, restart marker, per-row debounce, row state, styled info |
| AX4 | Terminal cell reads, frozen snapshot, history text, modes, foreground process, `screen-changed`, `user-line-submitted` |
| AX5 | Pane lifecycle intents: freeze, unfreeze, replace command, terminate process, resize with refusal |
| AX6 | Tree structure intents and atomic restructure batches with undo |
| AX7 | Title provenance (`source`, expected revision), inferred icon, attention marks |
| AX8 | `open-external` intent through the host allowlist |
| AX9 | Tree and chrome contribution points; lazy virtual-row children; drops on virtual rows |
| AX10 | Rich decorations: styled spans, tooltip, frame animation, trailing segments, hover visibility |
| AX11 | Pointer model: view pointer with sub-cell coordinates, drag-over feedback, terminal move and modifier gesture |
| AX12 | Settings views may embed display widgets; `preview` and `location` rows; `location-picker` widget; `location.geocode` service |
| AX13 | Picker widgets: `color-picker`, `path-field`, icon and glyph choice through catalogues; `icon` widget |
| AX14 | CLI plain text, stderr, bounded stdin, TTY test, caller pane, server-less commands, pane-selector group, cross-session list |
| AX15 | Surface v2: glyph plane, owner ids with receipts, font handles, video from bytes or ranges, `video` widget, pre-rendered loops, larger assets |
| AX16 | `fs` atomic write with expected revision, read with revision, tail with cursor, agent home scopes for Gemini and Antigravity |
| AX17 | Menu model: dynamic items with click context, submenus, icons, disabled reasons, toolbar submenus |
| AX18 | Click targets in styled text; Markdown task clicks and images |
| AX19 | Streaming HTTP (SSE, NDJSON, chunked), `@unstable` WebSocket, politeness; hosts taken from a setting with consent |
| AX20 | `send-input` stages with delays, raw bytes, mouse; preconditions; input lock; interactive `terminal-view` |
| AX21 | Agent facts: typed transcript, model fact, prompt epoch echo, `signal-changed`, `agent-model-changed` |
| AX22 | Embeddings and a host-held vector index |
| AX23 | In-app `toast`, `notice` row and widget, `notify` coalescing |
| AX24 | `chart` gains resampling, gaps, text-line rendering (asciichart parity) |
| AX25 | Form widgets: tri-state toggle, `check-list`, `key-capture`, focus order, secret reveal, slider and stepper styles in views |
| AX26 | Table column priority and minimum width, follow-tail, panel placement and mode label |
| AX27 | Streaming child processes (`process.spawn`) |
| AX28 | Durable timers and a journaled `send-input` with `uncertain` reporting |
| AX29 | Read-only kernel settings and keymap reads |
| AX30 | Limit tiers (`limits_tier: "first-party"`) |
| AX31 | Editor viewport, pointer, minimap marks, token provider export |
| AX32 | Command palette: kernel surface; commands gain `category` and `keywords` |
| AX33 | GPU kernels run by the host, `@unstable` |
| AX34 | Server-to-client requests between the two sides of one plugin |
| AX35 | Shared cache bucket for a plugin's processes |
| AX36 | Record lists: object items of up to 8 fields, item status, remote confirmation |
| AX37 | Small items: text debounce, `when` keys, basic pane activity and dirty flag, `map` row, pane event journal, reduced motion and density tokens |
| AX38 | `list-editor` widget and typed list items (glob, URL, host, path, regex, chord) |
| AX39 | Layout additions: `split` with draggable divider, `separator`, `dialog`, `scroll-view` |
| AX40 | Data display additions: `progress-row`, `meter`, `minimap`; `meter` row |
| AX41 | `diff-view` widget |
| AX42 | Status and feedback family: `badge`, `spinner`, `notice`, `icon` |

The decisions of the extended contract that need explanation are these:

- **Kernel keeps the engine, plugins own the choice.** Every addition names the part that stays in the kernel: dithering and the shared look, the vt100 emulation, the tree layout solver, the toast stack, the command palette, the syntax engine and every GPU shader. The plugin supplies content and intent. The kernel draws and decides.
- **Intents, not mutations.** Pane lifecycle, tree restructure, attention, status segments, frame slots, toasts and `open-external` are intents. The kernel checks them against the grant and the current state, and a submission completes with one outcome. A new outcome case, `ok-epoch`, carries the new prompt epoch for `send-input` on an agent pane.
- **Read paths are typed and redacted.** Terminal cells, scrollback, transcripts, kernel settings and the keymap are read paths, each behind its own grant, and all of them are read only.
- **High risk is explicit even for T1.** The nine high-risk grants always need an explicit grant, and the dialog shows them in the warning style.
- **Streaming, not polling.** HTTP streams, spawned children and screen changes arrive as events whose delivery policy is stated per event: coalesced, or never dropped with back-pressure.

## What the user sees

- The review dialog lists every capability a plugin requests, before the first run. The user grants or declines each one. High-risk rows start unchecked.
- A T2 package is shown with its publisher and signature status. A T3 package carries a dev badge for as long as it is installed.
- A bundled plugin with high-risk grants asks once at its first start. The first open of a site, a new host from a setting, and the first place lookup each ask once.
- A plugin that is disabled after three failures shows a notice in the tree footer. The user re-enables it in settings or on the kernel recovery page.
- A refused install shows the three-line message from D5 and leaves the other plugins running.
- Plugin rows in a built-in Settings tab sit under a divider that names the plugin, with a `▏` gutter.

## Errors and edge cases

| Situation | Result | Code or text |
|---|---|---|
| T2 or T3 package installed on Windows or macOS | Install refused | `Cannot install <name> <version>.` |
| `process.run:sh` requested by a T2 or T3 package | Install refused | `manifest.grant-tier` |
| `limits_tier: "first-party"` in a package that is not a bundled `ilium.*` plugin | Install refused | `manifest.limits-tier` |
| Package assets above the tier limit | Install refused | `manifest.asset-size` |
| Limit request above the tier ceiling | Clamped to the ceiling and logged | warn line in the plugin log |
| Third failure within 10 minutes | Plugin disabled with a notice | tree footer notice |
| Capability revoked during a call | Call fails and the plugin is re-activated | `revoked` |
| Old `.iliumanim` package installed | Refused, rebuild required | the loader does not accept the format |
| Declined `open-external`, geocoding or a new host from a setting | The call or submission is refused | `not-permitted` |
| Journaled input in flight when the server stops | Reported once, never replayed | `input-uncertain` |

<div class="note">
<p>The restart delays after a failure are 1 s, then 5 s; the third failure in the window disables the plugin. A failure counts for 10 minutes. A manual re-enable resets the count to zero. A revocation, a disable, an upgrade or a shutdown never counts as a failure.</p>
</div>

<div class="warn">
<p>Do not promise Windows or macOS support for a T2 or T3 plugin. Until a sandbox exists there, a third-party package does not install on those systems at all. Test third-party plugins on Linux, and state the platform limit in the plugin description. Check this page before a release.</p>
</div>

### Security

**SD1 No unconfined fallback.** If the sandbox cannot be built, the package does not load ([SEC-055]). **SD2 Fail closed for high veto points.** `on_failure: refuse` is the default ([SEC-287]). **SD3 Project values untrusted by default.** ([SEC-310]). **SD4 Key pinning.** ([SEC-142]).

## D27: an optional registry protocol

**Question.** D3 said there is no registry and no download. Packages now need discovery, updates and revocation. Does that contradict D3?

**Decision.** Ilium defines a TUF-style static registry: a folder of signed JSON files and package blobs on any HTTPS host or file share. The client verifies the metadata with a root key that the user or administrator pins. Ilium ships with no registry configured and operates no central store. Ratings are out of scope for 0.1. Automatic updates are off by default. A package file install keeps working with no registry. Mirrors and offline bundles serve isolated machines.

**Reason.** Static files need no server code, no database and no account system. A user or company can run one. Revocation and update checks need signed, expiring metadata, and TUF gives these properties in a known form.

**Effect on authors.** You can still pass a file on. You can also publish to a registry with `ilium plugin publish`. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/), [Signing and trust](/pages/reference-signing-and-trust/) and [Publishing guide](/pages/guide-publishing/). D3 stays valid for its signing and trust-per-key parts.

# Glossary

## Glossary

This page defines the terms that the other pages of the plugin manual use. Each entry gives the meaning in the contract `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. Where a term has a page of its own, the entry links to it. Read this page first when a term is unfamiliar.

A plugin is a WebAssembly component that the host loads, checks and runs. It reacts to events, sends intents that change Ilium, and uses only the rights that the user has granted. Most terms below describe one of four things: the package that carries the plugin, the rights it holds, the calls it makes, and the lifecycle that runs it.

### You will need

- Nothing installed, to read this page.
- To write a plugin, the toolchain from [Getting started: toolchain](/pages/getting-started-toolchain/). The `ilium plugin` commands are part of the `ilium` binary, so installing Ilium installs them.
- A Rust or TypeScript project. The examples below use the SDK import paths from the API pages.
- Basic familiarity with JSON, because the manifest is a JSON file.

## Terms

**Action.** A user interaction with a widget, delivered to the client side as a `ui-action` event with a kind, such as `activated` or `changed`, and a value. See [Events and intents](/pages/reference-events-and-intents/).

**Activation.** The moment the host instantiates a plugin and calls `lifecycle.activate`. A plugin is activated at startup, on the first use of one of its contributions, or on one of the triggers in its manifest `activation` list. See [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/).

**Authorization epoch.** A counter that the host increases each time a grant is revoked or added. A host call compares the epoch it started with against the current one. A call that is still in flight when the epoch changes returns `revoked`.

**Bundle.** A folder that holds signed registry metadata and the packages of chosen plugins, copied to a machine with no network. `ilium plugin export-bundle` writes it and `install --from-bundle` reads it. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/).

**Capability.** A named right that a plugin requests in its manifest and the user grants. Each host import and each event is behind one. See [Capability table](/pages/reference-capabilities/).

**Channel.** A release track of a plugin, `stable` or `beta`. A plugin follows one channel for updates. See [Versions and dependencies](/pages/reference-dependency-resolution/).

**Component.** A WebAssembly component: the compiled form of one side of a plugin, named `server.wasm`, `client.wasm` or `scene.wasm`. A package holds one component per side that the plugin uses. See [Rust SDK](/pages/rust-sdk/) and [TypeScript SDK](/pages/typescript-sdk/).

**Contribution.** Something a plugin adds to Ilium: a command, a keybinding, a settings page, a panel, a pane kind, a decoration slot, a scene or a help topic. A static contribution is declared in the manifest. A dynamic one is pushed at runtime. See [Manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/).

**`.cwasm`.** A WebAssembly component that has already been compiled for the host. The release embeds the bundled first-party plugins in this form, so they start without a compile step. See [Design decisions](/pages/design-decisions/).

**Decoration.** A short styled text or a Tabler icon that a plugin sets on a tree row, in a slot that the manifest declares, such as a badge or a footer. A decoration with `persist: true` survives a server restart, marked as stale. See [Manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/).

**De-duplication key.** The optional `dedup-key` field of a submission: 1 to 128 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9._:/-]`. A submission whose key the same plugin reserved within the last 10 minutes completes as `duplicate(original)` and has no effect. A refused submission does not reserve its key. The Rust helper `dedup::key_for` joins its parts with `:`. A `send-input` or `agent-action` submission must carry a key. See [Events and intents](/pages/reference-events-and-intents/).

**Deprecate.** To mark a whole plugin as no longer maintained, with an optional successor. Installs still work. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/).

**Editor primitive.** The host-provided pane kind for editing text. It is native. A plugin may provide an editor only after v1. See [Design decisions](/pages/design-decisions/).

**Extension point.** A named slot that one plugin owns and others fill. A `collect` point gathers data entries. A `hook` point runs handlers from other plugins in the owner's flow, in one of four modes: observe, transform, veto or first. Its id is `<plugin-id>/<point>`. See [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/).

**Grant.** The user's approval of one capability for one side of a plugin. A grant string is a name, or a name with an argument, such as `fs.read:project`. See [Capability table](/pages/reference-capabilities/).

**Hook.** A handler that a plugin contributes to a hook point. It answers `pass`, `replace`, `refuse` or `answer`, within a short deadline. A hook that is late or fails counts as `pass`. See [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/#hooks).

**Host.** The Ilium code that loads plugins, checks their calls and runs them. The host is the kernel together with the plugin host.

**`.iliumpkg`.** The one package format for plugins. It is a deterministic ZIP archive that holds a manifest, one or more components, assets, help topics and a file inventory. It replaces the old `.iliumanim` format. See [Packages](/pages/packages/) and [Porting from .iliumanim](/pages/porting-iliumanim/).

**Intent.** A request that a plugin sends to change Ilium, such as `rename-node` or `send-input`. An intent travels inside a submission. Each submission completes with exactly one outcome. See [Events and intents](/pages/reference-events-and-intents/).

**Job.** A unit of background work that a plugin starts with `jobs.start`. A job runs the `job-runner.run` export in a second instance of the same component, with its own deadline and memory limit. The plugin reads the result with `take-output`. See [Background jobs](/pages/background-jobs/).

**Kernel.** The part of Ilium that is native code and not a plugin (tier T0). It owns the tree, the panes, the settings store, the snapshot and the recovery page.

**Key id.** The fingerprint of a publisher public key: the SHA-256 of the key bytes, written as 8 groups of 4 hexadecimal characters. See [Signing and trust](/pages/reference-signing-and-trust/).

**Lock file.** The file `ilium-plugins.lock` in a project. It records the exact version and package hash of each plugin, so `install --locked` gives the same set everywhere. See [Versions and dependencies](/pages/reference-dependency-resolution/).

**Mirror.** A copy of a registry on another host or share. Clients check the signatures of the original registry, never the mirror operator. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/).

**Namespace.** The first part of a plugin id, such as `com.example`, that one publisher owns in a registry. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/).

**Outcome.** The result of a submission: `ok`, `ok-node`, `ok-epoch`, `duplicate`, `refused`, `failed` or `cancelled`. See the table in [Reference values](#reference-values).

**Pane.** A node of the tree that shows a running process, an agent, an editor or a plugin's own view.

**Pin.** To hold a plugin at one version so that updates skip it. See [Distribution commands](/pages/reference-plugin-distribution-cli/).

**Preopen.** A directory that the host opens for a granted file scope and passes to the component through WASI. A plugin sees only the preopens of the scopes it was granted, such as `/project` or `/data`.

**Primitive.** A host-provided pane kind that a plugin can build on or extend. The four primitives are `terminal`, `agent`, `editor` and `basic`, imported from `ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives` in Rust. See [Primitives](/pages/primitives/).

**Provider.** A plugin that supplies a service to others: a service provider for a named interface, or an inference provider for model calls. The host routes calls to the provider. See [Services](/pages/services/).

**Publisher id.** The identifier of a publisher, stored with the signing key and equal to the start of every plugin id that the key signs. It is different from the display name in `publisher`. See [Signing and trust](/pages/reference-signing-and-trust/).

**Registry.** An optional source of plugins: signed JSON files and package blobs on an HTTPS host or file share. Ilium ships with none configured (decision D27). See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/).

**Replacement.** A plugin that lists another plugin in `replaces` and provides its whole `surface`. The replaced core plugin is turned off while the replacement is on. See [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/#replace).

**Reproducible build.** A build in which two machines make the same package bytes from the same source. See [Publishing guide](/pages/guide-publishing/#reproducible-builds).

**Restored state.** The bytes that a plugin returns from `deactivate`. The host stores them and passes them back as `restored` on the next activation. The limit is 1 MiB. Larger bytes are dropped, and the next activation receives no value.

**Retained mode.** The rule that plugins run when an event arrives or a timer fires, and push their state to the host. The host keeps that state and draws it. A plugin's `views.render` is not called on every frame. See [Retained mode](/pages/retained-mode/).

**SBOM.** Software bill of materials: a list of the libraries inside a component, kept in `sbom.json`. See [Publishing guide](/pages/guide-publishing/#sbom).

**Scene.** An animated background, written as a `scene` component that implements the `renderer` export. A scene draws into a surface, and the host applies the shared look to the result. See [Scenes](/pages/api-scenes/).

**Scope.** A named area of the file system that a `fs` grant refers to, such as `project`, `data` or `cache`. See [File access](/pages/file-access/).

**Shared look.** The colour, style and dithering settings that the user sets once and the host applies to every scene and surface. A plugin does not add its own brightness or palette controls. See [Accessibility and theming](/pages/accessibility-and-theming/).

**Side.** One of the three places a plugin runs: `server` (S), `client` (C) or `scene` (A, animation). Each side has its own component, grant list, instance, state and failure count. See [Worlds and sides](/pages/worlds-and-sides/).

**Surface.** A pixel buffer that a plugin writes into. It is shown either by a `surface` widget or as the frame of a scene. The formats are listed in [Reference values](#reference-values).

**Tier.** The trust level of a plugin: T0 for the kernel, T1 for bundled first-party code, T2 for signed third-party code and T3 for unsigned local code. See [Security model](/pages/security/).

**Tree.** The hierarchy of nodes that Ilium shows in the sidebar, made of groups and panes.

**Trust store.** The file in which the host keeps the publisher keys that the user or administrator trusts, each with a tier. See [Signing and trust](/pages/reference-signing-and-trust/).

**Widget.** One visual element of a plugin's view, such as a `block`, a `paragraph`, a `table` or a `tabs` widget. See the widget pages, starting with [Widgets index](/pages/widgets-index/).

**WIT.** The WebAssembly Interface Types language. The plugin contract is written in WIT, and the Rust and TypeScript bindings are generated from it. Names stay kebab-case in WIT. The SDKs convert them, as shown in the naming rule below.

**World.** The WIT name for the set of imports and exports that one component may use, such as `ilium:server/base@0.1.0`. A manifest names the world of each component.

**Yank.** To withdraw one version from new installs and updates while installed copies keep working. See [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/).

## Further terms

**Cookbook.** The set of tested recipes in [Patterns cookbook](/pages/guide-patterns-cookbook/): debounce, throttle, cache, retry and others.

**Data version.** The integer `data_version` in the manifest. A change makes the host run `migrator` before `activate`. See [Data migration](/pages/guide-data-migration/).

**Display width.** The number of terminal cells a text takes. Wide characters take two. Measured with `display-width`. See [Internationalisation](/pages/guide-internationalisation/).

**Fingerprint.** The SHA-256 of a raw publisher public key, shown in the trust dialog. See [Publishing and support](/pages/guide-publishing-and-support/).


**Anchor.** A named place in a built-in Settings tab where a plugin section can attach. Anchors are only ever added. See [Plugin settings extension](/pages/settings-extension/).

**Attention mark.** A flag on a node set with `mark-attention` and cleared with `ack-attention`, behind the grant `tree.attention`. It drives the Attention display mode.

**Catalogue.** A named, typed list of options that a `choice` row or a widget uses as its `source`. A plugin declares its own in `catalogs`. The host serves read-only ones named `ilium.*`, such as `ilium.palettes`.

**Chrome.** The parts of the client around the content: tree toolbar, row actions, status bar segments and pane frame slots. A plugin fills them with the grant `ui.chrome`.

**Client request.** A call from one side of a plugin to its other side, declared in `client_requests` and sent with `client.request`. It is always granted and reaches only the plugin's own sides.

**Consent prompt.** A question the host asks the user at the first use of something that is not a grant by itself: the first geocoding lookup, the first `open-external` to each origin, and the first request to a host taken from a setting. See [Security model](/pages/security/).

**Durable timer.** A timer made with `timers.at` that survives a restart. It fires once, late, as `durable-timer-fired`.

**First-party limits tier.** The value `"first-party"` of the manifest key `limits_tier`. It raises the settings caps and is allowed only for bundled `ilium.*` plugins (error `manifest.limits-tier`).

**Frame slot.** A place in a pane frame (header icon, header text, footer row or banner) that a plugin fills with `set-frame-slot`.

**High-risk grant (H).** A grant that is off by default in every dialog and always needs an explicit user choice, even for a bundled plugin. Nine grants are high risk in the contract.

**Host catalogue.** A catalogue owned by the kernel, such as `ilium.palettes`, `ilium.dithers`, `ilium.filters`, `ilium.style-presets` or `ilium.icons`.

**Input journal.** The record of `send-input` submissions made with `journal: true`. An entry without a recorded outcome after a crash is reported once as `input-uncertain` and never replayed.

**Intent, lifecycle.** An intent that changes a pane's process: `freeze-pane`, `unfreeze-pane`, `replace-pane-command`, `terminate-pane-process` or `resize-pane`. It needs `panes.lifecycle`.

**Limits tier.** The class of caps that apply to a plugin: `standard`, or `first-party` for bundled plugins.

**Long-lived child.** A process started with `process.spawn` that keeps running and streams output as events. It needs `process.long-lived` and a matching `process.run:<program>` grant.

**Prompt epoch.** A counter of the prompts sent to an agent pane. `ok-epoch` returns the new value.

**Restructure batch.** A group of tree changes sent with the intent `restructure`, applied atomically and undone with `revert-restructure`. Undo tokens do not survive a restart.

**Row state.** The enabled, disabled or hidden state of a settings row, set with `settings.set-row-state` or computed from `visible_when`.

**Section.** A block of settings rows that a plugin adds to a tab. In a built-in tab it sits under a divider that names the plugin.

**Snapshot, frozen.** A copy of a terminal screen taken with `terminal.freeze-snapshot` so that a plugin reads one consistent state.

**Token provider.** An optional export that supplies syntax tokens for a language declared in `languages`.

**Toast.** A short message drawn by the client, sent with the intent `toast` (grant `notify.toast`).

**Unstable feature.** An item marked `@unstable(feature = <name>)`. It is visible only to a plugin that lists the name in `unstable` and only in development builds for T2 and T3. `gpu.kernels` is one.

**Plugin host.** The part of Ilium that loads components, links their imports, runs their exports under deadlines and enforces their limits. It is the crate `ilium-plugin-host`, and one instance of it runs in each process that hosts plugins. See [Host architecture](/pages/reference-host-architecture/).

**Dispatcher.** The task inside a plugin host that takes events, intents and calls from the kernel, batches them, and hands each call to the plugin executor in priority order. See [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/).

**Execution quota group.** The token bucket `ilium-execution` of one plugin side: 2,000 ms of CPU time that refills at 500 ms per second. An empty bucket makes submissions return `quota-exceeded`. See [Errors and limits](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/).

**Worker bank.** The pool of threads, `min(4, cores / 2)` and at least one, that runs background job instances so that jobs never block the plugin executor. See [Background jobs](/pages/background-jobs/).

**Store and instance.** In Wasmtime, a Store holds the memory and state of one running copy of a component, called an instance. Ilium uses one Store per plugin side instance. See [Host runtime](/pages/reference-host-runtime/).

**Epoch tick.** A 10 ms step of the engine clock that Wasmtime uses to interrupt running guest code. The host sets the deadline to `ceil(d / 10) + 1` ticks after the call starts, so a guest that spins traps no earlier than `d` and no later than `d + 20` ms. See [Host runtime](/pages/reference-host-runtime/).

**Sandbox helper.** The separate process `ilium-plugin-helper` that hosts one T2 or T3 plugin side inside a Linux sandbox. See [Sandbox helper protocol](/pages/reference-host-helper/).


**World variant.** A base world (`server/base`, `client/base`, `anim/base`) plus the optional export fragments, such as `with-hook-handler`, that a plugin implements. See [Worlds and sides](/pages/worlds-and-sides/).

**Plugin envelope.** The record `PluginEnvelope` that carries plugin traffic between a client and the server on the existing connection: submissions, outcomes, messages and control. See [Plugin traffic over IPC](/pages/reference-host-ipc/).

**Contribution delta.** The record `ContributionDelta` that carries changes of retained contributions (decorations, status segments, virtual rows) from the server to each client, as a snapshot followed by numbered increments. See [Plugin traffic over IPC](/pages/reference-host-ipc/).

**Caller deadline.** The timeout the caller sets on a request, for example the `timeout_millis` of an HTTP call or the client-request timeout. When it passes, the caller gets `timed-out`. See [Reply deadlines](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/#reply-deadlines).

**Ceiling.** The largest value a tier may use for a `limits` key. The host clamps a request above the ceiling and logs it. See [Errors and limits reference](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/).

**Grace.** The 100 ms after a soft deadline. A call that is still running when the grace ends traps. See [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/).

**Hard deadline.** A deadline at which the host interrupts the call. The call traps and counts as a failure unless its call class says it does not. See [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/).

**host-capacity.** The reason shown when the host refuses to start an instance because of session limits, such as the memory pool or the helper count. It is not a failure. See [Errors and limits reference](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/).

**Near-miss.** A call that ended within its deadline but used at least 80% of it. See [Health and watchdog](/pages/reference-health-and-watchdog/).

**retry-after-ms.** A field of the `plugin-error` record. On `quota-exceeded` and `rate-limited` it says how long to wait before the same call can succeed. See [Errors and limits reference](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/).

**Soft deadline.** A deadline that does not interrupt the call. The call finishes, the host discards a late result, and the breach counts toward the streak limit. See [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/).

**Streak limit.** The number of consecutive soft-deadline breaches of one call class that trap the instance: 3, or 30 for scene frames. See [Host scheduling](/pages/reference-host-scheduling/).

**Trap.** The instance aborts. The host counts one failure and restarts the side after 1 s, then 5 s, and disables it at the third failure within 10 minutes. See [Errors and limits reference](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/).

**ABI fault and semantic fault.** An ABI fault is a breach of the binary contract, such as a bad pointer or a malformed record, and traps the instance. A semantic fault is a valid call that the host refuses, and it returns an error code to the plugin. See [Errors and limits reference](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/).

### Internal decision ids

Some pages cite short ids such as L2 to L6, AX5, E9, C78, A21 and X5. They come from the design notes. L2 to L6 are section labels in [Errors and limits reference](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/), and AX5 is a decision in [Design decisions](/pages/design-decisions/). E9, C78, A21 and X5 have no page that defines them, and a reader can ignore them. The requirement ids written in square brackets with a prefix and a number are the ones that tests use.

## For users

These terms appear in the Plugins tab, in dialogs and in `ilium plugin list`. Each entry says what the word means for a person who installs and manages plugins. The longer pages are [Plugins for users](/pages/user-plugins-overview/), [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/) and [Permissions explained](/pages/user-permissions-explained/).

| Term | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| Plugin | A small program that adds a feature to Ilium. Thirty come with Ilium. Others are installed from a `.iliumpkg` file. |
| Core plugin | A plugin that comes with Ilium and has an id that starts with `ilium.core.`. Badge `T1`. See [Core plugins for users](/pages/user-core-plugins/). |
| Package | One `.iliumpkg` file. Ilium has no store. You get the file from the author. |
| Permission | The plain-language name of a grant: one thing a plugin may do, such as read files in this project. You answer for each one when you install. |
| High risk | A permission that can read private data or change things outside Ilium. It starts unchecked. |
| Signed | The package carries a signature from a publisher key. Badge `T2`. |
| Unsigned, `dev` | The package has no signature. Badge `T3` and `dev`. Install it only if you built it or reviewed it. |
| Publisher key | The key you trust to sign packages. You see its short fingerprint when you trust it. |
| On, Off, Failed | The state words in the Plugins tab. They are defined in [Settings, plugin rows](/pages/core-plugin-settings/#plugin-row-states). |
| Blocked by policy | An administrator rule forbids the plugin. See [Administration](/pages/guide-administration/). |
| Safe mode | A start of Ilium with third-party plugins off for that run. See [Troubleshooting plugins](/pages/user-troubleshooting/). |
| Recovery page | The simple plugin page that works when Settings does not. |
