## Reference values

### Tiers

| Tier | Who writes it | How it is loaded | Install rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | The kernel | Native code | Not a plugin |
| T1 | First-party, bundled | Precompiled `.cwasm` | Granted the manifest ceiling, except high-risk grants |
| T2 | Third parties, signed | `.iliumpkg` with an Ed25519 `signature` | Review dialog, normal grants checked |
| T3 | Local, unsigned | `.iliumpkg` without a signature | Review dialog, normal grants checked |

Windows and macOS refuse T2 and T3 packages until a sandbox exists on those systems. The refusal reads: `Cannot install <name> <version>.` followed by `Third-party plugins need the plugin sandbox, which is not available on Windows yet.` and `Bundled plugins keep working.`

### Sides and worlds

| Side | Component file | Base world |
|---|---|---|
| S, server | `server.wasm` | `ilium:server/base@0.1.0` |
| C, client | `client.wasm` | `ilium:client/base@0.1.0` |
| A, animation | `scene.wasm` | `ilium:anim/base@0.1.0` |

### Outcomes

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ok` | The submission was applied. For a call, the typed result is ready to take. |
| `ok-node(node-id)` | The submission was applied and created this node. |
| `ok-epoch(u64)` | A `send-input` on an agent pane was applied and carries the new prompt epoch. The SDK treats it as `ok` where code matches only `ok`. |
| `duplicate(original)` | The dedup key was reserved. `original` is the reference of the first submission. |
| `refused(code)` | Not applied, for a check that ran before acceptance. The key is not reserved. |
| `failed(code)` | Accepted, but the host failed to apply it, for example with `io` or `timed-out`. |
| `cancelled` | Stopped by the plugin, the user, a shutdown, or a refusal of its batch. |

### Error codes

| Code | Meaning | Retry |
|---|---|---|
| `not-permitted` | No capability, the user declined it, or the path leaves its scope | No |
| `not-found` | The node, pane, file, command, plugin or other named thing is gone | No |
| `invalid-argument` | The call breaks a rule the plugin can check, such as a size cap | No, fix the call |
| `conflict` | The state changed, or a lock or claim is held | Yes, after re-reading the state |
| `quota-exceeded` | A stored or held quota is full | After freeing resources |
| `rate-limited` | A rate rule throttles the call | Yes, after `retry-after-ms` |
| `busy` | Transient capacity is full | Yes, later |
| `timed-out` | A deadline passed | Yes |
| `cancelled` | The request was cancelled | Maybe |
| `unsupported` | The host or platform cannot do it | No |
| `pane-not-ready` | A restored terminal pane has not started its process | Yes, after the pane event |
| `revoked` | The authorization epoch changed during the call | No, the plugin is re-activated |
| `io` | An operating system I/O error other than a missing file | Maybe |
| `network` | DNS, connect, TLS or transport failure | Yes |
| `internal` | A host bug, or a trap inside a job | No |

### Grants

A grant string is `name` or `name:argument`. The first colon separates the name from the argument, so later colons belong to the argument.

| Grant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `agent.read` | Read agent state. No argument. |
| `fs.read:project` | Read the project directory, mounted as `/project`. |
| `http:api.example.com` | Call one exact host. |
| `http:*.example.com` | Call any subdomain, at any depth. The bare domain is not included. |
| `process.run:git` | Run the program `git`, resolved through `PATH`. |
| `topics.subscribe:build/*` | Receive every topic under the prefix `build/`. |

Grants are recorded per plugin, per side, and per user configuration. They are not recorded per project. A high-risk grant (H) is never checked by default in the install dialog.

### Further grants

Twenty-three grant rows are new. Ten are high risk (H).

| Grant | Sides | Meaning | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `terminal.read-cells` | S C | Terminal cells, modes, foreground process, frozen snapshot, `screen-changed` | |
| `terminal.history` | S C | Scrollback above the screen | H |
| `terminal.input-lock` | S C | Lock user input for at most 2 s while typing | H |
| `terminal.raw-input` | S C | Raw bytes and mouse events to a pane | H |
| `panes.lifecycle` | S | Freeze, unfreeze, replace command, terminate, resize | H |
| `tree.restructure` | S C | Create groups, folders, projects, splits; restructure batches | H |
| `tree.attention` | S C | Attention marks | |
| `ui.chrome` | S C | Tree toolbar, row actions, status segments, frame slots | |
| `open-external` | S C | Open a link or file through the host | |
| `sessions.cross` | S | Reach the same plugin in other live sessions | H |
| `process.long-lived` | S C | Long-lived child processes | H |
| `settings.read-kernel:<tab>` | S C | Read one built-in tab; `api` is H | H for `api` |
| `settings.write-kernel:<kernel-tab-id>` | S | Own one built-in settings tab; T1 only | H |
| `keymap.read` | C | Read the keymap | |
| `agent.transcript` | S C | Typed agent transcript turns | H |
| `location.geocode` | C A | Place search through the host | |
| `inference.embed` | S C | Embeddings through the selected provider | |
| `notify.toast` | S C | Toasts | |
| `journal.read` | S C | Host and other plugins' journal entries | |
| `gpu.kernels` | A | Host GPU kernels, `@unstable`, development builds only | |
| `panes.create-command:<program>` | S C | Create a pane that runs one named program; needs `panes.create` | H |
| `extensions.provide:<plugin-id>/<point>` | S C A | Own one extension point and receive its contributions | |
| `extensions.contribute:<plugin-id>/<point>` | S C | Contribute to one extension point; high when the point declares `risk: "high"` | |

New argument forms: `http:setting:<key>`, `fs.read:agent-sessions:gemini`, `fs.read:agent-config:gemini`, `fs.read:agent-config:antigravity` and `settings.read-kernel:<kernel-tab-id>`.

### Further events and intents

| Kind | Names |
|---|---|
| Events | `screen-changed`, `user-line-submitted`, `signal-changed`, `agent-model-changed`, `pane-lifecycle-changed`, `attention-changed`, `kernel-settings-changed`, `keymap-changed`, `editor-pointer`, `editor-viewport-changed`, `durable-timer-fired`, `input-uncertain`, `display-mode-changed`, `client-request` |
| Intents | `freeze-pane`, `unfreeze-pane`, `replace-pane-command`, `terminate-pane-process`, `resize-pane`, `create-group`, `create-folder`, `create-project`, `create-split`, `restructure`, `revert-restructure`, `mark-attention`, `ack-attention`, `set-status-segment`, `clear-status-segment`, `set-frame-slot`, `open-external`, `toast`, `dismiss-toast`, `set-bookmarked`, `set-expanded`, `set-inferred-icon` |
| UI actions and values | `ui-action` kinds and values grow with the 51 widgets; see [Events and intents](/pages/reference-events-and-intents/) |

### Further manifest errors

`manifest.catalog-unknown`, `manifest.contribution-limit`, `manifest.contribution-target`, `manifest.row-format`, `manifest.limits-tier`, `manifest.when-key`, `manifest.client-request-unknown`, `manifest.asset-size`, `manifest.visible-when`, `manifest.menu-depth`, `manifest.settings-source`, `manifest.cli-field` and `manifest.scene-prerender`. Each refuses the install and names the key path. See [Errors and limits](/pages/errors-and-limits/).

### File scopes and preopens

| Scope | Preopen | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `package` | `/package` | Always, read only |
| `data` | `/data` | Always, read and write |
| `cache` | `/cache` | Always, read and write, evictable |
| `project` | `/project` | Granted |
| `picked` | `/picked/<n>` | Granted per pick |
| `path:<template>` | `/paths/<n>` | Granted, high risk for a literal absolute path |

Templates can start with `{home}`, `{config}`, `{data}`, `{cache}`, `{project}` or `{worktrees}`.

### Activation triggers

`startup`, `event:<event-name>`, `command:<id>`, `view:<id>`, `pane-kind:<id>`, `scene:<id>`, `cli:<name>`, `http:<path>`, `service:<interface>`, `topic:<topic>` and `settings:<tab-id>`. Without an `activation` list, a plugin is activated on the first use of any of its contributions.

### Deactivation reasons

| Reason | When it happens |
|---|---|
| `shutdown` | The server or client stops. The plugin has its deactivate deadline (500 ms by default). |
| `disabled` | The user or `plugins.set-enabled` turns the plugin off. |
| `upgrade` | An update or `ilium plugin dev` replaces the running version. |
| `crash-restart` | Declared in the WIT enum but never delivered: a trap drops the instance without a call. |
| `revoked` | A capability was revoked. The plugin is re-activated with fewer grants. |
| `granted` | A capability was added. The plugin is re-activated with more grants. |
| `detached` | Not a deactivation reason. A client that disconnects cleanly deactivates its instance with `shutdown`, and the instance returns restore bytes for the next attach. |

### Surface formats

| Use | Formats |
|---|---|
| A scene surface (`ilium:anim/surface`) | `gray8`, `rgb8`, `rgba8` |
| A `surface` widget | `mask8`, `mono1`, `gray8`, `rgb8`, `rgba8` |

A scene row is `width` bytes for `gray8`, `3 x width` for `rgb8` and `4 x width` for `rgba8`.

## Worked examples

### Rust: a keyed submission

This server-side function builds a submission that sets a badge on one node. The key names the node and the change. The same change sent again within 10 minutes completes as `duplicate`.

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::dedup;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SetDecorationSpec;

/// Sets the `hello` badge on one node. The key names the node and the change.
fn badge_submission(node: NodeId, change: &str) -> Submission {
    let node_text = format!("{node:?}");
    let intent = Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
        node,
        slot: "hello".into(),
        content: vec![Span::plain("hi")],
        icon: None,
        sort_key: None,
        persist: false,
    });
    let key = dedup::key_for(&["badge", node_text.as_str(), change]);
    Submission::keyed(intent, key)
}
```

### TypeScript: a client plugin that answers a command

This client-side plugin answers its own command with a desktop notice. The dedup key makes a second invocation within 10 minutes complete as `duplicate`.

```ts
import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'command-invoked') continue;
      if (event.val.command !== 'com.example.hello/greet') continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'notify',
          val: { title: 'Hello', body: 'from a plugin', urgency: 'normal', sound: undefined },
        },
        correlation: 1n,
        dedupKey: 'hello:greet',
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});
```

### Manifest: the grants for each side

Grants are listed per side. Each side has its own grant list, and the host checks each component against its own list.

```json
"capabilities": {
  "server": ["agent.read", "tree.decorate", "fs.read:project"],
  "client": ["commands.invoke:com.example.hello/*"]
}
```

## What the user sees

When a plugin's first activation needs high-risk grants, the host shows one prompt per plugin. The user can allow the selected grants or refuse for now. A refusal is asked again at the next server start, at most three times.

<span class="t-err">err</span>  example.hello-badge 0.1.1  stopped by the restart rule
     <span class="t-dim">Stopped after 3 failures: handler.on-events trap.</span>
     <span class="t-dim">See notice N14 in Lifecycle.</span>
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. A plugin list after the restart rule disabled one plugin.

## Edge cases

- A refused submission does not reserve its dedup key, so a retry with the same key after fixing the cause is correct.
- A submission that was accepted and then failed keeps its key. A retry of a failed action needs a new key.
- A capability revoked during a call makes that call return `revoked`. The plugin is re-activated with the smaller grant set, and this is not a failure.
- Three failures in 10 minutes disable a plugin on one side. The first failure restarts it after 1 s and the second after 5 s. The third disables it. Details: [Lifecycle](/pages/lifecycle/#failure-counting-and-restart). A manual re-enable resets the count.

**Component mode.** A test mode in which the harness loads the built `.wasm` component in a WebAssembly runtime and enforces the limits. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).

**Conformance case.** One check of the conformance suite with a stable id such as `CONF-LIFE-02`. See [Conformance suite](/pages/reference-conformance-suite/).

**Dev badge.** The mark that Settings > Plugins and the plugin list show for a plugin installed by `ilium plugin dev`. See [Debugging tools](/pages/reference-debugging-tools/).

**Expectation file.** A JSON file next to a fixture that states the submissions, logs and outcomes the plugin must produce, with the match modes `exact`, `ordered` and `subset`. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).

**FakeHost.** The test double that stands in for the host for one plugin on one side. See [Testing plugins](/pages/testing/).

**FakeSession.** The test double that runs several plugins, both sides and core extension point stubs in one fake session. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).

**Fixture.** A JSON file that sets the starting state of the fake host and lists events to deliver. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).

**Golden file.** A text file that holds the expected render of a view, compared by `assert_golden`. See [Testing plugins](/pages/testing/).

**Lint rule.** A named, severity-ranked check of `ilium plugin lint`, such as `lint.grant-unused`. See [Check and lint rules](/pages/reference-check-and-lint-rules/).

**Native mode.** A test mode in which the plugin runs as a plain library on the host machine, with no component and no enforced limits. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).

**Replay file.** A JSONL recording of the inputs of a session, written by `trace --record` and re-run by `replay`. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).

**Snapshot.** A stored value, pretty JSON with sorted keys, that a test compares with `assert_snapshot`. See [Test harness reference](/pages/reference-test-harness/).

**Trace.** The ring buffer of 1,024 records per plugin instance that shows events, submissions, host calls and outcomes. See [Debugging tools](/pages/reference-debugging-tools/).

## Conventions

**Correlation number.** The `u64` a plugin puts on a submission. Values below 2^63 belong to the plugin, values from 2^63 up to the SDK. See [WIT reference conventions](/pages/reference-wit/#2-conventions).

**Dedup key.** A string of 1 to 128 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9._:/-]` that makes a submission happen once within 10 minutes. See [Intents](/pages/api-intents/).

**epoch-ms.** A `u64` count of milliseconds since the Unix epoch, UTC. Durations are millisecond counts in fields that end in `-ms`.

**Colour.** A `u32` written `0x00RRGGBB`. The top byte is zero.

**Id types.** `node-id`, `request-id`, `client-id`, `buffer-id` and the other ids are unsigned integers that are opaque to the plugin.

**Character limit.** A limit in "characters" counts Unicode scalar values. A limit in "bytes" counts UTF-8 bytes.

- [Manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/)
- [Capability table](/pages/reference-capabilities/)
- [Events and intents](/pages/reference-events-and-intents/)

### Security

**Audit log**: security record of grants and policy events ([Audit log](/pages/reference-audit-log/)). **Admin policy**: system TOML file that limits plugins ([Admin policy](/pages/reference-admin-policy/)). **Project trust**: user decision that a repository's `.ilium/` values apply ([SEC-310]). **Blocklist**: signed list of banned packages ([SEC-146]). **Safe mode**: start with third-party code off ([SEC-328]). **Data class**: label for kind of data in a point field ([SEC-281]). **Toxic combination**: read grant plus egress grant ([SEC-004]). **Key pinning**: a package keeps its first signing key ([SEC-142]). **Rotation statement**: signed move to a new key ([SEC-143]).

# Roadmap

## Roadmap

The plugin platform is built in ordered phases. Phases 0 to 6 make up version 1 (v1). Phase 7, which moves the native editor and the native board into plugins, is the first milestone after v1. This page lists every phase, the gate it must pass before the next phase opens, the rule that keeps v1 plugins working after v1, and the decisions that closed the open questions of the plan.

A gate is an ordered list of checks. A phase opens only when every check in its gate passes. A feature reaches plugins in the Ilium release that closes its phase.

## What you need

You need no tools to read this page. To write a plugin against a phase, you need:

- The API version `ilium:plugin@0.1.0`. The manifest `api` key is `"0.1.0"`, and it must match the component's `ilium:api-version` section.
- For Rust plugins: stable Rust 1.90 or later with the `wasm32-wasip2` target, and the crate `ilium-plugin-sdk`.
- For TypeScript plugins (from Phase 3): Bun 1.2 or later and the package `@ilium/plugin-sdk`. The SDK pins its own component tools, so nothing is installed globally.
- An Ilium release that carries the phase you use. Features of a later phase are not in an earlier release.

## Phases

| Phase | Name | What it delivers | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Decide and measure | Records the decisions, measures the benchmarks against their targets, and proves the toolchain path | Decisions recorded, benchmark numbers recorded, toolchain path proven |
| 1 | Registries | Replaces each closed enum with a registry that has native implementations | All existing tests, clippy and fmt pass. No visible behaviour change |
| 2 | Contract and host | The WIT packages, the plugin host, the Rust SDK and the first live contract | A Rust hello plugin installs from a package, receives events, sets a decoration, contributes a command and a settings page, survives a forced trap, and hot-reloads in dev mode |
| 2A | Ratatui-mirror UI API | The `ui` import, the `ui-tree` model, host-owned widget state, the popup stack and theme tokens | A widget gallery plugin, in Rust and in TypeScript, renders every widget case, and the golden buffers match for both |
| 2B | Pane primitives | The `terminal`, `agent`, `editor` and `basic` primitives | A board prototype builds a three-column card board as a basic pane kind, with drag and drop, persists it, and shows it again after a server restart |
| 2C | Scoped file access, codec and jobs | The `fs` import, the preopens for every scope, codec helpers and background jobs | Escape tests pass: `..`, absolute paths, symlinks and hard links out of every scope are refused, for direct calls and for `std::fs` through preopens |
| 3 | TypeScript build path | The TypeScript build, the `@ilium/plugin-sdk` package and the animation contract | The same conformance fixtures pass for the Rust and the TypeScript guests on Wasmtime |
| 4a to 4e | Early feature migrations | Features move from the kernel into first-party plugins in five waves | The common wave gate, plus the extra gate of each wave (see below) |
| 5 | Late feature migrations | Features with crash-safety contracts move last | Crash-safety tests pass for each feature (see below) |
| 6 | Third-party readiness | Package signing and the trust store, the review dialog for every capability, the `ilium plugin` commands, and the complete guides | A plugin written only from the published docs, by an agent with no access to the Ilium source, builds, installs and passes its own tests, in Rust and in TypeScript |
| 7 | Editors and boards as plugins (after v1) | The editor and the board move to plugins | See the Phase 7 section |

Phase 2A comes before Phase 2B because a basic pane's body is a `ui-tree`, so the widget API must exist before the pane primitives are built on it.

## The common wave gate

Every migration wave in Phase 4 must pass this gate before the next wave starts:

- The feature behaves as before, and its existing tests pass after they are ported.
- The frame and processing budgets in the [performance page](/pages/performance/) are met with every wave plugin loaded.
- Crash isolation holds. Kill a plugin's instance during `on-events`. The server keeps answering IPC within 50 ms, the plugin restarts after 1 s, and a third kill within 10 minutes disables it with a notice.

The crash rule replaces the older "second crash within 60 s" wording, so the restart rule below is the one that applies.

## Phase 4 waves

| Wave | Features | Extra gate |
|---|---|---|
| 4a | Pilots: agent toolbar buttons (client side), sound and notification selection rules (server side), one extra agent signature through the signature registry, text triggers limited to notify and sound actions, and tree sort-key providers | None beyond the common gate |
| 4b | Presentation: agent messaging, cost, titles and naming, Smart Copy, terminal links and context menu, the git status line, chatroom views, goal tracking, bookmarks, locks, workspace search, help and guided setup | None beyond the common gate |
| 4c | Portable scenes that need only the `package` and `cache` scopes, with no network and no media service, then inference providers as services. The V8 animation runtime is retired at the end of this wave | Each scene's output matches the native scene by the parity method |
| 4d | File-reading, caching and live-data scenes: live-data scenes, the maps and Wikipedia scenes, and image scenes, through `http`, the picked and template file scopes, `cache`, `codec` and jobs | Each scene matches its native output within the frame budget. With the network off, live-data scenes show cached or empty state, never an error loop. The cache stays within the `data` plus `cache` limit and evicts the oldest entries first |
| 4e | Saved-world scenes: the voxel scene reads saved worlds through the `minecraft-saves` scope, `codec.inflate` and jobs | A fixture saved world renders identically to the native voxel scene. Parsing runs in a job and never blocks a frame. The plugin cannot read any file outside the saves scope |

## Wave gate tests and what stays native

Each wave has one named gate test and a list of what stays in the kernel while the wave runs. The core plugins that each wave delivers are listed in [feature traceability](/pages/reference-feature-traceability/) by wave. [COR-060] [COR-061]

| Wave | Core plugins delivered | Gate test | What stays native |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4a | Agent toolbar buttons, Notifications rules, Text triggers (notify and sound actions), agent signatures, tree sort keys | `wave-4a-parity`: replay the baseline agent fixtures and compare toolbar, sounds and tree order | PTY, tree model, detection loop timing, sound output device |
| 4b | Fleet, Cost, Titles, Smart Copy, Terminal links, Worktrees, Chatroom, Progress, Recap, Voice, Scheduler, Sessions, Compaction, Settings, Keys and help, Search, Diagnostics, Agent setup, Session convert, Tree, Layout | `wave-4b-cli-and-settings`: run every example of the CLI reference and compare every settings tab with the baseline | Config store, snapshot writer, keymap, HTTP listener, recovery page |
| 4c | Inference, portable scenes, Ambient look | `wave-4c-scene-output`: each scene output equals the native scene by checksum | Look painter, dither, scene host, raster |
| 4d | Live-data, maps, Wikipedia and image scenes | `wave-4d-scene-budget`: native output within the frame budget | Scene host, network egress policy |
| 4e | Voxel scene | `wave-4e-saved-world`: fixture saved world renders identically | Scene host |
| 7 | Editor, Kanban | `wave-7-editor-board-parity`: editor and board scenarios of the user documentation | Pane kinds registry, file system scopes |

The editor and the board stay native until Phase 7. Their pages ([editor](/pages/core-plugin-editor/), [kanban](/pages/core-plugin-kanban/)) describe the plugin form and say so at the top.

## Phase 5 and crash safety

Phase 5 needs two kernel additions first. The keys of `send-input` are journaled in the snapshot before the PTY write, so a server restart does not repeat input. Progress of a decoration is persisted in the decoration store.

Each feature in Phase 5 passes its own gate. Kill the server in the middle of the operation, restart it, and check that no delivery is duplicated or lost. The features include scheduled input, the prompt queue, progress monitors, worktree workflows, session resume and conversion, voice, the file explorer on the basic primitive, the settings UI with its kernel recovery page, and the chatroom router.

## Phase 6: what v1 ships

- Packages are files that work with no network. They are signed for tier T2. An optional static registry protocol (decision D27) adds search, update and revocation. Ilium ships no registry and runs no central store. An unsigned or tampered T2 package is refused with a message that names the failing check.
- A separate sandbox helper process runs every T2 and T3 plugin on Linux. A T2 plugin that opens a file outside its scopes, opens a socket or spawns a process without a grant is denied by the helper.
- On Windows and macOS, installing or loading a T2 or T3 package is refused with a message that names the missing sandbox. Bundled T1 plugins keep working on every platform.
- The v1 contract is frozen at the end of Phase 6. The WIT packages are snapshotted, and from then on only `@since` additions are allowed.

<pre class="term">
<span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin install ./agent.iliumpkg
<span class="t-err">error</span> manifest.signature-invalid  bad signature
<span class="t-dim">step</span>  install stopped before any code was loaded
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. A tampered T2 package stops at the signature check, and the error code names the failing check.

## Phase 7: editors and boards as plugins

Phase 7 is the first milestone after v1. It moves the native editor and the native board into plugins built on the `editor` and `basic` primitives.

- An editor plugin provides the editor primitive. It covers editing, saving and autosave, the minimap, line numbers, syntax highlighting through an annotator, large-file source windows, and the Markdown source and rendered views. It is added as the export `editor-provider` with the grant `editor.provide`. The provider receives the open buffers with `adopt` and returns them with `release`, and while it runs the kernel routes every other plugin's `editor` calls to it.
- A board plugin, built on the basic primitive, covers kanban boards and boards created from Markdown files.
- The native editor and board code is removed once both plugins pass. The kernel keeps only the `code-view` hot path, which serves both the native provider and the plugin provider.
- A snapshot written by v1 with open editor and board panes restores into the plugin-provided panes, with the same files, cursor positions and board contents.

The Phase 7 gate is strict:

- No ABI break. A WIT diff between the v1 snapshot and the Phase 7 packages shows only additions marked `@since`. Every v1 conformance fixture and every first-party v1 plugin loads and passes unchanged.
- The editor and board feature tests from v1 pass against the plugin versions.
- Keystroke latency in the editor and board stays within the performance budget, measured with the same harness as Phase 2B.

## Contract additions by phase

The contract has 42 additions, AX1 to AX42, so that plugins can express every Ilium feature. They are part of the one contract. Each addition lands in the phase whose features need it, with conformance fixtures and a Rust guest and a TypeScript guest in the same change. An addition that ships before the Phase 6 freeze is part of the v1 contract. One that does not ship by then stays unreleased and breaks nothing. The decisions D12 to D25 are final (see [Design decisions](/pages/design-decisions/)).

| Phase | Additions placed here |
|---|---|
| 2 | The nine new contribution keys and `limits_tier` with their 13 manifest error codes. The 19 new grants, the new argument forms and the high-risk rule. `catalogs` and the host catalogues. The new settings rows and row-state calls. `kernel-settings.read` and `keymap.read`. Command `category` and `keywords`, the new `when` keys. The intents `toast`, `dismiss-toast` and `open-external`. `client-requests`. The `shared` cache bucket |
| 2A | The 19 new widgets and their props. Hover, tooltips, anchored and pinnable popovers, focus order, view pointer events and drag feedback. The menu model and the `menu-provider` export. | 2B | Terminal cell reads, history, snapshots and modes. Pane lifecycle intents. Tree structure intents and `restructure` with undo. Title provenance, inferred icons and attention. Tree and chrome contribution points, status segments, frame slots and the `virtual-rows-provider` export. Rich decorations. Staged, raw and mouse input, preconditions, the input lock and interactive `terminal-view`. Agent model, prompt epoch and typed transcripts. Editor viewport and minimap marks. Basic-pane activity and dirty flag |
| 2C | `fs` revisions, atomic writes and tail, and the Gemini and Antigravity agent scopes. HTTP streams and hosts taken from a setting. `process.spawn` with the `child` resource |

| 4c to 4d | `vector` embeddings once inference providers are services. Live-data and map scenes use HTTP streams and the shared cache |

### Extra gates for the additions

- **Phase 2.** Every high-risk grant of the additions is refused without an explicit grant, for a T1 fixture too. `limits_tier: "first-party"` on a package that is not a bundled `ilium.*` plugin is refused with `manifest.limits-tier`. A `settings.read-kernel:api` read never returns a secret.
- **Phase 2A.** The widget-gallery fixture renders all 51 widgets in Rust and TypeScript with matching golden buffers. The `location-picker` and the `location` row render cell for cell like the native world-map picker. The filterable choice dialog over `ilium.icons` pages in as the user scrolls and filters. Tooltips, spinner frames and decoration frames make no plugin call. A settings view that embeds a refused widget is refused with `invalid-argument`. Leaders follow the `…` rule: grey, one blank cell each side, blank under 5 cells, never part of a hit target.
- **Phase 2B.** A failing operation inside `restructure` leaves the tree unchanged, and `revert-restructure` restores the previous structure. The input lock never exceeds 2 s and no user key is lost. `resize-pane` refusals name the limiting neighbour. An inferred title never replaces a manual one.
- **Phase 5.** Killing the server between a journaled `send-input` write and its outcome produces exactly one `input-uncertain` after restart and no replay. A durable timer due while Ilium was stopped fires once with its lateness.

<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin install ./other.iliumpkg
<span class="t-err">error</span> manifest.limits-tier  limits_tier first-party refused
<span class="t-dim">step</span>  install stopped before any code was loaded
</pre>

Illustrative, not generated. The first Phase 2 gate check for `limits_tier` fails like this on a third-party package.

One risk is open. The additions bring 13 host interface groups and 19 widgets, so the placement above ships each group only with the feature that uses it. The outcome `ok-epoch` stays a separate case of `outcome`.

## The additive-only rule after v1

After v1, a contract change may only add items. Each addition carries `@since(version = <version>)` with the version that introduced it. Nothing exported in v1 is altered or removed. This covers the editor and basic primitives, the widget variant cases, and the event and intent cases. New widget cases are appended to the variant. A change that would alter or remove a v1 item is redesigned rather than shipped.

Plugin ids are part of the public surface too. Pane kind ids, command ids, settings keys, decoration slots and topic names keep their spelling across plugin versions. The kernel stores them as strings in snapshots.

Compatibility works in two steps:

- The host loads the current minor version and the previous one through hand-written adapters.
- A plugin built for a newer minor than the host is refused at install. The message names both versions.

Experimental items carry `@unstable(feature = <name>)` instead. Such an item is visible only to a plugin whose manifest lists the feature in the `unstable` key. In 0.1 there are two of them: `ui-calendar`, which enables the `calendar` widget, and `plugin-services`, which enables `services.call`. The `chart` widget is stable.

## The restart rule

The restart rule applies to each plugin on each side. On the client side, each client counts separately. A failing view counts against its plugin, not against the view.

| Event | Result |
|---|---|
| First failure | The plugin restarts after 1 s |
| Second failure | The plugin restarts after 5 s |
| Third failure within 10 minutes | The plugin is disabled on that side, and a notice names it |

A failure counts for 10 minutes and then expires. A successful run does not clear it sooner. A trap or a missed deadline counts as a failure. A `revoked` re-activation, a disable chosen by the user, an upgrade and a shutdown never count. Re-enabling the plugin by hand resets the count to zero.

## Decisions that closed the open items

These answers replace the questions that the plan left open. Each one is recorded in the decisions file with its identifier.

| Question | Answer | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Background-job model | Every job runs in a second instance of the component, in its own store. The plugin's own instance is never used | A21, X5 |
| TypeScript compiler | `componentize-js`. `componentize-qjs` is not used | U8 |
| Optional exports | Checked against the component's export list. The manifest lists only the optional exports | N9 |
| Settings and payload schemas | A JSON-Schema subset, draft 2020-12, checked by one pinned validator | N28 |
| Resource limits | The 0.1 defaults in the [errors and limits page](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/). A measured value may replace one, and the change is dated in the decisions file | Section 3 |
| `calendar` and `chart` | `chart` is stable. `calendar` stays unstable behind `ui-calendar` | W19, N33 |
| Prompt text for plugins without the grant | Nothing is sent, not even a length or a hash | C3 |
| Key-release events | Delivered only when the terminal supports the kitty keyboard protocol | C45 |
| `device.gpu` | Not part of the contract (`gpu.kernels` is `@unstable`). A manifest that names it is refused with `manifest.grant-unknown` | Added by page writers (`porting-iliumanim`) |

# Security model

## Security model

A plugin gets only the rights its manifest asks for and the user grants. First-party code runs inside the Ilium process. Third-party code runs in a separate helper process that the operating system confines. Every host call is checked against the grants in force at that moment. When a grant is revoked, the next call fails, and a call that was already running fails with `revoked`.

This page is the overview of the security rules and the entry point to the detailed pages. Statements that carry an id such as [SEC-013] are normative: they use MUST, SHOULD and MAY as in RFC 2119 and are collected in [Security and policy requirements](/pages/reference-requirements-security-policy/). The pages [Threat model](/pages/reference-threat-model/) and [Sandbox reference](/pages/reference-sandbox/) say what is defended and how.

**[SEC-013]** Every host call MUST be checked against the grants in force at that moment, for every tier except T0. A grant that is missing, declined, revoked or forbidden by policy MUST refuse the call with the form given under "What a call returns without a grant".

**[SEC-014]** A third-party package MUST never run in the Ilium process. If the sandbox cannot be built, the package does not load ([SEC-055]).

### You will need

- The capability table, which lists every grant and its risk mark: [Capability table](/pages/reference-capabilities/).
- The manifest reference, for the `capabilities` object, the `signature` entry, the `publisher` key and `limits_tier`: [Manifest reference](/pages/reference-manifest/).
- The package layout and install checks: [Packages](/pages/packages/).
- A language: the rules are the same in Rust and TypeScript. Each example below is shown in both, with the SDK paths of the [Rust SDK](/pages/rust-sdk/) and the [TypeScript SDK](/pages/typescript-sdk/).
- A Linux machine for any T2 or T3 package. The sandbox runs on Linux only ([SEC-057]).

## Trust tiers

| Tier | What it is | Where it runs | Grants |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 kernel | Native code built into Ilium | In the server or client process | Everything |
| T1 bundled | First-party WebAssembly embedded in the release | In-process Wasmtime | The manifest ceiling, granted automatically. High-risk (H) grants are asked for once, at first activation |
| T2 signed | Packages signed by a publisher key the user trusts | Sandboxed plugin helper, mandatory | A review dialog. Grants are remembered |
| T3 local and dev | Unsigned local packages | Sandboxed plugin helper, mandatory | The same review dialog, and a persistent `dev` badge |

In-process Wasmtime is trusted only for T1 code that the project builds itself. A third-party package never runs in that process. A T3 package is installed with `--allow-unsigned` or through `ilium plugin dev`.

The tier also decides three other things. These rules are enforced when the package is installed, not when the plugin runs.

| Rule | T1 bundled | T2 signed | T3 local |
|---|---|---|---|
| `limits_tier: "first-party"` (8 tabs, 2,048 value keys, 64 rows per section, 1,024 list items, 512 choice options) | Only when the id starts with `ilium.` | Refused: `manifest.limits-tier` | Refused: `manifest.limits-tier` |
| Package assets (`package_assets_mib`) | Up to 256 MiB | Up to 64 MiB | Up to 64 MiB |
| `sessions.cross` (commands in other running sessions) | Allowed with an explicit grant | Allowed with an explicit grant | Refused: `manifest.grant-tier` |
| `process.run:sh` | Allowed | Refused: `manifest.grant-tier` | Refused: `manifest.grant-tier` |

The first row is decision D12 and the second is D24. The `sessions.cross` row is D16. The `process.run:sh` row is [SEC-031]. All three are final decisions; see [Design decisions](/pages/design-decisions/).

## The sandbox

Third-party code runs in a helper process that the operating system confines. The full requirements are in [Sandbox reference](/pages/reference-sandbox/); this section is the summary.

- **[SEC-020]** One helper per plugin and side. Plugins never share a helper.
- **[SEC-021]** The helper has its own user, mount, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces, no network, no controlling terminal, a rebuilt environment and only the dispatcher channel as an open file ([SEC-022] to [SEC-028]).
- **[SEC-029]** Memory, process count and CPU are limited by a cgroup per helper.
- **[SEC-024]** A seccomp allowlist and `no_new_privs` apply before the first plugin byte is read.
- **[SEC-032]** A child started with `process.run` or `process.spawn` runs in the same confinement with no network, at low priority, under the plugin's CPU quota. Dropping the child handle or stopping the plugin ends the child with SIGTERM, and SIGKILL after 2 s.
- **[SEC-055]** When the sandbox cannot be built, T2 and T3 packages refuse to load with `sandbox.unavailable`. There is no unconfined fallback.

On Windows and macOS a T2 or T3 package is refused at install, and only T1 bundled plugins run (decision D5). The lines below are wrapped to fit the page. macOS shows the same text with its own name.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-err">Cannot install example.demo 0.1.0.</span>
Third-party plugins need the plugin
sandbox, which is not available on
Windows yet.
Bundled plugins keep working.
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. The install refusal for a T2 package on Windows. On macOS the same text names macOS.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Verifying a package

Before any code runs, the loader checks the package. There is one ordered list of install checks, and each step has its error code. The list is the table in [Grant review and consent](/pages/reference-grant-review-and-consent/#the-install-pipeline) ([SEC-100]). The first failing step stops the install, and each refusal is written as one JSONL `error` line that carries its code. The operational pipeline of 12 steps in [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/#the-install-pipeline) wraps the same checks with locking, staging and commit. The table below says which check belongs to which step of each list.

| Check order | What is checked | Error codes | Step in the 12-step pipeline |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 to 3 | Archive, layout, API version, file inventory | `package.zip-*`, `manifest.api-version`, `manifest.unknown-key`, `manifest.file-*`, `manifest.asset-size` | 2, 4, 5 |
| 4 | Signature (T2) and publisher match | `manifest.signature-invalid`, `manifest.publisher-mismatch` | 3 |
| 5 and 6 | Blocklist and administrator policy | `package.blocked`, `policy.*` | 6 |
| 7 | Key trust and key pinning | `trust.declined`, `package.publisher-key-changed` | 3 |
| 8 and 9 | Grant strings, tier rules. A grant denied by policy is not an install failure: it is locked off in the dialog | `manifest.grant-*`, `manifest.limits-tier` | 5, 6 |
| 10 | Review dialog | the user cancels | 7 |
| 11 | Commit | `install.write-failed` | 8 to 11 |

- [USR-170] Install, update and the Plugins screen MUST run the checks in the order of the table above, and MUST name the failing step's code in the error. Test: build one package for each failing check, install each, and assert the code and that nothing is written to the store.
- [USR-171] The error text for a refused install MUST begin `Cannot install <name> <version>.` and MUST name the check in plain words after it. Test: assert the first line for a hash failure and for a tier failure.

The review dialog is one dialog for every capability. Each row is a capability, grouped by side. A high-risk row is unchecked until the user checks it. The wording of each row is in the [Capability table](/pages/reference-capabilities/). A package that fills other plugins' extension points shows a separate group, **Adds to other plugins**, a package with `replaces` asks for a separate confirmation, and a package that reads data and sends data out shows the toxic combination row ([SEC-004]). This render is the canonical review dialog: other pages link here and do not redraw it. The dialog is drawn by the client with the same rounded border, grey `…` leaders and footer hint bar as every other Ilium dialog; a plugin never draws or restyles it ([SEC-102]).

## Grant strings

A grant is written as a name, or as a name and an argument separated by the first colon, for example `fs.read:project`. The name is one or more dot-separated lowercase segments. Later colons belong to the argument, so `services.use:ilium:inference/provider` has the name `services.use`.

| Grant | Argument | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `fs.read`, `fs.write`, `fs.watch` | Scope name or `path:<template>` | `fs.read:project`, `fs.watch:data`, `fs.read:agent-sessions:gemini` |
| `http` | Host pattern, or `setting:<key>` | `http:api.example.com`, `http:*.example.com`, `http:setting:server_url` |
| `process.run` | Program name or absolute path | `process.run:git`, `process.run:/usr/bin/git` |
| `commands.invoke` | Global command id or prefix | `commands.invoke:ilium.git/*` |
| `services.use`, `services.provide` | Service name without version | `services.use:ilium:inference/provider` |
| `settings.contribute` | One built-in tab id, no `*` | `settings.contribute:terminal` |
| `extensions.provide`, `extensions.contribute` | One global point id `<plugin-id>/<point>`, no `*` | `extensions.contribute:ilium.core.smart-copy/recognisers` |
| `settings.read-kernel` | One built-in tab id, no `*` | `settings.read-kernel:terminal` |

Four argument forms deserve a note: `http:setting:<key>`, `settings.read-kernel:<kernel-tab-id>`, and the agent scopes `agent-sessions:gemini`, `agent-config:gemini` and `agent-config:antigravity` of `fs.read` and `fs.watch`. The agent scopes are read only, and `fs.write:agent-sessions:<agent>` is refused at install with `manifest.grant-scope`.

Grants without an argument, such as `tree.read` or `agent.read`, take none. The [Capability table](/pages/reference-capabilities/) lists every grant.

Each grant has a risk mark. `always` grants are always on. `normal` grants are checked by default in the review dialog. High-risk (H) grants start unchecked, and the user checks each one. H grants include `panes.signal`, `terminal.write`, `agent.read-prompts`, `agent.control`, `process.run`, `panes.create-command`, `inference.provide`, `clipboard.read`, `location.observer`, file writes outside `data` and `cache`, file reads that reach a sensitive path ([SEC-061]), and the nine grants in the next section. Grants are recorded per plugin and per side in the grant store ([SEC-112]).

## More high-risk grants

These nine grants are high risk. They follow the same rule as every other H grant: a T1 bundled plugin still needs an explicit grant for each of them, and the dialog shows them in the warning style, never pre-checked.

| Grant | Sides | What it allows | Why it is high risk | Extra rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `terminal.history` | S C | Read the scrollback above the screen: `terminal.history-text`, `terminal.search-history` | Scrollback holds everything the user ever typed or printed in that pane, including secrets | A reply keeps the newest 4 MiB |
| `terminal.input-lock` | S C | Hold the user's keyboard for a short time with `terminal.lock-input` or the `lock-user-input` field of `send-input` | A plugin that holds the keyboard can hide what it types | At most 2 s per lock, one lock per pane. The user's keys are queued, not lost (D17) |
| `terminal.raw-input` | S C | Send raw bytes or mouse events with `send-input`, and make a `terminal-view` interactive | Raw bytes drive any program in the pane, as if the user typed them | Goes through `send-input`, with its check order and its dedup key |
| `panes.lifecycle` | S | Freeze, unfreeze, restart with a new command, terminate and resize panes | A plugin can stop or replace a running program | Freezing is refused on Windows with `unsupported` |
| `tree.restructure` | S C | Create groups, folders, projects and splits, and run atomic `restructure` batches | A batch can move or ungroup the whole tree | At most 256 operations per batch, all or nothing, and `revert-restructure` undoes one |
| `sessions.cross` | S | List the user's other running sessions and run one command of the same plugin there | It acts outside the session where the user granted it | T1 and signed T2 only, and only commands of the same plugin that the other session has also granted (D16) |
| `process.long-lived` | S C | Start a streaming child with `process.spawn` | A child outlives a single call | The program must also match a `process.run:<program>` grant. Children run in the helper's confinement |
| `agent.transcript` | S C | Read typed turns of an agent session | A transcript holds every prompt, answer and tool call | The host parses and redacts it, so a plugin never reads the raw file (D22) |
| `settings.read-kernel:api` | S C | Read the `api` tab of the built-in settings | The `api` tab holds the keys for model providers | Secrets are always returned as `<redacted>`. Other tabs are normal risk |

Four more grants are high risk and available to T1 bundled plugins only: `settings.read-all`, `settings.write-all`, `plugins.manage` and `settings.write-kernel:<tab-id>`. A T1 plugin gets each of them through the first-start prompt like any other H grant, and a T2 or T3 install that lists one fails with `manifest.grant-tier`. `settings.read-kernel:api` is high risk at every tier: T1 is asked at first activation, T2 and T3 see it unchecked in the review dialog, and no tier refuses it at install.

These grants are normal risk: `tree.attention`, `ui.chrome`, `open-external`, `keymap.read`, `location.geocode`, `inference.embed`, `extensions.provide:<point>`, `extensions.contribute:<point>` for a point with `risk: "standard"`, `notify.toast`, `journal.read`, `settings.read-kernel:<tab>` for a tab other than `api`, and `terminal.read-cells`. Two further grants are high risk because of what they receive or start: `panes.create-command:<program>` starts an unconfined program in a terminal pane ([SEC-040]), and `inference.provide` receives every prompt that other plugins send to the AI model ([SEC-007]). The development-only grant `gpu.kernels` is `@unstable(feature = gpu-kernels)` and appears only in development builds (D18).

### Consent that is not a grant

A grant is a standing permission. Four extended features also ask the user at the moment of first use, because the target is only known then. Each answer is stored in the consent store ([SEC-112]) and can be withdrawn in Settings > Plugins or with `ilium plugin consents` ([SEC-120]). Prompts are rate limited ([SEC-105]).

| Feature | Who is asked | When | If declined |
|---|---|---|---|
| `open-external` | The user | The first time a plugin opens each target origin (D25) | The intent completes as `refused(not-permitted)` |
| `http:setting:<key>` | The user | When the setting holds a host the plugin has not used before (D23) | The request fails with `not-permitted`, and the host is not contacted |
| `location.geocode` | The user | The first time a plugin geocodes. The host service is Photon, with Nominatim as fallback (D14) | Calls return `not-permitted` |
| Bundled plugin with H grants | The user | Once, at the first activation of a T1 plugin | The plugin runs without them. The question comes back at the next server start, and after three answers of Not now it stops ([SEC-111]) |

## What a call returns without a grant

A declined or revoked grant changes what a call returns. The function's signature decides the form, and the refusal is always written to the plugin log.

| Kind of function | Declined or revoked grant | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Returns `result<T, plugin-error>` | `not-permitted`, or `revoked` when the grant was removed during the call | `fs.read` on a path outside its scope, or `geocode.search` without consent |
| Returns `option<T>` (no error channel) | `none` | `location.current` returns `none` |
| Returns a list | An empty list | `tree.children` returns no nodes |
| A submission with an extended intent | `refused(not-permitted)`. The key is not reserved | `freeze-pane` without `panes.lifecycle` |
| Function whose grant the manifest never requested on that side (also when requested only for the other side) | A trap `host.capability-not-requested`. The instance ends and restarts after a delay. An import of an interface that no requested capability unlocks fails the install with `manifest.import-not-requested` | `process.spawn` called without a request |

The first refused call of each kind writes one `warn` line to the plugin log for each plugin instance. The line names the grant, the function and the reason.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-prompt">$</span> ilium plugin logs pane-tools --tail 4
<span class="t-dim">09:14:02</span> <span class="t-warn">warn</span> refused terminal.history
       by history-text (declined)
<span class="t-dim">09:14:09</span> <span class="t-warn">warn</span> refused open-external
       by open-external (declined)
<span class="t-dim">09:14:09</span> <span class="t-err">error</span> geocode failed: not-permitted
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. Refusals of high-risk and consent-gated calls. The last line is the error the plugin logged itself.</figcaption>
</figure>

The reason is one word from the closed list in [Refusal reasons](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/#refusal-reasons). The most common are `declined` (the user left the grant unchecked), `revoked` (the grant was removed), `policy` (the admin policy forbids it, [SEC-184]), `offline` (the offline switch is on, [SEC-084]) and `unavailable` (the target is absent or the caller lacks the grant to learn about it, [SEC-373]). A manifest that never asked for the grant is not a refusal reason: it is a trap. For `not-permitted`, `quota-exceeded` and `network` the error `message` starts with `<reason>: `. The log line has the form `refused <grant> by <function> (<reason>)`, and its JSON form is `{"type":"refusal","grant":"<grant>","function":"<function>","reason":"<reason>"}`.

## Revocation and the authorization epoch

Each plugin has an authorization epoch. Every grant change bumps it. A host call compares the epoch it started with against the current epoch, so a call in flight during a revocation fails closed with `revoked`.

Revoke a grant in Settings > Plugins > Capabilities, or from the command line:

```text
ilium plugin grants notes --revoke fs.read:project
```

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭─ Plugins · pane-tools · Capabilities ────────╮</span>
│ terminal.read-cells ………………………………………… granted │
│ terminal.history …………………………………… <span class="t-warn">HIGH</span> granted │
│ process.long-lived …………………… <span class="t-warn">HIGH</span> not granted │
│ notify.toast …………………………………………………………… granted │
│ settings.read-kernel:api    <span class="t-warn">HIGH</span> not granted │
│                                              │
│ <span class="t-dim">Space grant or revoke · Esc close</span>            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Rendered at 48 columns. Illustrative. A high-risk grant carries the HIGH mark whether granted or not.</figcaption>
</figure>
A revocation has these effects:

- A call records the epoch at entry. When the epoch changes before the call returns and the change removed a grant that the call needs, the call returns `revoked`, and a pending request that needs the grant completes as `failed(revoked)`. A call that does not need the removed grant completes normally. A call that enters after the bump is checked against the new set and returns `not-permitted` with a message starting `revoked: `, until re-activation and after it.
- The plugin receives `deactivate(revoked)` and is activated again with the reduced grant set. The re-activation is not counted as a failure.
- Contributions that need the grant are withdrawn: decorations, toolbar state, grabs, claims, highlights, filters, watches, routes, and the status segments, frame slots, toolbar buttons and row actions of `ui.chrome`.

A grant added later bumps the epoch too. The plugin then receives `deactivate(granted)` and is activated again with the new set.

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 120" role="img" aria-label="Trust chain from package to host call">
  <title>Trust chain</title>
  <desc>A package passes the signature check, then its grants are recorded. Each host call checks the epoch.</desc>
  <defs>
    <marker id="trust-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">

    </marker>
  </defs>

## File access

Scopes are resolved by the kernel once per grant, to canonical directories. A plugin never learns a path it was not granted.

| Scope | Root | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `package` | Unpacked package `assets/`, read only | Always |
| `data` | The plugin's private data folder | Always, read and write |
| `cache` | The plugin's private cache folder, may be evicted | Always, read and write |
| `project` | The session's project folder | Grant |
| `picked` | Each path the user chose in `fs.pick` or a `path-field` | Grant per pick |
| `worktrees` | The setting `workspace.worktree_root` | Grant. Write is H |
| `agent-sessions:<agent>`, `agent-config:<agent>` | Agent transcript or configuration folder, read only. includes `gemini` and, for configuration, `antigravity` | Grant, H |
| `path:<template>` | Template with `{home}`, `{config}`, `{data}`, `{cache}`, `{project}` | Grant. Literal absolute paths are H |

Each write is atomic. The kernel writes a temporary sibling file and renames it over the target, so a reader never sees a half-written file. With the `write-atomic` call, the write also carries an expected revision and fails with `conflict` when the file changed. Writes outside `data` and `cache` need an explicit user grant, even for T1 plugins.

## Extension points and replacement

An extension point lets one plugin add data or code to another plugin's flow. It is a grant, not a back door.

| Grant | Risk | What it allows |
|---|---|---|
| `extensions.provide:<plugin-id>/<point>` | S | Own a point. A plugin may own only points that start with its own id |
| `extensions.contribute:<plugin-id>/<point>` | S, or H when the point declares `risk: "high"` | Add an entry or a handler to that point |

- There are no wildcard grants. `manifest.grant-wildcard` refuses them, and `extensions.contribute-any` does not exist. The user sees each point by name.
- The review dialog groups a package's contributions under **Adds to other plugins**, for example `Text triggers > Before fire: can stop a trigger from sending text (high risk)`.
- A handler gets only the payload of the owner's `payload_schema`. It runs inside its own plugin instance, with its own grants, under a deadline of 5 to 50 ms.
- Hooks fail open. A handler that times out, traps or errors counts as a pass, so a slow handler cannot veto anything. Three breaches in a row stop that extension until the plugin restarts, and the user sees a notice.
- `replaces` needs no grant, but the user confirms every replacement. The built-in plugin is turned off while the replacement is on. Its stored data stays on disk and the replacement does not read it. `ilium.core.sessions` and `ilium.core.settings` cannot be replaced.

See [Extension points](/pages/api-extension-points/) and [Extending core plugins](/pages/extending-core-plugins/).

## What the kernel never lets a plugin do

- Read or write outside a granted scope through `..`, an absolute path, a symlink or a hard link.
- Open a socket or an HTTP connection it was not granted. A component that imports `wasi:sockets` or `wasi:http` is refused at load [ABI-024].
- Run a program it was not granted. `process.run` and `process.spawn` need a grant for that exact program name or absolute path.
- Read or change another plugin's settings, unless it holds `settings.read-all` or `settings.write-all`. Only first-party T1 plugins can receive them.
- Write a kernel setting or the keymap, except a T1 holder of `settings.write-kernel:<tab-id>`, who can write the keys of that one tab. `settings.read-kernel` and `keymap.read` only read, and any other plugin that wants a change links the user to `ilium://settings/<tab-id>#<key>` through `open-external`.
- Send terminal input, signal a pane, drive an agent, freeze or restart a pane, or restructure the tree without the matching high-risk grant (`terminal.write`, `panes.signal`, `agent.control`, `panes.lifecycle`, `tree.restructure`).
- Hold the keyboard for more than 2 s, or hold two input locks on one pane.
- Read an agent transcript as a raw file. `agent.transcript` returns typed turns that the host parsed and redacted.
- Send a command to another session that is not its own command, or to a session where the grant is missing.
- Print raw terminal escape sequences. Plugins draw through the UI tree only. The extended widgets (`terminal-view`, `video`, `surface`, `location-picker`) are drawn by the host from typed props.
- Replace the kernel recovery page, or hide the switch that disables the plugin.
- Change a built-in setting value, or draw a section in a built-in tab without `settings.contribute:<tab-id>`. A built-in tab never shows a `preview` row or a view-rendered plugin widget (SE10, D19).
- Cover the screen with toasts. A plugin may send 3 toasts per 10 s with `notify.toast`, and at most 3 are pending (D20).
- Lose a never-dropped event silently. An overflow restarts the plugin instead.

## Limits that protect the user

The extended contract adds limits whose purpose is safety. They are fixed by the host. A manifest may ask for less, and for some of them for more up to the tier ceiling.

| Limit | Value | When exceeded |
|---|---|---|
| Input lock | 2 s per lock, one per pane | The lock ends. The user's keys were queued, not lost |
| Toasts | 3 per 10 s per plugin, 3 pending | The oldest pending toast is replaced |
| Status segments and frame slots | 10 updates per second per segment or slot | Updates are coalesced |
| Geocoding | 1 request per second per plugin, 10 s timeout, 24 h cache | `rate-limited` with `retry-after-ms` |
| Open HTTP streams | `http_streams` (default 4, T1 up to 16) and `session_http_streams` (64); see [Errors and limits](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/#requestable-limits) | `quota-exceeded` |
| Pending HTTP requests | `http_pending` (default 256, T1 up to 1,024) | `busy` with `retry-after-ms` |
| Spawned children | `children` (default 2, T1 up to 8) and the shared `session_processes` (16) | `quota-exceeded` |
| Concurrent `process.run` | `process_runs` (default 4, T1 up to 16) and the shared `session_processes` (16) | `busy` with `retry-after-ms` |
| Durable timers | `durable_timers`: 64 (T1 up to 256) | `quota-exceeded` |
| Package assets | `package_assets_mib`: 64, T1 up to 256 | `manifest.asset-size` at install |
| `restructure` batch | 256 operations | The batch is refused |
| `screen-changed` events | 10 per second per pane | Coalesced |

The full list is in [Errors and limits](/pages/reference-errors-and-limits/).

## Worked example: a refused grant

The plugin reads a project note. If the grant is missing or was revoked, the plugin shows no note and logs a warning. Any other error is logged as an error. The first read asks for a path outside the scope, which the kernel refuses with `not-permitted` whatever the grants are. The second read is inside the scope.

**Manifest:** `"capabilities": { "server": ["fs.read:project"] }`

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::fs;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;

const MAX_NOTE_BYTES: u32 = 65_536;

/// Returns the note text, or `None` when the note cannot be read right now.
fn read_note(path: &str) -> Option<String> {
    let target = FsPath { scope: "project".into(), path: path.into() };
    match fs::read(&target, 0, MAX_NOTE_BYTES) {
        Ok(bytes) => String::from_utf8(bytes).ok(),
        Err(error) => {
            match error.code {
                ErrorCode::NotPermitted | ErrorCode::Revoked => {
                    log::log(Level::Warn, &format!("note unavailable: {path}"));
                }
                _ => log::log(Level::Error, &format!("note read failed: {}", error.message)),
            }
            None
        }
    }
}

#[ilium_plugin(side = "server")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Notes;

impl Lifecycle for Notes {
    fn activate(&mut self, _context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        let _ = read_note("../secrets.txt");
        let note = read_note("docs/notes.md");
        log::log(Level::Info, &format!("note loaded: {}", note.is_some()));
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for Notes {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { read } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/fs';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

const MAX_NOTE_BYTES = 65536;

/** Reads a file under the project scope. The kernel refuses paths that leave the scope. */
function readNote(path: string): string | undefined {
  try {
    const bytes = read({ scope: 'project', path }, 0n, MAX_NOTE_BYTES);
    return new TextDecoder().decode(bytes);
  } catch (error) {
    if (!(error instanceof PluginError)) {
      throw error;
    }
    if (error.code === 'not-permitted' || error.code === 'revoked') {
      log('warn', `note unavailable (${error.code}): ${path}`);
      return undefined;
    }
    log('error', `note read failed (${error.code}): ${error.message}`);
    return undefined;
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'server',
  activate(context) {
    readNote('../secrets.txt');
    const note = readNote('docs/notes.md');
    log('info', `${context.plugin}: note loaded ${note !== undefined}`);
  },
  onEvents: () => [],
});
```

Outcome: `../secrets.txt` leaves the scope, so the call fails with `not-permitted` and the plugin logs a warning. With the grant declined, `activate` still succeeds and the warning is written once. A revocation during the read returns `revoked`, and the plugin is activated again without the grant.

## Worked example: consent that the user declines

A client plugin looks up a place name with the host's geocoding service. The first call asks the user for consent. If the user declines, the call returns `not-permitted` on every later call too, and the plugin falls back to a plain text field.

**Manifest:** `"capabilities": { "client": ["location.geocode"] }`

**Rust**

```rust
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::geocode;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::log::{self, Level};
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::task;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::host::geocode::GeocodeQuery;

#[ilium_plugin(side = "client")]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Places;

impl Lifecycle for Places {
    fn activate(&mut self, _context: Activation) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        task::spawn(async {
            let query = GeocodeQuery {
                text: "Lyon".into(),
                near: None,
                limit: 5,
                language: Some("fr".into()),
            };
            match geocode::search(query).await {
                Ok(places) => log::log(Level::Info, &format!("{} places found", places.len())),
                Err(error) => match error.code {
                    ErrorCode::NotPermitted => {
                        log::log(Level::Warn, "geocoding declined, the place stays plain text");
                    }
                    _ => log::log(Level::Error, &format!("geocode failed: {}", error.message)),
                },
            }
        });
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Handler for Places {
    fn on_events(&mut self, _batch: Vec<Event>) -> Vec<Submission> {
        Vec::new()
    }
}
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { definePlugin, PluginError } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { search } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/geocode';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

async function lookup(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    const places = await search({ text: 'Lyon', near: undefined, limit: 5, language: 'fr' });
    log('info', `${places.length} places found`);
  } catch (error) {
    if (!(error instanceof PluginError)) {
      throw error;
    }
    if (error.code === 'not-permitted') {
      log('warn', 'geocoding declined, the place stays plain text');
      return;
    }
    log('error', `geocode failed (${error.code}): ${error.message}`);
  }
}

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate() {
    void lookup();
  },
  onEvents: () => [],
});
```

Outcome: the consent dialog appears once. After a decline, the plugin logs the warning, the host never contacts the geocoding service, and the host writes one refusal line to the plugin log. A declined `open-external` is handled the same way, from the outcome `refused(not-permitted)` of its submission.

## The manifest side of high-risk grants

A manifest lists the grants per side. The manifest is JSON, so it is the same for Rust and TypeScript plugins.

```json
"capabilities": {
  "server": ["terminal.read-cells", "terminal.history", "process.run:rg", "process.long-lived"],
  "client": ["notify.toast", "ui.chrome", "settings.read-kernel:terminal"]
},
"limits_tier": "standard"
```

Three of the server grants here are high risk: `terminal.history`, `process.run:rg` and `process.long-lived`. `settings.read-kernel:terminal` is normal risk, because only the `api` tab is high. A manifest that wrote `settings.read-kernel:*` would be refused with `manifest.grant-wildcard`.

## Settings rows in built-in tabs

A plugin can add rows to a built-in Settings tab, but only under a label the user always sees, and only with its own values. The kernel draws every plugin row under a divider that names the plugin and the word `plugin`, with a dim `▏` gutter on each line, so the user always knows where the rows came from. The text of a plugin row (titles, descriptions, info text, notice text) is plain text: the kernel strips control characters and bidi overrides, so a plugin cannot draw a fake kernel divider or a fake close button. Plugin values are stored only under `[plugins."<plugin-id>"]`, and a plugin row never writes a built-in value. A built-in tab never runs plugin code while it paints. The grant `settings.contribute:<tab-id>` allows drawing sections in one built-in tab and nothing else. It is shown in the review dialog as `Adds settings to the <tab> tab`. See [Plugin settings extension](/pages/settings-extension/) for the rules.

<figure>
<pre class="term"><span class="t-hi">╭──≡ ● · Terminal────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</span>
│ Scrollback lines …………………………………………………………………………………… - 10000 + *  │
│ Cursor style ……………………………………………………………………………………………… ← Block → +  │
│<span class="t-dim">── Notes · plugin ──────────────────────────────────────────────</span>│
│<span class="t-dim">▏</span>Highlight colour ………………………………………………………………………………………… [ Amber ]  │
│<span class="t-dim">▏</span>Keep history lines …………………………………………………………………………………………… [ On ]  │
│<span class="t-dim">▏</span><span class="t-dim">Plain text from the plugin; the kernel drew this divider.</span>      │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
</pre>
<figcaption>Illustrative, not generated. A built-in Terminal tab with the section of a plugin. The kernel rows come first, then one divider for the plugin, and the dim gutter on every plugin line.</figcaption>
</figure>

Reading a built-in value is a separate, read-only grant. `settings.read-kernel:<tab-id>` returns the JSON values of one tab with secrets replaced by `<redacted>`, and a `kernel-settings-changed` event names the keys that changed. It does not allow any write.

## Signing and distribution

The rules for updates, trusted keys and lost keys carry the ids USR-120 to USR-129. They are in [Packages, updates, trust and keys](/pages/packages/#updates-trust-and-keys) and [Install and manage plugins](/pages/user-install-and-manage/).

Packages are files. A registry is optional (decision D27). In both cases the user decides whether to trust the key that signed a package, and a registry adds signed revocation. See [Signing and trust](/pages/reference-signing-and-trust/) and [Registry reference](/pages/reference-registry/).

```text
ilium plugin keygen --publisher "Example Corp" --out ~/keys/example
ilium plugin sign ./dist/example.notes-1.2.0.iliumpkg --key ~/keys/example/publisher.key
ilium plugin trust add ~/keys/example/publisher.pub
ilium plugin install ./dist/example.notes-1.2.0.iliumpkg
```

`keygen` writes `publisher.key`, an owner-only Ed25519 private key, and `publisher.pub`, which holds the publisher name and public key. `sign` adds the `signature` entry atomically. `trust add`, `trust list` and `trust remove` manage the trusted keys. Anyone who holds `publisher.key` can sign packages as that publisher.

An unsigned package installs only with `--allow-unsigned`, as a T3 package with a `dev` badge. A lower version of an installed id is refused unless `--allow-downgrade` is given.

## Edge cases and errors

| Situation | Result | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| Capability revoked during a call | `revoked`. The plugin re-activates without the grant. Not a failure | Plugin log |
| Path leaves its scope through `..`, a symlink or a hard link | `not-permitted` | Plugin log |
| Import the manifest never requested | Trap. The instance ends and restarts after a delay | Plugin log, with the trap frames |
| Install of a T2 or T3 package on Windows or macOS | Refused, with the message in the sandbox section | Install output |
| Unsigned package without `--allow-unsigned` | Install refused | Install output |
| Signing key the user does not trust | Install offers `Trust publisher` with the fingerprint. Declining refuses it | Install dialog |
| `publisher` differs from the key's recorded publisher | `manifest.publisher-mismatch`, install stops | Install error line |
| `process.run:sh` in a T2 or T3 package | `manifest.grant-tier`, install stops. The shell grant is for T1 only | Install error line |
| `limits_tier: "first-party"` in a package that is not a bundled `ilium.*` plugin | `manifest.limits-tier`, install stops | Install error line |
| Package assets above 64 MiB (T2, T3) or 256 MiB (T1) | `manifest.asset-size`, install stops | Install error line |
| `settings.read-kernel` without a tab, or with `*` | `manifest.grant-argument-missing` or `manifest.grant-wildcard` | Install error line |
| T1 plugin with a high-risk grant that the user never granted | The call is refused as `not-permitted` (reason `declined`), though the plugin is bundled | Plugin log |
| Server restarts between a journaled `send-input` and its outcome | One `input-uncertain` event. The input is never replayed (D21) | Event, plugin log |
| User declines `open-external` for an origin | `refused(not-permitted)` for each later open of that origin until the answer is withdrawn | Outcome |
| `sessions.cross` in a T3 package | Not available to T3 packages (D16) | Install output |

## What the user sees

The review dialog grants capabilities, Settings > Plugins > Capabilities shows and revokes them, and `ilium plugin logs <id>` shows every refusal, trap and process run. A first-start prompt appears for a bundled plugin with high-risk grants, and a small confirmation appears the first time a plugin opens a site, uses a new host from a setting, or geocodes a place.

#### Lifecycle and trust

A package that policy blocks, or that is refused at load, never runs plugin code. Safe mode ([Safe mode and recovery](/pages/user-safe-mode-and-troubleshooting/)) turns third-party plugins off without changing grants. Install scope is global in 0.1.0 so that opening a repository cannot run code ([Plugin scope and sessions](/pages/reference-plugin-scope-and-sessions/)). An uninstall removes grants; see [Install, update and uninstall](/pages/reference-install-update-uninstall/). [LIF-281]

- [LIF-281] Uninstall MUST remove the plugin grants, and a project folder MUST NOT be able to install or enable a plugin. Test: uninstall and read `grants.json`; list an uninstalled package in `plugins.toml`.


## Author duties

A signed package carries the trust of its publisher key. The author is responsible for the key and for the support of the release. An author MUST keep the secret key out of the package and out of version control, and MUST announce a leaked key with the fingerprint of its replacement. [AUT-322] The practice is in [Publishing and support](/pages/guide-publishing-and-support/), and the review list before each release is in [Quality checklist](/pages/guide-quality-checklist/).
